Who's Your Daddy is a fun game to play with friends over Skype, but I never got much enjoyment playing with strangers. The baby is way more powerful then the dad. I had much more fun playing as the baby then the dad, as playing as the dad is a lot harder then you would think, there is so much you need to do. I'm going to list a ton of ways the baby can kill itself.
- Electrocution
- Poisoning Itself
- Eating Glass
- Drowning
- Burning to Death
A lot of these are very easy to do, such as the electrocution. Electrocution is an instant death and knives and forks are very common and easy to find. Once you get to a certain point, it is almost impossible to stop a baby from drowning. Eating Glass is an almost instant win. Plus, the babies can also travel through vents. Some of the vents are RIDICULOUSLY overpowered. The baby can get down into the kitchen with the use of vents in about 12-15 seconds, leaving almost no time for the dad to prepare.
Here are some improvements that I think would help the game.
- Nerf the vents
- Reduce the spawn rate on knives, forks, hammers, and baby keys
- Improve the spawn rate of locks, outlet covers, and pills
- Add more healing items
- Add more time for the dad to prepare
FINAL RATING:
7/10

All in all, this is a good game and worth playing. I was a bit skeptic, due to the mixed reviews (especially some people were still negative even by getting it in sale at 15€). I must say, at 15€ it's absolutely a bargain even with its flaws.
Mankind Divided continues the story of human revolution, so i don't understand how some negative reviews bash this aspect of the game. It's a sequel, what did you expect?
Some people hate the fact that there isn't a real tie-in to the choices taken in human revolution, in fact, you don't need a savegame. Did you save somebody? Did you pick a certain ending? It doesn't matter, the game will recap the first chapter and skip all these customization through careful dialogs and skilled story telling. It's a bit annoying, i can agree, but really, not that big deal like somebody tells.
This game has a huge problem for many people: it's not human revolution. HR set the bar very high (especially considering the franchise. Do you remember the time when deus ex 1 was the only good deus ex?) and beating that was going to be a challenge: some people will never be happy.
The game has a few flaws, and, in my opinion, are all cause of possible budget cuts or crunch time. Often you see a lack of variety (for example the underground loading screens) which should not be present in AAA games as this one. Do they break immersion? A little. Are they game breaking? Absolutely not. It is true, in order to shove a lot of content in the game (with side missions) many things are sospiciously convenient. Need to do side mission X? What a coincidence, it's just 20 meters over there, just the apartment in front side mission Y.
Yet, the story is not bad (although take a few hours to get you engaged) and although i didn't like --- MINOR SPOILER AHEAD ----
-------- END OF MINOR SPOIELR ----  i overall had fun.
The final mission especially is my favourite part of the game even if it's probably a little too short.
Some other minor annoying stuff are there, but really, it's still a very good game. If you liked Human Revolution, this game is for you too.

It bothers me that I can't find the motivation to beat this game. Loved the original, Invisible war and Human revolution, but this one is lacking something. It might be the absence of humorous side quests. I remember going to the club in Hong Kong (original Deus), funny accents, weird dancing. The game felt alive. Also remember the club side-quest from Human revolution (the one where you put the voice recording of that dude on the billboard outside). This game lacks those moments. The side quests are generic, go here and find this, beat this dude up, come back to me.
Main Quest Impressions (only played half):
The main quest feels too dramatic. In the original, you were in an episode of Law and Order. There was an overarching plot but each encounter was a component of a largery mystery. You had to find out how people were murdered in their apartments, Track down missing technology on boats. You were a detective doing somewhat tedious work. In this game, I feel like superman. You wanna kill the mob boss? Call in Jenson. Need to negotiate a hostage rescue? Where's Jenson?!? Dudes with Gold masks in Dubai causing a ruckus, Bring Jenson in with the SMG. You don't get those beginner mysteries and quests that build intrigue into the story.
Graphics:
Amazing. If you're playing this maxed out you're experiencing some of the best graphics PC gaming has to offer at the moment. The Art is also something to behold. That spire in Prague looks like something out of a high budget sci-fi movie. Also the encampment where they keep all the augs gives a sense of scale. It's a video game version of the CGI in the new Total Recall Movie.
Gameplay:
Boring. They added a few augs and you'll spend most of your time sneaking around if you want to be the good guy. It would be nice if they had more options to use force to change the pace of the game. It's odd that they added these cool looking weapons but discourage you from using them unless you want to get less XP and become a villain. The hacking game is lame. I'm not sure what to say about the Dialogue options that hasn't already been said about Afghanistan.
Conclusion:
It bums me out that I can't recommend this game. They nailed the Art and Graphics design. Maybe next time around cut the budget on that department a little bit and hire some quality writers?

Holy awesomeness, Batman!
The freeflow combat will make your mouth water. The gadgets will bring tears to your eyes. And the voicework of Mark Hamill as the Joker will have you screaming for more. This game's visuals are wonderful. I felt like I stepped into an old episode of Batman, the Animated series. And that is a very good thing.

This review comes from an FPS-biased gamer, so it took some time (i.e. 4 years after this game launched) for me to play it, mostly because I bought it late, and partly because I was waiting for steamworks.
Now that it's supported, GFWL is gloriously gone and the steam achievements are seamless. As for the game, the intro is nice and the visuals are impressive, but I found that the game really assumes that you know what you're doing and where you're going. The map system is terrible, and I found myself doubling back down corridors over and over to figure where the heck I was supposed to be.
Half the items you see as you play the game you can't collect until after you've unlocked certain upgrades, which is frustrating, and frankly a poor way to convince a completionist to go back through all the levels he's gotten lost in and ask him to go find more trophies. Nevertheless, I did it all.
The main campaign has a solid story and - as a person who is not intimately familiar with every villian - I enjoyed reading the back stories on the characters I unlocked. The immersion level is very good, and the controls are intuitive.
Challenge mode gets a little frustrating, but it's worth it to see the achievements pop at the end.
Overall: It's a solid Batman game with some flaws, and while it doesn't stack up for me with the top games, it's still a worthy endeavor.

The original and still the best in the series.
It's more focused environment leads to a more tightly crafted game that just begs to be explored. While the later games in the series offer a more open ended approach with arguably more things to see and do, in practice they seem to offer little more than filler between heavily scripted events. While collectibles, secrets and side missions often feel like chores in the later games, they feel like meaningful reasons to fully explore the asylum with appropriate rewards on offer. Each area is filled with unique assets and small, rememberable details. The riddlers side missions task you with photographing scenes that are unique to various characters from the Dark Knight universe which helps to direct the player toward these specially crafted, and unique in-game assets.
The combat system, while arguably too simplistic, is a delight to control as you see Batman stringing insane combo's together effortlessly disarming, and countering incoming attacks. Every kick, punch, grapple and counter is animated well making fights seem appropriately realistic and violent. The combat is assisted by some excellent audio leading to some satisfying crunches, cracks, and smacks as bones break and fists collide with faces.
The metroid-vania aspects of the game are implemented well, with each upgrade offering the oppertunity to revisit locations throughout the game.
The story is well told and the voice acting is excellent throughout, although I felt the final parts of the story were anticlimactic with the final boss fight in particular being tedius and frankly, rather silly. Seeing the Joker turn into a roid-raged meathead seemed rather out of character, and a little far-fetched - even for a comic book super villain.
On a technical level, the game still looks great to this day and runs exceptionally well. A mid-range pc should be able to run this game on maximum settings with a solid 60fps.
All-in-all it's a ground breaking game and in my opinion one of the best games of it's generation. A true masterpiece.

First of all, Romopolis is not a city management game.
Romopolis is mostly a puzzle game with a theme of city management, where you have a limited time and building areas to finish all given tasks. Every level also has a medal time (if you finish before it runs out, you also get a medal), and a Trophy task (optional task that gives you Trophy if you finish it).
As for the gameplay; you have 4 resources Denarii, Wood, Stone and Workers. Denarii is used to buy blueprints and other resources and is collected automatically via taxes from built houses. Workers are a resource that is not spent, but used during construction.
Tasks include number of residents, upgrades to houses, specific level of happiness (each house needs some services and increases happiness with adjacent parks), sum of Denarii, etc...
So, Romopolis is a nice puzzle game with lovely theme. And if you know what you're looking for in it, you are in for some enjoyment...
7.5/10 Recommended :)

This game is a level base challenge game. You build buildings for income and parks to make people happy. Each level is a new "challenge" with a medal if you do it within a certain time limit, with a bonus trophy if you complete the extra task as well.
It's games like this one that make me wish Steam offered a "Meh" button. The Polis Series by Lonely Troops are all on the cusp of being good games, but are just lacking a bit. I give this a thumbs up because it has a great foundation to be a great game and I did get several hours out of it, but after about 2 hours I was bored with the repetitive game play. I enjoyed the sandbox mode the most, but felt a bit limited with it. I would have liked larger maps, but this isn't an empire building game. It has an android app feel to it, which I don't mind but I know a lot of people aren't interested in that.
A pleasant casual city-sim, so long as you don't mind being timed.

In this game, you are an architect hired by the Roman Empire to build cities. Each time you succeed your notoriety increases and you will get better (though harder) jobs.
It is divided in 24 levels of crescent difficulty and complexity. Each level has 3 obligatory objectives (
): all 3 are required to complete the level and they must be done before the deadline. Completing a level unlocks the next one.
: There is an option to disable the "deadline". In this case, all you have to do is complete the objectives at your own leisure (unless you are after the medal).
To build the cities you have at your disposal: money, wood, stone and workers. Training workers, mining or  cutting down trees costs 1500 Dn, ordering wood or stone costs 500 Dn.
Money is gain from the people living in properties (like rent), so the better the properties and the happier the residents are, the more you earn.
Before building anything though, you must purchase its blueprint. Properties (houses/ apartments) require other buildings like temples or markets, otherwise the residents won't be as satisfied (happy). High-end properties require even more structures.
Concessions allow to upgrade your properties, so more money can be earned.
All buildings deteriorate so, from time to time, repairs are needed.
Since part of the rent is decided by the residents'
, you have to manage it carefully. Being near the wreck of any destroyed building or near a few specific structures will bring the happiness down by 1. Gardens, on the other hand, will make residents in the neighboring properties happier (+1 happiness).
That's the fun part of the game weigh the pros and cons of what and where to build; what to have near that building; if it is worth it spending money in upgrades, mining, cutting up trees or training workers (they are expensive but mid/late game they are worth the price, allowing you to multi-task and build more complex structures); etc., while trying to complete all goals as fast as possible.
During the Campaign, you can also earn trophies and medals in each level.
Besides Campaign, there is also Sandbox where you can create your own maps, set the goals you want to achieve, determine the deadline, etc.

A plus to this game is the fact that all you need is one "Imperial Protection" to use and all your buildings are protected from damage, unlike Townopolis, where you had to Inspect each and every buildings, although the extra step is nice, I like that Inspections are not needed once you get "Imperial Protection" which is basically Global Inspections.
The final verdict of this game is a clone of Townopolis, not sure which came first, and is also a clone of "Build-A-Lot", if you liked "Build-A-Lot", or games like it, then I recommend buying this game. It's alright, for how cheap it is, but you might not be getting exactly what you expected in this game.
Romopolis only appears to be a city builder simulation game on its surface, but after a couple missions it becomes clear that the game is in fact a puzzle game. Each scenario you are given a 5x5 squared grid to build on with obstacles (either in the form of tiles you cannot build on or buildings that impose a negative effect on your nearby structures. Objectives usually require you to have a certain amount of specific buildings or have a set amount of resources, which requires you to plan your city's layout.
This is all done with a time limit, too, so you either need to make use of the pause button a lot or know the game well.

While not nearly as sophisticated as higher end (and high cost) city simulation games out there, this game scores very high in my book due to it's very low price tag!
Watch my First Play and Review video right here:
24 Challenge Scenarios with different goals are included with the first four having a "hold your hand" tutorial to show you everything you need to know to succeed with this game.  Add in a Sandbox mode where you can make your own custom maps with your own goals to accomplish to defeat it and even add a timer to further challenge you... and you have a pretty impressive little strategy game for the price tag here.
As long as you buy this game without expectations of military conquests, seeing your workers move about the screen, and that it's the next Civilization game, I think you'll be quite happy with this game for it's price.

Romopolis is an old game that has been brought to steam to make the game more accessible to gamers that enjoy these sorts of games on the PC market.
Romopolis is a great game for it's genre, though if you're looking for the same experience as Sim City or Cities Skylines, you won't find that here. Romopolis is not a bad game, in fact, it is quite good in the gameplay style it covers, however, I fear that for many people on the PC this could be a let down. You have a campaign mode which provides you 24 different missions to complete. Each level is more difficult than the previous and the time limit to acquire the medal/achievemnt is the biggest challenge which I find quite fun.
Outside of that you have a sandbox mode, however, the sandbox mode doesn't work like most games. It doesn't give you an empty map and let you create your city, no, it is more of an editor to allow you to develop your own scenarios and share them with your friends. While this isn't a bad thing, it isn't really the traditional sandbox mode we all know and love.
The maps are small and scenario orientated. Once you're done with the scenario, that's pretty much it.
All in all it's a good fun game to play here and there. It has great visuals, the gameplay and upgrading systems are well thought out and the sounds are pretty good too. Overall. For $3.99, it's good value and will provide several hours of fun.

Gnomoria is a really fun game. It doesn't take too long to figure out the controls or how to play the game. There are lots of dangers your gnomes will face. Pros
+ Easy interface/controls to use and understand
+ Lots of various materials to build with
+ Several different types of hostile creatures
+ Resource trading with foreign kingdoms
+ Mods supported
Cons
- Bugs
- End game demands a lot of resources from your pc (disabling beetle spawning helps)
- Some aspects of the game might seems a bit simplistic compared to other sandbox games
With all that being said I still think Gnomoria was well worth the money I spent on it. I've had many hours of fun with it while watching my gnomes struggle to survive.

How does it hold up in 2017? Quite honestly.. just finished the main campaign and it took me 7 hours. I did it however with the help of quicksaving. It used to be one of my all time favourite games, and oddly enough playing it again after so many years took nothing away from the fun. It´s challenging, enjoyable and a rewarding game that worked without any issues. I am going to tackle the expansion packs next, these are new to me and i have never played them before. Some thoughts.
-This game does not hold you hand, only way to advance is to learn and be better Extremely rewarding and fun.
-Not having visible weapon model and iron sights actually adds to the immersion, i wish modern games would do it too.
-Shooting in this game still feels very satisfying. Guns are very powerfull and you need to take your time aiming.
-Your squad mates are surprisingly good. Competent in firefight, seek cover etc. If you give orders sensibly they rock.
-Campaign is very well paced. After a tough one theres 1-2 chill ones to just have fun with.
-Game runs at 1920x1080 without any issues. Take note that menus are still 800x600.
-If you worried that playing it again makes it lose the magic, certainly didn´t for me.

I've probably played almost every military shooter out there, across all console and PC titles, all the way up to the most recent Tom Clancy's Wildlands. But this game....
Look, just buy it and both its expansions for dirt cheap, search out the Heroes Unleashed mod on ModDB. which is the 15 year long masterwork of one man, and then find the first and third person view mod on the
forums which brings the game up to modern FPS speed.
Then enjoy the feeling of tension, the feeling of actually being scared to get shot, or scared that one of your teammates will get gunned down, but also the feeling of victory when your tactical plan comes through and you eliminate all tangos.
You will literally never need another shooter. Ever.

This game is incredible, even if you aren't an active reader or follower of the DC Comic Line. The storyline is amazing, even following the bare amount is enough to be interesting, but when you go and get all the extra parts of the story, it gets even better. The world is extremely interactive, you still have to follow a general line, but you can just spend forever exploring each well detailed area. Needless to say, some of the scenes will put you on the edge of your seat. Now, if you are one to follow the  Batman story line in depth, it is an even more impressive game. Many- if not most- of Batman's official Rogue's gallery, is included in cameos. From Firefly to the Madhatter to Humpty Dumpty to more than you can imagine, they're all here in some aspect, and that itself is exhilerating. Despite being a decently old game, first coming out in 09, its graphics are up to par with games released today. Having incredible fighting movements, various different types of enemies and a utility belt full of gadgets with you to choose from, the combat in this game is good enough for anyone who just wants to go around beating up every thug in their path. In my opinion, it is by far one of the best comic book based games out there, along with its two sequels. So, I seriously recommend this game, it is an incredible game.

Batman: Arkham Asylum is a proof that you don't have to know the story of Batman (if you're one of the 5 people in the world who don't know him :P)  to enjoy a ridiculuosly satisfyingly good blend of action adventure with some RPG elements.
Batman Arkham Asylum sets a story of the dark knight when he captured the Joker and sent him to the Arkham Asylum, when things happens and everything blows up, now it's up to Batman to unravel and stop whatever evil plans that cooked up in the asylum.
The first satisfaction comes with the fighting, as you already know Batman relied on both stealth and strength to tackle his enemies, hand to hand combat included chaining combos and takedown manouvers to finish a group of un/armed enemies, stealth moves can be used to divert the attention of enemies and terrifies them to bring advantages of yours
Don't forget, Batman is the world's greatest detective right? find all Riddler's trophy with (sometimes not so) vague  clues from the villain itself, use your nifty gadgets and upgrades to find them all
The plot are gradually interesting, on the journey Batman will be greeted with his iconic villain like Scarecrow, Poison Ivy, and Bane, which sometimes served as bosses on several level, the fight with them are interesting enough to keep you engaged. The setting of the Arkham Island itself is dark enough to give you a solitary and shadowy feeling,
But IMO the star of the game is Mark Hamill which delivered Joker's line of insanity  with really good voice acting, it almost like that you want to catch this super villain as soon as possible but the game defied you to that, it's the opposite of 'you'll be boring and hope that you will catch him ASAP' feeling, it's a good mixed feeling which helps you got through the game
Overall: it's a must have, there's some things in here like Leaderboards, combo battles, stealth challenges, riddle challenges, and other challenges that will keep you on this game even after you finished the main story, you won't get bored even after 60s hours of playing, mind you, don't look at spoiler or guide: it will crush those feelings

I'll be honest, I'm not that interested in the DC or Marvel universes or any superhero kind of person, but Batman is a pretty cool guy in my eyes. Seeing as how I got it from the recent Humble Bundle I decided to check the game out. I'll start with saying that this game has a wonderful atmosphere and feels very satisfying to walk around in as Batman and stalk the various enemies in some very vertical levels. Pretty much everyone knows how the fighting in this game works by now and I am probably one of the last people to have played it so I'll just leave it at "it's pretty darn fun". When I wasn't in full blown Batman wrecking ball action, I found the other most compelling part of the game to be the stealth. At times it did seem a bit ridiculous with what Batman could get away with, but in the end it was incredibly enjoyable to stalk the unfortunate few who were trapped in a room with the one and only Dark Knight. A nice complement to the game were the various gadgets Batman acquires throughout the game. I'm not sure why he didn't have these items on his person already, but it added I nice dash of Metroidvania into the game as well as fun mix-ups to the combat. The last big item that I would like to mention are the Riddler challenges. They can be extremely addicting and frustrating all at the same time. They were a fun activity to be distracted by whenever I wanted make myself to not plow full speed through the story. Even if you don't think you will enjoy the combat or stealth in the game I would still recommend to play it on easy just to enjoy the story. There are plenty of characters that make an appearance along with a ton of audiologs and others inclusions, all of which are enjoyable to take in.
I give the game a "Yes" out of "Go Play It Now"

There is cleary a lot of content here, and it seems to be a labor of love. That said, there are some issues here that make it difficult for me to recommend. Most of these issues boil down to learning curve and how much time you're willing to commit to figuring the game out. There are a few in-game tutoials, and the manual is easy enough to find on-line, but it's still a very difficult game to get your arms around. The tutorials are enough to get you started, but probably cover about 1% of the in game scenarios.
The manual gives a broad overview, but didn't shed any light on issues that I had with playability. I found units behaving contrary to orders that I was giving frequently. I had no doubt that the behavior was rational given the rules of the game, but became frustrated trying to figure it out without any feedback from the game. This was a shame, because the level of effort put into historical accuracy is impressive, as is the amount of control the designers are trying to offer.
I really wanted to like this game, but after three hours of wrestling with the interface, I decided to try something else. Maybe I gave up too soon, but with the number of available games on Steam at this price point, it seemed like I was needlessly banging my head against the wall instead of enjoying myself.

This game was great to begin with, but it has recently undergone some major updates in the form of version 1.09. Sadly the latest patch is not available on Steam, but it can be downloaded from Paradox forums, where you can register your game and get access to the patches
There is even a 1.10 patch in early alpha stage, the patch will attempt to adress the ancient bugs and problems with the game engine.
Graphics arent anything wonderfull, but this is about grand strategy, not fancy fireworks.
Game in itself is straight up Hearts of Iron, if your a Paradox fan, then you will love AoD aswell. Multitude of variation in strategy, tactics, diplomacy, large techtree, plenty of unit types and so much little details to think of that after years of playing, you still learn new things every now and then. It has the best replayability value that I have ever seen in a strategy game. If you have not played Paradox games before, then you are up for a long and hard path of learning the game, but it is very much worth it.
The AI is not terribly challenging once you master the game, the difficulty setting just grants it more bonuses rather than intelligence, but luckily there are alot of mods that improve the AI and gameplay generally, such as my own mod which can be downloaded here:
Best way to enjoy this game however is in multiplayer, there are various forums where you can sign up and try to find an MP game to join, Paradox forum is a good place to start. You need GameRanger to get access to online game as the game itself has no lobby function anymore.
In multiplayer the game springs to life, as you can co-op as Axis or Allies, or a desperate struggle as Poland/Czechoslovakia with your friend, the choices are limitless. But best games are the ones where all the major powers are controlled by a human player, that is where things get real. The games progress relatively slowly due to amount of players, but in also forces you to cooperate with your allies and form plans and strategies which can be equally fun as playing the game itself.
All in all, this is my favourite WW2 Grand strategy game and has been since its release. No other game has come even close, so I can recommend it with all my heart.

Still the best Batman game in the Arkham series and probably the best Batman game ever made. The story involves Batman catching Joker easily after a recent robbery and, coincidentally, Joker's gang moved to the Asylum because of an issue at the Blackgate Prison - once inside the Asylum, the Joker escapes and taskes control of the Asylum and prepares to unearth something far worse than what you initially suspect. You play as Batman trying to unearth this plot and once again stop the Joker.
To this day, this game still has amazing visuals, Batman himself covering around half the screen, looks the part and stands strong and confident as the character should as well as the texture work on his suit are top notch - the rest of the game fairs the same, since the game has been given an outstanding amount of care and work into every area you go through. Not one area in the game feels exactly the same as another even if they look similar. Very stellar work of textures all around overall.
I don't say this is the best Batman game out there for no reason - gameplay is pretty basic "Brawler" style with very minor puzzle solving, but what makes this game different, from, say a game like Assassin's Creed - is the "Free Flow combat system" the game has. The combat is slightly similar to the first Assassin's Creed, except - the flow combat system allows Batman to basically jump from one foe to another in a very fast manner, almost rythmically, to get a combo counter to go as high as you can while still making it challenging by giving the foes still standing a fighting chance and implementing counters.
You can also explore the entirety of the Arkham Asylum as you unlock areas and you can do a variety of things while exploring, you can face groups of enemies scattered around, you can do Riddler Challenges - whom are a bunch of mini puzzles scattered around the Asylum that involves the use of Batman's Detective Mode, these range from finding a specific item found in the area or marks that require the Detective Mode to find and a "Complete the Mark" type of game that involves you scanning the area from specific places to complete a full mark, etc - Riddler trophies, and a bunch of case files to find out more background information on Batman characters and villains (as well as the history behind Arkahm Asylum) that are often very well realized and fun to hear.

The Detective Mode & Gadgets: You'll be using these a LOT on your trudge through Arkham Asylum. Ranging from the standard Batarangs and Grappling hook (used for mundane objectives such as getting to and pulling out vents from hard to reach places, etc), the Explosive Gel (Used a lot to surprise enemies, to find weak walls to find trophies and secrets and to progress in the story as well!) and a bunch more. The Detecive Mode helps you analyze weak walls to use your Explosive Gel on and other gadgets as well as analyze enemy/allies conditions and, more important later on in the game, to find out which enemies carry weapons or are special enemies.).
So in general, if you ever wanted to know and feel what a life in the day of Batman is, this is definately your game, more so than the sequels (imo). From the excellent assets and sound to follow it up with, and the pitch perfect gameplay to go along with it, this sits as one of my favourite video game experiences and currently my best experience playing as the legendary Dark Knight.

I Am Alive is easily one of my favorite games, it has a decent plot and fairly well acted voice-overs. The gameplay is a mix of Resident Evil style scavenging and Prince of Persia-esque climbing sections.
Your characters stamina bar plays a huge part in how you play this game. Most every action causes it to drain. Running, climbing, and struggling to break locks. When you enter the areas the NPC's refer to as "the fog", which is dust and ash in the air caused by storms your stamina constantly drains. Do you risk a few more moments searching dusty streets for vital resources, or climb back up to saftey and let it recharge? You will find yourself constantly watching it well into the later ares of this game.
You will come across other survivors and you must decide what to do. Some may be hostlie, some may need help, the intimatation combat is very well done in this game. You are actually able to hold hostiles at gunpoint even when you may not have any ammo. Don't wait too long to act or they may realize your gun is empty and attack.

So, Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon is a standalone expansion to Ubisoft's Far Cry 3 (obviously). This time players are not put into the modern day jungles, rather a post apocalyptic world, with you playing as Rex "Power" Colt, a cyborg with a robotic arm and a bad attitude.
Gameplay is very similar to the base game, with the player able to free roam around the island, liberating outposts or, if you are like me, running away from the deadly wildlife. Blood Dragon introduces a new type of predator to the wild, that being the Blood Dragon. These hulking beasts are deadly in battle and have a hunger for fresh cyborg hearts (don't ask me why they have hearts, just play along!)
These new beasts add a new mechanic to the game, with the player being able to throw cyborg hearts around, which attracts the Blood Dragons, which can be a huge help in liberating outposts. Just throw a tasty heart into the outpost, and watch the bad guys flee in terror from the onslaught of a hulking beast that will rip apart anything in its path. (did we mention it can fire lasers from its mouth?)
Blood Dragon, for an expansion, is a decent size, with myself getting at least 10 or so hours into it.
One thing i do wish is there to be more sidequests, rather than there just be the main story, as the island feels very empty once you liberate all outposts, with there not being much to do afterwards.
This game is great, and you do not need Far Cry 3 to play it, meaning new players can pick up this game and play right away, without necessarily having to play the base game.
This game is highly reccomended for fans of old, cheesy, 80's sci-fi media. There are tons of 80's cliches, ncluding a badass synthesiser soundtrack.

I could write a long review, comparing and describing various aspects of this game, explaining mechanics or just pointing at errors and issues, which H&G definietly has a lot of. But I don't really want to do that, so I'll just explain why and under what conditions should you play it.
IF YOU WANT TO HAVE A GOOD EXPERIENCE WITH HEROES AND GENERALS, YOU DEFINIETLY NEED TO BRING YOUR FRIENDS ALONG AND PLAY WITH THEM, OR JOIN A CLAN.
When playing alone, H&G is mostly an utter pain. It might seem as a small issue at the beginning, as early game modes (Encounter and Skirmish) can be pure fun even without dragging a squad of mates with you. But as you begin to play Assault, then move on to War battles and finally acquire your very first assault team and begin to play the RTS, you will notice how helpless you are, when you and an army of random dudes take a stand against a clan. You will see teams consisting of 10 infantrymen and a bunch of snipers and tankers getting wiped from the face of Earth by infantry-focused teams capable of attacking an objective and defending the previous one at the same time thanks to their skilled commanders, coordinating their efforts. You will see bunches of random noobs running around and wasting precious equipment and constantly dying, while you will be the only one trying to take or defend objectives. And you will begin to hate this game deeply.
I've been through this, and then I took a few weeks off and decided to join a clan. Now I feel that this is how it should be played: tactically, with coordinated squads where each and every member knows exactly what he is supposed to do, and good leaders capable of commanding their men to maximize their efficiency on the battlefield. So, just find some friends and play together and you will have a lot of fun.

This has to be one of the best FPS games I've played in a while. There hasn't been a lot of innovation in the FPS genre in a very long time, but this game actually does some really new stuff.
First, I'll voice my one annoyance: this game is not roguelike. True, it has permadeath and procedurally generated replay value - but that does not make a game roguelike. So while this game is more roguelike than any other FPS I've seen, roguelikes are turned based tile games. Words mean things for a reason!
That being said, this game is amazing:
(1) Permadeath with permanent unlocks make death exciting but still "productive"
(2) Procedurally generated levels with random bosses and layouts make for lots of replay value
(3) The levelling system is very clever, and also adds to replay. Each game plays very differently depending on the weapons and upgrades you get access to
(4) Super fast and smooth controls make for incredible action
(5) Meaningful traps and jump puzzles which are difficult, but equally rewarding
(6) Unlockable classes that have simple, but profound differences for even more variety of game play
(7) Rarely seen fantasy genre in FPS, and very well executed at that
In short, this game is well worth the investment. For most FPS fans it will be a long time before this game gets stale to play. Still hasn't happened for me after numerous play throughs!

I can't believe I waited so long to pick this up - the negative reviews kept me on the fence, but now I know that most of those reviews are knee-jerky vitriol in the same vein as the spew about Mass Effect: Andromeda (which is a great game as well.) Seriously, people - you're only hurting yourselves (and the rest of us!) If you have issues with a product, then critique and even criticize it, but do so constructively; throwing tantrums and screaming hatefully at the developers does NOT encourage them to address issues OR provide more (and better) products in the future.
Deus Ex: Mankind Divided is a solid - and fun - game. The graphics are great, and voice acting is as good or better than other titles on the modern market, and the story continues the tradition of the series and follows up on one of the ending-options from Deus Ex: Human Revolution. Focusing on the main story will net a good 20-30 hours, and adding the side quests (which are definitely cool and involving) adds that much again or more. And, common nowadays, there is a New Game+ feature. Time-to-play of course depends on playstyle, but that is heart of the Deus Ex series: Take your time, read, hack, and explore everything for backstory, interact with NPCs, then stealth through the zones and missions, or go in guns blazing with full combat augs and beeline for the end. Or any combination thereof.
For those unfamiliar with the series, your character is a cybernetic-enhanced human in a world of conflict between the "naturals" and the "augmented" very similar to the conflict of the X-Men movie series (humans vs mutants). In the RPG-style of the game, as you gain experience you can improve your implants/augments and focus on various improvements such as stealth, physical power, social interaction, electronic manipulation (hacking/disabling), and/or combat defensive and offensive options and actions. How you play is as much about getting into (or avoiding) combat as it is interacting with others. Decisions in social interactions as well as mission tasks can affect "the world" around you, and they bear consequences that may be immediate (talk your way out of/into a fight) or long term (make a deal with a mobster who will expect a future favor).
The plot in DE:MD follows the protagonist working for a counter-terrorism division where, in the course of "normal" investigations, it is revealed that there is more going on behind the scenes - fairly typical plot device. The main character essentially has to wade through disinformation and clues to get to the point where he understands WHAT is going on though, in keeping with Deus Ex universe, it is not quite fully revealed WHY. This may be why some people claim the game is "unfinished" - things are not neat and tidy at the end, and it can feel "sudden". Fortunately, this leaves room for more story in future DLCs or expansions; unfortunately, the series title has been shelved "for now" because of sales (see above about negative reviews and discouraging further commitment.) Considering the series ranks so highly with many players, I like to think we will see more eventually. Still, something to consider if you are on-the-fence about picking up this title.
However, this does not mean it is unworthy of playing - getting to that untidy ending is still a great journey. Some of the characters are not as fleshed-out or memorable as in DE:HR, but all were suitable to the context and story and only one annoyed me (and I'm pretty sure that one was the point.) The scenes and environment are, at times, breathtaking, though to experience the best graphics will require a decent rig. I actually am upgrading my video card just so I can play this (and ME:A) again in full glory. The music is also great; not blasting, in-your-face distraction but low-key techno quite suitable to the dark cyberpunk Deus Ex theme. The dialogue carries the plot well, with some parts having much snarky humor goodness, and the background dialogue (random NPCs on the streets, etc) is immersive without being overly distracting. The controls are configurable and work great with trackball and Nostromo n52 gamepad (though until I decided on my main weapons/playstyle there were almost too many control choices.)
I have very few complaints with Deus Ex: Mankind Divided. Several quests and tasks demand you go from point A to point B and back again - common in RPGs - but the size of the Prague hub and the load-times from the travel tram often left me heading to the kitchen for a snack or reading a book while waiting. The load-times are my own system/hardware, but still I could do with less back-and-forth quests (in this or any game). The number of possible inventory items also feels excessive: 2 or 3 different ammo types for each weapon, weapon mods, "ammo" for some augs, half-a-dozen hacking items, a dozen or more vendor-trash items, plus a rudimentary crafting system... It's quite a bit much, especially adding to the travel back-and-forth bit to get to vendors. These complaints, however, in no way reduced my motivation to play (or play again when my new vidcard arrives.)
Overall, I think Deus Ex: Mankind Divided is a top-notch game. For me, it does not quite live up to the DE:Human Revolution reputation (which I am installing to play again) but it is great in its own right and it does remain true to the Deus Ex universe/experience. I can understand how some people might feel let down by it because of its predecessor, or because of the untidy ending, but clearly that didn't stop most of them from playing it. If you're considering picking up this title then do yourself a favor and note the nearly 2:1 ratio of positive to negative reviews. It is a good game - even a great game - and I highly recommend it. If you are concerned about cost-to-enjoyment, simply wait until it hits a discount (the Steam Summer Sale should be just around the corner) but in any event if you're a fan of the series, or a fan of FPS action/RPGs, don't miss this!

I got the game for 15€ on discount. And yet it was absolutely not worth it.
Let's get into the details:
Technically:
- The performance is horrible. Even on a 1080 the fps drop frequently (obviously the gc (garbage collection) is not dealt with).
- Bugs everywhere. Mostly small, non-gamebreaking ones.
- 21:9 support is.... well, there is none. Of course you can play it in 21:9, but there are way too many things that are not supported on that resolution. For a AAA title not tolerable.
Gameplay/Story:
- The story is absolutely boring (at least as far as I've seen it, I stopped playing quite early though).
- Conversations are linear. You can choose what to ask / say next, but you don't really have a choice at all.
- Gameplay mechanics like moving in sneakmode are horrible. It feel clumpsy, not smooth at all. For a game, that states you can play it entirely non-lethal, this is not acceptable.
- "Multiple ways to complete a quest" is a lie. Well, you can ether shoot your way through or sneak past the npcs. But other than that, there is only one way in and one way out. No open world (for example only a VERY limited number of houses / flats etc are accessible. Mostly through the windows, since the front door can't be opened at all).
Conclusion:
I am really happy I didn't buy it for 50€. Because even the 15€ I spent on it feel like a complete waste.

A very enjoyable title, to such an extent that a non-fan of Batman like me can play and love it. The combat is meaty and extravagant, rewarding good timing and skill. The better you fight the more XP you earn, with that XP you can upgrade your health, gadgets and fighting capabilities. There's also a good variety of enemy types that get introduced as you progress, forcing you to adapt and change your style.
It's not just the combat that emulates the feeling of Batman so well, but you gain a wide variety of gadgets to use either against your enemies or to find secrets on the rather large island where the game takes place. Not to mention the aspect of the dark knight, stealth will be a necessity, as your enemies won't always be unarmed. Armed goons in a room will start out confident and tough, but as you take them out one by one, they'll be reduced to nervous and panicking wrecks. The feeling is fantastic to say the least.
The story and voice acting is quite excellent, with an extensive character archive that details and explains many of the characters (mostly villains) in the Batman universe, these get unlocked with collectibles known as Riddler Trophies.
This game is a must to own if you simply enjoy a great game.

By far the game I've played the most the last decade! And it's great!
Other than appearance of a gnome without armor, you can customize everything about a gnome, even its name. Want a Miner to tend to the Farm when no stone-working is needed? Sure thing! Want the warriors to do menial Hauling after training for half a day? You bet. Want a guy who does nothing but slouch around all day? That too!
Crafting stations can also be assigned to a specific gnome, so no other gnomes will take jobs from him. Great if you want to train a single gnome in a job. Gnomes need water and food though, else they die. Make sure those jobs are a priority.
Gnomes can also be given default uniforms, which means any armor and weapon you want. You can design a military formation with ranged and melee gnomes, which has their own custom uniform as well, even the quality grade can be set, keeping the best armors and weapon for your best gnomes.
There are Position Perks which give you bonuses to almost whatever you want, and there is synergy between perks. You can set one position to Knock Em Down, which will result in more knockdowns, and another position can have Finish Him, which does more damage to knocked down enemies. Ranged units can be set to aim for the eyes, making it easier for your melee units. Having at least some diversity is important, and that counts for weapons as well! Enemies are stronger and weaker against certain weapon types.
Lastly, putting gnomes in a squad will allow much, much greater control over them, and a squad can be given a Perk as well, which becomes more powerful the more gnomes are in the squad.
Lastly, a gnome have skills in every weapon and every profession, but they need to be trained. Your starting gnomes start off with good skills in their profession, making the beginning a bit easier, but nomadic gnomes who want to join you have random skills. If you want someone to be really god at a specific thing, you need to train her by setting her to train or work as often as possible. Don't allow your gnomes to idle!
Personally I take it slow, and just build stuff. I really like the building aspect of the game. Gnomes just chop down, mine ore or stone, and you can use these to build block walls, effectively allowing you to create your ideal fortress or any other building you want. There is a huge variety of trees, farmables, stone types and ores as well. And everythinghas value of different kinds. A Gold sword will be worse than a Steel sword for instance, but will sell for more. That's right! There are merchants who can visit from time to time!
There are so many, many, many more layers to Gnomoria, so I recommend going to the steam community and read some while you play. The controls become very easy after a while, so study them a little to avoid annoyances. There is also a gnomoria wiki online with valuable information. Also, watch some videos on youtube; some of the castles and creations are really good.

I have played this game a lot. It is, overall, a simple graphic update to dwarf fortress that is a tad dumbed down. That said it is one of the most complex town/ colonization sim I have played that keeps you entertained for a long time. I played it before it was on steam and was excited to see it come out finally, but since it got on steam there hasn't been a whole lot of development. I'm really waiting for the end product to show up. As it stands once you have built everything you run out of things to do because you can literally walk away from the computer and your town will do fine most of the time. Its worth buying as is, and I can really see the potential in the end product. But its like getting halfway through a book and finding out the author of the series you are halfway through died without writing the last books, and unlike Robert Jordan, the author didn't leave notes that someone else could follow to write the ending to a monumental series.
Pros
-Manage a settlement of gnomes
-You can micromanage as much as you want
-Simple graphics, but not a text game
-Addictive, way too much of my life
-Challenging
-Customizable difficulties
-Diplomacy looks promising if it ever gets improved, like maybe I want to conduct a raid on a neighboring goblin kingdom instead of just insulting them
Cons
-Stupid zombies and beetles
-Steep learning curve
-Not much developement on the game, snails pace
-Produces a lot of activity that I never get from other games on my CPU
-No tiered crafting system- the Gnomes can make everything as soon as there are materials and the skills involved don't change the end product enough that it matters- only skills that improve anything are fighting skills, and farming.
-Trade doesn't really change over time- you get wealthier but your neighbors stay the same
I realize I have a lot of cons but some of them I enjoy like the steep learning curve, and just the way the game works.

The incredible story of our evolution from ape ancestors spans 6 million years or more, and features the acquirement of traits from bipedal walking, large brains, hairlessness, tool-making, hunting and harnessing fire, to the more recent development of language, art, culture and civilisation.
Darwin’s The Origin of Species, published in 1859, suggested that humans were descended from African apes. However, no fossils of our ancestors were discovered in Africa until 1924, when Raymond Dart dug up the “Taung child” – a 3-million to 4 million-year-old Australopithecine.
Over the last century, many spectacular discoveries have shed light on the history of the human family. Somewhere between 12 and 19 different species of early humans are recognised, though palaeoanthropologists bitterly dispute how they are related. Famous fossils include the remarkably complete “Lucy”, dug up in Ethiopia in 1974, and the astonishing “hobbit” species, Homo floresiensis, found on an Indonesian island in 2004.
Walking tall
Humans are really just a peculiar African ape – we share about 98% of our DNA with chimpanzees, our closest living relatives. Genetics and fossil evidence hint that we last shared a common ancestor 7 to 10 million years ago – even if we continued hybridising long after.
At around 6 million years ago, the first apes to walk on two legs appear in the fossil records. Despite the fact that many of these Australopithecines and other early humans were no bigger than chimps and had similar-sized brains, the shift to bipedalism was highly significant. Aside from our large brain, bipedalism is perhaps the most important difference between humans and apes, as it freed our hands to use tools.
Bipedalism may have evolved when drier conditions shrank dense African forests. It must have allowed our ancestors to spot predators from further away, reach hanging fruit from the ground, and reduce exposure to sunlight. Evidence that Australopithecines walked upright includes analysis of the shape of their bones and fossilised footprints.
One famous member of the species Australopithecus afarensis is the remarkably complete fossil found by palaeaoanthropologist Donald Johanson in Hadar, Ethiopia in 1974. The 3.2-million-year-old fossil was named Lucy, after the Beatles’ song Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds.
She stood around 1.1 metres (3.5 feet) tall and although she walked on two legs, she probably had a less graceful gait than us, since she walked with them bent.
Scientist’s have modelled her gait using computers. Their characteristic long arms and curved fingers suggest that at least some Australopithecines were still good climbers.
Hundreds of other fossils of Australopithecus afarensis have now also been discovered. Other related early human species include Australopithecus africanus – i copied this from
– 3.5-million-year-old Kenyanthropus platyops, 5.8-million to 4.4-million-year-old Ardipithecus, 5.8-million-year-old Orrorin tugenensis and 6 million year old Sahelanthropus tchadensis.
Tooled up
Australopithecines are thought to be the ancestors of Homo, the group to which our own species, Homo sapiens, belongs.
However, Australopithecines may also have given rise to another branch of hominid evolution – the vegetarian Paranthropus species. Around 2.7 million years ago, species such as Paranthropus bosei in east Africa evolved to take advantage of the dry grasslands. This included the development of enormous jaws and chewing muscles for grinding up tough roots and tubers.
By 2.4 million years ago, Homo habilis had appeared – the first recognisably human-like hominid to appear in the fossil record – which lived alongside P. bosei. Their bodies were around two-thirds the size of ours, but their brains were significantly larger than Australopithecines with a volume of about 600 cubic centimetres.
H. habilis had much smaller teeth and jaws than Paranthropus and was probably the first human to eat large quantities of meat. This meaty diet, acquired through scavenging, may have provided energy required to kick-start an increasing brain size. A mutation that weakened jaw muscles and gave our brains more space to grow may also lie behind the big brains we have today.
H. habilis – which means “handy man” – was also the first early human to habitually create tools and use them to break bones and extract marrow. This tool-making tradition, known as Oldowan, lasted virtually unchanged for a million years. Oldowan tools were made by breaking an angular rock with a “hammerstone” to give simple, sharp-edged stone flakes for chopping and slicing.
Despite their own increases in brain size, the Paranthropus group of species had become extinct by 1.2 million years ago. Some experts speculate that it was learning to work as a team against predators that gave Homo the edge.
Modern lookers
At around 1.65 million years ago, another early human, Homo ergaster, started to create tools in a slightly different fashion. This so-called Acheulean tradition was the tool-making technology used for nearly the entire Stone Age, and practiced until 100,000 years ago. Acheulean tools, such as hand axes and cleavers, were larger and more sophisticated than their predecessors’. They may have been status symbols as well as tools.
Homo ergaster first appeared in Africa around 2 million years ago, and in many ways resembled us. Though they had brow ridges, they had lost the stoop and long arms of their ancestors. They may have been even more slender than us and were probably well-adapted to running long distances. Some experts believe that they were the first to sport largely hairless bodies, and to sweat, though another theory puts our hairlessness down to an aquatic phase.
One famous example of a more modern looking early human is the Turkana boy, a teenager when he died, 1.6 million years ago in Kenya. The shape of this fossil showed that the human pelvis had reached today’s narrow proportions. Combined with the growing size of the human head and brain, this had far-reaching implications: human women now need help for a successful birth; and human babies are born earlier, and need a longer period of childhood care, than those of apes.
Meat-eating, however, may have allowed us to become early weaners.
H.ergaster may have been the first early human to leave Africa. Bones dated to around 1.75 million years ago have been found in Dmanisi in Georgia.
Shortly afterwards, Homo erectus appeared – the first early human whose fossils have been seen in large numbers outside of Africa. The first specimen discovered, a single cranium, was unearthed in Indonesia in 1891. H.erectus was highly successful, spreading to much of Asia between 1.8 and 1.5 million years ago, and surviving as recently as 27,000 years ago.
This species, with a brain volume of around 1000 cm3 would have interacted with modern humans. They may have been the first people to take to the seas and habitually hunt prey such as mammoths and wild horses, although there is some debate about this. They may also have harnessed the use of fire and built the first shelters.

In 2009, Rocksteady Studios, a video game studio with virtually no history restored gamers' hopes all around world with Batman Arkham Asylum. The UK based studio revived a genre long forgotten and delivered a superhero action game which is worth every cent you spend on it.
Yes, yes, there hasn't been a shortage of superhero games in the 21st century, but none of them really delivered on its potential. And there is a bunch like the Iromnan or Superman games that aren't even worth talking about. Batman always had the better track record when it comes to games, but Arkham Asylum fires on all cylinders. Great graphics, incredible sound effects, a mad story and the little details will engage gamers and not only Batman and superhero fans.
The game takes place on the famous Arkham Island where an Asylum has been build many-many years ago for the worst criminals Gotham can offer. It happens that The Joker has been captured by the Bats and taken in, but the Dark Knight suspects there is something going on in the background and takes his nemesis in himself. Shortly after a riot is started and The Joker gets loose. Now it's clear that the clown has something on his mind and Batman has to stop him. The story is intense and interesting as Bruce Wayne slowly puts together the pieces of Joker's grand plan. As you progress several of Batman's greatest foes will try to stop you, most notably Killer Croc, Poison Ivy or Bane, but others are introduced too. Some of them get bigger space others are bit players, but the point is that they are in the game and by their presence they make it richer.
The graphics are decent, but there are flaws here and there. Batman and The Joker look superb, but detail of minor characters aren't on that level and some even look ugly. Other than that, the island is looks beautiful and from the distance you can see Gotham, the city of sins. The game is very well optimized on the PC so gamers with older rigs won't have problem running it.
Even tough the island isn't overwhelmingly large, there is a lot to do. The main campaign will take around 8 hours to finish plus you can solve the puzzles and collect the question marks The Riddler left for you. By doing those you unlock character profiles, concept arts and more, so it's far from time wasting. Also by specific scanning stone tables on the island you can unlock recordings that tell you about the story of Arkham Asylum narrated by Amadeus Arkham himself. Probably the most interesting collectibles are the patient interview tapes that are scattered around the island. Some of the villains were interviewed in the facility and you can listen to these well composed dialogues. If you want to complete the main story with all the collectibles you will spend around 14+ hours on the island. When this is done you can try challenge missions where you have to beat scores by beating thugs. Sounds interesting and it adds to the game. This is the place where you can perfect you combat skills as the challenges get more and more difficult. The other half of them puts you in rooms where you have to complete 3, mostly skill-based tasks.
With the near perfect free flow combat Arkham City is a near perfect game that finally delivers not only to fans of the genre but also to Batman and superhero fans. In fact, those who are not really in comic books should consider this game for first. It's a joy to play every second of this game. Arkham Asylum set the bar for every single superhero game that comes after 2009. It's a benchmark and an example to follow for every publisher and developer.
Rating: 90/100; Replay Value: 3/5; To Beat: 8 hours (main campaign), 14 hours (campaign with collectibles); Played on: normal.

The combat, using an XBOX 360 controller for windows, is not much more involved than bashing a few buttons but is crafted in such a way that it's a marvel to watch Batman jump from enemy to enemy and even change the direction of his punch mid-swing to stop an incoming attack.
He's not limited to just hand to hand combat though and can take advantage of high-placed gargoyles to swoop down on unsuspecting enemies, taking out a heavily armed contingent one by one. There's nothing more satisfying then watching the last remaining bad guy panic knowing his doom is imminent.
I played on EASY difficulty because I was only interested in the story and the combat was an easy experience but I think it added to feeling like I was The Batman. Smashing through groups of armed toughies wouldn't have seemed so epic if the harder difficulty made for a slower experience (I'm not sure if it does, just speculating).
The boss fights however, even though unique in their mechanics, were probably on the easy side. Especially the finale. A player wanting a more challenging experience should probably bump up the difficultly at least to Normal.

The exploration is fairly minimal, the plot is generic and never feels like it's really resolved, the survival aspect is somewhat tame.  I had an issue on my laptop where the ground would pop in and out depending on camera angle (I did not have this problem on my desktop, though my laptop more than meets system requirements as well).  There was one section that I was entirely unable to complete, but found a way to climb around it after a couple hours (much of it spent getting there from the previous checkpoint which was some way back as they are not very frequent).
Ultimately, I think there's a market for this game, but it wasn't me.

"Hidden gem" my bum bum.
I stopped enjoying this one 30 minutes into the game, maybe even before that point.
In general this is a usual Ubisoft game - rushed, glitchy, feels unfinished, at times simply annoying.
Obnoxious camera with broken sensitivity if you're using mouse and keyboard - I had to switch to a controller 'cos I simply couldn't handle it. There are two different sensitivities for when you're running in 3rd person and when you're simply walking. Only the second one can be changed, which results in the camera being utterly glitchy when you're running with high sensitivity options.
Weird and annoying retry system that makes close to none sense when the game restarts you a second before you pick up another retry. Now, if you somehow still want to play this game, I'd suggest starting on easy. I went with survival and switched around 2h to easy simply cos of the game being made so poorly.
Combat is.... it's something that made me rage internally at least a dozen times, even after switching to easy. It's this... I don't even... It's a mess. It tries to be realistic but fails so many times due to it feeling rushed and glitchy (as the whole game). At times you will kill 1 out of 3 guys and be left pointing your empty gun at 2 of them. Now if you don't have anything else and are forced to melee, you can already restart since if you want to kill one of the remaining two bad guys you will have to go into this QTE which resolves around you MASHING one button but since it takes around 3-5 secs to finish that, the last enemy will just rush to you and interrupt that leaving you basically dead. The only thing that you could do in this situation is spam "back off" till one of them is at the end of the map so he won't be able to interrupt you. Or somehow try to be stealthy (there's no stealth system btw) and pray to the RNG gods as well as the bugs gods. It's possible to do but in no way fun.
Add to that some delay when pulling gun at enemies - sometimes they'll still feel brave even though you can shoot them easily. The delay is usually around 2 secs and can result in your death most of the time.
Oh, and yes.. At some point the game introduces the "kill the though guy, rest will surrender" mechanic which worked... you've guessed it.. once. You will never do this because your priority will be to kill the guys with guns first and pick those up as fast as you can so that you don't have to waste more ammo on other enemies that will pick up said guns and be the threat again.
To finish the combat bit I will add that AI is just.. marvelous. In this one instance I SHOT 2 people but one of the enemies felt somewhat brave and went with the line close to "Can you even shoot? I bet you won't have the balls to.". Yeah...
The game doesn't feel fun in general. It's like a chore... I'd understand the game being difficult, but the game being difficult 'cos it's an unfinished piece of Ubicrap? Sorry, no.
Story is.... uninteresting at best with the ending being a huge middle finger to your face and a cliffhanger saying "want to actually finish the game? Buy the next one." (which afaik will never get made). Not to mention that what you're doing has hardly any meaning for the main protag. The game is a pack of side quests resolved around other people and their problems. You're always helping someone, everyone else has 2 left hands and you're this knight on a white horse. Meh.
Not a single interesting/likeable character. Protag is this shell of a character, stating the obvious for the most of the time and following commands of other people. The kid with the head that's 50% of her body in the first cutscene is your typical sick child needing rescue with 0 personality, same as her guardian and mother. Not to mention people you can rescue/help. I really wanted to shoot that starving woman who said she wouldn't touch the meat but wanted 2 cans of vegies out of me. For the record, there were 2 types of meat in the game - human meat and rat meat. Afaik she didn't state which one is a no-no for her so... yeah...
"So, Extinox, have you enjoyed anything in this game?"
Actually yes. Not greatly but I still enjoyed it, I guess.
Climbing was somewhat fun. Of course not at all times 'cos of well.. glitches but it was mediocre and thus better than the other parts of the game.
EDIT: Oh, I forgot to add how it somehow uses 90% of my CPU most of the time and how sound is broken if you're running 5.1. The middle speaker will simply produce no sound. I will never forget the moment when there was a storm going on around me but when I set my camera to a specific angle, I wouldn't hear anything.

Think Tomb Raider only with a male protagonist set in a post-apocaplyptic world.   The main character is a hero in a decidedly non-heroic world.  Gameplay alternates between climbing/exploration and combat.
Climbing/exploration is tomb-raider like, although a little more on-rails in that if the game doesn't want you jumping, you won't be able to jump.  The second difference is a stamina meter which drops the longer your are climbing.  If it depletes, you fall to your death.  I liked this approach, although the "scary" music that starts playing when you are at 75% or lower stamina starts to get irritating.  I enjoyed the climbing aspect of the game, once I got used to the mechanics of it.  There is a fair amount of backtracking, though.
Combat is not the game's strength.  Since there is limited weaponry, you have to intimidate your enemies and push them off ledges, into fires, that sort of thing.  The idea is interesting, but the execution really didn't work well.  Some enemies don't back off.  Some enemies start shooting right away.  The only way to know which is which is to die and restart.  Until you get the bow-and-arrow half way through, this mechanic gets quite frustrating.
I finished the game in about 6 hours.  That's pretty short, but I bought it on sale and feel like I got good value for the money.  Despite it's weaknesses, I found the game as a whole compelling.  I was invested in the world and the characters.  The story of a man who, having lost his own family, decides to risk his life to safe someone else's is a common trope, but very well done here.  Some levels, like the ship or climbing the second office building, were a lot of fun.  On sale, I recommend this game to fans of the Tomb Raider genre.

I am SO VERY HAPPY that I purchased this game as a Halloween special, I think I paid $3.00 for it. I have a special liking for post-apocalyptic games, but if I had paid full price for this I would have been very upset.
The game starts off promising, with a bleak color scheme and appropriate moody music as you're placed in the shoes of a character who's arrived at his home town, and is trying to find a way to his dwelling. You have a gun but no bullets. OK, fine. Mad Max didn't have bullets for his gun half the time, but it was still an unforgettable experience of a movie. You come to a bridge which has been blown to pieces, and the tutorial system helpfully prompts you to jump the gap here, climb the post there. OK, fine. Normally I have little patience for jumping puzzles, but Half Life had its share, and that was one of the best games I ever played.
And this is where the game betrays its console roots. And no, I'm not a PC purist. I own a PS2, and PS3, and a Wii. I grew up playing Nintendo. There are some wonderful console games out there. This is not one of them. Here is why: While climbling, you have a stamina meter. OK, fine. Realistic. No one can hang by their fingers indefinately. You have to climb smart, or you'll run out of energy and fall. But, the game doesn't merely expect you to use common sense. It presents a jumping/climbing puzzle that demands perfection. You have JUST ENOUGH energy to make it where you need to get to. If you waste ANY time, even so much as a tenth of a second, you're going to fail. And fail. And fail some more. After ten tries I was able to get close to my objective. After ten more tries I was able to begin a final reach to the sanctuary of a ledge. And that's as close as I got. After the seventh time of running out of energy and falling to my death within that final reach, I gave up. Any game that throws a puzzle like this at you, a puzzle where literally one tenth of a wasted second counts, at the very beginning of the game... Well, to quote Eric Cartman, "Screw you guys, I'm going home." Some players would view this as a challenge. More power to them. I view it as frustrating and as lazy game design.
To be fair, I'm not doing this game justice by reviewing it after only an hour of gameplay. But I say if the first bite of a sandwich contains excrement, you have no one else to blame if you take a second bite. Or, God forbid, finishing the entire thing just because you paid good money for it. And scanning other reviews has indicated that this opening puzzle of frustration is only the tip of the iceberg.
The funny thing is, I've spent far more time writing this review than such a game deserves. But if I save even one gamer from throwing away $15.00 on this, then my work is done here.

The Triennale Game Collection is a showcase of 5 experimental works each developed by an indie designer, strongly displaying their features and thoughts in games and beyond. That said, they can be both highly insightful or pointless, depending on how you see them. All five of them, to me, show a very different angle of interactivity in gameplay. A bit too artistic at times, but overall interesting and powerful.
The art style in the main screen is good, but not great,
kind of modern Scandinavian style. (My thanks to Serotoninphobe for pointing that out.) The collection is produced by
, maker of MirrorMoon EP and FOTONICA, but personally I think they didn't work their aesthetic charm right this time. I guess there're some semiotics stuff they try to convey, but again, I'm never into semiotics.
The following are my thoughts on each of them, individually.
From Mario von Rickenbach of
and Christian Etter of Drei comes
, the wire conductor. A nifty interactive animation I'd say, just like Plug & Play, but smaller, more obscure and better looking. In this game you control a cord (and later a set of cords) and by which you manipulate the still objects insignificantly. It can be frustrating sometimes, but at the end you may (yes, may) find it worth it.
The music is especially remarkable, composed by
.
Boy, this one will be one of my all-time favorites.
A modern presentation of classical cosmographia developed by
, the developer of Sunset, Luxuria Superbia and other projects. From their former works one distinctive trait is featured, that is, minimum interaction combined with maximum expression of their ideas. Though with the nature of the industry Tale of Tales's games are, more or less, failures, commerce-wisely, their games are beautiful.
Not unlike their previous works,
is more of a presentation rather than a game. Unlike their previous attempts in Triennale Harvey and Samyn (the dev) are set free from breaking even, so here it's: A pure, clear and astonishingly gorgeous modern presentation of classical celestial spheres (Petrus Apianus's Cosmographicus liber, to be precise). Each sphere is interpreted with magnificent imagination beyond our dimension. Among all five games this is my personal favorite, partially because of my love in mysticism and theology, mostly because it's fascinating and delightful to play around with.
Created by Cardboard Computer, the creator of
, a fantastic adventure game that has been taking some year of development and the last episode is still missing. While waiting for the fifth episode, you may wanna play a bit of
, since it's very KR0-esque. In a desert valley you are a nameless person -- or you are the crystal object that roams about indicating where does the person go or investigate. The effort they put to make the crystal object exceptional vivid and lively successfully established the notion that you can't tell whether you are the crystal or the person.
Just like the trilogy by
the game is intentionally filled with interactable objects that virtually do nothing. But it's less fun to poke around, as the protagonist walks as slow as any normal person would do in reality. After you goof around for a while, the game comes down to three things: shopping -- which grants you new stuff and is the only means to advance time in this game -- offering things to a book-sharped white wall -- which then leaves new stuff to you -- and talking to a mysterious neighbor that rarely visits, and the talks are brief, enhancing the sense of solitude.
The ideas behind this game are very interesting and current, according to my interpretation. But I won't bother to share with you, because we can all interpret differently and that's the charm... and it'd be too long. Aside from that, the music and graphic are hearty.
In
(by
) you are fixed in an empty room with nothing but a projection machine, which you cannot see, but can interact with by dragging your mouse. By doing so, the image projected changes direction and distance, displaying the views in different parts of a city and its woods, skies and shores. Atop that, you can add a layer to it and change the content in that layer. An interesting attempt to present motion in still pictures, I myself take the projected images the minimized fragments of parts of, well, let's say a game, and the things on the layer sprites in that game. Or beyond that, the former places that are fixed, and the latter people and other animated things. Depending on what you make out of it,
can be either interesting and insightful, or just nonsense (that also applies to other ones featured in Triennale XXI).

Dead Space 1 was an amazing and unique sci-fi survival horror that till holds up today. Dead space 2 is a competant sci-fi spectacle shooter; but it's no survival horror.
With more dark areas, weaker torch and more predictable jump-scares than Doom 3 , Dead Space's encounters quickly become more irritation than entertainment. Add to the fact the lore and story revealled in DS2 is completely at odds with DS1 (The inconsistencies explained away eventually by a supplemental comic-book) means there really isn't a whole lot there for fans of the original who appreciated the games pacing and horror elements.
If you enjoyed the original for it's
elements, you'll be pleased to know Isaac still handles like a greased up hippo and takes up almost half the screen space, resulting in stupid situations like an enemy standing right in front of him but being hidden from the player's PoV. Necromorph dismemberment is as memorably rote as it's ever been - and the introduction of the seeker rifle means you can one-shot most necromorphs without even having to dismember them if that feels too much like work.
Dead Space 2, like Mass Effect 2, follows a predictable downward arc from the original's format. Polishing and refining down the formula for commercial interest, but losing it's soul along the way.
