Really nice fantasy 4X game, kind of similar to Civilization 5 or 6 because of the way combat works (one unit per tile) but with some elements taken from Master of Magic.
It's the basic 4X stuff: explor your surroundings, build cities and develop them, get resources and make research, defeat all enemies. The fantasy mechanics shake things up quite a bit, though: instead of the usual planet map, you have multiple worlds (lumps of rock floating in space) with specialized climates. You can research and cast spells that improve your units, change the terrain or damage your enemies. You have different factions, but when you capture their cities you can (at a cost) keep them and build those factions' unique stuff. Economy is somewhat simple, with relatively few resources and buildings, but military units have a nice variety and possible upgrades and buffs.
The rival wizards are really incompetent, but the game still provides a good challenge just through the huge number of monsters you find around the map and the scripted super-enemy, the United One, that is your real adversary in the main game mode.

I’ve always been into first person shooters and I love cyberpunk-themed worlds. Not so massive on stealth type games as I do like to gun, but the main thing I never liked about the Deus Ex franchise was the look of Adam Jensen, the main character. It’s like not liking an Actor in a movie. To me he looks stiff, like Neo but so not, and generally just trying too hard. With every new game release the character never changed so I never bothered to pick up the game until now.
I decided to play the most recent 2016 Deus Ex: Mankind Divided and was instantly thrown into a vibrant detailed world with impressive graphics, turbulent windy environment (which sadly doesn’t impress again after the initial scene) with tons of litter everywhere for me to pick up and interact with. It’s not open world, feels it at first but the world feels smaller as the game goes on. There’s a crafting system which I didn’t use at all, the main guts is in how you upgrade your character’s body augmentations, some of which will make or break the way you can get in and out of spaces, and this game offers you even more ways than Prey does.
My playthrough was 27hrs start to end doing a fair few of the side missions. I’m still not into the main character and thus didn’t get into much of the rather simple story (delivered with stiff cut-scenes). Prague/the world is awesome and I liked the general gameplay feel and how effective each upgrade I invested in worked. Although it’s a stealth game I still did 50/50 stealth and attack and I think I got the best of both worlds (IE: satisfaction from sneaking around in vents to avoid enemies to get to point A, or blasting my way direct to point A).
Gun play wasn’t amazing, the guns just didn’t feel powerful, but hey Deus Ex isn’t primarily a shooter. The ending was a let down as it’s a cliff hanger to a part B DLC, one which I didn’t pay for and glad I haven’t to be honest. Am I a Deus Ex fan? Nope. Really enjoyed the game, but kinda knew it wasn’t for me, still isn’t and it’s primarily because I have to play Adam Jensen.

TLDR: don't let complaints about "ending in the middle" stop you from getting this.
Think I'll start by bluntly addressing what was probably the most talked-about "negative" point: the ending. It's solid. Period. It makes all the sense in the world to wrap things up when they did. It's not as spectacular as Human Revolution, but it's definitely climactic, in a more subdued way; and if you do everything right, it's actually more *satisfying* than the previous game's. In Human Revolution you had to choose the lesser evil. In this game, there is actually something resembling a happy ending.
I'm actually very thankful that they decided to tone down the "epicness" for this installment. Trying to turn it up time and time again without ever reaching some sort of equilibrium can only lead to the agonizing death of the franchise. Case in point, Warcraft.
The problem which left a lot of people feeling let down, I believe, is that there are a fair number of non-trivial threads that this game starts up that never get resolved... and at least a handful of them are *much more* than non-trivial. So yes, after the end, you're very likely to go "whoa, whoa, whoa, hold on just a second! What about that other thing...?" But if you can appreciate the fact that, in a world of secrets and conspiracy, you don't get all the answers you want when you want them, then this game has a way of growing on you after the initial letdown. It did for me at least.
Gameplay wise, it's solid. I felt that the cover mechanism was a fair bit clunkier than in HR, but it seems I'm one of the few who thought that, and you get used to it after a while anyway. There are a few annoying collision and movement quirks but far from anything game breaking.
I found the new augs actually well thought-out and useful, though I do wonder what else they can possibly add in future installments - if Jensen was a one-man army in HR, now he's... I dunno, a one-man army of Greek demigods?
The arsenal is pretty standard, no gravity guns here, but it's better fleshed out than HR. Too bad they removed the armor-piercing upgrade for the pistol, but it does force you to employ a bit more variety, which is interesting. Coupled with the new augs and the ability to grab ledges, I'd say it makes for a somewhat improved combat experience. It's pretty fun to snipe through a level in frustration when someone spots you, before loading the game and retrying the stealth approach.
The world-building is probably the game's strongest point. It's equal to and sometimes better than HR, I'd say, though the outlines of the conspiracy are blurrier (which can be frustrating). I thought at first that the whole "mechanical apartheid" thing was a politically correct gimmick, but they deliver splendidly on the feeling of inescapable oppression. (Well, you can still run and jump around in the streets of Prague while wielding a sniper rifle and no one will lift a finger to stop you, but at least the cops growl threats when you do it.)
That trademark Deus Ex feeling of spending most of the game not knowing who to trust is very much there. Indications of shady activity retrieved via hacked emails and pocket secretaries are plentiful. Characters are believable and relatable, even the ones for whom the most compassionate thing you can feel is a desire to put him out of his misery quickly. All in all, impressive.
In conclusion, if you want some tens of hours of more-cerebral-than-average entertainment that will give you plenty of leftover food for thought, I'd definitely say grab this.

A highly entertaining and bright 3D platform game, that seems to feature some wonky controls (and seems to take some pride in it) to crank up the difficulty of the game; but it's actually not all that bad. Unlike countless other games the likes of Egg Returns Home that shamelessly rely on it's cheap wonky controls entirely for their difficulty, Totally Unbalanced's 'wonky' controls are actually bearable and manageable. You slip every once in a while, but your skill would, at the very least, actually matters; you can learn it and get used to it fairly quickly.
The game also boasts fantastic background music. The majority of the music I heard were pure bliss and they resonate very well with me, with the easy standout being the music they used for the very first level. I have no complaints aside from the fact that they didn't use that for more levels, considering I only heard it used in one other instance.
Overall, Totally Unbalanced is a great game, especially considering it's price tag - which considering how it features easy achievement and trading cards as a cherry on top, becomes even more impressive.

Arsenal of Democracy: A Hearts of Iron Game. The hint is in the title, a Hearts of Iron game. This is not really a game however, Arsenal of Democracy is a free mod available to all Hearts of Iron 2 players and this retail version only has a few minor advantages over the free version.
If you want to know whether this game is for you then you should not be reading this review, rather you should find a review for the regular Hearts of Iron 2, everything said in there is true for this game. With one notable exception however, none of the Hearts of Iron 2 mods will work for this.
It is a strange sense, to pay money for the retail version of a mod only to be denied access to, what is otherwise one of the strongest modding scenes around. Arsenal of Democracy does have some mods available made specifically for this game but they are few and far between and none have the scope or polished quality that is readily available for Hearts of Iron 2.
All in all, do not buy this, simply don't. If you are such a big fan of the genre that you must play every incarnation out there then save yourself some money, go get Hearts of Iron 2 instead and download the Arsenal of Democracy mod free of charge, you won't be missing out on much and should you want a slightly different total conversion of the World War 2 Grand Strategy experience, you simply download another mod.

Robin ponders for a minute.

Astrologically, it tells me that Saturn is in Leo.
Chronologically, it appears to be approximately a quarter past three.

Batman is silent for a moment, then speaks:

This is my first review so any constructive criticism and advice is welcome. Im also a fan of this game so this review is a bit biased.
Gnomoria is a game where you (the ruler of a race of small ethanol fuelled Shroom addicts) must forge a new homeland for your band of merry drunkards in the plains and mountains (read hills) of a hostile world populated by malevolent entities such as gnome sized bears, Golems made of Pure stone and metal... and wheat, hordes of Subterranean insects, armies of goblins and ogres that have gained the ability to slowdown and stop time itself, and when these threats are dealt with/detained/have a picket fence in front of them new problems shall emerge, such as  The flawless timing of your gnomes when something can go horribly wrong, your own boundless greed and  all those moments when you dig to deep.
But neither you nor your valiant dwarv... i mean gnomes need worry as when life gives you lemons you make lemonade, and when life gives you an honourable opponent who just wanted some pet rocks, you do the only sensible thing and make them into sausage.
In all seriousness though Gnomoria is a procedurally generated village/kingdom/hovel management game in which you are given control of a band of gnomes and a plot of land for you to do with as you wish. The best thing to compare it to is the game Dwarf Fortress as Gnomoria takes some heavy inspiration from it. The essential goal of the game is to create a thriving kingdom where your gnomes arent the first meal of the day. After the point where survival, just food and water (read booze), is no longer an issue the game opens up and you can focus on building your own unique kingdom.
One of Gnomoria's many strengths is the variety of ways the game can be played: do you want to make a castle? sure, do you want to make a subterreanean (sorta) Steampunk city? why not, do you literally want to make hobbition? be my guest, are Floating sky fortresses with gnomes who outright refuse technology your thing? you can do that. Despite the variety of ways to play the most common and effective way is to make a fortress with traps.
The traps system of Gnomoria is another of it's best features it allows for insane amounts of customisation and experimentation. The system involves two types of traps the unpowered traps like spike and blade traps and the more end game focused room sized traps. The unpowered traps trigger when an enemy steps on one and require resetting after it has been triggered, whereas the large room sized traps (usually) involve you making an elaborate gauntlet designed to either let you capture enemies for use in an arena or target practice or you may go the straightforward route and build a crushing trap to kill invading goblins. Unfortunately a fortress becomes extremely difficult to maintain without an advanced trap system and people who dont research any technologies will have a hard time surviving the lategame. I would still recommend using the trap system no matter what though as elaborate mechanisms such as arenas, lava rooms, drowning traps, fall traps, crushing traps and many more unique configurations can be made.
Among the other best features of the Game there is a building system which allows for complex structures and a combat log that allows you see how your Gnomes and Enemies are faring in battle. The combat itself is also quite indepth as injuries to certain body parts can injure or kill a gnome, with a possibility of gnomes losing limbs and dying of blood loss.
Now for the things i dislike about Gnomoria which in my opinion are far outweighed by the positives. The Diplomacy system is very bare bones at the moment with it consisting of whether you want to host an ambassador to enable trading with other gnomish kingdoms and whether you send tribute to the goblins for decreased hostilities.
On the more technical side the game doesn't have multithreading so unless you have a one core Cpu that is insanely good the game will at same stage start slowing down (This usually doesnt effect the gameplay to much as it is usually just a bit slower or there is a lag spike at the start of an invasion).
Unfortunately the game also doesnt have an awefull lot of variety in regards to location, enemies,  and unique events as you are more than capable of experiencing everything in one
lifetime (note however more features and locations are planned on the roadmap so there will likely be more added).
Another of my Gripes with the game is that it will absorb your time, to the point where you will lose track of time if you are not careful, and with all the new features being added such as Prosthetic Limbs and Automatons i can only see the game getting better in the future.
To end with i feel that i have more than gotten my $8.00 of fun from this game and it remains one of the most complete early access titles i have played and i would heavily recommend that you consider purchasing the game to support the developer. One final thing if you are considering buying the game id recommend watching a LP of it to help get your head around the basics and you should keep the wiki on when you first start work on traps and mechanisms.
Edit- just doing this for the 2017 steam awards, ideally this review is still relevant. whilst not being updated regularly anymore there is still a wealth of content to be found within the game that makes it worthy of its price and more as a stable and enjoyable DF like

Still one of the most hardcore and tactical shooters. Runs with no issues on Windows 10.
The graphics and sound still hold up well. The game is showing its age in areas from a gameplay perspective, but never in a way that greatly detracts from the experience provided you can adapt to some of the issues. For example, squad commands are limited and given from an overlay and you can't direct your squad to a position from the first-person view, which is a little clunky. In addition, your squad generally feels like a backup selection of playable characters that tag along with you as opposed to a group of AI you'll feel you can often use tactically and trust to perform without getting themselves killed.
Other issues I had included the way the game occasionally cheap-shots you by spawning a tank or truck full of enemies out of nowhere, which rolls up to your position in complete silence; and whilst the large, open maps still feel unique and fun to play on, you can't climb or step down many hills or cliffs, which tends to limit your tactical ability.
Still, as I said, none of this greatly detracts from the experience as it really never feels hugely misaligned with the gameplay--they're more just indications of the game's age. The atmosphere and intensity remains intact. I wouldn't hesitate to recommend a playthrough if you're into tactical shooters.

After playing 20 hours of Deus Ex: Human Revolution switching to Mankind Divided becomes an excercise in tolerance. The weak voice acting of the opening sequence makes readily apparent that this game was not the beloved child of the small team of Eidos Montreal as with the previous game.
This isn't a bad game off the bat.

Here it seems combat is the focus. If the combat system is the reason you play Deus Ex then you're not going to be dissapointed. However the openening of the sequel already feels lackluster

When I first started playing this game, I didn't understood why there was so many complaints about it because I was having such a good time
But after I got to the end credits I was like "that's it?, this is the whole game?"
If you liked Human Revolution, this is more of the same, it doesn't feel like they bring anything new to the table in Mankind Divided, which isn't necessarily bad since Human Revolution is really good even after all these years.
The gameplay is good, the characters are "meh" at best because you never really get to know much about them or even interact a lot with them, the graphics are good and the game runs fine on mid settings on toaster laptops like mine
Like the characters, the story is "meh", but the biggest disappointment about this game is when you get to the ending and realize that this is not a full game on it's own but just setting things up for the obvious sequel and you'l feel like you've accomplished nothing after you finished it, I guess you could think of this game as a much longer Metal Gear Solid Ground Zeroes, the gameplay is awesome but the story itself is short, uninteresting and doesn't have any conclusion to it and just sets things up for the sequel or "real game".
This is a fun but short game, and when I say "short" I mean when compared to other big budget AAA games like The Witcher 3 and Metal Gear Solid the Phantom Pain, in the aforementioned games you'll get +100 hours of gameplay while on Mankind Divided you'll get around 30 hours.
In resume, If you really liked Human Revolution, this is a must have, but buy it when it's on discount because it is certainly not worth 50€ or even 40€ in my opinion.

Im going to try to address some of the complaints about this game, most of which are unjustified. I'll admit right now HR is probably the best game i've ever played.
First things first I suspect most people complaining about the length of the game bought HR; Directors Cut which included all the DLC. Clearly the base game of MD is not going to compare with that. I am at time of writing 24 hours in, I've explored as much as i can, found as many side missions as i can and im on mission 14 of 17. Its only short if you make it short by speed running, skipping the side missions and not exploring. If your doing that, then why have you bought a Deus Ex game????
Pay to win. There is a 'Shop' button in the ingame menu, never clicked it, world didn't end.
The story is definately not as epic as HR but engaging, certainly not as bad as being made out but a little dissapointing. Some of the side missions are quite inventive, I really enjoyed playing detective. Being set in prague with only a few excursions does make the game look a bit similar, but its very well designed and I cant say after all this time im bored of seeing it., especially as the city evolves. The game also seems more geared up for stealth than HR, though by some of the latter levels combat seems more appropriate, but how you play is up to you.
Only real complaints are the loading times, upto 2 minutes when initially loading the game and travel from area to area and some of the voice acting isnt great cough....Miller. I've had 2 crashes in 24 hours of game time.
Im not going to lie, HR is superior in almost every way bar graphics. Why developers at the moment are going backwards with thier fanchises (Andromeda, DOW3 etc) I dont know. I suspect its cost/corner cutting. All that does is lead to annoyed customers who give bad reviews which in turn, make people like me wait till the price drops to what I think the game is worth, in this case £8.99 off CD KEYS.
Taken on its own merits, MD is a good game, maybe not great, but certainly not deserving negative reviews. But it just makes you think of what could have been...... 7.5/10

Deus Ex Mankind Divided was a worthy succesor to Deus Ex: Human Revolution in my opinion. The game truly excels at level design and side missions. I bought the game a couple of days ago and finished it today. What an amazing game it was. Personally, I find the negative reviews very pretentious and often unjustified. DEMD comes with improved graphics and an evolved gameplay that differs from Human Revolution. Mankind Divided is different in the UI experience but it's not anything bad described in the game's comments.
Mankind Divided comes different from its predecessor because it evolved, otherwise it would have been an expansion of Human Revolution. I appriciate the developers giving the game more space for the story narration while breaking from the typical boss-stage development. I understand this is not common, but the old matra had to be broken at some points.
Nonetheless, the game focuses more on the stealth approach which increases the climax in many missions. You can still go ahead and face the enemies full frontal and you will be glad to find out there's a balance between the tactical approach for each mission.
I played tha game with the standard difficult settings without changing anything and I found it a a bit easier than its predecessor. In order to advance stages you don't have to expect a boss for every act of the story. It works better since there are other things to focus on the game, like your combact abilities, hacking, weapon experties, and so on.
The changes of locations where the game takes place are a refreshing element. When reaching Prague you have the feeling that's how Half Life 3 should have tasted because of the similarities with the European setting. Perhaps the game focuses too much in Pragues shortening any other possible location that could have given the game ten more hours of game play. There I can see people poiting out the game being shorter than Human Revolution.
In conclusion the game is an awesome experience even at full price. Eidos placed a lot of work in this title and it was worth the money. Do not expect a replay of Human Revolution, rather embrace the progression of the whole story setting.

Wow, This is gonna hurt.
When I first started Deus Ex Human Revolution, my start into the franchise i was not impressed at first then lost intrest afterword an hour in. BUUUT, when i try to play again with a fresh face , I was blown away by the gameplay, the upgrade tree, the level design that no other series in my opinon cannot top and just the fact that really i have so much freedom to do while playing. Love the Intresting addictive story, rememberable characters and in awe of the cyberpunk world i was in.
But we're not talking about Human Revolution, we're talking about Mankind Divided, the long-anticpated sequel from the same devs, so it got to be good right?!! Well..... it is okay... i supposed. Let's get staright to the point.
STORY:
Well, that one of the weakest parts of MKD, the story continues after two years after the 'Incident' where without spoilers: naturals (people who don't have any augmentation) became afraid and discriminative towards the augmented people. Who before in HR are the rich and famous as augmenation is very expensive and considered a luxery now have their property and wealth taken from them and live in slums segregated away from the naturals.  Our protagonist, Adam Jenson has now left Sharif Industry the corporation he used to work for back in HR and now a member of the sercet special forces Task Force 21 hunting down terrorists but also hunting down the antagonists that caused all of this.
So why is the story not as good as the first game? Well what MKD really lacks in it's narative is it not really interesting. Firstly, the first act is really unfocused as their are plot points all over the place with hunting down terrorists, working with hackers, confronting Gerorgian Mafia all in a few hours makes it feel like the story goes nowhere. Secondly (and this is pretty critical) that the new characters are really not interesting. No, there not bad just dull especially comparing HR's cast. Adam's boss in MKD compared with HR is a boring shell that gives orders to Adam and ahve no real sense of an relationship to him. All I remember from him is that he's Austrailian and that about it but the problem is that he's an important character that is the only few compared with others that has a backstory and after that i STILL find him dull. Thridly and what kills my enjoyment is that the new conspirarcy IMO is nowhere near intresting and mndblowing as it was back in HR and the antiagonists that in the previous game is like a boogyman tale that people are not sure if it does exist. But now in MKD, are protrayed as the most genertic way possible and even reveal these characters openly now and without thier mysterious shadow appearences, it loses the charm. but hey, at least their are cameos and references to the orginal Deus Ex.
Gameplay: Now, the story in my opinon is rather disapointing but the gameplay is still a strong point in the franchise and i still enjoy it. The weapons are still statfising to use and the legendary level design is still there. what's different is that there is are new augs to use and but it comes at a cost at least in the first half of the game. The new augs powers can be used but Adam's body would be over heating and need to be balanced by permentanly removing other new aug powers. It's not that bad as it sounds, becuase it gives the player a decison for what type of build to play in the game and focused on strengthing that build. There are also different functions you can used on the weaposn to be used in different situations. For example, a taser-like ammo that work on 9 ml pistols to disable drones and cameras which is cool but no neccessary. But besides that the gameplay is very similar to HR but in cases a bit streamlined so in comparison it is more easier than HR.
Conculsion:
After, writing this review for half an hour and you guys properly skipping most of the text to see the point of all this, read this: I knwo i'm not reccommeding it not because it's bad. If i review this game on it's on merits  i would reccommed this despite it's flaws. But for those who are unsure if you don't mind a weak story for expansive, freedom of engagment combat and streamlined but still deep upgrade trees, AT A SALE then grab this a soon as possible you won't regret it. But PLEASE PLAY HUMAN REVOULTION FIRST. It's cheaper, have a better story and IMO one of the best RPGs and FPS in years.

This game is great. Many of the reviews talk about imbalances in the game. 9/10 of these "imbalances" only occur because the players don't know how to use what they have to their advantage. Getting sniped while trying to run through a field? Hop in someones car when you spawn or go around through the woods. (You don't have to run in a straight line to the cap points, dummys.) Repair costs too high? Stop using mods that you don't need. Tired of getting farmed by planes? STOP RUNNING THROUGH FIELDS WHEN YOU CAN GO AROUND!!! STOP BEING OUT IN THE OPEN!!! I have 6 pilots in the game and hundreds of hours flying. I constantly see people running out in the open, dying, then running out in the open again. They can just look up in the air, and see when the plane is facing their direction thenwait for a chance to run.

There are a few complaints about the game that I agree with, however. One being the anti-tank commandos. This can be very frustrating when learning to play as a tanker. There are ways to avoid them, but it's difficult when there is one guy on a motorcycle who has a hard on for your tank. (IMO anti-tank grenades should cost much more to use, or some other way of disincentivize their use.) Tank armor will soon be drastically changed, so this may help to balance them.
The squad system is absolutely awful. It's possible for a rank 15 infantry with a maxed out squad leader badge and full auxilary seats to be put under the command of a rank 6 with none. This means that if you want to play as an infantry with the option of switching to another class during the battle, you need to queue up for a match, and retry several times until you get into a fitting squad.
People often complain about the devs "ignoring the community". This may have been true in the past. (I'm not sure if it was ACTUALLY true, or if it just felt that way due to the lack of transparency.) Recently, the devs have begun to hold a  "Q&A&Y" in which they livestream themselves taking suggestions, and answering questions from the community every two weeks.
Some players have raised concern over the fact that the devs have been releasing cosmetic changes and new content instead of fixing what currently exists. At first glance this seems like a problem. However, the devs ARE working on fixing code issues and other problems. The problem is that these fixes often break other parts of the game. So, rather than fixing the symptoms of the problem, they are fixing the CORE of the problem, the current code.

It's always bittersweet to find a free game that you want more of. Such is the case with Mandagon, a 2D exploration game set in a Tibetan vision of limbo. You don't know why you're there or what you're doing or why you're a cheeful-looking stone head that can jump, but all will be revealed as you wander the serene temples and ruins of this magical place. There's no real puzzling to do, other than sussing out the story from the cryptic rhymes shared by ancient statues, but the exploration is more than enough to keep you engaged for as long as it lasts.
The heart of Mandagon's appeal is its environment and atmosphere, which would be remarkable even for a full-priced game. The graphics are finely-detailed pixel art, showing off every crack and bit of moss on stones and every groove in the pillars holding the place aloft. You'll start your adventure in a stony valley of pools and cliff dwellings, but soon your adventure will take you to etherial ruins floating in the sky, their banners and wind chimes tossing gently in the breeze. With no enemies to harangue you and no challenging platforming to speak of, the art turns Mandagon into a peaceful trek across a gorgeous and fantastic world.
It's not a big world, of course, and you should be able to see all its sights in 30 minutes or so. Your goal is to place six tablets back in their proper places, and there aren't a whole lot of places where they could be hidden. The arches where the tablets must be placed also serve as the fast travel points, making it easy to get back to where you need to be at any time. You won't find any abilities or upgrades, just shortcuts to activate and one special travel method high up in the ruins. There are a few little secrets tucked away that also build on the excellent atmosphere as well.
The story's not bad but it's told in terribly vague terms, so unless you want to really puzzle out the rhymes you'll just be here for the journey. And it's an absolutely lovely, imaginative journey for the short time it lasts, so there's no reason not to give it a go if you like exploring. This feels like a title for people who loved the Knytt games, because it definitely pushes a lot of the same buttons for me. Here's hoping Mandagon's creators are hard at work on a full game, because this little slice of heaven left me hungry for more.

Let me begin by saying when first seeing the original announcement trailer for I Am Alive, I was extremely excited. The concept was very interesting and while it seemed to be an action game there were large psycological aspects to the play style that could make for a dynamic and unique game. After a long while I had forgotten about the game and assumed it to be vaporware only to suddenly find it alive on steam, no pun intended. I immediately seized it and excitedly dove right in. Disappointment set in quickly and I now wish it had stayed lost, maintaining my fantasy of what it might have been.
I Am Alive is a post-apocalyptic survival game. Food, resources, and ammunition are scarce and people have devolved into animalistic cliques who follow a kill or be killed morality. You come in one year in the aftermath of a great earthquake which has destroyed your home town of Haverton. Looking for your wife and daughter you meet with Mei, a young girl who you connect with and decide to protect. My first qualm with this game comes with its flimsy plot line. The game immediately begins with a clear set goal in mind and then immediately falls off track and begins following a long series of tangents to a quite unfinished ending. Along this way you meet various crooks and characters of whom you only learn of three names leaving the rest as expendables with whom you make no connections. Rewards for helping these people are generally bland and unsatisfying despite considerable effort and padding in order to help them. Worse, while many could easily have something interesting to say or do, they rather instead go straight to a generic need item, recieve item, thank you formula. Enemies are just as bad, consisting of roughly 4 or five different character models and all resulting in the same action to solve the problem, kill the one with the gun first, kill the rest second. The game gives the appearance of giving options without presenting the other choices. There isn't really a diplomatic way to deal with enemies (ordering to surrender, bribing them to leave, tying them up), and if you're lucky after killing half of them, one may offer to let you knock him unconcious. My initial interest in this game came from the idea of having alot of ways to handle enemies and being given the choice between the easy way, murder, and the hard way diplomacy and mercy.
Items are scarce in the game, but not very scarce apparently. There are some 20 different items in the game all performing some combination of the same three functions, restoring stamina, restoring strength, and restoring health. While a particular item may be scarce there seems to be no end the items to fill any one of these purposes. If you only have a single soda can you most likely have come across 6 or 7 water bottles, for example. Each of these items at some point can be used to help a victim solve a problem but it is frustrating when you do not have an item on your one chance meeting with a particular victim. In many cases its even more frustrating when an item serves no other real purpose but to help this victim, despite the item being readily available (cigarettes and wine). Along with this many of the victims seem to need this item only for the purpose of giving an item something to do (again cigarettes and wine). It again adds to the unfinished feeling the game gives.
The environment in the game is . . . well, gray. Exteremly gray in fact. I understand the idea of soot and ash covering the town making it this way but there is a serious lack of any color in this game indoors or out. I mean orange fire, yellow dust, red brick,  and blue water bottles should not be outside the realm of possibility. I originally thought that my character was severly injured and this was some sort of indicator of his deteriorated state, similar to other survival games, however that is the entire game. While the intent was clearly to give the player the feeling of depression washing over the city, it goes from sad to boring quickly. Action scenes feel drab and uninteresting when not only repetetive  but also made up of a single constant color throughout the short five hour playthrough. Did I mention short? Cause five hours was the entire game, padding and all. The core gameplay of I Am Alive could be broken down to one hour of actual play time and 4 hours of walking through dust cloud and climbing. While climbing mechanics in certain games such as Uncharted or Tomb Raider have been made exciting by quick time events, and active gameplay through the process, I Am Alive has made the sequence tedious. Adding the stamina bar would be an interesting twist on the game if it did not add to the padding between actual gameplay.
Overall probably the biggest let down in game history, and that includes Duke Nukem. I hope the developers can sleep alright at night.

If you're a fan of post-apocalyptic games then this is a must have. You play as a survivor of the apocalypse searching the forgotten city to find your family. This game shows quite a realistic view of what it would be like in an apocalypse with it's dark atmosphere, having to scavenge for food, ammo and survivors. I Am Alive is very similar to The Last of Us in many ways as they are both post-apocalyptic survival games.
The combat in I Am Alive has a more strategic approach as you have to take in the amount of ammo and health you have, also whether the enemies have a gun or a machete or even armour. Also what was awesome was how you're able to use the environment to kill an enemy, e.g. Holding your gun out to an enemy who has only but a machete and forcing him to walk back into a fire or off a cliff.
The overall gameplay gives you more of a restricted feel as you can't explore a lot of the areas and a lot is just blocked off. One thing that got my frustrated a lot was the camera view. One of the last of the traditional MMOs, a game with the complexity and epic feel of the old days of Everquest and vanilla WoW. A titanic map of Middle-Earth, an intricate class balance that all but mandates broad utility over narrow specialization, extensive immersion and roleplay systems, all set in the epic world of Tolkien's writings. That said, the game does have its flaws. It is obviously dated in several ways from graphics to gameplay, suffers from occasional lag issues or disconnects, and the Free to Play implementation has some aspects that may or may not appeal to casual players in addition to occasionally high costs for its items. Acquiring the store currency without paying cash can be very grindy for those determined not to spend anything on the game, and the game's complexity may not appeal to newer or more casual gamers looking for easy and cheap entertainment.
For those who want to relive some part of the olden days of MMO gaming, however, Lord of the Rings Online is a solid bet and worth at least a try.

Now, the game is met with sup-par development and dedication from the staff, false promises, and a growing veteran pool that makes growth for this game look more like mold on a cadaver than a fruit bearing tree. Despite the communities growing interest to support the game, for free even, the devs seem to have no interest of expanding their staff or following through on the multiple promises for advancement that have been waved in front of the players faces like a carrot for years.  As a new player, the game itself is already overwhelming for most, so the move to Steam fell embarrassingly short simply because the game is stagnant and the devs released a dead game to hoping it would be resurrected.
I have seen this games potential, and it's no longer there. Not that this game couldn't be taken from the incompetent devs to  skyrocket it's success to new extremes, but it's not going to happen. At best, this game has 700 players on at a time, and their one server is a global one. Just do yourself a favor and skip this one. The community used to be generous and mature, now it's just a bunch of sour old people that are too technologically inept to play anything apart from browser games.

Warlock 2: The Exiled is a turn-based 4X strategy game set in the fantasy kingdom of Ardania (and in the many connected shards/worlds). You play as one of the Great Mages and either try to defeat the United One and his allies in Exiled mode or fulfill one of the other victory conditions in sandbox/outplanes mode. In many ways the game plays and looks like a fantasy version of Civilization V, although there's a much bigger focus on combat.
I haven't actually played the original Warlock: Master of Arcane, but the sandbox mode in Warlock 2 is supposed to be quite similar to the original game.
The hex-based maps look great and the various shards have strong unique visual styles. The beautiful graphics are probably the strongest part of the game.
The spell effects and the unit art are not quite as impressive, but they get the job done too.
Sound effects and music are both decent enough. Voice acting on the other hand is of very mixed quality. The narrator voice is passable enough but the voice acting for many individual units is pretty terrible.
The core gameplay has clearly been inspired by Civilization 5. The game uses hex-based maps with one unit per tile (1UPT) rule and battles are fought on the world map. Unfortunately, this leads to similar issues as in Civ 5/6. The AI is pretty terrible at dealing with the 1UPT rule and you can easily defeat much bigger armies on the field. At least the existence of heroes and other super units means that armies are often quite small.
Out of the four Xs, eXterminate is clearly the main focus here. While the game provides a number of victory conditions, defeating the other Great Mages is usually by far the easiest way to win. The other Xs (eXplore, eXpand and eXploit) feel rather shallow in comparison, and the city management in particular feels quite underwhelming.
While dealing with the monster lairs and other neutral enemies is fun at first, the constant respawns get quite annoying later on. Unlike most games of this type there does not appear to be any way to stop these spawns. Especially in the late game dealing with these monsters can get quite tedious.
The diplomacy system and the strategic AI are pretty much a joke too. All the AIs I met were either extremely passive or constantly declaring wars they had no hope of winning. On normal difficulty the AI Great Mages felt like complete pushovers who had trouble just dealing with the monster spawns.
I wasn't a big fan of the hero system either. The heroes can be extremely powerful, especially if you can get a good one early on and level them up. Too bad recruiting new heroes feels extremely random and there doesn't seem to be any way to target a hero you want.
On a positive note the game does at least have some unique features that help differentiate it from other 4X games. The huge variety of different magical attacks, buffs, summons and other powers is certainly a nice touch. In practice many of the spells feel rather underwhelming, however, and for the most part I ended up using a small set of powerful core spells.
The ability to travel between different shards gives the game some unique flavor, too. In sandbox mode the outer shards are quite heavily defended, but in return you gain access to various special resources that can be used to create powerful new units and unit upgrades.
The Exiled mode is a rather weak attempt to provide a more story-driven experience in the 4X framework. You travel through progressively more difficult shards on your way back to Ardania where you will face off against the lieutenants of the United One. Personally I didn't like this mode much and found it a tedious slog to complete. The mix of heavy scripting and random maps doesn't work particularly well and overall I enjoyed the sandbox mode much more.
The AI Great Mages don't really provide much challenge on normal difficulty and can be defeated quite easily. The main challenge comes from the constantly spawning neutral units and monsters. Entering one of the outer shards in sandbox mode or Ardania in Exiled mode takes some planning too, as these worlds are quite well defended.
The UI is very similar to Civilization V and functional enough. Lot of the information is poorly presented, however, and the game lacks a Civilopedia-equivalent. An option to better highlight special resources would have been nice too. I also felt it was way too easy to accidentally move units and quite often I sent an unit heading towards a completely different shard.
Overall the writing is passable but not particularly imaginative. Ardania (the fantasy world originally introduced in the Majesty games) is one of the more generic fantasy worlds and none of the races or leaders stand out. The story in exiled mode is rather basic too and mainly acts as an excuse to fight progressively harder foes.
The DLC for the game looked rather underwhelming and I didn't purchase any of it. The game does have one proper expansion (Wrath of the Nagas), but based on reviews it is more or less broken and the new faction seriously unbalances the game.
The game has lots of small bugs. I didn't encounter any game-breaking issues, but many of the features and spells suffer from minor glitches.
Warlock 2: The Exiled is a pretty mediocre effort to create a fantasy-themed 4X game. The visuals are certainly nice and hopping from shard to shard is fun enough diversion. Unfortunately the core 4X gameplay is quite shallow, the combat suffers from poor enemy AI, the Exiled mode is quite disappointing and the diplomacy is just a mess. I can't really recommend this, you are much better off playing the Fall from Heaven II Civ4 mod or Endless Legend if you are looking for a fantasy-themed 4X fix.
Before this review I played some sandbox and Outplanes games and defeated the United One in Exiled mode. I felt the game suffered from a number of core issues and I'm unlikely to continue playing it.

I just love this game. If I look at the info Steam provides me, I played over 122 hours of this game... and I still am NOT bored!!!
Most games these days last maybe 20 hrs around cost often over 5 times the price of Gnomoria... so you sure get more than your money's worth with this game.
What about the game itself: basically it is a "Dwarf Fortress clone" with very nice looking "retro" graphics intead of ASCII symbols. It is not as complex and "deep" as DF, but this game is also still in the early access stage. The developer seems to be intentioned to add many more features in the (hopefully near) future.
In any case: AS IS the game is already huge fun!
Actually I ma very thrilled to see what the developer will add next (I have read rumors of magic and more complex diplomacy coming into the gameplay and I am quite excited about that).
One thing I like a lot is CUSTOMIZABLE DIFFICULTY: not only you can choose how hard the enemies are and how pentyful or scarce the raw materials are, but you can also select the mobs you want in the game. Want goblins and Mants to harrass you but you want to dig for metals in peace? Select only goblins and mants as enemies! Want hardcore gaming? You can have that too! Or, if you like the casual gameplay, you can have a relaxing peaceful game with no mobs at all. Although games like minecraft give some of these options, Gnomoria makes it much more tunable and customizable!
As it is you can really customize your game as it suits your gaming needs.
There are some minorr bugs and glitches here and there, but nothing really game breaking. The game is stable and smooth... although I am experiencing a bit of a slowdown (nothing major) if I have many gnomes or have dug really deep. I must mention my system is not top notch, hence better systems might not have this poblem.
NOTE: I must say that from v.0.9.17 onward the problem mentioned above has certainly been improved a lot.
In any case the game works great.
As I have seen until now, the developer(s) are still working on it actively, interact with the gamers, hence it seems to me this is a game that will suffer death by abbandonment some early access games suffer.
Also this game, in terms of development, reminds me of Minecraft: a fully playable fun game, with more content always on the way.
CONCLUSION:
I can only recommend this game!
AS IS, it is already a great game and my 122+ hours of gameplay at this moment is a testament that this game does not bore easily, especially if you are into games like Dwarf Fortess and similar stategy games.

As much as I love playing creative indie games, it is really refreshing to play a game with a huge budget where they worked closely with Nvidia to optimize the graphics and make a 3D Vision ready game. What I mean by all of this is: Batman: Arkham Asylum looks gorgeous! There were even a few scenes that had a lot of PhysX effects going on that my GTX 670 struggled with. I wouldn't have guessed that it came out in 2009. One of my biggest pet peeves is when games that look great have cutscenes that have been rendered in 720p (I'm looking at you, Mass Effect series) but the only difference I could see in Asylum was that the cutscenes were not in 3D.
I'm not a huge Batman fan, so I don't know who most of the villains are; I only learned about Two Face when I watched The Dark Knight. Arkham Asylum does a very good job of introducing the characters and giving their backgrounds. They even have a little bio section for each major character with both in-universe and real life facts about them. I could tell that most of the character designs were new takes on those characters, and I definitely think that they were done well. I found it a little odd that almost every single person in the game was ripped, but this is Batman after all.
Mark Hamill did a phenomenal job voicing the Joker. He was easily the most interesting character tho listen to, and I intentionally died a couple of times so I could listen to him taunt me.
Each main villain had a couple of levels devoted to them. My personal favorite were the Scarecrow levels because I got to relive some of the defining moments in Batman's life. By that I mean I got to see his parents die.
The gameplay is pretty basic: left-click to hit people, and right-click to counter when they try to hit you. Some enemy types switch this up a little by making you stun them first or dodging behind them before you can hit them, but ultimately it only adds one extra button that you have to hit before taking them down.
My favorite parts of the game were the rooms where there were a bunch of armed thugs in a large area, and I had to figure out how to take them down without being seen. It reminded me of the scenes in Batman Begins down by the docks where Batman did just that. Unfortunately I wasn't quite as good at it as the real Batman.
The detective "puzzles" were fairly interesting, but usually very straightforward. I felt like I was doing less detective work and more just following a trail that the developers would only let me see if I turned on the special goggles.
My least favorite parts by far were the boss battles. They were clearly constructed exactly the same way that boss battles were made back in the 90's. I was usually stuck on a platform below the much larger boss, performing the same actions multiple times while looking for patterns in their attacks so I knew when they were vulnerable.
It took me a little over 10 hours to complete the story. It seemed like I wasn't missing much by not exploring heavily; the main missions took me all over the island. It would have been nice to have gotten more of the audio logs, which were pretty amusing, and I only found a fraction of the Riddler trophies. I'm definitely not a completionist.
Overall I enjoyed the game a lot, and I would recommend that anyone who thinks Batman is the coolest play it. It's currently $20, which is a pretty reasonable price.

UPDATE: With Dwarf fortress newest release 42.05, it really blows Gnomoria out of the water in terms of depth. Still recommended, just less so. I've probably spent 2-3 times the hours played in Dwarf fortress than Gnomoria since I last wrote the Gnomoria review, so I definitely prefer DF.
If you loved Dwarf Fortress, but wish it was just a little easier on the interface and the eyes, look no further than Gnomoria.
Gnomoria vs. Dwarf Fortress Comparison:
Interface: Average versus Horrible.
Graphics: Average versus Horrible.
Overall Depth: Good versus Amazing.
Combat Depth: Average versus Great (Upgraded DF's combat depth due to recent release that have mercenaries and more usable war animals).
Mechanism/Trap Customization: Average versus Amazing
Simulation/Realism: Average versus Amazing.
Learning Curve: High versus Colossal. (2 hrs versus 12 hrs)
Pacing: Superb versus Good.
-----
Further comment on pacing: Gnomoria imho has amazing pacing, it takes forever to achieve things in Gnomoria, but it doesn't feel that way until you stare at the clock and realize you just lost 5 hours setting up 5 rooms because of the four intervening goblin raids with Ogre support and food shortage. Yet, you were having a blast and didn't notice how much time went by. This sort of time loss never happens to me these days; it says a lot that this game is able to recreate it.

I'm not really into the batmans, which is probably why I wasn't really into this game.
But its a gloriously realised metroivania style game in the batmanverse full of kewl stealth, kewl combat, kewl gadgets, kewl villians and overall is pretty kewl.
However as kewl as it is, I didn't find it terribly involving. Combat looks impressive and flashy as hell, but really, you could probably beat the game pretty easily by mashing one button.
The stealth is pretty well done and its satisfying to pick off enemies one by one, but the levels are littered with gargoyles and vents that are an immediate 'I win' in terms of vanishing into the shadows. Knock out dewd, go on/into one of those, then rinse repeat.
Speaking of vents, they become pretty annoying when you need to crack open the 100th vent cover, the constant requirement of mashing the action button to break open the covers or pull down rocks just seems redundant and a way to pad out the gametime.
The gadgets are all very handy and perform well, no complaints there.
The villians are the best bit, the joker, harley quinn and poison ivy all feature heavily, and are miles more interesting than bats.
There are some genuinely challenging moments where the game mixes up certain encounters by taking away things you take for granted, such as the gargoyles, and forcing you into a different playstyle to accomplish your goals, something which really impressed me.
Another cool little thing is how batman collects various cuts and bruises, and his suit and cape become progressively more tattered throughout the course of the game, something which really sells the plight of bats and brings home that he's a hero, but also just a man.
If you like batman, then this is probably the best superhero game I've played, and you're likely to love it. But I didn't.

Every now and then there are games that achieve every single ambition their designers had. Arkham Asylum is among them. It both redefined the action adventure and is among the best representations of Batman, comics and movies included.
Batman is possibly the only superhero I still find interesting in any way. This is because he fits the tormented hero archetype without simply repeating it. He also has no superpowers which make other superheroes so limited. Instead he uses his brain and never kills anyone. There are two extremes to the character: the Brooding Batman wallowing in human misery and the smart-as-a-whip Gadget Batman. Here he is somewhere in the middle and this works well.
The other thing that makes Batman so interesting are certain villains. The conflict between Batman and The Joker is always interesting and has inspired many creative minds. Mark Hamill delivers one of the best VA performances yet, equal to Jack Nicholson or Heath Ledger. There are far too many villains in the Batman universe and the game veers dangerously close of being a Con Air stuffed with supercriminals. This more-is-more tendency also extends to the silly collectibles, but thankfully there are clever puzzles involved so they are tolerable. Scarecrow is used to the fullest of his potential as well. Robin is one of the most unnecessary characters in comics history (and there are many contenders) and I thank the makers that they left him out completely.
The close combat system was an instant classic in game design and no subsequent effort can escape it's influence. Clearing rooms of gun-wielding thugs has many alternate routes and the entire "moving puzzle" idea is always fresh. The Gothic asylum setting is also interesting to explore, and the various Bat-gadgets are fun and natural to use. Graphical presentation is incredibly detailed and life-like, and every single sound I heard was just-so as well. There is simply no reason to skip this 15-hour adventure.

If I had to think of any cons to this game, it would be inconsistent controlling, especially around the water areas for some odd reason. But that's a nitpick at worst.
I'd highly recommend this game to anyone interested. (Especially since it's free.)

Ahh the beauty of Indie games. 2016 has been an incredible year for me in terms of Indie games I have had the chance to find and play, both old and recent. The games I have played throughout 2016 had helped remind me time and time again of my passionate love for video games and my never ending search for the next story.
Although released in 2016, Mandagon was the indie game that started 2017 for me, and oh boy was it one hell of a beautiful game!
Created by developer Blind Sky Studios, a small UK games studio composed of four coffee loving people, Mandagon is a short and free indie, adventure and pixel styled game inspired by Tibetan theology and philosophy, in which the focus is Bardo, the Tibetan word or version for “Limbo”.
In Mandagon you play as a sort of statue or part of a totem, and you explore and climb a sort of temple, in which you are given samples of a story about a man, his daughter, and a choice. Although Mandagon is quite straightforward in its gameplay and purpose, a rather simple and not particularly challenging gameplay of hopping your way to the top and around to access the inside of a temple, the mystery of the story is what will give you the desire to keep hoping, to find out what is on the other side, and, ultimately, what will make you keep thinking about Mandagon even after you are finished with its story.
There are also two other elements of Mandagon that caught my attention and still has it, the aesthetic of the game and its soundtrack. Although simplistic at first glance, Mandagon is an incredibly gorgeous game in which I encourage you to stop at times and observe your surroundings. See how tapestries move with the wind, the birds flapping their winds, and every other sparkle of color and detail that were a very welcomed surprised for a free game. The soundtrack of Mandagon was also a surprise. A single 22 minute composition seemingly designed for you to meditate your way through the universe, the story and the game, with themes of contemplation and sacrifice. Though available for free on steam at the moment, a digital art book, soundtrack and extras are available as a package for 4.43$ on steam, which I highly recommend not only because it’s awesome, but because I truly believe that Mandagon has too much to offer to be a free game.
In the hour or so that I spent in its universe, surrounded by its music and its themes or death, life, purpose and sacrifice, Mandagon gave me more than hours and hours long game have been giving me: it gave me an experience.
10/10 – Will purchase the art and OST package, and would purchase anytime if it means putting my money where it belongs, in the pocket of true artists.

I really dig this game for a lot of reasons, but foremost is the combat. Here's how the last encounter I had went when I finally nailed it after running low on the hard-to-come-by retries.
I walk into an area and am surrounded, 2 guys behind me and 3 in front. I quickly note that 2 of the guys are armored (one being behind me), the second man behind me has a gun, and the other 2 simply have knives. I also notice a bonfire in the corner. Then I make my plan and execute.
First I back up without revealing that I'm armed or willing to fight. However, the guy who approaches me is the armored guy who was behind me. Since he's armored, I can't kill him with a quick knife. So I continue backing up for a couple seconds until the only guy behind me is the one with a gun, and then I strike.
I attack the gunman with my surprise strike, killing off the gunner and leaving the 4 others in front of me without a way to get between me to the dead man's gun. I then have to immediately toggle to precision aim, and aim quickly to shoot the armored man who was harassing me before he slashes me and while the other 3 enemies approach.
Once I shoot the first armored man pointblank, I can quickly cycle between the 2 unarmored men and convince them to start backing up, realizing that I have a gun with ammo. The 2nd armored man continues approaching with his bulletproof vest, so I have to quickly switch to precision aiming and shoot him in the head.
At this point there are 2 men with knives left. I tell them both to keep backing up, separating them and forcing one to back up to the fire. I then kick the poor man into the fire to die, and quickly turn as the final man starts sprinting at me when he realizes I'm still looking to kill. I choose to save the 1 round of ammunition that I have left, and catch him in a one-on-one knife battle, knowing that I can finally win it without his buddies around to save him.
I walk away from 5 dead bodies with only 1 round of ammunition left, wondering how I can make it out of an even larger battle next time.
I highly recommend this game. It has its flaws, but it's easy to look past them with combat as thrilling and intense as this.

First off, I would like to state that I have yet to complete this game out of sheer frustration.
Though I will keep on attempting to finish the game,
granted if I can win the race between me finishing the game and my controller breaking.
That being said, here are my two cents about this game.
I will start off with the bad side of the game in order to create a critique that feels like you are eating a pudding with glazed sugar layered at the bottom, where the further you go and eat in more of the chunks, the sweeter it gets.
was once an extremely anticipated game when it was first leaked on 2009, and announced to be completed on 2010, but was later pushed back several times before finally being released on 2012. This gave potential buyers the time to ponder about the game.
When news first befell unto my ears, I heard so many rumors that this game would become the ultimate open world survival game with a good storyline to follow through. However, like any fairly hyped games, you are bound to be disappointed.
The final product released into the market looked like a stillbirth compared to what people were expecting from the game.
As a result, the game's popularity sank faster than a fat lady trying to water skii whilst wearing lead shoes.
Granted, this is not entirely the developers' fault, as speculations may have created greater expectation, but could be easily diminished by not being so hush about the game's situation and deliver actual information and updates rather than popping up ever so often just to deliver push-backs.
Over the course of some five hours of me playing this game, I can sum up the game in three words, "Trial and error."
By using new players' naiveté, the game would constantly throw you into situations where you are required to know beforehand what you are facing, to which usually results in death, and because of the limited retry system, this is like someone giving you a slap in the face and then proceeded to light your head on fire, as the system adds more than a big slap to the face, to which I will elaborate in a moment. I have found myself setting the game to the easiest difficulty to allow myself to go through all the death hoops the game presents to me with my trial and error technique in order to become acquainted with said death hoops, just so I would not light myself on fire on the normal playthrough.
The second thing is the delusion of difficulty, not illusion, but delusion. For some reason, the developer thought that simply by limiting the amount of retries the player can have in a trial and error game, the game would be interesting and challenging. If that were the case, then Honey Boo Boo's mother is a supermodel, and telling people to limit the amount of times they can urinate a day is a good idea.
Look, we have all gone through the age where that formula worked, where you played, died, and subsequently receive a game over screen. That was when the existing technology limited the amount of content that could be present in the game, and so by using that retry formula, the consumers would have the illusion of getting their money's worth. I have had my fair share of
and
already back in the days, I want to be able to play a game that would not tell me how many times I could go pee-pee in the waterbowl.
The three things I also absolutely hated in this game are: The grappling hook mechanic, the death conditions, and the bullet scarcity formula. When I first acquired the grappling hook, it was a complete nightmare for me. The swining momentum is just so bad that it makes swimming through a tub full of mayonaise seem that much easier. It took me seven tries before I could finally get the gist of it and finally not fall off and become the next cannibal's grand slam. Talking about falling and dying a horrible death, I never understood how the main character sometimes manages to die from a half-meter drop. Those areas obviously have absolutely nothing there, and if I were sliding, my momentum was just about enough to rub a gum off of my shoe, but yet, those spots still somehow manage to kill me. Perhaps messing up the sliding gave the main character so much emotional distress that he died of pure embarrassment.
Within any survival games, I am one of those players that tend to hoard anything that I can find and use as little of them as possible, this game was no exception, but what definitely has gotten to me was the fact that the game will attempt to, in any manner and time as physically possible, to keep your bullet count around one or two. Now, this may sound like an excellent mechanic, and I am the one who is whining about something mundane, but the fact that any time you kill a gun-wielding assailant with two or more bullets in your possession, the gun you get from them is always empty, really ticks me off. However, if some other baddie picks up the gun, he would start shooting up the place like a twelve year old kid playing Rookie Mode on
. This is not a good mechanic, this only manages to show the player a huge sign written thusly, "You are in my pistol theme park, and you will never have more bullets than I want you to." Why bother doing the whole survival aspect when you are not letting me worry about using resources? Since I know for a fact that I will always get bullets somewhere for a necessary fight ahead of me.
Talking about bullets and fights, the staticity and linearity is absolutely flabbergasting. You would think that despite not being the ultimate open world survival game,
would still provide the fundementals of the genre, right?
Wrong.
For the majortiy, if not all, of the cases, there is only one way to climb to the destination, only one way to swing somewhere with the swing hook, and only one way to defeat foes. There are some hidden items here and there given out for looking a bit further, but would also usually mean wasting precious foodstuffs and dying; they might as well place big pieces of paper with, "I owe you, invalid upon death," all over it, as this was mentioned to be a trial and error game with limited tries.
As for its staticity, every event and item placement are always at exactly the same place, even with static events, you would at least expect non-static placements for loots, and hope that perhaps that one time when you recheck that mundane corner again, a flashing item surrounded by an white aura would appear, like a young kid hoping to find
in their grandmother's wardrobe, only to find an abundent amount of mothballs located within.
Oh, and the save system sucks harder than an industrial grade vacuum cleaner.
Despite so many factors, including the menu being complete and utter stinking fecal matter, that make this game so frustrating, I cannot get myself to hate this game.
All in all, I am just so very intrigued by the world, the environment, and the idea of this game.
Despite the frustration
makes me deal with, during the immersive moments of the game, when I truly looked, especially into the story and the world, this game makes me feel in awe, and delivers so many other emotional impacts, like a pyromaniac seeing a forest on fire for the first time (to which the aforementioned person may or may not have been the cause of).
I realize that I am on my own in the broken world.
I realize that this game is not be for everyone, hence I would not recommend this game.
However, if you are willing to overlook the many flaws I have already pointed out, and the ones I may have forgotten about, go ahead and try it out, but I do not in any way guarentee a frustration-free playthrough.
TL;DR:
You most likely will not like it, but if you are willing to look at the game in a different perspective, by all means, go for it.

So, I'm gonna make this one short. I really enjoyed I AM ALIVE but once you look at the game on the paper it pretty much sucks.
On the plus side we have:
+Fun.
+Good Story.
+A decent morality system that I will talk about in a second.
+The difficulty is nothing crazy but satisfying.
+SOME good character dialog.
On the other hand we have:
-The awful Graphics.
-The bad combat system.
-The game took me around 5 hours to complete and I also did most of the side missions.
-Minor bugs(nothing too bad)
-That annoying dust filter in sequences where you are outside of the dust.
The (kind of) morality system:
Now there isn't much of a real morality system other than a few things like "don't steal", don't eat humans". Those things will give a small boost to your endscore. However I found myself thinking about my victims as you will often find yourself in a place where YOU raid a camp. The bad thing  about this that instead of actually putting some people that are innocent where you can kill them to make you think about who you shoot. I only killed 3 innocents while playing and every time there was a way around them, the game however does not give you the possibility to skip "bad" guys(yoiu CAN skip some but it is usually much harder). Then again you have the possibility to execute your enemies which will give you no bonus other than the feeling of justice/douchbaggery(maybe, that is).
Final Verdict:
I had a lot of fun with this game and it didn't frustrate me at all, the story is good but the price is a bit too high. I'd say buy it but maybe wait for a sale, unless you are a huge fan of post-apocalyptic games then grab a paysafe card and buy this little UBI pearl.

First of all, the title of this game is very misleading. This isn't a 4X game at all. It's a browser-building game that, despite it's depth, still doesn't break itself free from it's grindy core.
You do not eXplore or eXterminate. There is no exploration whatsoever, the full map is revealed already. There's no extermination at all, since the community has taken a pretty "pacifist" attitude as to not scare new players away. You are seriously berated if you attack someone who is active in this game, veterans might gank on you if you decide to go that way repeatedly. For one, this is great if you're starting. Everyone gives you resources and everyone treats you nicely. However, if you are looking for a brawl later on, you'll find yourself terribly disappointed.
There's also, as you might have expected, not an ending. This is a game of YEARS. Not days, not months, YEARS. Just to get your first city going in this game takes weeks if you don't buy/use prestige.
I recommend this game for those who take and enjoy it as it is: a free, browser-based, spare-time, chat-room time-killer game. It's supposed to be played while you do other things, to distract you from time to time, not to be taken as a primary source of entertainment. I do not recommend it for people who don't like sitting for hours watching the paint dry while chatting with strangers.
Side note: If you expect something special about the Steam launcher, don't. Besides achievements, full screen, 5 tracks of music and improved chat room, there's nothing different from the browser version. You're indeed just paying for 200 in-game premium currency.

I've only been in the game for about two weeks, but think I have a decent feel for where it is going.
Yet another "build your city, make friends, maybe go to war" game ... but one that seems to have avoided some of the problems that have plagued others. If you like this type of game, you'll be quite satisfied with Illyriad. Its really about knowing what to expect. To be happy in this game you should be aware:
- This game is primarily a "city-state" builder. the successful players seem to build a network of cities, which take months...putting in a little effort with multiple sign-ins per week.
- This game is not one for folks that want to quickly become a "top player" in the game. Top players - those with large empires, have been playing for months or years.
- In spite of that, a new player can be comfortable and experience everything pretty much without fear of getting wiped out by some ganker. This is because:
- the community is very friendly and welcoming to new players. They know they need them to keep the game going.
- while there is a currency you can buy, there is no way you can use the currency and "pay to win".  I could spend $500 and nothing I can do will allow me to suddenly become powerful in the game. The game mechanics simply won't allow it (all progress eventually ties to your level of research, which cannot be sped up)
- After spending my $5, I've not used more than 20% of the currency I bought - and doubt I would ever need to buy more. Frankly,
- One drawback of these games is that you need to log on periodically to keep production, etc. going, but most of us have a life to live. As an HTML5 game, you can log on with any browser. It works tolerably on my phone (at least enough to queue up production, etc.) I've played it on iOS, Android, and Windows. That's a nice convenience. (Getting more common - but thought it worth mentioning)
- Wars - if you want constant battle - find another game. While I hear that there have been some pretty nasty wars - I also hear they were very specific battles between particular alliances. So far, the several thousand players have been largely at peace.
So, if you are a "patient" game player that likes to spend time thinking and planning while building up a network of cities that gather resource and support your friends, you'll probably be happy here.

I don't normally review, but I feel this game deserve a little more love than it gets. Definately a great game. Let me break down my reasons so this becomes an actual review:
1: Performance
Never had any hitches in my entire playthrough. I never actually checked what settings I was on, as I don't really care. the textures were pretty well detailed and the game looked pretty good so I assume I was at least on high. i7-4790K, 20 GB RAM, GTX 980
2: Story
This argument I could see, the game feels a little, light, for a Deus Ex game. It's a few hours shorter than Deus Ex: Human Revolution, but I still had a 27 hour long playthrough (all side missions and I took my time/screwed around a bit).  While the story missions are a bit lacking I feel the side missions really shine through and while aren't necessary to beat the game I really recommend giving them a shot! Mankind Divided focuses on a single hub as opposed to the other Deus Ex games so take your time to explore Prague.
3: My Impressions
I started playing right after a playthrough of Deus Ex:Human Revolution, a prequel to this game. I have to say that the gamplay feels improved over DE:HR overall even if I had some trouble getting out of cover quickly. This game makes me feel that Square Enix is positioning to try to turn the series into a cash cow, which is where a lot of the negative reviews comes from I guess; the season pass, the ending, even booting up the game one of the splash screens seems to be a Deus Ex branding. While I'd say it's a single notch or so below DE:HR, I'd say it's definately a solid entry in the series and an easy recommendation to fans.
If you still have any doubts, just put it on your wishlist then. The game seems to go sale for 15 USD fairly often.

I have played bad games before but being from the generation (I am old) who just played games and either liked them or didn't and then moved on I have never felt the need to write a review however this game really irked me. First and foremost is the AI or actually the serious lack of AI. I played games similar to this 20+ years ago and the AI was better. Seriously, getting to turn 200 on impossilbe difficulty and finding an AI player with only one city and two units becuase it started on an island and didnt research the correct spell which could have been learnt by turn 50 is stupid. I downloaded a community mod to improve the AI which helped but didnt change me next issue however before getting to that I just want to mention how insane I think it is that a member of the community who I didn't pay any money to is able to actually make the game halfway worth playing however the company who sold me the game couldn't. My second issue is the fact that there are a large number of units which you can pick from and temple units you can create later in the game and after you get your first hero they are all largely pointless. The heros are insane, unbalanced and about the only thing worth having once you get a good one. Every game I played ended in exactly the same way, my four indistructable heros roamed around the world killing everything whilst the units I built or summoned hung around near my cities just in case a randomly spawned mob attacked one of them. The only reason to use anything other than your four indistructable heros is to maybe speed things up a little bit but it really is just a little bit. My final gripe is the fact that I had to restart every game multiple times just to find a good starting location. Now, i have played other games where this was the case, i'm looking at you Civilisation, but that was many many moons ago and it isn't something I expect from a game these days as it is just pointless. When you start and your area is so small you can barely fit a city on it and can't get anywhere becuase there are mountains in the way I know you can just research the lower land spell but why would I want to click End Turn for 40 turns just so I can actually move from my starting location and play the game? I don't want to spend 20 minutes trying to find a map i can actually start on.
I would not recommend this game to anyone and this is the first game i have bought where i seriously considered asking for my money back and i have bought a lot of games in the 30 years since I got my first Commodore 64.
