Coming from Warlock 1, I was hugely disappointed that the developers cheaped out on its sequel. It's basically the same thing all over with some new units, spells and map tiles, but everything else is the same. The concept to win is the same: hire legendary hero or temple unit, pimp it out of this world and then just left-mouse-click your way to a boring victory. Considering how beefed up the campaign boss units are, there's simply no other way of winning the game. The AI is still terrible, particularly around water. The enemy mage will just swarm the seas with units, but finds it almost impossible to make landfall.
Would I recommed this game? Depends. If you've never played Warlock before, then this could be an enjoyable game for a week or so. However, if you've already played Warlock 1, this game doesn't really bring anything new and exciting to the table.

Extremely addictive game.  I enjoy building up my base and my gnome's skills so was not a fan of random monsters wondering in and killing some of my precious few gnomes.  Fortunuately, you can reduce the monster's strength and occurrence to 50%.  Which is low enough to keep your gnomes alive without spending too much of their time training to be soliders.
Sure there could a lot more done, and there is room for a lot more growth, but as it is I'd give this game a 10.
Of you enjoy base building, farming, keeping animal pastures, and slowly building upon materials and exprties of your minions to be able to build better and better things, you'll love this game.  Nothing I've seen is remotely as good.
ps.  There are a few things that you need to worry about in the first year:  Make sure you alter your gnome's professiosn so that some of them have the skill you want (crafting skills, so they will actually build thing, hauling, so they can take built stuff out of your workshops, and that you build a small wheat farm right away, and build a distillery asap so they will have liquids to drink.
ps2. Make sure of, just becase a gnome has a skill, doesn't mean he'll do it if he has a million other things setup ahead of it.  So go to the population/professions tab and make sure the stuff that you want done are setup in the correct priority on the right hand side.

Gnomoria is a watered down version of Dwarf Fortress.  Unlike DF, it is designed from the start with a graphical (rather than ASCII) representation in mind.  It is much less complex than DF, but also much more readily accessible.  Although development seems to have slowed, it has not stopped.  For the price, Gnomoria can offer many hours of fun in curating one's very own gnome home.  For those who want a great deal more complexity with a much less user-friendly UI, Dwarf Fortress is free.

For what it is, this game is decent. Basically, it is a Facebook game (i.e. you click things to increase your abilities/affection in certain areas). And like a Facebook game of that type, it is a time and money-sink. You may think that last term is not correct for a free-to-play game, but the game has an option to acquire time slots (very important) for diamonds. And a function where you can get more diamonds for real money.
Also, if you notice, this game has Trading Cards. Well, Steam has a funny little foible for Free-to-Play games and Trading Cards. Whereas any game that you buy with Cards gives you a number of free slots equal to approximately half the number of cards in a set (rounded up), for a Free-to-Play game like some MMOs (DC Universe Online, for example), they only unlock those free Cards for each $9 you spend in the game. Which means for this game, you have to spend $54 to unlock the 6 Free Cards you would get for a game with the same 11 card set you bought... even for as little as $0.99 (you may think I'm kidding but Shan Gui, for example is $1.99 with a 5-card set, which is 3 cards for those $2 approximately).
Just a word of warning.

I was really impressed by this game. It's immense atomsphere of post-apocalyptic city with no usual zombies aboard just made me forget about all the weak spots (and there are lots of them). Really deep immersion into the setting. You feel alone, scared and depressed all the time. As I already mentioned there are no zombies or aliens or any other fictional stuff. It is a sad grey quest through desolated concrete jungle filled with murderers, rapists and few normal people who are mostly busy with... well, dying. Some gameplay mechanics (such as stamina loss when climbing or suffocating on the bottom levels covered with dust) came out to be very good ideas for making the game closer to real life. Lack of supplies makes it more challenging - you won't be running around with pockets full of different types of ammo and various goods.
However, if we speak about the tech part, I Am Alive is far from perfect. I would say that the graphics are very avearge for a product of 2012. It feels more like a game of 2008. The makers did pretty bad job for a product that has been in development for like 5 or 6 years. Sometimes it felt like the they didn't put much effort in this title (especially when everyone were waiting for The Last of Us which came out a year later).
Anyway, I do recommend this game for anyone who likes post-apocalyptic settings. It has a unique atmosphere and is definitely worth trying.

Lets start with the good things as there are few.
1. The levels itself - are in itself atmospheric, it really gives you the impression how a town could look like after a series of earthquakes.
2. The climbing mechanic - that you loose endurance/stamina if you climb is a nice change.
3. Overall interesting take on survival in a town after a global catastrophic event - without the obligatory zombies.
Yeah...that's it.
Now to go on with the bad things where do I start:
The graphics are washed up and even if you use the highest settings you can't change the fact that this piece of crap was meant to be played on an XBOX or PS2. Yes I know - it is developed for the XBOX 360 and PS3 but I can't drop the feeling that I have seen better graphics in part on a XBOX or PS2.
The music at the beginning is good and adds to the little bit of atmosphere there is at all - but it gets so repetitive after a time (especially as you loose stamina constantly and with you loosing stamina the music builds up and always the same tune) that you sometimes just want to mute the whole game.
So now we know that the game itself is just a common stone between pearls and diamonds in terms of audio and graphics, but there are these rare jewels that suck at this too but still have great gameplay and story.
This game is absolutely NOT one of them.
The gameplay is overall horrific with the exception of the climbing mechanic.
Combat or stealth - it gives you no choice - you have to fight.
There is no sneaking (although they implemeted the sneak button how cool is that) at all, the moment you pass a certain point the game spawns enemies and you can not get around them either because they detect you on the spot or you desperately try to get by the ones that are already somewhere in the level - and the level is created so that you have to get through them.
This is no "THIEF" at all.
So lets "fight" which comes down to coerce the AI in getting stuck or other "special" movements.
Why?
Because you either have guns - for which you practically never have any ammunition or you can use your mighty machete.
Nonono, not hacking and slashing, you have to wait until your enemies have reached you and then you can draw your machete for one hit.
If it is someone with a machete he will block it and you have to go through button smashing, it is easier if the enemy has a gun, then no button smashing.
The only problem is that these guys come in packs.
So the moment you have to buttonsmash and are locked in the scripted killscene, our enemies friends are hacking you to pieces OR his gun equipped buddies just kill you with one shot (ok,ok @ higher difficulty)
The AI can shoot at you forever but if you loot them they magically have emptied everything they had after 1001 shots (one of the many bugs in this game shows you that fact when you get stuck somewhere in a wall and they use you as invincible target practice or you just run around eating up your health items just to see how often they can fire) if you are lucky there is one bullet left after you killed them, about 50% of the time the gun is empty although the owner of it WILL kill you with it if you believe that you could reload the level and just walk past by him.
Yes I have the feeling that the people working at this game desperately wanted to shoot themeselves after they saw what they had created and implemented this thoughtful underlying message of the last bullet.
You can get a shotgun in the game but first you really have to do some climbing and exploring and the few shots you have are the only ones in the whole game.
After around 75% of the game you get a bow with one arrow - oh and you won't believe it - YES!! you can reuse that arrow.
The story is pretty mediocre, you should have encountered it somewhere else already and probably better told but worst of all it is pretty shortlived (around 8 hours and I took my sweet time) and cut at the end.
The ending is one bad joke.
I couldn't help but think that at some point of production they really believed they had born a new superloved AAA title hence the dream of producing dlcs and a second game.
But when at the end they realized what a boring abomination they helped to bring into this gamingworld they just hurried up and forced some kind of ending in and a really bad one too.
The bottom line is that if you really want to try out this game buy it in a Steam Sale...for up to 3 $/€.
Anything more will make you wish you had tossed that money in a blender and watched it blend - more entertainment for the buck.
Don't buy. Unless it's on sale for a few bucks.

Well, what to say? This game is prime example of missed opportunity for something extraordinary, but it failed on some crucial steps... but has shine on other. Game has some interesting and decent game mechanics and it plays good for most of time. There is occasional fighting with controls and weird key mapping on PC (you can change it) but nothing serious or unfixable. Atmosphere of game is phenomenal; torn up town looks amazing and feels real; even if at closer inspection lack of texture details and low poly models are quite visible, that is not "deal breaker".
Main problem with game is story, ending and length; game can be finished in some 5h (I have repeat some areas to help all victims, so my overall play time was longer) and I got feeling like I just have started to play it. And even game it self went in direction like it will continue for at least 10h... but then it cuts and roles credits...
Main character story never get's resolved while ending ruins any potential for sequels (I won't spoil it).
Over all, game looks like it was rushed to be finished while production was still at 1/3 of development, so they just made cut there, made up some stupid ending and "VOILA!" game is done! And it's sad that potential this game had, was ruined in such stupid way...
And I can recommend it, but keep in mind what I have said; if that doesn't bother you and you want to feel great atmosphere game has, go for it (but get it on some BIG discount).
Over all rating: 5/10

I've been playing browser war/strategy/building type games (Evony, Lords of Ultima, Ikariam, Tribal Wars, and quite a few others for years). One of those literally for 6 years every day. I can honestly say Illyriad is the most mind-blowing browser game I've found so far. Infact it's got more content than many installed MMO games I've paid for.
There's so many features in this game that I'm not sure I'll ever find them all. Unlike pretty much all of hte other games, you don't just build up the same stuff as everyone else and whoever has the most (or can use them the best) wins. You actually can't build everything in a city on this game. There's so many different buildings you can't fit them all in a single city, and so many weeks/months of different research that you most likely wouldn't ever finish it all - I could be wrong on that point.
I've only been here a few days now, but the community is a throw-back from the internet's much kinder and more mature years. Global chat is welcoming, helpful, and respectful. It's also ridiculously active. Even at 3-4AM there's people out there chatting away. I've seen a couple spats break out between the vets, but they were still handled without the name calling and flaming you'd see on every other game these days. Just saying "hey" will often get a new player drowned in incoming free resources. I've not ran out of anything yet, and I've not asked for anything. You also won't be pounced on and killed when you get out of newbie protection. It's just really so refreshing to see respect and people that genuinely care about the long-term viability of a multiplayer game these days.
For those new to these kinds of games, or unsure of whether they could handle learning the potentially overwhelming amount of content, don't be afraid. The community has also made a TON of guides on the forums, everything from where to start, to advanced topics. There are also training alliances to join that exist solely to teach new players the game and graduate them onto their future "real" alliance. Even the folks in global chat will answer your questions happily.
For those vets of browser war games.. this one has more than just war available. There are weapons, armor, and critters craftable to use with your army or other crafting. There's a magic system. There's quests. There's tons of different troops. There's a building and research for everything you could imagine and a lot of stuff you couldn't. I'm not sure if there's a total number of cities limit, but if there is it's pretty high.
This game is not greedy. It's not pay to win. You get 25 prestige (in game currency) just for starting. You get another 200 for playing on Steam. Prestige is used to speed up buildings, cavarans that are marching to/from you, and provide minor boosts to production for a length of time. You can't buy troops or research or anything game changing with prestige. You won't be obliterated by someone outspending you. And if you do decide to spend, it's cheap!
You can play this game free on the browser, or you can buy it on Steam. I started on the browser to see if I liked it first, then bought it on Steam the next day. It's absolutely worth buying it on steam, the 200 prestige is a big help in getting you going faster. If you started on the browser and then buy on Steam, you CAN keep your account. Just link them when Steam gives you the option.
---------------------
Some CONs:
I'm not gonna lie, this is not a quick game. This is a game for people looking to casually play long term and build up their stuff. If you need instant gratification or immediate wars, this is probably not the game for you.
You will start as a newbie amongst monster sized players that have been here for years. Don't let that intimidate you. They're not gonna bother you, they will help you build up. They will shower you with love because they WANT you to play.
The interface is a bit clunky in some places, it's not that they suck at GUI making, it's more that there's just so much stuff they have to have menus under menus to fit it all, lol. I figured out where to click for what I wanted by the 2nd day, so don't let that scare you off. I gotta admit I spent my 1st day clicking everywhere trying to remember where I saw whatever I was looking for. It does have a newbie tutorial that guides you through building a few things and such, you'll likely forget half of what it said by the time it's done. At least.. I did :)
The world map is crowded with graphics. It makes it hard to find resources or goodies on the map to loot. Unchecking the "terrain" box makes it a thousand times easier. Once you remove the images of mountains, forests, etc. then it's all clear and good.
---------------------
Overall, I'd highly recommend this game if you're into these kinds of games. I'd also recommend checking it out if you're unfamiliar with these kinds of games.

If you're a fan of fast paced arena shooters, magic, upgrades from failures or successful runs, tons of weapons in three categories, plenty of characters to unlock, procedurally generated dungeons with a wonderful aesthetic, permadeath, and quite the challenge... This is the game you've been looking for.
It plays like old school arena shooters where movement was fast and fluid and killing was about how well you could aim. The magic aspect adds a host of wonderful components to the game. You have four weapon types: wand, spellbook, staff, and arcane. You start with your wand and a random weapon in one category at the start of each floor. There's quite a bit of variation and I have found few weapons that feel the same.
Floors are generated differently each time and I can tell you that they are gorgeous. The base "game" has five floors, which takes quite a while to get through before facing the final boss. Each floor has a boss at the end and random rooms that can contain shrines where you might sacrifice health or mana in exchange for random upgrades or be punished with a downgrade. Treasure rooms, puzzle/trap rooms, lore rooms, etc are all scattered throughout as well.
As you kill minions and progress through the floors, you will level up. Upon level up you can select a perk that could drastically change the way you play from there on, or you might elect to refill your mana before a boss fight. You can find shrines or select perks that allow you multiple perks per level or even grant you free levels. There is a true sense of growing stronger to deal with harder enemies.
The game is not easy. You will feel totally prepared to enter a room only to find out that your staff only does 50% of it's normal damage so you need to use something else to complete it effectively. Playing on easy feels like you're playing normal in other games and even then there is no hand holding.
Be prepared to die over and over again.

Torchlight II does some things very well. It does other things very poorly. Whether you like the game will come down directly to what type of RPG you like.
Comparable game: Titan Quest.
You will like Torchlight if:
1) You enjoy character building. Torchlight II has 4 distinct character types that each have at least 2 clear build paths. The replayability is there- From a run-an-gun shotgunner to a life sucking mage.
2) You enjoy the intracacies of finding and equipping the best armor/weapons and grinding/searching for more.
3) You enjoy doing multiple playthroughs.
You will not like Torchlight II if:
1) You want a story driven RPG.
2) You want an RPG with battle mechanics that are more then button smashing.
3) You cant stand 'guns' in a classic RPG.
4) You want a 'deep' RPG. Beyond character building TLII is pretty shallow.

First of all, the music in this game gives me goosebumps. It's an amazing soundtrack!
A lot of the reviews here are bad because of Square Enix' DLC policy. I think that is unfair to the game. The model does not affect the game in any way. The DLC stories are just giving you something extra, and the prison DLC is quite good. I understand that some complains about the DLC "cheat pack", because it's an "one-time-only-pack". But still. A lot of people also forget that when making movies you have to cut a lot of scenes, because they don't make the picture better. I feel like the DLCs here represent that thinking. This Season Pass is like when you buy a special edition of a movie to get deleted scenes, bloopers and behind the scenes stuff.
Some of the recent reviews are bad because of low fps. Geforce Experience tweaks the game for you (60 fps) and in this case you should really let it do so. Geforce Experience has a 0-11 quality scale. I have a GTX 1070 GPU and it plays the game on 0/11 on 2190p and 2/11 on 1440p. With 1080p it's 7/11, so the game demands a lot of your GPU. Have that in mind when you try tweaking the game by yourself. Modern games are GPU-based, so if you have a five year old i5-processor, it does not affect the game. I had the same settings in Geforce Experience before upgrading to a quite better i7-processor. If you want a better performance you have to buy yourself a better GPU or more of them and put them in SLI.
So is this a good game? Absolutely, but it's not perfect. I loved Human Revolution and I had a replay before playing Mankind Divided. Gameplaywise Mankind Divided is far better by giving you more options. Storywise I find Human Revolution a bit better. Both games do repeat their environments trough the whole game. So there are no big suprises in level design. Unfortunate, because things do feel a bit repetitive. The amount of augmentations help a lot, but there is something missing here. The game wants you to explore all the vents and there are many vents. It's fun to find hidden places, but exploring 10-50 vents in a building complex to see if there are some hidden objects feels like lazy game design to me. In the next game I want more variation and not have to do the same things all over again, and again, and again. Apart from this I like that you can choose if you want to do things stealthy or like a maniac. The augmentations makes a solid variation in fighting enemies. Overall the gameplay is quite good, the story is good and the music makes the game even better. If you like Sci-Fi you will love this game.

Ive played this game for a while now and I'm sad to say that its just not living up to what it could be. Heres the epitome of the game summed up in my experience:
I grinded for hours and hours to get my first tank, and that was really fun, it added a new angle to gameplay and felt balanced and fair, at least in the lowest level tank. The grind itself was fun as playing inf is actually pretty cool and enjoyable, especially in lower teirs (no tanks/planes). I recently payed £6.50 during an event and bought my first plane to save more grind. Also really fun. However now im on my first medium tank and plane. The matches are constantly unbalanced and their is a clear bias towards russian vehicles etc. Going up against second and third teir medium tanks is infuriating as my tank cannot even peirce armor. I am never placed in matches with tanks on a similar low level, in fact the same is true of the 2nd light tank you unlock, where you are constantly placed in matches with teir 3 light tanks whos armor you cant peirce and who can 2 hit kill you. This has killed the game for me and I would no longer reccomend this game because of it.
The devs have, to my knowledge, been repeatedly informed of the balancing issues, and yet have done nothing to fix it. The fact that the entire community feels this is an issue and a simple stat change could solve it sums up for me what the devs attitude is to this game and their fanbase.
So to summarise
Pros:
-brilliant idea behind game
-free
-fun/semi realistic gameplay
-brilliant low teir gameplay with fun inf combat, equally enjoyable to battlefield or cod.
cons:
-horrendous balancing issues
-russian bias kills too many games
-community is pretty aweful in game (13yr old edgelords)
-server issues are constant and nearly always crashing for some reason
-devs refusal to fix issues.

One of the first Tom Clancy titles that took FPS gameplay to the next level. I recommend this to everyone who seeks a challenging and strategic type of shooter. However it is recommended that beginners play the training mission first.
In Ghost Recon you have to be careful before you take each step. It's like being a soldier in real life, where if you run out in the open you'll get spotted and shot within seconds. Enemies are often equipped with camo suits so they can hide themselves between trees, bushes and dirt. The same realism applies to the damage dealt by weapons, most of the time kills are achieved with 1 shot (except if you hit arms or legs).
Although the game is based on levels, the map design makes it feel almost like a sandbox game. There are always many ways to complete the objectives. Not to mention that the quality of the foliage and nature environment is phenomenal for the date the game came out. There are also different classes and weapon sets that you can choose, which means variety in your playing style. In most games where you choose a class, you can only do that in multiplayer. You can also boost the stats of your soldiers after every mission, which in my opinion makes it a little more balanced because of the AI being challenging.
Definitely recommended.

Would I recommend this game? Yes!
Trine 2 has every issue fixed I had with the first installment.


Most importantly, the controls are SO much better! Much more crisp and responsive, this time it feels like you're actually in control of your character instead of waiting for them to respond. The biggest frustration I had with Trine 1 is dealt with in this game!
More positives: The game looks even better than the first one, the puzzles often require use of more than one of the characters and their abilities (not solely conjuring a boatload of Wizard boxes and planks anymore), there are cutscenes now and the narration is sped up, the voiceacting is much better.
The negatives: Story is still bland. Some puzzles simply can not be solved if you don't have the right skills levelled up in your skilltree, and there is no real indication when that's the problem. That gave some frustration every now and then.
Overall, GREAT game. 9/10, buy it, especially if on sale, though it's worth full price as well.

That is my first statement and an important one to put right in the open. That being said this game is fantastic. The first time I saw this game was on youtuber's channel called Aavak. After a couple 30 minute episodes I decided I was done watching and wanted to start playing the game. What made me think this?
1. The game is in a state that if it were abandoned it can still give a well rounded experience it is a sandbox game so it doesn't really ever end until you want it to but it's pretty complete regardless.
2.The game has a wonderful premise that it actually delivers: A sandbox game where you command gnomes to build a kingdom and defend it from enemies. There isn't anything missing from the core idea it has enemy ai that attacks three different factions of them infact (goblins, mants, misc creatures), gnome ai is good enough there is some room for improvement but it works which is more than other early acces games can say, building things works, there isn't any incomplete or nofunctioning objects they all have some purpose.
3. The game has a great dev. Robobob has been very open about what holds him back from delivering a new update he also has decided to split the updates up into an official and an indevelopment which allows him to make sure everything is working properly before he releases the update as an official update greatly reducing the number of bugs that could destroy your kingdom should you have not realized the game recently updated.
4. The game is pretty fun. You might not have the same taste as me so you might want to watch some videos on it before making you final purchase, but something about controling minions to me is satisfying and gnomoria does it pretty well. There are plenty of quality of life options and settings that make managing your forts easy and an easy drop-down menu whenever you right click allows you to quickly switch between the tools of the trade no hotkey memorization required. The game can be entirely mouse driven with no real reason to use the keyboard except for a few of those quality of life systems like dropping the walls of your fort to see only the floor or removing the gray blocks that represent unkown areas to see your spiral staircase in its semi-3D glory or rotate the camera to get a better view or zoom in to see the action up close. There is quite a bit in this game already with great potential in the future if this game continues as it is.
I recommend this if you like sim games have always wanted to play Dwarf Fortress but could never figure out the controls and if you have ten dollars sitting around (you may want to watch some youtube videos or have the wiki opened before purchasing or playing this as it doesn't come with a user's manual or tutorials)

For what it is, this game is decent. Basically, it is a Facebook game (i.e. you click things to increase your abilities/affection in certain areas). And like a Facebook game of that type, it is a time and money-sink. You may think that last term is not correct for a free-to-play game, but the game has an option to acquire time slots (very important) for diamonds. And a function where you can get more diamonds for real money.
Also, if you notice, this game has Trading Cards. Well, Steam has a funny little foible for Free-to-Play games and Trading Cards. Whereas any game that you buy with Cards gives you a number of free slots equal to approximately half the number of cards in a set (rounded up), for a Free-to-Play game like some MMOs (DC Universe Online, for example), they only unlock those free Cards for each $9 you spend in the game. Which means for this game, you have to spend $54 to unlock the 6 Free Cards you would get for a game with the same 11 card set you bought... even for as little as $0.99 (you may think I'm kidding but Shan Gui, for example is $1.99 with a 5-card set, which is 3 cards for those $2 approximately).
Just a word of warning.

Batman: Arkham Asylum is an hybrid between an action and a stealth game taking place in the Batman universe. The plot revolves around Batman capturing the Joker one more time and bringing him to the titular Arkham Asylum, only for him to escape and take control of the facility. Batman must then uncover Joker's real plan and stop him, his henchmen and the super villains he will send against the Dark Knight.
The main gameplay is generally splitted in direct combat and stealth or predator sequences. Hand-to-hand combat revolves around the so called "freeflow system": in order to bring down a lot of enemies without losing health Batman must hit one enemy after another using his moves and gadgets (and countering enemies' blows when necessary) in the longest combo possible. Later combat sequences are made harder by enemies carrying special equipment that requires you to deploy special countermoves and very though mini-bosses. The predator sequences are instead classical stealth-based encounters: since Batman can't resist agains severe gunfire, you are forced to navigate several maps carefully, picking up enemies one by one without being discovered. You can use your gadgets and vantage points to plan your moves more carefully.
Defeating enemies allows you to gain experience that can be used to gain "levels": each level unlocks an upgrade point which can be spent in either better equipment or new moves.
Arkham Asylum allows the player to choose from three levels of difficulty: easy, normal and hard. The latter offers the greatest jump of difficulty, since it makes enemies more aggressive and resiliant in combat, counterattack icons disappear and gunfire more damaging to Batman.
The whole game takes place on the Arkham Island near Gotham: aside from three main hub zones, the majority of the action takes place inside the facilities of the asylum, like the Gardends or the Medical Bay.
The only side quest featured in the game revolves around the challenges the Riddler set up for Batman: these can either be about finding Riddler's trophies hidden in more or less plain sight around the island or scan specific points of the scenary and solve Batman universe-related riddles.
Aside from the main campaign, Arkham Asylum offers a challenge mode too, which is about playing through different combat or predator maps and try to achieve the best possible score and unlocks medals.
Not only Batman: Arkham Asylum is considered one of the best licensed and superhero game around: it's also a great piece of story from the Batman universe and a very damn fine example of the action genre, and a long time favorite of mine

Batman Arkham Asylum is an action\adventure "super hero" game.
So after many average and horrible batman games is Batman Arkham Asylum
worth trying ? well I can answer your question right away.
You start the game when batman caught the most famous villian the Joker
and sents him back to prison ( Arkham Asylum ) where he should be belong,
even though the guards should be able to do the rest, batman sense that something isn't quite right and that he should keep his eye on Joker after all Joker gave up so easily almost without a fight. After what it seems that the Joker well be sent to his place, Joker escaped killing the guards in his way and somehow controlling all the asylum in a blink of an eye. Now it up to batman to stop Joker and find out what was Joker's planning all this time.
Gameplay : the combat is great and fluid almost perfect, it combines stealth approach, puzzles and riddles and of course brute force.
This is the first game that will make you feel that you are the batman
that you are in cotrol of your gadgets, fighting style and detective's skills.
I can rest assure you that Batman Arkham Asylum gameplay is one of the best
there is to offer.
Story : its been a long time since I was so interested in a game's storyline,
the cutscenes\dialog\twists are just great.
You will be suprised and thrilled by what will come next, also lets not forget about the characters which all of them are amazingly done.
Graphics : What can I say ? beautiful,amazing,outstanding and perfectly fit to the batman's art style. One of the best I have seen in 2009 and even today its just plain impressive.
AI + difficulty : this is where I think that Batman Arkham Asylum could be better,
while the game has diffrent enemies and every boss fight is unique, still the game
is too damn easy even on the hard difficulty, only the challenges gives the feeling that I might actually lose.
Music + Sound : I can't say too much cause the only thing that comes in my mind is the word "Perfection"
Summary : Batman Arkham Asylum trully deserves the "Game of the year" title of 2009, one of the most suprising,impressive and outstanding games there is to offer and God help those who didn't play the game yet. The only thing that bothers me was the difficulty which was too easy for me, but overall I'll give this game
a 9.5\10

Firstly the game is free to play if you go to their website. You can even sign in through your steam account there. I encourage you to check it out.
Secondly, what you are paying for here is what in game is called "Prestige" it's a premium currancy that allows you to speed certain things up like building, or boosting resource production. Understandably some people may find this feature to be a "pay to win" style of play, however, there's a massive time sink involved with research that has to be done with each and every single one of your cities. Research can not be sped up.
Production can also not be sped up in the terms of spending prestige to do so. Plus you can get 1 free prestige per day, and most of the speed up options only cost 3.
1. The community on the game is absolutely amazing. I have met more friendly and helpful players in this game than in the last 16 years of online gaming.
2. The game is fairly easy to pick up, follow the tutorial, and check out a couple guides for more in depth knowledge.
3. The premium currancy is given out for free just for logging in once every day.
4. The map is insanely huge, with tons of territory to claim for yourself, or your alliance.
5. The political system is intriguing and fun.
6. Trading within your region is easy.
7. Even the large alliances are willing to help out new players.
8. Great depth within the game and plenty of avenues with which to play by.
9. The steam sound track is enjoyable.
10. Four races to choose from with different play styles.
1. No animations or sound effects for things within the game.
2. It takes a long time to get established within the game. (i love this fact, but some more casual folks will not.)
3. The game can be daunting for anyone not familiar with grand strategy games like Hearts of Iron, Crusader kings 2, or the like.
4. The learning curve can be steep. Although the information is readily available, a lot of the generation of need it now will find it less enjoyable with out a little bit of research.
5. Sometimes in the game you will end up in a time sink where you are unable to do anything but wait. I use these times to play other games, or attend to that weird thing called life.
6. It is rooted in a browser game style. I tend to avoid these games like the plague as they are usually just money sinks, but after looking around in game, and researching, I find that this is not like that. However, due to the browser origins, there's not much to look at in terms of animations, and things you might find in games like Hearts of Iron.
All in all I have been playing the game for a little under a week now, and love it. I feel that the game will keep my attention for quite some time into the future. Given that you can check out the game completely free you really have nothing to lose. Though for the cheep price here on steam you get the music sound track and plenty of the premium currancy for half price of the normal.
If you enjoy grand far reaching slow burning strategy games this is one for you.

Alright, let's see.
This is a game that runs in the same strain as games like Evony, Travian, Etc.... If you aren't interested in this style of game, This one won't get you into this genre either. You either like it or you don't.
Before you scream "PAY TO WIN!!", no. This game is not. And that's probably one of the things that sets it above other games in this genre, that and it's outstanding and mature community. This is not a game you have to throw money at in order to play at a high level. You don't have to spend any money at all, or even use prestige. Should you so wish to use prestige, you can purchase it with in-game currency (And it is not impossibly expensive in-game to buy!), and any options using it are very cheap, so it will last you a while any way you get it. You also get the option to gain 1 prestige daily, and considering that 95% of options that use prestige cost 5 at the most, you will still be able to use prestige perks fairly regularly, even if you are a free player who decides not to buy prestige with in-game gold.
With this said, I can safely qualify my statement that this game is NOT pay to win. You don't have to spend a dime, and you can still be the best. But I will still recommend you to buy this on steam. The amount of prestige you get is very generous (225!), and this game is worth supporting just on principle. $4-5 is very cheap.
That aside,
THE GOOD:
-First and foremost, excellent community. People in this community have a high level of maturity and are very friendly and helpful. They will send you gifts. They will shower you with advice and acceptance.
-FAIR RL money (Prestige) system. You cannot gain an insurmountable advantage using it, nor do you need to use it often at all. At most, you can gain a temporary 10% boost to attack or defence on 1 specific unit type made in 1 specific city. Given the game mechanics involved in war, it is entirely possible to outplay/nullify such a minor advantage. Skill and timing beat brute strength. Prestige does not change this.
-HUGE map. 4 million squares total. Really impressive size, gives plenty of space for players to set up their own kingdoms.
-Actual lore
-Warfare is not 100% mandatory. You can engage in it at your leisure. People here are polite enough that you are unlikely to be assaulted for no reason, especially as a newbie. People will actually come to your defense if a troll tries to siege you and harrass you just because you're a newbie and can't defend yourself. Once again fantastic community.
- THE BAD
-The map has a dated aesthetic. This is not necessarily a bad thing, some will find it quaint.
-They still have some kinks and oversights to work out with their steam client. I would imagine that this will be fixed soon.
-The game can be slow as molasses at times, once again not necessarily a bad thing.
Overall I think this game is really worth a try if you're willing to give this genre a chance.

With Arkham City out is this game still the definitive Batman game? in many ways yes. The story might be more linear, but the experience is tighter as a result. The hub world is amazingly realised and each building has its own unique character together with a ton of Batman references, easter eggs and secrets just for good measure. There certainly are flaws, but for every one flaw Arkham Asylum has it does 2 things right. Bane might be embarrassingly depicted but Batman, Joker, Scarecrow, Ivy and Harley, are all well-voiced and authentic. For every boring boss fight the game throws at you there are intense scarecrow confrontations and tense hostage-stealth situations that stand out from the normal fights (which are also amazing and slick). Arkham City might be bigger, more refined and more immersive, but Arkham Asylum doesn't suffer from having a better sequel. Its a damn fine Action game, and a great Batman story.

The combat. Oh sweet god of this universe, the combat! Never have I seen such simple, responsive, satisfying and fun combat in a game like this. Dating back to the 60's television show we've all seen Batman take on a group of thugs, but Arkham Asylum displays this stalwart of the character like a ballet of brutality. If only Assassin's Creed were as streamlined...

Mandagon is a perfect example of how heart and story can carry a game. Games aren't great because of their graphics, gore, fantasy, etc... but because of the story they tell. This game tells a very complex story simply and lets the player discover what is going piece by piece causing them to want to continue playing to learn about the character. This heart and storytelling is an aspect of gaming that I would like to see more of. With advances in technology many developers have relied on graphical content to carry their games, but completely forgot about the reason why we should play their game. Games have evolved into a medium for storytelling and this game proves that you can successfully get a message across without fancy asthetics and long drawn out quick time events. It also shows (by the already overwhelmingly positive reviews) that gamers want to care about their characters and the story they tell. I hope to see more games like this in the future and would love to see this developer's future projects.

Mandagon (mantis/panda/dragon) teleports you straight away to a Tibetan Buddhist concept known as 'Bardo' a limbo place between death and rebirth. Buddhists mainly believe that if you do good deeds you get rebirthed into a higher lifeform or do bad deeds and your soul will get rebirthed into a lower life form.
The objective of the game is to simply find six keys and a number of totems (optional) and open the big door where you will find a 'god' who will then cast his vote. The totems give you back ground information as to your background story as you can't tell much just by looking at yourself since you look like an Aztec version of pacman.
Tom Kitchen the main designer behind this game, suffered a family loss in death and looking through various answers though he is not a religious man himself found 'some' comfort in the Tibetan book of the dead and it's the information from that which gives you the background information to your game character as well as to what may have helped Tom get through his grieving process and helped him to move on with his life.
Since morality is an integral part of all of our lives, improving ourselves, being our better self, ascension will at some point play an essential role in both our needs and desires. Likewise this game is all about ascension, moving up (forward) to find answers. Tom Kitchen is all for 'exploring' concepts of an afterlife. Unfortunately only one concept is displayed in this game and I would have been equally impressed if the game went onto explore other concepts, Mormon, Hindu, JW, Catholic, Atheist, phansigar. Maybe that could be a sequel. But the game does do more than just explore afterlife, it also explores the concept of what sacrifice really means too.
While this is a free game there is also some DLC available for purchase. It consists of one soundtrack, some art concepts that never made it into the game and finally it places the totem poem in its correct order so it makes sense.
I appreciate that Tom Kitchen was able to move forward as I also looked into Buddhism and read the 'book of the dead', but personally I was never able to get my head around one thing. I haven't always been a good person, so there is always a good chance according to their beliefs that I could come back as a lower life form. Ok fair enough. I have come to appreciate that things like stealing, lying, murder is bad. So here is my question. How can one be a good crocodile or a bad crocodile? Once you started going down in life forms surely you’re doomed!?

There are a lot of mixed reviews on here about the game.  I bought Warlock 2: The Exiled for quite the bargain and didn't buy it when it just came out years ago and when it was still full-priced.  The reason for bringing this up is because its pricecard is very important. I feel that the game is good, but I wouldn't have been as satisfied about the game if I payed the full price for it.
The game is pretty good!  But why? There are a few reasons, but let me start out by stating that which I found the most enjoyable: its gigantic, open feel.  There is so much to explore, so much to see, and so much to figure out.  The whole world is out there for you.  Aside from its sandbox feel, there is pretty intriguing lore available, the Lords (heroes) are enjoyable and unique enough, and the art is far from displeasing.  It's not a fantastic game, let me pop that bubble, but it's fun and customizable.
It's a turn-based, challenging, customizable, exploration, strategy game that will suit your needs -- if and when -- for the right price.
Now, about its flaws.
The game has quite some bugs in its system.  I had moments where I couldn't click/attack an enemy unit for no reason and also encountered problems when alt + tabbing back into the game, such as, a complete game interface freeze (I could still move the screen around) and clicking not working.  Some weird spells were missing too, the gamed 'Unity' spell.
A really frustrating part about its gameplay so far is the random AI spawn.  They spawn random turtles/dragons/skeletons around the map to '♥♥♥♥ around' with your previous bases in other dimensions/worlds, but all it really does is make it a horrible grind fest where you have to keep behind somewhat stronger units to defend older bases.  These older bases become a bit redundant as they barely level up and just offer sustainability in the shape of magic, food, or gold.  But for the rest, this world has been conquered, captured, and is LONG IN THE PAST.  But what we consider to be done becomes a horrible grind-fest of killing 'new enemies' who aren't challenging and really just ruin your progressive game-plan.  It's also quite annoying when the enemy mage shows up and messes with your land and turns it all into volcanoes/snow/whatnot.  I just want to move on-- but wait, oh ok, a random aggressive turtle shows up and it's snowing in my otherwise very lucrative city that I conquered fifty years ago -- great.  Just GREAT.
The game does a pretty well job of being decent on its own for the rest, but I have to admit that the challenge is a bit hard to find after a while and battles turn a tiny bit boring.
Don't let this faze you, though!  It has been a worthile experience so far and I can't wait to play more.  There is strategy, economy-building and balancing, exploration, and much more involved.  A world of lore awaits.

Breathing In The Life of San Andreas
=========================
Some games are picked up, played by a gamer, and then they are laid down left to dust. Other games are picked up, admired by the audience from the trailers, and like a good episode of Game of Thrones, the audience will automatically know that this will be "the one". Or in GTA V's case, the "Big One". As you play the game, you can't help but notice the small, minute details that Rockstar puts in the cariacture to present San Andreas as it is an actual real, breathing place. This is the first game which really showcased that. Sure, there was Sim City but that was a city simulation game. This is an open world game, and while you may argue that Skyrim or Fallout: New Vegas were good games, which I admit they are, this game is the first one that started to blur a scripted game to reality.
You can see it in the AI. Take for example the cars that people drive down the roads of Blaine County & Los Santos. Each one is wearing some different; each one drives a different car depending on the area where they live in; each one has a seperate gender & race which doesn't make it feel like it's an illusion of generated cars & vehicles that are set to spawn in certain locations as you drive by which applies to most vehicles that naturally spawn. Then, there's the fact that they always seem to be there, never popping in like God himself placed the car with the people in there.
One of the other areas you can see it in the game is the interactions between the characters. Take the characteristics of Michael for example. He has a surely defined storyline within the game's main storyline itself. All the characters in this game seem to work together 'in harmony", minus that French yogi & that accursed tennis coach! The small viligant villans will try to ruin your character, while the rich will as well. The good thing is you will always have a "little help from my friends" which is a real good thing! One of the other things that you won't ever forget is how much depth that goes within the storyline and the famous quotes that come from the game. Overall, it's a splendid singleplayer experience.
Then there's the multiplayer which is always evolving and changing. There's a variety of different tasks for you to take on whether it's managing your Motorcycle Club or partying on the Yatch having fun with the ladies. Whatever your most inner-heart desires are, just remember one thing from this review: DO and I repeat DO NOT let the money rain on you! Report it as fast as you can and you will be saved from spending another $60 dollars plus the Shark Cards you buy.
One last thing: Fire rockets at Michael's house. He will really appreciate it. Personally he should upgrade to the crib that Franklin owns OR BETTER YET, buy a trailer out in the Grand Senora Desert! Trevor will really appreciate being neighbors with you. You can deal drugs like it's hasta manana!

Despite the flaws of microtransactions, short story and optimization issues due to an unethical production studio, for what it's worth Mankind Divded is a competent Deus Ex game. The music and art style are neat and a bit over the top at times in true DE fashion, and the graphics are gorgeous. The voice acting is mostly well-written and absorbing, being one of my favourite parts of the game. The actors put a lot of effort into their lines and it shows. The level design is absolutely phenominal, leaving you tons of room to decide how to approach situations. You could hack, or find a vent, talk your way through or take multiple combat approaches, lethal or non-lethal. Choices feel important still to the story, but have less of an immediate effect than in previous entries, and feel less restrictive than before. You might not notice the impact your actions have until later on, and deciding one route to take may not always bar you from other things, unlike HR. The main questline is a little sluggish and hard to follow at first, but picks up quickly after the first few missions. Sidequests are all entertaining and rewarding; one of the earliest sidequests you can start allows you to have access to al your augs without overheat, for example.
Overall opinion: 8/10, stay away from the iffy stuff and the game is still very enjoyable. I wouldn't buy it on full price, but if you can find it for 50% or more than it's completely worth it.

It’s a shame really. I loved Human Revolution and I really looked forward to Mankind Divided. Everything I saw from their marketing made it clear to me that this is the kind of sequel I wanted to a game I greatly enjoyed, the same polished gameplay enhanced by a story and setting that at least tries to be about something. Unfortunately, some things started popping up that made me lose faith somewhat.
They were called “augment your pre-order”, single-use consumable items for pre-orders and season pass owners and microtransactions.
Thankfully, the actual game is in no way worse off if you don’t use these consumables, because it’s actually properly balanced for the player to master whatever the game may through at them. Because holy sh
it did I love every single second of actually playing this game. This is what I was referring to by calling it a shame. Square tried to cripple a game with gameplay polished to a point where I’m not sure if they can even surpass it outside of some minor technical kinks and I really can’t fathom why.
In Human Revolution, I never really committed to any single playstyle the game offered. I tried going stealthy when I could but it didn’t really matter to me if a hacking attempt failed or whenever I got into a fire fight, because I didn’t go for a non-lethal run. And I know that the ability to do that didn’t sit well with purists, but the game did still offer everybody the chance to play the game with self-imposed restrictions, outside of the boss fights in the original edition that only offered direct confrontation as the only way of dealing with them. But this time around I went for a complete non-lethal stealth run and actually managed to get the pacifist achievement for not killing a single person. And that’s saying a lot for someone like me, since I’m legendarily bad at stealth gameplay.
The reason for this decision is twofold: I wanted to test myself here and see if I could manage to actually do it. And the second reason was that I somehow feel that this is actually the intended way of playing it. That is not to say that you’re not given tons of offensive firepower along with a bunch of pretty cool augmentations for killing people, but sneaking and hacking are far more rewarding here in terms of narrative as well as fleshing out the world and I somehow feel that not doing that would have you end up with a lesser experience.
Sneaking through these levels was tons of fun and finding all the routes in and out of offices through traditionally oversized vents hidden behind vending machines, hacking open window blinds, awnings and ladders or disabling lasers, cameras and turrets and generally eluding everybody or picking them off silently one by one had me on the edge of my seat. It’s the kind of horror game anticipation of not wanting to get spotted by the monstrosity that’s stalking you, only it doesn’t rely on cheap jumpscares and a black screen all the time.
But what really was the most useful feature in this game, is the save option. I’m not kidding, I save-scummed my way through most of this game and I really feel like this is a legitimate strategy, since the game basically lets you save absolutely everywhere. Because even a maxed-out hacking ability won’t guarantee that you’ll be able to unlock a door or computer 100% of the time, since a random number generator still decides the probability of any step alerting security measures even with a detection rate of 15%.
But it can also entice you to do things you ordinarily wouldn’t if you’d face losing progress. At one point, I snuck my way through a part of some vents that lead to a room filled with noxious gas. And instead of turning around, I simply saved the game, filled up my health bar and sprinted through the room to the other side where I found the valve that controls the flow of the gas. And this is a valid approach to take, because sometimes these rooms are dead-ends with no other way of entering so you’ll just have to take a leap-of-faith like this and the game encourages it with its save feature. Coming back later with the lung upgrade doesn’t really add any challenge to this room, you can just saunter in, close the valve and you’re good to go. And there are numerous instances where I used similar tactics by saving and trying unconventional stuff just to see if it would yield a satisfactory result. Because to me, this is what Deus Ex represents: Playing it the way you want. And save-scumming is just another way the game lets you do exactly that, pretending to  this stealth god that hacks absolutely everything without getting caught or cut off at any point.
So while the gameplay in my opinion is absolutely sublime and far more engaging than most other modern games, the narrative unfortunately deserves a few criticisms. Now the overall story isn’t the problem. I really like the setting here, showing the aftermath of the aug incident and how humanity reacts with justifiable hostility towards augmented people, because to the general population, there’s no real guarantee that something like this wouldn’t happen again. And the ensuing terrorism from augmented people is also believable in the face of current events. I feel the line at the start of the game “If you treat people like animals for long enough, they’ll start acting like animals” rings true.
What I felt was really a letdown is the whole conspiracy aspect that wasn’t fleshed out to a satisfactory point. And this is where the rumors of this game originally being bigger and getting cut into pieces by Square seem to gain a lot of traction, because the game unfortunately ends on a sequel bait cliffhanger that gives no closure to any of the plot threads we see in the game. Sure, TF29 manages to save the day, but the direct impact this had and TF29’s connection to the illuminati is not all that fleshed out. The same is true for Janus and his Juggernaut Collective. The Augmented Rights Coalition a bit more fleshed out, but only to a point where they serve as a scapegoat for the terrorist attacks, and the people behind the illuminati are never elaborated upon except for one single person in a post-credits cutscene that only further complicates matters and brings even more layers to this story that need to be uncovered.
This is only exacerbated by the fact that the major players from Human Revolution barely make an appearance. Tai Yong Medical is namedropped quite often and Belltower is certainly present, but other than that, there isn’t much there. Megan is mentioned but never shown, Sarif makes a few token appearances that don’t amount to much and Pritchard is only mentioned once in passing. Same thing with the Tyrants, they and their actions don’t really play into any of the events now. It feels like there’s a lot of stuff missing here, even in spite of the fact that Eidos really try to tie everything together with the story of the original, setting up the pieces, when realistically it should probably not do so and just try to go forth with its own continuity and eventually revisit the events of the original Deus Ex in a new game, since the original has aged so go
dda
mn poorly that I still haven’t managed to get through it all.
In the end, Mankind Divided provides a phenomenal gameplay experience in an interesting world, that is unfortunately let down by some narrative shortcomings and an ungodly amount of corporate meddling that made me stick with my pledge of not buying this game on launch or anywhere near full price just because I’m absolutely opposed to the bulls
hit Square Enix tried to pull with this game. And I seriously hope that Square realized that they fuc
ked up here. It wasn’t consumer apathy towards the franchise that resulted in fewer sales. It was their absolutely despicable behavior as a publisher that kneecapped this game and the future of the franchise.

"Batman Arkham Trilogy" [ Batman Arkham Asylum, Batman Arkham City, Batman Origin (incoming)  ] is a milestone game in all Action Game history of humanbeings,  a game that  has all the critical amazing elements of a blockbuster RPG would possibly have!!
And if you do play this game, you HAVE to play it all in order to discover the unique "Batman Arkham Universe", and unveil the biggest mystery of the Gotham city crime conspiracy...
Scarlet's Score: 9.2/10

The gaming world was a different place before Arkham Asylum.  We had wanted a hero, a villain, nay anybody whose shoes we could step into and viscerally and believably beat the living crap outta people and feel like Jackie Chan.  Until Batman Arkham Asylum arrived, we didn't know just how badly we had been missing a game that could make you feel like billy big ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and boy did it deliver.  Gaming brawlers had come a long way since Streets of Rage and now they would never be the same again.  Indeed, this style of combat system has become the norm for 3rd person melee combat RPGs but not all manage to recreate the fluidity and satisfying perfection of Rocksteady's design.
In my eyes, the combat is what makes this game.  Its freeflow design is so tactile, responsive and has fantastic, bone crunching feedback that it feels unbelievably satisfying.  With such a simple set of inputs (at least initially), the game encourages you to perfect timings and combos rather than simple button mashing, and the skill and complexity only rises as the Batman acquires more gadgets and skills himself.  The combat system is so well honed and refined that by the end of the game, a skilled player can launch feet first into a large group of henchmen and seamlessly take every last man down with well over 10 distinctly different moves, a variety of gadgets, dodges, blocks, stuns, jumps, kicks, punches, throws and numerous other martial art moves, all tied together into a 50 move combo without ever taking a single hit.  The end result is simply stunning to watch and pure joy incarnate to execute yourself.  To top it off, the skill balance is just about perfect as to do something like this is neither unrewardingly simplistic or frustratingly impossible.  Admittedly there is the very rare moment when the Batman doesn't mercilessly assault the particular henchman you intended him to and it throws off your combo as you try desperately to think ahead to the next limb mangling move, but this is so rare as to be no more than a petty annoyance.  The one thing I'm not so sure about though is that the Batman only seems to knock the goons out.  Now I've cracked some skulls as the Batman and I'm sure it's been well beyond the stresses and forces the human body can take, no matter how muscle bound the henchmen may be.  I'm pretty sure the Batman kills some people here.
But Batman is so much more than the combat even though the game could probably stand up on its jaw crunching merits alone.  The other set of mechanics that play so perfectly into the theme and gameplay of Arkham Asylum is the Batman's ability for stealth and this really does enable you to approach situations in a variety of ways and is particularly great at enabling the Batman to take down enemies unawares or launch into combat with the element of surprise at hand.  Similarly to the combat, the Batman gains gadgets and skills that enable more advanced stealth techniques and takedowns and again enable the player to develop some quite complicated and nuanced tactics.  Combine these skills with the combat and here you have the perfect marriage of mechanics that makes you feel like the Batman more so than the vast majority of games make you feel like the intended protagonist.  That feeling of swinging from gargoyle to gargoyle before gliding down, batcape unfurled, onto a completely unsuspecting group of goons and perfectly beating them up in a flawless combo is quite simply, unmatched.
Additionally, Arkham Asylum is a deep dive into who is, in my humble opinion, the greatest and most interesting super hero going, with a ton of lore and atmosphere that really makes you feel like you're not just the Batman but you really are walking through his world.  The plot is fantastic, although arguably shoe horns so many Batman villains into one place that it feels a little too dense at times but even this plays well into the compact setting of Arkham Asylum and the wider plot.  Overall, the presentation and content is outstanding with even the little extras, that are commonplace in free roam worlds, forming an interesting addition to the game and provide a view into Batman lore.  You can either take it or leave it, but at least it's not pointless fluff like so many other games seemingly have with audio logs that add sod all to the story or atmosphere.  These really do add a little bit of extra detail which as a Batman fan, I genuinely enjoyed.  Finally, it's the little details that I really noticed on my second playthrough on PC that just made me fall in love with the game again.  The wear and tear to the batsuit and the Batman himself as the night at Arkham progresses, and the five o' clock shadow that develops through the night just cements that feeling of immersion this game achieves so well and really makes you feel you're battling through a protracted nightmare of the Joker's design.
A particular highlight for me is the voice acting which is just outstanding and not since Metal Gear 1 with David Hayter's rough, gravelly Solid Snake have I been so enamoured with the voice behind the mask.  Kevin Conroy as the Batman hits the nail on the head, returning to the glorious Michael Keaton style of Batman; unassuming, suave and charming richboy in a batsuit.  Arleen Sorkin is great as Harley Quinn, Wally Wingert pulls off a toned down Jim Carey style Riddler which I think strikes a great balance, and Dino Andrade as The Scarecrow is utterly menacing, matching his sinister presence in the game perfectly.  Perhaps Tom Hardy's Bane would have been the icing on the cake but the star performance undoubtedly goes to the legendary Mark Hamill of the Joker who plays him perfectly and creates a really interesting counterpoint to the Batman and helps deliver the whole game.
I'm yet to play the remastered edition but rest assured, I certainly will and I'm looking forward to what will be my third playthrough.  This will undoubtedly go down as a classic of its generation and a mechanic defining game to boot.

Years years ago, when I finally had my second computer (my first computer, that I got back when I had 5 years, was just obsolete at that point), this is one of the games that came with it. And let me tell you, even back then I knew this was a great game. Does it hold up for today's standards though, after SO MANY YEARS? Well, yes. You can keep reading, and find out why, but as usual on my reviews, I'll start with the bad stuff:
Sadly, the worst part of the game is also the best part of it: The difficulty. Have you played other FPS games? Back then, FPS games were all about being a generic American hero who could take 9001 bullets, carry over 10 guns at the same time, jump insane distances, run like hell non-stop, and basically be a God. This game was one of those that stopped and did the complete opposite. Enemies die in one or two shots, yeah. And so do yourself. Gameplay is slow, enemies at times come out of nowhere, you get the idea. While people like me would love this, I can tell a lot of people would NOT enjoy it's difficulty at all.
Another thing that might turn people away are the graphics. Now, while I don't really hate them, the game has not aged well at all on that matter. Leaving how pretty the game is, there seems to be some weird bugs and glitches related to the game and graphics: At times stuff can be seen weirdly clear through the fog, both enemies and allies trying to shoot people through walls, parts of enemies clipping through solid objects and more of the same kind of stuff. Also, while the gameplay can be played in Widescreen, which surprises me for a game this old, the menus run in 800x600, which is just weird.
The last thing I will complain about this is the AI. Everyone seems to be a bit... Stupid. At times soldiers act in really weird ways, and the enemies can also act in unpredictable r#tarded ways as well. Infact, in the 4 missions I've played so far, I've also gotten teamkilled by my teammates 3 times, because they seem to enjoy using the grenade launchers at close-range. And I'm not even joking with that, the AI really loves that weapon.
All of that being said, what you have left is a gem that still packs more and better Gameplay than 70€ sh#ts we get today. Just to remind you, this is a game that got close to KILL CALL OF DUTY AND MEDAL OF HONOR (which killed itself anyway, rofl). It's all about being stealthy, taking enemies properly. You have a squad of 6 soldiers, which you can control and jump from one to other if you feel like changing. There are also 4 kind of soldiers, without counting the Specialists, which you unlock by winning missions. You're given liberty to do the missions as you please. Wanna rush them with machine-guns, or rather snipe them one after another? SUIT YOURSELF!
There's also multiplayer... But well, it's an old game. Good luck finding people to play with. I played once a few years ago with a friend using Hamachi, and it was indeed insanely fun. If you do find people, then you'll enjoy it. People call this "Like the Dark Souls of FPS", but I find that dishonest. It's just what a serious FPS should be, not these sh#tty casul CoD games that you could buy these days. That being said, ignore the sequels. Some of them are decent, but Ubisoft has destroyed it with the Free2play title which is filled with Pay2Win bullsh#t. They deserve no respect for that crap, so play this one instead. It's cheaper, it's better, and it even feels more rewarding.
Oh, and you're killing Russians, so you could always go full♥♥♥♥♥♥and be an idiot, if that's your thing.

The map is just garbage to look at.  Rather than pick between pretty but slightly less functional or purely functional (i.e. just having a key and having shapes/symbols on a grid make up the map) the devs chose to incorporate the worst of both worlds.  So you have atrocious functionality and an eyesore of a map where they just repaste the same clipart mountain/plains/forest.  What's more they mix two and sometimes even three art styles and it's just visually displeasing and even somewhat upsetting.
-Chat client takes up half the screen.  Can you make it smaller?  Of ♥♥♥♥ing course you can't, don't be stupid!
-You're being asked to pay for a game... that is pay to win.  It's a freemium game that ISN'T. EVEN. FREE.  Right?  Right?!
I love browser games along this vein so this game felt like a personal injury.  As much as I wanted to learn about the mechanics I actually physically couldn't make myself play for more than about eight minutes as the above realizations dawned on me.  Trust me, I tried.  And I love Utopia, which has NO graphics and is all just text-based.  I'm fine if you go minimalist like Utopia.  I'm fine if you go all pretty like Dominion or a couple others that slip my mind now.  Just, for the love of God, don't hamfistedly try to do both and fail.

tl;dr review: This is a cute game but it has a lot of flaws--the most glaring of which is that you can't "win" without spending real money. That's a cardinal sin for an f2p game and so I do not recommend it.
Long review: Crush Crush is an incremental dating sim. For those not familiar with incremental games, you do a series of simple tasks (clicking on things, waiting, etc.) until they become too difficult and then you start the game over and you are given a boost to your clicking/waiting abilities based on how far you got. Rinse and repeat. Crush Crush is a dating sim in that the clicking and waiting represent you trying to woo a series of stereotypica girls (twintails tsundere; gamer girl; catgirl; the ditz; etc.) by chatting with them, buying them gifts, and working jobs and learning hobbies to impress them. Each girl has ten affection levels from Adversary to Lover. There's not a lot of story persay--just an intro cutscene for each girl--but there's an impressive amount of dialgoue that you get for clicking on them and it gets updated every few ranks. The girls also each have eight cgs--first meeting, friendship rank, sweetheart rank, lover rank, and then one for each date--moonlit stroll, beach, sightseeing, and movies.
The mechanics are pretty straightforward. You gain affection by poking girls (clicking on them), chatting with them, giving them gifts, and taking them on dates. Chatting is almost always better than poking but has a cooldown until you get a couple hours into the game. You also get different reactions for poking than chatting so it's fun to do a few times even once the mechanic is obsolete. It's easy to forget that gifts and dates also give affection because most girls need an amount of gifts or dates to progress and money is often scarce.
You get money from working jobs. At the start you can only work at Fast Food as a Burger Flipper which works on a standard idle system--every 5 seconds you get paid, once you've been paid 24 times you become a bun toaster which pays a bit more--if you do it long enough you can eventually become a Beef Chief. You unlock other jobs by learning hobbies.
There are twelve Hobbies randing from Dancing to Sky Diving. Each hobby raises a stat (Dancing raises Style, Sky Diving raises Luck, etc.). You raise hobbies by idling--it takes 30 seconds of Dancing to get to rank 1 Style, 42 seconds for rank 2, 1 minute for rank 3, and scales on and on (each rank takes 30*1.425^[current rank] seconds). You unlock jobs by reaching various ranks, girls will often require you to be at certain ranks to progress, and each girl has a favorite hobby and that hobby affects how much affection you gain with her both passively and by chatting.
Time Blocks are the game's second currency. You start with six and you gain one for every four "achievements" you unlock. Achievements range from reaching a new rank with a girl or job; getting all of  your hobbies to certain thresholds; or miscellaneous things like # of clicks, affection gained, dates or gifts purchased, and time played. Hobbies each require three time blocks to work at; jobs require a varying amount; and dates take between three and six, depending on the date.
Every time you reach a new affection level or unlock an achievement during your current run, you gain prestige points. Whenever you do a soft reset, those prestige points become a multiplier to all of your idle activities (hobbies/jobs/passive heart gains).
The final currency is diamonds, which is the RMT currency. Unlike other incrementals, there is a fixed amount of free diamonds available--11 per girl (you get one per affection levels 2-9 and three at 10 but only the first time for each girl). You can spend these on cosmetic boosts like outfits or on gameplay improvements like time skips and speed boosts (both overall and hobby specific).
Overall the game has cute artwork and dialogue and plays really well through about the 30-40 hobby level and then the scaling just completely falls off a cliff for many reasons, which follow.
Prestige doesn't affect affection gains at all. Sure you level hobbies faster which gives better chat affection but the multiplier on that is insignificant. Meanwhile, you get a huge boost (10x-ish) to chatting for every girl you get to Lover. This railroads you into getting every girl to Lover in order every time you play unless you feel like clicking thousands of times extra.It's made worse by girls who are unlocked earlier having harder late game requirements than later girls so your options are "click thousands of times extra" or "wait around for my hobbies to get where they need to be for earlier girl". This leads to the game being almost excessively idle as you'll spend most of your time waiting on hobbies and occasionally logging in to click on a few things for a few minutes once your hobbies have leveled sufficiently. There's really no other option unless you want to do super quick resets to grind out prestige (which is technically the most effiicient way to do it in the early game but is incredibly tedious).
Later girls also just require a ridiculous amount of affection so an auto-clicker is mandatory (unless you like clicking 1000-10k times per rank on a girl).
Scaling is also off in other ways. The 7th girl you encounter requires 40 in your hobby ranks to get to her 8th and 9th levels. She requirse 60 hobby to get to her 10th level. It takes 1191 times as long to go from 40-60 as it does from 1-40 in a hobby. So she'll get to rank 9 reasonably early and then just sit there for real time weeks or months through multiple prestiges. Many other girls have similar problems where their requirements skyrocket dramatically and lead to a game curve that encourages you to just do a lot of early, fast resets because you can't make any real incremental progress from one playthrough to the next without weeks of idling.
I think the worst idea, though, is splitting the prestige boost you get from the speed multiplier you can buy in the store. And the devs have artificially capped the f2p boost at 2048x but the bought multiplier caps at 8192x and they stack. If you don't spend any of your limited RMT currency on speed boosts, the game is straight up unbeatable. At 2048x, it takes multiple real-time years to get through some of the later girls (again, because the devs thought having hobby requirements jump in increments of 10 rather than curve gradually was fine for some reason). If you spend all of the free diamonds on speed boosts, the later girls still take 3+ months of idle time to get enough money and hobbies to pass them. If you spend money to max out the speed boost and the hobby boosts, that gets down to a matter of weeks.
It's especially disappointing that the devs decided to add an overarching plot to the game (you accidentally open a space-time rift) that only shows up on the last six girls which means it takes weeks/months to even get to the start of it and most people will never see it.
So again it's a cute idea and the art and dialogue are top-notch but game balance just falls off a cliff around eight girls in and it's just not beatable without spending real money.
I'd recommend trying it out for the early game and being ready to make the call of whether you want to spend money on it or not before you invest too much time.
