This game is definetly the most addictive clicker game I have ever played (and I have played quite a few in my experiences with middle school computer labs).  I have spent 160 hours playing this game according to Steam, which means it is my most played game in my Steam Library, with the only game coming even slightly close being Stardew Valley at 130 hours.  That's a lot of time spent clicking my mousepad over and over again.
This game has a very unique feel to it in pretty much every aspect.  I bet you, without looking it up or going into the game, I could name all of the girls in the game in order of appearence (Cassie, Mio, Quill, Elle, Iro, Bonnibel, Ayano, Fumi, Bearverly, Nina, Alpha, Pamu, Luna, Eva, Karma, Sutra, The Dark One, and QPernikiss), and remember what they look like and how they act.  A lot of anime-styled games end up with the problem of the characters being too similar to be memorable, but I remember and like all of the girls you date in the game.
The art is also really cute and detailed.  I love all of the pictures they show when you take the girls on dates or reach a certain heart level with the girls.  I never get tired of looking at them.
One thing I especially love about this game is how well it runs.  Since all I have to play games on is my laptop, I'm unable to play a lot of games because of hardware limitations.  But this game can run well on the highest graphics quality and doesn't cause my laptop to explode.
One of the only critiques I have about the game is that I wish there were more music tracks.  The music is very catchy, but I have no real reason to listen to it while I'm playing since it just loops.  Other than this detail, this is a great game for people who like dating hot girls (like me) or have nothing better to do than waste their life playing video games (like me).
P.S. Alpha is best girl.

Certainly one of the most underrated 4X games on Steam and a lot deeper than it might appear at first. One of the rare 'easy to learn but hard to master' types of games. Especially the building system where you have to decide what you build instead of just building everything *cough*Civ*cough* stands out. You have to specialize cities since you can't have everything in just one mega city. Special map resources often allow different buildings to build upon forcing you to make a decision what is more important to you. Economy seems simple at first until you suddenly go banrupt because you were underestimating the upkeep costs of certain buildings and units.
This would be one of the best mulitplayer 4X games if it would support simultaneous turns, but unfortunately it does not *sigh*. Research and diplomacy is also a bit lacking, but otherwise it's a very good game which also doesn't take as long as Civ and is also more fast paced. It's a shame that these days every hex-based 4X game is suppressed by the Civ franchise.
Renaissance mod is also a great mod for it, adding several races, heroes and lots of other stuff.

Fantastic satire of the DLC/fix it later publishing culture we live in right now.

The game is cute, with minimalistic, 8-bit graphics. Its core mechanic, of buying DLC in order to progress, is incredibly clever.
However, there is a laundry list of criticisms I have with the game.
Which you can unlock for the low, low price of $2.99!

Firstly, an important note - you do not spend real money on the DLC within the game, it is "purchased" using the coins you collect in game.
The game does a great job at poking fun at the recent trend of fremium games where you need to pay to really get anywhere or games with a lot of DLC that add features that should really have been in the main launch. I'll not spoil what the DLC is, as this is probably the most fun aspect of your playthrough. Things are taken to extremes where you will not be able to progress until you've collected enough coing to buy the correct DLC.
You'll defintely find yourself smirking at the absurdity of it all and you'll be pulled in by the uniqueness of a game that purposely blocks your progress until you "buy" DLC.
It's good for a quick laugh but don't expect an expansive game that will keep you going for more than a few hours.

Before playing Arkham Asylum, I would never have thought that Batman could be adapted into a game featuring both satisfying action and a top notch story, but Arkham Asylum accomplishes both in top form. Featuring a scenario and dialogue crafted by Paul Dini, one of the finest writers of Batman The Animated Series, this very much captures the noirish tone of that excellent show and its very distinctive character personalities, particularly the rogues gallery of villains, while also incorporating more mature themes and hard hitting action than could be presented in a mere cartoon. The experience is definitely gritty and at times intense, but the violence never goes over the top. There's also a very nice balance between linear missions - including stalking portions that require refined stealth tactics and sneak attacks - and open world segments where you explore the exterior of the island setting, all presented with exceptional graphical detail. Mark Hamill also delivers one of his best perfomances yet as the Joker, the devilish clown prince of crime. Four stars.

Torchlight II is a sprawling, ambitious game that does one thing very, very well. It gives you a world you'll want to explore, filled with enemies you'll love to destroy.
Over a period of about 40+ hours, completed the story on normal difficulty, mostly solo. Played several different multiplayer scenarios, and tried the game with two of the other character classes.

Full of mod options to customize your gameplay for non-stop grinding with your friends. I recommend adding mods to reduce the level requirement for your skills, I believe Synergies has a mod for that called SKILL UNLOCK. Otherwise, if you stick with vanilla level sequences then it will take you quite awhile to unlock new skills.

Greetings!  Torchlight 2 is an improvement of the original in every way; it is rare I get to say that but this is game exactly that.  If you didn’t know Torchlight 2 is a dungeon crawler similar to Diablo or Pillars of Eternity and although many would argue it is not as good as either I enjoyed myself playing this game.
Refined and Magical:  The game feels like Torchlight but better in every way.  From the graphics to the audio the world is beautiful even 8 years later; the mechanics continue to be classic but still relevant and playable providing multiple play styles over the 4 playable classes (one more than the previous game).  In regards to Quality of Life (one of my biggest talking points) the game improves a great deal solely on the inclusion of Item Display:  An option that allows you to control what quality of items your GUI highlights for pick up.  This alone made game the game many times more enjoyable.
Mods, Mods, Mods:  Just like its predecessor this game has a great modding community and the developers encourage this.  You can find everything from new levels to new classes and this provides hundreds of hours of extra content.  The game itself has plenty of content as well:  Including a decent length on the campaign (took me about 30 hours) and extra content in the form of random levels that you can purchase (with in-game currency not real money) with modifiers.
Cracked Ember:  There are some weak areas in the game however.  The story is interesting (though D2 wants their plot back) but kind of slows down beyond the initial moment.  The final two bosses’ need a lot of work with next to no dialog or plot other than ‘kill this person…because it is why you are here’.  I would have liked to see more unique weapon types that really change the way you play (there are several already however).
It should be fairly obvious that if you don’t have this game you should. One thing I did forget to mention:  I really enjoyed the base of the story and how it included the original characters (and the way my favorite class, the Alchemist, interacted was the best!).  So, if you like dungeon crawl games this should be in your library regardless of which ones that are already.  Worth a buy, even at full price and worth your time regardless.

So basically this is old-school twitch gaming, like DOOM, but with a randomized level/weapons/level-up bonuses/etc.  It's not for everyone, I guess, but it's the perfect way to combine the two genres of FPS and roguelike.  Roguelite?  Whatever.  One of the best things I can point out is the ability to choose between two level-up bonuses, so the RNG isn't quite so cruel - but on the flip side, you don't get into the rut of building your character the same way every run, since the same choices aren't always available.  It's a good mix of player-in-control vs. randomization, and I really like that.
The comments about a lack of variety in environments and design and such are perfectly fair; this isn't an extremely deep title, or extremely long, I would guess.  (I certainly won't be making it to the end any time soon, because I am terrible at FPSes.)  But for what it is, it's very pretty (the art is luscious) and gripping (my 90 minutes was all in one sitting - couldn't put it down).  And wonderfully smooth, as any good twitch shooter should be.
In fairness, I did get this on sale when it was like $6, so definitely well worth the money then.  $15 might be a touch steep, but all things considered, this is a really well-produced game and I've had it on my wishlist for a while - and I am more satisfied with this than with a lot of my other purchases, to be perfectly honest.

It’s a shame really. I loved Human Revolution and I really looked forward to Mankind Divided. Everything I saw from their marketing made it clear to me that this is the kind of sequel I wanted to a game I greatly enjoyed, the same polished gameplay enhanced by a story and setting that at least tries to be about something. Unfortunately, some things started popping up that made me lose faith somewhat.
They were called “augment your pre-order”, single-use consumable items for pre-orders and season pass owners and microtransactions.
Thankfully, the actual game is in no way worse off if you don’t use these consumables, because it’s actually properly balanced for the player to master whatever the game may through at them. Because holy sh
it did I love every single second of actually playing this game. This is what I was referring to by calling it a shame. Square tried to cripple a game with gameplay polished to a point where I’m not sure if they can even surpass it outside of some minor technical kinks and I really can’t fathom why.
In Human Revolution, I never really committed to any single playstyle the game offered. I tried going stealthy when I could but it didn’t really matter to me if a hacking attempt failed or whenever I got into a fire fight, because I didn’t go for a non-lethal run. And I know that the ability to do that didn’t sit well with purists, but the game did still offer everybody the chance to play the game with self-imposed restrictions, outside of the boss fights in the original edition that only offered direct confrontation as the only way of dealing with them. But this time around I went for a complete non-lethal stealth run and actually managed to get the pacifist achievement for not killing a single person. And that’s saying a lot for someone like me, since I’m legendarily bad at stealth gameplay.
The reason for this decision is twofold: I wanted to test myself here and see if I could manage to actually do it. And the second reason was that I somehow feel that this is actually the intended way of playing it. That is not to say that you’re not given tons of offensive firepower along with a bunch of pretty cool augmentations for killing people, but sneaking and hacking are far more rewarding here in terms of narrative as well as fleshing out the world and I somehow feel that not doing that would have you end up with a lesser experience.
Sneaking through these levels was tons of fun and finding all the routes in and out of offices through traditionally oversized vents hidden behind vending machines, hacking open window blinds, awnings and ladders or disabling lasers, cameras and turrets and generally eluding everybody or picking them off silently one by one had me on the edge of my seat. It’s the kind of horror game anticipation of not wanting to get spotted by the monstrosity that’s stalking you, only it doesn’t rely on cheap jumpscares and a black screen all the time.
But what really was the most useful feature in this game, is the save option. I’m not kidding, I save-scummed my way through most of this game and I really feel like this is a legitimate strategy, since the game basically lets you save absolutely everywhere. Because even a maxed-out hacking ability won’t guarantee that you’ll be able to unlock a door or computer 100% of the time, since a random number generator still decides the probability of any step alerting security measures even with a detection rate of 15%.
But it can also entice you to do things you ordinarily wouldn’t if you’d face losing progress. At one point, I snuck my way through a part of some vents that lead to a room filled with noxious gas. And instead of turning around, I simply saved the game, filled up my health bar and sprinted through the room to the other side where I found the valve that controls the flow of the gas. And this is a valid approach to take, because sometimes these rooms are dead-ends with no other way of entering so you’ll just have to take a leap-of-faith like this and the game encourages it with its save feature. Coming back later with the lung upgrade doesn’t really add any challenge to this room, you can just saunter in, close the valve and you’re good to go. And there are numerous instances where I used similar tactics by saving and trying unconventional stuff just to see if it would yield a satisfactory result. Because to me, this is what Deus Ex represents: Playing it the way you want. And save-scumming is just another way the game lets you do exactly that, pretending to  this stealth god that hacks absolutely everything without getting caught or cut off at any point.
So while the gameplay in my opinion is absolutely sublime and far more engaging than most other modern games, the narrative unfortunately deserves a few criticisms. Now the overall story isn’t the problem. I really like the setting here, showing the aftermath of the aug incident and how humanity reacts with justifiable hostility towards augmented people, because to the general population, there’s no real guarantee that something like this wouldn’t happen again. And the ensuing terrorism from augmented people is also believable in the face of current events. I feel the line at the start of the game “If you treat people like animals for long enough, they’ll start acting like animals” rings true.
What I felt was really a letdown is the whole conspiracy aspect that wasn’t fleshed out to a satisfactory point. And this is where the rumors of this game originally being bigger and getting cut into pieces by Square seem to gain a lot of traction, because the game unfortunately ends on a sequel bait cliffhanger that gives no closure to any of the plot threads we see in the game. Sure, TF29 manages to save the day, but the direct impact this had and TF29’s connection to the illuminati is not all that fleshed out. The same is true for Janus and his Juggernaut Collective. The Augmented Rights Coalition a bit more fleshed out, but only to a point where they serve as a scapegoat for the terrorist attacks, and the people behind the illuminati are never elaborated upon except for one single person in a post-credits cutscene that only further complicates matters and brings even more layers to this story that need to be uncovered.
This is only exacerbated by the fact that the major players from Human Revolution barely make an appearance. Tai Yong Medical is namedropped quite often and Belltower is certainly present, but other than that, there isn’t much there. Megan is mentioned but never shown, Sarif makes a few token appearances that don’t amount to much and Pritchard is only mentioned once in passing. Same thing with the Tyrants, they and their actions don’t really play into any of the events now. It feels like there’s a lot of stuff missing here, even in spite of the fact that Eidos really try to tie everything together with the story of the original, setting up the pieces, when realistically it should probably not do so and just try to go forth with its own continuity and eventually revisit the events of the original Deus Ex in a new game, since the original has aged so go
dda
mn poorly that I still haven’t managed to get through it all.
In the end, Mankind Divided provides a phenomenal gameplay experience in an interesting world, that is unfortunately let down by some narrative shortcomings and an ungodly amount of corporate meddling that made me stick with my pledge of not buying this game on launch or anywhere near full price just because I’m absolutely opposed to the bulls
hit Square Enix tried to pull with this game. And I seriously hope that Square realized that they fuc
ked up here. It wasn’t consumer apathy towards the franchise that resulted in fewer sales. It was their absolutely despicable behavior as a publisher that kneecapped this game and the future of the franchise.

If you like/love cyberpunk then you will like/love this game.
Let me just say, back when this game was announced with the ‘augment your pre-order’ system, I was not impressed. However, I feel it is unfair to review a game based on its pre-order system. Not to mention that was a long time ago and was scrapped before release.
I had an amazing time playing this game and really got sucked into the atmosphere of the game, which hasn't happened in a long time for me. The art style/graphics are fantastic, the music is immersive and the story is interesting to follow (even if it is cut a bit short at the end). Walking through a rainy cyberpunk city is an incredible feeling and well worth a purchase, especially with the subtle synth music playing in the background.
The augments are a lot of fun to use and the new augments bring a fresh take on the game compared to HR. I went down a hacker/stealth/passive run through of the game and was able to complete the game with no kills. You don’t need to kill the bosses in this game either. You can either smooth talk your way out of a fight with the social augment or simply stun them. Play around with the augments and see what works best for you. Stealth or combat are equally fun in the game.

Weapons are great. The weapons have a great sci-fi feel to them even though they are based mainly on current technology. If you want to go for a full assault build there are plenty of weaponry options to choose from. However, the stealth options are a bit limited. Some augments are weapon-like and cater to either combat or stealth, which add to the roster of options.
The story was interesting and enjoyable to follow through. There are some good ‘Witcher’ style side quests that take you on their own mini stories. The story does continue on from HR so I recommend playing that first but you could get away with playing it as a standalone game. I’m not going to say anything about the story as that is for you to enjoy. However, one complaint would be the ending does feel like it was cut short in order to create the next game. And sadly, we have no idea when we will get the next game due to poor sales.

Overall, this is a fun, immersive game that was a great experience from start to finish. If you enjoy sci-fi/cyberpunk themed games then you will have a blast playing through this. I would recommend this game at full price but if you get it on sale then you have yourself a steal!

Dead Space 2 is not a perfect game but i love it anyway. The first Dead Space is one of my (if not the most) favorite survivor horror shooters and Dead Space 2 improves a lot of things compared to the first while keeping what was already good:
- Your character is not a silent dummy anymore
- More weapons
- More enemies
- Zero Gravity is done well this time
- Puzzles are easy but still fun
- Some great "WOW" moments
- The objective tracker is a small quality of life improvement
- Still feels like a survivor horror
- Still scary
On the other hand there are still some problems:
- Character developement is almost completely absent
- Objectives feel the same
- Aiming and movement are a bit clunky
- Some parts of the gameplay feel recycled from the first title
Aside from this small problems i absolutely reccomend the game for the fans of the genre and those who already played the first game.
9/10

This isn't gonna be like one of my normally stupid long reviews, more off the cuff, but still very rambley
TL;DR:
Dead Space 2 is a tightly paced Action game. It loses the claustrophobia that made DS1 an effective horror game, instead trimming away anything that might slow down the pace of the game at all, and turning it into an excellently paced, and extremely enjoyable, Third Person Shooter.
DS2 isn’t a great horror game, or even really a good horror game. The monster design might be considered disturbing to some, but if you’ve any nerves at all, there's very little here that will legitimately frighten you. Unless you have an aversion to eye related horror, which I coincidentally have (and I blame on this game directly,
).
The tradeoff for losing the horror aspect of Dead Space is that this 6-8 hour campaign just
. It moves so quickly, and is so concerned that you're going to get bored that it just never slows down. Isaac is much more mobile to boot. You move more quickly, stasis is ready pretty much right off the bat, and side to side movement is much faster than before, allowing you to strafe when necessary. Zero Grav now has a jetpack, so that's just automatically better.
Dead Space 2 is a logical continuation on the first. Isaac is already experienced with all this horror♥♥♥♥♥♥ so he behaves less like an engineer, and more like a doomsday prepper. His character is a bit generic, and the writing isn't the best, but I love the story anyway. It's like a schlocky horror flick that you don't have to take too seriously, but still manages to be fun. If Dead Space 1 was just a video game version of Event Horizon, then DS2 is Event Horizon ala Aliens, where its Vietnam in space but with Cronenberg abominations instead of H.R. Geiger's lustful fever dreams, and all with a healthy dose of schlock.
I ended up rambling anyway, and this review is incoherent and scatterbrained because of it, but DS2 is just plain fun. I don't know the best way to put it into words, but I just always enjoy playing it. Whatever parts may factor into it or not, it controls tightly, and it’s just good because of it.
There's the whole steam awards thing going on, and I find it a good fit for the "No Apologies" award. Its parts aren't exceptionally great, but the whole is just a goddamn blast for some reason.
Plus, who doesn't love a game where the story is just that Scientology is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, but in space?

Tom Clansy's owned Ghost Recon is a tactical shooter in which you get to control the squad during the mission itself while being able to take control of any of them. Yep, one of realistical tactical, where you die from one shot. It was developed by Red Storm and published in 2001, with being ported onto various consoles in following two years, that are Xbox, GameCube, PS2. And yes, it was made by same people as who made Rainbow Six few years ago, and now they were challenging players by moving action from close-range to long-range open combat. Just like Delta Force, but with fog. And squad tactics.
And yes, it got two more expansion packs that you can buy on Steam as well.
Technically, well, it's actually fine. Sure, game came out before widescreen monitors happened, but engine can support such resolution and allows you to select it from options. Main menu and such will stay as blocky low-resolution 4:3, but as soon as you get into gameplay, it will switch to what you set in options. FOV however will not increase, so people are still chubby.
Not sure about multiplayer. Never got to playing it and Internet browser in the game itself appears as completely empty. No wind, no tumbleweeds. Perhaps server browser is broken. But as far as I am aware, it's dead. And multiplayer was the main positive point of this game, so we are left with less positive single-player.
So, the plot is that in 2008 ultra-super-hyper-nationalists come to power in Russia and are now going to conquer and merge with countries that were part of USSR, starting with finding the way to take on Georgia. Funny how game predicted that in 2008 there will be conflict with Georgia and Russia, though it wasn't the one where Russia is your everyday demonized baddie. Anyway, you then go and take on various mission to kill people and do objectives, being world's judge. Until you beat final mission. And then get thrown into main menu immeditly. Because screw you, it's realistical tactical lack of ending!
Graphics look kinda nice, I dig the enviroment for sure. Death animations do the job. Lack of gun in view is silly though. Music is fine, just randomly placed in main menu and then sometimes playes when somebody in your team dies.
You got 15 single-players missions to complete and boy, it's not going to be easy. And it wasn't supposed to be easy. As fun as it could be. Anyway, you look at the map which doesn't tell you about verticality, then pick your platoon out of 6 members, that is divided into 3 squads, each having max to 3 people. Mind it, you can order only to whole squad, so better keep specialized people, like sniper, in separate special squad. And Demolition for enemy armor and mission objectives. And Support for having big magazine. But mostly riflemans. You can actually auto-assign people, and game handles it well, even though it never picks anybody from Specialist category. Who are powerful soldiers who may even have unique weapons.
You can get Specialists by completing bonus objective. Where game can screw you up, because it ends mission as soon as either you done all main objective or if killed all enemies if last objective was moving to extraction point. That, and soldiers who died in battle will not reappear. At least they level up between each mission.
And so you will run, you will walk, you will duck and crawl toward enemy, to get into position to shoot them all. Well, mostly running, otherwise you will run out of patience on these big maps covered in fog. And lean around. And notice threat indicator at the bottom of the screen showing red. And snipe enemies. Who will then run toward trees and hide and wait for a moment to lean around and put bulets into your dumb AI teammate. Who you will thankfully kill first. Until you realize that somebody threw grenade and you will be hopelessly trying to switch to each member and micro-manage them to run away. But they all die and so you restart mission as you don't want to have even less soldiers to pick in next mission.
A thing to note, is the way that they did aiming thing. You see, unlike other games, the aiming will drop when you are turning around. Actually, turning around punishes you more than just walking slowly! As a result, it makes flanking more important in this game.
With no planning phase for giving actual order, like in Rainbow Six, Ghost Recon lets you control team during gameplay. Just bring out the map, choose the squad, and click on a map, setting waypoint and where they are supposed to look. Then erase it and do it again, as map UI seems to be unreliably at selecting the team for some reason. But at least I prefer to be able to do it during gameplay. You can also set rules for each team, one for movement: Stop, Move but stop if being supressed, Move at any cost. And rule of engangement: Recon, shoot only if shot back, which is good for ordering troops to get into good position around enemy point. Assault, shoot accurately, sometimes, which is good when on the move and don't know where enemy is. And Supress, which makes them trigger-happy, good when you set them to defend or assault from one position.
And well, now that you wonder what tactics there are, here is what to expect: Always come from unexpected side. If you need to assault inner building, then switch to soldier on one side, kill one enemy, switch to soldier on opposite side, kill another enemy and so on.
As far squad tactics, well, they aren't reliable. But expect to use them to cover your flank. And sometimes to assault base while staying in one position. And moving people them around on map to get closer to objectives, so you could then control a soldier from squad, with others being like your "lives".
Yep, AI teammates aren't reliable and soon you will feel divided. As it turns into mix of FPS action and Strategy game where you can't trust either part. Because sometimes AI can actually save you, but it's rare. Most often you will be wondering why your squad keeps being wiped out, then quickload and see person ignoring 9 sneaking soldiers, after all he is behind tree, he is INVINCIBLE!
The fact that command map shows no verticality in level means you will have to manually position them anyway, often.
Oh, and yes, I said quickload. Which means that there is quicksave. Which means that you can shove tactics into armor's rear and quickscam your way to the victory! No, really, Rainbow Six or Delta Force never allowed you to do it. But I guess that this cheapness counter-balances against the game's cheap difficulty where enemies can always aimbot you up. For knowledge is the main decision point in this game, and if you know what to expect, you don't need to crawl. You come in and kill all ten of them. Quickloading many times to get out from ambush.
And let's be honest. Most of people who praise the game had it as the first game. And others who praise it do it because of how difficult it is. Mostly of how you can die randomly easily. And thus is somehow makes you feel better if you somehow manage to pull though. Not sure, I didn't feel anything like this, just a chore. Because well, when I died, I didn't feel that it was always fair, thus I just didn't care and reloaded a save.
But I still can recommend the game. Well, not fully. Mostly above average. Because sometimes it works and makes you feel rewarded for positioning your team properly. Other times, it just screws you.
Actually, when you just play some missions separately - it's a blast of trying to survive and setting good positions and tactics! Then there are some missions that feel messy and less fun. Look, stealth mission! It's just that main campaign, which makes me feel that I must be overprotective as it punishes you if your soldier dies by not having him in next missions, is where I just start to abuse quicksaves and grind it and get impatient.

I hate to say this, especially considering how much fun I had with FC3, but FBD is pretty meh. Visually it looks great, and in terms of art and sound direction, it totally nails the exaggeratedly ridiculous action feel that it was going for. Unfortunately, there are too many self-effacing nods to the player/audience that slow things down, plus too much required stealth that totally kills the momentum of what should have been a fun shoot-em-up at its core. I loved stealth in FC3 and all the challenges that it posed, but here it feels silly, tacked on, and turns an enjoyable romp into a tedious crawl in too many places.
I hate to be a nay-sayer on this one, since novel spins on tired tropes in gaming should be encouraged, but I'd give this one a pass nonetheless.

When this game was released back in 2009, it put the world to its knees when Batman fans finally got what they've always wanted: A good Batman game. Not only it's a good superhero game, it's one of the best games of all times.
Story:
You are Batman.
The Joker has surrendered to you so easily, you start wondering what is it that he's really planning.
You take him to Arkham Asylum, the place for all of Gotham's most dangerous psychopaths.
After entering Arkham Asylum, the Joker breakes loose when you are forced to stay behind while he's being escorted to his cell. With the help of Harley Quinn, the Joker takes over the asylum, and now you have to stop him from getting what he wants.
The story is excellent, and it involves other villains such as Scarecrow, Bane and Poison Ivy.
Gameplay:
When the freeflow combat system was introduced to us, fans and gamers in general were blown away by how amazing it is. It's one of the best, if not THE best combat system that I've ever encountered in a game before. It is fluid, easy to learn but takes time to master.
The stealth gameplay is fantastic.
It truly shows how Batman can take down a room full of armed men without anyone seeing him.
He is a bat, and bats live in the dark. That's why he's called The Dark Knight.
Boss fights are great, each boss is different from the other ones and they're all awesome in their own way. Aside from the gameplay and the boss fights, you also have over 200 Riddler Challenges to complete, that includes trophies, riddles, interview tapes and arkham chronicles.
There's also challenge mode which is super fun and is also necessary in order to 100% the game.
Visuals:
The game has a great atmosphere, it's dark and can be creepy at times, and it shows how scary Arkham Asylum is, with it being a madhouse and all, and the atmosphere fits perfectly with Batman.
The graphics are fantastic, the game is one of the best looking games of 2009, and it still stands even in today's standards.
Summary:
When the game was released, it raised the bar for superhero games to a whole new level.
The game is the reason to why Rocksteady is my favorite game developer.
I give this game a 9.5/10.

This is one of the most enjoyable games I have ever played and I've played a lot. What I like about the game is that the action is immediate and continuous;  it constantly surprises you with it's depth and new features and because of the complex spell system it gives you a ridiculous number of strategic options during any given turn.
The basic combat system is similar to Civilization,  but really more like Heroes of Might and Magic,  although it does not have separate explore modes to combat modes.
Resources are critical in this game.  It is expensive to research and use spells and to hire heroes and combat units.  The number of towns you can build is normally limited so it's quality not quantity that's important.  Placing your town near critical rare resource items is a must.
Similarly it is quality not quantity in your choice of units to recruit or build.  Experience upgrades, equipment upgrades and other perks are the key to victory.  Again that creates a lot of strategic use of your resources and upgrades.
By contrast I find the more highly rated age of wonders 3 plodding and just plain boring. This game can be chaotic.  It keeps you on your edge.  Age of wonders 3 is about spamming units towns and sucking resources.  It's just flat, not sure why.
It's just unfortunate that this game was not promoted very well.  The sales were too low and the series is now dead.  Paradox has abandoned it.

So the short answer to "Do you reccomend this game?" is yes I do, but I feel a longer answer is needed. You see I play the Civilization series quite a bit and it's one of my favorite games. After experiencing Civ Beyond Earth I was curious if there was some fantasy based game that was similar to Civ. Warlock 2 is pretty much that without being that. While I would overall say it is a good game, it does not come close to measuring up to Civ high bar that may be. There are many things I wish Civ would take from this game IF they were to make a fantasy version. But there is a LOT of basic things this game could have taken from Civilization. Breakdown as follows:
Things that SHOULD have been taken from Civ:
-Diplomacy: The diplomacy here is really lack luster. There's no trading of reasources because the reasources act differently. Your stances with rivals are pretty much non-aggression, alliance, and war. There are no real reprucussions for breaking the first two. Your relationship with them goes down but who cares you're fighting them. It reallys lacks the diversity in Civ where you can denounce a rival leading to possible make shift alliances. Betraying an ally or breaking non-aggression has an impact on how other nations view you, Instead you trade spells or currencies. That's about it.
-Minor Nations: Warlock 2 has small independent cities much like Civ 5's city states. Unlike Civ 5 these cities are always and perpetually hostile. This is boring. One of the beutiful things about City States in Civ 5 is their ability to switch sides as they are courted by other nation and the benefits derived from such an alliance. Here your options are bypass them entirely or take them over. This is particularly irksome when they happen to settle right on or near a world portal.
-City Upgrading: Another key difference from Civ 5 is that you have to build your cities buildings on surrounding tiles instead of in the city. I can see why they did that but it's made complicated by some of the ludicrous building trees. Some of them are so convoluted it's a wonder if you can ever access hire tiers and still have reasources. It pretty much means you have to build entire cities devoted to a reasource with a base city where you produce all your units which is not ideal should your food city fall to an enemy for example.
-One More Turn: Oh you just won? Game over. No one of the coolest things about Civ is being able to continue playing your empire even after victory. Closet thing you can get to that on this game is trapping you opponents on their starting shards.
-Hotkeys: Dear Lord this game needs some hotkeys. In Civ when a unit needs orders it sends you directly over the unit. Here it just sends you to the shard it's on. Now for Civ it wouldn't be a problem. You press C and it centers on the unit. In Warlock 2? Nope just scroll following the units movement path which is frankly another thing that needs work.
Things to praise about it that are different from Civ:
-Currency Resources: I love the way army upkeep works in this game with units not only needing gold but food and mana. I like the fact that your food feeds your entire empire and not just your city. I know sometimes in Civ it is annoying trying to settle cities in food scarce areas for a reasource and then it can't grow. I like that all excess food is converted to gold. In this way I feel Warlock 2 actually does a better job at simulating a real economy with areas of various terrain contributing differently to the overall empire.
-Different Races: Obviously a game about history like Civ is not going to have Elves and whatnot. But seeing the unique units and architecture for each race is unique. Each has a varied playstyle with Svarts having strong expensive units or the Undead consuming mana instead of food.
-Leader Customization: Choosing a leader in Civ basically amounts to a civlization bonus and a couple of unique units. In Warlock 2 you can allocate points to different bonuses as well as choosing your race. It makes for a unique experience each time until you find that combo you like most.
So if you're looking for a game that's a Civ fantasy game you're going to either have to download a mod or wait for them to make one. But if you're looking for a fantasy turn based strategy game with slightly clumsy controls and a decent backstory this is it. I won't compare it to Warlock 1 because frankly I never played it. I'd advise choosing this one over 1 simply for the new races. If you already have the first one just wait until this one is on sale. I'd also reccomend downloading the mod to prevent the rare crash problem.

This is a good game, but it is sad how few things would have had to be changed in order to make it ACE.
I like the game's clear focus on warfare. This is a streamlined, military themed game where conflict is inevitable. This makes it way faster to kick off than most 4X games.
There are also interesting game modes apart from the standard sandbox. Conquering the planes is fun, their themes are well-implemented, and I like how you have to adapt to the challenges each type of world poses.
The Renaissance mod gives a huge boost to the game, making it actually challenging and the AI difficult to tackle.
This is all well and great, but I just can't get over the overall WACKYNESS of it. I mean I get it, let's make fun of the fantasy tropes everyone knows, ha-ha. But it's just too blatant, too intent on making itself a parody. I had the same problem with the Age of Wonders series transition from serious-style Tolkienesque high fantasy to "oh-look-at-me-I-dare-make-fun-of-myself" fantasy. Humour has its place but there is "funny" and there is "too much". If I play a 4X wargame, I want its atmosphere to be epic instead of watching Monty Python's blood rabbit fight donkey riding knights.
But if you don't mind the wackyness of the style, this is a very good strategy game (when modded with Renaissance).
Get back to me when it has multiplayer.

Broken Game, Full of bugs, Ignorant Punishments, Fragile Situations and the worst DLC to come out of a company that isn't EA.
Big Issues, Bugs:
The number of times I have had to restart the game because it has frozen on a load, or at some random point, it WAY too high for what is supposed to be an experienced developer. Issues that are not only well known, but that are very, very old. Game breaking bugs or unclear issues that can ruin an entire playthrough.
The worst so far, and most recent for my playthough is the Telescope in Daria's apartment.
DO. NOT. TOUCH. IT. You can barely move it once you are in, and you cannot get out. You cannot quickload to get out and if you try to load a game, you will get slapped so hard with a crash and a memory leak that even restarting your own computer is a challenge.
There is no excuse for this sort of issue to be in a Deus Ex game.
There are other issues in the auto-save system saving over previous autosaves, leaving you high and dry if you have not used a quick save in a while.
And in playthough issues, the random auto alarm in the Swiss hangar mission is devestating to anyone trying to do a Fox run, especially since without a quickload or hard save you cannot even go back far enough to make a different choice in who to contact when you wake up. Why would you put this in your game? So someone can waste an entire day on an achievement run, just to get screwed over?
DLC:
You get special weapons with a gold skin if you get the deluxe version of the game or some DLC. However, you can only use them in 1 playthrough. You can't put them on other saves. Why? I bought the damn thing, I should be able to play through with them as much as I please. Why would you ever do a single redemption in a SINGLE PLAYER game?
Combat:
You have 2 choices that carry through the entire game, and netiher of them makes even a tiny bit of different.
1. Kill no one(which also means not being seen at all, ever)
2. Kill everyone. Or knock everyone out, which is literally the same thing, let's be honest. They never wake back up, so close enough.
Guns are as useless as they are unrealistically quiet. The machine pistol especially, it is so common and ammo for it is everywhere, but why on earth would you ever want to use it?
Shotguns are great if you want to get close enough to kiss them but use the loudest weapon in the world instead of just a takedown.
The stun gun is the only actually useful weapon. At least it can take pretty much everyone out without drawing attention. Though that isnt exactly combat.
If you do get into a gun fight, no problem! Just literally muder everyone. There's no consequence to killing every single person in the city. You don't even get scolded for it.
Pros:
Pretty.
Overall 4/10 and those 4 coming only from the style and look of the game. It looks amazing, and the settings are extremely creatively put together, esecially the details in the Aug city. But pretty does not make a good game when the mechanics fall flat and the story is as intricate and interesting as a cardboard box.

For starters, I really love Deus Ex series, and I really enjoyed Mankind Divided. I can also fully understand those who declare it inferior to Human Revolution. HR was a sci-fi techno action blockbuster starting with terrorist attack involving mass murder, mayhem and destruction, and ending with a global zombie apocalypse. You must try really, really hard to beat that in terms of fascination, and I don't think the MD team really tried to do that. Instead they created a dystopian conspiracy thriller about shadowy Illuminaty infusing the ranks of potentially problematic civil movement with their agent provocateurs who turn it into violent terrorist organization which can be easily blamed for many problems while simultaneously turning their sympathizers into partners in vicious and bloody crimes. A simple yet effective scheme, and frighteningly realistic, too.
Still, there are problems. Some of them are purely technical bugs, such as vendors' behaviour during the second and the third Prague episodes (every time they meet you as though for the very first time, and their reaction to your buying and selling balance seems random). But there are also problems with the world logic. Of course, they could be deliberate decisions to make the players' lives easier, but I think the world of DX is so rich, convoluted and realistic that these compromises make things not better but worse. Still, fixing them could really make gameplay harder, so it could be done in a separate difficulty level or as a New Game Plus Plus mode.
Here are my ideas.
Problem #1 - Crafting. The most disbalancing feature. You can dismantle almost everything you find and turn even some tubes or whatever from garbage piles and from under kitchen sinks into hi-tech weaponry and equipment. Hand-made Typhoon or TESLA ammo? Improvised multitool? MacGyver's emerald green with envy! As for me, it's just wrong.
How to fix it. There are several ways to do it. The simplest one is multiplying the crafting prices by at least five. But it would be only a cosmetic change. The true solution would be to replace the ordinary hi-tech equipment and ammo with something truly makeshift that would feel like truly desperate measures for a really tight spot. Improvised power cell which would only give you 5-10% of charge. Makeshift multitool which would only reduce the hacked device's security rating by 1. Terminator-style pipebombs. Lethal or non-lethal tripwires... The list can go on and on. Introduce recipes for some advanced and intricate thing which can be bought from vendors, found on hacked computers during missions or received as an award for quests. Turn all those 'for sale only' parts (processors, gyrostabilizers, hydraulic pumps) into ingredients for your gizmos, and suddenly the game gains a whole additional layer of depth! Isn't that cool?
Problem #2 - Vendors' goods. Alright, you can't make RPG without vendors. But vendors must not be omnipotent. Typhoon ammo sold by a street thug? It's military experiment grade hardware, for God's sake! It must not be that easily available! It must be distributed strictly by Task Force 29, namely by Aria, who would provide you with, like 5 pieces of lethal Typhoon/nanoblade if you chose lethal path in the very beginning or non-lethal Typhoon/TESLA/PEPS if you chose non-lethal on each visit (but, say, no more than 20 of each per Prague episode - it's experimental and thus scarce, after all!) Of course you would be able to find some of it in Alps and on Golden Masks' bodies, but nowhere else. Careful resource management is also an important part of good RPG, don't you agree?
Problem #3 - Weapons upgrading. Well, making your swords/spells/guns more poverful and versatile has always been a part of RPG character development and leveling up, but I think you'll agree that it's really hard to make assault rifle clip contain more ammo with household appliances parts, since it involves some metallurgy and exhaustive reingeneering to make the weapon balanced, accurate, and, well, useful. Of course, weapon customization is a eal and huge industry, and that's exactly what DXMD is missing and needs - weapon masters, who for a cash or a service would improve your weapons a little. But only a little! For real quality boost you would need to look for magic artifacts... I mean, custom-made weapons belonging to very special and very resourceful people or organizations. DX series already have those - a golden revolver from The Missing Link and the EMP assault rifle from MD immediately come to mind. But it's too little! We need more! Super sniper rifle in Miller's closet. Exquisite machine gun in Radich Nikoladze's wall safe. Exclusive stun rifle as a reward from hacker vendor in exchange for some info from the metro station security room... Plenty of options! And one more reason to look around very-very carefully.
Not-Really-A-Problem #4 - Inventory. I think you would agree that Jensen's inventory capacity is inhumane. No one can really go around the city with full-sized rifles under his coat. Pistol, revolver, stun gun, machine gun, shotgun - that's the maximum. Assault rifle, sniper rifle, tranq rifle - suitcase is needed. Yes, like in Hitman series. That would be great, don't you think? ...Well, maybe not. There is a thin line between enjoyable realism and headache. History knows super realistic games which were playable only by REAL hardcore lovers ('Robinson's Requiem' and 'Deus' by Silmarils immediately come to mind). Simple and physically impossible inventory is one of the genre's conventions which is there to stay to allow us to just sit back and enjoy the plot and forget all those real-life packing problems. But I wouldn't mind playing some mode like 'Trenchcoat' from Deus Ex: Revision in MD, if only just to try it out.
Well, that's all that comes to mind as of now. Hope my ranting will give some ideas to DX:MD team or mod-making community. Don't get me wrong, I really love DX:MD in its present state, but that's exactly why I feel obliged to point out aspects which can be improved to make it even greater.
Thanks for your patience and attention!

While I respect this game for trying to be fresh, it ended up feeling clunky and poorly-executed. On the good side, the story can be interesting and it's a fresh change from zombie apocalypse. Confrontations can also sometimes feel rewarding if you outsmart a group. The problem is that these good parts are rare. While the game teaches you the basics of combat early on, it also defies these at times. Also, the ending was horribly underwhelming.
Confrontations:
The game does a great job early on of showing you ways of dealing with multiple people and when you are underpowered (lacking ammunition for your gun) but it breaks many of the conventions established early on. For example, the enemy will rarely recognize the bow and arrow as a weapon and so, rather than stopping, they keep charging you. The enemy will also, after a while, charge you when you have a gun out (believing you have no bullets). This breaks the mechanic of shoving the enemy into fire or off cliffs since it takes so goddamn long to maneuver them into position while keeping your crosshairs on all the enemies. Another issue is enemy spawning. One particular sequence annoyed me to no end. You had to walk forward and get the attention of one group before a second group would open an impenetrable door and attack you from behind. You weren't allowed to sneak past one group or deal with them one at a time; you were forced to let them flank you.
Puzzles:
The game has a lot of climbing and maneuvering puzzles. I actually think this is its best quality and wish the game consisted purely of these sorts of puzzles and left out the clunky combat. Your climbing time is restricted by your stamina, which decreases over time as you climb. The first problem with this is that your character is incredibly difficult to control while climbing. I routinely found myself shifting along edges when I was pressing down to slide down the goddamn pole I was clinging to! Secondly, climbing is introduced in one of the hardest climbing puzzles in the game. With no guide or direction, the player has to complete one of the longest and hardest to deduce climbing paths in the game.
Story:
The story is pretty generic, but by the end I had some hope for it. We were saying goodbye to some main characters and the protagonist renewed his effort to reunite with his wife. And then the game ended. The game progressed to a state where, while not great, it was certainly improving. But instead of continuing the game, it just abuptly ends in a vague cutscene. I had only just gotten a second arrow for my bow.
In the end, this game seemed like it was trying to be a lot of things and failing at all of them. It was made by what appears to be a primarily Chinese team, so this may be their first entry into American games, but it felt very lacking in ways that cannot simply be excused by considering other cultures. Get this game if it's on super sale. If for nothing else, the guy who voices Adam Jensen in Deus Ex: HR plays a guy in a wheelchair here. So, if you want to hear the moody gravel voice, this is the game for you.

Arkham Asylum is simply the best game based off of a comic book ever made, along with the sequal Arkham City.
I was skeptical when I first heard about a new Batman game but those doubts were very quickly put to rest. This game has everything that makes Batman great, very cool gadgets that are vital in keeping Batman true to his roots of non letal takedowns. This game keeps with the theme of Batman appearing as nothing more than a very intelligent detective that has no actual "super powers" and instead uses his mind and his many gadgets to overcome his foes.
The graphics are a solid 10/10 with the character models being a rather striking feature as they are incredibly well done. The soundtrack and sounds are great as well and really help pull the player into the atmosphere of the game.
Perhaps this games strongest feature is it's combat system. It is so fluid, simple and complex at the same time that many games have since tried to imitate it, in fact most critics regard the combat system in this game as well as Arkham City as simply the best.
The story grips you from the start and with plenty of plot twist that you will not see coming, it keeps you on your toes from start to finish. It isn't one of those cheesy tacked on stories either, true to the Batman franchise the story and the classic characters that play important rolls are all fantasic.
I could continue to rave about how great this game is but there is a reason this game is widely regarded as one of the top games to be released in the last decade. While most games metascores are to be taken with a grain of salt, this is one of the few instances in which the critics are correct. I honestly can't think of a single significant negative of this game.

** [[Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon]] **
"Tactical" is a word many game publishers love to abuse for lacking first person shooters; Ghost Recon is not one of those games. Expect stellar gameplay with a variety of missions ranging from the jungle to the desert, weapons and customization. The campaign(s) are straight forward with a realistic approach focusing on establishing a democracy in a war-stricken land. The gameplay if a first-person shooter with a few HUD items along with a tactical map on which the player can direct his/her troops. Don't expect to get attached to the characters unless the player renames them after close companions in real life. There is a small skill tree on which the player can update units' skills including "Leadership", "Marksmanship", and more. Once the player's soldier dies in that campaign, they lose him and his skillset forever. There are a few classes to choose from with specialized weaponry corresponding to each class which makes each class valuable in its own respects. The multiplayer is dead, unless the player play it with a friend; unfortunantly, this is where the game shines. Strategizing on the map allows for dynamic gameplay; putting the player and their friends' minds together really makes the player feel as if the player is operating in a real spec ops mission. One of the downfalls to the gameplay has to be the difficulty, I recommend saving often with the "quick-save" and "quick-load" features; one wrong move can put a world of hurt on the player's team. Expect to run this game at a solid-locked 60FPS with ultra-high graphics. There is still a pretty decent modding community providing the player with extra campaign missions including a WWII campaign! Even though this game was made way back in 2000, it is still the most tactical game on my list.
PROS:
+ Solid Gameplay
+ 60 FPS
+ Variety of Mods
+ Easy Integration of Mods
+ Great Multiplayer With Friends
+ Endless Hours of Gameplay
Cons:
- Brutal Difficulty
- Dead Online Multiplayer

I played Ghost recon when it first came and was instantly hooked. Since then the development of military FPS have rocketed away from what was – back in 2001 – quite an advanced game. Both the original game and its expansion packs (Desert Siege and Island Thunder) was built around huge maps, the management of a small team of six soldiers and sharp punishment for not thinking tactically and proceeding with some caution. The enemy had a deadly aim, even if their AI wasn’t always on top.
Then came various games like Call of Duty, Battlefield, Ghost recon Future Soldier and Sniper Ghost Warrior, and more work and less time to play made me give away my Ghost Recon Gold collections box to a friend. It was just by pure chance that I earlier this year suddenly discovered that Steam sold the original Ghost Recon with its official expansion packs for “pennies” and I could not resist buying it. It can be a risky business to return to old pleasures; like a movie or a book, you remember from the past, but I found myself enjoying the gameplay as much as I did back in 2001.
In addition, with the mods like frostbite and CENTCOM you may have hours of fun. Just forget about the old graphics and focus on the thrill of the mission.
My advice: Play it on elite difficulty for maximum challenge and fun.

Let me be cliche and compare this game to Smash Bros right off the bat, because that's what everyone pays attention to:
While Brawlhalla lacks some of the complexity of Smash (not every character has a fully unique set of heavy and light attacks), the weapon system is an interesting alternative. Each character essentially has 2 move sets, 1 for each weapon – however, character specific attacks only exist for heavy attacks, or "signatures". The ability to switch between move sets depending on situation/matchup adds another layer of strategy to the game.
The problem with the weapon system is that some characters feel samey – often two characters with the same weapon play the exact same way. However, the large array of weapons makes up for this, and there are plenty of characters to choose from with different weapon combinations.
One bonus over Smash is the constant updates. Despite being "early access", there are very few bugs, and they use their development time to add new characters, gamemodes, and balance changes. It keeps the game interesting over long periods of time.
Aside from that, the controls are tight, the animations are top notch, and the gameplay is much, much smoother than I expected it to be going in. Overall, a great game. If you enjoy Smash and want something to play on PC, pick this up.

Arkham Asylum is one damn good action game, surprising for a western-developed title, and one damn good stealth game, surprising for a modern video game (ded genre etc). The combat is simple but also somewhat complex, with quite a few gadgets and moves, and a LOT of ways to take down enemies. The stealth and combat in Asylum can be mixed together at will, (except when fighting armed enemies, in which case it is too dangerous to fight them openly) providing a lot of different gameplay possibilities for the player. While learning the advanced uses of moves and gadgets is not necessary for the player to truly succeed in the normal game, the challenge mode is where the game's combat shines. On top of the base game and the challenges, which are all reasonably difficult, the game also comes with a harder difficulty mode that will really wreck your♥♥♥♥♥♥ It's a little bit broken because the game's combat is very reliant on the appearence of shining attack indicators over enemies before they strike, which are gone when playing the hardest difficulty, but overall it remains one of the hardest action games I've played in the last few years.
The stealth is also wonderful. It's very fast, and requires proper use of your gadgets and tools. There's never a moment in Arkahm Asylum's stealth where you're doing nothing or waiting for something to happen. It also has a very interesting system of fear tactics, where you can get various effects out of enemies with fear.
Arkham Asylum features my favourite depiction of Batman and Gotham City, it being in my opinion a perfect blend of the style of the animated series and the more realistic versions of the live-action films. The art style (and graphics) is fantastic, and that's without even mentioning the amazing Scarecrow segments scattered throughout the game.
The biggest problem with this game is probably the integration with Games For Windows Live, even on Steam. But if that doesn't bother you too much, you should definately give this game a try. You won't regret it.

Now here’s a game to remember. Batman: Arkham Asylum is a breath of fresh air for superhero games. Instead of leeching off the success of the Nolan films, Warner Brother Studios have managed to use the original comics as a great basis for developing a rich and intriguing game world.
Batman Arkham Asylum is really a game that I consider to be a pioneer of the new “free flow” combat system. Third person combat has never been more fun for me. You can string together different moves and quickly move from one enemy to the next or even attack more than one at the same time. It’s incredibly satisfying.
The story of Arkham Asylum is another star of the show. Focused around catching the joker after he escapes and proceeds to cause havoc on the Asylum, it’s up to Batman to save the island before things go from bad to worse. Along the way you get to meet (and in some cases fight) some familiar enemies from the Batman comics including Scarecrow, Poison Ivy, and The Riddler. Despite the focus being around the Joker, I found myself so engrossed in each of these villains back stories as they featured in their cameo appearances. Having more than one villain made the story more robust and gave it very good pacing. As I progressed through the game, I kept many memories of these great bad guys and the levels they belonged to. When a story is able to do that, you know it’s been well made.
Speaking of memorable levels, I was very impressed with the level design as well! Each area of the Asylum has its own unique appearance and although they all share similar features that are needed for gameplay, they all feel different. You’re given a lot of ground to explore and extra missions to complete for unlockables and extras. The Riddler riddles are particularly well done, although not exactly deep. At times you’ll even get to re-visit areas you’ve already been through and use newly unlocked equipment to reach previously inaccessible sections.
In addition to the main story, there are also challenge maps which are small test rooms to well…….challenge you. They focus on fighting, stealth, and even unique situations. Although a good way to spend more time after you’ve completed the story, I didn’t find them necessary. Because they lack the story of the campaign, I wasn’t as interested in playing them. It’s that part of the game that feels more like a game rather than an experience, and that’s not for me.
Arkham Asylum doesn’t feel cheesy, it doesn’t feel forced, and it really sucks you in. Whether you’re a fan of the comics or not, Batman: Arkham Asylum is a thoroughly enjoyable experience.

"This game is seriously handicapped in comparison to dwarf fortress. This game has some issues, and it does not let you see from a top down perspective. It can't beat dwarf fortress in  any way."
"Although I would recommend the game to newbies."
That was my first review of this game. However, I found out that there is not much to say about dwarf fortress either. There's tons of "things" just thrown into dwarf fortress for the fun of it, badly integrated. At least this game is well integrated with all its parts for the time being, and perhaps it becomes even better when it is finished. At first, I got irritated by the 3D controls, since Dwarf Fortress lacks any kind of advanced graphics which means it gets a lot of things for free. But I learnt that, once upon a time, I struggled with dwarf fortress aswell. And now I got to play this game the way it was meant to be played. I learnt the controls and overcame the struggle with the initial "but do gnomes only eat berries" kind of scepticism. I think it is kind of nice that the game has a few good things like rotation of the view so that you can see the floor where you otherwise wouldn't. And there's the potential to have a lot of things put into this game. Imagine modding this game in order to add new plants and stones, crafting, workbenches, new things in general. Imagine, since it is still alpha, that this game could potentially gain a lot of features. I don't promise it, but I would really like to see this game finished.

Old school feel, new school design. Ziggurat was a bit of an impulse buy, and I'm glad I am impulsive. There is a ton to love about this game, if you have any interest in roguelikes and/or FPSes, you may enjoy Ziggurat. While nothing about it is going to blow your mind, if you enjoy game loops that involve killing hordes of enemies using a varied arsenal and slowly levelling and upgrading your avatar to take on increasingly difficult maps/bosses, you will find plenty of that here. Tons of unlockables from heroes to weapons to upgrades and randomly generated maps composed of hand built rooms, Ziggurat is built to be played over and over. The game is sufficiently difficult to challenge you and draw you in, and the highly polished gameplay and randomized content will make you say, "One more run, I can do better."
Worth full price, easily.

A decent follow-up to the excellent Deus Ex: Human Revolution. First of all I want to say that I am not sure what the hoopla was over the microtransactions. You could buy ammo or praxis points with money, but the game never really made you do it, as it was easy enough to come by these things. The graphics and detail in this game are impressive, I stopped frequently to gawk at the scenery. My trusty old Geforce 970 was able to play this game on high without any fps issues.
Most of the game plays in futuristic Prague, which is beautifully designed and chock full of detail. It seems Eidos went with quality over quanity, as there aren't as many locales as in Human Revolution. In return Prague and its stores etc. are full of detail, and rivals Witcher 3 cities in atmosphere and believability.
The story is passable, but nothing to write home about. Augs are being discriminated against after the Pangea event, the game does a good job portraying how it feels to be  a second class citizen. If you take the  metro meant for non aug people a police office will remind you of your error. Great little touch.
Apart from this game is very similar to Human Revolution, which some people see as detriment. I thought they build nicely on the last game, and am not certain how much they could have changed without upsetting people for being too different.
All in all a decent follow-up, that seemed it was cut short for dlcs or a sequel, as the story apruptly ends. Otherwise than that I got my money's worth, as I got around 32ish hours out of it, and paid only 20 bucks for it. I am saddened to hear that Deus Ex's future is uncertain, as it did no perform up to expectations.  Perhaps in the next iteration they can drop the stupid PR crap, microtransactions and deliver a whole story to avoid upsetting a large segment of fickle gamers.

Three adventurers get tied together by the Trine, and now forced to explore a large world to beat a great evil.  Yada yada yada.
Trine was a pretty solid game that incorporated three characters that were able to switch abilities as characters.  Trine 2 tries to recapture that greatness with a few switch and ends up becoming a very frustrating and pointless exercise in annoyance.
Trine and Trine 2 are physics basic puzzlers, and while I remember liking Trine, Trine 2 just frustrates me, it frustrates me to the point that I'm trying to play it a third time, and while I get through a few levels I just mostly get annoyed after playing a level.
Where Half LIfe 2 had really simplistic physics based puzzles, Trine 2 has the opposite problem, their puzzles are too free form and you constantly feel like your breaking the game to beat them.  You have an annoying puzzle and if you pull this piece to the right, you can jump against it and get this hop jump off the side of it to reach the top.
The problem is you never know if you're doing something right or just glitching the system, and in fact I don't know if there's ever really a "Right" way to do many puzzles.  In portal, I can use plane english to tell you how to beat a level in a few lines.    I could try to do that in Trine but a lot of times it's "you'll have to try to force the puzzle."
That's really the problem with the physics puzzle of the whole thing, and the fact is much of the game is physics puzzles.  Though there's combat, you're going to be able to easily beat it with the warrior, and with a little  work the thief.
But that brings up the other problem.  A lot of these puzzles feel like only one character can pass.  Where I enjoyed the first game, it feels like all three characters had equal power, and use.  In Trine 2 after a few levels, you will stop using the wizard.  The wizard feels slow, weak and under powered.  They also removed the triangle step that really made the wizard powerful and instead made him almost worthless.
The point is the main idea of the game (use all three characters) doesn't really apply here, you can beat levels with only one character, and often you'll only really use 2, maybe having the wizard summon ONE square.
But that's the other issue, quite often the solution to a puzzle is focused on one or two characters, so if you lose one or even worse two  you'll feel like you have to go back and revive all three characters so you can be assured to win.
Hell if you don't have the thief's low gravity shot by the end the game is extremely hard, with that shot, a lot of puzzles are simple, on the other hand, some puzzles feel like they require the shot, so a game breaking shot is required?
It feels mostly tedious to play this game.  Here's a new room that doesn't feel clean, then you'll beat it, sometimes having to sacrifice characters in the way and when you beat it you'll feel like you didn't properly beat it.  To me, that's not a good feeling.
There's more issues I have with the game.  The levels feel too long, the characters are uninteresting, and the story is weak, but overall, I just really hate the feeling I get from the gameplay, and too me I could forgive almost anything else, but the gameplay makes it really impossible to even try to recommend this.
If you really want a 2d platformer puzzle, VVVVV is very good, as is Limbo,  Thomas was Alone, Braid, or maybe even Fez, but I'd skip this game unless you really need a little frustration with your puzzles.

-No regenerating health.
-One shot, one kill difficulty. Occasionally you may get wounded.
-Frag grenades have a good 20 foot kill zone.
-Rocket launchers have realistic back blast that can kill/wound you and your squad.

-Missions areas are very large. Learn by trial and error.
-All maps can be played in adversarial or coop modes.
Graphics
-Supports 1080p resolution in game. (Game menu does not)
-Game says it caps out at 32fps but actually runs at 60fps.
-Game is from 2001 so don't expect crazy good textures.
Recommendation?
If you buy this game I recommend Desert Siege and Island Thunder expansion packs since they are also on steam.
Also do yourself a favor and download the Heroes Unleashed mod from here.
When you're all said and done the game has about 175 coop missions to play. I have no idea how many weapons.
If you want to use a controller I recommend Anti-micro.

War is hell, but if you're gonna do it, you gotta do it right. This game is as relevant and riveting today as it was when it first came out. It makes no bones about what it is: A pure tactical simulator, geared toward getting your team out alive and completing objectives from rescuing hostages to full-scale assault on armored patrols.
My only gripe with this game is that, while it has good singleplayer, the AI of your team cannot often be trusted. Sending the computers into combat situations often results in friendly casualties, meaning it is best to take control of the squad you're sending into battle at one time. This is just my experience of course, but it does hamper you in that you cannot have two teams conquering two objectives at the same time.  However, they can act as sentries if placed right, and will defend points and shoot enemy soldiers with great accuracy, just not while they are on the move.
Really though, this isn't a big issue, all it means is that the missions take a little longer, and even so, time flies when you are having fun!
The AI of the enemies is very good, and they'll give you a bit of a bite even on recruit.
This is not an arcade shooter, its a milsim on a tactical level. And I guarantee, if you take it as that, you're gonna have a helluva time.

Okay, so this is going to be an in-depth review of the game, and my opinion will be expressed at the end with a tl;dr. If you don't want to see the entire review, and just want a quick explination, please just scroll down.
Brawlhalla is a smash bros esque 2d arena fighter that is free, bar skins that are entirely optional. it can run semi-well on potatoes, so if you are using one, this may be the game for you, however, if you're running a gaming rig, you'll be hitting a capped 60, as all animations are based on this frame cap. Each character holds two weapons, which are used with the same animations per character, however each character has 3 signitures per weapon, down, side and neutral. the weapons available are; Sword, Hammer, Spear, Blasters, Katars, Gauntlets, Bow, scythe and rocket lance.
Pros
The game is fast paced, and the controls are fairly tight, however floaty they may be, which helps to give the game a little more focus on maneuverability. This aids the game's play-style very well, as reading the opponents movements is rewarded well.
The game is generally fun in short bursts, and the dev's are constantly adding to both the game, and the community, hosting livestreams, and some of the community is based around tournaments which are usually friendly, and help those new to the game learn.
The match-making isn't as bad as many make it out to be, as those who are being matched with bad times are most likley playing at down times in their servers.
Cons
The community in general is very toxic, I have been called a spammer more times than I can count, to play you really need to be ready for insults to be thrown your way, and to be able to brush it off.
The game gets boring, or is changed in a negative way at times. I had to take a 3 month hiatus to  even start to enjoy the game again, but even then, the game was so different, with movement being slowed down, and many moves having a much lower combo potential, which sucks if you have learned through muscle memory
The hitboxes are very odd, since they are circular, they always extend further than they should, leaving some hits to be judged as unfair.
Some weapons are simply better at certain tiers, lower tier play needs more spamable weapons, which require little skill, such as rocket lance, however, using rocket lance at higher tiers requires much more skill than other faster weapons in the same tier, which means balance is a little broken, which isn't great for such a legend based game.
There is really only one playstyle, the more reading play style, as it is the only one which pays off, or isn't called "scummy", but you're gonna be called a spammer if you use it!
Only the first 300 hours are actually positive, the rest is a slew of either anger, or very little skill, as you either cannot climb due to the previous weapon diadvantages noted, or, like me, you got the hang of a faster character, in which you'll be in platinum for around 100 hours.
Want to download a game? Want to do it while playing brawlhalla? Tough luck, you really can't. You will lag to hell and back, and then some. Even if it isn't taking up much of the bandwidth, the game will tank like hell.
The platinum problem
There is such a huge skill divide between gold and diamon that there really should be a much higher end to the ranking system, as diamond is simply not enough, this leads to the platinum problem, at low platinum, either you are an advanced gold player, or you'll climb quickly as you are much more skilled than the golds which are peeking through into the tier, however, there is a large skill divide between this and high platinum, verging on diamond which is simply unexcusable. There needs to be a higher rank than diamond, like masters, or such, as there is too large of a skill gap, as only the elite can reach higher diamond, and this leads those who have more skill than the golds with a hard time in mid platinum, and they will remain there for a long time.
tl;dr
Honestly, I think the game is okay, if you want to have a few fun hours with friends, or if you're really dedicated to the game, and become the next best player, but if you're somehwere in the middle, and will spend about 650 hours, and feel under acomplished, then don't bother, get another game, or emulate smash, I hope this helped.
