Night Blights is a very fun, and charming, little horror game. It pulls off being simultaneously cute and stress-inducing so well, as the things you must manage drastically increase with each night. If you like jumpscare-based games, this one might be for you.
You play as a child who must defend yourself and your family from the gremlin-like Night Blights prowling around your home. You do this by closing doors, pressing various switches, and many other things each night. The game relies heavily on audio and sound cues, so playing with headphones is very much recommended.
No matter how much I've played that Survival Mode to get that top score, the game still manages to make me paranoid when I do play it. My favorite part of the game is the amount of random little things there are to troll you; random things may open or appear to freak you out, or to open areas that you might not get a chance at on a different attempt. There's also many, many Easter eggs to other horror games and movies as well. The dev did a wonderful job on this cute little game, and while it may get a bit frustrating at times, it's overall quite silly and fun; I think it deserves a bit more attention than it gets here on Steam.

I loved the game over on GameJolt, however, I'm seriously dissapointed in paying money for this game. Not only has the game somehow disabled itself?!- it says that a newer game version is available and my copy has been disabled- the email I sent to Night Blights support has been bounced back. The email account simply doesn't seem to exist. It won't update, I've spent about 4 hours verifying and making sure it wasn't an error on the account of my computer. I deleted and redownloaded the game files, restarted my system, cleared out some uneccesary data. 

Then I changed the update for Night Blights to high priority, but it won't work and what I wanted to be fun has become severely frustrating. Until this issue is fixed, I feel obligated to warn people away from downloading the game. Stick to the demo version over on GameJolt for the time being until this gets fixed.

UPDATE:

The problem is now fixed. Kudos to the developers for responding so quickly to the problem, although, seeing how their update system penalizes people possesing older copies of the game, it does detract from my overall enjoyment. Regardless, I think it's time I talk about what I love about Night Blights. 

Although one could draw comparisons between this game and Five Nights at Freddies, it's clearly paved it's own path from it's horror-genre cousin. Playing this game always keeps you on your toes, as you listen to audio cues signaling which location you'll need to quickly visit. Constantly bombarded by creatures called Night Blights, keeping you or your family safe is no easy feet.

In this game, you control and direct the movement of a child. Level game play is also directed by a mysterious book detailing your gruesome encounters in common storybook fashion. Our poor protaginist seems to never be able to catch a break, since staying awake all night to fend of murderous and mischivious creatures must be quite taxing.

All around, it features a unique style of game play, with penalizing consequences for ignoring gameplay ques. Although lacking player custimization, it does boast an immersive environment with hidden suprises to continue its underlying sense of dread. Overall, I would recommend to a friend. In this game, it helps to be strategical, and keep the fire lit.

Before reading my review, first thing you need to do is watch the E3 trailer from 2008.
Did you watch it? Looks great right? I remember E3 2008 and said to myself, "This game looks great!", although I knew it was a cinematic trailer, it was the initial concept of survival and escape from hordes of other humans that were possibly your friends prior to "The Event", as it's called in the published version of the game, that stood out to me.
The game we got? Well, it went through a lot of changes as it was already in development for like, five years prior to E3 2008, and then released in 2012, went through even more changes. The biggest change is that you don't experience "The Event", okay, it's a big f*cking earthquake. But how awesome would it have been to experience that as part of the game?
Instead, I Am Alive takes place a year later as your character returns to the city of Haventon to find his wife and daughter, how original. Instead, you find some girl named Mei who's just crying in the playground by your house, so you help her find her mother instead, as well as some bloke in a wheelchair.
During the game, you can help strangers that actually need it, or kill people that are hostile. It's a very black and white game, literally too. Instead of the nice, yet muddy, colors of the initial trailer, Ubisoft Shanghai rapes your eyes with an over abundance of black and white, mostly white, film grain. The dust is thick, foggy thick.
Let me remind you that this game came out in 2012. The textures and models from Super Mario Sunshine are better, and that was 2002. The gameplay tries to emulate the Assassin's Creed climbing, but somehow messes that up. And the shooting mechanic switches you from 3rd person survival game, to 1st person shooter.
This game's just doesn't really do anything right, except for the limited ammo which would make sense considering the stuff doesn't just appear out of nowhere.
It's mediocre.
5/10

After playing Warlock and enjoying it, in spite of some niggling issues, I looked forward to trying Warlock 2. Anticipating new features, cleanups of quirks, and hopefully expanded content, I purchased and began playing. At first things looked good, however, after getting further into the game I quickly encountered several issues that caused me to throw my hands up and remove the game from my system. To whit:
Building buffs (like unit armor, combat training, resistance potions) are now limited to a very small quantity. For example, i was only able to outfit 5 units with basic armor. So once equipting my 4 heroes, I had to pick one lucky unit to get the last set.
Random monsters that spawn quite a bit more frequently than before (on default setting) now include creature types like shadow dragons, units with 300 hp, immune to a variety of usual attacks, and flying. So much for several of my cities.
After building up what seemed like a decent force of heroes, strong (100+ hp melee units) and ranged units (casters and archers), I daintly sent my forces into an outer plane. The horde of shadow dragons, deadwood elementals, gold dragons, and evil warlocks promptly showed me the error of my ways. And this was on the easiest difficulty level.
While the gameplay has indeed improved, it feels like the AI was improved by the use of power boosts rather than intelligence. I am not a big fan of 'meatgrinder' type campaigns, especially after the game was modified to restrict me to 5 starting cities (bumpable to 8). I simply could not generate enough quailty units fast enough to replace lost units.
If you appreciate running a constant stream of units to be killed while trying to achieve your goal, this game could certainly hold your interest. It does not appeal to me in that it pretty much makes the leveling, buffing, and equipting I prefer in building a fighting force completely moot.

Warlock 2 is a confused 4x game which has broken the playfield up into a series of small maps connected via portals which you must cross to defeat the final opponent.  Nearing the portals with a unit triggers random events for activating the portal and other allies of the end boss will create random events of their own to trip you up.
Resource management is very strict.  It may be difficult at first to balance your cities so that they are able to grow and remain happy.  The number of cities you are able to control at a time is also kept very low (5-11 as the game progresses).  Although this can be changed with an option in the game settings it is marked 'Not Recommended'.  Developing advanced units can also be challenging as each is produced by a specific building which has other buildings as a pre-requisite and each building must be placed within a limited area in which other structures for wealth and food must also exist.  This forces the player along rather narrow paths which greatly limit the viable choices that can be made.
This is my main complaint about the game.  It feels too rigid.  The player is locked into a very limited set of choices while forced to face randomly appearing enemies and AI opponents which greatly outmatch you at every step.  This creates gameplay in which there is perhaps only one narrow path to victory and only by discovering that single formula can the player succeed.  This is in opposition to the general appeal of a 4x game which to me is that you can discover many paths to victory.

That feeling you get when you just barely KO your opponent with only one stock left on either side, or that feeling you get when you make a ridiculous comeback when the odds are stacked against you.
The player base is quite strong. You have people of all skill levels playing, which can make for some laughable matches or some ridiculously enraging ones.

That being said, the community (especially ranked) can be quite salty. One of my first team ranked matches (that I lost) had the other team cussing and spitting every time of racial slur and derrogatory expletive my way. I couldn't believe what I was reading and all I could do was simply laugh. So yes, you have a lot of young people playing.
Overall,  I'm very happy I found Brawhalla. I wouldn't hesistate to reccomend it to anyone; which is why I am now playing regularly with my girlfriend. Great relationship building experience.

Ziggurat is an FPS rogue-like\lite in the vain of Hexen or Heretic using the ever titular BoI formula and for the most part it succeeds but it still falters along the line for me.
+ Feels very smooth, no stutters, frames drops or crashes.
+ Movement in this game feels very fast, I can get from point A to point B extremely quickly and this makes dodging any hazards an easy task.
+ Some rooms have a special trait which boost your wand\stave\magic combat proficiency and that's pretty cool i.e +50% damage with wands, -50% other.
+ Interesting room layouts where some have various hazards scattered throughout them while others have presents at the end only if you manage to progress through.
+ It's a very beautiful game, I love the art style chosen. It feels like a dark twisted cartoon themed world at times and that's really nice.
+ The audio (for the most part) is well done. The music at times is mystical however the weapon sound effects do lack some umpf behind them.
- For some reason it feels too repetitive early on as you encounter the same type rooms and enemies very frequently.
- There's nothing really to do in the rooms, you just enter and fight spawning enemies. It'd cool if there were some kind of interactables in the certain rooms.
- Some room special traits are f*cking awful and not fun in the slightest i.e. Can only attack when in air, Scavenger (can only attack enemies after you've collected some scattered orbs).
- Feels like I have to grind to unlock the majority of items\perks which gets pretty boring.
- The perspective feels off. It feels like the player is too close to the floor. Either that or you're playing as very short characters.
- The bosses, I hate all of the bosses I've fought so far, they all behave in the exact same way. Spawn in, summon some ads, charge at you (give or take) and do a large attack. I would've love some variety in this aspect because as it stands you've basically encountered all bosses after your very first boss fight.
- You don't get experience after defeating enemies it drops to the floor which does disappear after a while.
- Why do the items left on the floor vanish, I mean I feel like this shouldn't even be a thing any more. Player's computers are extremely powerful these days to accommodate the excess memory usage required for the items. For me, items should only disappear of the player's pc does not have enough memory to allow for extra optimisation.
- Weaponry feels a bit samey or too similar to present day military weapons. For instance the base wand is an automatic weapon, you get a grenade with distance notches. How about some charge weapons where the longer you charge it the more powerful it becomes. Or how about some cursed weapons which have a negative connotation for the player but is generally stronger in all aspects.
- The perks feel a bit lacklustre it's either that or I haven't unlocked a ton of them.
While the gameplay for the most part is fun, it's marred by some odd design choices which detract from the fun at times. I feel like this game just isn't for me or that I just don't have the patience to soldier through the repetition as I was simply performing the exact same things I did in my previous runs being enter room, fight enemy, pick boring perk, circle strafe boss. Also, I found myself saying these lines "Why can't I attack", "What's hitting me" and "Well that room was annoying" way too often while playing. And while I've only played a meager 3Hrs as of this review I don't feel like I'll miss out by not continuing. So while I do like what I've played so far I cannot recommend it.

I start games off with a 10/10 and then subtract for any reasonbly-construed faults.
Gameplay- Check; was very fun and intuitive, but deep; enhanced the work of previous game without departing too far from the winning formula; allowed for multiple methods of solving problems and overcoming obstacles, as well as greatly enhancing the depth of gameplay driven by dialogue choices.

Audio- Check; good foley; immersion felt complete and satisfying.
Score- Check; Bulb knows his stuff (I expected nothing less from him), as does whomever made the overworld music; combines symphony with synths and djents; very moving.
Graphics- Check; on a high-end PC, this thing kills with graphical fidelity; even lower settings do not compromise the overall aesthetic
All told, I found no overbearing fault with it. 10 x 10 = 100. S Rank.

First impressions of the game when trying it out was really good. It reminded me of "Binding of Isaac" in some areas and the customization possibilities you got when choosing where to place boss rewards on your character sheet made for interesting choices based on what kind of playstyle you wanted to try.
Decent flow of combat, nice graphics and all in all it was a decent experience.
All of this comes to naught because of one feature in the game, though.
Event rooms.
There are some rooms that are "event rooms" where you get the chance for a reward if you do something. This could be a simple as jumping unto a pillar that stood in the middle of the room, to beat a swarm of enemies, to feed a hungry shark or to... get killed by spikes.
Actually, the last one is the effect and not the actual event. It sums up to the same thing, though. With one roll of the die, when you enter the room everything you did up till that point is nullified ("the room strips you from your powers"), so your customization and choices doesn't matter. Furthermore, it's not a matter of 'beat this challenge', but 'how long time do you want to spend in this room before suffering the inescapable death'. These 'event spike rooms' stand for the 'instant death' mechanics we should have left in the dark ages, even though the game tries to shine them up as 'hard challlenges'. The end result is the same. your choices and good gameplay before you entered the room doesn't matter and you won't get past the room.
This was especially annoying when a game session is not a "quick thing" but something that can take hours. Hours of playing well and customization thrown away at the roll of a die. That's not good gameplay.
My suggestion: Find another roguelike that actually feels rewarding without these 'instant death' rooms.

Building a Deus Ex game has to be one of the most frustrating projects in game development.  To live up to what some people call the best game on PC or even of all time is virutually impossible.  That being said, I think Mankind Divided follows in the footsteps of Human Revolution by delivering on what I'd call "fairly close" territory.  The spirit of the franchise continues with planty of cyberpunk twisting stories and environments with a semi-dystopian view of the period lying between Human Revolution and the original Deus Ex.  While I think the writing doesn't quite live up to Human Revolution, it improves upon many mechanics and the feeling of freedom in the gameplay.  Rather than a host of hubs with moderately explorable knooks and crannies, you're relegated to essentially two main hub areas that offer wide collection of secrets to unlock.  Side missions feel more involved than ever and, though it still imparts the standard open world RPG feelng of "shouldn't I really be on the main quest," you'll find yourself running all over reading e-mails and hacking everything with a screen just because it's there.
It's sort of unfair to look to me for a recommendation of this game since this genre is one of my favorites (and sadly one of the least populated), but I can say if you ignore the stupid microtransaction forced in by the publisher, it's really a fun experience that delivers plenty of bang for the buck.  Especially if it's in a decent sale.

Most superhero games have fluctuated in quality for the most part, from the horrible, to the somewhat enjoyable quality.
While Batman games have had a far more generous treatment than Superman's (Superman 64 anyone?) one can hardly say that these games have ever been as amazing as they should be.
Well, up until Batman: Arkham Asylum. Yes, finally. This game not only portrays the Batman universe accurately and with detail, it does the one most important thing. It makes us feel like the Batman.
Everything about this game screams high quality. From the detailed menus, to the flawless fun combat, it remains true to Batman and gives the genre the epicness it deserves.
Let's begin. Arkham Asylum basically starts with you, the Batman, apprehending the Joker and taking him into custody into this facility dedicated to rehabilitating psychos, which Gotham is home to many. However, the Joker had a plan up its sleeve, and you'll have to stop him before he, his henchmen, and many other villains from wreaking havoc upon Gotham. The plot may be pretty standard, but it's excellently done.
The voice acting is phenomenal, as is the immersive scenes you'll come across. The villains themselves are many, some with their own hidden agenda, some well known such as Harley Quinn, the Joker, or Poison Ivy, to some more obscure ones reserved for avid fans. It's great to see them all so accurately portrayed, given how diverse Batman's opponents are throughout his long history of crimefighting.
The Asylum itself is actually pretty big. Beyond the various facilities, the entire island is available for you to explore, albeit sections of it may be closed off either for plot purposes, or because you're missing a certain gadget or skill in order to be able to reach them. This, combined with the rather closed and linear feel of the game overall, gives it a pretty big Castlevania vibe. You'll notice areas wondering how to get to, until you get that one gadget and then it just clicks with your brain, allowing you to get there.
But is the exploration worth it? Yes, yes it is. The game rewards you lavishly for exploration, as all games should. The main part of the collectibles make sense in the Batman lore, as it turns out the Riddler himself has planted them all over the Asylum, and as his namesake demands, also  placed riddles for you to solve. He will start out sarcastically complimenting you as you solve the first ones, gradually becoming nervous and afraid you'll solve them all as you progress further. It's great fun just hearing his reactions couples with juicy collectibles, like optional challenges, character biographies providing detailed insight into each character in the Batman mythos. Other collectibles include recording tapes from interviews made by the medical personnel to certain villains, letting you know just a bit more about them.
This is all fine and good, but I could not end this review without talking about the strongest point of this game, its phenomenal gameplay. It plays so well on the PC it's unreal. Kicking groups of thugs, dodging about, sneaking up on them and taking them out. The AI's great, they'll actually freak out if you're good and take them out one at a time.
It feels like you're the Batman, I can't stress this enough. And that's exactly what these games should be about. Can't wait to get my hands on Arkham City. Arkham Asylum is a must play, and even if you don't care about Batman, you'll end up loving it.

Ghost Recon is one of the all time classics of the tactical FPS genre. I have played this game many times over since the early 2000s, and it still plays great. Even if the graphics are slightly dated, the game play more than makes up for it. You have to be smart and tactical in your approach to combat and as such this game is a rarity nowadays. If you don’t plan the approach, more often than not, you will be spotted and taken out. This is also an open map style game so you can achieve your objectives from many angles, only helping its tactical appeal. Another interesting aspect is the ‘command map’ in which you can control other squads and have them move as a separate entity. Each squad has maximum of three members and you can have 3 squads but a max of 6 total characters. Each of these characters is playable through selecting him or her in the command interface.
This game truly is the pinnacle of the genre so if you’re not hung up on graphics but are interested in realistic combat, then this is definitely the game for you.

Overall a fantastic game in my opinion. The gameplay and the way you interact with the enemies is really done in a way i've never seen before. However the graphics are lacking a bit, and the game is rather short. Like i said though, I think that despite a few shortcomings it really is a great game.

The game play mostly consists of 2 things: climbing and combat. Both are done a bit differently than usual.
For climbing there is this whole stamina mechanic. The time you can spend hanging is limited and all actions drain it, some more than others, which can make things tense as your last strength fades and you are about to fall to your doom. So just plan your path when you can and rely on your wits when you can't.
Combat is more tactical. A bullet is enough to kill. But those are rare and valuable. Thus it boils down to how many guys you can take out with the least amount of bullets. There are some options to achieve this, mostly through scare mechanic - pointing your gun at the enemy and manipulating them to some degree. Also, don't worry about missing your shots - the auto-aim is strong in this one.
The story is simple and straight-forward. Optional exploring exists, but it's quite minimal. Visuals may look ugly at first, but the whole feel of it helps getting into the atmosphere. The one word that will come to your mind when reminded of this game will probably be ''gray''.
If you have read this far and plan on playing, I can offer you these 2 tips:
- Don't torture yourself too much with exploring the dust filled, lower streets. You will
later on.
- Helping the mysterious stranger will yield a cool and powerful weapon, which widens your combat options. Use it wisely.

TLDR; Brilliant game. Be ready to spend money eventually. If you enjoy Tolkien/Middle Earth, give it a go. You will get sucked in. 15/10, would play forever.
My hours on record is off. I've been plaing at least 650-700+ hours, on and off, over the last 4-5 years. I'm a casual player, I don't grind, but I LOVE this game! If you're a Tolkien/Middle Earth fan at all, you NEED to try out this game! Immersing myself with a character backstory and "living" in the scenery of Middle Earth is the best thing about it. The graphics are gorgeous, the music is phenominal. The storyline is a mix of following the Fellowship and a fictional side storyline, but everything still intertwines and works together.
The game is (mostly) free to play. There are in-game transaction options to help progress your story, character, and level better, however none of these are mandatory. Everything is OPTIONAL. You are able to grind for "LOTRPoints" to afford in-game items instead of paying for them, which I personally did for quite a while before buying anything, and waited even longer before I decided paying for a VIP account was worth it (which again, is optional. VIP doesn't really give you much of any bonus for shelling out the money for it). Some sections of territory are locked to any quests, though you can still freeroam around the lands with no problem. Have fun exploring! However you WILL run into a wall in your storyline/quests between East and West Rohan (right before you hit Edoras), and at that point you have to buy expansion packs, or become a VIP member to get free access to Rohan and Gondor, although once you reach that point, you'll have hopefully played enough of the game to realise if you want to keep going or not and spend the money.
There are TONS to do and explore in this game! You can run into all the traditional characters and iconic locations around Middle Earth if you're interested in easter eggs and lore. You can power your way through the game for free with grinding kills and leveling up your character without paying a single cent. You can spend the money to jump your character to near the current level cap (95/115) and get straight into quests levels of Gondor. There's plenty of races and classes to mix and match choose from (some paid, most free), and fun seasonal festivals to collect limited edition items which bring the entire server community together! Roleplay specific servers, international servers, etc.
With the game being out for as long as it has, it's just now released access into Mordor. I, myself, am worried that it'll be the end of everything now that this main storyline is more or less finished, but I also have fingers crossed that they'll expand on a post-Hobbit storyline and introduce Mirkwood/Long Lake/Lonely Mountian exploration. However, if they don't, you need to get in on playing LOTRO now before they shut down the game completely and you miss the entire experience! 15/10 Would play forever.

A perfect Batman game....

What on earth can I say about this game to convey how awesome it is? I don't know what to even start with. But let's start with the total revamp of Batman's world; everyone from major players like Two-Face to obscure baddies like Calendar Man get references in the game, with clear signs of their presence within this world. Arkham feels like it should while overrun by the inmates, with everything from the PA system to the foliage turned against the Dark Knight. And oh how Batman has changed. He's still the righteous, self-sacrificing hero we all know, but now he's gotten an upgrade: brand-spanking new tech. And not only that, but the game finally lets us control Batman in combat as he should be; no more clumsy high kicks like in the old side-scrollers, or even the stiff moves in MK/DC. No, now he has an array of combat moves so big I'm not sure anyone could possibly get them all, and they all are guided by the combat system so that you feel like Batman, orchestrating the ballet of combat while letting your training and reflexes do most of the work. The gliding is spectacular too; despite the achievement for it, you'll find yourself wanting to get to the highest point in the asylum and glide for whole minutes around, just enjoying the feeling of flying high above the ground. But, as much as I love this game, I feel almost obligated to warn of the few major downs. For one, get used to seeing the world in blue and orange, because detective mode is the most addicting thing in any game I've ever played, besides maybe the Konami Code. Also, I hope your stomach doesn't quiver when thinking of grotesquely mutilated body parts sticking through the floor and walls, because the physics are hyper-realistic, but bug out easily, causing thugs to suddenly become marrionettes in the hands of some twisted, sadistic god in the machine. And, I'm sorry, but this was the worst final boss in the history of final bosses. After all the excitement and action of the game, it comes down to a boss fight you can't wait for... Until you realize that it's not a real final boss fight, but an almost exact repeat of an earlier boss. The replay value of this game is also extrememly low, as the island is almost deserted after you've completed the Riddler Challenges (which aren't that challenging). And, much as I hate to say it, even the extra challenge maps get either boring or impossible quickly, and after a few hours of frustratingly trying to do that one perfect thing and failing every time, you will inevitably end up going back through the story, hoping for something better and new. All in all, the game is definitely recommendable, BUT I would just like to caution any non-Batman fans: a lot of the references and jokes are going to go sailing way high over your head. Also, if you do buy this game and aren't satisfied, or don't like the negative comments I've made, buy the sequel instead; the story is easy to pick up on, and the studio fixed literally every single problem I listed. I certainly hope this was helpful, and have fun Batmaning!

Survivor Squad: Gauntlets is a game I would describe as a Top Down Squad-Based Action Strategy Game.
(My my, that's a lot of genres smushed together, isn't it?)
But of course, as much as it's mashed together, it's an appropriate description. Survivor Squad: Gauntlets is a game where you control a single or group of 'survivors' in real time. You can tell them to perform actions, and they also have their own passive AI that can be adjusted in behavior depending on the situation or task at hand. The controls are very simple, but show enough complexity that you can be clever with your strategy. The main goal is to eliminate all enemies (zombies in this case) and survive till the end of the level. Sounds simple, right? Well dependant on the level, sometimes it will become a little more difficult to defend your survivors, putting them through a 'Gauntlet' of sorts, hence the title. Smart decisions and positioning matter a lot, as do who has what weapon where, and the like.
Oh and of course, I forgot to mention one of the most important features. The level editor. Yes, the game comes with a level editor, and it's very well put together. It's easy to understand, yet rather in depth and has a lot of content to it to truly make your own 'Gauntlet', if you will. This is where I think the game truly shines, in that, you, the devs, and the community can make this game grow by developing their own levels and posting them for other people to try. Similarly to how the game "Happy Wheels" grew to fame is because it featured a level editor with some rather basic gameplay.
Overall, the game is good, especially for the price point at $8.99 USD or your regional equivalent. I'd recommend picking it up, and playing around with it. The programming work put into this game is great, and I do support the dev in his hard work!

Survivor Squad: Gaunlets is a top down, zombie horde survival game, with various "gauntlets" (challenges/missions) to complete. At the conclusion of each Gauntlet, you'll get a chance to view details of the gauntlet, edit it to see how it works, and comment on the gauntlet, before moving onto the next one. There are many community made gauntlets that are available for Survivor Squad, extending replayability and also difficulty. I really like the graphics, simple and clean, sort of cartoonesque. The sounds are good, and do add to the ambiance. Gameplay wise, it has simple controls (Mostly RMB) and a fog (well black sections of the map) which "unfog" as the survivors move about (or their view changes)- so you do get lots of "surprises"! Line of sight is very important! It is a challenging game, and lots of fun. For me, it's a new spin on the zombie survival games of today. With only two hours on the clock, I haven't yet seen all this game has to offer, but right off the bat, I'd recommended it as a good title to add to your library. If your a modder, maybe the gauntlets could give you, your next editing experience?

This game is loaded with pros. There's a great story with great voice acting that is true to all the characters. Parts of the story revolving around Scarecrow are very creepy.
Combat is excellent. I love the various ways Batman attacks, counters, and evades all into combo chains. There are 20 upgrades available to your attack, armor, and tools, though I only found about half worthwhile. On the final blow in many combo chains, there are cinematic animations that zoom in on the knockout blows. You can attack from above, below, around corners.
Boss battles are varied. Scarecrow levels are unique as they are a completely different gameplay mechanic that is a bit more 2D. Objectives are clear with map markers to point you in the right direction. The battle with Killer Croc wasn't what I was expecting, and I mean that in a good way. Strangely, the final battle is probably the easiest in the game.
One of the best aspects of the game is exploration. You can crawl through ventilation systems, find structural weaknesses to tear down or blast your way through, and countless places to fire your grappling hook into. And there are 240 challenges to solve from the Riddler scattered throughout Arkham Island. Many of these lead to back story and character bios. Others unlock new challenge modes.
Graphics are great, though the faces on the characters could use a bit of work. I have Radeon HD 6350 graphics built in to the motherboard, 8 GB of RAM, and an AMD Quad Core 3620, which was one of the cheaper desktops I could find in summer 2012. Nothing fancy, and I was able to max out all graphics settings without a glitch. I couldn't enable the enhanced physics, since it seems to only let you set that if you have specific Nvidia cards.
My only real complaint about this game is that the controls can be a pain sometimes. I used keyboard + mouse and Batman didn't always do what I wanted him to. This was a negligible issue though.
Looking forward to starting Arkham City.

I played this game when it was released, and I was young and stupid so I died every couple of minutes and got frustrated. Re-installed it in 2006 and oh boy, what a joy it was !
► The graphics don't matter here, it's a 2001 game so you can't expect much but you can set it to high resolutions. The good thing about its graphic engine it's the way in which both the enemies and your team can blend in a huge variety of environments. It is sometimes very hard to tell an enemy from a bush for instance, forcing the player to advance slowly, recon the area with the right team member, use the binoculars or the sniper before assaulting a given objective. Despite its age the game provides you with a great variety of environments starting with open woodlands under clear sky, cities, farming areas at night, snowy mountains, foggy marshes with low visiblity ahead and so on. And if that's not enough for you there's Desert Siege and Island Thunder , the game's two add-ons, adding desert environments ( DUH ) and treacherous jungles. This kind of variety is rarely seen in most tactical shooters , making Ghost Recon a must have for any player who likes the genre.
► The A.I is also great. You may experience some pathfinding problems with some of your squad members ( especially in closed environements such as houses - they sometimes get stuck behind a table or block your way upstairs, which is annoying but it doesn't happen that often , you may even finish the game without having these problems. But then again you can control any of your squad members and get them out of the way. ) The enemies have good reactions when a firefight starts, you will see them splitting up instead of sticking together like magnets or just married couples. They will try to get behind you, they advance a little, they stop for a few moments, they go right, they go left and you cannot predict the path they will take in order to find you and kill you. So hiding behind a rock and waiting for 20 russians to pop in one by one so you can shoot them is a no-no. Even in easy difficulty you'll find it challenging ( especially if it's your first time trying this game ).
► Speaking of challenging, let me say a few words about something I didn't like in this game. You can save your games. Now it might sound stupid but save game options for this genre tend to ruin the experience a little bit. It is way more rewarding to finish a mission without saving your progress, it forces you to think twice before doing something, but if you fail 30 seconds before completing the last objective then it is very frustrating to start it all over again. Saving your progress is good for players who are new to tactical shooters, but the more experienced you get the less help you want to get from the game. And speaking about help, there's a radar at the bottom of the screen telling you if there are enemies around you. It doesn't tell you the number of enemies, the small circle turns red if you're approaching an enemy ( or being approached by it ). It also tells you from which direction the gunshots are coming, which is another small cheat. The problem with these tools is that they are distracting. I sometimes get shot because I spend half a second watching my radar to check the coming direction of the gunshots. Other than that, the HUD is alright, it shows your stance, level of injuries, remaining ammo and weapon used. The remaining ammunition in the magazines is another thing that should have been removed..
► Overall the gameplay is good, simple but effective. You can bring up to six Ghosts to the battle, and assign them to Alpha, Bravo and Charlie squads. This gives room for nice pre-planning, you can therefore create a recon squad equiped with silenced weapons, an assault squad carrying assault rifles ( DUH ) and a sniper squad involving the sniper himself and a teamate to protect his back. This is one example among many you can use before pressing the start button. During the mission, you also have access to a tactical map, which is actually a very basic one offering you the possibility to adopt different behaviours ( Assault - fire at will /// Recon - Don't shoot /// and so on ) . You can assign waypoints to the teams allowing you to coordinate an assault for instance. But then again, careful with that tool, if the squad you're not controlling gets stuck behind a rock... there goes you planning. The map could have been greatly improved but it hasn't been, and that's a shame. Finally, the map menu also shows where your troopers have been injured. Being shot in the leg will make the Ghost move slower or will be forced to walk, whereas  an injured arm will greatly reduce his ability to shoot accurately. The objectives you have to complete stretch from capturing a high profile colonel ( and bring it back to the base - yes, you will have to go all the way back to the insertion area so pay attention more tangos incoming !! ) , blowing up planes, clearing an old castle's courtyard, assaulting a farm and a house, destroying tanks, rescuing NATO soldiers and so on and so forth. The diversity of Ghost Recon is amazing for such an old game !
► It comes with 15 singleplayer missions , which is not that much but if you buy the add-ons you'll have enough for weeks . It also has a multiplayer, which I haven't tried, yet. You can also replay the missions, trying different approaches, using different squad members such as specialists ( you can unlock them by completing side objectives and they are very valuable squad members, they come with higher skills in every domain ( stealth, weapons, command, endurance ). You can upgrade the skills of each Ghost by assigning skill points, earned at the end of each mission. I recommend to upgrade the stealth skill as much as possible, I'm just saying...
As a conclusion I would say that this is one of the best tactical shooters out there, and it comes at a cheap price ! What else do you need ?

DE:MD is very much like its predecessor, Human Revolution, in all the good and all the bad ways.  It shares the same gameplay and the same mechanics. It shares the same shiny gold aesthetic and the same weapons. There's the same 50 hours of game play.
So, I think the primary determinant of if you're going to enjoy this game or not is if you enjoyed Human Revolution, because aside from the updated visuals and different story arc, this is the same game.
I'm very much on the fence about Deus Ex games. I love love LOVE the visuals. I love the architecture and the design and even the fashion. I love the world it describes. But I have a really hard time with the gameplay. Although the very first question this game asks -- again, just like DE:HR -- is if you want to be leathal or not, it turns out that the game really *really* wants you to go full-stealth, and the sooner you bend to the game's will, the quicker you'll find enjoyment. It drives me crazy that the game hands you a sniper rifle, then won't let you use it.
The main story arc is a little over-baked, while the side-missions are still raw. The forced story-choices are sort of ham-fisted. They'd be better to just ask, "Press A for the Bad Ending, and Press B for the Other Bad Ending."
I spent far too much of the game save-spamming, and had to rage-quit a few times. I spent the usual time lugging around weapons I'd never actually get to use, while balancing out the storage space constraints of the same. But in the end, I enjoyed my 50 hours of game.
This is easily a $30 game. But because it insists on driving you through a story with limited forks, the replayability is lacking. The spaces, though large, aren't large enough to really incentivize exploration, and even my usual completionist feelings were pretty easy to submerge.  This is no Skyrim, no Far Cry, but it's worth playing.

Ascendant isn't a terrible game... it's just not a very good one. The combat system is fun at its core, and I like the way it gives you slightly more control over your items than some games, but repetition kills it. You're forced to kill the same enemies so many times that it becomes hollow--especially since you can almost always pick them off a few at a time, and 75% of enemies in every room are either flies or normal grunts. And you're forced to replay the same levels over because the difficulty is very high. And there's not enough bosses either, so you'll face the same ones almost every run; nor are the bosses remotely balanced against each other (one of the early bosses you can kill unscratched on your first try, another one is ludicrously difficult even with great items and a full health bar).
Production values don't help it--the soundtrack and graphics are both totally forgettable, and you will get bored of the appearance of the early levels very quickly.
It's plainly, painfully obvious that this game is trying to be The Binding Of Isaac as a sidescroller. But ultimately, you're better off just replaying Isaac again.

I was a big fan of Diablo 2 back then and played it a ton, so I was looking for a similar game. I wanted an Action RPG which captured the same feeling and enjoyement you got while playing Diablo 2. Torchlight 2 basically does that perfectly, but even improves on a lot of the bad aspects Diablo 2 had and turns them into good ones.
For example, remember how limited the inventory space was in Diablo 2? Well, in Torchlight 2 you get an animal companion, which will not only fight for you, but also has its own inventory space and you can send it back to town to sell all the items in its inventory on its own just be the click of a button. This is honestly an amazing addition in my opinion and only one of the many additions this game has to offer.
Aside from that, Torchlight 2 at its core is a pretty standard Action RPG. You got your classes, your skill trees and you hack and slay your way through big maps while solving quests. But it does all of this extremely good and really captures the feel a ARPG should have. The combat - the most important aspect of an ARPG - feels extremely satisfying.
The only negative thing I have to say about this game is that it only features 4 classes. All of these classes are really fleshed out and feature three skill trees, which lead to a huge amount of combinable skills and several viable builds, but I still would have wished for some more variety.
If you are a fan of ARPGs or if you liked Diablo 2 and want a similar game, Torchlight 2 is a damn good game you should definitely check out.

I Am Alive was the very reason I started using the screenshot taking feature Steam offers. Probably most of the pictures I took were uploaded for this game only. I am still perplexed why people call this game ugly. It's environment is simply gorgeous. I look at the big picture here not tiny details such as not near perfect antialiasing or the highest HD textures available in current generation video games. Simply the city our protagonist arrives to looks stunning and depressing and superb. This desolate city is characterised by grey and white colours due to the fog, dust and toxic waste present and the beams of the sun shining through the sky are the most beautiful I have ever seen in a video game. Those being more expert in this area will probably challenge me - I have found this game visually stunning, regardless. I took numerous pictures especially when you climb the skyscrapers - those sequences are outstanding.
Gameplay-wise I Am Alive is a rather difficult TPS game. Even a single enemy can easily kill you. You have melee weapons at your disposal and any firearms you have provide you only with limited ammo. You need to plan every single encounter very carefully. The only letdown when it comes to this game its shortness. It can be completed in 5 or 6 hours with all side missions completed and collectibles obtained. Still, it is forgivable considering the budget was rather low for this one and also it's easy to catch this gem at a discounted price.

This is  a lost oppertunity for Paradox. If you've played the orginal then you will know the appeal of the a game which combines the best of Civilization with elements from the 90s "Master of Magic" and Stardock's more recent Fallen Enchantress. The  Warlock series is steeped in Ardanian lore from games such as the Majesty collection and so has quite a bit of inspiration to draw from. And this, sadly is where Warlock 2 falls short. It is little more than a carbon copy of the orginal with a few changes to the mechanics, some additional units, races and spells. As some have already posted it's more like a combo DLC than a stand alone game. Paradox could have done so much more by expanding gameplay, improving diplomacy and building on the mid and late game events introduced in the Armageddon expansion from the first Warlock game. It is clear that the game engine is the same as the original however.
The game is also buggy even as of the latest patch with, in my experiance at least, constant crashes, freezes and stalled AI turns. The AI, is also somewhat flawed and does not give the level of challenge in later stages of the game that you would want. By around turn 80 you know who is going to win. Your greatest challenge mostly comes from the monster lairs and the occasional random event.
So should you pay for this?  Well it depends. If you like the Civ-type game with magical elements then yes you probably will find it interesting for a while and you will get a moderate amount of replayability. If you are a fan of the orginal and are looking for some modest evolutionary changes, then again you will continue to enjoy the franchise. If you, like myself, are looking for the next step in magic based strategy games with lots of intricate gameplay, deep diplomacy and challenging AI then you will be disappointed.
For those who do play I would strongly recommend the Renaissance Mod from Chumley - it's practically a DLC in its own right. You can find it here:

It's easy to tell if a developer puts care, ethusiasm and energy into a release and when they just phone it in for the sake of a few dollars. I never recommend paying full price for games which fall into the later category and unfortunately Paradox on this occasion are well and truely in this space. There is only one sure fire way to make developers take notice and thats through poor sales. At the time of this review, the game is several years old. I would suspect that you can pick it up on sale or relatively cheaply.

(Full Disclosure: The developer is a friend of mine and I provided some voice acting in this game. With that said, I can recommend this game in good conscience because I think it's genuinely fun, challenging and well-designed. It has a lot more content than many of its survive-the-night peers like Wick, Emily Wants To Play and Sophie's Curse, to boot.)
"Night Blights" is a survive-the-night game that combines Five Nights at Freddy's time management with 3D exploration. You play as a child, seeking to protect their family from home invasion by pesky, hungry Blight monsters who would love to eat your family but will settle for eating toys instead - provided you feed them in time. The game features seven levels in the core campaign, plus a survival mode and unlockable extras via a star rating system for each level.
I've played a lot of games in this style, some of which I mentioned in the disclaimer. Night Blights is, by far, the most content-rich of all of them. Each level brings new threats to the fold - on the first night, you'll have just a couple things to keep track of. By the second, you'll have a couple more. By the third, a couple more.
The objectives stack as new areas of the house are unlocked, and it provides a decent challenge curve without growing repetitive. With each new challenge comes a wrench to your previous strategy, and winning subsequent nights requires adjustment.
Like any game, Night Blights is not flawless. The platforming (Yes, there is platforming - one of the many ways this game stands out from its peers) is a little rough, and grabbing objects like toys or stools can feel too slippery. Minor complaints and personal frustrations aside, the game controls magnificently overall for a two-dev game that tries to do as much as Night Blights does.
Couple things before closing out: 1) This is not supposed to be a super-serious horror game. The main attraction for the game is gameplay and fun. 2) If you played the free GameJolt version of this game released last summer - Yes, the Steam version is MUCH different and is definitely worth $5.
Overall, I'd recommend this to anyone who like this style of gameplay. Come one, come all, disenfranchised FNAF fans! In all seriousness, "Night Blights" is much more than its time-management mechanics. At its core, it is a fun, light-hearted B-movie homage that was treated with plenty of care and attention to detail, and features more than enough content to warrant the price tag.

Night Blights is a "Horror" Game, which at first glance looks really similiar to FNaF4, however it came out originally before FNaF4 did, and the game itself is completely different.
I've originally played this game when it was released on Gamejolt, and it was a really great experience. The Steam version is a lot more polished, has more features, and is in general a lot better, that's why I recommend buying it.
Now, the "horror" here isn't supposed to be taken COMPLETELY seriously. The game can be scary, however it focuses more on gameplay mechanics, that being scary. So if you're looking for the same horror experience  like in Amnesia or SOMA, you're out of luck.
Now, each night of the game, it becomes harder, and more ways for the Blights to enter your house are added. You will have to take strategies to where organize the toys, which path should you take first if a Blight is about to enter from 2 different entrances, and such. The fact that you have to constantly do things, or you will die, is giving a lot of tension to the game, making it more exciting, and adds to the scary factor. This game, I can guarantee, is not a jumpscare fest.
During the nights, various things can happen, such as a painting falling, or a Blight just staring at you from the top of a staircase. These little things add a lot to games like this, and make it a lot better.
There's also a Survival mode and Free Roam mode here, which gives the game more replayability, so you can come back to it just to play for fun and try to survive the longest.
In other words, Night Blights is a Horror game which focuses more on the gameplay factor than the horror, and in result provides great gameplay, with simple, yet good mechanics.
So if you like the FNaF Games, or just want a small bit of scares, I recommend this game greatly. I only have less than a hour on Steam as of right now, but I spent a lot of time on the Gamejolt version, and I definitely say its worth it.

If you like the old school serious sam point and shoot intense FPS shooter with tons of enemies and twitch actions, then you will like this game. Very smooth. Very simple. It works.
It also has the graphical vibe of Orcs Must Die. The shooting component is similar but without the traps and enemies are more focused on you as opposed to hitting the exit. The AI is not complex, many enemies just stand or move around towards you in a predictable pattern/speed. They will shoot patterned shots at you, in mass, that with skill you can avoid. There are bosses that will have unique spells/abilities.
This game is easy to drop into and out of. You don't need a ton of time to play. Overall I would say it is pretty casual. There is no story. No commitment.
You can upgrade your character with light RPG like impacts that have some effect on playstyle. You can also unlock new characters that also effect playstyle. Kind of like orcs must die skill trees really. There are definite things this and orcs must die have identicle. It is a great game, with a distinct feel, like a blend of serious sam and orcs must die is exactly what it is. If you have played both of those games, and liked both of those games, and you mashed them together, then this is it, and you will most likely like this as well.
But because of so many of the identicle components found in orcs must die, I have to deduct a star, even for the price.
Also it crashed on me when another program forced it into window mode just now. And there is no really noticable battle music, although that could be a plus for some, if there is any music, I don't remeber any, and while I didn't notice it detracting from the atmosphere, and generally the sound was good from the minions and spells, I would say the music feels non-existant.
I don't regret the purchase (got it on sale for around $5 I think), it is nice and casual shooter with solid mechanics, nice graphics, and smooth gameplay. I'd say the metascore in the 70's range is accurate.

Ziggurat is a fast-paced FPS roguelike where you play as one of many Sorcerer's that has to ascend 'the Ziggurat' to prove your worth of becoming a powerful wizard.
The story is interesting; you are an eager Sorcerer that believes you're ready to participate in 'the Ziggurat'. A test in which you prove your worth to the Daedolon Brothers, the most powerul wizard guild that rules the lands. But be forewarned the journey is far from easy and very few manage to get out of the dangerous fortress alive; only the strongest will make it - usually not without physical or mental wounds.
Before you start your journey you have to choose between a variety of characters, each favours a certain playstyle. After deciding who you want to be you're thrown into 'the Ziggurat', which is made up of five randomly generated floors with various types of rooms. Your goal is to find the key room on each floor to open the portal in the boss room. On the way you'll find one of many artifcats which are your weapons. While fighting monsters they drop MAGIC orbs which is your ammo and EXP orbs. Once you level up you get to choose from one of three random perks to build your character.
The controls are very easy to get used to and everything you do just feels so smooth, you can either walk or run and have an option to do a quick-turn. If you want you can fully rebind everything if the basic layout bothers you and the game plays fairly well with a controller if you prefer that.
Graphically this game doesn't fail to impress, it's cartoony yet dark; silly but serious at the same time and you can really tell the developers put a lot of love into the art-style they went with. Each floor has its own unique aesthetic that really helps to bring 'the Ziggurat' to life and make it an enjoyable experience.
I also found the soundtrack to be pretty enjoyable, it's nothing ear shatteringly amazing but it is really well done.
This game offers a surprising amount of replay value to it for those who wish to play multiple times. There's over 10 characters to unlock, more than 100 perks and numerous weapon unlocks in the game as well as a decent enemy variety. Rooms can have a modifier that is either negative or positive to the player. Also there's three difficulties; easy, normal, hard as well as an "endless mode".
I would highly recommend this game to anyone that's a fan of roguelikes and knows what they're getting themselves into; it has a lot of depth and content to keep you coming back for more. If you're not into roguelikes or not really sure but think the game looks interesting then pick it up on a sale, you won't regret it.

An old, but still very good tactical game. You control a squad of elite soldiers with their own stats that will improve over time. The game has perma-death so you'll have to be careful with your veterans or else they'll be replaced by rookies.
The game is also fairly hard for todays standards if you play on normal/hard. You get killed in 1-3 shots, so you must use your brain. If you survive a shot you may get penalties, like moving much slower or being easier to detect.
In my experience this is an harsh game where you constantly have to think of how to make your squad survive the next mission, instead of just blowing things up 24/7. If you can look past the graphics it's a very nice tactical experience, particularily in co-op.
There's a mod called "Heroes Unleashed" that will add more than twice as many weapons to the game, fixing the weapons variety issue.
One of the best tactical shooters on the planet.

Ghost Recon is a realistic tactical shooter with squad control, similar to Rainbow Six Rogue Spear, but different in that it is more "play as you go" and depicts U.S. Army Special Forces fighting out in the open instead of the more methodical preplanned close quarters counter terrorist manuevers.
I'll compare this to its rivals; "Operation Flashpoint: Cold War Crisis" / "Arma: Cold war Assault" and "Delta Force: Land Warrior".
This game costs around $10 without the two expansions, $20 with, and isn't on sale frequently. DF:LW has the same price, but includes more missions and a greater number of larger and more diverse maps. OFP/Arma ranges from $6 to free, goes on sale frequently, and has much larger maps that are fewer in number (though commmunity maps for ARMA outnumber GR's).
GR controls are simpler, but more limiting than OFP/Arma and DF.
GR total squad and fire team sizes are limited to six and three, respectively, while the OFP/Arma limit is twelve for each category and even has a high command module allowing for control of more.
Squad control is less developed than OFP/Arma, but moreso than DF.
GR's smaller numbers of vehicles and craft can't be entered or operated as in OFP/Arma, but they play more of a role than in DF.
The GR tactical map is less informative, and there is no compass, watch, gps, or radio as there are in OFP/Arma.
GR view and engagement distances are shorter, usually being within 130m (though fogless mod can extend that out to 500m).
GR lacks the external ballistics effects of DF and OFP/Arma.
Movement is more restricted in general, though GR allows one to lean whereas the others don't (without mods).
Weaponry and munitions can't be picked up, and total selection is smaller.
GR has wind effects, but no day/night or weather cycle like OFP/Arma.
GR's AI can navigate tight spaces better than the others.

This game is  the best rougelike there is, in my opinion. It incorporates brawler mechanics that keeps the player engaged and consistantly interested; to me it is stronger then the likes of Binding of Isaac, gameplay wise.
The game also succeeds Aesthetically aswell. I was introduced to ancient mythology through picture books and games like Age of Mythology as a kid. These normally carried with them a more classical interpretation of ancient myth that I've grown accustomed to, with mythical creatures portrayed in a more literal sense, and ancient Gods being represented by rennaissance-inspired, realistic portraits.  However Ascendant tackles it's mythology theme in an abstract way that reminds me of Greek Pottery; grande, fantastic tales brought to life with minimal capabilities... and I think it works. The myths of Theseus and Gilgamesh in this game FEEL mythical.
Aside from that, the effort that went into this game oozes out of everything. The Mythological refrences are often abstract and exotic; until playing this game I had never heard of Kamohoalii (The Shark God of Hawaii), or even the existence of an Irish pantheon of dieties which is well represented in this game. Even the tooltip descriptions of blessings and characters are poetic and well written. Clearly the developers put alot of time aside to touch up on the little things and make everything about this game worthy of the players time.
The only real criticisms I have is that the soundtrack, whilst suiting the visuals most of the time, is repetitive and lacking in variety. Also, the Boss variety is severely lacking. The designs for bosses like The Burrower and The Maw and unique bosses like that are exceptional, but the majority of the bosses are just superstrong versions of regular mobs in the game. Boss rooms being a big part of the game, the lack of variety easily halfs replayability for people who don't have the patience to wait for Son of Grunty's shield to go down for the millionth time.
Overall, I think this game, as a first title, is perfect. There isn't anything missing, and what is there is expertly crafted. That, to me, warrants a sequel with funding that allows for the extreme variety this game deserves.

Ascendent is an interesting game that has a lot going for it, and a lot going against it.
Pros:
-Interesting art style
-Good soundtrack
-Good amount of characters with unique attributes
-Variety of weapons and upgrades for your character
-Each run feels unique with different layouts, bosses, and items
Neutral:
-Combat is not the best but it works to an extent
-Controls can be awkward at times but are generally not too bad
Cons:
-Obnoxious boss fights
-Difficutly is overall too high
Summary:
Ascendent is a good game overall but it is flawed in many areas. For example the bosses are quite obnoxious as many of them have shields that make them invincible for a period of time while you get beaten senseless by them. Also some of them have attacks that are really hard to dodge. Another problem is that the game is just too difficult at times. There are a lot of enemeis and a lot of them have hard to dodge attacks. On their own its not too bad but when they are stacked up, you are bound to get hit. Add in the little amount of hearts the game gives you and the obnoxious bosses (where you generally get hurt the most) and you will find you die quite a lot.
But while those points hold the game back, I still had a lot of fun. The game always had me coming back for more because each run felt different and had me going further along in the game. I like the way you power yourself up by gaining blessings from beating bosses or buying them at the shop. Each blessing had a unique power depending on how you used it. Also the weapons were cool and each had a unique effect. I have heard that other people didn't like the controls too much and felt the combat is awkward, and I can't say I disagree, but it didn't ruin the fun for me. While both could be better, they work well enough to enjoy the game. I was originally put off on buying the game due to some of the negative reviews, but I ended up getting this game from a Humble Bundle, and I really enjoyed it. Overall, its a fun game and I do recommend it. It has its problems but if you are not very critical of games or are not too picky, you can learn to overlook them and have fun with what the game does right.

This game has a lot of flaws, but it still manages to create a unique experience unlike anything you've ever played.
Unlike most post-apocalyptic games, you don't have any zombies or monsters to fight. Your biggest enemies are the environment, the lack of resources and the other survivors.
Getting places is hard. Roads are blocked and bridges are broken, and your climbing skills are the only thing keeping you alive. Problem is, you have a very limited amount of stamina that drains every time you climb or run, and when it's drained fully - you fall. As if that's not enough, dust storms make the air outside unbreathable, and when inside the fog your stamina will constantly drain until you die, or reach high ground.
Resources are very limited, and you will rarely have more than 2-3 bullets in your gun. You will often have none. Combat is not based on who shoots faster, but on psychology and bluffing. Raise your hands to let the enemy come near enough for a surprise attack, or aim your empty pistol at him and tell him to back off up to a cliff, then push him over.
This combat system makes you get very creative when fighting 5-6 enemies, since you probably wont have enough bullets to kill them all.
Some survivors will only fight you if you get too close, and backing off will prevent a fight. Others will ask for your help, and you will have to choose wether or not to spare your very limited supplies.
With this combat system and the constant pressure of the draining stamina, this game keeps you stressed throughout it all. And as if that's not enough - you have a limited number of retries before having to restart from the beginning of the chapter!
The game is flawed, though:
Controls can be a bit clunky while climbing, sometimes resulting in a pointless death and waste of retry.
It's not always clear where to go, especially in heavy dust where you can't see♥♥♥♥♥♥ and you might end up walking in circles trying to find the entrance to a building, and it can get quite frustrating.
The story is very lacking. You learn pracitcally nothing about what actually happened and the story just seems to stop rather than end when you finish the game.
While the game is semi-openworld, you have little to no motivation to explore. Yeah, you might find other survivors or some food and water, but is it really worth running around in a dust storm for?
Overall, this game is a solid 8/10 and I highly recommend playing it.

I Am Alive was one of those games for me. It’s sort of a survival game set in a post-apocalyptic United States of America. You play as some guy with a forgettable name after he has walked across the entirety of the United States after “the Event” to find your wife and daughter. I remember when the demo came out and I tried it having mixed feelings about it. You can tell that Ubisoft really wanted to show off the climbing engine they use for Assassin’s Creed in other venues. Unlike Assassin’s Creed where you can use your free running to get around the city in a number of different ways I Am Alive simply has you going on one set path. The climbing and exploration is done well in I Am Alive, the stamina bar was a nice touch. You can only run or climb until you run out of stamina and after that you have to mash the right trigger which will deplete how much stamina you can recover, if not you’ll end up falling to your death. And if that sounds like too daunting of a challenge fear not! You can scavenge different supplies as you make your way through the city like food, water, and medical supplies. So if you’re running out of stamina you can just drink a bottle of water as you’re climbing and you’ll be alright.
Combat is the other major obstacle that you’ll encounter and it wasn’t done as well as I expected. You start off the game with empty pistol and some enemies you intimidate and some you have to kill but it always seems to be random chance. You’ll run into other enemies with guns and even though bullets are really hard to come by and it would seem that you can’t have any more than four bullets in your gun your enemies will have full magazines and extra clips. Combat is messy and I always dreaded walking into a conflict but perhaps that is what the developers were aiming for, trying to drive home how hard it is to survive in a post-apocalyptic world.
I came into I Am Alive being on the fence about it. The demo left a bittersweet taste in my mouth and the entire game isn’t very long at all. The game ended right when things were getting good and I left with more questions than when I began. There are other NPC survivors that you can help by getting them certain resources in exchange for information about your family and maybe doing that would have given a better story ending, I’m not sure I don’t usually strive for 100% completion when I struggle with a core mechanic of gameplay , like combat. I think I Am Alive would work really well as an episodic game with what is already released being the first episode. I thought that they were working with an interesting premise which I wouldn’t mind seeing a little more of once it’s been fine-tuned and had some of the bugs worked out of it.

Set two years after the events of
,
takes place in a world where augmented people have been marginalized to the point of segregation as non-augmented people fear a reprisal of the ‘Aug Incident.’ The truth about the secret organization manipulating events, the Illuminati, never reached the public because it was never transmitted, as
chooses the fourth ending of
to set the stage for Adam Jensen’s newest adventure.
No longer working for David Sarif, as his company went bankrupt and was forced to sell their assets to Tai Yong Medical, Adam finds himself working for an anti-terrorist intelligence and response team known as Task Force 29, determined to put augmented terrorists behind bars. At the same time, Adam’s also secretly working for the Juggernaut Collective, a global hacktivist group that is equally determined to bring the Illuminati secrets into the public eye, led by a man named Janus. It is an interesting situation for our protagonist as he splits his loyalties between the two groups, made even more dangerous by the fact that TF29 has been infiltrated by the Illuminati and Adam doesn’t really know who to trust.
For better or worse however, a terrorist bombing early on in the game diverts the focus of the game to solving this case and putting an end to further terrorists attacks rather than going after the obvious masterminds behind them. There are naturally subtle (and not so subtle) hints that the Illuminati are working behind the scenes in order to spur sentiment against augmented people and Adam eventually finds evidence to that effect but don’t expect any poignant revelations like in
. Indeed, the fact that Adam doesn’t require Neuropozyne given his augmented condition is referred to in passing and dismissed. We do not get to investigate the mystery of White Helix’s research into modifying human DNA nor do we get to finish our chat with Megan Reed, who’s conspicuously absent from
, as is our pilot friend Faridah Malik (whom we fortunately did manage to save in the previous game).
While I must admit that the investigation into the terrorist bombing is not as appealing a premise as looking for the people who nearly killed you and kidnapped your (former) girlfriend, it’s still a competent one that succeeds at creating a more gripping atmosphere than its predecessor. This is partly due to the fact that the whole of
takes place in a single city filled with interesting side missions that constantly reinforce the narrative and change as you enter Act III. Indeed, the ‘side’ missions in
are more often than not very good, so well integrated into the world and events surrounding them that they never felt like a chore to do. At times, I must admit I enjoyed some of them more than the main narrative of the game like ‘01011000′, where you meet an old friend from the previous game; ‘Fade to Black,’ where you investigate the disappearance of a fellow Task Force 29 agent; or ‘The Harvester’ and ‘The Last Harvest,’ two (linked) side missions where you investigate a series of murders and track down a serial killer on the loose.
Of particular note are the headquartes of TF29 that are constantly bustling with activity, even more so after the terrorist attack at the beginning. Whenever I entered that place I felt like people were actually working there and that they had other ops going on while I did my own thing. They even set up a (very pretty) psychiatrist for Adam to talk to (and maybe hook up with?) after the bombing. Competing for Adam’s attention is another fellow (and augmented) TF29 agent, Aria Argento, who unfortunately doesn’t get the chance to join Adam in his investigations. The one who does join Adam for a stroll from time to time is Alex Vega, a former (also augmented) VTOL pilot for Blacktower and his contact in the Juggernaut Collective. I can’t shake the feeling that
would be so much better if it embraced the more investigative side of Adam Jensen and gave him a partner for certain side missions (or even in sections of the main narrative), like in
.
Gameplay-wise it follows the trail laid out by
, with augmented abilities that need to be unlocked and upgraded via praxis kits and the tetris-like inventory management. As before, multiple paths are available to tackle each mission depending on your abilities and even Bosses can be taken down in other ways besides blowing them to kingdom come. Furthermore, the narrative provides a reason why Adam doesn’t keep (or, rather, resets) his abilities from the previous game and introduces even new and very powerful ones, like the TITAN skin and TESLA, that are tied to the mystery of what happened to Adam after he blew up the Panchea facility. This is also explored through another side mission though nowhere near the degree I would’ve liked, instead planting the seeds of intrigue and baiting our curiosity.
Indeed, while
provides a beginning, middle, and an end to the terrorist bombing plot, it still manages to raise many more questions than it conclusively answers regarding the overarching narrative of the Illuminati’s secret agenda and Adam’s place in it. This has understandably bothered many fans who perhaps expected Adam would take a more direct approach in seeking out the masterminds behind the events of
instead of laying out the groundwork for future sequels in
. For my part, the gameplay and atmosphere in
far surpassed its weaker (main) storyline, delivering as good an experience (in some aspects better) as
did in 2011. One can only hope Jensen’s next adventure is not too far off into the future and that we’ll see familiar characters from both entries return to help our favourite augmented cop uncover this worldwide conspiracy.
