What is happening to the gaming industry? We live in an age of almost circular mistrust and exploitation. With piracy and second hand sales apparently ever increasing and a CONTINUAL drain on the potential earnings of game studios, it's time for them to hit back. And they do this with DOWNLOADABLE content.
DOWNLOADABLE content is the scourge of the consumer, a desperate grab for more money from the creators. We know you bought your game, but pay more! Pay more to see the ending, to see the plots, to improve your power... Pay more to complete your experience!
Okay, that might be slightly unbalanced (and not representative of my actual views, that's for another time), but it was only an introduction. It is hardly going to be news to anyone that some of the practices creeping in to gaming are unpopular, or at best divisive. There are some thoughts that, with the birth of microtransactions and freemium set-ups, we are heading toward some sort of dystopian future for games.
That's where DLC Quest comes in! An indie developed 2D platformer which pretty much bases itself in this vision of the future of gaming, where anything you could possibly want in a game comes...as an extra!
Of course, this doesn't mean that the game becomes extortionately expensive, as this is done with tongue planted firmly within the cheek. It serves to ridicule not only the poor practices that are heading this slippery slope, but also other parts of the general gaming world.
DLC Quest offers two separate, but linked, campaigns – DLC Quest and Live Freemium or Die, which are both provided in the package. Fortunately, the developers obviously resisted the urge to forge a bond with the ironic and hypocritical by making Live Freemium or Die into paid downloadable content.
So what's the context behind the parody? Well, in DLC Quest, the player takes control of Player, a sprite-come-hero that is dragged into the the perils of the village, aided in his various quests by the magnanimous shopkeeper offering all sorts of goodies that are necessary for defeating the bad guy and saving the princess and all of the other gaming clichés you can think of. It must be said that DLC Quest is very short and to the point, with some (but not a lot) of exploration to be done before even 100% completion.
Live Freemium or Die is a “direct sequel” of sorts to DLC Quest, and provides a much more fleshed out experience than that of the former. Continuing the rather contrived storyline to this point of DLC Quest, Live Freemium or Die CONTINUES following Player as he investigates a recent string of related deaths in the village, providing a much larger scale of map for exploration and a slightly more directed story than the first part of the duology.
Gameplay-wise, the DLC duo doesn't really do anything to innovate, nor does it do anything particularly wrong. The game plays as a fairly simple 2D platformer, with each game providing a slightly different platforming mechanic to get around with. It must also be noted that Live Freemium or Die adds a little more of the challenge that DLC Quest was pretty much devoid of. That being said, it's hardly Super Meat Boy and won't provide too much of a headache to anyone. This isn't necessarily a bad thing, as it allows many people to enjoy the concept and humour within, but don't come in expecting to be tested.
So if DLC Quest isn't going to win awards for its gameplay, what about the graphics and sounds? Well, once you've unlocked the audio and visual packs, it can be seen that it is a fairly basic affair. The 8-bit visual style pays good homage to the early days of gaming history, whilst the fairly catchy (albeit short, much like the game) chiptune background music also adds to the aesthetic. These provide a great contrast to the issues of modern and future gaming models that the game attempts to address.
So, if you're wanting a AAA blockbuster that's going to provide you with hours of content and the complexities that come with it, then you are looking in the wrong place. If you're wanting a technical masterpiece or keyboard smashing difficulty, then your experience is not here. If, however, you are looking for a short and simple distraction, at only a fraction of the PRICE of a map pack, with plenty of satirical amusement (As such, it could be described as a much more concise version of what Duke Nukem Forever tried to be), then look no further than DLC Quest – and be happy that the industry haven't quite plunged to the depths that the game attests to!

This is the game that started me off with this franchise, and what a game this is. In all honesty this is one of my favorite games of all time - I first owned it on the 360 and played through it 3 or 4 times, and I recently started a playthrough of the whole series to complete the other two and to relieve what has got to be one of my favorite game-universes to date. So I will be a little bit biased.
This game makes a few QOL improvements over the first one. Immediately you'll notice the better-feeling movement, which feels more fluid rather than clunky (that's not to say the clunkiness of the first game's movement was terrible.) The locator system being able to toggle between your objective/bench/store/save station, showing you where the nearest one is at the click of a button. Reloading can be done while you're not aiming, which is a wonderful addition that was sorely missed on my playthrough of the first game. Stasis can now recharge on its own, though this takes awhile and depending on the situation you may want to use a stasis pack - which now stacks up to three rather than single slots in the first one. It also seems that the guns are more responsive with their alternate fire modes, which is welcome in tense moments. Also, the new stomp. Hell yeah.
All around the guns have been improved - a few new ones, reworked alternate fires on some of them, and they just feel great to shoot. Really well animated too, in my opinion even better than the first one's animation. Kinesis is now really effective, being able to impale enemies with rods and other enemy's parts can deal quite a bit of damage and even tear off limbs if aimed correctly - allowing you to save precious ammo on the higher difficulties.
The game is more focused on action rather than horror, but still retains many horror elements from the first. While I'm not a fan of jumpscares (and this series has a lot of those) I don't find myself as annoyed with them as with certain movies or other games. What I recommend trying after the first playthrough, is turning the music all the way off so that it's only ambient sounds and no 'orchestra heart-attacks' every time a necromorph jumps out at you. It's amazing how much work they put into the ambience, and it can make for some very tense traversal because you'll hear something jump out, and not know exactly where it is. The game also uses lighting very effectively - even better than the first one due to the upgraded engine. And some of the redesigns on the necromorphs are just creepy.
The story is good, though I would hesistate to say great because it's not very complex or emotional, but it does have its moments and it's fun to go through. The set pieces aren't the most interactive, but it's fun to see Isaac get thrown around, and some of these set pieces are just so crazy it's fun to see how crazy it gets. I'd even say there's a bit of comedy here and there in the writing; for example, at the end of Chapter 5 there's a crazy set piece where Isaac is thrown about and chased by two different things trying to kill him, gets thrown out into space before finally being launched back into Titan Station via a window. The next line he says is, "What do you want Stross? Look, it's over. All my plans just blew out the window." That is some funny♥♥♥♥♥♥
The game lasts about 10 hours or so on the first playthrough, and depending on how much you're exploring and what difficulty your on it can vary, especially for subsequent playthroughs and ng+. There's new suits and schematics on ng+ so it's definitely worth going through a second time. One thing to keep in mind though is that all of the DLC from the consoles is unlocked from the start on PC, so for the first playthrough it's best to just ignore them so that you don't get the armor and inventory bonus from the start.
On PC the bodies and other physics items can glitch out at 60fps (this is a console port after all), so be warned. The game is also a little too-reliant on jump scares, but you'll get used to it and expect them/get desensitized to them after awhile. It's not the scariest game in the world, but if you play it as an action-game with some horror elements it's a ton of fun. There are quick-time events as well, though I think they're used sparringly enough to not be annoying. Also, if you're looking for a more survival-horror-esque experience, go on one of the higher two difficulties. Otherwise, you will be swimming in ammo and medkits like the opening of Dead Space 3.
Overall, I absolutely love this game. It's not perfect by any means, but it's probably the reason why I love gritty sci-fi and horror, and why creatures like necromorphs just unnerve me to this day. It pains me to see that we won't be getting any more installments or even spin-offs with new characters, but I think it was a good run while it lasted. I guess I'm one of the few that is enjoying my time with the third one so far, and at this point I'll take any new Dead Space experience while I can. If you've never played any of the games in this series, do yourself a favor and give it a shot. These go on sale (1 and 2) quite often, so there's no reason not to get them for cheap and spend a weekend in the shoes of CEC Engineer Isaac Clarke.
Rest in peace, Visceral Games. Thanks for all the fun times.

survivor squad: gauntlets is, simply put, survivor squad + improvements, and most of what i have to say about survivor squad has already been said in my review of the first game. but rather than talking about the first game, lets go into what this game has done to improve and change what survivor squad has already established.
first off, a rather minor thing at best, is the charactors and voice acting, its generally better here, but it is, again, a minor detail.
the aiming machanic is greatly improved (or something i hadn't noticed in the first game due to lack of tutorial*). aiming in this game works better here due to 2 good features, locking aiming direction and moving while looking a specific direction. these 2 abilities allow you to better secure areas and check corners. good things to have in squad based game play.
the inventory system as been reworked a bit, but i hardly noticed due to not having to pick up everything i needed like in the first game.
where the first game was procedural generated, gauntlets allows for user created maps, and knowing how creating some users can be, great things can come from it. but this comes with a slight downside, there was only a few non user created maps (last time i played), meaning that most levels have to be user created. but then again, the map editor is built in, so, get bored, build your own level. simple...
other than that, i've run out of things to say about the game in the rather short time i've played it, it was as simple as the first game and in the end, it felt almost the same in most aspects
*another improvement the devs added was the inclusion of a basic tutorial for basic controls, whereas the first game has a brief opening sceen that allows you to move, nothing more

I would first like to note that this review comes from a free-key that was provided by the developer in exchange for late beta feedback and/or a promised review and they get both out of me, though the fact that the game was free in no way sways my review.
Though never reviewed by me, I have put many hours into the initial Survival Squad and though it had and still has a few quirky behavioral bugs, for the most part it is a solid game that is well worth playing, but this is not a review of the original, but of the second game: Gauntlets.
Gauntlets uses pretty much the same mechanics as the original game and in it you lead up to 4 characters in a pausable real time zombie fighter but with larger possible maps and a small handful of improvements and fixes over the original, as well as other changes.
Though I realize that likely a majority of readers won't understand the comparison and thus I will explain it after, I would compare this game very much to Jagged Alliance: Deadly Games (which is available at GOG at the time of this review). The original Jagged Alliance (already available on Steam) is an open campaign of a game where the player moves between zones and tries to reach the conclusion of an over-arching in a very free-roam open-world environment, which is sort of what Survivor Squad is. Deadly Games, which was the second game in the series was to Jagged Alliance what Gauntlets is to Survivor Squad. It gives up the openworld, free roam format for a more story driven, level or mission based play style that possesses a much more detailed and linear story than the original, which is also much shorter than the original. The campaign it comes with is 6 missions long and I honestly have yet to finish it, but have played enough that I have a good idea of how it plays out. It's fair enough but in itself not enough that I would actually recommend this game. It would be, as many of my reviews a negative review with a caveat that focuses on a specific niche audience that I recommend try it anyway... Gauntlets is more than just a 6 mission campaign that uses a similar engine though.
Survivor Squad: Gauntlets has is a lot more intricate and has a degree of complexity to what can be done with the engine that the original did not reach, including the ability to have much larger maps to play on.
In addition, Survivor Squad: Gauntlets has an editor that lets players use the engine to craft their own missions and campaigns, giving it a much larger possible scope than the developer produced content it starts with and it is for this reason that I'd tilt my verdict from a negative review to a mildly positive one.
In all, at the less than $10 price point, it's worth a try for anyone that likes the zombie-horror and survival genre, and a must-try for anyone that was a fan of the original Survivor Squad and what it may lack in initial content has great potential to be added to by the community as well as additional content from the developer through additional Gauntlets  (or missions) that can easily be found through the game itself and already consists of enough additional Gauntlets to give it much more potential playtime than the handful of challenging missions it starts with.
Though I wouldn't call it one of the best games I've ever played, I would consider it no less of a waste of money than the original was and is definitely entertaining enough to be worth it's price.

Brawlhalla is yet another SSB-esque Brawler, however unlike many other games of it's kind it has some things about it that benefit it very greatly, which are:
+ It is Free2Play AND Free2Win. Yes, you can unlock Legends (Characters) that are not in the current rotation with real money, but you can do so with in-game currency earned by playing too. Plus the game is so ridicolously well balanced that the character that suits YOUR playstyle the best is the best character. PERIOD. (There is one character that is a little stronger than the rest of the cast IMO but it is not broken in any way, trust me.)
+ It is the only brawler where items are actually well suited for competative play. Every match starts with both player's characters being unarmed (bare hands). When unarmed all Legends have the exact same moveset. To get one of the two Weapons your Legend can have you have to pick up a special item which spawns fairly often. You can even throw your Weapon at your opponent for mixups, snipes etc. There are three additional items, none of which are op but certainly help you out if you are practiced at using them
+ The game keeps a good balance between not being too complicated and offering a lot of options so you are never limited to one option
+ There is only one advanced technique (Gravity Cancelling) which is really easy to use. I told my brother how it works and he nailed it almost every time after that right away.
+ It offers a solid variety of game modes so you can either compete with others in bloody serious matches or troll around in Dodgebomb, Bombsketball etc. - There is something for everyone
+ The training mode allows you to choose any Legend, even those that are not currently in the rotation so you can test characters before buying them with your hard earned gold. Plus the training mode has lots of very useful tools (Showing hitboxes, hurtboxes, tag frames and the time your opponent would have to dodge out of your combo, Slow motion, Frame advance - You get the idea.)
+ You can use so-called stances to reduce one point in one of the four stats (Attack, Defense, Dexterity and Speed) to increase another one. This seems marginal at first but might be just the tweak you needed for your main to suit you best.
+ The game automatically records EVERY match you had (Unless there was a patch that changed the Legends involved) so doing compilation videos or video material for tutorials is much more convenient
+ It is only ~300MB big (how is that even possible?!) so you can just quickly download it and have fun. I especially liked this because I am limited to 10GB per month until my connection gets slowed down significantly
Here are some things I dislike about the game (mostly nit picks)
- You have to unlock color palettes and stances for your character by leveling it up. The first is no bother to me, but the latter puts new players in a disadvantage
- Some characters are super easy to spam Signature moves with (Especially the Side Signature of Nix is almost not punishable for instance). Since Ember is in the current rotation this made me very salty until I figured out how to punish it and probably leads to new players chosing exactly this tactic
- The ranked match making is not too good IMO. It is way too easy to smurf and sometimes I get thrown into a 1v1 with players that have 100+ more elo than me. EVERY loss reduces your Elo, no matter how good the opponent was (I once had to fight a Diamond Player with 1500 Elo when I was Bronze with 1200 Elo. I got 3 stocked.)
- ~80% of the community consists of toxic and/or salty idiots. Look at my Profile Page - I played for a little more than two days and already had two comments with people insulting me for beating their♥♥♥♥♥(They both spammed)
Overall this game is still super fun and I recommend it to EVERYONE who likes Super Smash Bros. even a little. However, even if you never played any game of the series this could still be fun to you and if it is not, you did not waste any money.

I wouldn't recommend it unless you can ge♥♥♥♥♥on the cheap and you're really hard up for 2d brawler action. The nods of various mythos and deities and mythologies form a cool framework for the game, and the combat is passably fun for what it tries to do and has a decent skill ceiling, but... I don't know. Just finished this game on Casual level and thought to write a review.  The simple way to review this game is to say that that if you liked Warlock: Master of the Arcane, you will like this game as well.  If you didn't like the first part or haven't played it, but are looking for a turn-based strategy with lots of variety, challenging AI and reward for your strategic decisions, then this is not a game for you. As someone who really enjoyed the first game, I liked this one very much.
I thought to go further and write the differences between this and original game, but other people already covered that and you can read it on internet.  I'll just add a few things that I thought were the worse than in the original, for those people that expect everything to be same or better.
1. Even more than in the original game, the location of your initial capital can make big difference, from a very easy ride, to an impossible to finish.  Don't be shy restarting the game a few times until your capital is in good location.
2. You can safely only control a certain number of cities (starts with 5, but increases as you research some traits to maximum of eleven - yes, like with spells, you can choose to research traits that help you manage your realm).  If you go over this number, people get unhappy which gives penalties and I believe can lead into some sort of riot - I've never got that far.  You can have unlimited number of specialist cities (those that only make gold, or are like a fortress, or temple cities to a deity that improve relations with that deity and produce some mana).  This is really a shame when you conquer some good cities (but still not better than those you already have) - you just have to destroy them, or wait for 10 turns for "plundered" status to disappear before you can convert them to a specialist city.
3. When a building give you perks to use, it's only a limited number of uses.  For example, a smithy will give you only 5 armours, which means you can only give the perk to 5 units.  This is applicable to each smithy, so if you have 2 smithies, that's 10 units to give the perk to.  But with the limited number of cities, you don't want to build smithy in each one.  Not to mention buildings that require a few other buildings to be built before you can have them, like University, or buildings that need a resource tile to be built.  You will never be able to control all resources.  So you have to choose carefully which unit you will give a perk to.  Heroes are the obvious choice, but even with them, a healer lord that stays out of fights may not necessarily need all the armour upgrades.
For the end, there are a few bugs (for example, mass heal spell doesn't heal all the units in the range), but not enough to make the game too frustrating.  I didn't have a single time that the game crushed during the play, so that's obviously a good thing.

I Am Alive had it's highs and lows, although nowhere near perfect, was still a wonderful game...

The parkour was occasionally choppy, espesially with rails on building sides, and anytime you walk past a survivor in need of help, they would repeat their entire problem to you no matter how many times you passed them, and if you walked away to go find what they're looking for, they would say somthing like, "Dammit, knew you couldn't care less. You are a terrible person and you should feel bad." The game itself was linear, and don't get me wrong, linear games are fine, but with this game's "survival" label, I felt too cooped up when the game told me that 'I should't be going there yet' as soon as I veered off the correct street thinking I saw a better way to a destination. Even on the correct route, sometimes there was no breathing room. Fallen rocks and barbed wire barricaded nearly every nook and cranny at certain points.
The game was certainly good, but with every good thing about it comes tiny bad things that add up. Though the color scheme was like no other, but somtimes things just looked drab and colorless; the combat was brilliant, yet a tad repetitive; the story was intriguing, just not developed enough; and the ambient suspence music was great, but goes on and off like a toilet around a group of bored six year-olds. It fades out way too quickley, and if I'm just going for a safe leisurly jog, it sounds like I could be♥♥♥♥♥♥♥any second from behind because my stamina lowered a bit. Perhaps the only element not having a down side was the atmosphere, I can't leave that out.
To finish up, I thought the game's ending was abrupt. There were still unanswered questions and little loose ends that could have been tied with just one or two extra missions. A DLC would be fitting for the wrap up, so I really hope one comes out! If you just skipped to the end of this rambling set of paragraphs, just get the game. It's pretty good.

This has got to be one of the most addicting games I have ever played. Originally recommended by my boyfriend, I decided to try it out and now I've gotten completely addicted to it. Not only are the controls easy to manage and use, but the gameplay itself is extremely entertaining and can keep me hooked for hours. I do wish there were more maps to choose from and the option for even longer rounds (usually when I have the max amount of players and 20+ lives, time runs out before the chance to knock everyone else out completely comes), and maybe even more players. But everything else is great! This game has definitely got to be one of my favorite games, if not my favorite. I love it! I hope to see more characters and maps added in the future. This game is totally worth the time, as it is one of the 4 games I play the most, and I highly recommend it. "Trine 2" is a 3rd person side-scrolling puzzle game that uses 3 uniquely skilled characters within a team. It is hours of mentally stimulating fun with a beautiful visual style and fuild movement. It's so good. Play it for the thoughtfulness but stay all the way to the end for the sheer joy of it.

Pluses and minuses.
+ E for everyone

+ Lots and lots of puzzle solving that can be solved in a variety of ways
+/- This isn't really a pro or a con, but.. playing alone was extremely boring for this type of game, at least for me. I only began to have fun when I was playing with others.

This is a rogue-like FPS dungeon crawler. The action is fast, the enemies are fast, this is not a game for the faint of heart. Hours of replayability, in that you can unlock different mages (stat differences only, no actual cosmetic difference), new weapons to fill 3 of your 4 weapon slots (first slot is always your trusty wand), and the dungeons are randomized every time. Plus, even on the lowest graphical settings, the set pieces are gorgeous, and the monsters are hideous.
Ziggurat is a great game that combines different genres very well; I can't recommend it enough, even though I haven't put much time into it . . . yet.

A fantastic dungeon crawler/FPS hybrid that definitely brings back a lot of memories of the hectic action in Heretic, keeping combat very fast. The concept of progressing via failure is something you have to catch on to at the beginning, since with so few perks and very little experience playing, you're going to die a lot. But you always unlock more stuff, so it is still advancing you further. Once you unlock several characters, you see a lot more of the inherent replay value.
I think the game could still use a "wildcard" build-your-own-character feature, maybe with some points to distribute, and/or a degree of control over what perks might appear, as once everything is unlocked, the game is a pure slot machine. These are minor things though, and you can always end a run if it looks like it's going nowhere. Great fun.

A fast-paced, rougelike, dungeon crawler mage game that shows similarities to The Binding of Isaac.
You are to use 4 different weapons which are gained at each level to fight through the Ziggurat, which no one has survived from. Leveling up will give you perks to use to your advantage to clear rooms with ease. Each floor/game is randomly generated and every enemy has their special kinds of abilities. Bosses are trying to stop you from progressing after you get the portal key to go to the next floor, to survive the Ziggurat.
You have 4 magic weapons to work with: Your trusty wand, spells, staves, and alchemy. Each weapon has their unique ablilities (wand differs with different characters) and has a secondary fire mode, which uses more mana, but is more powerful. Weapons also are unlocked by just playing the game and keeping up your score. Amulets, which are found rarely, gives a temporary, reusable power that will help you tons. Leveling up will give you 2 perks to choose from that either gives benefits or a curse with it, same with offering rooms, where you take your chances of giving mana or health and gaining blessings, indifferences, and curses. To fight the boss, you'll have to find a portal key that is in any random generated room and to progress to the next level. Lore scrolls help you learn about the story, but if you don't care about them, at least they give you the XP.
I'd pick this game up on a sale if you're not thinking to play it that often. It is repetative, but it keeps itself moving with ramdomly generating your games.

Ziggurat- A game I learned about from the one and only Jim Sterling
Ziggurat is one of the few examples of an Early Access game done right (which isn't THAT hard to do!), before and after its official release. It's basically a dugeon-crawler game, but in first-person instead of a top-down perspective.
You're a wizard trying to pass his final tests in order to join an elite guild of wizards. But this isn't a written test like Hogwarts has; it's a matter of LIFE AND DEATH!!!!
Seriously though, Ziggurat is an extremely fun game due to:
+ Uniqueness
+Combat
+Large variety of spells and weapons (like a pistol that shoots out lava)
+Largely detailed environments
+Large variety of monsters to fight
+Fun boss battles
+High replay value (due to multiple characters you can play as)
+You can fight demonic carrots (that'd be funny if every other review on this page didn't say the EXACT SAME THING!!!)
In short, an awesome game.

Drawn Story is a game with potential. It’s also something a little different. A game with a concept where you must literally draw your own solutions. Of course, you are provided with suggestions in some of the puzzles and are left to your own devices to draw them. The title has the potential to create a very enjoyable game and it’s final release is one that I await with anticipation.
The big positive is that the game has the potential to be a very calming and soothing game. Drawing and illustrating has for a long time been considered a relaxing psychological activity. I can definitely see where this has the potential to be perfect in that type of a way. However, at this stage of development it doesn’t provide that sensation for me although the potential is there for everyone to see.
The problems in this stage of development are major sticking points for me and outweigh the game’s potential. First, what you perceive to be as the right solution may not be. It took me about fifty attempts to draw the oar for the boat in the first scene. So many of my drawings the game recognized as sabers, swords or even bombs that killed my special little blue guy resetting the puzzle completely. Ultimately it took me loading a YouTube video before I was able to successfully complete the first level. I would argue that the game has too large a library of images to draw upon at this stage of development. As a result close never feels good enough and that can be eternally frustrating if you’re not the most talented artist or your idea looks the slightest bit different than that of Rekubratskiy.
Further, I have a big problem with the fact that you have to press the control key to actually draw which diverts some attention away from the act of drawing itself. I’m used to playing video games but have never been much of an artist therefore I must qualify what I say as being from the perspective of a gamer rather than that of an illustrator. In fact, back in my school years my art teachers would consistently advise my mother that I was much better off doing other ‘brain work’ (maths, English, sciences, etc.) than sitting in on their classes. Interesting concepts for art work were always in my head but I lacked the technical ability to convert the image onto the paper or whatever craft work we were in the process of working on during that time. I’ve always been much better at the written word. I am reminded of that here because constantly focusing my left hand on control forces me to put less than one hundred percent focus onto what the drawing hand is doing. Surely there are superior ways to enable players to draw than drawing their attention away from this facet.
At this stage the game gets a pass (a tentative negative) from me but is certainly one to keep an eye on.
Note: This review has no bearing on the fact that my first two installs came without an executable file or the DLLs required to run the game. That problem was solved rather quickly.

The game is off to a good start.  The game is normally $8, I bought it when it went on sale.  At such a low price I felt that even if the developer had jumped ship the instant I bought it, I would be getting my money's worth.  The developer has a demo available on their website, and I tried an... "extended demo" before purchasing so I knew what I was getting.
If you haven't played Dwarf Fortress, Gnomoria is a sort of sandbox-y building game; it's like if you owned a Minecraft server and could tell all the players what to do and they had to do what you said.  There are enemies, but you have huge control over the difficulty between choosing what types of enemies can spawn in the world and how tough the enemies are in general.  I recommend checking out this game if you like building/sim games or 4X games.
If you have played Dwarf Fortress, I also recommend giving this game a try.  It may be a clone, but the developer has his own ideas about where to take the game and it doesn't feel like he's just trying to take advantage of an established franchise.  The best thing about this game compared to DF is that the menus are intuitive and easy to navigate.  You won't need any third-party programs to assign jobs to your Gnomes, you won't tear out your hair trying to set-up the military.
In short, although the game isn't finished and lacks extensive content, the pieces that are in place are high enough quality that anyone at all intruiged by the premise would be doing themselves a favor by giving it a chance.

Ascendant is a decent cross between an action platformer and a roguelike, but it's far from perfect or even all that great. Think The Binding of Isaac meets Dust and you'll have a good idea of what you're in for. The game's amateurish art and uninspired sound hardly make for the most aesthetically pleasing package, and the steep learning curve will probably lead some to shelve this one prematurely. If you can stick with the game, however, you'll find that it really is a solid platformer with some relatively deep RPG mechanics and an intelligent procedure for generating levels. This game's biggest problem is that it falls into the same trap that a lot of indie games that attempt to implement roguelike elements fall into: Luck trumps skill in a big way. Ascendant is tough, and like The Binding of Isaac, your odds of success are determined almost entirely by how lucky you got with treasure chests early on in the game. There's a lot going against this one, but it still manages to be a pretty good game.

This game is probably one of the harder games I own. The melee enemies aren't too tough because just using the light attack to weaken them then satisfyingly smashing them with the launch attack does the trick, but I find the projectile-launching enemies are all just stupidly unpredictable a-holes that make the game a frustrating mess of dodging and pinpoint counterattacking.
Let me get one thing straight: The counterattack works. It DOES work, and is very satisfying when pulled off, but doing so is, to quote JonTron, "like trying to pull the addiction out of a heroin addict: HARD AND FRUSTRATING." The window of time on this counter is TINY. Teeny-tiny. You ever play Smash Bros. and find that the counterattack windows are rather short? Well, this game takes the window of time that someone like Marth would have and crushes it with a STEAMroller (get it?). We're talking probably 4-5 frames of counterattack availability. It's annoying when you're playing a game like this that has a lot of unpredictability in the enemy attack patterns, but to throw in a 5-frame counter window is just unecessarily cruel. The counter window CAN be expanded if you happen to find a 4-leaf clover under a blue moon while a shooting star flies over your head and somehow manage to get the weapon enchantment that does so, but I only got that on one playthrough, and died because a projectile-using enemy knocked me into a pit of spikes and killed me, FANCY THAT.
Don't get me wrong: this game IS fun, it's just hard. We're talking giant T-rex turds hard. Adamantium hard. The kind of hard that even a Metapod couldn't achieve and...yeah this metaphor is over.
What I'm saying is, if you're the kind of person who's gotten good at avoiding things in Rogue Legacy, maintaining twitch reflexes in Hotline Miami, and love the roguelike item-collecting enhancement-gaining world of Binding of Isaac, this is your game. Oh yeah, and if you're one of those sadistic f***s that likes Dark Souls, get this game. You'll be (un)pleasantly surprised. Can I say, Prepare to Die? ;)
Thanks for reading!
TL:DR This game is hard, get it if you like roguelikes that are hard and have fast reflexes.

I don’t really have anything to preface this with other than I ended up being disappointed. Let’s get going.
I – Story [1/10]
Ascendant is a roguelike platformer from Hapa Games. The story is as follows: you (the player) assume the role of a demigod who has taken it upon his/herself to invade the realm controlled by your rivals. And that’s all she wrote folks. The premise is decent I suppose, but that premise is all there is.
II – UI [10/10]
The user interface isn’t bad. Health and mana are clearly displayed in the top left corner of the screen. The minimap is located in the top right and, to be fair, is one of the better minimaps I’ve seen in a game lately. It has multiple view styles and the game cycles through them automatically to best suit your needs. This feature was probably my favorite thing about the game as a whole. The menus were good and I had no trouble navigating around them.
III – Gameplay [3/10]
Despite the gameplay being rather solid for the most part, Ascendant gets old in a hurry. Puzzle solving, a staple aspect of platformers, is weak and scarcely found. The combat is okay.  You’ll cycle through the same few attack animations by mashing either attack button. One is a direct attack and the other can catapult your enemies across the screen in a direction of your predetermination. The magic ability the player has at their disposal is boring. It only has one function and  that is to shoot a projectile in any direction you want. On top of this, while you can parry enemy attacks, it’ll be a cold day in Hell before you can get the timing down.
There is no persistent upgrade system and the game institutes permadeath. You can take this to mean that every time you die (which may or may not be often) you’ll be starting from scratch. While that doesn’t generally bother me in most roguelike games, it started to irk me after a time in this one.
Levels and items found in the levels are also randomly generated. When done correctly, this is my favorite thing about any given roguelike game, but it almost felt like that was broken in Ascendant. Levels varied slightly, but enemies became overly familiar (especially finding the same bosses repeatedly life after life) and finding the same items over and over. It was unimpressive to say the least.
IV – Content [8/10]
Ascendant has a lot of content. Whether you will see it all is iffy, but it is there. There are about 16 different weapons to find/unlock during the course of the game. There were a lot of enemy types, but you may not see many of them. There was even close to 100 other items, which was a decent amount for a game such as this. Also, you had the ability to unlock other characters to play as; reach having their own pros and cons. Although the random generation seems to tamper with the content appearances, I can’t really fault the content itself.
V – Visual [9/10]
The art of Ascendant was, initially, what grabbed my attention when it came to the game. The graphics are very stylized and unique. It really makes it standout in the genre. The environments can be a bit homely at times, but I was never left wanting with character and enemy designs.
VI – Audio [1/10]
A final weak link in the chain, the music of Ascendant was very much disappointing. While it does change, it’s very quiet and easily drowned out by the sounds of combat and various other sound effects. It also becomes repetitive very quickly. If you were looking for an aural pleasure, you came to the wrong place.
VII – Overall [5.3/10]
Overall, I wouldn’t waste my time with this one. I’m glad I got it out of a Humble Bundle and that I didn’t for over the entire price tag.

TL:DR Summary - This is a classic free to play MMORPG experience in the vein of WOW which does definite service to the Lord of the Rings intellectual property.  If you are interested in a video game romp through middle earth then give this a try.
The Lord of the Rings Online (henceforth referred to as LOTRO) is a standard free to play MMORPG game set in the Tolkien universe.  You have the standard choices of race / class to complete the holy trinity of tank / heals / dps, and completing quests that take you through the books / movies as you level up.  Your adventures take care of some behind the scenes action that complement what the major characters are doing at the time.  If you have played any MMO over the last decade you will find the controls to be familiar with tab through / click targeting, and button activated powers with effects that are based on your statistics that improve as you level.
The Good to Great:
If you have any love of Tolkien's universe you will likely enjoy this game.  The quests are rife with references to the major story events while not making you feel as if you are doing nothing while the major players are taking care of all the important business.  I very much enjoyed that many quests deal with characters that did not get as much time in either the book or the movie, and are rendered in interesting ways (the Witch King of Angmar, and Tom Bombadil are examples).  I also enjoyed the fact that if you were unable to find a group you were not completely unable to progress the story, and could solo much of the content.  The caveat to this is that as a solo player you had to grind a bit more to keep your level near where the main questline's level was at, but this is not an issue as there are tons of quests everywhere you travel.  The holy trinity of character classes is not a requirement to complete much of the group content which is a blessing, but a more well rounded ground certainly makes life easier.  The questing is very deep, and takes you through the major events chronologically with you completing tangential tasks.  I found the writing for the main questline to be good to high quality with little distractors.
The Bad:
The gameplay is dated, and can be boring.  The quests many times are go here, kill this, and come back to talk to me.  This would not be so bad, but given the high quality of the main quest these little kill tasks seemed odd to me & kind of "phoned in."  The graphics are dated as well, but hey this was released in April 2007.  It can be a bit of a chore to get a group for some of the more difficult content as the playerbase is small.  This is especially true when compared to other games of the genre.  The game is free to play, but there are creature comforts that you may wish to spend real cash on (a mount).  There are 5 expansions now that if you really get into the game you will wish to purchase as well.  Unfortunately, to purchase all the expansions will run you over $100.  For me this is a bit of a tough sell given the repetitive nature of much of the "added content", and the age of  the product.  On the other hand my love of the lore may overpower my cheapness in order to run around Rohan & Mordor on a pixelated horse.  I have made a few smaller purchases for cosmetics, and a mount.  I have not yet purchased any of the expansions as the free to play content has met my needs.
My ladyfriend loves this intellectual property, and this was an easy gateway drug . . . er . . game to try out the MMORPG genre.  I have enjoyed the nostalgia of the gameplay, and the rendered world.  Do not expect new gameplay, cutting edge graphics, or any breaking of new ground of any sort.  This is standard MMO fare in a different flavor, and did not dissappoint.  As it is free to play what do you have to lose?

I love this game.
It's got everything an MMO needs: A great story, fun gameplay, and one hell of a way to addict you.  I will debunk some negative reviews and show them in their least exaggerated form.

As in most free to play games nowadays there are microtransactions, at this day and age its improbable to find a game without them. You can get almost every paid feature for free. I know a couple of people who are at the end of the game and haven't spent a single penny.
2) Old Graphics,
Personally I don't care but for some people this is a big no-no. Keep in mind this game is over a decade old so if it doesn't exactly reach the standard today I think it should be excused. I do feel some negative reviews exaggerate how bad they are, on Ultra High settings this game looks about 5 years old. (I do think they should remodel the player characters however.)
(I've been taking screenshots whenever I see something that looks amazing, they are slowly racking up on my account if you want to check out a few)

The LotRO community is friendly and mature. The Free to Play model is one of the best if not the best there is out there. There is also a Subscription option that is reasonably priced and includes such perks as mail-anywhere and an opening of abilities and other game play stuff that F2P has to grind for, but would be expected to have access to in a Subscription-only game. The Crafting is well thought out and helpful; unlike some games you aren't at the next teir of gear before you can craft the gear you need. It does have housing consisting of 'hooks' with limited but adaquit mobility including new massive-sized housing. Cosmetics from armor and weapons to pets and mounts are varied and numerous, hiding but not replacing one's actual stat gear. Gold Sellers are not overwhelming and are banned very quickly although other GM or customer service support normally takes three or four days to get around to a person via email, but once they do they are generally very helpful. The differant classes are well crafted, beyond 'balance' and work well either solo or in groups, each having their own CC and some sort of self heal.
Then there is the story of aiding in the War of the Rings and even aiding Frodo along on his adventure as an unseen hand helping to carry the load.
Beautiful game about universe of Tolkien -  M-E. But generaly just a nice MMORPG too.

Thought it was about time that I review this game.
I am only 75 hours in so far, but I am having a great time!
As a long time WoW player I was looking for an MMO to sink my spare time into and this game has delivered.
I will say straight up, this games graphics/mechanics are NOT as good as WoW but to me it satisfies me in a different way.
Firstly the community is very friendly, in the last 75 hours I have only seen 1 or 2 trolls in the World chat channels.
Ask a question and you get an actual answer, unlike WoW in my opinion has a very toxic playerbase.
Questing is the same sort of thing in both WoW and LOTRO, kill X amount of this, collect X amount of that.
Dungeons and instances, I would say that WoW does a better job here. Although the few lower level dungeons I have done in LOTRO are pretty fun.
Now onto the UI, the UI in LOTRO is absolute aids. Mods only help to a degree but the UI in WoW is alot friendlier.
Plenty of side quests, crafting and hobbies to be had in both games, and again WoW seems more simpler to get on with.
To summarize, both WoW and LOTRO are your pretty standard run of the mill MMOs.... BUT
And this is the shining and winning factor for me, its LORD OF THE RINGS.
If you are a huge Lord Of the Rings fan then just that fact alone will make up for all of LOTRO downfalls, the size of the map in LOTRO is amazing, all the places you know and love from the LOTR series are here, Mordor was released recently but that is endgame content so I can not comment.
Real life cash aspect? 3 classes are locked behind a paywall, you get less inventory space and a few other small restrictions, but if you enjoy the game then just subscribe for VIP status, its priced at £8.99 per month and is very cheap in my eyes considering what this game brings me.
TL;DR  You will love this game if you love LOTR

Survivor Squad: Gauntlets is a squad management zombie survival game with a top down PoV and a focus on the line-of-sight mechanic.
You have control over a group of survivors, as a whole and independently from each other, and have to micromanage these aspects of control in order to complete each gauntlet or mission. You will need to tactically plan ahead of every movement you make or you'll end up suffering the consequences of poor foresight, which often include having your arm chewed on by an undead.
But what control does Survivor Squad: Gauntlets give us in order to avoid such a fate? Well, firstly there's movement, you will need to move and you will need to do it in different ways according to each situation you encounter. Maybe you want to make a run for an exit and risk gathering a horde behind you... Or maybe you'd prefer to be safe and sound and walk, guns held tight and ready? Maybe you want to send each survivor in a direction to collect supplies and save time, because you never know what can happen as the night progresses... Or you'd prefer to keep it tight and take your time? Whatever you decide, you will need to get a move on sooner or later, so you better think well where you're going.
Another mechanic you'll need to master to achieve success, and one the game puts a special emphasis on, is the Line of Sight. Your survivors can't shoot at what they can't see, much like in real life. Line of Sight interacts with your surroundings as well, including getting narrower vision if you're in a small alley, or being able to see through a crack in the wall or a window, or even security cameras if you can access them! Remember that your survivors can act independently and as a group, and if one of them sees something the rest of the team will notice too, so take advantage of this and make each of them cover as much ground as possible to avoid any sneaky zed from suprising you. If you want, you can also make them focus on their line of sight only and to ignore the calls of the others, really useful if you're caught in a horde in a place with more than one entrance and need all the entrances to be covered at all times.
Of course, what would a zombie game be without guns? So far I've encountered pistols, shotguns, rifles, flamethrowers and even grenade launchers. Each one has its own stats and each one is useful in different situations, for example, a grenade launcher might be ideal if you're entrenched in a building and covering an entrance, but it might not be the best thing to carry if you're in the open or in a tight building.
Then there's items. As you progress through a gauntlet you may find a variety of items that could be of use in your mission. Ranging from videocameras to teleporters, passing through autoturrets and sonars and a myriad more, you will find a use for every single one in multiple situations: Need to hold of an horde whilst waiting for an evac? An autoturret will mow down the incoming zeds in a hail of bullets. Collecting supplies and need to drop them off at your transport? Teleport away and avoid walking in the open and risking getting caught by a random horde (just make sure you don't run out of energy for it!).
And then there's what I'll admit are my absolute favorite parts of each gauntlet: the interactivity and the situations. Normally you will have a more or less specific objective to accomplish, but the game lets you decide how to fullfil it. Apart from that, the map is full of little curios that you can interact with (or not) to achieve a certain outcome. Each one is different and sometimes you won't be sure of the outcome, but you might want to risk it anyway, who knows? Maybe it'll open a secret path, an armory or a shortcut if you press
button... Or it might trigger an alarm, a bomb or who knows what! The situations are also great, this game achieves an atmosphere of uncertainty that really gives it a special charm and that I think more games of the zombie genre should strive to achieve. You can never be sure of anything, you might think you have everything planned beforehand and start walking, but who knows if a random horde will trigger that you didn't prepare yourself for? Or the way might be blocked without you knowing, or there might be a bomb in a building that you just entered and will have to risk your life disabling it, or let it take the building and whatever valuables might be inside, and lose a potential stronghold for later on in the process. This interactivity combined with variety of situations and feeling of uncertainty works really well in Survivor Squad: Gauntlets. Other games with similar mechanics (squad management) often become a bit stale because you basically just click and wait, click and wait, click and wait because everything is easy to plan for and there's nothing to put you under stress or make you react; in Survivor Squad: Gauntlets you certainly click, but I wouldn't wait if I were you, better keep an eye up because anything can happen... and will probably happen.
On a more technical note, there's the graphics and sound. No, it's no Crysis, but it's got a nice style going on and it looks good to the eye and sounds good to the ear, what else can you ask for? The style works well with the game and the main non-gameplay feature (the gauntlets), where a more cumbersome style might cluster your vision too much, but Survivor Squad: Gauntlets manages to find a nice equilibrium. The sound is good too, not spectacular, but good enough. On a note, but reiterating that it IS in fact still Early Access, the music is not too varied and can get repetitive to listen to the same tracks over and over, if the developers are planning on adding more tracks, then all the better, and if not you can always disable the ingame music and play a custom playlist of yours for a more personalized experience.
Lastly, and what I think sells the game better than anything, is, as the title of the game would suggest to you, the gauntlets.  These are the scenenarios on which you play each time. The developers have made quite a bit of them that act as a story, but what's really awesome is that you can create custom ones and share them or play in gauntlets made by other players like you! This feature is awesome and ensures that you can always pop up the game and have a new experience even if you have wore out the rest of features the game has to offer.
All in all I really, really, really recommend this game to everybody regardless of their preferred genre, even if you haven't played a squad management game the tutorial and first missions will teach you fast enough so that in ten minutes you can work your way around the game intuitively. And if you've played them, then you will love this one.
So grab your shotty and remember, leave no man behind!

My first impressions of this game are positive. When you first start it up it asks you to go through a simple tutorial to learn how to control your survivors. After that you get to the real fun of the game: Gauntlet missions.
These missions are player made scenarios made using the in depth editor. I was not expecting the editor to be so robust. You can make whole stories inside this thing. It's pretty amazing. There is also a tutorial for the editor so you can get a feeling for how it works.
When you are in the game you control your survivors RTS style by selecting them and right clicking a spot to move them. You can order your survivors to face a certain direction and focus on it so you have an area covered. Covering an area is VERY important in this game. Line of sight plays a big role in this. If you cant see it, it will kill you. This means you will want to either have all your corners covered or be in a place that only has one entrance.
If you aren't used to RTS games it will take some time to get used to moving the survivors. If you ever get flustered the game has a quick pause button so you can plan out what you want to do.
Overall this game is a fun thing to play with. If the community picks up for it there is no limit for the amount of things you can do with it.
I give this game a 9/10 overall.

Simply put this game is an innovative breath of fresh air from the otherwise rather static genres of both strategy and zombie games. It manages to blend the two in a uniquely positive way that feels different and new. Commanding hordes of zombies is extremely satisfying and seeing the puny efforts of man come to nothing as all human civilizations burn is quite enjoyable. But, like any EarlyAccess game it still has a lot of room for improvement.
The number of gamemodes the game offers brings a lot of variety to the table. So far the Skirmish and the World Domination are quite well developed, with room for improvement. Being a fan of similar strategy games I found the World Domination gamemode more akin to my tastes. The Skirmish is enjoyable but the World Domination is where things get really interesting, personally. I am very excited for the other planned gamemodes the Campaign and the Multiplayer.
The soundtrack is beautifully composed and provides quite a good amount of immersion. However the tracks that play are irrelevant to what is actually going on, so you may find yourself leading the final attack on humanity's last city while the music is relatively calm.
Obviously the game has some room for improvement. It could be because of my slow computer, but I found it a bit difficult to effectively select and control the units. Also in World Domination when my hordes were being attacked I found it difficult to counterattack, as selecting the target proved a bit tedious. However apart from that and the music issue, all the game needs is a bit of polish and its good to go. It is ofcourse still in Early Access so such things are expected at this stage.
In short, the game holds great potential. Its innovitave, fun, and quite challenging at times. A great way to waste away a couple of hours. To those seeking to buy this game I suggest you do not expect too much out of the game as it is, or you might be disappointed, however for such a low price the content it already has is worth it. I expect a lot from this game in the future, as its foundations have a lot to offer and the idea behind the game just draws me in, and I believe the developers will deliver. The game is frequently updated and its come a very long way in a very short time. I recommend to fellow strategy game as well as zombie game lovers, to keep a very close eye on this game. Even as it is, its well worth a playthrough.

Warlock 2 is a truly fantastic game, despite what some of these reviews may say. If you're a lover of 4X strategy games and fantasy lore, get this game -- you won't be sorry.
One of the reasons this game has so many harsh ratings is because it can be a little buggy. But on the right system (Windows 7, 8 and 10 all work well), it's a ton of fun and you'll encounter few bugs. I can safely say this after 2000+ hours of game play.
The developers were forced to abandon the game before they were fixed, so avoid this game if you're using one of those OS's.
- Tons of flavorful units (15+ for each race, several more 'wild' creatures)
- Varied and unique races
- Interesting lords (hero units)
- Simple but highly strategic combat system
- Wide variety of fantasy resources
- Strategic spells (terraforming, empire boosting, unit enhancement)
- Great game modes (sandbox maps, shard worlds, boss-killing campaigns)
- Rich lore (with a good sense of humor)
- Excellent replay value
- Tons of fun -- one of the best games I've ever played
There are a few stubborn bugs and the developers are no longer able to work on the title to fix them. On Windows, none of the bugs are game-breaking.
To give you an idea, roughly 1 in 20 games I've played have crashed at some point. (Games are usually 20+ hours long.) The good news is that you can usually "correct" a game-crash bug by loading an autosave from just a turn or two prior and doing your turn a little differently.
Note that there are also a few mods that fix a number of minor bugs -- Renaissance Mod fixes many of them.
As a beginner, the AI seems quite strong. But once you know what you're doing, the AI is lackluster and you'll catch it making some bone-headed moves, even on the most difficult setting.
Luckily, a number of mods improved the AI -- Legendary Mode AI is one and Renaissance Mod is another. The AI still makes the occasional poor move, but the games themselves are much more challenging with either of these mods.
Despite what the description says, users agree that the game is not in a playable state for Linux and Mac users.
The first Warlock was widely criticized on two counts:
1) It looked like a Civ 5 clone. True, it does have a very similar feel to the UI in Civ 5, and it has retained this feel for the sequel. But the gameplay is quite different than a Civ title, with only passing similarities.
2) The game lacked strategic depth. To win, all you really needed to do was to "city spam" your way to victory. There was no downside for having multiple cities, making most games feel like a race to see who could expand the fastest.
You could also "perk" (buff) as many units as you wanted just by capturing a single resource tile. Very easy to abuse.
Warlock 2, however, changed both of these things for the better by adding some much-needed limitations.
Some people who enjoyed the freedom Warlock 1 granted with regards to city spamming and limitless unit perks are likely to be turned off by the sequel. I know I was at first ... until I played a bit and realized how much these changes improved the game.
In fact, fans of the first title pushed back so hard on the city limit that the developers added the ability to turn it off when you create a new game. But just as the developers noted that disabling the city limit is "not recommended," I strongly concur. The gameplay is so much richer with some scarcity and consequences for overextending -- just as it is in the best 4X games.
As I learned to play with the newly laid out limitations on number of cities and availability of perks, along with the new unrest system, I discovered that the developers really did know what they were doing. The game has TONS more strategic depth than Warlock 1. So again -- take some of these negative reviews with a grain of salt.
The developers really did a lot to improve the game with these simple changes. When people say Warlock 2 is just a clone of the original with more content, they are sorely mistaken.
In Warlock 1, researching spells is entirely random. When it's time to research a new spell, you're given a small selection of random spells and are able to chose one.
The sequel offers an actual research tree, with clearly laid out paths to acquire new spells. This gives you the ability to navigate the tree and strategically chose your preferred research path. Many players consider this the best improvement over the original.
Aside from World of Warcraft, I don't think I've ever spent so much time playing (and enjoying) a game.

The cons I described above should be fair warning to those who are concerned about getting this game.

Gameplay
--------------------
This is easily TL2's biggest flaw as it has a myriad of problems. One such problem being that it's too easy. Playing as a mage on the hardest difficultly setting I was still able to opt for a 100% glass-canon style build for nearly an entire playthrough. Completely ignoring defensive-based statistics and crowd control-based skills. Dying was a rarity, but, even in the circumstances where I did, I didn't care, because the death system is so ridiculously unpunishing. For non-hardcore characters death is handled similarly World of Warcraft, in the sense that the only major cost is the time it takes you to travel back to where your character died. Your given the option of either reviving in town, at the entrance of the dungeon where you died, or exactly where your character died, with the last two options costing a measly amount of gold. The biggest problem with this system is that TL2 hands out gold like there's no tomorrow so you don't care about the costs. And because the amount of gold taken is a percentage based on your total gold at that point in time, it's easily exploitable by stocking up on tons of commonly used items (such as health potions) beforehand to decrease your total amount of gold, and therefore, the amount of gold lost upon death.
Playing on the hardest difficultly as a hardcore character (i.e. character death is permanent) somewhat remedies these problems of it being too easy as it forces you to play more defensively. But, even this mode is flawed because of the sheer amount of grinding you'll have to do in addition to the deadly traps strewn throughout act 2. This grinding is the worst, as TL2 features a loot drop system like it's spiritual predecessor Diablo II. Which means, you'll be spending several boring hours killing the same act bosses over and over again in order to get equipment that's good enough to safely proceed to later areas. It also doesn't help that often many of the statistics featured on equipment are awful, even on rare and unique items. However, all this gear grinding won't matter at all if you accidentally step on traps in act 2. Because they ignore all forms of damage mitigation even being on them for more than a single second can kill your character. Even having a high health pool only buys you about half a second-more worth of time to get out of a trap. The only saving grace is that these traps tend to be easily avoidable, however, then we get to the next biggest problem with act 2 traps - The Genie's Trial. This main quest featured midway into act 2 forces you to go through a tiny enclosed area littered with dozens of traps and constantly spawning enemies that are every where. Getting through this area without dying is nearly an impossible task, especially if you haven't done it once before.
Aside from these major problems there is also a bunch of other smaller problems. Health and mana potions are one such problem. Because TL2 hands out silly amounts of gold and potions are so cheap you'll find yourself buying and stocking up on dozens at a time, tediously pressing a hotkey to use one whenever you've even taken the slightest amount of damage. It begs the question why the developers didn't remove potions altogether and opt for a high health/mana regeneration-based system instead, as it would've achieved the same results without all the tedious clicking and hotkey-pressing. Class skills and spell scrolls are another issue with TL2. Many have terrible descriptions, are extremely situational, or just outright terrible, which ultimately makes designing characters far more annoying and confusing than it ought to be. What makes the bad descriptions even worse is that TL2 has no true character-respect system, so, if you make a major mistake based on one or more of these descriptions, tough luck, there is no way of taking those points back without making and leveling up an entirely new character. Another perplexing design decision is that there are twenty-one activatable skills for each class but only nine passive ones. This makes no sense considering you can only activate one activatable skill at a time. And since most of these activatable skills do the same thing, deal damage, it stands to reason there should've been far, far more passive skills to balance out your character/s.
Story
--------------------
Finally moving pass gameplay, we get to the story, which, there practically isn't one. Like TL1 it's heavily inspired by the Diablo series, particularly in this case it's D2. You'll be chasing one guy through four acts, always being one step behind him as he sows chaos throughout the world. There is absolutely no character development to any character you meet along the way and therefore, you don't care about any of them. In fact the character who received the most development in the first Torchlight game (what little there was) is immediately killed off in the opening cinematic. You can't even have animosity toward the main villian for any of his actions because he's being manipulated by the same sort of corruption effect that was seen in the first game. Even the final boss/es have absolutely no backstory what-so-ever.
Music and SFX
--------------------
This is another aspect you don't care about. Again, it lazily borrows from it's spiritual predecessors (Diablo), so if you played those games, you'll hear those same tunes remixed, quite often. Everything else you'll hear is pretty standard-fare to below-average. While TL2 does feature some notable voice acting, which is appreciated, there is too far too few of it to make a lasting impact.
Aesthetic
--------------------
If there is one nice thing I can say about TL2, it is it's aesthetic. It's colorful (especially spells), is nice to look at, and different. But, it's also disappointing as well, mainly in regards to how the PC looks. Every PC despite their differences in class look exactly the same to each other when wearing the same equipment. The only thing that makes a Embermage look like a mage and an Engineer look like an engineer (gender differences aside) are there class-restricted armor, which, you rarely find or want to use because they tend to have awful statistics. It's extremely disappointing if you look up original character art for the game, because the PCs look nothing like their final in-game models.
Conclusion
--------------------
Overall I'd say TL2 is an extremely generic and bland action RPG. It borrows far too heavily from predecessors of the genre while not doing anything exciting, new, or innovative, in addition to not having enough charm with it's own license to make it worth a purchase. I strongly urge you to buy or save your money for better games.
Scores
--------------------
Gameplay: 2/10
Story: 2/10
Music and SFX: 4/10
Aesthetic: 7/10
Overall Score : 3/10
*Note* that the Overall Score is not an average of the other four scores. This is because aspects like gameplay and story are generally more important in a video game than the music, SFX, and aesthetic. That's not to say these aspects aren't important, they are, just not as important.
Disclosure
--------------------
All my play time was spent over the course of single player games on the hardest difficultly setting, playing primarily Embermages, which were mostly hardcore characters in the level 20 to 40 range. My one, non-hardcore Embermage reached level 80+ and completed NG+. My recorded steam hours for this game are not accurate as I spent many hours allowing this game to run in the background while I researched various aspects of the game or did other things. This review has received two large updates in order to fix grammar, make it shorter, more easily comprehensible, and for accuracy.

This game is brilliant. The depth and immersion of this game is unbelievable. There's no zombies. No irradiated monsters. Nothing like that. There's just people. And they act like people. Some just want to defend their home. Others want your stuff. The way you fight is fantastic as well. You fight with psychology, rather than your muscles. You'll almost always be outnumbered. You almost always won't have any ammo. Use your mind, surprise the bandits, and make them -think- that you have a bullet chambered in that pistol you're pointing at them. If you go in, gun up, you'll find yourself dead before you can even -try- and threaten them.
Overall, you'll hardly ever see the ruined city you're in. You'll barely be able to see a few feet in any direction. But then you'll climb up and out of the dust, and the world will just open up before your eyes.
One downside though, is it can occasionally go a little funny with the controls. This is a game where at times, it's quite plain that it's a port. But the slight irking from having your character shimmy along a ledge to the right, rather than climbing further up a building, is quite easily forgiven once you take everything else into stock.
I'd heartily recommend this game to anyone who is fond of the survivor Post-Apocalyptia genre, with a heavy emphasis on realism when it comes to combat and exploration.
