A worthy successor to Astral Masters.  Some rules have been simplified and it's faster paced, but still the same idea.  Build a deck out of your cards and battle opponents in the league, or with random decks or draft tournaments.  The cards come a bit faster if you pay, but it's absolutely not necessary.
Skill counts for a bit more than in some games, but it's not chess and the decisions on each turn won't take forver to think about.  The basic rules are simple, and each card's special properties and abilities are clearly described on it.  Cards are divided into creatures and spells - creatures all have a special ability as well as attack and defence.  There are few options to hit the opponent directly, so although spells are powerful and creatures don't tend to live very long, the creature battle is nevertheless central.
There is a single-player campaign with daily missions, including a good few at the start to get you familiar, but I think it's fair to say that multiplayer is the core of the game.  Multiplayer is painless - click on 'Play League Game' and in a few seconds you'll get an opponent in the range of 0.5-2 times your current level, or failing that a bot will arrive to take you on.  So getting a game is also fast.
Definitely worth checking out if you enjoy this type of game,

If you're really good at it, try playing on hard mode where the game does not display counter-attack indicators over attacking enemies.  I am also happy to report that the combat (and the whole game really) works flawlessly with keyboard+mouse, which isn't always the case with third-person action games.
Now that GFWL has been removed, there's nothing preventing me from recommending it.  I even started over with a new save and 100%'ed the game after the switch to Steamworks since it's so fun.

Gnomoria is a game in which you manipulate, rather than order directly, your colony of gnomes as they reshape the landscape into their kingdom. Farms, groves and pastures, workshops built underground or in buildings, forts and castles, crossbows and rifles, swords and hammers, armors and ... well other types of armors. Mines. Lots of mines. Dangerous mines full of skeletons, zombies, spiders, beetles and the occasional golem. Also gems, valuable metal ores but mostly less valuable dirt and rock. That you can bake/chisel into more valuable ceramic blocks, bricks or crafts for trade or showing off.
The essence of the game is manipulation. Each gnome can be assigned a profession which can be entirely customised by the player. Dedicated chefs, carpenters that double up as farmers, jewelers who also help tend the wounded or build things when there's no jewels to make or wounded to tend. Both the specefic jobs for a profession and their priorities can be customised and here is where the learning curve comes from.
Even though the game is still incomplete, there is much to discover and learn about how to best organise and grow your workforce. Giving orders is relatively easy, but seeing them carried out sensibly and efficiently is an entirely diffrent matter.
The game is difficult yet mostly peacefull at the same time. Expect lots of restarts but also expect your next kingdom to fare better than the last.
There is maybe little point past survival, or survival in the prettiest and most efficient kingdom you can build, but in that regard Gnomoria is similar to Lego bricks. You don't play much with what you create, you reach a point of satisfaction (or more likely late game instability) and start thinking about how to build another world.
Have loved ones on standby ready to hit you over the head with something sturdy but loving, preferably a hammer. The game is far more addictive than it seems.

The game shines in the non-linear, non-restrictive gameplay that has plagued many linear corridor shooters (to include Ghost Recon Future Soldier). Players have a map, and a team of men, and must apply critical thinking through mission analysis in order to be successful.
The game also has an outstanding damage model that still outshines most shooters; A single 5.56mm round will kill, and players can sustain arm and leg wounds that affect their ability to shoot and move. Third person animations also reflect player damage in the form of limping and visible blood stains and gunshot wounds.
There is also an RPG-like system that allows players to develop their Ghosts and apply personal attributes that will improve their performance.
My only big gripe is the use of a reticule system instead of a first person weapon. Unlike Ravenshield, there is no on-screen, first person weapon. There are only a series of recitules that can be zoomed in to simulate weapon sights.
The best FPS ever.

However, the game is rather inconsistent with these things, and you can stumble upon world-changing information without anything changing or the characters (even the protagonist) reacting to it.
Overall a competent continuation of Deus Ex:Human Revolution. Worth about 30$ imo.

I am not much of a rewiwer, more of an analyst. This review is based on experience both with the game and the genre, at the time of writing sunk 40-50 hours into this game. I will not play a bad game for 40 minutes let alone 40 hours. If you are a fan of the genre buy it, game is excellent. If you would like a more detailed reasoning behind why keep reading, there wil be very very minor gameplay/story spoilers as it is impossible to talk about certain mechanics of the game without referencing them.
The plot of the game is simple. You are a Demi-god, There is a God, Overthrow the God, Become the new god. Each Demi-god has its own story and reasons for wanting to be God. The level structure is similar to Binding of Issac, there are multiple floors in groups of two with semi randomly generated rooms between you and the boss of each floor. Every odd numbered floor has a random boss from a select pool of possible bosses for that floor, and every even numbered floor has that levels guardian which is the same every time but there are two possible variations of it. Each boss is a challenge in its own right and each has its own set of attacks, attack paterns, weaknesses to exploit and most have multiple phases. Some are more challenging than others and some can end up being trivial if RNGesus loves you but personally that is half the fun.
Before I begin I will say the game has an excellent Tutorial that covers pretty much everything I am about to cover. If you buy this game play the tutorial, it is not boring and gets straight to the point.
Combat boiled down is - Attacks, launch attacks, Magic Attacks, Parry and evasion. You may also occassionally find a 1 use items called Breaths which offer numberous effects for the room you are in. Most are combat focused but for the most part you'll be depending on either your weapons or magic to clear the path between you and the next room. Attacking an enemy with either magic of spells will also do stagger damage. Stagger damage is a separate  health bar of sorts. Once an enemy has taken enough stagger damage they will glow yellow allowing you to use a launch attack to send them flying across the screen taking massive damage and doing massive damage to anything they collide with. Its a very simple mechanic and very satisfying. Feels very meaty especially if you are able to stagger and ping a larger foe across the room. For survival you can dash left or right through enemy attacks and flank them or parry the attack sending them flying (or in the case of projectiles reflects them). Timing is key, you'll have to be rather skilled at the game to successfully pull it off especially in the late game or against certain bosses but using the room to your advantage is also a viable tactic, You don't have to parry or dash through attacks, you can always jump over, run away, lure foes out of position among other things. It is very well done.
As for what you'll encounter there is quite a bit of enemy variety but you will not notice it at first since each season is tiered. The first season will always have a mix of melee flies, Grunts, mage grunts, worm brawlers, worm hitters and suicide grunts, The next season will expand this roster adding elite versions ontop of new enemy types with their own elite versions. Many enimes especially later ones are a challenge in their own right and their mere presence can change the whole way you tackle the room. You may also encounter one of many many possible event rooms which range from being ambushed, blessing themed obstacle courses, mini games, gambling and straight up "Here is a awersome free thing, have fun". You won't know until you enter what it is and it took me around 20-25 hours of playing until I was finally able to experience all of them. Adds a lot of depth to each floor if you decide to explore them especially if they are locked costing you a valuable key.
Every playable Deity in this game (7 in total) has its own strengths/weaknesses which cater to certain playstyles which you'll disvoered as you unlock them. Every floor has at least 1 item room and a shop. Items rooms contain 1 gold chest either locked or unlocked which can provide you with high level stat boosts, breaths, weapons, a chunk of influence (the shop currency) or something else that I won't spoil. Shops on each floor are always locked and always have 4 items for sale and are one of the few ways to get a new spell. Each spell replaces your magic attack with a new one which can range from tripple shots to spread fire or mines.
There are two levels of passives in this game. First are spirits which are straight up passives, you pick them up and you get a bonus. There are 57 to collect in all and most have a chance of appearing on weapons you'll find to. There is no limit to the amount of passives you can get and they pretty much all stack flawlessly naby offering very cool interactions with each other. Bklessings are the second teir of passive in the game and each Deity can only hold a limited number at a time but they are very powerful. Blessings are rewards for beating the levels boss and can be placed into 1 of 3 body slots augmenting your attacks, magic or passively. Each blessing has its own unique effect depending on where you socket and they all interact with each other. 21 blessings with 63 passives in total to discover and many many combinations and synergies to experiment with. Because of how potent blessings are they will shape your run meaning no two runs end up the same but that should go without saying, its the whole point of the genre.
Overall the game is fantasic and a must have if you are a fan of the genre. There is a lot of depth to be had but it will require a little investment since you will have to learn encounters and most likely need to unlock new items before you are able to get a successful completion. It does have a few balance niggles mainly when you encounter a room with multiple shielded enemies which will be very intimidating at first but apart from that the game is paced very well and is very rewarding to play and much more than a simple 1 button combat system that is the fault of many other games in this genre.

So I NEVER write reviews. Like literally I've only done two recomandations years back for games I no longer play. But for the madness that is Crush Crush, I feel with the time I have invested in it, I am obligated to do so.
I love Crush Crush for it's art, it's humor, and it's gosh darn addictive quality (Having played every single version from the Kongregrate original on the day it first came out to the Steam Version also on the day it first came out to the Nutaku version also you guessed it, on the first release day) . Having invested at least over a day in active play time with this version (And possibly a lot more in the kongregate version and less in the Nutaku version since I wasn't in the mood for a grind) and with the two last girls still on my to do list, I can personally say I've invested a lot of time into this game. As for the recommendation?
Well that's a bit more of complex subject. Although I love this game and I hate to say it, but that recomandation is based on my personal style of play. So you only need to ask yourself a few questions as to whether or not Crush Crush is for you;
1) Are you a perfectionist?
2) Do you have free time?
3) Are you addicted to achievements?
4) Do you like anime waifus?
If you anwsered yes to one or more of the above questions, congrats, Crush Crush is for you.
So here comes the part where I lay into Crush Crush...
So the biggest problem I have and many others like me, is that the difficulty curve for this game, in particular at the end game, is H*CKING high. You will grind, you will farm, you will grovel on your knees and beg for mercy. But those last two girls Karma and Sutra will burn your soul alive. (And Luna to because the mystical slippers literally can not be bought without a massive grind of cash or forking over a diamond). I am not joking in saying that despite having near max multiplier AND store diamond based multipliers, it STILL takes a silly amount of time to get anything done for those last two girls. The difficulty curve is just to darn high. That in itself is my only real complaint for the game. I love everything else. But if your not playing this for the long haul and or are not willing to fork some real life cash for diamonds, the end game hell awaits you. (Which technically is my other complaint but I don't mind forking over a little cash to help the devs.)
(But seriously, I love this game and recommend you give it a go. Just don't expect any breaks once you get to the end game because buddy, your in it for the long haul.)

well... where do I begin? It was a bright and sunny tuesday morning, the birds were chirping, and the sweet morning dew covered my front lawn. The crisp cool air, rushed through my hair, as I walked down my front steps to go retrieve me mail. I opened the mailbox door and pulled out the papers within. Running my fingers along the lightly damp envelops I noticed a peculiar letter. "To whom it may concern," it read. "This coming Friday Feburary the 10th great things will happen." That is all it said; nothing more was to be found within the envelop except for that letter. I looked up and turned around to retire to my home. I waited three days until that friday, and that's when it all started. When I woke up that morning I felt odd. Something wasn't right. I could feel it. I went about my day, tending to my spice garden, and tinkering with the toys I once played with as a child, reminding me of the days when resposibility was as distant figure standing in the shadows, only to emerge years later as a grotesque beast, that would entomb me. The memories of a long lost childhood, returned for a moment, allowing me to experience the joyous days of years past. I looked up from my desk full of toys only to notice a shimmering light coming from behind me. I turn around only to notice my computer had awoken from sleep, only to display what would be the most terrifying entity in existance. The screen simply read, "crush crush." I walkover to my computer and pull my chair out from my desk. I take a seat and put my hand on my mouse. I move the cursor to the button that would forever change me; "play." I press my mouse down and the screen goes blank. An instant later a creature with horendous bodily proportions appears on my monitor. My stomach immediately began to churn and my room began to spin in my head, The nausea, although overwhelming, could not stop me from noticing the pain given to me from the game from enslaving my eternal soul. Like a demon from the eternal fires of hell it latched onto my soul, morphed it, violated it. Before I could think again the most vile creature that I have ever encountered. The ears stood tall, but the body stood taller. the creature, a neko girl. My heart raced and a sharp pain raced down my arm. My breathing grew heavy, then silence. My pulse was no more. I shattered the screen with the last ounce of strength I had. The screen went blank and the glass that made up the panel was shattered into thousands of shards. I looked at my monitor and could see my distortred reflection in the fractured panel of glass. I watched as I took what I was sure would my last breath. My vision went dark along with my thoughts. I awoke in a hospital bed. lines from bags of saline ran down and into my arm. The doctor walked in. "you're lucky to be alive he said." "what happened?" I ask him. He looked at me, then glanced down to the right, "crush crush."
Please save yourself the pain. If you value your life go nowhere near this detriment of a game. Stay strong, stay safe, and goodluck if you refuse to heed my warning.

There are some games that, when I see them, I get hooked and tend to ignore most bad reviews. Sometimes, that is a wise choice, as I have found MANY games that I've loved that had terrible reviews all around. But other times, that is a terrible move, as the reviews are true.
In this case, the bad reviews are true. I am Alive is, well, terrible.
I was hooked since the first trailer ever released, and I never played it until now. Now, I wish I hadn't. I didn't want to just drop the game, as I hate doing that, so I just tried to play through as quickly as possible, ignoring the in-game achievements. Thankfully there are no Steam achievements, as I would hate to see the partial completion in that.
Anyway, to the point: Don't buy this game. The controls are horrible. Getting a controller helps, but it's still wonky. The combat is no good. You can sneak attack someone, which is cool at first, but it wears off. Besides that, you can shoot people but ammo is TERRIBLY scarce. I understand that this game is survivalist, but your guy has been out there forever, and he begins the game with like a water bottle and that's it.
The only other way to fight is with your knife. If the combat was more action-oriented, then it would have been better. Instead, you're usually screwed when fighting gangs. Your only knife attack (besides the sneaking one to get the first edge-up) is to run up to someone's face and proceed into a button-mashing event while you're left open to all other baddies. Your guy can't just stab and slash in an active manner. Instead, he can only lock his knife with the other guy and sit there while being shot. And each time he's shot, the event has to be restarted.
Therefore, combat is terrible. It should have been more fluid and action-oriented.
And as for the climbing... God, such a pain. I liked what they were trying to do at first, but then got over it quickly. Again, it's a survivalist game, but it is just too much. You have a fatigue meter which, when you lose enough fatigue, also will lose its capacity. If you don't have items to restore capacity, you're screwed and usually find yourself in a vicious circle of needing to find items which require either (a) ammo to shoot a lock or (b) you to climb somewhere. But chances are you're looking for ammo already, or you're looking for an item to help you climb. So often you're forced to restart places or re-attempt entire sections.
And the graphics--they look like someone digitalized sawdust and filtered it through the imagery. The game can still look ugly and apocalyptic without looking... THAT kind of ugly.
There's more issues, as I found many glitches along the way, the story was lackluster, and on and on and on.
Overall, I was terribly disappointed. Do not play this game.

Pros: Clever "threaten with gun" mechanics that make confrontations tense. You can practically taste the bleak, hostile and claustrophobic post-apocalyptic world. Climbing mechanics that are closer to Prince of Persia than Assassin's Creed, and add further tension and intensity with a Stamina meter and the chance of a lethal drop every few steps. The survival aspect is well-done, with exploration being about equally likely to lead to more of the sparse number of much-needed inventory items, as to another potentially deadly confrontation. Largely captures the grey moral nature of the post-apocalyptic world, like the movie The Road; no one can trust one another, and someone pointing a gun at you and/or threatening you may not be looking to kill and/or rob you, they may just be scared. Challenging. Once you've slid down a slanted skyscraper, jumped the gap in a modern bridge or barely made your way through a collapsed building, you will never again feel completely comfortable in our otherwise seemingly strong, sturdy buildings.
Cons: Unless you're playing on Easy, the Retry feature is pretty ridiculous: you have to complete a level without running out of them(in spite of the trial-and-error nature of much of the game), meaning without making very many mistakes(you can earn extra Retries), or you have to start it all over - and trust me, in this, you will make mistakes. Once you've completed a level, you can do it over, but if you go back to a level before your current one, it will delete your progress beyond that level(forget about replayability)! If these aspects were something hardcore gamers could activate to challenge themselves, that would be fine, but with it being the way the game is designed, it loses a lot of potential fans. Ending is unsatisfying. The last third of the game is prepostorous - it's as if it was developed by someone else, and they thought it was a regular shooter, rather than a "make every last bullet count" survival game.
My recommendation: Give it a go if you love at least one of the following: Prince of Persia style climbing, a survival challenge, dark post-apocalyptic fiction and unconventional approaches to taking out enemies.

Ok, just made it through the game, which seems to be a mixture of survival, adventure, climbing and TPS/FPS. Here's the results:
Pro:
+ Story. Grounded, realistic - not off-hook or with irrational twists.
+ Setting/atmosphere. Dark and dusty, gloomy undertone without being pathetic.
+ The voice-acting! A real big plus. Little Mei has the most realistic and beautiful voice for a kid I ever experienced in a video game.
Cons.
- Graphics. Obviously it's a console port. You have to live with that.
- Game time. It only takes about six hours for a complete game. Well, as there are survivors to save, this time could be extended if you want to find and help them all (20 altogether). Otherwise replayability's low.
- Controls. They are a pain. If you're used to play FPS games, you will have a hard time learning the controls. don't be frustrated to lose your first fights because you pressed the wrong buttons. It's a console game after all, maybe the devs did not want to screw up the game mechanics by changing controls on pc. who knows.
Conclusion: You might have a look if you're into survival, like a gloomy atmosphere and don't expect innovative gameplay or experiences.

Warlock 2 is one of those games where I want to like it, and every time I play it I wish it was better. While this game has many qualities that I like, there are many things about it I do not. I will skip the nonsense and go straight to the pros and cons.
Pros:
*There are many game settings you can choose from in the sandbox mode, which is great for giving you just the right amount of a challenge.
*The game has a nice selection of characters to choose from. Each one very customizable, and many different races to choose as a starting city.
*The variety of units and enemies are very expansive. I never felt like every other race was just a clone of another.
*The game has a large amount of replayability. The above mentioned items, as well as completely random worlds and situations make each session unique.
Cons:
*For many users, this game encounters random crashes with no warnings or crash screen to explain what happened.
*The AI is extremely annoying. Almost every single game I play, the opponents constantly bug me for non-aggression pacts and alliances every 2 or 3 turns. I got to one point in a game where I met all 8 of them, and every 2 or 3 turns, all 8 of them asked for an alliance. You almost have to declare war on them just to make them shut up. But then they just ask for peace every few turns. This does not change based on difficulty.
*It is too easy to steamroll enemies. Honestly the most challenging parts of the game I have found to be exploring the other worlds with extremely hard wild monsters. Even on the max difficulty though, once you build up to it, you can just mow through every faction with little to no resistance. Their combat AI is no better than their diplomacy AI.
Other than that though, the game really has some potential. If someone out there was good with code, and could mod it to have a decent AI, I would recommend this game in a heartbeat. Or if the developer ever desires to finish what could have been an amazing game. As it stands though, I do not recommend it. At least not at full price. Wait for a Steam sale, and if you are dying for some new 4x, give it a shot.

It's basically the same as Warlock 1 (which in turn was basically the same as Master of Magic, which was also a game I liked), but it's a bit more balanced, the alternate worlds (which I found to be one of the most interesting parts of the first Warlock game) play a much more signifcant role in the game (and in Exiled mode include a world which is more closely equivalent to the alternate world from Master of Magic), there are more playable races, and the game runs more smoothly.

What should I say, really? Parts are too easy, parts too hard, and all of it is - at least to me - boring.
Let's begin with enemies. You get the first blaster after a few seconds, and... well, if you don't stupidly jump into deep caves or something, enemies pretty much won't touch you. Yes, some of them have ranged attacks. You learn to avoid those - quickly.
The only exception: Bosses. The first boss is too hard, with any equipment you are able to get until you encounter him. It's frustrating, and after an hour of trying again and again, I gave up.
And mining? Well, shooting at dirt with a... mining blaster? That's probably the best word. So, shooting at dirt with a mining blaster, collecting an infinite stack of dirt... and some decidedly less than infinite amounts of useful materials. If the floods of non-threatening enemies don't annoy you to death first.
Lastly, crafting. It's quite easy to create the first three crafting stations... which are needed for many items, the materials for which are probably available after many weeks of playing non-stop. The few items you can craft in the beginning are nearly useless.
Seriously, this game needs a manual just to explain which parts SHOULD be enjoyable...
So, really, nice try, but I really can't recommend this game, as much as I'd like to.

This game is well made, polished, balanced, beautiful, and has a uniquely colorful art style.
It's also criminally easy.
I'm not a difficulty junkie by any measure. I play basically all my games on Normal, with a few exceptions. I bought this game to play with my older brother, just as something to do to spend some time together whenever we have the chance to see each other.
But neither of us could get into it. It was simply too easy. The puzzles were simple, the combat forgiving almost to the point of patronizing, and the platforming was almost impossible to fail at.
I can easily see people enjoying this game if they're new to gaming, don't spend enough time getting truly good with the controls, or are wholly unused to puzzles or puzzle games. And I don't mean that in a derogatory sense: it would genuinely be perfect for someone like that. And people like that are more common than you'd think.
But if you been around the block a bit, this game isn't going to challenge you. As I said, I'm not a difficulty junkie, but every game needs to have a baseline level of difficulty (relative to me personally, not in general) for me to remain engaged. This game just didn't do that for me.

In Spectromancer, you got all the cards you could possibly play right at the beginning of the game, and so you could proceed along a longer term strategy.  Here you have a hand and draw at the end of your turn like a normal card game.  Frankly it's a lot less interesting.  The core game is good, but I'd just go buy Spectromancer if I were you.

Astral Heros is a card game that uses a mix of mechanics you can see in other card games.

You can literally play for 2000 hours (yes 2000) hours of this game, over a year and a half, and not get bored of it.  It's that good.  You can create limitless amounts of new kingdoms with each new game, set difficulties, peaceful or not, metal/gem/coal resource abundance etc.  There is much more than meets the eye of simple gfx and sound.  After a while you figure out that if you want to build a stone temple, you have to dig a hole down and get stone, turn it into stone blocks (with workshops for each type of thing) and craft the blocks and tell the gnomes where to build.  It's total freedom but with that comes the complexity of running your own little kingdom.  Are you up to the challenge?  It's like simcity or warcraft meets minecraft.  For those that don't like FPS games or need a break from them, this is a great break.  Actually... it is more like a black hole from which you won't want to escape.  It is that fun.  Oh, and development is constant.  No fears as with some in-development games... the dev is at the ready and giving many new features on a consistent basis.  Don't starve, die of thirst, or get killed by bears, or anything that spawns below level -7 (that is where monsters can spawn, at level -8 and below).  Monsters also spawn on the surface but they are usually wild animals only.  Occasionally, depending on difficulty you get goblin raids (not too rough at first, again depends on your settings), but after a while they can get pretty tough.  You will have to grow your own food, or forage from the naturally occuring fruit trees, or clip and plant some more of your own to make sure you always have plenty of spare food.
Performance, for most this won't be an issue, though this game is entirely cpu-dependant ghz-wise.  SINGLE CORE
Any relatively recent CPU will run this game on anything up to including a medium sized map, but for those that want to build on large or huge maps with many gnomes (40-50+) and mine deep, a pentium-anniversary edition OC'ed,  i5k or i7k cpu is recommended.   At 4.2ghz on an AMD FX will run a small or a medium kingdom up to 60 gnomes.  On a 4.6ghz i7 4790k cpu a large and huge sized map will run well with the same amount of gnomes at a better frame rate.  Older cpu's such as Athlon II's will incur stutter a bit when mining deeply (past -50 or -60 deep) when you have.  A newer i5/i7 overclocked past 4.4ghz will pretty much let you build anything without too much framerate lagging associated with mature kingdoms.  Don't let all my talk about performance scare you away, but this game is so awesome, you might just want to upgrade your computer if it's a few years old just to build more :)  A fancy video card won't do you much justice with this game so if you video card isn't too recent don't worry a bit.  Just give this game a shot.  In it's current state, it rarely to almost never crashes, and with autosaves, you wouldn't lose much progress even if it did.  It is feature-complete enough to surpass most other early-access (and some fully released) games.
This game, at it's price, is an absolute steal.  The community on steam discussion forums here is very helpful if you have a question to ask or some hurdle you cannot overcome (expect to lose once or twice, or three times even when you first play, this is how you learn!).  For those wanting to build more above ground instead of living in a hole in the ground I personally have made a simple gfx mod that adds windows to some of the game textures, you can look it up in the steam discussion forums under 'mods' for this game.  Visit
for help with various ambiguous parts of the game, and see
for some (RECENT!) let's play videos.  RECENT being the key.  You want something from spring 2014 or newer since this pre-release game is still-a-changing.  A demo of this game is available.
THIS GAME HAS NO BUILT IN TUTORIAL.  EXPECT TO DO SOME READING ON THE WIKI (or on steam discussion forums) FOR HELP.  I have been playing this game for almost 18 months, it's a vortex that sucks you in like no other, and if you need a game that you can just quick walk away from (to tend to the pets, or your kids, or do the wash) then this is the kind of game for you, things will still be (usually) where you left them.
New features added just this past month include AUTOMATONS!  Yes!  Gnome-cyborg-robot things that do the work for you!  Prosthetic Limbs can now mend limpy gnomes back into action again.
Did the goblins attack your kingdom and now you're angry and want to throw a stone back at them?  Do one better, have one of your gnomes hand-deliver 1000 Goblin-meat Sandwiches to the Goblin kingdom and watch the mayhem ensue!
Build a mud temple that Adam Ant would long to live in, a Stone temple or pyramid reminiscent of civilizations of yesteryear.   ... or just a bunch of red brick townhomes that look like a gov't housing project!  It's all up to YOU!
Combat is handled in the beginning with sticks, stones, logs, soon onto swords of various materials (yes, material each has different strenth), bronze, iron, and steel being the best options.  Research can be done via Tinkering at a specific workshop to research various new technologies.  Just a few are ranged weapons (bow and arrow, blunderbuss, pistol), prosthetic limbs, traps of various types, power-plant type devices to power mechanical walls, and now automatons.
You can (after researching) even build pumps to move water, make water, or move LAVA and make a volcanic eruption!
Water+Lava=Obsidian, a very very tough stone.
Basically, the skinny on all of this is, no matter what you want to build, if you like a game where the goal is only to survive and the rest is up to you, this is totally it.  You are limited only by your brain, and ability to cope with situations that arise.  A little bit of simcity, a little bit of warcraft (1 and 2), a whole lot of inspiration (admittedly so) from Dwarf Fortress... and new features all the time.
After you spend a few dozen hours figuring things out and getting yourself adjusted to this game, to peruse the discussion forums for cool kingdom seeds and figure out how to use the custom-map-generator in the game,  With the right digits and a bit of trial and error you can have a map that's 40-50% water and easily surround your kingdom with a moat... or dig enough small holes on any map and eventually they'll fill with rain water and you can make it that way.  This is what makes Gnomoria so fun...there is just so much to it.  So deceptively simple, yet so deep.  The combinations are endless.  Smart Kings can also make their kingdoms self-sufficient to a point, or just wall in for total safety and stand atop the kingdom walls to watch the wild animals beat each other up.  Either way, give it a shot, it's only a few bucks and what's a few bucks for what may very well be thousands of hours of fun.

I've put in about 350 hours into Gnomoria and I feel confident that I can give an informed review. The game is quite polished for an early access game. There is a large amount of content but your enjoyment really depends on whether you like this type of game or not. I personally enjoy it because i can set goals and Queues and then leave it for a couple hours while my gnomes work. The updates are frequent and fairly timely.
The one big complaint I have is the slowdown and drop in frame rate on bigger maps or when you get about 50 levels down. I have a decent comp but even on small maps when I reach about -65 down I start to experience significant lag, it makes the game borderline unplayable hence why I have around 20 different save slots. Also you can't save without exiting, however you can just ctrl+alt+delete and shut down the game to get around that (really useful when you have a beetle invasion). Even if the game isn't changed at all before 1.0 it is definatly worth the price of admission.

I can definitely recommend this game, but I'm going to be honest about everything I say and this game is not amazing in any aspect at all. It feels like the game is missing the key component of variety.
Allow me to explain.
First and foremost all the levels in the game have barely any variety in graphical design. Sure there is fire spewed from cracks on one level and water on another, but they kind of blend together when there is no cohesiveness. For example you might have a lava room right next to a water room. Not just that but you don't get anything like you do with say binding of isaac where you have the basement and then the caves. It doesn't work like that. There is no jungle followed by castle it's all the same and it really hurts the game aesthetically. With that said the game is not ugly. It's fairly stylized and for what it is it's quite nice to look at. The spell effects are nice and it's very colorful contrasting the greys of the concrete wonderfully.
The next thing to note is pretty similar to the previous, but based in the basics of controls and gameplay. So controls works and they work well. You move somewhat fast and you can jump easily and things work. But they don't work very flavorfully. Dashing is done in literally one direction and there is barely any in between speeds. No crouching, no bouncing off walls, no climbing, no double jumps as far as I can tell, no crawling, no swimming, no variances of any kind. As soon as you get the movement down you get it and you undestand it and that's that. There will be very little to learn extra. It's not bad at all because it 'works' for sure. It just isn't great.
Alright lets move onto the combat, weapons, spells, etc. Combat is another form of 'it works' and just so. Enemies are stricken by attacks and they flash to let you know you hit them. They get hit by your attacks and take damage and then die.
With that said I want to say that enemies really don't do much else in terms of you fighting them. You engage, you attack and then they die or you die. There is poison and slowing for the enemies, but there isn't anything like enemy weaknesses or anything like that. Enemies don't really flinch they just keep goin. Combat works, but its not very satisfying. With all that said combat works as in it functions very well. I do have some complaints like when I can't hit a skeleton with a shield from behind with a bomb because you have to hit them when they lift it up. I also don't like that the game feels like a first person bullet hell especially when some of the rooms are uncomfortably small and hit detection on some melee attacks is terrible and it's impossible to avoid some of them.
Ok lets talk about the spells you use. They're pretty neat initially. The wand shoots some pew pew purple blasts. It can alt fire for a shotgun style blast too which is pretty nice and it recharges. It's kind of a backup weapon though considering the power of the other weapons. And while the pew pew is nice, it gets old especially when most weapons just fire projectiles. And there's no variety with different characters they are just very mildly different mostly. one is good with the wand, another is better with the mana based weaponry that has limited ammo and one is faster. Not a lot of variety.
Like, so you can get a staff and the staff shoots projectiles just like the wand, but it fans them out. Having a weapon like this is nice to have, but there's more than one staff that functions this way. They just have small differences like one poisons, one slows, one shoots fast, etc. Same with the bombs, one explodes, one explodes into poison shards, one leaves fire. Not to mention some of the weapons are OP as ♥♥♥♥ compared to others poison bombs OP. The variety in functionality though leaves a lot to be desired.
To explain what I mean I'm going to compare to some other games so bear with me. In hexen you have three characters you can play with. The mage, the cleric, the fighter. They are vastly different for numerous reasons. The fighter has fists where he goes 'Punch, punch, POW' while the cleric has a mace that just swings and does damage and the mage has a staff that shoots a little weaker laser pew pew. That's their starting weapons. They are very different from each other and as you play through, they have red, blue, green mana weapons and the weapons they all get looks and function differently. For example, the blue weapon for the fighter is a lightning axe that blasts targets in melee with lightning. It can even be used when it's out of charge for less damage. The blue weapon for a cleric is a staff that can shoot bolts of energy or it can suck the enemy's life at close range. The blue weapon for the mage is frost hands that does a big shotgun effect at range or freezes opponents at close range and then they can be shattered to bits.
It's not like this in ziggurat. most weapons have a primary fire that does something in that school and and alt fire and just does that thing more for more mana and that's it. Examples like spells in the blue mana category that do a shotgun effect. There are like 3 to 4 of these and their alt fires just do a larger AOE of them. The freezing one can freeze enemies for a second, but it doesn't do much else. It's not really very satisfying at all. Then there's staves that just shoot a buncha projectiles like a fan and more projectiles with alt fire. There is like the eagle staff which is heat seeking, but it hardly matters as it's alt fire is just more projectiles! And alchemy? It's explosives pretty much. Bombs and a rocket gun, etc. Alt fire? You guessed! It's just more projectiles!
And this kinda blandness is all over the game. The perks you can get are really meh. Like ooooo more hp, big deal. In a game like binding of isaac getting extra HP is rarely the first thing you care about. That's more like something you are happy to get, but not super excited over. People like brimstone, monstros lung, ipecac and other unique and enjoyable modifiers. Stuff like that does not exist in the game. You dont' get something that makes your projectiles multiply. There is no 'your staves becomes laser beams' or 'your bombs stick to enemies' or 'when you get hit you belch explosive vomit'. Nothing that makes the game really stand out.
One last thing to note and it's the secrets in the game. it's kinda annoying that when you find a secret you're treated to the devs showing you other games. I don't get this. Why is it done? You don't reference your old games directly. Why do this at all? I dont' care about your others games and if I did I would google your company name. If you wanna reference an old game you do it subtly.

A genuinely fun to play FPS that's setting harkens back to Heretic/HeXen, with added replayability thanks to its rogue-like elements.
There's a good sense of movement with the characters and options to upgrades speed, which you don't see in many modern fps games.
You can also hold 4 weapons (one of each type) and there are a good amount in the game.
A fair amount of variety among weapons, which ones you get though depend on the luck of the game.
I often don't like rogue-lite/procedurally generated games, but this game gets a rare pass just because it's so fun as an FPS alone. The elements didn't really bug me, and in fact added to my enjoyment.
My complaints are that it's a bit short at just 5 level themes. I also wish there was some sort of multiplayer.
I went in wanting to get a game like Heretic or HeXen but I honestly didn't expect to get one.
I'm so glad I found this game, as I've ran through the Ziggurat successfully 4 different times and I am still addicted to this game.

Ziggurat is a game clearly made by some clever buggers, because it's water-tight and polished to a mirror shine. A game can take approximately 90 minutes and will be packed with Serious Sam dodging, persistent RPG elements and dungeon exploration with unlockables aplenty and Binding of Isaac fashion item/weapon discovery at the end of each run.
While much has gone into the design, it's no slouch in either visuals or audio though - it's crisp and clear on the eyes from start to finish and I can't say I found any real fault in either the music or the sound design.
It could be expressed as a sum of others of its type - Serious Sam with Heretic's aesthetic, Hexen's weaponry and spellplay - but make no mistake, the setting and overall theme gives it its own identity, although I'm sure it could have benefitted from some more characterisation here and there.
Regardless, I'll be quite happy to keep this in my library for future visits.

I'm a pretty big fan of the first game. Can't say the same for this sequel. To go and exclaim that I hate this game would be stupid. But I will say that it's extremely overrated and completely mediocre. It's certainly not /bad/ but it is lacking some of what made the previous title so refreshing.
Dead Space was all about immersion. No HUD, no pause menus, no cutscenes where characters would forward the story. While the sequel maintains the diegetically implemented menus and lack of heads up display, they changed Isaac into a rather talkative character.
The use of a silent protagonist in a horror situation has worked really well in many games in the horror/action genre (Dead Space 1, Half Life, Dark Souls, Bioshock 1). But now I'm sitting in front of a locked door, waiting for Isaac to finish a conversation with his dead wife before the door magically unlocks. They didn't try to explain why your path is blocked. The reason is always just "because videogame" and that really takes you out of the atmosphere. There's also a bunch of actual cutscenes, instead of just having them on the diegetic with no pause in gameplay. (This is bad for the genre, not good)
The game is also littered with jump scares. And those are just the worst. Yes, when you play a loud noise out of nowhere, you will scare people. There's nothing to it, dozens of ♥♥♥♥♥♥ horror movies do it every year.
The combat is relatively unchanged. Obviously it will never be like the first time you dismembered a necromorph, which was quite an eye opener back in 2008. But the shooting is still solid, and Isaac now has smoother controls (maybe it's because I'm playing the sequel with a mouse, I was on 360 for the first installment). This game is a LOT easier than the first. For comparison, 2 on hard difficulty is easier than 1 on normal difficulty. An annoying gimmick here seems to be trapping the player in small areas, and spawning waves of enemies before letting them free. This method is repeated at neausea and you'll be preparing for this predictable barrage every time you climb into a larger elevator. The first title gave you a lot of larger areas to work with, à la RE4.
The weapons carry over from the first game. Throw the pulse rifle and rivet gun in the trash where they belong. Always have full force gun ammo. That thing is overpowered af.
The first game had boss fights, this one did not. (Besides that excuse for an ending) That last boss is pretty pathetic. In presentation and difficulty.
The zero gravity segments return, but this time you are completely free to fly around as you please. But the way they have you turn is quick to disorient.
You get to use the character's "engineering background" by completing puzzles that look like they belong at a kindergarden playground.
It doesn't make him look smart.
Oh yeah graphics, this game looks great. Nice wrapping paper on a mediocre present.

I've never played a first-person dungeon crawler before, so this game was a new experience for me. Full disclosure: I played this game using a controller. You can use either K&M or Controller, but I prefer using a controller when it's adequately supported.
It was definitely a cool experience when I first started. It didn't occur to me until after a handful of attempts that this game feels so familiar because it's essentially playing Binding of Isaac or Legend of Zelda, in the view of Isaac or Zelda. While I don't believe this game has a comparable number of items compared to BoI or LoZ, it nevertheless has a good feel when playing.
Much like BoI, it's rogue-like, so each level is randomly-generated, items and stats are reset before each new run, and deaths are permanent. A main difference I see between the playstyle of BoI and Ziggurat is that Ziggurat has a levelling system, where your character can gain experience, and more-or-less can guarantee an upgrade for direct ability. BoI, while guarantees an upgrade at the start of your run, does not guarantee any upgrades beyond the first.
Don't forget that this is a rogue-like game, so your level resets after each run.
Overall, if you like the Binding of Isaac games, you'll probably like this game.

well... where do I begin? It was a bright and sunny tuesday morning, the birds were chirping, and the sweet morning dew covered my front lawn. The crisp cool air, rushed through my hair, as I walked down my front steps to go retrieve me mail. I opened the mailbox door and pulled out the papers within. Running my fingers along the lightly damp envelops I noticed a peculiar letter. "To whom it may concern," it read. "This coming Friday Feburary the 10th great things will happen." That is all it said; nothing more was to be found within the envelop except for that letter. I looked up and turned around to retire to my home. I waited three days until that friday, and that's when it all started. When I woke up that morning I felt odd. Something wasn't right. I could feel it. I went about my day, tending to my spice garden, and tinkering with the toys I once played with as a child, reminding me of the days when resposibility was as distant figure standing in the shadows, only to emerge years later as a grotesque beast, that would entomb me. The memories of a long lost childhood, returned for a moment, allowing me to experience the joyous days of years past. I looked up from my desk full of toys only to notice a shimmering light coming from behind me. I turn around only to notice my computer had awoken from sleep, only to display what would be the most terrifying entity in existance. The screen simply read, "crush crush." I walkover to my computer and pull my chair out from my desk. I take a seat and put my hand on my mouse. I move the cursor to the button that would forever change me; "play." I press my mouse down and the screen goes blank. An instant later a creature with horendous bodily proportions appears on my monitor. My stomach immediately began to churn and my room began to spin in my head, The nausea, although overwhelming, could not stop me from noticing the pain given to me from the game from enslaving my eternal soul. Like a demon from the eternal fires of hell it latched onto my soul, morphed it, violated it. Before I could think again the most vile creature that I have ever encountered. The ears stood tall, but the body stood taller. the creature, a neko girl. My heart raced and a sharp pain raced down my arm. My breathing grew heavy, then silence. My pulse was no more. I shattered the screen with the last ounce of strength I had. The screen went blank and the glass that made up the panel was shattered into thousands of shards. I looked at my monitor and could see my distortred reflection in the fractured panel of glass. I watched as I took what I was sure would my last breath. My vision went dark along with my thoughts. I awoke in a hospital bed. lines from bags of saline ran down and into my arm. The doctor walked in. "you're lucky to be alive he said." "what happened?" I ask him. He looked at me, then glanced down to the right, "crush crush."
Please save yourself the pain. If you value your life go nowhere near this detriment of a game. Stay strong, stay safe, and goodluck if you refuse to heed my warning.

Glitchy and slightly overpriced, but nonetheless amazing. This addition to the Deus Ex series was desperately needed after the success of Human Revolution in 2011. The gameplay is formidable, the story is compelling, the soundtrack is inspiring, and Adam Jensen is back and better than ever! Though the game falls short of being flawlessly developed, it was still such a "worth it" purchase in my eyes.
For a full ~30 minute video review, check out my video!

One of the few criticisms leveled at "Deus Ex: Human Revolution" was that it - in many ways - felt like a beat-for-beat re-creation of the original game. Yes, the specifics varied but the general pacing and plot were extremely similar. Personally, I didn't find this a major issue; the familiarity probably allowed players to more gracefully accept the changes that were made, while at the same time offering a useful baseline for the developers working on to reboot a much-beloved franchise. But if we accept that "Human Revolution" was "Deus Ex 2012", does that make its sequel, "Mankind Divided" to be the 2016 equivalent of the much derided "Deus Ex" sequel, "Invisible War"?
Unfortunately, it seems the answer to that question is yes. Now, it should be stated that from a gameplay and story standard, Mankind Divided is far superior to "Invisible War", which suffered from a gross simplification of its mechanics and level design due to the limitations of game-consoles; compared to the original game, "Invisible War" was shallow and disappointing. This definitely cannot be said of "Mankind Divided"; its gameplay is a virtually untouched replica of "Human Revolution".
Where "Mankind Divided" fails, however, is in its scope and direction. It is a far smaller game than its predecessor, both mechanically and narratively, forced as it is to squeeze its storyline into the increasingly narrow time period between the original and "Human Revolution". Unable to add anything significant to the backstory - the plot feels like a shaggy dog story; a pointless addition that doesn't really go anywhere (in this one area, at least, "Invisible War" was superior as it advanced the storyline significantly). It feels like a game added simply to cash in on the franchise's marketability rather than a necessary continuation of the tale.
Like "Invisible War", much of "Mankind Divided" takes place in one single locale - Seattle in IW, Prague in MD - with short diversions to other areas. Prague is, at least, impressively large; although nowhere near the size of maps seen in games like Grand Theft Auto 5 or Watch_Dogs, the amount of detail is high. However, compared to the world-spanning conspiracies of the earlier games, this focus on just one city makes it feel less like fighting against a global conspiracy and more like busy work. It doesn't help that the game has terrible pacing, both in the overall narrative and the individual missions; it's really not until the last few levels that there's any intensity at all.
The gameplay, as mentioned, remains a solid re-creation of that introduced in "Human Revolution", albeit with a few new powers. On the surface, this might sound intriguing - who doesn't want more powers? - but these new additions seem to be added more to add tick-marks to the back of the box than to significantly change-up the gameplay and for the most part I stuck to the older abilities; the new powers seemed unbalanced and unnecessary.
All in all, "Mankind Divided" was an average game but it felt pointless and rushed - in development, if not pacing. It probably could have used another year just to hammer out the story, and more to build out the world.

While it is still enjoyable, it doesn't seem to feel as grand as previous titles. All-in-all, I would still say the game is worth playing if you enjoyed the previous games.

I *REALLY* wanted to like this game... I really did -- but the bottom line is that it is convoluted and stupid. Close up, the game is AWESOME. Lots of different units, spells, monsters... Plenty of everything you'd expect and desire in a game like this. Why does it suck? I'll give you some examples -- The campaign world is a series of linked world-shards, or planes, or whatever -- these are connected by gates. It may take several turns for a unit to travel from one connected plane to the next much less to a plane several links away. Your economy cannot support large stacks of units for every city you have on every plane -- so the bulk of your army has to be at the forefront of your campaign. However, no matter how domesticated the planes you conquer become, wild monsters always pop up there. You're forced to summon or send back units to places you've conquered over and over again. It also gets confusing which planes are connected where, and it just seems there should be an easier way to move around and control things. Also, city development is based on a flowchart where to build more sophisticated buildings you must have prerequisite buildings -- this is a common element in this genre of game. HOWEVER, despite this being done right in almost every other game where this is an element, it manages to somehow be opaque in this game what structures a city should have to enable you to build higher tier buildings -- you can either constantly refer to the flow chart button (annoying, and sometimes doesn't scroll anyway) or try to figure it out which the tutorial itself says is just going to lead to frustration and wasted effort. Why not have the city building be done ON THE FLOWCHART, then? Beats the bloody hell out of me. Instead you're wondering why one city you have can only build a million craftsman districts while another one can have a bank and a mint in it... is it because the other city in question has a granary? WHY THE HELL SHOULD THAT MATTER, and if it does why isn't it more obvious!? It's so sad that this game sags under it's weight like it does, because there is plenty to recommend it if such key aspects didn't suck.

Highly addictive and highly playable, even in the unfinished state.  This game has been described as "Dwarf Fortress Light with a twist", which is... honestly really accurate.  If you've ever wanted to try DF, but couldn't get past the ASCII, then this is a good way to start.
That said, it still doesn't hold your hand by any measure.  In fact, since it tries to be more "gamey" than DF's bent towards "realism", it can actually be somewhat harder to start, since there's a real penalty to just walling yourself off, and you can't just go with pure traps and crossbows behind fortifications from day 1.
For those of you that don't play Dwarf Fortress, the nature of this game is that it just plunks you down smack in the middle of some randomly-generated grassy field with no particular instruction but to try not to starve.  Dash for the tutorials/guides/Let's Play now.  If you want to live, you better be planting some wheat, pronto, and it's not a bad idea to do a little foraging and deforestation, while your miners dig a ditch around your encampment and burrow into some hills to set up a little cave to huddle in.  If you find some stone, congrats, you can make a "crude workshop", which bootstraps your economy from pounding rocks together to having a couple basic workshops like the sawmill and carpenter to finally getting basically one of every workshop in the list as you can find the materials it takes to make them, and have the space to squirrel them away.  After that, goblins come to kill you, so hopefully, you created a military and trained it, or you die.  You didn't? Oh, well, it's your fault for not taking time out to train your troops, rather than using their labor to farm to survive the coming Winter.
That said, it's not THAT hard, and there are difficulty sliders, but it's not a walk in the park, and there's basically nothing there to tell you when things are about to go seriously wrong.  (Kingdom Wealth, determined by what goods you produce, brings stronger enemies, and at 30k wealth, which is VERY easy to hit, you get very strong enemies starting to spawn in seiges... fanatically keeping wealth down is critical to survive.)  At least you have options to tone down the enemy...
The crafting system is also somewhat detailed to a somewhat pointless degree.  There are intermediate steps for many crafting projects that seem redundant.  You can't simply make a torch out of some log you chopped down, you have to first saw the log into a plank, then split the plank into a stick, then turn one stick and one coal into a torch.  Making a shield takes two intermediate products, a shield boss and a shield backing, the shield backing only being used in that one specific recipe, so there's no reason to stockpile them.  Hypothetically, it can make certain projects take longer, but why not just make specific workshops slower to compensate?  It can wind up with clutter, both on the map, and in the menus.
There is a significantly drop in variety from Dwarf Fortress, but they do at least make the individual monsters, creatures, and plantlife mostly unique.  Goblins attack based upon kingdom worth.  Mants (giant ants) attack for food. Golems are created inside your mines when you don't clean up your mine debris. Skeletons, zombies, and beetles are found in unlit deep mines.
That said, there's definite room to grow here.  The game seems mostly focused upon the survival aspects, so the game is more based upon offering harder and harder fights at this moment than DF does.  However, it is not (yet) as sophisticated when it comes to engineering/physics exploits, or the capacity to create a compelling story.  Dwarf Fortress is such a great game because it allows for drastically different playstyles, from the challenge of modded super-invaders to crazy terraforming to creating a narrative from randomly generated characters.  The challenge is here, but the story is missing.  Gnomes differ only in what skills they have power-pumped so far, and there's no sense of a world beyond the boundaries on your play map.
In total, it's more akin to what Dwarf Fortress was back in the 2D era, where it had more obviously "gamey" elements, and a clear sense of progression when you cleared obstacles like chasms that spit out tougher monsters as you progressed, but rewarded you with better ores to build weapons.  DF has gone on to be more a "Performance Art Project" about being a simulation, while Gnomoria tries more to be a game with a difficulty curve.
If you want to have challenging fights and a sense of progression, Gnomoria has what you're looking for.  It's yet to even start on the epic world-building that DF has, so if you're more into playing a game to grow attached to some of the characters or see a story play out or play dollhouse or pretty princess dress-up, it's not there yet.  It has yet to even offer any terrain but grassy hills...

EDIT: I have over 1,000 hours on this game now, so I'm editing this review again to improve it.
This is a Diablo-like fantasy dungeon crawler in a magic-steampunk setting.
A former hero has turned evil, and is on a rampage toward the clockwork core of the world, hoping to harness its power. Your quest takes you on a long journey following their trail of destruction, fighting off the forces of evil (who have seized this opportunity to invade) along the way.
Mouse/keyboard controls for this game took some getting used to for me. You control your hero with a visible mouse pointer, which is used for movement, pickups, and attack. Left-clicking in any empty space starts you running toward the pointer, left-clicking a nearby item picks it up, and left-clicking a monster either attacks if you're in range of your weapon, or moves you closer if you aren't. You can left-click and hold to lock on to a monster and follow it wherever it moves, attacking whenever you get close enough. (This approach can be very helpful with teleporting monsters.) Right-click uses whatever skill or ability you have assigned to that. Combat skills that are aimed at a target monster or area work much the same as your weapon attacks. You can hold Shift to attack without moving, or hold Ctrl to only move/attack when you click a valid target.
The 1234567890 row on the keyboard are your hotkeys, corresponding to a row of icons at the bottom of your screen. These can be bound to anything you like, from potions to spells, and can be changed with a mouse left-click via a pop-up menu. They can also be triggered with a mouse right-click on the icon, which can be handy for potions and skills that don't need to be aimed.
All of this is rebindable through the options menu, so if you'd rather have your hotkeys somewhere else it's doable. There's a key to swap weapons, a key to toggle between two assignments for the right-click for each weapon set, and hotkeys to drink the best health or mana potion you have.
Combat is easy on Normal at the beginning, but you might want to finish the game once on Normal if you're new to this, because the last few areas of the game are very dangerous due to sheer enemy density and traps. There are also Casual, Veteran, and Elite difficulty settings. Elite is especially brutal, as aside from boosted monster level, you will frequently encounter monsters which have had special powers added, like a shock aura or teleportation ability.
The game relies on an autosave system rather than manual save slots. Death is relatively speaking a slap on the wrist here: You can respawn in town for free, pay a small percentage of your gold to respawn at the start of the current area, or (on Normal) pay a larger percentage to respawn exactly where you fell. (This is not always a good idea, as whatever killed you is probably still nearby.) You get to keep all your inventory and experience. However, there is also a checkbox on the difficulty select during character creation for a Hardcore mode that adds permadeath: Get killed once and that save is disabled, time to make a new character. Hardcore can be added to any difficulty level. Difficulty level or Hardcore status can't be changed midgame.
I had the game crash a few times from my old desktop PC getting overworked, but the autosave system managed to recover most of my progress each time. I have yet to lose a character entirely to save corruption, which is appreciated.
The game allows four classes: The Berzerker, Embermage, Engineer, and Outlander. The game system used is incredibly intricate, and had a great many stats and mechanics to juggle that the average player will probably not understand very well. Criticals, fumbles, double-strikes ("execute") when dual-wielding, dodges, blocks, and so on all have different modifiers depending your stats, skills, and gear. In practice, you can ignore a lot of this detail and still make a viable build, and enjoy the game without thinking about it too much, most of it takes care of itself.
There are ten gear slots not counting weapon slots, and two pair of weapon slots to fill. Most ranged weapons can reach about halfway to the edge of the screen, except shotguns and cannon, which have very short range but a wide spread that damages all targets in an arc. Most melee weapons also have broad sweeping arcs, although they do less damage to secondary targets than they do to the primary one.
Many armors/trinkets (and some weapons) are part of sets that have a list of bonuses unlocked by the number of pieces you're wearing. The last few bonuses from having a complete or nearly complete set are usually pretty awesome.
Every character starts with a pet chosen during character creation. (This Steam version also includes a headcrab from Half-Life as a selectable pet, because sure why not.) They have slightly different combat strengths and weaknesses, and their own inventory for holding loot. You can even send them back to town to sell off whatever loot you've given them, and buy potions and other supplies to bring back! This takes a minute or two, during which you can keep adventuring.
Slaying monsters and opening chests often gets you gold and/or new gear as loot, and experience points that eventually raise your level. Every new level, you can improve your attributes by a few points, and buy a new skill from the skill tree menu, or improve an existing skill. Some active skills get new perks when invested enough, but some passives are very powerful and not to be overlooked.
In addition to abilities from your class and skilltree, you have four spell slots to learn new abilities from scrolls, and so does your pet. I ended up using my pet mostly for summon spells (temporarily creates friendly monsters to help you in combat) and set it to aggressive to make sure it re-summoned them at every opportunity. I also ended up using my own slots mostly for passives, since I already had enough active abilities to juggle, but the passives are good enough that this is no loss if you decide to go that route. There are also attack spells like Frost, Fireball, Silence, and Web available from scrolls.
The game gives you big visible health and mana meters in the corners of the screen. The most powerful active abilities have a cooldown in addition to whatever mana cost they have, and are balanced pretty well. Every class also has a Charge meter you build up while attacking continuously, which temporarily grants special powers once it fills up.
I was altogether very happy with the action in the game, the sound and music are lovely, the art style is adorable, combat is very "crunchy" with lots of spectacular spell effects and gory damage animations, the steady progression schedule gives you plenty of new toys regularly, and there's a New Game Plus mode.
Gripes? I really have no idea how players of games like Diablo and World of Warcraft manage all these abilities. Even while keeping my builds as simple as possible, the action sometimes feels like playing the piano during a bar fight. EDIT: I did get used to it with experience, and it's very fluid for me now. I can rattle off a series of buffs or summons with ease, and having several spells and abilities instantly available instead of having to scroll through them is very convenient.
There's a lack of respawning areas to grind if you find yourself under-leveled, but it usually isn't an issue, except on Elite. Things like sidequests, the Phase Beast challenges, and the Nether-Realm portals provide all the experience you need. (EDIT: Areas eventually respawn if you've done several other areas of the same type, but it's not clear exactly how that works. As a workaround, you can force areas to reset by starting a LAN game and clicking the "re-roll" checkbox.)
I haven't tested modding or multiplayer yet.
Overall, I had a great time with this, and would recommend it to action RPG fans in search of something different.

Torchlight II is essentially an embodiment of the generic, loot driven, action RPG. If you were to ask me to specifically point out an area where this game excels, I wouldn't be able to. The Graphics and Storytelling is mediocre at best, it brings nothing new or revolutionary to the table in terms of innovative gameplay, and the soundtrack isn't all that great. However, when you look at the game as a whole, it all seems to fit. There is something immensely satisfying about simultaneously using over a dozen spells, potions and attacks available at your disposal to clear out large hordes of enemies in the game that cannot be described. The devs have gone out of their way to ensure the player's comfort while still keeping the game challenging. The game offers to the player a wide variety of loot from the start of the game, there are convenient hotkeys that can be assigned to take care of every action, there is also a pet, who follows you around, helping out in battle and carrying excess loot. Torchlight II is simply the game I tend to come back to for relaxing, and it has always been a pleasant experience. There is also some pretty good mods for this game, so I would recommend checking those out as well. Peace.

I looked at the description in the store for I Am Alive and thought it was a neat concept.
I played the game, and there wasn't a moment I wasn't happy with it.
It wasn't ground breaking, nor was it particularly beautifully - it's visuals obscured by a constant miasma of dust.
The thing that won me over with this game was it's humanity.
It's a touching story, with fun climing, fun stealth, and interesting interactions with NPC's.
It doesn't pull any punches with it's content, and it gives a brutally honest opinion of what it would be like in a post apocolyptic world.
If there's one drawback for this game, it is its length. You'll easily blow through the game with it having around about 10 hours gametime, give or take, if you're trying to complete it all on normal difficulty.

I recommend this if it's on sale, or for its full retail price if you're bored and want to play something with a bit of charm.

I Am Alive is a flawed, but surprisingly enjoyable survival game. You play a man searching for his family after a catastrophe destroys a large American city. Survivors live amongst the ruins, and many of them are willing to kill over a bottle of water or a can of food. Other survivors may need your aid, and it's up to you if you want to help them or not.
I Am Alive is something like a survival-horror game, even though it doesn't have traditional monsters. Combat sequences aren't that numerous, but they do require some planning since enemies usually outnumber you and bullets are very hard to come by. I Am Alive often puts you in situations where you're facing four armed enemies and you only have one bullet and your trusty machete. Combat in I Am Alive works but it's kind of clunky, with button prompts often appearing just a bit too late; It's manageable, but could have been better.
Not everyone in I Am Alive will be hostile towards the player: there are numerous survivors who require assistance of some kind. While you can help these folks out by parting with precious supplies, you don't have to. Saving some people might involve taking someone else's life, but do you want to waste a precious bullet to save a stranger? It's up to you, and the game never judges your actions (or inactions). I Am Alive tries to subtly steer players down the virtuous path but if you want to keep all the goodies for yourself, you can.
I Am Alive also has some platforming sequences where you have to scale crumbling skyscrapers while making sure your stamina doesn't run out. These parts can be tense, but they aren't very hard.
All these things combine to make I Am Alive a fairly engrossing experience. What the game really needed more of was some extra polish as it feels a bit cheap, with mediocre character models and animations. The graphics can be atmospheric, but Unreal Engine's "Sand Blasted" filter is horribly abused and makes nearly everything look the same after a while; fans of the color grey will love I Am Alive. Enemy artificial intelligence leaves something to be desired too, as baddies will  often cower when you point a gun at them only to instantly forget you had a gun when you lower the weapon, only to suddenly remember you have a firearm when the gun comes back up and quickly go back to pleading for their lives. This behaviour is comical, but it kills the tension in a lot of parts.
I Am Alive's ending also needed some work. The cliffhanger conclusion feels really rushed, and it leaves a couple of major plot points unresolved. It's a very disappointing finish, with almost no payoff. It feels like there's a level missing.
Flaws aside, I Am Alive still manages to be a pretty good game. Try it. You just might be pleasantly surprised.

If you have one team mate, you can each switch off as the missing class, and if you have two team mates, you can each dedicate yourselves to playing your one role. you can trade your roles if both players agree by hitting the class-switching key at the same time.
Trine 2 has much lovelier backgrounds than the original game, in my opinion, and the whole game just felt smoother in general. I probably would never have completed Trine 2 on my own, just as I never completed the original Trine on my own, but co-op really helped to add a missing element to the first game and kept me on track to completing this game and having a nice time with it. Mandagon is a short but interesting plataformer game. Developed by Blind Sky Studios, Mandagon It's inspired by Tibetan theology and philosophy, and the story is about a sacrifice or something like that (sincerely, I don't get the whole story since is kind of cryptic, so if you're someone that doesn't like this kind of stories, I warn you), but the point is: we are a totem who, through exploration, needs to find pieces to uncover the truth of his searching. During our adventure we can find other totems as well as simbolism that tell us what we are looking for (again the story is cryptic).
The art style is fantastic, a lot of people says that it looks like FEZ and yeah the inspiration is pretty obvious, not only in the art style (great pixel art) but also in its relaxing way of telling the story and in letting you to explore as you pleases. The ambientation is other thing that game does well, reminds of the Tibet (as you can imagine) but since is just a sngle screen it's not something so impressive. The music is good too, even though it's more a simple companion rather than a memorable ost.
On the "negative" side (isn't bad at all, just not too well performed) the jump in Mandagon isn't very good and as a plataformer, this could be a problem, however the game is very short and the plataforming good enough to forget this problem. And talking about duration the game is no longer than an hour, I think the game lenght is around 35-45 minutes.
In conclusion Mandagon is a short game with some mistakes and not too memorable, but it's free and good enough to play it out and relax. It's not something that you'll remind for years, it´s what it is: a short, relaxing videogame that is definetively worth the hour that takes from you.
