My favorite 4X.  I like that the different campaigns are very different.  You can play a conquer your neighbors game like any other, on either a series of worlds or on a large world with the other worlds attached as possible, though not necessary places to explore; or you can compete to be the first to finish a series of increasingly difficult quests in what maybe shouldn't be the default game mode;  or if you have the expansion you can play against a single strong opponent who appears in the middle of your civilization, nagas this time rather than dremers as in the first game.  I like that this final mode encourages you to work together with your opponents whether they are computer players or human players, and I like that computer allies really will help you.  This is something very lacking in really all the other 4X games, where it is just a fight for supremacy.
The other thing that sets this game appart is the focus on tactical combat and exploration rather than civilization building or roleplaying (as in the Age of Wonders or HOMM series).  I like this. You start off right away with an army and your army grows just as much as you want it to, as you can build units at the same time as buildings in your cities.  (a bizarre restriction in the Civ games and in the Endless games)  There are so many different types of neutral units that hide great rewards in their spawn points.  Much of the early game is just plain survival, and it's a lot of fun.  It never seems like you've explored everything.  Even after 100s of hours that I've spent in both Warlock 1 and 2 combined.  In multiplayer turns are turn-based rather than simultaneous, but as everything happens on the main map, and you can watch your allies, things don't seem as boring as HOMM (which I would never play multiplayer).
I really am liking Endless Space and Endless Legend as well, those really have a lot to discover, but this has a pick up and play quality and a, I must play just a few more turns, quality that keeps me playing this even when those are available.  I suppose I would play those when I want something more serious, and this when I want something fun, while the old standards of Civ and HOMM are really starting to feel more OLD than standard in their current iterations.
Unless you like a buggy game that the devs have abandoned, look elsewhere.

I Am Alive might have been a great game but it manages to fall over itself in several critical categories. The first is atrociously awful combat, where you are saddled with an avatar who has only two combat moves and both are ridiculously hobbled. The first is shooting a gun, which is effective in dealing with enemies but ammunition is purposely in extremely short supply. The second is melee combat, but the only move you can make is to grapple with an enemy and jab a knife into their midsection, and that move can be interrupted by getting hit. Essentially this means you are helpless against groups, because you won't have enough ammunition to take down all the enemies and melee is impossible against more than one person. Of course, the game frequently throws you against groups. Toss in a hobbled save-game system (save-points, and only a handful of retries before you have to restart the entire level) and combat becomes a game-killer.
The platforming, the other half of the game, is too cumbersome and limited to make exploration enjoyable, and the dreary, limited graphics mean you won't want to wander the world anyway. The game does open up some after a while, becoming far less linear than its first few levels make it appear, but there's really not that much to do in the world so there's no point. And just when you think you are starting to make progress, the game suddenly ends, with no resolution or even a climax. It's a disappointing game on so many levels.

TL;DR - This game is quite fun. It's probably a 9/10 if you like this kind of gameplay. 7/10 otherwise.
I'm not into this kind of hack n' slash games. I much prefer to fight fewer and stronger enemies in games like Dark Souls than to crush down hordes upon hordes of weak monsters like here in Torchlight. That said, I had a pretty good time.
Pros:
+ Well made RPG mechanics. Lots and lots of different builds possible for each class.
+ Interesting enemy moves. I didn't expect it from a game like this, but most monsters have cool and varied attacks.
+ Pet companion. I normally go "ugh" when I see pets in rpgs, but here it's very well done. No, you don't have to feed it. Tough if you DO feed it, it'll transform. It can also hold loot for you, so double inventary space. You can send it to town to sell your loot from wherever you are, it'll come back in merely 2 minutes. You can also teach spells to it. My pet became a goddamn necromancer, summoning different kinds of skeletons!
+ Loot! Lots of loot. Trash loot, rare lot, very rare loot. It's always satisfying to see loot showers.
+ Nice dungeons. You'll be in dungeons 70% of the time, and they're all very nicely made with hidden rooms, treasure chests and traps.
+ Actually this game should be called Dungeon Crawler Simulator because after the end they give you many more dungeons to go through and get loot.
+ You can toggle your helm on/off. Some managed to be uglier than my character's face.
Cons:
- Story is pretty uninsteresting, in my personal view. No memorable characters or moments at all. It's also very linear. But I guess you can get into the gameplay so much and just forget about it.
- Art style isn't my cup of tea. That's another personal point, I guess. The characters look silly, have huge hands and tiny feet.
- Unless you're wearing a complete gear set (which isn't very easy to get) you'll probably look very ugly. At the end I went against my build a bit to wear a (almost) complete set, because I was tired of looking like a clown.
Yeah, I don't have a lot to complain. The game is very well made. I'm not a fan of this gameplay so I probably won't play it again, but there's lots of replay value. You can try different classes, builds and difficulties.

Worth it! However, I prefered Deus Ex: Human Revolution.

To be honest, my relationship with Deus Ex has been hardly the coziest or most consistent. But Human Revolution made me reconsider my feelings and then came along Mankind Divided. The premise made sense, the gameplay promised a few things and the asking price wasn't unreasonable. I bought it. Now 40 hours later, here's the review.
PLOT - I know all things aren't supposed to have definitive endings. But as almost everyone has said, the game feels incomplete. More so because the prime characters of the previous game (Sarif aside) have little role to play. It seems they've just been cast aside so new ones can come in. Also, the whole police guy vs rogue guy thing isn't well developed. Unlike HR, there's no riveting plotline. So story wise, I would really like to hope the future isn't as bad as the present.
GAMEPLAY - Smooth, though with some annoyances. Most of the things haven't really been changed drastically, and that suits me fine. Those new powers should have been easier to acquire, since I ended up getting things like remote hack very late in the game. By which time I'd become totally used to using the last game's skillset on this one. And it suited me fine.
ENVIRONMENT - Future Prague is a small, confusing but beautiful place. It's small because there are only a few districts and Golem City is no Hengsha. It's also small and confusing because of the subway movement system. There should have been special markers for when the rail stations were involved. But I spent much time roaming around wondering where something was, only to realise it wasn't in that district at all. Finally, it's beautiful because of the great play of light and shade, the detailed textures on EVERYTHING and the excellent physics. I wish they would work on facial expressions the way Ubisoft does but regarding looks, that's about the only growl I'll make. And it's not a loud one.
PERFORMANCE - Pretty good. On HD I could run at max settings with a GTX 960, FX 8320 and about 4GB of RAM. Glitches are few and far between. Given what disasters Ubisoft puts out (and then there's Dishonored 2), I honestly didn't find anything very amiss. There was the one time when I had to persuade a goon to let off a shopkeeper. I killed the goon and the shopkeeper spent the rest of the game cowering on the floor. But that was pretty much the only problem.
RATING - 8/10. Polished, good looking and filled with fun missions that keep vintage DE in the mix while remaining fresh. Story is jaded and incomplete, and the GPS system is utter BS. Overall, a decent buy if you've enjoyed the previous iteration or are looking for a mix of FPS and sci fi stealth.

The game is nice but, like the first one, unplayable with a mouse.
Basically the camera has a maximum movement speed, and if you move the mouse too fast, then the movements buffer.
So, if you just move the mouse very fast for a few seconds, you can go get a drink and when you come back, the camera will still be moving.
When you have to control your minions to solve a time-sensitive puzzle, it is virtually impossible to get them to go where you want to go.
I never wanted to throw my mouse into my screen this bad since... well. since Overlord I.
Also, if at some point you are stuck, there is no such things as "going back to train so it's easier the next time". Already visited areas are void of enemies.
TIP: If you set "mouse sensitivity" in the game settings to the maximum, and lower the sensitivity in the mouse itself, puzzles become feasible. Still, you will hate them.

Overlord 2 is a really good game for a really good price. It does everything Overlord 1 did, but even better. It also added plenty of new things likes new items used in crafting, creatures your minions can ride for extra damage and affects, a new spell system, better control over minions, etc. I will first go over the things this game did great, starting with:
1) The game looks great (for the time)
The game, at least in my opinion, looks exceptionally well for it's time, especially in one of the first areas you are let free in, the Overlord and minions look really great also, the NPCs are a little less detailed and don't look that great but this was 2009. To this day, I am still surprised how nice this game looks.
2) The art style is fantastic and fits the "fairytale" theme perfectly. None of the Characters look like they are out of place, especially the Minions and the Overlord, many of the areas of the game fit well with the plot and theme, overall the art style is very nice and does make up for the game with it's slight loss in it's visuals (which still are really nice).
3) The Minions are the mascot of the series, the Browns, more than others, they control well and bring in really good strategy to the gameplay, all of the different minions have different aspects to them to make them unique to each other, the Browns are as basic as you can get with a minion, they have the most health and do the most damage, they will only run up to an enemy and beat them senseless, the Reds use fireballs and are great for a ranged attack and is the second type of minions you will obtain and it brings some strategy into the game, Greens are the third type you get and will jump onto enemies and stab enemies with their claws, finally, Blues, the only minions that can swim and will revive other minions that have recently fallen, Minions also can pick up items to make them stronger and deal more damage.
4) The customization of your character, or the Overlord, is really good too. You can make a variety of different weapons and armor, you can upgrade a series of spells, your health, and the amount of magic you can hold, you can also customize your tower.
There are MANY more things that make this game REALLY good but I think this review is already long enough and I should start addressing the things that aren't so good about this game. Starting with:
1) The NPC animations are absolutely HORRENDOUS, especially in this game's cutscenes. They all look wonky and odd, where as the Overlord's Animations look fine, and the minion's animations as well, although this is a very minor thing, as in it doesn't have a real affect on the gameplay, I felt like it was my biggest problem with the game.
2) The Sidequests ARE TEDIOUS, emphasis on the "TEDIOUS" for example, one of the quests is kill a thousand gnomes, which I completed at the end of the game, grinding in an area where there is a nice amount of them, expecting a reward for this TEDIOUS task... I got nothing, other sidequests are the same thing, kill a absurd amount of something for no reward, basically wasting your time, so don't even bother with the "conquer the town" quests.
3) Some parts of the game, it is necessary to control minions on a wall.... under a time limit with plenty obstacles, it will take you some time to do but it is a pain in the A S S and probably the worst section of the game.
Overall, this game is a classic and I enjoyed replaying it. The Overall Score for this game is: 9/10

If nothing else, Batman: Arkham Asylum is at least definitive proof that superhero games can be good, if not downright fantastic. The visuals are dazzling. The combat is smooth. The story flows. There are enough Easter eggs to make Batman fans jump with glee. The list of pros is so long that it'd probably be shorter to point out the flaws.
First and foremost is linearity. Having played the sequel, Arkham City, it was difficult for me to return to a game which constantly forced me down a singular path. This limitation on what I can see and where I can go not only took away from the feeling of realism, but made Arkham Island feel devoid of life.
The second most gripping issue is Batman's detective mode which allows the player to track enemies even behind walls. Many players, myself included, will play through the game with this ability on. Unfortunately, while activated, nearly everything becomes monochromatic, leaving the beautiful and vibrant environments unnoticed.
Grade: B+

What is there to say about the famous Batman that has not already been said? Batman is my favorite hero, hands down. Maybe that makes me slightly biased in this review, but Batman: Arkham Asylum is exactly how a Batman game should be for long-time or even newly-born fans. I am not inclined to lie about him being a "super" hero, because he ultimately does not have super powers. His gadgets make him a super being, BUT he does not have super-human abilities, unlike his nemesises or other "super" heroes in likeness of Superman and whatnot.
He drives a Batmobile; I mean, who does not love this guy? The two main parts about this game that stood out to me the most are not only the constant action throughout the entirety of the game (fighting mechanics, flying mechanics, and the like), but the Scarecrow and the Joker are what make this game what it is. Without spoiling the game for anyone who has not indulged in this experience yet, Scarecrow plays an epic part in this game; it is one of my favorite parts in gaming history. The Joker is hilarious; he kept me laughing consistently, which is a plus in any game. This game is stunning, graphics wise; the gameplay is absolutely one hundred pecent fun, one hundred percent of the time; the story-line is full of character, as there are an extensive amount of villians in it; basically, this game is perfection at its finest hour. Everything about it is exhilerating. Sometimes, more so than not, games are disappointing when they are hyped up, but this one is as pleasing as pie, unless you are into cake. It is not by any means a short game either, so if you enjoy a decent amount of gameplay, this is your match. You will not be disappointed, trust me! I have played over 1,000 + games, and this is one of my favorites.

There are some games that build themselves around a gimmick, and if you don't enjoy that gimmick for very long you quickly part ways with the game. There's another game (not this one) that has goofy control that was funny at first but that I wasn't really willing to cope with to actually finish that game past its second stage.
In this case, this game does a lot of jokes about the bad DLC practices that happen a ton in some modern gaming where, instead of true bonus content you can buy if you want more, they nickel and dime you for things you need to enjoy the game in the first place. There was a point in the game where I saw the reviews that said the makers drew the game out too long and the joke gets spent up and trying to complete everything becomes tedium instead, and I could see that they had felt the game had outstayed its welcome on its gimmicks.
I could understand that perspective but not personally share it. While I won't try to get every single achievement (I've got all but two of them, and seeing what those two are I don't think I want to get myself out of sorts getting them)... I really enjoyed the jokes this game pulled and the bits of commentary it did. It turned its DLC jokes into actual gameplay mechanics in some cases, and each thing it had you 'buy' or do felt like a little unique bit of commentary under the overall DLC subject or in some cases actually ended up being things you would buy with in-game money anyway like better weaponry. I personally got a kick out of the guy who said he had nothing to say now but would be important later - I've seen plenty of RPGs that did just that, and were less upfront about it.
Anyway, I guess what I'm saying is I personally enjoyed this game and the different DLC jokes it pulled instead of feeling like it outlived its fun like some other reviewers feel. At the very least, it's inexpensive enough that you can give it a go and walk away when you personally feel sated without breaking the bank, even if your experience doesn't mirror mine.

This game is, without a doubt, fun. It is very fun, can provide quite a few hearty laughs, and even can prove to be a bit of a challange, as the game is, even admitted by the developer, asymetric favoring the baby. The gameplay quickly turns father players into either bumbling panicked messes trying to baby proof anything and everything as fast as possible, or a cool and collected father, going from drawer to shelf, covering power outlets and locking cabinets. Meanwhile, baby players turn into death machines, trying to find every way possible to get an edge up on their dads, drinking bleach, using their blocks to reach high places, etc. etc.
While I do rather reccomend Who's Your Daddy, this reccomendation comes with a bit of a disclaimer. The fun and laughs this games offers wear off rather fast, at least in its current state. Some of the most deadly items to the baby spawn in the same location every game, while all the items useful to the father are completely randomized, and the time it takes trying to search through all the drawers and cabinets to find them, is just time that the baby is given to find one of its, rather easy, deaths. Objects like knives and forks are a dime a dozen, and it makes it very easy for the baby to overwhelm the father and get an easy, yet entertaining, death by electric shock.
Overall, for its (current) $5 price tag, Who's Your Daddy is a fun little package filled with good laughs and somewhat addicting gameplay. The game is still in Early Access, and still has room and time to improve on its formula, but until then, be aware that the $5 you're spending are going to yield abour 2-5 hours of fun gameplay, before it starts becoming a bit stale and unfun. I hope to see the game improve, and I can see potential, but at it's current stage, it's only good for a short laugh, before the game becomes a bit boring. Buy at your own risk.

I'm on the fence whether I should recommend this game or not. On one hand, i've gotten a decent 20 hours or so of actual play time out of it. On the other hand, I've completely discarded it and returned to Dwarf Fortress, which is free.
I suppose I will recommend it based on the fact that it is decently enjoyable. For me the game was painfully easy to learn and master, which is the only real issue I have with it. There is no real end game. Once you have a sizeable fortress and a decent number of gnomes, all manner of goblins, ogres, beetles, and skeletons will become trivial.
I suppose for 8$, 20 hours is acceptable. Keep in mind that I love this type of game, and have sunk hundreds of hours into games such as Dwarf Fortress, Dungeon Keeper, Majesty, The Guild 2, etc.
However, I loathe Minecraft which has a similar draw of "make structures that look pretty." So if you enjoy games like that, you may find more appeal in this one after you've conquered the challenges it presents.

The game has promise in concept but the jerky movement, confusing interface, and lack of a smooth gameplay make me feel like going back to my old Commodore 64 instead. At least I get nice sprite animations that way. This game reminds me of those old 1990s games for Windows you would find on a Freeware CD. Old-looking graphics are fine but at least it would be nice if the characters would not pop around from tile to tile in a Japanese Seizure Robots way.  It's a chore to play, like a better version of the infamous "Towns".
I come back to the game from time to time and check out the features. I am waiting for a really slick UI, a tutorial that makes sense, but I doubt I will see it.  There are no tips in the game and I should not have to watch a 20 minute YouTube video explaining how to play when I have played games for decades. Perhaps if I spent 3 hours learning how to play well I would be one of the positive reviewers, but this one does not inspire me to play at all. I click on the ground and it tells me what the terrain is with an annoying box that says "grass" I must close. Really?

Updated: The Paradox forums indicate no further patching will be done on the Mac or Linux versions of this game:
The game remains broken in a number of key ways on these platforms and should not be purchased. Extremely shabby practice.
Original review:
This game seems to be very solid mechanically. I wish that what buildings were available was tied to a tech tree of some kind, but that's a minor complaint. What sticks out is that Warlock II solves the late game micro Hell of most 4X games without sacrificing early and mid expansion and development play by making it prudent to convert your cities into automated gold or mana or piety batteries. I think this is a brilliant design decision. Compare it to Civ V BNW. In BNW, hard nerfs to science left four to six cities optimal for most of the game, which means that decisions about city placement and development are kind of limited in scope. By mid game these cities will be strong enough to each build everything useful, and because there are so few multiplicative national or great wonders there's little incentive to specialize. Here, because you're constantly expanding outwards and throwing your initial core cities onto automated gold production, you have all kinds of opportunites to specialize your new settlements according to the local terrain and to make decisions about whether to maintain a well-built research city that puts you over your limit and will never be strategically useful as a unit production center.
So while I think this is one of the most ingenious design decisions I've seen in a strategy game lately, I can't recommend this game. First, there are major problems with the AI. I don't especially mind this because the game's emphasis seems to be on using your empire as an engine to reach and generate units powerful enough to defeat powerful NPC units rather than on direct competition with AI empires, but it bears mentioning that the enemy empire AI basically can't play the game.
The most major issue, though, is the huge array of bugs on the Mac and Linux ports. I bought this without looking into its technical side because I was under the impression that Paradox had really cleaned up its act in terms of publishing non-functional products, but these versions of the game are virtually unplayable. I was most hit by the fact that the quests system, which is integral to progress in some places, is completely broken on both platforms in both release and beta versions, but browsing the Paradox support forums reveals a huge number of other issues from broken saves to constant crashes. After the backlash Paradox has had from putting its name on busted stuff and its subsequent attempts to up the standards for both its in house development and its publishing side, it's extremely disappointing to see something in this state for sale. Presumably they're working on fixing these issues, but these ports have been out for months and are not playable in a meaningful way.

Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons is... difficult to explain. It is maybe less of a game and more of an interactive experience. There is no real dialogue and it is very atmospheric.
About the game itself:
You play as two Brothers who go on a journey trying to obtain medicine for their sick father. I can't really say much more about the plot as this game is all about living through the journey with these Brothers. The gameplay consists of moving and climbing with said protagonists around caves, edges, all that good stuff.
Pros:
-While the graphics are pretty simple and somewhat cartoony, the world and the surroundings are beautiful
-The overall atmosphere is very dynamic, sometimes changing from soothing and wonderful to dark and deadly in very short amounts of time
-Innovative fusion of narrative and gameplay
-Quite a few little things to discover along the way
-Climbing mechanics are fun and somewhat diverse
Cons:
-You need a controller to play (though the gameplay pretty much works off of the controller, so it wouldn't make sense to play with mouse and keyboard anyway)
-No interaction with the story
-If it is hard for you to get emotionally invested in stories without dialogue or very atmospheric scenes you will probably find this boring
-Short (took me about 2 and a half hours to complete)
Personal Opinion:
Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons is one of my favourite media experiences. I recommend it to everyone who enjoys a short, atmospheric little journey with some emotional moments along the way. No dialogue, just you, the two Brothers, the adventure and the world. You can probably tell if this is of interest for you by my ravings, so try it out for yourself if it is.

I picked up this game after having seen it at PAX and have not regretted it a moment since.  The art is beautiful.  Colorful, expressive, and a very coherent style.  The music is haunting and evokes very well the emotion of each scene.  The characters, from your party down to even relatively minor NPCs, are interesting, complex, and relatable.  The story will grip you from the moment you first step off the ship until the very end.  This is an excellent example of a game that knows exactly what it wants to be, focuses on doing that very well, and delivers a first rate experience.  If you're looking for a huge Skyrim or Fallout type open world sandbox, this isn't the game for you, but if you want a game with top notch story and characters, prepare to spend many amazing hours exploring this rich, lovingly crafted world.

Short answer: Great story. Well-defined characters. Fun combat. Interesting world. Incredible music. Definitely recommended. Sequel or I riot.
Long Answer (trying to remain spoiler-free):
I've played this game basically non-stop since I bought it. It's without a doubt a spectacular and lovingly-crafted story. All aspects of the game have been built around this. There is a massive tonne of lore, but you don't need it to understand what's going on. It will absolutely add fantastic depth to what you're experiencing however. The combat can be engaging or it can be a cakewalk. It is not a massive tactical hurdle to overcome, but (without giving much away) how combat in the game progresses serves to accentuate how both the story and the characters have developed.
As stated above the characters you meet are all well-defined and flawed people. You get to experience their journeys throughout the story and how said journeys contribute to the overarching themes that this game is putting forward.
The game is delivered with a great and detailed visual flair. Some wonky physics here and there with outfits, but it didn't distract me too much.
The sound delivers on all fronts all the time. Period. The voice cast gives it their all to help realise the characters they portray and the soundtrack is simply wonderful and on point. I'm a big sucker for this sort of thing so it definitely helped.
There are a couple of nitpicks I should mention in the interest of fairness:
The sheer amount of lore can hit you like a tonne of bricks at first. You just need to keep in mind that it is not necessary reading, although it is recommended to read most of the character-based stuff to get the most out of the story.
The companion AI is not going to please everyone. It occasionally got on my nerves, but it didn't turn out to be too much of a hassle. To be honest I just thought of every Neverwinter Nights/Baldur's Gate game I've ever played and it really didn't compare poorly. There are decent AI customisation options for those that get picky.
Finally there is the accusation that the game railroads you. It absolutely does. But frankly (and this is from someone whose favourite game is still the Witcher 3), not every game needs to have multiple endings to be considered good. If you're interested in this game then chances are you're happy experiencing a good story and interesting world above all else. This the game delivers in spades.
It's clearly made by folks who are invested and passionate. They've got me hooked for a sequel. I certainly hope they make one.

Masquerada is quite the conflicting game. On one hand, it is clear that it was made with a lot of care; it has a unique look and world, and it truly tries to be something special. On the other hand, it clearly doesn't live up to the ideal that it strived for, with heavy flaws and too many things crammed into too small a game. It's difficult to recommend, since the main hook (the story, supported by the voice actors) just doesn't deliver in quality. The fact is, if you are tempted to buy this game off the premise, you'd do well to lower your expectations, in the same way you would if you watched an amateur play. Sadly, that is what Masquerada reminds me of the most.
For the details, we'll start with the positives. The game looks quite good, at least in terms of art design. The voice actors do a good job, as you would expect since the cast is well known in the VA business. The combat system is also pretty damn solid, with a focus on team synergy (sadly, the team only consists of three characters, but it's easy to overlook) in an ARPG-like way, but with a pause function (something like Dragon Age: Origins). You can set party AI behaviours, or take full control yourself; when you get used to the specifics, it makes for a quite engaging experience. As a concept, the story is actually pretty good and it does take time with the different characters, making sure that you know them, which results in some good moments.
But here's the major, MAJOR problem with the game: It railroads you. Hard. We're talking straight roads and thin corridors from A to B throughout almost the entire game. Anything else is either finding new masks (or Mascherines, as the game calls them) in order to get new ultimate abilities (ranking from pretty poor to decent) and some other, small upgrade items. Thing is, those are all marked with big, glowing circles on the ground, in a way that is almost insulting; no actual looting, just running around the levels looking for giant, multicolored circles in order to get the extras. Most of the circles are not items, however; they are lore drops. If you play Masquerada, I hope you enjoy reading, because there are a LOT of lore drops per level. Now, you could skip over them and probably get out fine, but a lot of the worldbuilding is done in the lore section. They didn't seem to be able to fit all the story in the actual game, so instead I imagine that they wrote it out and crammed it into the lore section. I spent more of the game reading than I did actually playing, as a result.
With all of that said, I think that all of those problems would have been at least tolerable if the story was as great as it could've been. However, it just isn't. The pacing is all over the place: in one minute, you are talking with your crew, basically being able to play with one hand; the other, you are zipping from place to place, while the main character puts together clues. Most of this is made through cutscenes, with some battles sprinkled in between - no dialogue choices, no agency, just going from cutscene to cutscene, going through a corridor to a glowing circle, and then another three cutscenes. Missions that would have been side missions in other games (like companion quests) are tinkered together with the main plot, with no choice if you want to do them or not. It's a game that acts as if it wanted to be a TV show.
The consquence of this is that everything feels overdramatic and awkward, because there is no space in between "moments" that happen. Even in the companion quests, everything has to be SUPER important ALL of the time - every cutscene has the characters sharing their innermost feeling, or sighing deeply, or screaming at eachother, or emoting about how much doubt they have. The frustrating thing is that some of those moments are truly good by themselves, but in the bigger picture they aren't allowed to actually stand out because something else superimportant has to happen in the next cutscene as well. If fleshed out properly, with proper time given each moment, I wouldn't be surprised if this game could've been 50 hours, if not more. And it probably should have.
For all my frustrations, there are good things hiding in Masquerada. It had promise, the characters are memorable and I don't necessarily regret having played it. But I can't with a clear conscience recommend it either. It just doesn't work in the end, which is a sad thing.

A small, short adventure of growth...
Mandagon is a basically like a cup of water. It sort of does your body good, and it's very, vey simplistic. It is a 2D platformer featuring only one solidly designed level whose mechanics include jumping, elevators, teleports, and underwater jet streams that launch your block entity upwards. It is very quick to satisfy you with reward.
The primary rewards is a sort of interpretive mystery that I wont spoil you here. Suffice to say there are no enemies, only obstacles, and that growth I mentioned first is sort of designed for your block character get reach what it does not know it needs or wants. There is no real narrative other than the atmosphere, so that’s why there’s room for a fair bit of interpretation of the values hidden amongst notes around the level (actually, they are totems with humming inscriptions reading you two-sentence anecdotes and proverbs). I would say that this game could actually benefit from playing it twice. It wont take your more than 30 minutes to get through all of it, so perhaps stopping to observe every nook and cranny would be fair idea.
Also, the soundscapes are intoxicating. They sort of carry you along. They aren’t filled with melodies; it’s more like listening to a synthesizer with ocean and wind sounds being played as music. That’s the best way I can describe it. They’re meditative sounds and very relaxing.
All in all, I’m surprised to say that a one-level game is as solid as this. So, good job to the developers. I look forward to other ideas from them.

Let's just start things off with the fact that I've played this game through over 20 times. I'm not joking. This was the first game I owned for my PS3 and I don't think that I've ever enjoyed a game so much before. I finished the game with 100% completion and all trophies collected on PS3 and I would do it again and again if I could. It's a bummer that the PC version doesn't have achievments, but who cares? It's a ♥♥♥♥ing masterpiece.
If I could go back in time and replay this game again, I wouldn't even hesitate.
Let's do some basic facts on why I think it's so good.
For starters, it's more story focused than the first game. I'm not saying it's the step a lot of people would prefer when it comes to a series like Dead Space but it's one that I felt fit perfectly for this franchise. It fits the tone that the desperate engineer Isaac Clarke starts questioning all the things he's seen and you can clearly see the barrier in his mind breaking at the stress he's put through. Maybe I'm reading too much into it, who knows? But it fits just right with the intention I'm sure the developers had in mind.
Secondly, the engine and combat system are just borderline perfected from the first game. It's fluid, smooth and it FEELS good to use the different weapons. For example, The Force Gun creates hilariously powerful gusts of kinetic energy and it's hilarious to see a Necromorph's limbs just fly all over the room.
And thirdly, I couldn't help but love the entire premise of how the series turned into this in general. This is a broad subject, but bear with me.
When it comes down to it, your experience as a player is completely and entirely formed by how sucked into the atmosphere (no pun intended) you are by the game you're playing.
Some people would think that Amnesia: The Dark Descent is the ultimate experience. Some people would say Dark Souls is the ultimate in atmosphere. And these are both great options, but I feel that nothing even comes close to the feeling I had in this barren, alien-ridden space station.
The first game was fantastic, but the second one just tops everything the first one did by a mile. We don't speak about the third game, as it never happened.
If you've decided to even read this far, I'm sure that alot of the things I'm saying sound biased and not really suitable for a review to help you decide if you should buy this game or not.
Let me be slightly more subjective.
Dead Space 2 is an atmospheric, sci-fi, survival horror thriller.
Being awoken 3 years after the incident of the USG Ishimura, haunted by the past and under the influence of the mysterious "marker", you have one goal in mind.
Escape.
Dead Space 2 has offered me well over 100 hours on console and it feels just as fun to go back and try different weapons as it did way back when it first came out.
In my honest opinion, I give this game an un-ironic
10/10.

Dead Space, the dismemberment simulator. Not much has changed in the sequel. A viscera-spraying game from Visceral Games. The most noticeable change is that of the environment. You are no longer stranded on the mining vessel Ishimura but on a sprawling cosmic city. The city of Sprawl built near Saturn's moon Titan is somewhat less ominous than the first planet-cracker marooned somewhere in deep space. It's just that the first one was so delicate in its atmosphere-making and much more Alien-like while the second one is more Aliens-like which isn't a bad thing and I guess it's an evolution of the series to a more action game feel. You'll get a lot of that here, with stomping corpses being ever so satisfying and the return of classic deep space miner equipment followed by many new additions. For the sake of survivability, I chose to fully upgrade the staple tool of Dead Space: the Plasma Cutter. So I didn't really have time for experimentation, especially on Zealot difficulty which was a lot of fun to survive and I recommend playing it. The last chapters of the game were the most nerve-wracking with that limb-regenerating pursuer and a tough final boss fight. Isaac Clarke, the protagonist, now talks all of a sudden and the script is much more elaborate which again is a bit detrimental to the horror atmosphere, but the game will still make you jump and keep you on the edge of your seat from the beginning to the end. The OST is much less prominent and essential than in the first game. The game's graphics are top-notch and with amazing optimization. You still have to turn off in-game Vsync to get higher FPS. Is there multiplayer in this game?
8/10
+ a lot of dismembering action, graphics and environment, BioShock-esque dystopian city with twisted Unitologist ideology
- a significant loss of horror atmosphere compared to the first game

It takes a little while to get going, but after a few hours it gets the Deus Ex feel back and the end is really well done. Totally worth playing if you liked other entries in the series or stealth games in general.
The beginning feels a little rocky (especially if it's been a while since you played the first one) since you start off with a bunch of pre-picked augmentations for the tutorial level. I understand what they were going for, but it still felt weird to go from 0 to fully aug'd right off the bat instead of the slower progression of the other games. These augs are then scrambled and you can't use most of them until you complete a few early quests. I get that they wanted you to spend some time wandering aroung Prague, but it's a jarring change to go from 0 to unstoppable then right back to 0.
Once you get past the beginning though the game gets a lot better. Conspiracies start popping up everywhere again, you do some double agent work, and basically become a cyborg batman leaping across the roofs of Prague. It's really fun. The game can get pretty heavy handed with it's message at times, but it also has a few twists that I was completely wrong about. The ending is really good and connects back to a lot of previous events in the game instead of being just a 'pick your button' ending. One cocktail party sequence in particular is awesome. There are a couple of big branching paths that will make you want to start a New Game+ to go check them out.
It would be nice if the weapon augs like the taser mapped to weapon controls so you wouldn't have to do finger gymnastics holding down an F key while you aim, but overall the new augs are good additions that expand your options.
If you try it and you don't like the first hour or two, just push on through it a little longer to get to the good stuff. It'll be worth it.

If you aren't already aware, Mankind Divided picks up where Human Revolution left off. Being a huge fan of Human Revolution, and playing through it 3 times, I can say that I also love this game. My first playthrough was in "Give Me Deus Ex" mode. If you've played HR, there's no reason why you shouldn't give yourself more of a challenge. I tried to get several achievements such as "Pacifist" and "Foxiest of the Hounds" and ended up spending over 50 hours in a single playthrough. I didn't get the latter as I must have set off an alarm somewhere. Do car alarms count?
There are many reviews about gameplay that you have already read. It has received a lot of criticism. I will try and address why I disagree (at least partly) with the critisisms below, as well as offer my thoughts as to why I think it let some people down, so that you won't be disappointed when playing it.
#1 - The game offers in app purchases.
* I do agree that $60 AAA games shouldn't offer in app purchases, please let's stop the madness! However, to be fair, they don't put it in your face or beg you to spend more money. If I didn't know it offered IAPs ahead of time, I wouldn't have gone looking for the menu, and probably would have never seen it. As of this review I have put in 56+ hours into the game and have seen the IAP menu once, because I went looking for it.
#2 - The game has too many loose endings.
* I'm not sure why people say this. The game wraps up quite nicely. At the beginning of the game you find out that Jensen has experimental augs and you never really find out from where. But, this is all to setup a third game, and it's dead obvious that this is what it's for. There is a surprise cliffhanger in the middle of the ending credits regarding these augs, but again, this is to setup a third game and is quite exciting to know that the developers want to continue the story! :) However, if you follow the main storyline from the intro mission in Dubai all the way to the end, it wraps the primary story up, while leaving just as much mystery as Human Revolution did when it ended. You didn't think that Pancea was the ultimate goal of the Illuminati at the end of HR, did you? Of course not :)
#3 - The game just doesn't have the same mood as HR.
* You're right, and I suppose this is due to the fact that HR is consistently dark all the way through the game, however, MD starts out in the middle of the day which makes the mood a little lighter and much more settling. Don't get too settled in though, the mood does change from there and I think is a great storytelling element far superior to HR :)
#4 - The gameplay feels identical to HR.
I hope that nobody who makes this comment also thinks Mass Effect 2 or 3 were great games, because they suffer from the exact same problem, but I would argue they were worse in this area. That's not saying those two games are bad, they aren't, but for some reason people holds this game to a different standard.
#5 - Unstable and buggy.
* I only had one crash bug that got fixed when I was about half way through the game. The developers obviously want a high quality game and didn't just put it out and just rake in the cash. Some advice... don't buy games (or anything technology related) shortly after they release! I'd think this would be common sense by now, but apparently not. Wait a few months. If you wait, the bugs will get ironed out and you'll end up paying less for the game. The same goes for new CPUs, GPUs, games, software, etc. If you get something immediately when it comes out, expect bugs, including major ones.
Overall, I really loved the game and am going to play through it again. I can understand some of the critisisms above, but many of them I believe are from people setting their expectations far too high, or getting on the hype train. Also, I hate to say it, but I think we are at a point where games are getting large and complex enough that you can expect bugs for the first few months after release. This is just how software is. Early adopters always get bitten by bugs, and games are no different. If you want to have a more bug free experience when playing games, then wait at least 3-6 months until after a game is released.
To cap it off I would like to add in something I did miss from HR (Director's Cut). I really enjoyed the Director's Cut boss battles. They were like challenging/intense milestones that helped break up the story, but also offered a non-frontal assault approach to defeating the bosses. I know this makes it harder with the "Pacifist" style gameplay/achievement, but if you can't figure anything out, adding that "bosses don't count" again is perfectly acceptable, at least to me. :)
[Update] Now that I've also played through the "Criminal Past" DLC I can say that it feels like a fun, unique, standalone DX game where you can literally play through it with the old Aug system from HR, or the new Aug system from MD, or no Augs at all. I've also played through the two other DLC missions and enjoyed them as well. Finally, Breach mode, although not my favorite of what DX:MD has to offer, is quite fun too and adds even more gameplay if you want more DX style gameplay.

The devs made a fine game, then ended it where they shouldn't. A Criminal Past as a DLC is pretty decent though. Recommending it only because this game is good before being terminated, and cyberpunk is cool.

What started out as a joke on
from a despised, sad cat man, turned into the family friendly game of the year. "Who's Your Daddy" is the sleeper hit of 2015, the brain child of Thehumanidiot, turning decades of volunteer dad work into a full hands on simulated experience.
The goal of 'Who's your daddy' is to make sure that your spawnling doesn't remove himself from the gene pool too quickly (High School is the most appropriate time for this.) You do this by making sure that the baby can't eat dozens of batteries, stick forks into electrical sockets, and drinking blue juice under the sink. Alternatively, if you are playing as the baby character, it's your job to be as much of a little♥♥♥♥♥♥as humanly possible. This is more choice than a Telltale video game.
The graphics are nothing to write home about. The dad is a heteronormative cis white male, with the baby able to change its appearance based on what actions it has undertaken. It's possible to turn the baby into Shrek if you eat too much blue juice, for example.
The soundtrack consists of one song that constantly loops. It is actually the newest hit single by young money rapper Drake, where he dances like a complete bozo on film. The song plays in the main menu, and from the in game radio, a statement of how every single song on the radio is exactly the same. Not only are we treated to a parent trainer, we also have a strong message about the media today.
All in all, 'Who's your Daddy' is an ideal game for anyone that wants to have a nice friendly game. The price is cheap, the graphics inducing nostalgia, and the gameplay is simple yet effective. I fully anticipate when we're treated with 'Who's your Daddy' at EVO 2016.

Imagine Earth is a fun & uniqued little game, its been a long time since devs had the kind of freedom to experiment when making games.

So if your looking for a nice little original strategy game, I whole heartedly recommend this one.
PS note to devs, players tend not to trust early access after being ripped off by many devs since its introduction. Staying in early access too long (4 years in 2018 for you), is not a good idea for that reason. I first played LOTRO in 2009 and stopped because it was subscription-only at that time. I returned to LOTRO last year (2016), tried all the free content for a few months, and enjoyed it so much that I started subscribing. I'm still loving LOTRO now. This has been the longest time I've stuck with any game ever. I've played several MMOs before. Mostly the storytelling content in LOTRO is what keeps me interested. Some of the voice acting is superb. The landscapes are beautiful. The atmosphere is immersive, especially adventuring solo. Crafting is great. Character cosmetics customization is fun. Combat mechanics is balanced enough for my limited abilities. Player community is older, mature, and friendly. I don't think I qualify as a Tolkien fan because I haven't read the books, but I like how there are so many other players in the game who are. The huge Tolkien fanbase provides another source of players and even brings in non-gamers. Hopefully there are plenty more years of LOTRO to come.

Lord of the Rings Online was my first MMO that I started playing around 2008. I stopped playing it when I tried other MMOs but Lotro is by far the best MMO I've ever played and is the MMO I keep going back to. It does have dated graphics by 2017 standards, and newer MMOS have better quality of life improvements, but those are really minor shortcomings of Lotro given everything else. It's got a great community, the world is expansive and fun to explore, and the map designs and quests remain faithful to the books (read: not the movies).

Dead Space is a sci-fi, survival horror game that happens to be one of the best and my personal favorite in this ganre. Dead Space 2, just like Dead Space is an awesome game. The story continies with Isaac trying to deal with his inner demons and dementia. Many new gameplay elemets are presented with the 2nd game and most of what was good in DS1 is still here. It has been said that a good villain or antagonist makes a great story.
How often have you played a game where the big bad is just some insane, evil monster out to destroy the world just because it is evil? Or an unbelievable cardboard caricature of a power-hungry evil dictator? Or just some angry, rampaging dragon that's angry because, well it's a dragon?
No one is like that in Masquerada. You may not agree with the primary antagonist, but you get to understand where she comes from.
All the characters feel grounded, from the heroes to the villains. They are people with believeable motivations, which makes the story soar.
And the story is beautifully done. From the immersive world building and art design, to the dialogue of all the characters (all of it voiced), to the high quality codex entries.
Many a time in RPGs I skip reading lore entries or books, but not in this case because they are so well written. Perhaps the secret is also that it is a journal lensed from the protagonist Ciercero's perspective. It helps you understand him better and makes us care about the characters and lore.
If you are looking for an open-world, multiple branching choice RPG with tons of replayability, this game is not for you. It is entirely linear (like some JRPGs), relatively short (12 to 15 hours), and has zero sidequests. You are playing not as an avatar of yourself, but as a inspectorre (think detective) set in a fantasy renaissance Venetian setting. It is his point of view and story, and he is a man on a mission.
What you give up in terms of sprawling open world and a quest log full of entries, you get a tight storyline with well written believable characters that grow on you. I laughed; I teared up; I worried whether characters were going to die because I cared.
Combat wise it was passable but the pausable real-time action is not a key highlight. For me at least. I bought Masquerada because of the recommendations on the story and world, and I am happy to say that my expectations here were more than met.
It is uncommon to find games that pack a deep emotive punch. Like Transistor, or Undertale, this is one story I think I will remember for some time.

Some of my friends admitted that they had heard of this game but passed it by as 'just another indie RPG'. If you've got the same impression from the game's description, please, hear me - it is anything but! Not 'just another' anything. By no means 'generic'. And not even an RPG (well, not what we usually call 'RPG'). And though it is (kind of) indie, it has basically none of the flaws usually associated with this tag. It is beautiful. It is polished. It has amazing soundtrack and VA (it is fully voiced, by the way).
So, about what it actually is.
Witching Hour Studio did what I was hoping to see for a good long while. They approached the game itself as a mean to tell the story instead of way-to-popular approach: using the story to keep player from closing the game. It seems like a minor difference, but in fact it changes everything.
It is a story, in the first place. Beautiful, strong and completely linear narrative. And in this case I with no doubt put linearity as a 'pro'. Because not a once had I seen non-linear plot and choice-driven dialogs written at the level of a good book. Choices and branches simply put too many boundaries on the writers and the industry still has to learn to come over them.
Well, with 'Masquerada' developers decided that they want to tell a story and got rid of everything that got in the way. And oh, they did it splendidly! Everything that works towards immersing player in the world, everything that amplifies emotional impact is refined to the point of perfection. Everything else is toned down and done well enough to neither distract nor cause any annoyance (well, save for companion's AI and checkpoint system. They actually CAN be annoying at times. Nothing too bad, though).
I guess, it is quite obvious by now, that I absolutely LOVE this game.
It is like all my prayers being answered:
Actually, this is already enough for me to like the game, but there is more:
Now I need to stop with exaltation and say something about gameplay.
Personally I found it quite nice and entertaining. I've played on Storymode, though, so my opinion may be not the most worthy one.
Combat is real-time with tactical pause, you've certainly seen enough of the kind. Two companions at one time, fallen party member can be resurrected right during the battle if you manage to channel long enough. Battles overall are fast-paced, positioning is quite important, skills are fun, varied and look nice. Some combos, if you manage skills carefully. No stats, no loot, no inventory, no grinding. Skill points are awarded for plot battles. You can choose an element near the beginning of the game, it defines available skills. Skills can be enhanced through not-very-big skill trees and easily respecked since certain point in the game. You can find new Mascherines on the locations, these will provide you with different ultimate abilities. Also you can find inks and engravings which will provide some additional benefits. That's about it.
At Storymode combat obviously was pretty easy, I had no need to actually setup party behaviour (there are some options that may be usefull on higher difficulties) or micro-manage the party, save for couple of battles, where companions were adamant about entering every single AoE (and there are quite a lot of AoEs!). On higher dificulties those suicidal tendencies may become annoying, I guess.
I like so much how carefully every combat mechanics is woven into lore. It is a small touch, but it is so nice to feel during the combat that you are actually
this world, adhering to its rules, feeling how your actions
.
Exploration is pretty straightforward: you see glowing circle - you go to it. Some are at open sight, to find others you'll need to do some walking around, but nothing too long or complicated. Personally I like this approach, since I still have nightmares about Deep Roads and endless doors and chests with nothing of interest (and my interest is lore) inside. Some can find it too easy and obvious - well, you've been warned.
I also like how the tutorial is done - it is short story serving as a prequel to the main game. And even in tutorial you get lore, emotions and drama - to get you prepared for what awaits you in the main story.
My review turned out to be an ominous wall of text, so TL;DR.
Pros:
+ Story
+ Characters (all of them and specifically protagonist)
+ Worldbuilding
+ Visuals
+
+ Voice acting
+ Lots of well-written text in Codex
+/-  Linearity and pretty lightweight gameplay (I think it is for the best, but some may disagree)
- Companions AI
- No manual saves.
*If you are not well accustomed to high fantasy genre you may at first find yourself drowning in lots of Italian-esque terms. Brace yourself. It won't last long, though. Lore is given to you in thoughtful way, so after the first impact it won't be overwhelming. I am fan of the genre and had no troubles here, but I see how it may become an issue.
'Masquerada' is beautiful, breathtaking and heartbreaking story with uforgettable, flawed, growing and alive characters set in unique and amazingly well-thought world. Visuals, VA and wonderful soundtrack greatly add to the experience, and nothing detract from it. Gameplay is solid even if not the deepest one. Unfortunately almost unseen game, acting outside customary boundaries (which makes it hard to determine it's genre - certainly not what is usually expected from the western RPG) and doing it splendidly.

I finished this game yesterday, and I still don't know the words to do it justice, but I'll try my best.
Masquerada is an epxerience with very few equals. Transistor and Portal 2 come to mind, because this, too, is a game where everything just comes together and *fits*. It's beautiful, from the backgrounds to the character designs to the phenomenal voice acting to the music; I honestly cannot praise any aspect enough.
The battle system is tastical but never grinds to a halt. It's also a vehicle for the world building and so is everything else, because Masquerada never wastes your time. For example, the "codex entries" are not written like schoolbook texts. They are written by the main character and it's genius and refreshing. You get information about the world as seen through Cicero's eyes, and get information about him at the same time. I'm actually surprised this hasn't been done more often yet.
The world building is dense and everywhere, but never overwhelming (except maybe for the 'prologue', a separately playable tutorial that is thankfully not indicative for the game itself). There is no distraction in the form of sidequests, no long and confusing corridors that eventually lead to a loot chest. Open world games can be fantastic and fun, of course, but the balance between keeping you engaged in the story and distracting you with hundreds of markers on your map is very often a thin line, at least for me.
In Masquerada, there's only you and the characters and the story, and once it grabs you by the heart it's very difficult to take a break from it. There are no filler screens, nothing that doesn't further flesh out the world you are exploring or helps you understand what makes the characters tick or where they stand to each other.
Speaking of the story: you'll know some of the beats, some will take you by surprise. It's a story about redemption, about found family, about war and loss and coming to terms with your decisions and their consequences. There is death, but the game never crosses over into grimdark territory, never loses that spark of hope and humour. Cicero is now one of my favourite main characters, but honestly, there is not one character I wasn't emotionally invested in by the end, even the villains. They are just that human, that honest and *real*. The excellent voice acting does its part as well.
The love of everyone involved in this project shines through in every screen, in every line of dialogue, in every gorgeous musical note, and it's just a joy to experience them.
I hope this wasn't too confusing. I'm just still so stroked about having played this game, and looking forward to another run of it!

Players who try to rush other players tend to lose all their resources, when they could've tried and built up a resource pool to invade. You have to use long range artillery or massive, damage dealing units. Be careful if you see a player use the Shroud or play China, as you run the risk of dying to their Space Marine Tactical Squads or their Warlock Titans. This has shaped up to be a really good game. It is satisfying with the layers of content and systems. Consider an ecological Civ-ish game where the focus is mainly on building large or lots of cities and strong economy. Make money, but don't drive the environment into collapse.

These types of system add constant limits to what you can do, but there seems to be always a way around it. It results in a really fun gameplay loop that is always teaching you.

I started playing this game when my English teacher gathered me and 4 other students to play, so we could form one whole fellowship. Of course, I was super excited to play with him (because he's awesome, obviously), but I was a little skeptical about LoTRO. I'd heard some bad things about it, the main thing being that it's pay to win. Even though I was a little unsure about it, there was no way on earth that I would pass up an opportunity to play with one of my teachers, so I decided to give it a go. Let me just say, I was pleasantly surprised.
First of all, it's not pay to win. Although it's convenient to pay for a subscription, it's definitely not necessary. I've gone without spending a penny on this game (though, I am tempted to) and it's been going fine. Just do the deeds (which aren't even that hard) and you'll get the tokens you need for necessities, like riding.
Furthermore, for a 10 year old game, the graphics are surprisingly good! Although they aren't Rainbow 6 good, they still look nice. Middle Earth is huge and they did a great job of portraying it that way. The scenery is pleasing to look at, and often colorful. It's got a very memorable enviroment, and I definitely enjoy exploring it.
Also, gameplay! The gameplay is fun and intuitive. At first I thought "Incredible. They ripped of WoW's combat system, gave it a little spin, and threw it into a game". Then I discovered Fellowship maneuvers. I've never been so immersed in an MMO combat system before. Your position is important, and communication between your fellowship members is even more so. Fellowship maneuvers are super hard to pull off, but it's
satisfying when you get it right. Even questing is fun in this game! (Which is really really hard to pull off in an MMO kek)
Anyways, I love this game, and I love the people I play it with. Install this game, grab some friends, and give it a try. It's a blast. I hope I helped you decide if you'll get this game or not. Anyways, have a good day, and good playing!

The game has a great concept, a pretty lively community and an active esports scene.
I'm going to make this easy and make a list:

Gnomoria is a rather entertaining kingdom building sandbox game. Giving indirect commands through building instructions and management, you run a settlement of gnomes and eventually build it into a kingdom.
This game's got quite a bit of potential, and shows it well. However, like any early access game, you should take it with a grain of salt, and expect problems to surface. Overall, though, the good outweighs the bad.
Gnomoria's strengths come from it's crafting system and terrain editing. You can destroy, construct, or modify almost any block in the world, allowing you to build your kingdom however you want. Many choose to live underground, building multi-level dwarf-like caverns for the gnomes to live in. Others (myself included) build on the surface, building castles and walls. The gnomes are very good at managing jobs, where the ones that are dedicated (mining, farming, etc) will do their dedicated professions first, as there's fewer capable doing so. The resource management feels very fun and satisfying as well, stockpiling your goods in crates and barrels to conserve space. You start with only a few of these, and your gnomes sleeping on usually nothing but straw beds, eventually upgrading parts of your base to house your gnomes better.
Gnomoria's downsides are like any early access game's. There's a few pathing bugs, where gnomes will essentially paint themselves into a corner when removing floors. Also, the game is rather hard to understand without reading through the information section for about an hour. It's very detailed, but the game lacks a tutorial or "getting started" play guide. Gnomoria's also a logistics game, and if you don't enjoy base/kingdom management, it's probably not going to offer something you want.
However, Gnomoria is definitely worth picking up if you like games like Prison Architect or Dwarf Fortress. I bought it on a whim during the summer sale and after finally spending a few hours learning the ropes, it's loads of fun.

I wish I could recommend Warlock 2. I really liked the first game as a cheap, fun little Civ clone with a bigger focus on combat. I thought number 2 would address some of my complaints about the first game or at least change things up. But what I didn't like about Warlock 1 remains and also has some new annoyances: bare-bones diplomacy system, random AI opponent decisions (really alliances don't matter - you'll end up warring and clashing with everyone), limiting how many perks you can give to units, enemies spawning inside your territory at random times (especially when it decides to create enemies FAR too powerful you to deal with), random quest spawning that creates enemies that you need to fight, even if you refuse those quests...the list sadly goes on.
And while I understand the new Unrest rules and city limit, Warlock pretty much thrived on expanding and creating more and more cities and the Unrest system pretty much makes it so you need to play it small. And considering how massive some of the worlds can be you'll run out of effective cities really quickly. That means you need to convert old cities into special cities: free cities (like Civ puppet cities, only they only generate an insignificant amount of gold, fortress cities (which is pretty much a range 3 tower) or religious cities (which give a small amount on mana and improve relations with the chosen god). Maybe if people don’t like managing large amounts of cities they'll enjoy this focus but for me it just didn't work.
I did have some fun with Warlock 2. In the 70 hours I put into it I really liked going through portals and discovering new worlds in the Exiled mode. But honestly if you need a fantasy 4X game go with Civ 5 (with some of the fantasy mods), Fallen Enchantress and Warlock 1. If you do want to play 2, I recommend a really big steam sale.

Time to complete: 8 hours

This game is good for about the first hour... then it quickly becomes apparent that NOTHING will get better. "I Am Alive" hides some serious issues underneath a beautiful atmosphere, and honestly I didn't catch them at first.
Atmosphere/Design
I am a huge fan of post-apocalypic and survival games. Give me an ugly waste land, a single can of beans, and a stick and I'm in heaven. The atmosphere is probably the best thing about this game: cars are overturned and rusted from years of abandonment, buildings are crumbling with most of their windows broken out, the streets are empty, and small pockets of survivors/bandits can be seen scuttling from cover to cover. However, after awhile, I did notice some flaws. First, all bandits and survivors seem to hide out in buildings that are undergoing some kind of construction. The obvious reason for this is that construction offers a lot of pipes and ledges for you to implement the primary gameplay element of climbing/platforming. Logically, it's idiotic. The "event" that caused the apocalpse in the game has left most buildings damaged, and yet somehow these UNFINISHED buildings are left standing along with all of their scaffolding, tools, and materials intact? That's just stupid. Furthermore, EVERYTHING is gray. I get it, apocalypse= dirt covers everything, but dam, cars should still come in multiple colors at least! These two flaws combine so that every area is the same crumbling/under construction gray building, and it gets boring to look at really fast.
Gameplay
Don't believe the trailers, this game is a climbing/platformer. I would liken it to assassins creed, but it's not as fast or intuitive as that game. The climbing in this game is SLOW, but worse than that it is also tedious. You are given a stamina meter and it runs out extremely fast, which makes sense to make it challenging, but there are several moments that are absolutely unforgiving. There are areas where you literally have to scale a building, and there is a veritable maze of pipes and ledges that you must navigate absolutely perfectly, or your stamina runs out and you fall to your death. This wouldn't be a problem if you could just look and plan a safe route, but often it's simply trial and error because you can't see where there's a ledge for you to stop and regain your stamina. To top it off there is a permanent stamina loss mechanic, where you can extend your cimbing time using up the stamina meter itself! This mechaninc is completely artificial because the devs obviously set up some climbing puzzles to require you to use it, which means you would always have failed those sections without it. The combat is also idiotic. You have a gun and a machete, but combat only occurs in two ways: a stand-off/bluff and a quick-time event. You never have more than three bullets for your gun, so when you encounter enemies you have to quickly draw on them, shoot the one who has a gun first, (or he will shoot you even while you are pointing a gun at him), and then "juggle" the other two with commands, environmental traps, and your machete. Can you swing your machete? NO. It uses a ridiculously long QTE where the enemy always blocks your attack and you have to mash the button to kill him, which gives plenty of time for his friend to run up and kill you. So you end up telling them to back up until you can kick one over a ledge, or make him step in a fire, and then kill the last one with a QTE. It was this terrible gameplay that inevitably made me put down the game. I spent an hour at one point figuring out the perfect climbing path up a building that required the least permanent loss of stamina, and after I reached the top I was immediately greeted by three enemies, who took me around 8 tries to defeat. Ultimately, just boring!
Story
This isn't really a spoiler, but you are looking for your family. Surprise, surprise, you were separated from your family after an apoclyptic event! That NEVER happens! Don't get me wrong, the "find your missing family" storyline could have been great, and even starts fairly promising with a scene at your house where you pick up a few clues as to where your family may be. I was honestly looking forward to a story where your wife left litle clues behind everywhere she went that you would follow to inch closer and closer to her. But guess what? After that first scene in your house, you NEVER look for your wife again! Sure that is your "long-term" goal, but for the duration of the this game, you are on one long side quest to help out someone else. Yep, the entire game is spent helping ONE other person that your character is not related to or knows in any way. This is reason #2 why I stopped playing, I genuinely didn't care about what my character was doing. It doesn't even make sense! You encounter like twenty life-threatening situations just for this one stranger!
Technical Note
I have a very good PC and a newer AMD Radeon GPU, and I had to make some serious tweaks to my system to stop the environment from completely disappearing! I can run far Cry 4 on max settigns, but this game made me spend a few HOURS just to see the dam floor! Also, you cannot play it with anything but a gamepad. Using a keyboard and mouse make the camera stutter every 3-5 seconds and it is absolutely enfuriating.
Don't buy this game, because I am confident that you will have the same experience I had. You will be really excited about the apocalyptic story and atmosphere, and you will be wooed for the first couple of hours, until you start to smell something, and then the smell will grow and grow until it makes you stop playing. Later the next day you will realize the smell was coming from the sh!t this game is made of.

I have a hard time believing somebody can have a good time with this in three-player coop. This is the way we played and had an absolutely bad time with it.
Technical problems aren’t the reason. The game works fairly fine and I cannot really comment badly on things like graphics or music. Unfortunately, I have a strong beef with the game’s core mechanics, controls, and level design, which make the game unbearable mess to work with, especially in a coop environment.
The levels are cramped and small, full of physics-based junk that reacts to forces like being submerged in jam. The way of using those elements, manipulating them for various needs is hindered by the controls, which are extremely floaty and sloppy for a platformer. Overall feedback on everything you do in the game is also delayed or not really impactful – platforms act strangely, enemies don’t have stagger animations and you may not even notice when the annoying fireballs sap your health. In addition, fighting enemies is as deep as a puddle, with nothing exciting to offer. Puzzles are annoying most of the time, with hit-or-miss quality.
The game becomes frustrating to the third degree in coop mode, where there is no way that players will not make the lives of others miserable. Having so many tools at your disposal at once also murks the correct puzzle solutions, making the “incorrect” solutions that should seemingly work, leave you with nothing. Good graphics also contribute to the absolute mess of visual effects making the game borderline incomprehensible at times.
In one word, the game is just
. None of the aspects of Trine have any sharp edge to it. Everything, from platforming through fighting to exploration, is made without being impressive in the slightest. Lack of consistent feedback for players actions, no fair or engaging challenges, and the story and setting as boring as this year’s EA E3 conference convince me to not recommend this game, even if you seriously do not have anything else to do.

I first saw this game during the 2015 Playstation Experience event and was instantly smitten. A year and a half later I was totally eager to play the game and I'm so glad I took the time to sit down and try it out.
PROS
- The artwork is STUNNING. The details that exist in the world's environment, the character designs, the masks, all of it is wonderfully opulent and rich. The designs really work into the storyline, so no part of it really feels arbitrary. The animation sequences are done in an animated comic book format, which was really neat.
- The story and lore are great! There are some people who complain that the story is discovery-driven, vs. hand fed to the user. I personally really liked that, since a lot of the main plot and snippets of lore are fed through dialogue sequences. If they had tried to cram more of the lore and backstory in the dialogue options, it would've been quite bloated and conversation-heavy. Instead you find bits and pieces of the game's lore and character relationships with the main character in little points around the map. Reading through them is completely optional and won't detract from the story, but provide a lot of richness to it.
- Characters were enjoyable. They all start off a bit abrasive, but as you interact with them more, their depth and personal woes really come to light. Learning about the things that drive them and keep them going in that kind of society was a fantastic experience.
- The game is mostly (or fully? can't completely recall) voice acted, with a great cast of actors who really bring the characters to life. The music was also wonderful, and I would generally recommend it as a whole soundtrack.
CONS
- The game is, IMO, fairly battle-light/clunky. The mechanics are there, in which you have a skill bar, skill tree, and basically auto-attack near enemies. There are some skills that require specific targetting, which was the clunky part for me since single-clicking targets in hordes was annoying. It was still FUN overall, just not the most refined aspect of the game.
Overall, would highly recommend to anyone who enjoys solid stories and experiencing a game with enjoyable characters. If you're looking for something that's game-mechanic heavy, I wouldn't suggest it, but maybe watch a video or two to enjoy the sights and sounds of the game.
