I`m a huge Deus Ex fan right up from the start. I spent alot of time playing the original when it was released, and I also spent alot of time playing Invisible War, and was probably one of those people who did think that it wasn`t that bad even though it was a major disappointment.
Mankind Divided has big shoes to fill given that Human Revolution was so popular. It`s also a series first of having you continue the storyline of a main character from a previous game
When I first opened the game, it really feels like a true sequel though, and not just like a story expansion to Human Revolution. The Dubai map feels a bit of, and I feel that the story could have sticked there for a few hours at least and let me explore the city a bit, not just a going into a facility. It`s a bit of a disappointment that the game quickly moves on to Prague, but once I`m there I truly start to understand how beautiful this game is! The graphics are stunning and the feeling of walking around in Prague is just very immersing and a bit terrifying with police checkpoints everywhere and police asking for papers etc given that they are oppressing people with augmentations. Mankind Divided has really created an atmosphere of a fascist police state like in no other game I`ve played with similar theme.
The city itself is beutifully done. I almost feel like when I first played Half-life 2 for the first time and it`s representation of a futuristc eastern european city. This game can be played for only the graphics and effects themselves if you are more interested in that aspect of gaming.
Have you played Human Revolution, most of the gameplay options is familiar with exception for more augmentations introduced. It`s almost ridiculous now since the augmentations practically makes the game too easy to beat.
In the first episode in Dubai
you have the Adam Jensen you left at the end of Human Revolution. After that intro mission, you are arriving in Prague meeting up with a contact there, and quickly walks into a terrorist attack which resets your augs.  One of your first missions is to visit a tech guy for a reboot of your augs, and that results in you starting with an insanely bunch of praxis kits and you can pretty much choose to reactivate alot of those you had previous. So already from start you basically have built up Adam Jensen to his former strength from Human Revolution.
One of the best features of Invisible War as a follow-up to the original is quite simply that you play as a totally new character. I think this would have been beneficial in Mankind Divided. Adam Jensen could have been main character just like Paul Denton in the original, and his actions affects the players actions. This could have made character progression more interesting, but instead you pretty much continue playing the same character. I can iunderstand the reason why though given how well done that character is.
Deus Ex: Human Revolution was a game which I looked forward to and ended up playing for almost 60-70 hrs in one playthrough, and that was before the DLCs and the directors`s cut version. It filled the originals shoes perfectly with an intriguing plotline and the fact that you get alot of surprises along the ways fits well into the Deus Ex universe. You get flown around the world trying to make sense of plot. The ending is as intruiging as that of the original.
Mankind Divided does a beutiful job in making you get a feel of the world with a fascist police state, conspiracies based in mega corporations making bids for world domination, just like you would expect from a Deus Ex game, it even brings in character from the original Deus Ex making the feeling of prequel story all the more present. So what`s really the problem with the story of Mankind Divided?
Mankind Divided is just 15 hrs long and that`s even when I tried to solve most secondary objectives as well and concentrated on stealth all the way. And, making a reference to the original Deus Ex, story-wise Mankind Divided`s ending is just like if the original Deus Ex would have ended just when Paul Denton said that he was a traitor working for the NSF at the LaGuardia airport. For those of you unfamiliar to the original, this is basically in the beginning of the game and the first of it`s many big plot twists, with both Hong Kong, Paris and a few other places left for discovering. For more story in Mankind Divided you have to buy DLCs, which is a series new. DLCs were released to Human Revolution but never so that the plot was dependent on buying these DLCs.

Mankind Divided sticks just to Prague as a main location except for 4 smaller excursions, (a Dubai building in the beginning, an aug ghetto in the middle, a Swiss Alps research facility later on, and a London conference hall at the end). The most fairest comparison would be with the previous game, Human Revolution. most of the story plays out in larger maps of Detroit and Shanghai with several smaller maps in between and as already mentioned, several plot twists with a distinct feel of the original Deus Ex.
Adam Jensen is a good protagonist but it makes no sense starting a rpg game with a fully upgraded character. It would perhaps have been better with Adam Jensen being included in the game as someone working closely with the new protagonist or Adam Jensen being someone you have to relate to. This move have been used successfully in the other Deus Ex games.

The game lacks a more substantial Deus Ex story, with an unsatisfying ending not at all in line with the other Deus Ex titles. It feels more like this story is about selling Adam Jensen rather than a good Deus Ex story. For further story you then have to buy DLCs which is a shame if you ask me.
This is with out a doubt one of the most beutiful games I`ve ever played. I can`t stress that enough. If you are very much into graphics first, and storyline second, than this is a game I would recommend.
If you are fine with all the greivences I mentioned and like to continue the Adam Jensen storyline no matter what, buy the game! If you are a graphics and effects nerd and want to see a cool but chilly representation of a futuristic police state, buy the game.
For true Deus Ex fans: As I said, it`s fantastic just until you realize how short it is. If you expect an epic game just like human revolution or an epic storyline like the one in the orginal, save your money, and hope that the next Deus Ex release is better and longer!

I was hesitant if I would enjoy Mankind Divided based on everyones dislike on the story and ending; since that for me was one of the highlights of Human Revolution. After beating it I can agree to an extent and understand why people were and are frustrated with how Mankind Divided concludes. DE:MD doesn't start in a great way either, with little context or explanation of the events from HR; to when it ends without resolving plot points.
If you go into Mankind Divided expecting a strong story from start to finish that fleshes itself out and takes into account all the plot threads that you come across in the main missions, then you are setting yourself up for sadness.
However if you find Deus Ex is about an interactive world that has a a lot of interactions with NPC's/AI, level design with depth and secrets, with a great amount of replay value, then Mankind Divided will either meet or exceed those expectations. The gameplay loop fully works in hand with all the mechanics and systems it has to offer that sets up great gameplay and situations that can be unique to your playthrough of the game. In terms of gameplay and options given to you, Mankind Divided fully exceeds and expands upon Human Revolution in every way.
Even the presentation is amazing. The Dawn Engine that was used for MD gives levels a level of detail that is not seen often. Every corner and level have such a vast amount of detail its almost insane. This review is mostly based off of the performance of the game as that's my biggest hindrance. The game when it works is fun, beautiful and creative. Sadly it just doesn't run well at all. I'm using an i5440 and RX 480 8GB, while not top specs its certainly not crappy either. On medium settings this game chugs hard and constantly hitches on itself with framerate going anywhere from 25-60 in seconds some times. I've tried both DX11 and 12 but both have issues. The performance is a good deal better on DX12 but in certain areas, most notably the hub world major parts of it have these horrible graphics issues where giant black triangles obscure your whole vision. Sometimes there will even be torso-less NPCs with floating black spikes making up their midsections. So I try flipping between DX12 when doing indoor missions and DX11 when doing big outdoor areas. Of course this game has the longest initial load of any of my PC games so this can take forever.
That said there are still more problems. I tried playing in Big Picture Mode and 3 times in a row the game has hard frozen on me forcing a reboot of my desktop to fix. No other BPM game has done that to me. I really want to like it, but these are major issues that haven't been addressed and aren't likely to be either. There's also a memory leak problem so that if you play for a couple hours anyway the game is likely to crash too.
TL:DR Gameplay is fun but can't outweigh the horrible performance issues. Please fix this because I really, really want to keep playing it!

A very nice example that early access can be well done.
If you like building sims where you optimize your city (or colony in this case), you should definitely try this hidden gem. I have to admit the game got my attention over a year ago since it is about the consequences of environmental pollution. Since when I first bought the game the devs put a lot of work in the game with frequent updates. Keep up the nice work! Also, they focus (in my opinion) on the most important part of a game, the GAMEPLAY.
The game is about building colonies on different planets which can be done either in a couple of campaign missions, the endless game mode or in a competition mode against AI players. The world is a sphere with a triangular grid. The core mechanic is to place buildings on the grid and have and eye on the adjacency of buildings. There are some buildings that boost each other and buildings that reduces the efficiency of other ones. Of course, the environment also has influence on buildings, so it is a good thing to place a sawmill directly next to a forest but placing an oil platform next to a fish farm is not so good >.<.  So additionally, to optimizing the limited space you also have to manage the adjacency of the buildings too.
Basically, you are building both a city out of different parts and the industry supporting it. You have to balance between population, production and pollution. Overproduction of energy, food and goods can be sold. There is also a science tree where you have to choose what you want to build or upgrade.
They also added enemy factions which you have to deal with, additionally to environmental hazards. It really is difficult to maintain a healthy environment when you have to compete against an opponent.
Before concluding, I will list some pros and cons about the game.
Pro:
Contra:
Neutral:
Regarding the graphics, effects, 3D models and textures aside. I think the best improvement would be to add more animations. I have to compare to Anno2070 here, since what made the graphics so nice were the many details, the moving parts of the factories or the farming robots and the flying cars in the city. You always had stuff to look at. Maybe working with such things is a better improvement than cranking up the texture resolution or things like that.
All in all, I really enjoy the game 😊

I read the negative reviews.  I didn't listen.
I'm maybe 5 hours in, on the third storyline mission, and I'm done.
Caveat:  I know this is early access.
[x] Has overly complicated menus and inaccessible shortcuts.
I don't find this to be true.  Once familiarized with them, they are very cut and dry and easily accessible contextual menus.  The problem is, they spent so much time on this, it seems they forgot to use them to actually create gameplay.  One possible solution should be a starting tooltip that hovering a bit over options brings up an extended description.
[+] Seems like a mobile app/simple/quickly bored.
Have to agree here, as the gameplay is so simplistic, you quickly lose the will to continue.  That isn't necessarily a bad thing, but you do come away feeling you paid for more than was delivered.  Given the foundation they've laid with the gameplay, I don't think this will change.  There is no pull to continue as it is just more of the same.
[x] It is slow and perforance is bad.
I didn't have this problem, and it played quite nicely in that regard.
[x] Terrible graphics.
I disagree, I found them to be highly representative of what they needed to be for gameplay on the map, and found them unifying and endearing.  The characters, on the other hand, while trying to be uniform with accessiblity and simplicity, end up being cheesy and a mood killer.  They don't jive with the on-planet gameplay.  Or maybe I'm just old and can't stand childish crap anymore.
[x] Can only play one way - a tree hugger.
I didn't find this to be true, either.  There are plenty of upgrades/technology to assist with this and maintain a blended approach.  I mean, part of the game is to make sure the environment doesn't collapse, so you should at least have an inkling starting out that you can't wontonly pollute without consequence.
---
I do like several elements of gameplay that make it easy and accessible, such as the trading interface - no reason to be complicated there, very straight-forward.  I liked the influence indicators when building, which helped to find the right combos/locations for buildings.  Heck, looking back over this review, I guess the main problem is there just wasn't enough meat to the game.  I paid $20 to assist production, but didn't get that value from current gameplay.  A bit more depth with future development before release, and I'd probably change my recommendation.

Idle Games all follow the same pattern. You have resources (time), you allocate these resources to gather goods (money or hobby levels), you use goods to gather more resources (more time blocks). You hit a ceiling at some point in which more resources cannot be obtained; then you "reset" and in the next incarnation certain benefits take place (prestige bonus) that allow you to break through the previous ceiling.
This category of game is very little about gaming, and more about managing resources and achievement hunting. Usually the premise doesn't play any role, but CrushCrush tries to shine in its market by offering the "dating simulator" premise (which is VERY questionable), kawaii waifus and a very, very, VERY pink interface. But by far the most attractive point of CrushCrush is the fact that it is "F2P". Quotes intended.
As I said, the premise doesn't matter for this kind of game, but it has its touch of humour at some points which is a plus. The art is okay, awkward sometimes. What kills it - beware my friends - is the fact that there is a limit in "resetting". And it is not of the reasonable kind.
After the obtaining the modest 2048 multiplier, your resets give you no further benefit and by all means there is not a reason to reset anymore. Alternatively... you can keep going further by affording Speed Boosts in the "$$$ Store <3". Of f***ing course. Let me give you an idea of
it is, shall I? So if you spend, let's say, 10$-ish and get a x64 Speed Bonus, you'll have a 2048x64 multiplier. Having in mind the wooping 2048x8192 multiplier, it doesn't take a genious to realize that Speed Bonuses are
for this game. As a F2P you can afford some of these Speed Boosts with bonuses you get along the game, but nowhere near the 8192. Sadly, I did buy the bonus at the beginning before I realized that this game was unreasonably unbalanced.
Don't go on trying to defend the game devs by throwing the "it is supposed to last forever!!" kind of cards. According to the maths in the official forums, a F2P player would need, after obtaining the maximum Prestige and free Speed Bonus, 2 years to unlock the last two girls. I am not talking about two years of fun, dedication and love. I am talking about two years of
, because there is absolutely
more to do there, other than
. Even for a game that it is
about gaming, this has crossed the line between the "lulz" and the "wth? O.o"
Advice to the devs: tune your game down, Karma and Sutra are unreasonable. It takes about a week for someone with MAXED stats to get Golden Slippers. I'd wait a week if your game had something else to offer during this week, but when instead it literally tells me "forget me, come back next week" I might as well not come back at all. Lift the Prestige Bonus Limit, or at least raise it. A Lot. Add more girls in between Karma and Luna to help F2P to farm Diamonds for Speed Boosts.

Story:Plot wise theres nothing too unique about it. YOU KILL SPACE ZOMBIES NOW! Oh and scientologists have something to do with it, apparently. So yeah it is very one-note, quite silly at times aswell to the point where it doesn't make much sence, but who cares you get to massacre hordes of undead.
Graphics:Visually the game still holds up, given the fact it came out back in 2011. At the time, it's dynamic lighting was very innovative and it still looks good, it's just that the shadows show some age. In regards to textures, some are decent, where as others kind of look dated. Design wise, the developers decided to go for a very grim, futuristic look, which is there to create a very deprived, industrial atmosphere and they definintely delivered. It's spooky as ♥♥♥♥ mate. Well that and alien space mutant zombies are running around, trying to rip you apart.
Sound and music:This aspect of the game is one of Dead Spaces 2's strong suits. It is exceptionally good. Everything from the sounds that the evironment is emitting to the roars of  your guns blazing is top-notch. All of it is there to enhance your experience and keep you on your toes. Even though, the music is not something you'd listent to on your phone and what not but it does have its' purpose, which is to keep you on edge and never let you take a break.
Gameplay:The gameplay is very simple, it's a corridor shooter. This game has always been marketed as a horror survival game, but i think it's more of a action based shooter with some horror/survival elements. But i'm not going to nag on the marketing for not representing their game properly because ,honetsly, the finished product is absolutely fantastic. All of the guns are super satisfying to use. Every time you get to cut a limb off and see it fly across the room is such a treat to behold(i know i need help). But it is true, the guns feel very empowering and they all have their role in the game, which let's the player define his playstyle. You like to run and gun? Go for the pulse rifle/seeker rifle and slaughter everything in site. You want to be more tactical with your play? Go for the mine gun and stick a bunch proximity bombs on the walls, that will teach them pesky necromorphs to have such a uncontrollable hunger for flesh. There's also a mechanic called stasis, which allows you to slow down enemies. Very useful tool to have when your surrounded by monsters, that are ready to chow-down on your face. Combat wise, the only thing that's left to address is the telekinises mechanic. It's basically used for puzzle solving but it can also be used in combat scenarios aswell. You can toss things such as javelins, metal crates, severed necromorph claws(yes you can do that) at enemies, giving you  opportunities to conserve ammo. As for everything else that you do in the game, it's pretty standart exploring/puzzle solving affair. One thing that deserves a mention is the Zero G. In the first Dead Space the Zero G in terms of movement was very limited. Sure you could stick to walls, but it was very restricted. Now you can free-roam in Zero G. So now instead of just hopping onto a wall and walk on it that way,  you can fly around and fully explore your surroundings. To conclude the gameplay side of things, all of these little gameplay elements are wrapped with smooth character movement and tight controls. It's great. Oh and it has mutiplayer...who gives a ♥♥♥♥.
In conclusion:You need to buy this game. It's that good and it has a very humble price now. However, i will say this and it  might discourage some people. The game comes with DRM and sometimes you can run into an issue where the servers go out or some♥♥♥♥♥♥like that and you can't play the game. I've run into this issue once. Although, the problem seems to have solved itself apparently. I dunno the game has a mind of it's own i guess. So yeah keep that in mind.

Gnomoria is a rather entertaining kingdom building sandbox game. Giving indirect commands through building instructions and management, you run a settlement of gnomes and eventually build it into a kingdom.
This game's got quite a bit of potential, and shows it well. However, like any early access game, you should take it with a grain of salt, and expect problems to surface. Overall, though, the good outweighs the bad.
Gnomoria's strengths come from it's crafting system and terrain editing. You can destroy, construct, or modify almost any block in the world, allowing you to build your kingdom however you want. Many choose to live underground, building multi-level dwarf-like caverns for the gnomes to live in. Others (myself included) build on the surface, building castles and walls. The gnomes are very good at managing jobs, where the ones that are dedicated (mining, farming, etc) will do their dedicated professions first, as there's fewer capable doing so. The resource management feels very fun and satisfying as well, stockpiling your goods in crates and barrels to conserve space. You start with only a few of these, and your gnomes sleeping on usually nothing but straw beds, eventually upgrading parts of your base to house your gnomes better.
Gnomoria's downsides are like any early access game's. There's a few pathing bugs, where gnomes will essentially paint themselves into a corner when removing floors. Also, the game is rather hard to understand without reading through the information section for about an hour. It's very detailed, but the game lacks a tutorial or "getting started" play guide. Gnomoria's also a logistics game, and if you don't enjoy base/kingdom management, it's probably not going to offer something you want.
However, Gnomoria is definitely worth picking up if you like games like Prison Architect or Dwarf Fortress. I bought it on a whim during the summer sale and after finally spending a few hours learning the ropes, it's loads of fun.

This game is an aquired taste I feel. Initially I just thought it was okay, but when I played more and got better at it I really started to love the game. Now it's one of my favourite indie games.
Things I love about it:
- Balance: I feel like the devs spent quite a bit of time finetuning the difficulty of this game. It can be really difficult, but it feels really rewarding when you beat it.
- Variety: Even though this game isn't littered with RPG elements such as loot, the variety is this game is really amazing. There are quite a bit of weapons(with alernate fire modes) that really demand different playstyles, and the room are equally varied: From huge carrot enemy hordes to varied enemies, from trap room to mystic chests that offer trinkets. And then there are the bosses... quite a lot of them as well! Also, daily challenges are they to mix things up even further!
- The artstyle. I am a sucker for this kind of fantasy artstyle and it's very well executed. I suppose some will hate it, but it look crisp and the cartoony textures make the game playable on low spec machines.
This is a very focused product that revolves around one strong core gameplay mechanic, but the devs really utilize the strong shooting mechanics in an expertly way through variety, good diificulty levels and rewards.
Definately one of the best rogue-likes on steam. It still gets an update every now and then, and I think it's underrated.

When I first heard of this game, I thought it would be more akin to traditional western RPGs, in actuality it feels more as if Transistor (Supergiant Games) and Dragon Age came together to have a baby. That's not a bad thing. On the contrary, the linear narrative and set protagonist allowed for a much tighter story and some great character interaction and development.
As other reviews have stated, the writing, voice acting and music are the real stars of this game. These pieces worked together to create a really engaging tale set in a unique world. But while some might like the art style, it didn't quite click for me even if I did grow used to it as the hours passed--your mileage will vary.
Onto the combat... When I first put this game on my wishlist, I saw reviews saying the combat was hard. Naturally, being lazy, I set it to Storymode upon first booting up and encountered no troubles. Even then, some of the fights at the beginning were a bit tricky, but once you reach the end game and have your own system worked out it becomes pretty fun (on Storymode...).
Seeing as they brought up a lot of lingering questions in the epilogue, I'm sure hoping there's going to be a sequel.

The story is good (but not amazing), the characters are not that interesting and their interactions / dialogs remind me of a bad soap. As for the lore, it's not bad but instead of merging it with the game and getting the player to get to know the world naturally and gradually, you get pages and pages to read, as if you're studying for a history exam. The "messages" are not subtle in the least bit. There is no exploration, no sense of player agency. Might as well read a book or watch a movie. Stopped playing after about 8 hours. I wanted to give it a chance, the only reason I played that much, but I got incredibly bored. Towards the end I was just looking at the screen thinking "Please, not another dialog in which I have no part! Let me do something!"

Compared to earlier Batman titles, this game is probably one of the best in the series. The fact that this game has next to no flaws practically gives it the title of being a masterpiece.
Gameplay is fluid. From moving around the map to using your equipment, everything is very simple to control no matter how complex or versatile the resulting actions really are. Combat is extremely well-done and can be pretty difficult at times. Some of the boss-battles get to be repetitive but are done well enough that you shouldn't mind too much. Enviroments are also impressive but don't really encourage exploration since you'll run across over 60% of the game's "replay-encouraging-content" as you play (and for me, none of the content feels worth searching for). Finally, the story is top-notch.
The game isn't perfect, but it comes close enough to deserve being on a top-five list or something. If you like Batman, buy this game. If you don't, wait for a sale and buy it because it's that fun.

The bloated combat mechanics and lack of micro-management options killed this game for me.
While Masquerada boasts excellent voice acting, a unique game world and a solid visual style, the core gameplay made my experience impossible to enjoy. The combat simply doesn't know what it wants to be. Stances feel as though they do next to nothing. The control you have over character AI is far too limited and clunky, meaning keeping party members alive is an arduous task.
The lore is also a little on the thick side. It throws you right in the deep end, which wouldn't be so bad in itself if it weren't for the fact that you are bombarded with a lot of psuedo-venitian terminology right from the get go. Codexes offer some help, but the game quickly ends up in 'wall of text' territory.
I went into Masquerada hoping for a fresh new RPG experience with interesting combat and magic, but ultimately came away disappointed.

this is a game that, i feel, is almost vitally important in what it does and how it does it. the story is beautiful, grounded - so many other stories almost lose their humanity along the way of these grand tales of loss and rebirth, but masquerada keeps its feet on the ground firmly, making us believe even more in its lofty ideals and beautiful tragedy. it is not a game that has its happy ending without loss, and i appreciate that. the story is /real/, though its setting is fantastical, and its characters are  true in a way few stories ever truly achieve. i reccomend this game wholeheartedly.

Grand Theft Auto V is a game which at this point anyone must have played. While the singleplayer offers tons of hours of classic GTA madness, the multiplayer (GTA Online) has the ability to steal your life for a longer time than you perhaps wish for. The singleplayer has not changed much since the game was released during the older-gen on PS3 and Xbox 360, except for improvements in the game engine allowing more enhanced graphics and some more in-game customization options, the multiplayer has since had several free major updates, which is great.
However, the multiplayer has its downsides, as the Rockstar thinks their GTA Online is an MMO, which has the user heavily restricted opposed to older GTA games like GTA IV, where players could make of the multiplayer as they pleased. This restriction locks content like housing and vehicles behind huge expenses, that has grown exponentially for every update to the game. These obstacles requires a lot of grinding from the user and encourages payment with real life money.
All in all a product that is recommended, as there is still a ton of content worth the money, especially from a sale.

so, i’m going to get my one critique of the game out here first - and the rest of the review is going to be ridiculously positive. if you’re not into that kind of subjectivity, this might not help you, but i can’t resist:
for people playing on higher difficulties especially: the game should probably save more often - especially towards the end string of battles where a loss or a simple movement glitch can send you really far back for no good reason. for me playing on story mode, this was an occasionally relevant annoyance that didn’t detract from the experience - can’t speak to other difficulties.
as for everything else...
the environments, illustrated cutscenes, and animation are phenomenal, the sound design/music/voice-acting is top-notch, the costume/character design is stunning, the characters themselves & the world they live in are compelling, and the stories this game tells are those of survival, and hope - something i know i needed this year. (one of these stories is also my favorite gay male narrative to come out of any media in almost a decade - so make of that what you will.) these are people who know their stuff and they execute it exceptionally well.
the game opens beautifully, pulls off well the common fantasy trope of dropping you into the middle of a complex universe with its own laws. at about an hour in, when you’ve become accustomed to the game, you will probably begin to wonder if this is where the game plateaus - if (like many fantasy titles by bigger studios, even) the game will sort of, be impressive for this first stretch until it gets tiring, and the lofty worldbuilding will fall out from under it and crush the game under a lore slog that outpaces your desire to read it. i.e. impressive, for an indie game, A for effort, but ultimately too ambitious. i expected this! but for me, it never reached that point - such a pleasant surprise that this easily became one of my favorite games in recent memory.
combat is simplified, stylized Dragon Age - a little clumsy, although at least still very pleasant to look at. (disclaimer: i’m vastly more interested in stories in games, and could usually care less about combat unless the two are integrated somehow. the game’s story mode felt like a good balance to me - simple enough that i didn’t struggle very much, not so simple that it felt like repetitive busy work.)
which, of course, brings me to story - and i think the game’s environment shines on its own, but the story is what really blows the doors off everything for me. it’s Fullmetal Alchemist meets UNDERTALE, in a way - a starkly human war story with an incredibly vulnerable heart. i know “indie” is hardly a genre, but hear me out: much like UNDERTALE is so much more than the snappy jaunt through skeleton town it begins as, MSAS avoids the lofty, snooty, shallow narrative of political intrigue that so often plagues socially relevant stories full of complex lore. i think that deserves to be noted specifically - at many points, it would’ve been very, very easy to fall into that trap, but MSAS keeps its feet planted firmly on the ground in a way that exceeds every other title i’ve seen that’s tried. the dialogue is tight and the message is clear - far from getting in the way, the wordy codex (usually presented as endearingly vigilant cicero’s personal journal) flows with the direction of the narrative naturally.
this kind of dark storytelling can easily cross into the territory of either Edgy Kick-the-Dog Suckerpunch or that of Unchallenged Nihilist Escapism - MSAS on the whole does neither, balancing perfectly on the knife’s edge with the sort of subtle, deceptive brilliance of all enduring fantasy stories.
the game’s not perfect, but it was brave as hell - in my opinion, it paid off. well done.

A very fun game where you really feel like a super hero.
The combat is very fun because your goal is to chain as much combo as possible to take down numerous enemies, through using punches, kicks, batarangs, grappling hook, take downs, throws, etc. It is actually much simpler than it sounds and you just have to time your button correctly.
The game slowly teaches you how to use the various gadgets that batman has such as the explosive gel, grappling hook, batarang, etc in order to advance in the game.
The graphics and sounds are good. The story is good and introduces you to the villains very well.
The only con is that I got dizzy after playing the game for a while, presumably due to swinging around with the grappling hook in certain areas and getting motion sickness. An unfortunate side effect that may put me off buying Arkham City.
But if you have no such problems, this game definitely deserves its Game of the Year award.

I am skeptical of any game that stars an iconic character with a distinct feel, such as Batman, as it is very easy to screw it up. That was not the case here. Everything from the voice acting (using the actors from the animated series was an excellent choice) to character designs to fighting was done brilliantly. Its easy to overload a game like this by including all the villians, but it stayed focused on just a handful, which helped flesh them out and make their encounters more meaningful, while providing factoids about others in the DC universe. The combat system deserves special mention as it provided an excellent portrayal of what one would think the Dark Knight's prowess would be, and it does so in an user intuitive fashion, keeping it simple so that anyone could play without a fighting game button mash-fest.

Bunnies can work together, with the robot, solo or in small groups to make their way to victory, with their own aims in mind. The Robot's rise to victory is less subtle than a bunnies, but he has many tools at his disposal, and a good robot can control his bunnies with them - most of the time.
The Dev of this game actively communicates on the Steam forums, responding to comments and suggestions and seems to take an active approach to maintain game balance, which is fragile in a game with so many options, and so far - he's managed it.

I write this review after finishing the main story.
Man ! Did I want to love that game and invested some time in it though it felt like a betrayal...
This game has so many great stuffs in it though, it's like the guys didn't make a story to use the content of the game... Very strange feeling.
It started pretty well. Story, characters, cutscenes, different ways to reach an objective but then it failed:
- I was saving up ammos and guns in case big fights were happening and... nope...
Only one "big"(ish) fight at the end where you just hide in the vents and unload your weapons to the guy... ok...
What ?! is that the end already ?
For instance, I saved some rockets expecting to stumble on a launcher at some point and... nope... just carried rockets for nothing.
Same with the mines. I remembered epic situations in the previous Deus Ex where you had to sneak around a deadly robot an place mines on his path. but never had the occasion to use a single one on this game.
- Skills, some are pretty necessary but once unlocked (pretty quickly) all the other feel rather secondary and you feel that you didn't really develop your character at all.
- Story. Quite good ! The characters seem rather interesting, the story intricate though it ends so abruptly !!! Like, really ?
- I was naively hoping that the additional stories would enhance the experience. Again nope. A single MAP. Bored with the previous experience, I decided to go full loud and kill everyone despite the story not suggesting that this guys were bad guys. I litteraly wiped an entire company of security but the CEO was nice enough to make a communication to all his employees to say that they had to let me leave freely the building... Should I tell him they're all dead ? ah no, that's a bit rude isn't it ? *Sigh*
Overall, due to that huge disappointment at the end, despite a game rather enjoyable in general, it will be a negative score.
I'm assuming this is related to the DLC strategy they have where they will split the story in several releases and maybe that frustration will wash away with the next story but it kinda felt I bought half of a game.
Oh, and a negative point also for the never ending credits that lock your computer while forcing you to watch the crazy pictures of the developping team. They have no mercy.

Most of what can be said about this game you can find in other reviews, so this will just be some quick notes for fans of Deus Ex or Human Revolution.
One thing to note is that because of the open world design, it's pretty common to stumble upon the solutions for later missions much earlier just by exploring and following your curiosity. Sadly this kind of ruins it when you do find a mission that uses that solution. Several missions that were supposed to have twists in them weren't as impactful because I had discovered the twists already just by exploring.
So I don't think the open world approach was a good idea with this game necessarily, or at least they didn't manage to make it work as well as the standalone missions or large levels like the bank.
The main storyline of the game feels rushed compared to Human Revolution. It builds up satisfactorily until what feels like the halfway point, then you realize part way through the following mission that this is supposed to be the climax. It's like half the game was cut out (not at all unusual these days, and often in the service of making future DLC episodes). It doesn't even resolve simple plot points and instead teases them for the sequel/DLC. HR did a better job of making a self-contained story that still leaves enough open for sequels, possibly because with HR they didn't know if there would be any sequels yet.
One of the things that defined Human Revolution and the Deus Ex series as a whole was the theme of transhumanism. Surprisingly and disappointingly Mankind Divided actually moves away from that, using it only as a setting for a story that's more about racism, segregation, and police brutality and militarization of police. There being a cultural divide between augs and naturals makes sense and was explored in HR, but the extent that it reaches in MD never seems to be adequately justified. It's a shame because while I suppose this is more politically relevant, I'm much more interested in transhumanism than sociopolitics.
If you don't do the side missions, you could probably complete the whole game in five hours. Maybe the side missions were intended to be where you'd spend most of your time, but it doesn't seem like there are enough of them for that.
All-in-all, it's still a great game, but I wish this didn't have to have the marketing and budget of a AAA game where stuff is cut up for use in DLC and sequels. At $30 or less this game is a good buy and you'll easily get 30 hours if you like experimenting and exploring.

Of course there is also punch through weak spot in wall or.. ya know.. just shoot everyone. It gives some sense of choice but all being said it still feels very contrived.
The narrative is a bit topical, perhaps society just repeats this mentality. Raising tension in social and civil disobedience regarding (in some some cases) feigned or indeed real oppression. Officers using slurs such as “Clank” referring to augmented people pushing tensions further. Radical idealists associated with terrorism and how the media can misconstrue facts to fit the ongoing narrative for political or otherwise personal gain.
Not bad.  Had to upgrade my video cards for this.

Pros:
In terms of gameplay, Mankind Divided does everything Human Revolution did but with more cool augmentations and a lot better implemenations of previous game mechanics.  The "unstable" experimental augmentations are all awesome, particularly when you make enough progress in the game to really take advantage of them.  The leveling up system has a lot more options now and most of the rudimentary stuff starts already filled out so you don't really have to go through unlocking most of the stuff you already had in human revolution, which is nice.  Every particular level or area offers dozens of different ways of approaching the problem or knocking out the enemies.  It is pretty open ended about how you go through the game although the narrative itself is fairly linear.  The graphics are definitely an upgrade from Human Revolution, and the level of the game is pretty incredible.  Hacking is now a bit more complex with a bit more variety so they don't get boring or tedious to do, and if they do, there's multitools that you can craft to skip past it and theres never a shortage of crafting parts.  The crafting mechanic was pretty cool but I found that I rarely used it since I naturally conserve my consumable materials.  The game runs well on a good system (I never experienced any of the other technical difficulties others mentioned).
Cons:
The most obviously glaring issue with the game right off the bat is that the in-engine facial animations for dialogue are pretty bad, and somehow look even worse than in Human Revolution.  For a game that involves so much dialogue, its surprising they didn't put more effort into that.  The terrible lip-flapping can be pretty distracting at times and the characters are pretty emotionless looking.  The only other major problem with the game is the plot.  Human Revolution had an incredibly suspenseful and interesting plot with a wonderful cast of relatable characters.  Mankind Divided's cast of characters are all emotionless husks that do little other than argue with each other and grumble over comms all the time.  The plot itself is convoluted, and uninteresting.  It starts out well enough but eventually trails off around the time that you return to Prague.  Human Revolution had so much to offer in diverse levels and futuristic landscapes, and just about everywhere in Mankind Divided looks about the same.  There is ultimately no real climax to the game as it seems to be building up to whatever the plot of the next game will be, so don't expect any huge ending like Human Revolution had.   It honestly feels like filler.
Overall, I had a lot of fun playing it, the world was immersive as ever, and sneaking up behind enemies, knocking them out, and dragging them into compromising positions never gets old.  This game offers so many new ways to tackle any particular problem, I felt like I never got to the point where I was just doing the same thing over and over again, but always trying something in a different way.  My playing preference is toward stealth, so I can't speak for how the game plays for someone that likes to play more aggressively using the game's weapon system more than I did.  But that just goes to show how the game can adjust to anyone's particular playstyle so that you can make it your own experience.  I also can't speak for the new Breach game mode.  That being said, the story was a big let down, and although I'm still invested enough in it to check out their next installment, whenever that comes out, there really is nothing good to say about the plot.  If you enjoyed Human Revolution purely for the story and not the gameplay, then this is probably not the game for you.  But if you enjoy the gameplay enough that the plot isn't as big a deal, you will probably have as much fun with Mankind Divided as you did with Human Revolution.  Obviously if you haven't played Human Revolution, you should really play that first, as I think it still superior to this one overall, if only because of how much better of a plot it had.
TLDR; The gameplay and graphics are an improvement on its precedessor, but the plot is awful and so are the in-engine character animations.  If it goes on sale and you've played DX:HR, its worth the buy if you liked the gameplay of DX:HR.

An adventure game with a Swedish film director leading the production, which at first intrigued me to check it out. Set in a medieval world with Norse fantasy elements, you control two brothers on their perilous quest to find a cure for their father's sickness. Along the way, they will find obstacles where co-operation between brothers are crucial to overcome them. They'll also meet different characters along the way who will help or intend to stop them, which adds some further puzzle and action elements to some degree. The level design and contents are just about imaginative and holds many surprises along the road, keeping it fresh and with a wide range of obstacles to keep you adapting to progress.
The plot narrative is without translated dialogues in this game, where the words being spoken are either names or short dialogues in its own language. The game relies therefore on visual communication through the environment, the characters and the occuring events, which cleverly gives enough on its own. As there are light-hearted moments as well as grim or sad events throughout the adventure, the two brothers were given a lifelike, human quality for me to connect with. Warmly recommended for people who desires an immersive adventure gaming in cinematic environment but also in a less-is-more approach and emotional value.

Being a huge Civilization fan, I was very happy to find out about another series that is very very similar in gameplay style - but not that similar so is different having it's own theme.
Having played all the Civ games it was very easy to jump straight into this,  for those new to this genre you should play the tutorial and read a little online tips and tricks,  to get you off to a smooth start.
You build up your own civilization, you create soldiers to defend and attack, pioneers to found new cities, you construct buildings to help your city grow and research spells to help you advance.
There are many modes to choose from, you can play relaxed to impossible. You can custom design your starting lands which also come in a few flavours,  exiled, sandbox and one other - you choose your Mage (leader) and how many Mages you compete against.
Your armies are supplement by arriving lords, whom you can equip with special artifacts. They are very powerful fighting units-  and wise to keep them alive as long as possible.
You move your units and research/construct in turns- you make your moves and then the opposition make theirs and it is your turn again.
There are many enemies to deal with, not just from the Mages civ-  many creatures that spawn themselves for you to battle as you discover new lands.
It is not a quick game- you need to spend a lot of time just to play through one full game, but it is addictive and easy to keep having that one more turn before you log out!  It is very interesting and quite fun.
A couple of annoyances like always having to give your units orders each turn-  unless i am missing something there.
There is a  multiplayer option too.
i rate this game 8/10 and highly recommend it for strategy game lovers.

Ok, felt like I should edit my review since there were a bunch of noobs who apparently, before trolling around, haven't taken the time to see if this game is downloadable via other means or since when it's been on Steam.
In short: NO the game hasn't been on Steam since 2007. And YES, many players chose to download the game using the file on the official website even when the game became available on Steam (hence my few no. of recorded hours). Now, if your existential dillemas have been answered, we can get to what really matters.
I've been playing this game since launch (back in 2007 that is) and I can say these:
Pros:
- biggest map in any MMORPG (and getting larger). Plus, you have the chance to explore the whole of Middle-Earth
- beautiful and diverse landscapes (you can litterally just roam around, admiring the view)
- it induces a good feeling
- you can grind if you want, but it's not a must-do (it really isn't)
- nice housing system (best I've seen so far)
- it has really good instances, especially for the later parts of the game
- kingships (clans that is) are usually pretty well organized and friendly. So the game has a good, mature community
- Overall, the PvE is really good
Cons:
- the PvP is bad, just bad (after 10 years you'd think they'd introduce some kind of clan teritorial control stuff, like in EVE or Conan)
- graphics is a bit outdated, especially when in concerns the earlier content
- theoretically it's f2p. Practically though, there are some limitations that may make you feel like you should pay. Sure, you can play without paying (I am for example), but it's a pain at times
- prices for some stuff are just absurd. However, this is a player-ralated issue, not a game-related one
Conclusion: together with Lineage II, this is the only MMORPG I keep returning to.

As many other reviews have already put it, if you don't mind, or can get pass the linearity, heavy text reading, shortcomings in the UI, and streamlined mechanics, you're in for a wonderful adventure.
The best thing about the game is undoubtedly the narrative and character development. Each character is believable and fleshed out, having been voiced by some of the top voice talents of the industry. The trials and tribulations faced by each character are also told in a way that makes the player reflect upon him/herself. I've found this both enlightening and engaging. At times, I'm even drawing my own life lessons from the character's reflections in the journals.
It took me a while to grasp the combos with the combat mechanics, but when I understood enough to be proficient, I've found myself having fun optimising my tactics.
One of my favourite things about the game, though, is how the character talking portraits during the dialogue sequences are set up. Each speaker's talking portrait during the dialogue is quite literally a camera pointing at the actual character's avatar animating in the world. This may be a small detail, or even to save work separating a high poly portrait vs a low poly avatar, but because the actions in the portrait are directly from the avatar, it makes the dialogue animations feel more intimate and authentic for me.
All in all, if you're looking for an open world RPG with branching plotlines, look elsewhere. If you like an engaging story, with believable characters that take themselves seriously, and don't want to fiddle with complicated mechanics, this would be right up your alley. Be prepared for the slow start though, and the large amount of italian-named jargon to remember.

Backed the game out of principle to support a local studio. With its mixed initial reviews and my previous poor experience with Witching Hour, I wasn't expecting much from Masquerada.
Problems came soon enough with the lack of manual saves, a codex of quasi-Italian proper nouns, difficulty targeting during combat, missable achievement-tied collectables and a slow start.
Despite its problems, Masquerada's clean art style, emotional voice-acting, music and overall high production value kept me playing. After it's slow introduction, the plot picked up pace with twists and character development. By the end of it all, the party has grown on and I'm left wanting for a sequel.
While no studio, AAA or indie, has the right to expect players to wait beyond a couple of hours to get engaged, I would still recommend Masquerada to anyone who wants an RPG set in a unique world, done in the vein of classic RPGs of yore. I would also recommend not being too bothered with the codex entries as the game itself does a competent job of showing the world.

Crying softly. I love this game so much.
I have had this game in my Library for a while. I've watched the trailers for it and I figured it was a good game to make an investment in. But not until recently have I been actually able to play it for myself and truly experience it. I have to say this is absolutely one of my favorite games I have ever played. And it's really saying something since I don't usually have such strong feelings about games nor do I play that many in the first place.
First I love the style that the game is in from the 3-D elements such as the character models the the more handrawn looking elements as well. It is such a pleasing style that blends these two elements together. Not to mention the world building and the characters themselves. I just love everything about the artistic approach to this game and it is certainly pleasing to look at.
Next the story. God the story. I don't even know if I can put into words how much I love the story in this game. Not only to the stuff that we hear in game but all of the notes and Codex pages you can gather! Now I'm not usually one to try and read up on all the lore of a game if I am to collect pages and stuff but this game is just so engaging and interestingthat I just couldn't help but want more information! I took great pleasure reading up on all the pages that I have collected.
And let me gush about the fact that the game is completely voice acted, the character protraits actually move and are animated when major dialogue comes up, and just the whole animating of the characters! I love that the whole game is voice acted instead of bits of voice acting and then radio silence from the characters before coming to another part where they are speaking again. It was so wonderful and interesting to listen to. The dialogue was wonderful no doubt about that! It was all so well written. It was funny, it pulled at your heart strings, witty, serious, all sorts of things. Not to mention how much voice acting talent there is and how wonderful everyone pulled off their characters.
Honestly there is so much I could just gush about with this game. It is such a wonderful game I do hope that another Masquerada game comes out in the future. The set up is there and I'm sure that was the intent. I would love to see Cicero and the gang come back for more adventure around Ombre. Find out more about the about the past with the Gods and the Lady that we where introduced to. More about the Fey and the Mascherines and the Deminticate (i believed that's how it's spelled off the top of my head but I could be wrong) as well as this supposed impending Cataclysm. I want to see how Ombre rebuilds itself after everything. I want to know what happened to Damien. I want to know what plans the Lady has for Cicero. I want so many things and learn more about this gorgeous, well-developed, interesting world that I have been introduced to. I do hope this game does well enough for that to be a possibility to those that love Masquerada.
In short this game is honestly a must have. Even if the gameplay is not your style with it being a pause-for-strategy style type of game the visual elements, music, characters, and overall story would be well worth the investment.

Great game! Here's what I loved about it
Things that need work:

At first it was daunting to play the game, but once the story starts you get hooked waiting to see what happens next.
It starts like a detective story (in a Venetian setting) but becomes a saving-the-world type of thing, which is the case in most RPGs (or a Dan Brown novel). However, the story is linear and there are no sidequests. You also cannot return to rooms you've previously visited, so you have to make sure you've explored the whole place before going to the next one. If you're the type of RPG player who likes exploring the world, talking to NPCs, and doing sidequests, this is not for you. However, there are optional dialogues with some of the main characters.
If you don't like reading, this may not be the game for you. But I liked how very deep and well thought out the lore is, and the codex is massive! If you don't want to delve much into the storyline, then I guess you can ignore that. All dialogues between the characters have voiceovers, and one particular detail that I liked was how there's a 3D animated portait of the character as it speaks, with a banner in the color of their affiliation. Most of the game is in 2D art, but it's intricately designed and very detailed, especially the comics-style cutscenes. The soundtrack is also beautiful.
The combat is a bit complicated to master, but it helps that you can reset your skill tree and practice at the training grounds. You can try different ability combos among your party members and once you've found the best strategy that works for you, the battles are a bit easier to finish. However, I didn't care much about the stances and it didn't present any issues for me in the game.
There are still a few bugs in terms of achievements that the developers are already addressing (they respond promptly in the forums). Other than that, this is definitely a must play!

Definitely a hidden gem. I first heard about this game when browsing Steam and right off the bat the art-style, gameplay, story "rich" content, and of course, the VAs instantly caught my attention. I downloaded the demo and enjoyed what I had played. It took me a while to purchase the game, but I am glad I did.
First off, this game is not meant for somebody wanting an in-depth RPG with a "high quality" combat system that focuses on exploration and dialogue choices. This game is strictly linear where the game pushes you in one-direction and only that direction. There are no side-quests and all the dialogue is used to tell the story that they are telling. There are no "choices" during conversations that affect the direction of the conversation. As much as I enjoy games with options such as that, there is also room in the gaming world for games that control what you do. This is a perfect example of that. (If you're expecting something else, then don't buy it. Or buy it and refund it if you don't enjoy it.) This game is almost an "interactive story." And it is an amazing story. There is never a dull moment during the game and it isn't too short as too feel rushed and not too long as too feel drawn out. It was almost as if I was playing a book. There is a lot of dialogue betweens the characters and a lot of text if you choose to read the lore. The lore surrounding the world is actually interesting and collecting the tidbits of knowledge around the areas opens the world up and draws you in)
The Voice Acting is superb. This game has amazing VAs all-around excluding the obvious Matthew Mercer and Jennifer Hale.
There really isn't much I don't enjoy about the game. However, as most other reviewers point out, the combat isn't perfect. I personally didn't have many problems. I played on normal difficulty and, for the most part, it was pretty seamless (I could see hard being harder, obviously, but I don't think it would be too bad). It actually became pretty easy towards the end. I didn't have much micromanaging to do because I was able to build my companions to pretty much self-sustain themselves (Kalden is a great face-tank and has amazing AoE heals). That just left me to focus on using my abilities. I sometimes needed to control my companions, but that wasn't too often and it almost always worked out well.
Lastly, collectibles are a bit sporadic. It wasn't too bad and they were spread out far enough to allow you to read and not tire of reading the lore bits. However, the placements of the seemed pretty random, for the most part. Not a big deal though.
In the end, the game was amazing and I definitely recommend it to anyone that enjoys a game focusing on story. And more people need to get this game, it deserves more attention that it has gotten.

Imagine Earth is a sort of simplified city building game with an easily understood user interface and light hearted characters to meet with somewhat cartoonish nature. You are a colony manager and you build cities in sandbox or campaign with the limit of how much punishment the planet can take before eco collapse. It is a fun game to play if you have a little free time, but I will say that it gets somewhat boring after 20 hours or so. The game is almost to simple sometimes because once you build your city to a good size, then it is smooth sailing until you either stop expanding or destroy your colony with a environment collapse (unless you are in the campaign then you finish the mission). One thing I really found annoying was the tech tree because you earn tech points over time building cities to invest in the tree. You can also buy tech from traders, but once a decision is made, you have to live with it for every new game you start. You cannot start the tech tree over, but buy techs that counter it and this applies to every sandbox and campaign mission started. I will rate the game recommended because it in early access and still is updating regularly. It was fun for a short time, but I would have gotten it on sale If I had the opportunity to start over.

Most paid-game clients have had free games sections in the past. Plagued by demos, 12-second promotional material and trailers, they've rarely been worth the trouble. Steam has flipped the whole system on its head, wherein the Free Games section now has more of an illustrious allure than the disastrous paid quagmire.
MANDAGON joins the lineup in a fairly unexciting but gracefully prompt adventure.
There's 1 level to explore, with 6 collectables. A bit more if you count the chatterboxes, and you play as a cube. Your controls involve jumping, moving from side to side, and hitting buttons. There's no puzzles, no platforming profiency, and it's a couple of steps above a walking simulator in that you have the ability to fall off a ledge.
By all accounts it should be completely forgettable. But what MANDAGON lacks in any semblence of mechanical ambition it attempts to make up for with the novelty of Tibetan mythology, an ambient soundtrack, and production values which are definitely in the high region for independant game projects.
And there's not anything more to it than that. You hop around for half an hour, collect the tablets, see the ending sequence then leave. The story - a fairly vapid fairytale about a father who trades his own life for his daughter's - is talked up by the chatty totem poles before the ending sequence just plainly states it.
There's one secret, a couple of ambient tracks, and the ability to enter buildings. That's it. That's all this game attempts to be. And it's content with that and has the good sense not to wear out its welcome. It is exactly as serene as it seems.
For what little of you it asks, MANDAGON is worth your time. Just don't expect to be left with too much of an impression.

Crush Crush; yet another clicker game that demands you to waste your life sitting in a chair in your room clicking your mouse furiously with the ultimate reward of seeing some hentai nudity.
In the tags section of this game, you may have noticed a word called nudity, and maybe that was the driving force that sent you to check this game out, 'Oh boy, time for me to enjoy some good hentai!' But unfortunately, you'd be terribly mistaken. Because as of writing this review; there isn't any nudity.
"Crush Crush; yet another clicker game that demands you to waste your life sitting in a chair in your room clicking your mouse furiously with the ultimate reward of wasting your life."
Now for such a game, you'd think that it surely should have nudity. No. It doesn't.
So, what is the point of this game then? Well, the point of this game is to spend roughly two hours of sitting in your chair, secluded in your room, clicking furiously trying to woo this girl becuase you think that you will be rewarded with a pair of jugs. Nope. After roughly two hours (it really depends on how enthusiastice you are on seeing those jugs....not that there is any) All that happens is you achieve the status of her being your girlfriend. But once you have made her your girlfriend, what the hell do you do now? There is no more progression after that; unless you want to start all over with one of the other girls (which there are plenty of). But i''m sure as hell not sitting here, furiously clicking on my mouse for roughly two hours, when i don't even get to see the slightest piece of nudity in the end. Therefore, it really is rather pointless and is undoubtedly, a waste of time and, your life.
But that isn't all there is to the game! There is music and there is sound effects, though unsurprisingly, it is rather gay sounding; thankfully though, you can easily mute it on and off.
So, i've shared my piece on the games nudity, but that pretty much sums the game up itself in that paragraph. What do you do in the game? In layman terms, Crush Crush is a girlfriend simulator. You start off with a girl that you coincedentally meet somehow, and your ultimate goal is to keeping wooing her until you reach the status of her being your girlfriend. That's all. Naturally, as you progress through the different stages of the relationship (acquaintances, frenemies, crush, girlfriend) you require more points and skill points in order to advance. That is either a hell of a lot of clicking, or just wait 'till you have enough money from your job, and then take her to the movies which usually gives you all the points you need. But apart from the points, i also mentioned skill points; which you gain from hobbies that you undertake. In some cases, you need a certain skill point level to progress with a girl. You also need to have a job that they want. So, you need to change jobs frequently to meet their needs, obviously, different jobs have different income which you can spend on gifts and dates.
The game really is self explanatory in it's own way, so you don't need an instruction manual on how to play the thing.
That's about all there is to the game. You spend hours wooing a girl and you get nothing in return. Oh i suppose you get achievements, maybe you want to get a 100% achievement rating for a game; in that case, this game shouldn't be too hard to get that achievement.
But the game itself, really is pointless. Unless they release a nudity mod/patch or whatever, which quite possible could happen, (nowing the weeaboo community). But then again, it's a lot easier and quicker to just go on Google Images and search up hentai.
Crush Crush is free, so there is no harm in giving it a try, but; what on earth is the point of it?

I know that this game has been panned for multiple rather good reasons.  Yes, the plot begins and ends rather suddenly.  Yes, the plot does rely on the player knowing other parts of the Deus Ex universe to understand fully what's happening in the story.  Yes, the *main* set of missions makes up a rather short part of the game.  Yes, the game is a bit demanding.  Yes, it has some rather unnecessary microtransactions.  Yes, it's basically more DX:HR.  But you know what?  I still ♥♥♥♥ing enjoyed it.  Before I my judgement is dismissed, I have played both the original and HR, and I can say that this game does live up to its predacessors (maybe not entirely to story depth of the original and some elements are made simpler for newer audiences).  Before you rant on about how bad the "cliffhanger" ending was, I may as well remind you that this is still in prequel territory, meaning whatever final installment there's left will have to leave you hanging for the sake of leading back to the original.  I may as well get the flaws out of the way first before moving onto the qualities.
Cons:
-Does rely on the understanding of all that has happened in the rest of the timeline.  I.E., you wouldn't know Alex was from Deus Ex: The Fall unless you looked her up/bought the mobile spinoff, muchless how Adam went from head of security at the now bankrupt Sarif Industries to a member of an Interpol taskforce.
-Game is very demanding.  If you really do want to play this game, seriously upgrade your hardware.
-Ships with unnecessary microtransaction cash/praxis kits.
-We didn't need Breach.  The game is fine as is without it.
-Can't switch iron sights from press to toggle.  Also, if you are making the jump from Human Revolution to Mankind Divided, be wary that the original cover system has been reworked.
-While not a god-gun per say, the stun gun is rather ridiculous this time around.
-Nitpicky bits in terms of quality.
Pros:
-Whatever settings you may have this game at, it still looks beautiful.
-While it is only one hub, it has the size of Hengsha and Detroit put together, and has more cranies and nooks than you can be bothered with counting.
-Even on lower settings, the game looks amazing.
-Stealth is still good, even if the addition of sight indicators has made things much easier, and every stealth section is an impenitrable fortress until you find the one ventilation shaft that is the whole system's undoing.
-Game doesn't necessarily shove you into the stealth aspect of things, and grants augs which can allow more capability in combat than simply devoting to stealth.  While the game still does reward you for stealthing, it's only an extra 400 XP for ghost and smooth operator combined.
-Side missions do add great length and story onto the main story.  Some side missions do require more searching than others, unlike how Human Revolution does hand you most of the side quests.
-Interesting throwbacks to earlier entries added.  Biocells are *reappearing* and

-Another masterpiece to add to Michael Mccann's resume.
-Mix of crafting and weapon upgrades does help put emphasis on some resource use.
-Complication of weapon upgrades, ammo types, and in-combat modifications on the fly.
-Nice addition of cover-based takedowns, even if it can stealth easy at times.
-More of what you'd expect from earlier games in general.
-If you really are miffed by the addition of microtransactions, you don't need them, dumbass.  You can complete the game without them, and I easily got all the augmentations I needed by the endgame without any added praxis kits.
-Interesting roster of characters.
-Cliff Stephens as Bob Page again!
-Length averaged out more or less be the same length as the original and Human Revolution with all the missions tied together. At least subjectively.
-Verticallity does greatly add to tactical decisions.
-Dwells more into the transhumanism themes.  Yes it does somewhat monopolize on the inequality debates we have currently to get its point across, but like the devs said, Deus Ex is meant to be a mirror for us to better understand ourselves with.
-Arguably, a solid game at its core.  Maybe one final game to finish Adam's story arch and finish ties between 2029 and 2052, and it should be good.
Overall, I'd say a 8.7/10.  While it's various flaws do detract from its final value, I'd still say it's a good game, and is in equal terms with Human Revolution as a Deus Ex game.

I'm a longtime player of a variety of different types of strategy titles...
This one doesn't really do anything well enough to stand out from the pack.
- The spell and research system has a little potential, but it's not really realized.
- The tech tree, construction, city development etc. isn't anything special.
- The units don't have anything new for mechanics or elements.
- The unit progresison/advancement and lord development don't appear to have anything special about them either.
The big downside to me is the pathing and command system for units, it's a little clunky, and if you click through units it doesn't always center you on the selected unit, which leads to movement errors. It also gets increasingly clunky the more you have on the go to manage movement, especially with allies units involved - you'll wind up being blocked by their units from reaching goals - or using your units to block them.
All in all, it's a mediocre title that falls short of many similar titles already out - Fallen Enchantress: Legendary Heroes and Eador: Masters of the Broken World are titles that share a good deal in common with this one (Eador's "shards" and Warlocks are strikingly similar) - but both of those titles do a better job than this one, in my opinion.

Fun game. Essentially Warlock 2 is Civilization V with a fantasy twist, and the twist makes all the difference. Never enjoyed Civ 5, but I am liking Warlock a lot. Warlock 2 does a great job at making you feel like a badass mage, packing some powerful spells like the ability to warp the landscape and erect a volcano, or call in a lightning storm, and grant your troops the ability of flight. There's also a fun quest system, and NPC mages that will harass you until you complete certain quests.
If you never played the first one, then this is a great game to pick up. Most of the negative reviews come from people who felt Warlock 2 didn't add enough to Warlock 1 to justify the "2," but it's nevertheless a good game.
Contrasting to AoW3, then I find that AoW3 does everything better than Warlock. More customization, more detailed battles, more maps, two length single player campaigns (Warlock has none), and a better selection of avatars. However, you might still prefer Warlock over AoW because Warlock is more streamlined for quicker turns and games. It's probably, therefore, a better choice for multiplayer, unless you want long drawn out games amongst close friends with AoW3. All in all, if you're an impatient player, you might prefer Warlock, but either way you can't go wrong.
