I enjoyed DE:MD. I enjoyed the suspense as I hid in a ventilation duct, watching the pattern of guards as they patrolled an area. I enjoyed exploring areas, looking for alternate routes to a destination. I enjoyed the hacking mini games. I enjoyed the game quite a lot.
There are plenty of nits to pick, however.  I never finished DE:HR because I spent most of the game focusing on stealthily achieving my objectives without combat.  That didn't serve me well at all when I encountered a boss fight that required fast action combat. The same was true in DE:MD.  Fortunately, I found a way to shoot from cover and moved on, but it gives the impression that I may have been playing incorrectly up to that point.  The controls are a little unpredictable at times. Trying to escape from cover to move the extra distance for a takedown can be twitchy. The same is true for trying to hit some of the jumps, especially jumps to vents. When timing is critical to escape you can be certain that you'll be slowly crouch-walking towards the vent, mis-jump twice, then fall over dead as multiple guards swarm your position and fill you with hot lead.
Despite those gripes, the game has atmosphere and theme that appeal to me.  The story doesn't make much sense, but I didn't need it to.  If you go into FPS games looking for the S to stand for Sneak, this is the game for you.

The game is very good but has its flaws.
When the game first came out it had major stability issues. With those patched the game became playable. Add to that the addition of Linux support.
As far as the storyline goes. It was well balanced and had several good twists to it. If you played the first game (Well the one before this one) you will notice that the story is pretty slim and very straight forward. This leads to the linearity of the storyline. The side quests, you will stumble into most of them while accomplishing the main mission. Like most people say, there are so many unanswered questions. While the main story was completed, it left things open to multiple expansions and sequels. If the two DLCs currently out have any indication as to how further ones are going to go, I am definitely ready for  more DLCs…

One thing to note is how well they push the effects of the first game into this game. They even have a very detailed recap video explaining what happened in the first game if you started with this game and did not want to go and play Human Revolution first.

So then we go to graphics. Well this was definitely one of the major updates. The game looks sooooo good. The facial animations, the buildings, the garbage in the streets. Everything looks crisp and high detailed like it would look in real life. The different locations in the game are very detailed and have a look all their own. Unfortunately there are far less locations than what was in Human Revolution. The game is very well optimized. I was playing this with a 980Ti on Linux. Ran very smooth. (For those who do not have their large screen TV connected to your PC. This is one of those games that definitely benefits from the larger screen.)
The sounds of the game are great. I am a bit torn on this one. You can tell that they put a lot of effort into the music. It is never overbearing and blends well with the locations and action. However, due to the type of game, the music is a bit low key (Major props to the music cast though). If there were more locations to take advantage of their talents I might think a bit differently.
Gameplay! Basically the part that can break any game. The controls are very fluid and responsive. The interactions from fights, moving objects, transitions to cutsceens all great. The took everything good from Human Revolution and polished it up and added a few new bells and whistles without overburdening the system. The game gives players more options (better) when deciding how they want to accomplish each task. I felt the first game was quite linear in this part while this game opens things up a little.  One downside is the hacking. Through the first game it felt like an integral and optional part of the world. In this one however, it feels more like a necessity with little payoff. I played this game pacifist style so things are a little different. However the fact remains that it felt more like they slid it in to fill in certain parts of the game.
If you have read some of the other reviews, you know this game has micro-transactions and 1 use micro-transactions. I am not upset about these as they are optional for the main game and do not prevent me from effectively playing through. However, I have no idea in regards to the extra game BREACH as I tried it and did not have any fun. So I never went back to it.
This is a must have game, especially if you have played Human Revolution. In fact the expansions not only add new story lines, they add new locations and dangers. They were definitely worth the purchase AFTER finishing the game.

OBEY is a game that runs absolutely terrible on my turd of a PC. Nor does it run on my 2010 Macbook (Non-Pro) with only 2 GB of RAM.
With that being said, here is my semi in depth review.
Obey is a First Person multiplayer game that sets itself apart from most by focusing on team based play. It can be played online, or with bots, though the bots tend to be pretty easy. It can seem very chaotic and difficult to understand at first, although once one masters the gameplay it gets less confusing. The game's tutorial tries to teach you how to play a little, showing you what different items do and how the game works. Gameplay is basically like a very complicated King Of The Hill, in which players feed items into a massive robot controlled by one player in order to try to earn money so then the player controlling the robot can give back more items and money to the players. In terms that a sane person will understand, to win you basically need to make the most money.
Overall, the game is worth buying for people that are looking for an interesting multiplayer experience that strives to be different from your average online game.

Nothing I've ever played can compare to this game. There's only one word I can use to describe it: chaos.
You've only got one goal: get the most money possible.
It's crazy confusing at first. The tutorial helps, but goes so fast and is still not entirely clear (the easiest ways to play are either in the lobby with bots or by looking it up on youtube). You're thrown into a field full of junk, corpses, rocket fuels, etc. You can put these items in a "feed box" going to the robot, offering them different perks and giving you a small amount of money. However, the more loyal you are, the richer the robot gets. As a bunny, there's not much you can do besides feed the robot and hope he gives you money for being loyal.
Now, you can always go overthrow him and take control.
This opens up a whole new world of excitement. You have to constantly watch for disobeying bunnies attempting to steal your throne, pay loyal bunnies, order dropships with supplies for your bunnies to feed you, shoot disobeying bunnies, and much much more.
Overall, it's a great game once you get the hang of it. The bots are super easy to play against, so once you know what you're doing I recommend getting with actual people to play. Mics are also extremely helpful for communication.

Well this game has a lot of that trust & betrayal feeling to it, though instead of pretending to be some high calibre Mafiosi, you get into the flesh of small and cute little hamsters.
You and your furry little fellows must all obey one huge monkey looking robot that watches over it all. Do as he says, and he will most probably reward you and distinguish you among your pairs. Disobey him, and you'll probably just fall under his machine-gun.
Now, before you star assuming this developer has some sort of child induced fear to primates, let me tell you the twist of it all. The giant bad♥♥♥♥♥looking robot you see from anywhere on the map? That's actually a hamster. That's right, there's one of you just hanging in inside. That ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ got up there first to watch over you and your mates. To be the leader. One ham to rule them all.

Be a loyal feud to your master and gain his trust.
Be a revolutionary leader and lead your pack to subversion.

No matter what you choose, you'll see where the fun is.
Words are plenty, and meaning hides in between. Welcome to social multiplayer.

Obeying or disobeying an order; to be killed or to help. That is what OBEY is truly all about. OBEY is a completely new genre.  The asymmetry combined with the player-driven gameplay make for one of the best multiplayer experiences that I have ever had on PC.  It is a competitive multiplayer action game where you play as adorable fluffy bunnies that will do everything in their power to coerce others to join their side of the battle. OBEY is so addicting that it is the type of game that I cannot put down.  Winning a game is one of the greatest experiences, and knowing that you did it all through dishonesty and deception makes it all the better. OBEY is not just a game I would recommend, but what you'll find is one of the most innovative experiences on PC and you will become a part of the most friendly and entertaining multiplayer community out there.

OBEY is quite unique, which is pretty rare these days. The game is a king of the hill style game, you want your bunny to take control of the giant robot of doom. It's all about timing, and tricking your opponents so that they end up doing what you want them to do. You have to avoid doing the same for your opponent though!
I highly recommend you have a mic. It makes the game considerably more fun.
The game doesn't have a huge population, so I recommend finding some friends to play with.
The dev is pretty active and helpful. He's on hand to answer questions, and even takes his time to help new players learn the game.
OBEY is very solid. It plays well, even at this early stage and is something that's a little different from every other game out there.

Over 10 years ago now my significant other pre-ordered a lifetime LoTR:O subscription. I made a face and told him there was no way some crummy wow clone mmo could do justice to the LoTR legacy, despite the fact that I honestly didn't even like the books that much. I naysayed right up to the day he started playing, and with a rather skeptical, sour attitude I watched over his shoulder a few times while he played.
I didn't want to admit that I was surprised by how rich the world looked, but I found myself watching more frequently and by the end of the week I was taking turns playing on his account on days where I was off work and he was at school. Soon after that I was pouting for turns, much to his amusement. And then as a gift he surprised me with my very own lifetime account.
I played non-stop for about four years, in the book 8 SoA days I fell in love with LoTR:O, and though I've taken a number of breaks especially over recent years, I always find myself coming back. My last serious play was raiding in the Moria days, but every time I peek in for a few weeks of casual leveling or crafting catch up, or to take a go at new content, I again find myself awed by the enriched world, and the fun of cooperative play that I haven't enjoyed nearly as much in other games.
Be it taking the long walk from the shire all the way to Rivendell to experience the journey of the hobbits, or now pressing on into Rohand and Gondor, defying Isengard, saving the people of Angmar, exploring the frozen wastes of Forchel or even enduring Everswim(Evendim), the plethora of brilliant sights will satisfy anyone that enjoys immersion. While the various different instance types from puzzle like situations to outright tank and spank should provide plenty of opportunity for any gamer that enjoys a sense of story to go along with the content.
The game does have some hangups, certainly, and I do recommend a bit of patience - sometimes it can feel repetitive, and the engine being old doesn't run as smoothly as some might prefer. Overall though, I'd say this has been one of my favorite games for the last decade and definitely recommend it.

is best described as a mixture of puzzle, strategy and management simulation. Even though with a educational mandate, as it's main feature is the fragility of planets. As the title implies this game throws a shadow on the future of our earth. But first things first.
In this game you are the jr. vice president of Imagine Earth, Ltd., a coorporation that colonizes distant planets for big profits. The game comes with a nice campaign, introducing you to likeable characters that guide you through your first steps. Expect to fail in the second mission anyways. Even though the tutorial is very well designed and gives a good guidance, the game itself remains a challenge.
You start of every new colony by placing your first town centre on the planet. Soon enough new colonists will move in and develop a demand for food, energy and goods.
By the games triangular grid, every building has - yes, that's right - three sides. And as you place buildings next to each other they possibly gain benefits or detriments from each other. So in this way Imagine Earth actually resembles "Reus". For example, you can increase the energy output of biomass plants by placing them next to forests or farms. But your inhabitants will become unhappy if you build coal plants next to their houses. Since building space is limited, conflicts are inevitable and part of the challenge arises from the task to place your buildings in the most productive and proficient way.
On the other hand there are different types or tiles of terrain. So you want to place your farms on fertile land or your gas plants on top of gas resources to maximize outcomes. This task gets significant harder by the fact that all your buildings create pollution, eventually triggering a greenhouse effect on your planet. Fertile land turns into desert, tornados and volcanoes arise and ultimatly your facing meltdown of the polar caps, rising global water level. To cut a long story short,
[/b]]The graphics[/b] are a bit toony, which I personally enjoy very much. The planets themself looking like beautiful blue marbles that I - personally - feel a bit sad for, if my false management destroys them.
itself is not extraordinarily remarkable but fits the pace of the game very good. (The speed of the music actually changes with the set game speed - mindblown!)
is also not quite thrilling but gives enough motivation to play through the campaign which I perceived mostly as a tutorial introducing my to new elements. Once your done with the rather short campaign, there is sandbox mode, challenge mode and a free play mode. You can play on planets, that are procedural created according to player set parameters - for instance like in
where you can choose size of the map, the amount of resources, etc... - what makes the game
.
(It seems that there is the idea of exchanging planets with your friends, competing for highscorse, but I can not confirm this.)
are very simple and easy to pick up right away. One click opens the menu, one click lets you choose, one click places the building.
As much as I enjoy Imagine Earth, there are two downsides. Even though the planets look beautiful, they feel a bit sterile, as streets stay empty, for example. Where are your 1.5 billion inhabitants? Building big cities is fun and the realy look cool as large skyscrapers emerge, but there is now life in the game. There are neither people or cars (like in Anno, where you get the impression of a busy citylife), nor animals roaming on the map.
The other minor flaw is, that you cant buy 5 buildings in a row, as you have to open the menu, select the building and place it for every building. Which I find a little unpractical and thus ironic in a game, that focus on maximizing efficiency.
This game is what I expected when I first got my hands on "Reus". If you were, like me, disappointed by Reus - even though solely based on your own false expectations - then this game is for you. One of my favorite rogue-likes on Steam, and the best FPS available within the genre.  Interesting and colorful environments and enemies, varied room goals, and wonderful weapons/weapon abilities.  There are a bunch of unlockable characters to choose from, as well as a host of unlockable items and bonuses.  Ziggurat is fun, challenging and rewarding all at once.
While the amount of character-related content is staggering, the world itself is a bit... vanilla.  Opportunities that could have been used to add lore to the game are instead spent introducing you to the dev's previous projects.  Those rooms are particularly annoying because they force you to view the (thankfully brief) dialogue.  There are a few types of secret rooms, but they typically contain a single item and nothing else of interest.  If you're looking for dialogue and story content, look elsewhere.
A solid shooter, well designed and well taken care of.  Skip Paranautical, skip Heavy Bullets.  The voxel based entries in to this category can not hold a candle to the nuts and bolts of Ziggurat.

Edit (6/3/2016) - As soon as they wrapped the console port, the dev team swung back and added a new game mode (Gauntlet), and a boatload of bugfixes.  Likely the last update, barring balance/bugs with Gauntlet, which is not a disappointment in the least.  After a stint in Early Access, and two years of support beyond release, Milkstone have made Ziggurat the best possible game it could be.
Not only are these guys a shining example of Early Access done right, they are also a great tutorial for ANY developer on how to take community feedback, and how to improve your game even beyond the release window.
Now let's start talking about a sequel, Milkstone. ;)

Not terribly impressed with this title.
Plays like civ with magic. I was hoping to get a tast of old-school Master of Mgic, and this was a temporary fix. It's different enough from Civ to be fun and refreshing, but the game mechanics made it tedious in mid to late game.
Pros:
- Challenging - The wrong move could easily cost you a veteran hero. You learn to wander off into new worlds only with expendible troops, etc. You will lose troops. You will lose cities. The rise and fall is exciting.
- Different - Tile types and heros were different - you can build mana farms instead of farms. Perks provided by certain improvements were really interesting and fun.
- Variety - The tech trees for different civilizations were well-thought out and different enough to force you into a different strategy for each.
Cons:
- Very few options with excess mana. Can't increase your casting power, so you just accumulate excess mana if your economy is mana-focused. It's frustrating.
- Excess food means NOTHING. You have a minimum food for population and troops eat (a little) food, but towns increase in size at a fixed rate, so unless your people are starving, there's no benefit to extra food. Yes, excess is converted to cash, but if I needed cash, I'd build cash buildings.
- The economy revolves around money. There's a cap on how much mana you can realistically spend, and excess food is converted to cash, so you quickly learn that building cash is the only really valuable resource. This removes a lot of strategy and the benefits of any variety in the different races.
- Random events are devasating and often change the landscape, affecting the bonuses of carefully placed town improvements. They sometimes take out town population, which might have taken 30 turns to increase by 1 (at a fixed rate), leaving your economy in shambles with no way to recover for another 30+ turns: enough to cost you the game.
This game seemed promising, but in the end was just annoying. This game is being uninstalled.

full disclosure: I was a kickstarter backer.  Here's my quick run-down:
Narrative and story are clearly where the bulk of the energy went.  And it's a really good story. key to that are:
---- 1) wonderful world-building: start from the premise of "Renaissance Venice" + "Avatar: the Last Airbender" and that'll get you most of the way.  Do yourself a favor and read all the codex entries you find - they explain a lot of why you're in certain places or why the characters have particular reactions.  It's very text-heavy, but very rewarding.  Really want to play in this world as a tabletop rpg.
---- 2) superb voice-acting.  The game's dialogue is fully voice-acted and they hired professionals, and it shows.
Combat gameplay is... frenetic: basically, it's tactical and real-time w/ pausing to issue commands, and frustrating because the AI takes over very quickly.  I would recommend you do a mixture of the following:
---- 1) If you want to focus on it as a story game, vow to never pause.  Start the game on the easiest setting, customize the AI behaviors. Once you get used to issuing commands quickly you can ratchet up the difficulty.  Focus on playing combats as the protagonist and think of when you switch to other characters you're Cicero issuing commands.
---- 2) if you want to focus on it as a tactics game, take a look at some of the auto-pause functionality and turn off the AI entirely.  Every couple of seconds, pause and issue new commands.  Start on hard difficulty, focus on synergies (e.g. the tags and between different characters' abilities).
Exploration gameplay is... like going to an art gallery.  The environments are gorgeously rendered, but there's little interactivity and often you don't get to revisit environments once you've advanced to the next one (with some exceptions).  On the one hand, it's really easy to find individual objects (they're highlighted with giant beacons).  But on the other hand, you only get one chance to find each thing.  It would be helpful if the devs made it easy to figure out where you missed a codex entry or mask or ink or engraving or whatever. Maybe that's in there (you CAN go back and revisit subchapters you've already played), but I didn't see it.
Character optimization is fun, in that there are like a bajillion ways to customize each character (different abilities, different inks/engravings/masks). The game is well-designed enough where the abilities are roughly equivalent in power AFAICT, so you're free to choose the ones that seem cool (air squirrels FTW).  Unfortunately, a lot fo the game's mechanics are not spelled out.  What does Vulnerability do?  My assumption is that it means you take more damage.  That might be buried in a codex entry, but it'd be helpful if there was a little pop-up when you mouse over it.
Overall, I liked the game a lot, but I love narrative-heavy games.  Masquerada was certainly worth the $1/hour I spent playing it. I do wish that the investigation element, which is so crucial to the plot, was better expressed in the gameplay.
If what you want is a deep narrative-heavy experience in a wonderfully-realized world and you're cool not having a whole lot of narrative agency, Masquerada is awesome. Take your time to savor the parts of it where the devs really put their focus - narrative and world-building (read the codex entries).  If what you want is an open world that you can freely explore with super-crunchy gameplay, skip this one.
That said, my recommendation is a conditional but enthusiastic yes.

Masquerada: Songs and Shadows really took me by surprise, it really did. The game claims to be a RPG but there are very few elements to support that claim, especially given the fact that the story is quite linear and there are no choices for you to make, you’re basically just watching how everything unfolds. That said, there is a lot to say about Masquerada, both good and bad, and I believe it’s a game that went under a lot of people’s radar and I truly believe it deserves a lot more exposure and credit than it has received.
One of the key elements that make this a truly wonderful experience is the fact that all the dialogue is fully voice acted, with the exception of dialogue between background characters. What I want to say is that the voice acting, as well as the entirety of the OST, are really top-notch, I can't stress that enough. The music is of epic proportions and among the best I’ve heard this year in any videogame and, with that in mind, I’d suggest to even those that are not interested in the game to give the OST a try. I find the stylized visuals to be well put together and fitting with the theme the game is aiming for, even though some of the textures are rather low detail. The visuals of the characters actually remind me of Abyss Odyssey in a way I can’t really explain, but just so things are clear, that is a plus in my book. The animations themselves look really smooth but they seem a little off place in comparison to the 2d background, and that took me a while to get used to.
The game takes place in Ombre, a country widely known for its exotiqueness and magic. On the other hand, what really distinguishes it from the rest of the world is the use of masquerines, which grant its wearers control of the elements. Given the scarceness of these masks, Ombre’s society was divided into several factions, guilds and whatnot, and this is pretty much what shapes the entire storyline. That said, at first I felt like the game didn’t really do a good job in explaining what was going on and who you are but, slowly, everything started to make sense (reading the codex entries helps a lot). The tutorial, which teaches you the basics of combat, also serves as a prologue to the events of the rest of the game, which takes place 5 years after. I feel like even slightly resuming the initial part of the plot could potentially spoil some people so I’ll refrain myself from doing so. All you need to know is that this game pretty much has it all, from an enduring political conflict in a society characterized by huge disparities in terms of social and political structure to ever enduring friendships, betrayal, loss of loved ones, intrigue, mystery and the discovery of the secrets behind an old civilization. Not only the world but each individual main character is very unique and interesting in their own way, offering a different vision of the world that surrounds them. The game does have some jokes here and there, the overall theme of the game is rather grim and dark, but it does have its cheerful moments.
There is a lot to be said about the game story and its world building, and I do really mean A LOT. There’s tons of codex entries that you can collect and read, which provide an insightful look to Masquerada’s world, its locations, history, characters, culture and factions. The writing is exceptionally well done, and reading these is a joy and it certainly helps in getting you more immersed into the world and understanding everything that is going on in greater detail. When reading these, I often found myself lost in thought wondering about this place, imagining how the places it described really looked, how I’d fit in, what I’d do in order to change it for the better and so on. I really found it very hard to not lose track of time when playing Masquerada.
The worst thing in Masquerada for me, or the least good part of it, depending on how you see it, is the actual gameplay. While playing the game you’ll either be in combat or walking around these closed areas trying to get from one point to another. In the latter, you can find codex entries, upgrades for your characters but also other people talking to each other about their everyday life or about more important events. These interactions are sadly not voice acted, while the main dialogue is, which is a shame given that the voice acting is actually really really good.
Combat is fought in real-time but you have the option to pause. While in other games pausing would give you an advantage, in the sense that you could plan your approach and use your abilities in the best way possible, I didn’t find the need to do so in Masquerada, for I found the combat to be rather shallow and basically a spam fest. I must say the combat really disappointed me because, initially, it looked liked it had a lot of depth to it, with different possible combos with the various elements and other mechanics such as different stances that change how fast you can use your abilities and how much damage you deal/take. It’s also worth saying that the abilities that you have will be unlocked with points that you’ll get as you play through the game so there is some room for you choose what you think it’s best. Then there’s also your masquerine ultimate ability, which varies depending on the masquerine you have equipped at any given time.
One particular mechanic which I found to be really neat is the ability to set your companions behaviour, in the sense that you can tell them what skill should they use and on who. For example, you can make it so that they target the enemy with the lowest amount/highest amount of HP. Still, if you want, you can completely disable this entirely.
What the game offers in terms of story, world design and visuals, compensates the lack of depth of the combat system and overall gameplay, which really hurts how I overall feel about the game. Masquerada could pretty much just be an adventure game stripped of all the combat and it still would be just as good. That said, I do appreciate the fact that it was rather easy, for it allowed me to progress faster through the story without having to worry with my opponents. Still, just when I was starting to feel that the game was extending itself, it just suddenly got even more interesting and hooked me even more.

This game is an exemplary RPG, with a brilliantly executed storyline that matches its beautiful and immersive setting.
What greatly stuns me is how much this game gets /right/ that I found lacking in other games. Its in-universe lore - using familiar concepts of a built in 'codex' to explain concepts, collected by investigating objects of interest or eavesdropping on random conversations - is rich and detailed, yet not overly slapped in your face. The story itself is so strong, you find yourself wanting to quickly brush up on the protagonist's thoughts in his journal, or reading up upon what 'Media' means. (Not the press.) While in other games I found no need to touch the 'lore' journals, as most formulaic fantasy settings allow me to quickly work out the one or two differences in how 'corrupt church' 'drunk mining stubborn dwarves' fit into their world. In this rich, Venetian-inspired, creative and original setting, I was enchanted by its design and found myself eagerly learning as much as I could as I explored it.
When I say explored, it is more truly like being led through a story. Being fond of books, I'm no stranger to the idea of a well done start from chapter one to the finale, but most games that take this approach rely so heavily on a complex-yet-standard RPG system to do their work for them. Instead, writing is prolific, the voice acting is superb and touching, and the dialogue is plentiful. The protagonist is no copy-paste blank you-are-this-man type, but an interesting hero with his own displayable flaws and merits. I found myself able to relate to some of his issues quite a bit, so he came to me as a very excellent protagonist to walk through the story.
The companions' 'plot lines' are not done in a side-quest format (in fact, there is a total lack of side quests or backtracking entirely) but instead are part of the development of a story, not used as filler but as fuel to drive the narrative forward. It's refreshing to see such a traditional approach to writing rather than a rather shy walk around the issue of 'we don't want to bore the player' circle of laziness. The first companion I thought of as mildly interesting grew on me - a little at first, and immensely by the end. Every other companion, regardless of my first impression, eventually became such a strong and interesting character that I was pleased to hear everything they said and see their part in the story.
The music is by Josh Whelchel, whom I had encountered over a decade ago in the little-known 'Spirit Engine' series of side-scrolling RPGs. His music then was excellently suited to the them (with over 70 tracks being produced for the first game) and were so catchy, I still have them today. His music in this is drastically different in style, but suits the game to a tee. It perfectly suits the intrigue-filled tale, the very latin-inspired choral musics accompanying the folk music of violins, harps, and flutes to complete its 'medieval Italian' dark fantasy theme. The soundtrack, as well, has about 40 tracks, so it is well worth the price.
The art is gorgeous and simple, the backgrounds being splendidly well done, and the characters shown in a sort of cel-shaded manner with a Disney or Dreamworks-like drawing style, in the manner of the classic 2D style. I found the art style refreshing, and it belies the plot's sometimes dark or sinister twists in quite a (pleasantly) jolting manner.
As for the story, I won't go into any detail about it as discovering it without spoilers is an excellent way to experience it. The 'blurb' of the game you find in the steam store is sufficient enough to see if it piques your interest, but I assure you the writing is of the highest quality, the story strong from start to finish. I have never found a game which so excellently used the tutorial as a fascinating story hook.
Combat is very good, reminiscient of Baldur's Gate, Pillars of Eternity or Dragon Age in that one can switch between up to 3 characters, pause at any time to issue orders, let A.I. control your allies (with customizable priorities for energy usage and when to use their abilities) or just letting yourself manually control each aspect, although I did find myself wanting to manually control my companions more than once on occasion. There is no inventory or buy/sell system, instead customization is done with a very nice and transparent skill tree (for each character) and with ultimate abilites stemming from which Mask you currently have equipped. Multiple masks can be collected for every character and are an important part of mixing and matching.
I completed the game on Normal yet still found the combat a meaty challenge, I am rather sure Hard offers an excellent point for replayability (the other point being to completely collect all optional codex entries and masks, for a full-achievement run.) In addition, since different companions can be used at different times in the story, a replay allows you to see the dialogue of other characters in a previously played through segment. For example, I was very surprised that my healer had plenty of dialogue in a segment where I could have had him swapped out for my other characters.
All in all, a fantastic game. My leisurely first experience was about 12 hours of game time, I am sure a complete run - or a run on hard mode - would take around 14-16. It is well worth the buy, and is one of my best games I've played in 2016.

Gnomoria is a surprisingly fun and addictive game. If you've ever been curious about Dwarf Fortress, but were intimidated by the lack of UI and graphics, Gnomoria is a fantastic game to jump into. Orders you give to your gnomes will be followed according to the guidelines you set. You do not directly control them, but you affect how they behave by determining the gnome's professions, priorities,  and other parameters you impose. It becomes an extremely fun balancing act of figuring out exactly how to acheive true efficiency while also struggling to plan ahead. The more expansive and 'worthy' your empire becomes, the greater dangers arrive to destroy it. It takes hours to finally feel like you've gotten a foothold in the world you've generated, but when you do, you feel a great sense of pride in what your tiny gnome society has accomplished.
The only gripes I would have would be the lack of variety in environments as well as the flora and fauna. New biomes as well as new animals and trees would make this game way more replayable. Also, this game has no form of tutorial so the learning curve is quite steep. It took me 3 different restarts before I fully understood the importance of key aspects of the game like action priorities, training a strong military, and proper item storage to name a few. The wiki and video tutorials should definitely be used when first starting off. Beyond that, the game is definitely worth the eight dollar inevestment and is worth your time. If you've ever been inquisitive about these types of strategy games, Gnomoria is a charming and enjoyable place to start.

OBEY sets out to be a truly unique game and achieves that goal. Each player is dumped into the map as a harmless bunny/sheep creature whose only abilities are to pickup or drop items and perform an astonishing 1cm high jump + "squeek" combo of cuteness. There is a huge opportunity for personalising characters with accessories here, which is one of the many updates currently planned.
The gameplay is essentially defined by the actions of the players in the match in question, but I guess you could describe the overarching type as a strategic game of power accumulation. The winner is decided by who reaches $10,000 first. The way in which they achieve that is up to them and the other players.
A match usually begins with a mad dash to the giant robot/tower, whose occupant has a variety of extra actions available to them. If they play their cards right, they can make the other players collect resources for them which converts to money for
players. If they fail to carefully watch their subordinates, they can find sneaky ways to detract power and money or even overthrow their control of the robot.
This is where the unique gameplay mechanics come into play. As controller of the robot, the game provides some generic warnings and instructions to place on the map for your subordinates, but the real gameplay takes place through chatting with the other players, demanding one thing or offering payment for colecting resources or making demands on threat of violence (gun turret, flamethrower, rockets).
As an online-only game (there are A.I bots that work properly, but for me the fun was completely lost without human players), the availability of friends/strangers to play with will make or break your experience with OBEY. I would highly recommend purchasing a 4-pack with some friends or finding a group to play with.

Now, skipping the lyrical part, game is quite good generally. Game concept where you are supposed to behave in a cat-and-mouse way, with application of being more of an armed watcher tower ["cat"], who supervises his minions and guiding them to earn more benefits, while punishing those who dare to act suspicious with death penalty, - is quite rare to meet in the industry. If I am to describe this game in short, your winning condition is to gain 10 000$ prior to any other player by any means possible, which is either obeying the tower - "boss" and working hard to bring goods in a box to gain money both for the tower and yourself, or devote yourself to rebellion and try to overtake control over the tower, and become the "boss" yourself. Tower, in fact, must observe other bunnies and try not to miss any sneaky rambos [described in a previous sentence]. Not to say, you can't figure who is who unless you want to learn people's personal behaviour and mark them in-mind.
There aren't any critical issues and I didn't happen to meet anything what could distort my experience even slightly. For the mechanics, rabbits are moving really slow while map is rather big, but such does the tower, which only has a tiny illuminated area to see over the map.  Music is neat, controls are intuitive too. There could be some better explanation guide, aside from the starting tutorial, but it's easy enough to figure on your own during your first playthough (harder with bots though, ouch).
So far game is dedicated to reach its full potential only in online mode, and sadly said, it's almost dead by the time. Good part is that there are bots to replace real players, but this way the "drama part" of interaction and cooperation within a small group of bunnies goes to the second plan, leaving in most times meaningless world for you to toy with. So, I'd strongly advise you to found a party, or seek for random people on forums, to truly enjoy the game. Also, people say that devs are often present in-game, helping beginners and leading them through sometimes puzzling aspects of the game, which is a nice touch and really good attitude towards community. I am pretty sure too that there are more updates to come, with new modes, items, mechanics and improved AI (and bigger base of players), so that may be the point where you decide to give this game a try.
Well, this ends my review. I may have been subjective at points and didn't cover some of the in-game details, but still want to describe what I felt and found enjoyable while playing

LOTRO will come out with a High Elf Race soon in the future of 2017-2018.
You can choose to play solo in instances/skirms OR with a group ranging from 2-24.
At level 75 you can learn Mounted Combat and pick from 3 different "War Steeds". Light, Medium, Heavy.
The Level cap is 105 as of 2017.
The storyline in the game is at the Black Gates.
There is so much to do after you hit level 105 like earning deeds, which earns you LOTRO Coins/Points that you can buy from the LOTRO store.
You can play as F2P or P2P or VIP. (P2P is Premium to Play). So basically you pay one time and become premium forever until you change to VIP, if you want to.
There is Monster Play, which is only VIP, as far as I know.
You can earn as many pets, horses/goats in game as you want to. The best thing about mounts is their costumes and you can pick the costumes that you want on your war steeds.
You do get skills through a skill tree. Three colors being Blue, Red and Yellow. Blue is usually the defense. Red is the DPS. Yellow is the ranged or spells aka buffs and debuffs. However it all depends on what class you play.
I have enjoyed the game so far and still play it. If you are a player that loves the lore of LOTRO, the books, movies, poems, side books for the side stories, music and the animation story then you will love this game! If you are looking to play the game to run through it and get to the end game and finish it, then you probably won't be satisfied as you have missed a lot of side quests and details on how to pick your weapons, armour, legendary weapons and essences.
There are 10 servers to play on, all of them have their good and bad players and trolls.
Enjoy the game. I hope to see you in there. :)

(Originally written 2/6/2011)
Ready to get the mining suit scared off you yet again? Then strap in and start up this sequel to one of the most horrific games seen recently.
After three years, Isaac Clarke has resurfaced in the Sol system. After his adventures on and around the formerly forbidden world of Aegis VII, where the planet-cracker ship USG Ishimura played host to unspeakable horrors known as Necromorphs, Isaac was discovered to have been infected by the man-made Marker, which seemed to spawn these so-called alien monstrosities, with a self-replicating signal; the resulting dementia makes Isaac’s hallucinations worse than ever and will eventually kill him if he does not reach the resistance leader Daina, somewhere on Titan Station orbiting the moon of Saturn.
You get an awkward (in a horrifyingly good way) gameplay shift at the beginning; being committed to the asylum on the Station, you’re bound by a straitjacket and must evade the invading Necromorphs until you can get free. You regain the use of your powers of Stasis (which enables you to slow an object or enemy to a near crawl) and Kinesis (which lets you pick up any loose object and fling it as a weapon) through specific events near the beginning of the game; and once you step into your familiar suit, you’ll feel right at home.
The morphing of your fellow humans into the ravenous, unthinking Necromorphs is more hideous than ever; the first person you meet and who tries to help you, rousing you from a drug-induced slumber in the asylum, is impaled with extreme prejudice right before your eyes, and you watch every detail as poor Marco, Daina’s hapless emissary (and protagonist of the in-between game Dead Space Ignition for Xbox LIVE Arcade), is transformed into the demon who immediately tries to kill you. And you can’t fight back; you’re still bound.
The fact that Isaac now speaks on a regular basis forges an emotional attachment such that you more readily experience his trauma, pain and horror along with him. The other characters are voiced just as well.
Multiplayer is a new experience to the Dead Space franchise, bringing with it the opportunity to fight as an engineer much like Isaac himself, or become one of several Necromorphs which try to take the Engineer team down. Gameplay is objective based; the Engineers must take steps throughout each level to contain or destroy the Necros, while the Necros themselves must prevent the Engineers from accomplishing their goals. You choose one of four classes of Necro when you choose to play as one, from hardy, strong types to wall-walking tentacled creatures. One thing about multiplayer, though: you must use an access code to unlock it fully, so keep that in mind if you choose to rent it or buy it used, as the provided code may have already been entered and thus be useless.
All in all, a wonderful, scary game, full of both shock moments and psychological horror just like the first. Five out of five stars!

Think Binding of Isaac in 3D. This is basically a randomly connected set of 3D arenas, where you fight fantasy creatures with magical weapons. Throw in the occasional room with a new weapons or gods you can pray to, and the obligatory end-of-level boss that blocks the way to the next floor.
Permadeath is in, so when you're dead, it's game over. The only things that accumulate between runs are unlocked objects that add to the random pool of stuff you can find. So no built-in grinding like in Rogue Legacy or Full Mojo Rampage. However as I unlock stuff some sound really powerful compared to what I found previously, so I'm not 100% sure if the game is designed as a real roguelike, i.e. if you have the knowledge and skill could you possibly finish it on your first run?
The visuals are great with a lot of variety between floors.
If you compare it to Binding of Isaac the game has a lot of the features that make that game so great (even secret rooms), but there's not as much item variety and game-changing stuff to find. It has narrowed the gap with recent updates though.
Compared to classic shooters like Hexen from which it borrowed the combat, it lacks the complex level design and occasional interactive object or puzzle. Rooms once emptied of enemies feel empty.
I dislike that mana, xp and health drops from enemies disappear quite rapidly, but that's a design decision I suppose.
Overall this game has a few flaws but is a lot of fun and will get better if you give it a dozen runs.

The original Overlord tickled the black recesses of your evil heart and you fancy another helping.
A strong sequel indeed, though perhaps not quite to the same level as the original... Even if you do get to club baby seals and pick a fight with disgruntled hippie elves.
You're back! And the peasants haven't had a good smiting in decades. In the absence of evil, the Glorious Empire (essentially the Romans) have established a dominance over the once-corrupt lands and it's up to you to wrest it back from their regimented grasp.
The game returns with many of the strong elements from before: Same minion mechanics and same playful humour. The forging problems from before have also been given a welcome overhaul: Giving you the specific recipe-style we saw in Raising Hell... So no more canning thousands of minions to buff defence. Speaking of which, you can now resurrect the buggers (albeit at a price). Handy in one respect, but equally a pain where you have to spend a good 10 minutes resurrecting each minion one-by-one if you happened to have a bad day at the office.
You also now to get to play with Roman catapults, warships and the minions can play with mounts to make them even more fearsome in battle. Nice novelties (the catapult is particularly fun) but to ground expectations: These are relatively infrequent. The mounts, in particular, felt a little underused, only appearing at specific scripted parts of the story. The new ability to possess a minion at various points seems unusual... but it allows for an utterly exquisite stealth mission mid-way through the game. A really refreshing and creative play on the game mechanics, and definitely one of the highlights.
Unfortunately, despite the flashy extras... the game suffers somewhat in gameplay. I never thought I'd say this, but sacking an entire village is a hell of a slog - having to hunt down and dish out Overlord spells on each and every inhabitant. It's enough to make you a do-gooder! The bosses are very disappointing too. Whilst fighting a giant spider in its nest sounds terribly exciting, it was underwhelming and downright convoluted. The final boss also dragged on for more phases than it really needed to - all repeating the same thing.
So it left a poor aftertaste from a weak finale. But giving credit where it's due, the bulk of the game up to that point was very enjoyable and a cements its place a fun, dark successor to the original Overlord. It's unlikely to win over those who weren't blown away by the first rendition. But for a strong fans it should, at the very least, be worth a playthrough.

I played the original Overlord on XBOX 360 back in the day and found it to be an entertaining, if deeply flawed, experience. I didn’t have particularly high hopes for this title, but I have to say that I ended up being pleasantly surprised. While Overlord II still has its share of glitches and awkward controls it’s a lot of fun overall.

For those who didn’t play the original, in Overlord II you play as an “evil” Overlord bent on expanding his reign and building the tower that serves as his base of operations. I use the term “evil” somewhat loosely here as the game is overwhelmingly cartoonish and light-hearted. You choose how evil you want to be, but even at your worst you can’t do anything like what you could in a game like Fallout.

While you have a limited ability to control your Overlord in combat the vast majority of the gameplay focuses on controlling a variety of minions with different abilities. You point to order your minions to perform a variety of tasks: from attacking enemies, to retrieving treasure, to removing objects. Minions are generally pretty entertaining to watch, but you’ll occasionally encounter some frustrations in controlling them.

Overlord II isn’t an incredible game by any means, but it’ll certainly keep you entertained for close to 30 hours.

I've been playing for a few days straight
, and now I believe I can right a review on the game
(this is pretty lengthy, skip to TL:DR if you don't want to read it)
First, I must clear up three terms that I'll be using throughout the review. If you know them, skip to "The Game".
Legend. Legend is just another way of saying "character" or "hero".
Signature. Signature is your standard "heavy" attack, but it's specific to your legend (ie. Character 1 has moves Character 2 doesn't)
ELO. ELO is a system in ranked that tracks your skill via the skill of the players that you defeat.
First, combat. Combat is truly one of the best parts of this game. Unlike some other fighting games, the combat feels smooth and quick. You need to be constantly on your feet, lest your opponent use a well-placed signature and send you flying. To add to this, the weapon system is there. At the beginning of the game, you start unarmed, which has it's own moveset, and then you can pick up weapons as the battle goes on. Each character is locked to using two weapons (three movesets total), and learning to use them each is fun in-and-of itself, let alone trying to counter your enemy's weapons.
Second, Legends. The Legends are great. Due to the weapons and signatures (giving each legend a total of 6 unique moves), each character feels and plays differently, yet still being easy to get into if you've played a character if you have played with one of their weapons. They each also have different distributions of stats, making each character have certain stengths and weaknesses that you can play with or against. Each of them also seem to be pretty balanced
. Sure, there are a few stray characters that are better or worse than the average, but that's just about every game. If a character looks cool, that's pretty much all that's needed to make it viable. If you like the character, and find it fun, then it's a good character.

Third, ranked. Recently, ranked modes in games have become popular, so I might as well cover this. Ranked is pretty standard as things go. There are 1v1s and 2v2s, in which you have a set amount of lives (three), and you have to knock out each of their lives. The way they place you is by ELO and Rank (Tin, Copper, Silver, Gold, Platinum, Diamond). All-in-all, I haven't had many issues with it. Sure, there are a few times where I was put against someone better than me, but no system is perfect, and those players had most likely played in the last season.
I'm going to make this quick, primarily cause there isn't much to talk about. The community is pretty standard as competitive game. Most players just leave the game at the end, only saying "GG", but you have a stray player who insults you (which I ignore), or someone who gives you advice (which I cherish). I've seen many people complain about the community, but I see no issues.
Brawlhalla is a great fighter that has fantastic combat, great character selection, and a nice ranked system.
All-in-all, the game is free to play, try it, it's not like you'll lose anything
.

Played With: Mouse & Keyboard; Windows 10

-True Sequel: The game improves all aspects of the original: the visuals and animation highly improved, the voice acting is expanded, the writing is more humorous. Overall most aspects of the game have been upscaled.

-Mechanical Improvements: The crafting system has been reworked to use resources, gold and a small amount of minions so that now you don't’ have to sacrifice 2000 minions to have a decent weapon. The AI of the minions seems to gotten a large upgrade as they now follow the orders more closely, and if your minion gets stuck they despawn now instead of taking up a slot while on the other side of the map.

-New Mechanics: The game has a lot of additions since its predecessor. Mounts: browns, reds and greens all get new mount units, which are stronger and can traverse in terrain that normal units can’t. Possession: you can now become a minion and go through the places that the Overlord is too large to walk through. Boats/Siege Weapons: you can now send several minions to man a weapon or boat, you will be able to cover large terrain using the boat while the weapons tend to be turret sections that break up from the usual carnage and puzzle solving.

-Dominion and Destruction: The Evil system from original game has been improved now instead of being good or evil you can enslave everyone and let them live under your evil rule or you can murder and destroy everything.

-Spells: Similar to the original Overlord you have magic,now you have three spells for it, however the only useful one is the initial damage spell, while I never used the other two.

-Sweeping Camera: When you sweep your minions the camera may go completely the other way, you will have to do few tries sweeping your minions over areas. You may not be able to see what’s happening as the camera is looking behind you while your minions are in front of you.

-Manual Save/Choices: Because the game autosaves as a main method of saving, and I only discovered the manual save at the end of my playthrough (It’s in the mission select screen under all the quests) there were times where a choice or a kill I did not intend would be saved as part of my story. If you are going for 100% domination or destruction be warned you may kill a unit slave by mistake and then it’s all over.

-This game is a fantastic sequel to the original Overlord, everything has been improved and it has added plenty of fresh content to keep you engaged. Being an Overlord has never been this much fun.

As a computer animator, I've always had a strong respect for game developers and for games as an artistic medium, but Brothers was the game that made me realize that video game have the power to create an emotional experience unlike any other medium. This game takes full advantage of the way games force you to connect with the player character. STAY AWAY FROM SPOILERS BEFORE PLAYING THIS GAME. Seriously, you owe it to yourself to get the full experience. However, if the game has been spoiled for you, don't worry, the experience itself will still be worth it. That being said, brace yourself. I don't know who was responsible for the gut punch that this game pulls, but they are both a creative genius and a sadistic monster, and I both respect and fear them. No piece of media ever made me cry before this, but this game had me full on sobbing for 20 minutes.
Despite the emotional trauma, this is an incredibly fun, creative and well-made game. The mechanic of controling two brothers at once is brilliant and creative and makes for some uniquely challenging puzzles. Different levels have new ways to use the mechanic, which keeps things fresh and interesting.
Overall, this game is absolutely amazing. In my opinion anyone looking to go into game development should be required to play this game, as a reminder of the full potential of games as a medium.

Set in a dark and dusty post-apocalyptic world, I Am Alive is pretty damn gritty. When you first boot up the game you may think the developers are aiming for a monochrome art style to reflect the emptiness of the world and the protagonist. Nope - it's just really, really dusty. Everything (seriously, everything) in the game is black, white, brown, or somewhere in between, with occasional splashes of red (to create an industrial feel as well as the obvious reason).
Follow the exploits of Professor Brian Cox as he tries to find his family, help fellow survivors, and explain the Pauli exclusion principle to increasingly ignorant and hostile thugs. At times, this is deep, rewarding, and engaging stuff.
Unfortunately for the Professor, his resources are somewhat limited. Our Lancastrian hero's weaponry is limited to his machete and a pistol. However, the latter seems to be used more as a mechanic for conserving resources than as a weapon, as bullets can only be found from enemies who have...guns! Combat can therefore become frustrating as confrontations with thugs are common and it's difficult to know who to shoot first and who to leave for a struggle kill with your machete.
This isn't the only time tactics are needed for conserving resources, however, as Professor Cox regains health and stamina through the rare packets of food and drink that he finds perched on outcrops and crates by a fellow survivor who presumably didn't want to make things to easy for those after him.
The game revolves around stamina and climbing as Professor Brian must scale increasingly dizzying heights during each episode. Despite his PhD in physics, the Professor's stamina depletes frighteningly quickly making each section of climbing a nail-biting game of tactics. Thankfully, as seen above, Brian can have snacks while hanging from girders to give him a boost. How this is meant to work in real life exactly I have no idea.
So what happens when the Professor falls to his death, or some thugs grow tired of hearing about eleven-dimensional M-theory and slaughter him with machetes? Well, on "Normal" mode he'll be given three retries for each "episode" which will allow him to revert to a checkpoint a few minutes of gameplay back. It soon becomes apparent, however, that given the maze-like webs of scaffolding Professor Cox must negotiate and how difficult is to know which enemies to eliminate first on so few bullets, these retries really aren't enough. It's not uncommon to have to retry up to twenty minutes of gameplay following a clumsy death near the end of one "episode". The game only saves at the end of each 20-30 minute episode, so get ready to sit down for long periods at a time with this game.
Although we're used to Brian gazing dreamily up at the stars as though he wouldn't hurt a fly, the game's moral direction is altogether more ambiguous. You're rewarded for helping injured survivors and reuniting friends and family, but more frequently you're forced into combat you don't want or need. I would have liked to have seen a less linear path through levels, with some scope for stealth and avoiding conflict.
When the game works, it works well and flows nicely. Although some of the events in the game feel jarringly too convenient (early on an earthquake pushes over a building, allowing you to slide down the wall back to where you started form and the next checkpoint), a dark atmosphere draws you in and it's hard to resist helping Professor Brian back to the university in time for his next lecture on electron potential wells.

Ever heard of Dwarf Fortress? No? Well, you have now! If you know about Dwarf Fortress, imagine DF with graphics and a GUI. Yeah, it's that awesome.
Gnomoriais kind of a cross between a survival game, Minecraft, and a fortress building game. You get thrown into this huge world (however big you want it to be) and get a bunch of gnomes to order around. The thing is though, you don't really order them around, you just give them tasks that they'll do on their own time, but you can tell them what they should prioritize. It's like an RTS game where the units are all kinda rebellious but are smarter. It's a lot of fun if you love managing the logistics of operations - if you love "this goes here, that goes there, these things will turn that into this", this is a great game for you.

Gnomoria is pretty much "Dwarf Fortress: fortress mode, the good bits, with a better UI".  The simulation isn't as insanely detailed as DF, and doesn't have the adventure mode or "simulate-an-entire-world" bits that DF does, but in place of that you get something with good graphics and a *vastly* more consistent UI (mouse driven, keys always do the same thing regardless of which submenu you're in).  It's a lot easier to get into than DF (though still has one hell of a learning curve), and every bit as much fun.
There are some things that could be better: frame-rate suffers with larger settlements with lots of entities (although not as badly as in DF); the 'technology tree' is sort of incomprehensible without a guide; and the end-game can definitely get a bit stale.  It also doesn't really exhibit quite the same level of hilarious batshit lunacy that DF can sometimes generate (though it definitely has its moment), and lacks some of DF's ugly-kitten charm.
All that said, if you liked DF Fortress Mode back in the 2d/early 3d days when it was more game and less simulation, didn't really like the direction it took after that, and always hated the lack of graphics and baffling UI decisions, then this is definitely worth a try.

A surprisingly complex multiplayer game in which you're either in charge or one of many subordinates. Unlike others of its kind, it doesn't really rely on a system of honor or rules ("FREEKILLER!!!"); It's carefully designed so that an inattentive or needlessly violent ruler can be easily sabotaged or dethroned. Good fun to be had betraying and outsmarting friends and strangers no matter which side you're on. A few words of warning though: voice chat is a must, be prepared to take time to learn game's mechanics/strategies, and bring some friends along or prepare to coordinate with the game's community to play for the time being.
The goal of the game is to be the first to earn 10,000¢. You earn a very slow passive income which is increased by wearing a collar or greatly by being in the robot. Taking control of the robot is simply a matter of walking in the door. The game's maps are dark and unless you're under the spotlight of the robots's sights or wearing a collar you aren't readily seen. You can also hide behind hills or under water.
So being in the robot = earning the most money = winning, right? Why not just constantly shoot all that approach your thone? Well, being in the robot only really gives you the ability to kill. In order to restock you have to order supplies, dumped onto the map by a dropship, and coerce/bribe your subordinates into dropping them into a box. Bunny corpses that are dropped into the box heavily penalize the robot overlord. Killed players respawn in the dropship and have to wait for it to arrive... unless something were to happen to the dropship :) In its absence players spawn randomly on the map; You will quickly find out how hard it is to prevent the stealthy approach of many rabbits to your door at once.
The game's site has a wiki which goes over things in much more detail. The learning curve is steep, but it's surprising just how many different strategies there are.
A few negatives:
*Controller support is only partial. You need the keyboard to fully control the robot or purchase items.
*Uses mouse smoothing but has no option to disable it.
*The tutorial only gives a short introduction to the game's components. It will take a lot of reading on the wiki or playing a few sessions to start to understand how to play. Some scenario-based tutorials like strategy games have might be more fun while providing practical examples instead of text.
*The game has bots in the absence of human players, but apart from the obvious (not being able to trick you) you are unable to command them to do specific things. They're no fun.

---I received this game from the developer in order to review it. You will get my honest feelings about the game (both good and bad).---
This game is simple to play but impossible to master. You will never have the same game twice and at this point in Early Access, multiplayer is a must. With that said, I would fully recommend this game to anyone looking for a great time with a few friends.
The idea is simple, be the first to 10,000 and you win. How you go about getting there is another story. You are a bunny and can either hop around following or disobeying orders as you see fit. You will receive orders from whoever is operating the "Robot". If you should choose to do so at any point and are able, you can take over running the robot which will lead to quicker point accumulation.
I started with the tutorial and then played a round against the bots. I then repeated the above and thought I had it all figured out and was ready for my first game with real players... Boy was I wrong. There is a lot of things not included in the tutorial which you need to pick up in live games with real players. Games with bots (at this point) really aren't the same as with live players. Keeping in mind the game is still in early access, there aren't always a lot of players available for games all the time. The developer (Dez) is around and if he is free, he spends time teaching new players what to do in the game. There is a spectator mode where you can hear the players speaking over the mic and fly around anywhere in the level observing what is going on and I fully recommend taking advantage of this feature.
The game is very polished in its current state and with Dez continuing with updates and hopefully adding new features this game promises to be great when it makes it out of early access. Maybe new animals which have unique abilities and different game modes (I think that I was already introduced to a new game mode during the last event) will make this game even greater than it already is.

As of today December 2, 2015, Obey is in Early Access but it's already fully functional. The various in-game rules are what's left to be finished, but you can enjoy the game already. Its weakness tho is that it's online only, and although there are bots, they are mostly to fill servers up, and so playing with them alone is not viable.
Obey is simply a game about power. Big deal, you might think, any videogame involves power. True, but Obey pares it down to its most important aspects: what one does to acquire and maintain it, and what other people have to deal with. Due to this, the game is designed to be played live against other people, and there's no single player. Although there are bots, they are mostly to fill servers up, and so playing with them alone is not viable.
Every players starts being "created equal", as a harmless bunny capable of little more than carrying and dropping items, and you mission is to amass a pre-determined amount of cash. Somewhere nearby them is a massive, weaponized tower, as the stand-in for Authority. It's the prime source of cash, and it makes itself felt in that most primal form possible: violence. Oh, and of course, only one lucky rabbit gets to control over. You can see where this is going.
The player commanding the tower (Robosaru) can just plain kill every other bunny with little effort... except there's no point in that, as they can work for him and help him get money faster. Either with the threat of violence or financial incentives, the enemy bunnies are exploited in order to make the Robosaru player richer. But of course, that player most likely won't rule forever, and can lose his Authority if he doesn't pay enough attention to hi unwilling subjects.
And here we have the most interesting part. Each bunny not already in the Robosaru can choose to be a loyal little worker, or try to sabotage and overthrow him. Players who choose the latter can skulk around the map and use various items to hamper the ruling bunny's flow of riches, and similarly, loyalists might get a reward by acting against a rebel. Or he might not. It's all up to the Robosaur's occupant, really. He can be ruthless or relatively benevolent, and the other bunnies might exploit that.
Because of this social element, voice chat is very important (altho players can use text messages), allowing the ruler to better express his wishes, and other bunnies to ask for favors. It might not look like much, but these conversations are essential to keep the game dynamic, and not allowing a single player to hog the Robosaur. Add to it a variety of items (laser fences, landmines, ammo for the Robosaur etc.) and the power relations can get complex.
It's only real drawback at the moment are the lack of players, but that's something that ebbs and flows. Overall, a very clever experiment on powermongering.

Short story: Yes, yes, yes. Great idea, great execution, great fun! Best EarlyA game I've played so far!
*** Note: Headset strongly recommended! ***
Well here we have an Early Access game that acually feels finished and bug-free! And the store page doesn't lie: Obey is unlike any other game.
It's a bizarre marriage of co-op and PvP at the same time - and it's hell of fun! It's both fooling around, and trying to win. Although the mechanics are fairly simple, and kind-of "easy to learn, difficult to master", there is no single "will always work", golden road to victory - depending on the situation, different strategies can work.
Simply put, being a good bunny earns you cash, being the boss earns you more. Any bunny can be boss - if you manage to enter the "bosstower" alive! Bunnies make cash by feeding items to a dropbox, and can hurt the boss by feeding it trash. So you have to be a smart boss, or the bunnies will ruin you. On the other hand, the boss has a chaingun. As a bunny, your only weapon is: acting smart. If you are a smart bunny, you might win even without being the boss.
The first player to reach $10.000 wins. All this, while voice-chatting with the others.
It's about timing (but not FPS reflexes), and knowing when to work together, and when to screw the others - and about the enjoyment while doing so :) Sneaking up on the boss is so much fun, as is fooling around with other bunny mates, trying to steal their pay...
I wish there was a free demo, everyone should try this!
Highly playable, I didn't encounter any bug so far.
The price tag is a little high - I assume because the dev wanted a small, interested community while in EA. I feel like this is more of an $8 game - that said, the 4-pack is worth it if you have voice-chat multiplayer friends. If this is on sale, don't hesitate!
Obey a shining example of how a little team (1 guy!) can make a game that works, without resorting to season DLCs and other shenanigans - if they have a good, realizable idea, and follow it. This is the most complete Early Access game I've come across so far, and the only one that feels finished. Dead Space 2 is an awesome follow up to one of the greatest survival horror games of all time. It effectively adds so much more to the series while still feeling like its predecessor. If you enjoyed the first then you will almost definitely love this one.
Story: This game takes place three years after the events of the Original Dead Space. Isaac Clarke awakens aboard the Sprawl, a densely populated space station on the last remaining shard of Titan, Saturn's largest moon and site of the first planet crack. Isaac is almost immediately thrown back into the horrific chaos with no memory of the events after Aegis VII but this time he is hunted by Necromorphs and the Earth Government Soldiers. He is soon contacted by Daina Le Guin who promises to help him and give him a cure for his rampant Dementia that causes him to hallucinate the grim reanimation of his dead girlfriend, Nicole. Having no place to turn to, Isaac must fight his way through the Sprawl and reach Diana before he is taken down by EarthGov, the Necromorphs, or his own mind.
Overall Score for Story: 10/10
Gameplay: One of the coolest things about Dead Space 2 is that it plays almost exactly like Dead Space. The keyboard and mouse controls have been fixed while the controller layout remains exactly the same. The game has the same weapons along with several new additions and they function almost exactly the same. The Stasis ability returns, and the Kinesis ability has evolved to Advanced Kinesis, which allows you to pick up sharp objects and throw them at Necromorphs, including their own claws and spikes which is pretty cool. Other differences include the ability to reload while sprinting, the introduction to tons of new suits, the ability to hack control panels, and the introduction of zero gravity flying which was very different in the first game. There are also plenty of new and twisted enemies to dismember. Overall the game plays like an updated version of Dead Space which feels amazing and adds much more customization.
Overall Score for Gameplay: 10/10
Characters: The characters in this game are very convincing and develop really well over the journey. Isaac now talks and is much more emotional then he was in the first game. Ellie and Stross replace Hammond and Kendra as Isaac's main companions and they do a good job of it without feeling like a copy and pasted version of the two previous characters. The new antagonist isn't as creepy or scary as before, but he is certainly more intimidating and ruthless. The cast is voiced very well and complement the story and its themes very well.
Overall Score for Characters: 9/10
Graphics: This game may be older now, but the graphics hold up very well. The textures are simple, yet their art style make them pop out and look very colorful. It doesn't exactly look like a brand new game, but it certainly looks sharp and realistic, especially the characters models. The game is also very easy to run at 60FPS due to its age.
Overall Score for Graphics: 10/10
Soundtrack: The soundtrack in this game is very good. It has the intense and high speed tracks like the first to build tension and fear but it also has more emotional tracks that play during crucial plot points and emotional moments that give the game and its story a sadder feel. The OST does a very good job of putting you into the mind of Isaac Clarke.
Overall Score for Soundtrack: 9/10
Sound: The sound design in this game is exceptional and brings a great sense of weight to the Sprawl. The physics objects can be thrown about and they make dramatic noises as they crash into their environment. The guns don't sound as full as they did in the first game but that's to be expected considering the lesser emphasis on horror in this game.
Overall Score for Sound: 10/10
Dead Space 2 is a near perfect example of what sequels attempt, but often fail to achieve. It remains true to its roots and what made it great while also adding in a plethora of equipment, enemies, characters, and lore that further develop the series as a whole. While not as scary as the first, I think this game has some good action and a superior story compared to first. Definitely worth picking up at full price if your a fan, it does however go on sale frequently enough for you to wait though.
Overall Score for Game: 9.7/10

This game takes two big steps. I would never suggest, or approve, of this method...but they got away with it beautifully.
1. The Voice. When you make a game, the protagonist is either a silent, blank canvas for the player to project themselves into or their own character that the player must accept and enjoy playing as. Isaac is one of the few characters to transition between these two, and that's really risky business. I don't know how Visceral did it, but they pulled it off. I don't hate what Isaac has to say now, and most of the things he does line up well with how I played the game. The way he talks down the crazies, his occasional quips, and my personal favorite, the "♥♥♥♥ you" he gives to the final boss before the fight. It's all great lines and voice acting and I'm satisfied with the personality Isaac ended up with.
2. The Genre. This one is a little more subjective. I did not like the original Dead Space. It wasn't even slightly scary, the atmosphere was dull, and the enemies were laughably easy to dispense. What I did enjoy was the story and the boss fights, both of which were fantastic. I was upset that this great idea ended up with such dull gameplay in the name of "Horror". I wanted more of the creative and unique weapons, all of which I loved, I wanted more, cool looking armor, I wanted more bosses and beautifully grotesque enemies. Dead Space 2 gave me all of that. It wasn't going with that subtle "what was that noise???" scary, everything is just thrown in your face in a ridiculous "sudden loud noise" compilation and I love it. It goes over the top in all the right ways.
You can't give the player this arsenal of crazy weapons and then portray them as a helpless victim. Dead Space 2 is the perfect blend of action and horror that got lucky with the chances it took. I can't recommend this game without playing the first, but I also can't recommend the first without a desire to play the second. And I definitely can't recommend either at the full price.

I enjoyed this game very much - I mainlined most of it in one weekend because it was like a book I couldn't put down. The art is wonderful, the music is gorgeous, the voice acting is incredible, the world-building is fascinating, and the characters are engaging.
