I had it on "Normal" setting, so perhaps it's different with "Difficult," but most of the battles could have been won, I felt, with me simply sitting back and doing nothing, letting the AI (over which I had some control, as far as which skills the party members learned, etc.) take control and win handily.
Still, as I said, I was not in it for the challenge, but rather the story and setting. There were parts that had me literally gasping, covering my mouth in shock and sadness, and parts that made me all warm and fuzzy as the characters grew and had more revealed about them. The ending left me hoping that, somehow, a sequel might be made so that I could continue to travel with these characters and discover more about their world.
If you are interested in some great interactive storytelling in a unique fantasy setting, I do highly recommend this game.

I'm writing an actual review for this game because it deserves one.  Masquerada was something that I had tried an early build of back at PAX 2015, then backed when there was the Kickstarter call.  I remember being pretty impressed by the art and the feel of the world even back in the early alpha and was further intrigued when I saw the voice talent that got hired.
Even so, I honestly wasn't expecting a whole lot.  It's been a while since I've had any story draw me in after all, and I guess I've gotten a little disillusioned with the story based indie game market.  However, this one grabbed me by the throat and had me doing a few ill-advised marathon sessions to finish the game because I just had to know how all of the plot threads were going to resolve.
Two things really carry this game to greatness: its setting and its characters.  Ombre was a grand, beautiful and dangerous place that I never got tired of seeing more of.  The artists did a wonderful job of bringing various exotic styles and concepts to life.  Whether I was climbing the spiral staircases in the White Spire or scaling the Singing Tree, I was always excited to see what was around the corner.  However, what really sealed the deal for me was the little NPC conversations you can walk into, and the quality of the codex entries.  While it occasionally annoyed my completionist side to walk back and forth to see who talked and who didn't, the side conversation added a much needed extra oomph to the feeling that the Citte was a place of many different personalities and opinions.  Likewise, I read every codex entry that I got my hands on.  The writers made an interesting decision to have all the entries written from the perspective of Cicero, the main character, which added some lovely insights of the character's interior thoughts to the general world building.
Speaking of the characters, almost all of them were beautifully realized in both writing and performance.  I particularly liked watching Cicero through the course of the game, as Matt Mercer's performance was stellar as always, but Jennifer Hale somehow managed to surprise me again with how she played Lucia.  You'd think I'd be used to being impressed by her after all these years, but jeez, she did an amazing job.  It was immensely fun peeling back the layers of secrets back one by one, trying to figure out what each character was motivated most by, alongside Cicero.  There were actually several plot points that took me by surprise, in a non-bs way, which doesn't happen often anymore.  My only complaint is that Vasco kind of got the short end of the stick in terms of screen time.  He's the only one of the main party that I don't think got a super developed arc, though what was there was intriguing enough.
As caveats, I realize that this style of story telling is not for everyone.  I absolutely love reading codex entries, as I mentioned above, and I think that the game would be quite a bit thinner if you aren't the type of person who finds that sort of thing interesting.  Likewise, the combat in the game is not bad, but it's certainly not the main draw.  AI for your companions is a little wonky sometimes, but I didn't have the patience to play it as a tactical RPG as I'm sure was intended.  I played on Normal, and got by in fights with minimal pauses, usually to reposition characters out of AOE effects.  If you're just looking for a super deep tactics game, this is probably not the game for you.  Perhaps it becomes more important if you were to up the difficulty to Hard, which I might do at some point.  Masquerada is also a relatively short game; I'd say it's 10-12 hours.  So if you're looking for something that will give you more than that, look elsewhere.  It's also a linear story.  This is not a downside in my eyes; the writers had fully defined characters and a plot in mind, so giving "choice" to the player is kind of... not necessary for this plot to work.  I feel like in the past few years, story driven games have gotten extremely enamored with the idea of "choice in video games", and it's kind of nice to have a game that realizes it doesn't need to shoehorn moral decisions and a paragon/renegade bar in to tell a good story.  In terms of bugs, I found two typos and had one screen loading error happen in my 14 hours of play, which I find totally acceptable.
However, if you can put those caveats aside, I definitely recommend picking this game up.  It's been a while since I've had this much fun just exploring a -good- story.  Load it up and get sucked into Ombre for a few hours.  Thank you so much Witching Hour! I eagerly await a sequel :)

This is the first review for a game that I've ever written on Steam, and I'm writing this because I think it's important to share just how much I enjoyed this game. After reading most of the reviews, I feel like those who didn't recommend the game went into it with the wrong mindset, and while that's totally understandable, it's important to clear up what Masquerada is and what it is not.
The tl;dr is that this is a very linear, story-driven game that has a suitable (but not superb) combat  with questionable AI. There are no dialogue options, branching choices, sub quests, or exploring, but the game makes up for it with some incredibly compelling lore and world-building, a succint and satisfying story with its fair share of twists and turns, and an interesting cast of characters that are splendidly portrayed and voice acted. If you play games for the story and characters, buy this now. If you're looking for a sprawling sandbox with a deep combat system, you might want to look elsewhere -- but I'd still encourage you to give the game a try, just to get a glimpse at some of the storytelling and see if it's your cup of tea.
At its heart, Masquerada wants to tell you a story. It plays like a book or movie with some combat sprinkled in, and while it is extremely linear, there is a great deal of charm and heart in the game that more than makes up for its flaws. The tale takes place in a fantasy mirror of Renaissance Italy that is recovering from a tumultuous civil war between the Costadani, who are commoners, and the Masquerada, who are the 'nobility' that wear magical masks to tap into the powers of the elements.
The characters are well written and come alive as the story progresses through action, mystery, and intrigue in an incredibly innovative and interesting world. The music didn't have me humming after closing out of the game, but it adds just the right amount of atmosphere when it's needed. The real aural gem is the voice acting; there are some pretty heavy hitters in the gaming industry doing some pretty astounding work, including Matthew Mercer (various games and anime) and Jennifer Hale (Bastila Shan, Fem!Shep, every cartoon you watched as a kid), and it makes the characters and story so much more engaging to play through.
The game is a little brief by RPG standards. I spent somewhere in the area of ~15-20 hours on the game while playing on hard, and that's probably an above average playtime. The strict linearity and lack of sidequests makes it so that there's rarely a dull moment in the plot as it strides forward, and you never have to deal with filler that isn't somehow meaningful to the characters, if not the overarching tale itself. Masquerada is rife with world-building and awesome lore, which is further expanded upon by a codex/journal that the protagonist writes in first person about the world and his experiences in it, which add additional layers of depth to the characters he interacts with, their history, his thoughts about current events, etc.
The gameplay is an isometric, pause for tactics RPG. Each character is attached to an element (water, wind, fire, earth) and a style of fighting (essentially melee rogue, melee tank, ranged caster). Within the introductory stages of the game, the protagonist chooses his element and can then switch between the three styles of combat at will. Each element has a selection of six active ability and one passive ability, each with their own (small) tree of upgrades, but you can only every have your passive and four active abilities selected in battle, and you don't gain enough skill points in the game to max them out. Combat revolves around positioning around enemies' attacks while using your abilities to create elemental tags that you can then activate for a variety of effects depending on which elements are interacting together and your upgrades. Each character has a Focus arc -- an area in front of them that allows them to block attacks and avoid damage directly to their health until the bar depletes.
Combat can be clunky and finicky, however. Things move too fast and it's hard to keep up without constantly pausing. You have to make sure your characters' Focus arcs are facing the enemies that are attacking you while positioning your rogue archetypes to flank for extra damage, while lining up your abilities to do the most damage possible, while managing who is getting tagged with which elements and who is triggering those tags for the best effect, while trying to avoid your enemies' abilities when they're broadcast. This shouldn't be too complex to handle, but when there are a dozen or more combatants on the screen, things start getting muddled because everyone is attacking several times
.
These issues are further compounded by the fact that, although the AI has been adjusted in the most recent patch (for the better), trying to a) keep your characters out of enemies' attacks and b) make sure they aren't attacking the wrong targets... both still remain an issue. The most you can do to set up your characters' AI is determine how many targets are around when they use an ability, which isn't ideal. I ended up turning off most of my abilities for automatic AI use for a number of reasons. One character has a great attack steroid, but is mana starved and kept using an ability to open up combat on 3+ targets once the mobs got larger towards the end of the game, which made it so I couldn't use the steroid buff. Each character has an ability to trigger elemental tags, but your only options are to deactivate the AI for these abilities or have them immediately activate the closest elemental tag whenever the cooldown is up -- you can't specify which tags you want to trigger, or under what conditions.
But with some pausing, the combat does work, and it certainly isn't such a hamper that it made me enjoy the game less -- but there are some clear design flaws that could be fixed or worked on, and while I don't want to discourage anyone from playing the game, it's important to know what you're getting into, if only so that you can temper some of your expectations.
Overall, I loved this game. I was deeply impressed by the storytelling and the overarching plot. The characters and voice acting were engaging. And for all the quirks and flaws and linearity, I was incredibly happy and pleasantly surprised by my experience with the game. If you enjoy a good story, play this. None of the game's flaws are glaringly awful or make the game unplayable by any means, and experiencing the world of Masquerada is well worth any mechanical idiosyncrasies with the game.

PROS
+ Graphics/Visuals
Like the first entry, Trine 2 has a gorgeous art-style, but now even more so. The lighting, on the one hand, seems more natural and realistic; yet, it maintains the enchanted quality of the first game. The assortment of levels is impressive with a diversity of themes such as coastal, desert, aerial, gastrointestinal, and more. The environments are breathtaking, frequently causing you to pause while taking in the almost overwhelming scenery. Something I particularly liked was how the camera would occasionally shift its view to looking somewhat forward. This change in perspective gave a 2.5-dimensional feeling to the game which I found quite pleasing.
+ Music
Trine 2's top-notch soundtrack is a combination of orchestra and more unusual instrumental choices resulting in a captivating and unique listening experience. As great as the music was in the predecessor, I would argue that it is better this time around.
+ Improved Gameplay
Just about every problem I had with Trine gets addressed in this sequel. Combat, although nothing special, is now at least adequate and does not feel tacked on. Puzzles and platforming are not as exploitable thanks to the nixing of the triangle block that Zoya could use for grappling. The controls seem like they work better since I was not fumbling as much. The difficulty is consistent, and you should not experience any spikes. Characters have more abilities and upgrades adding a little more depth to the RPG aspect. Finally, there is more variation to everything: puzzles, enemies, levels, assets, etc.
CONS
-Game Length
My only complaint with Trine 2 is its' short length which is ironically made worse by the excellent level design and music. I may have to replay someday to get my fill.
CONCLUSION
Trine 2 manages to maintain the desirable qualities of the last installment while working on past mistakes. The result is a sequel closer to what Frozenbyte was trying to achieve with Trine 1. Ultimately, I give Trine 2 a PAR of 4.

The shortest way I could describe this game would be "Like the first game, but without most of the flaws it had."
The presence of beautiful environments seems to be the most consistent element throughout the entire trilogy, and this game is not an exception. Since this game is longer than the first, it also means even more amazing scenery to look at.
The music is rougly as good as in the first game, but with one major difference - the music tracks seem a bit longer, which means they don't feel quite as repetitive.
The story seems to have been given a bit more thought this time around. It's still not super-deep, but it's way more thought out than it was in the first game. It is also worth mentioning that a few story elements from the first game have been retconned.
Combat hasn't changed too much from the first game. It's had a few minor tweaks to improve it further, but remains largely the same. There is a greater variety of enemies, but most are reskinned versions of the same ones. There
some enemies that can kill the player in one hit, but all of them are either bosses or immobile environmental hazards. Some of the bosses are also more varied than in the previous game.
The first Trine suffered from major issues, such as inconsistent hitboxes and other problems. Luckily, in Trine 2, nearly all of those problems have been fixed. You no longer have to worry about unfairly missing platforms that you clearly should have landed on.
In the previous game, most of the puzzles were a matter of "How many boxes do I need to stack to get up there?" This game still has several bits that are like that, very many in fact, but it also has a couple of parts where you actually need to be observant or do actual thinking. So another improvement there.
Some exp orbs are unfairly placed, such as being so far above the top of the screen that you can't even see them unless you get to the highest point in the immediate area and build a full stack of boxes to climb up on.
This game fixes nearly all of the issues the first game had, and the result is very solid. This is a good game.

Too bad this game is random for the sake of being random.
You fail more by bad random setups than your ability to dodge or to efficiently output more damage, add-in a couple of other annoying factors, it gets frustrating when you fail.
I suggest watching a gameplay video before reading this review.
There are four types of weapons in this game; Wand(starting weapon), Spell, Staff & Alchemy.
You can't run and shoot and its on purpose.
So when you are in a room full of enemies that like to shoot high flying homing explosive mortars plus low flying homing shots at the same time, you have to walk & shoot, run for a few seconds, walk & shoot. While you do all of that you will get hit behind your back, on top of your head and you didn't know.
Too much enemy homing abilities going on at the same time.
The best recommendation when in a room full of homing nonsense, walk & shoot, run for a few seconds around so a few shots cleared then repeat. Generally this recommendation applies to every room except the last boss.
You can only run in one direction and thats forward and if you try to turn you slow down and slide.
Enemies don't give you experience(EXP) when you kill them.
They drop these EXP gems, you have to pick them up and they expire if you don't pick them up.
This brings up a lot of troubles. Slowers the game pace too much, you'll see why in the failing example.
At first you won't mind or care but when very bad random setups start ocurring you'll notice.
It also brings up the problem of resource management.
There are rooms in which killing enemies doesn't yield any EXP at all, these would be the Obelisk rooms and Scavenge rooms.
This is a problem because you might be indulged into spending either Spell, Alchemy or Staff ammo in return for no EXP but you can clear the rooms safer? Although with all the homing abilities going on and other rooms still left to clear I don't recommend it.
There are enemies you can't get close to them so you have to kill them from afar but at the same time you have homing mortars/shots/enemies plus a whole bunch of AoE damage going on, you have to decide when you kill them to give up health and positioning for a bit of EXP or no EXP at all.
Not putting it slightly, there are enemies with insta-hit shots if you are close to them or the hitbox for their shots and AoE is so big you can't be close to them while walking,
A failing example would be:
Second floor, very very small room and spawns four Storm Beasts and three Imps plus more combinations of them as you kill them.
Storm Beasts are flying slow moving fat gargoyle looking creatures who shoot lighting spheres, it can't be dodged if you are close and walking but the room is so small you might as well be running all the time but you can't shoot and run at the same time.
Imps are small flying imp looking creatures who shoot three flames across the floor in fan like style.
The best recommendation is to run around in circles and once in a while walk & shoot but if you walk you'll get hit by Storm Beasts shots, because their hitbox and AoE is big and you'll be against a wall every time.
Storm Beasts are bullet sponges so trying to kill them with any kind of "efficient" damage output you might have come up with in your run isn't revelant(unless luckily enough you got a good combinaton of weapons).
All the while you have these fans of flames shooting at you.
Its good not great, mostly you'll die randomly and in my opinion with more balance tweaking this could become great.

I'd reccomend this game if it weren't for a few things. Here are the pros and cons of brawlhalla.
(Skip to the overall review to see me explain myself about the main big problem)
CONS:
- Spam in ranked
- Dodge machanic is very spotty and you can be hit during a dodge which makes no sense.
- The sound is constantly too high whether you actually turn it down or not
- Combos and moves in the game are easily spammable making it hard to beat anyone who spams
- The game is kind of unbalanced as some characters are so fast that you actually can't hit them even with a speed buff
- Many characters are just a different skin and play the exact same, making little diversity
PROS:
- Microtransations are minimal and are only cosmetic
- Most of the community is nice and will joke around with you even though there are some toxic scum bags in the bunch
- The game is very addicting and has a lot of potential
- Grinding in the game is actually very fun when you come up against players who actually play the game and not spam.
- The design of the characters is amazing and is actually very well done
- The map design is also very well done
- You can get weapons skins and a certian character skins with glory points. (Sadly you can't gain many of these skins with glory points)
OVERALL REVIEW (skip to the end to see who I would recommend it for and why I personally don't recommend it):
I would Recommend this game if it weren't for one thing. SPAM. Many characters are exactly the same in a way but the main problem is spam. The game is unbalanced but if you use some tactics you can beat way faster characters. However the speed at which you can do attacks can easily result in uncounterable spam. It makes the game very annoying and rage inducing especially in ranked. Now that can be looked past if you just want to play it with friends, but the fact is so many high ranking players spam their heads off. If I fight Queen Nai, constant magic. If I fight Bodvar, constant sword and hammer knockout attack spam. If I fight another Orion, spear down attack, and lance spam. If I fight a Nix constant grab spam. It's honestly not fun. If you would punish people who do this then the game would be more fun, and maybe get way more traction than it already has. But you can't expect many people to play in tornouments if they see spammers in ranked because they are going to assume official tornouments are like that. However if you can't spam in tornouments, why can you spam in ranked? That question should not be asked. I stopped many games because cheesy things like this aren't punished. Halo 5 SWAT: The enemy team takes the center of the map and no matter where you come from they kill you extremely easily due to fortifying. Thats just one tiny example. It's just annoying and has the ability to be fixed or at least punished for being scummy. But is it? Not that I know of. It's unfair to the people who are at least mediocre at the game that can't get better because if they go against someone else they spam. Now if you just want with your friends, go ahead and get it. But they should fix this crap.

Whether you are playing it alone or with a friend, this game will take you to an ancient nordic world, inhabited by villagers and legendary creatures. Help the two title brothers find an ingredient for their father's medicine, make them cooperate in order to get through their magical journey, interact with everyone and everything; you won't regret it!
Pro tip: keep tissues at hand, there might be some crying!
Brothers is one of the best story experiences ever made - you really have to experience it for yourself.
Makes you work your hand-eye coordination in an entirely new way, and has a moving story told without dialogue to boot. Check it out.
This game is for someone who just want to relax and enjoy a beautiful story. The puzzle is not hard, but what makes this game amazing is the way this game deliver the story between two brothers.

In Brothers- a Tale of Two Sons you guide two brothers across a foreboding landscape on a quest to receive a cure to heal your sick father (I’m sure I read somewhere that its based of a Scandinavian folklore story).

Each joystick is used to control one of the sons, and it uses this mechanic quite well. Using each son at the same time to distract and manipulate the environment and enemies can be quite challenging at first, but after a while it becomes second nature. It also uses the mechanic of holding down a button to simulate the eldest son holding hands/dragging the youngest child around. If you have ever had to guild a child/younger sibling then this feels right at home, and I thought it was an excellent way to incorporate the sense of companionship. When that mechanic is removed from the game it actually feels like you have lost something, I can’t think of any other game that rams home a sense of loss or wrongness like Brothers does.
The art style is great, highlighting what you need to focus on while everything else just adds to the stage. You never get lost or not know what needs to be done, but you aren’t babied through it, it has just been designed that well. You need a controller to play this, but again with the above mentioned game mechanic I can’t see how it would work and convey the same sense of companionship.
The game won’t take you a very long time to finish, which is my only complaint, but I highly recommend playing it.
If you are chasing achievements then you can easily 100% this, as long as you take a little time to get some of the more scenic achievements.

On top of that, the mechanics meld with the story in a such a great way that Brothers really is a showcase for the unique type of storytelling capable through videogames.

TL;DR: You should buy this game because its graphics are good, gameplay is strategic, thought out and entertaining, controls are good and its humour is witty.
I've had this game for a while on my Xbox 360 and decided to get the PC version when it went on sale, and I've had lots of fun with it.
All of the Overlord games are very similar in terms of story and how they play. I've played the first Overlord game, Overlord II and Overlord: Dark Legend, though I haven't played Overlord: Minions or Overlord: Fellowship of Evil, so I can't compare to those two games.
Let's talk about the technical aspects of the game. Out of the three that I have played, Overlord II is certainly the best. It has the best graphics and massively improves on character animations over the first game. For a game that's considered "old" now, its graphics are quite good and the game runs absolutely fantastic, maintaining a high, smooth and extremely consistent framerate. The game's controls are also pretty good, and I much prefer keyboard controls to the Xbox 360 controls.
It's also a very stable game. On my Windows 10 laptop, I haven't had a single crash, though the macOS version is a whole other story. I'm happy that the game was ported to the Mac so I could play it on my MacBook while I'm out and about (it's not bad playing on the MacBook's touchpad and my MacBook's Intel Iris graphics run the game quite acceptably) but what I'm really disappointed about with the Mac version is that (for me, at least) it doesn't appear to run for any more than 30 minutes before crashing. Worse still, it won't launch again after a crash until I restart the computer, as it will crash again immediately after launching. Also, as it only allows you to save in the Dark Tower or when it autosaves at certain checkpoints, you can't progress on the Mac version because it won't stay running long enough to reach a save checkpoint.
Bottom line, if you want to play this game, you're best running Windows.
Technicalities aside, actual gameplay is great. Overlord II is a very linear game and there isn't much choice so it's not the most replayable game in the world, but it'll keep you busy for a while. The game involves a lot of strategy and thinking which mixes things up for me since I rarely play games that involve strategy though I wish there were more hints available because you can get stuck in some places, unsure of what to do next. As I mentioned above, the game's controls work really well on the console but moreso with the keyboard and mouse (though that's just my opinion).
The game's world is visually well-crafted and I really love the colourful fantasy theme and I love that there are a lot of different world styles. You'll get to explore worldspaces that are reminiscent of wintry Nordic culture, tropical Caribbean culture, jungles and worldspaces that look a lot like Italian countryside as well.
The game's voice acting is cheesy as all hell. It's not bad, but it's really cheesy. The game also makes use of some cheesy humour and some other humour that's really funny. In fact, there are some things about this game that makes me wonder how it was able to keep its Teen rating and not end up with a Mature rating - those faries you encounter, for example.
It's also a quite rewarding game as well. Conquering a village has many rewards. Instead of killing a village's inhabitants, it would be better to enslave them because once enslaved, the villagers will work to produce weapons and armour for your minions and gold for you to collect.

Fingered! is Edmund McMillen's weakest game compared to his other projects like Super Meat Boy and The Binding of Isaac, but it's still a fun game nonetheless.
Difficulty-wise it's damn diffcult.  It'll take you about an hour or two to learn the basics, and a few more to beat the game.  It doesnt help that some of the hints you're given can be very vague, and occasionally I was forced to take a 1/2-1/4 guess.
The art style is very McMillen.  If you like his other games, you'll enjoy his art style.  However if this is your first McMillen game, you'd probably be a bit grossed out.
My only real complaint is that you cannot fullscreen the game.  It's stuck in a small window.  Also, as far as I can figure out, there's no audio controls - not even a mute - and no .ini files from which you can change it manually.  I have no idea why tthat's the case, however I assume it's because Fingered! is a small side project by McMillen, and not a fully fleshed out game.
I'd give this game a 6.5/10.  I did enjoy it, despite it's shortcomings.  If it cost more I'd advise against it, but ~$2 for 6 hours to 100% isn't a bad price.  If you know you like McMillen games, I'd say pick Fingered! up.

Let's see, Obey is a multiplayer game in which bunnies compete against each other for making the most money. Meanwhile, there's a giant robot -which is controlled by one of the bunnies- that "employs" the rest of the bunnies. The player can choose to obey the robot or try to overtake his or her position. So basically that's the concept.
I had to play the tutorial a few times just to learn the ropes, because there are quite a few mechanics and I'm not used to multiplayer-only games... and then I found out that there weren't any players online. This has happened the three times I've tried the game, but I may have had bad luck. Luckily, there's a bot system that works pretty decently, so it's not like you can't play... but it's certainly not the way the game was meant to be played, I guess.
It's kind of fun though. The game itself is based on a cool idea and the implementation is not bad. The graphics are also quite outstanding for an indie game, I specially liked the robot. The way the giant robot looks from the point of view of our bunny is truly imposing.
The price is still quite expensive in my opinion, but once it gets a proper sale price, I guess it would be really cool to play this game with a few friends after buying the 4-Pack.
And well, I'm not sure what other features will be implemented in the future, but the game is quite playable already. I would like, for example, to have a sprint key or being able to hide the bunny underground or something. I haven't played for too long and I already felt it was sometimes too repetitive to go from one place to another carrying stuff just to be annihilated the moment I stepped out of the "delivery path" (yup, the bots are pretty smart)
I also think it would be cool if the robot had some kind of massive speaker and if it gave its orders through pre-recorded audio, rather than text. I think that would be a cool way to implement a bit more of humour into the game and for players to understand the game earlier. I mean, if I had heard "Bring me more uranium, or die!!!!!" I would have known right away what I had to do. The bots kind of already do that already through text, but I'd like to see it more often and, if possible, with audio. Just some suggestions.
I'll definitely come back once more things are added to the game. Specially recommended to those that really enjoy multiplayer games in which you have to interact a lot with other players, be aware though that there aren't too many people online, so be sure to bring your friends with you!

Few things you need to know before you get into this game:
This game is nothing like I’ve ever played before. You either play as a harmless bunny or a killer robot.
As a robot you command a bunch of bunnies (vocally or via text/on-screen commands). Bunnies have to bring you (robot) ammo, fuel, batteries, etc and do tasks like building defenses around you. You reward them by paying salary.
As a bunny you must
your robot overlord… or not. Robot has a “money generator” and you can sabotage robot’s income by turning generator off. There are other ways to ruin robot’s day. Most importantly, if you are sneaky enough, you can get inside the robot yourself and become the new overlord :) If you don’t obey and act fishy robot will send you to sweet bunny heaven in an instant.
It is a roleplaying game in sense that everyone has to play a role (there is no inventory, experience or anything like that). Quality of gameplay highly depends on the ability of players to be able to embrace their roles. Headset certainly makes communication more fun.
I applaud the developer for trying something unique rather than using Unity engine to make another minecraft clone and I do hope this game becomes successful enough for the servers to get populated. At this moment community is very small and there are barely any people playing.

OBEY is a really unique multiplayer game that's quite difficult to describe really. In each match you start off by playing a Bunny and in the arena there is a large looming tower that can be controlled by one player. You have a choice as to how you choose to play. The player who controls the tower issues commands to the other players and then they can choose whether or not you want to obey (hence the name!) those commands or not. You might want to obey the commands from the tower and play the game that way, or you might try to rebel and take over the tower!
The game play is very strategic, especially if you manage to get control of the tower. There are a ton of items in the game arena that can be used in different ways and add a huge amount of depth to the game. You'll certainly need to play through the tutorial but this isn't enough really. This is still in Early Access so hopefully the tutorial will be expanded in the future but in the meantime I'd recommend watching some Youtube videos to get a better idea of how it works.
You can play on a LAN using a private server or you can join an online one. When I tested it there were only a handful of empty servers online so hopefully more people will pick this up and the servers will become more populated.

Blasting the limbs off of hideous necromorphs remains tremendously satisfying, and although the pacing lags a bit during the game's middle portions, this second outing packs more than enough scares and surprises to make stepping back into Isaac Clarke's suit extremely worthwhile. In addition, a new multiplayer component successfully translates Dead Space's particular breed of dismemberment-focused combat into a pulse-pounding team-based experience that casts you as both humans and as the foul necromorphs.

Engineer Isaac Clark returns for yet another hair raising necroslashing adventure. I was quite interested in the first game, but always found the controls to be rather cumbersome. As a result I was pleasantly surprised how smooth the controls were in part 2, as Visceral Games have clearly taken the criticism on Dead Space 1 (DS1) to heart and done their best to seriously improve the solid fundamentals of the original game.
To those who liked the original I can say that Dead Space 2 is an instant must buy. The story is well put together and a direct continuation of part 1, the combat is fun as ever (Severing limbs of horrifyingly mutated humans never gets old) and the game is drenched in a sci fi horror atmosphere that is quite impressive (there's especially a rather disturbing section somewhere halfway involving mutated infants).
Safe for a rather annoying (but luckily quite short) gameplay segment just before the end of the game I can find almost no fault in how the story, sound, graphics and gameplay are presented. The weapons one can choose and modify allow for various playingstyles and safe for 1-2 all feel distinctly different in their application, enemies are tough and present a challenge (especially on the highest difficulty setting), I experienced zero graphical issues or game crashes and graphically the game still looks very good with proper quality texturing and models that move very smoothly.
Power up that UAV suit and ready that plasmacutter for a journey well worth taking.

I've had this game since it was released as early access. It's been consistently a lot of fun throughout development and the devs have been really active in updating and expanding the game. An example being I found a bug in Alpha 11, maybe they had already located it too, either way, it was fixed in 5 hours! So, this is not one of
early releases.
On the actual gameplay, it's an entertaining simulation, where you're having to develop a colony, with pre-set victory conditions in each level. You can't use all the buildings and techs every time, so you end up needing to be selective on what you develop and coupled with that is the risk of runaway global warming, which results in failure. Added to that is time trials, challenges, free play and planet creators, so it's got a decent amount of replay value to it too.
It's a pretty chilled game, which however can put the pressure on at times. For the price it is, I would definitely say it's entertaining and enjoyable enough to be totally worth it.

Imagine Earth first looks like a simple building game, but it quickly evolves into a complex strategy game. The missions where they include computer adversaries are quite challenging and they make for a fun game.

I purchased this game some time ago and have waited a long time to review it, due in part to some issues I had with it, but also because I wanted to be fair, considering that it is an early access game. So with that being said, my review:
So I was flipping through the steam games and I came across this game called "Imagine Earth" in the simulation section, I saw that it had a demo and decided to try it. At the time the demo only had a missions available, a simple interface and not a lot in the way of content... but I was hooked.
It reminded me why I like simulation games in the first place, giving me all the things I enjoy with the bonus of playing God to a newly created world to work with. I could feel the nostalgia of Sim Earth I played as a kid. So I jumped right in after playing the demo and purchased early access to the game.
Playing the early access version it was immediately apparent the game was slightly different than the demo that been made available, which is okay considering that demos are just that, demonstrations of what the game will look like. But one thing was clear, this was no simulation game.
What I got instead was a game that seemed more like a puzzle where your decisions didn't really matter more than getting the right pieces in the right order before you run out of time. I had many issues with the game, all of which I made clear by submitting emails to the developers who were very receptive and seemed opened to the community ideas.
Lorian the third world in the game gave me excruciating torment, where it seemed the developers were more interested in creating a game of torture than a game of fun, and it became discouraging to play over and over, failure after failure. So I took a break, quit playing altogether in the hopes some of the issues I had with it would be solved eventually.
So after months I decided to try the game again, and I am so glad that I did. All of the issues that I had originally had have disappeared. What was once an overly complicated puzzle of torture, had become a relaxing simulation/strategy game that was less scripted with super hard puzzle nonsense and although still difficult seems less locked into "their" pre-defined way to win strategy I sometimes felt when playing. Even when I failed a couple of times, I saw different ways to get to where I wanted and ultimately finished the things that were once overly difficult to beat.
The developers have clearly taken the community recommendations and made the game a lot more playable and fun, and that's why I felt like it was time to review this game for them.
I wholeheartedly recommend this game now, for its addictive playstyle that will keep you happy for hours on end. While the game is still unfinished, it’s very much where it needs to be now, and playing it no longer feels like an exercise in futility but rather an actual game that is fun to play. I'm excited to see more and cannot wait to see how this one ends.
For the people that like extra-long drawn out games, this one might not be for you, as the game only has a few missions, but it almost doesn't matter because the addictive nature of it will keep you coming back for more. I hope to see expansions or additions to the game after it is released because what they have here opens so many other possibilities. Certainly you will be left wanting for more, and there doesn't seem to be any reason why the devs couldn't keep adding on to the game.
For the people that love simulation, strategy, space games, this game is FOR YOU! For everyone else that loves fun quirky games, you'll want to play this game too. Beautiful, charming, and challenging. Highly recommended!

Though I don't usually play many strategy games I'm having a lot of fun with Imagine Earth, there is  good variety in missions and has many interesting concepts I haven't seen in other RTS games. I like that it tackles a "serious" issues like global warming in a fun an entertaining way and especially the sandbox mode is something you can probably sink says into.

I am writing a second review for this game because I just finished the main storyline. When I wrote my previous review, I was only in the middle of the game and I did not have an overall grasp on the game.
TL;DR version: DEFINITELY PLAY THIS GAME. Plus, Misha Mansoor from Periphery wrote the ending credits song.
Expanded version:
This game deserves so much more respect than it is currently recieving. AFter beating the game, I still don't understand why people are hating on it. Yes, there are microtransactions and it's annoying that SQUARE ENIX (not Eidos) forced them in. But, you can completely avoid using microtransactions and easily treat them as if they are not there. These easily avoidable annoyances are not detrimental enough to ruin this wonderful work of art that is Mankind Divided.  Seriously, people need to grow up and give it a rest. I only hope that this game starts to recieve more and more praise as the months go on, thus turning MD into a cult classic like it deserves to be.
Story:
MD's story-telling method is a bit different than HR's. I think this is because HR focused more on story building while MD focused more on world building. As a result, the gameplay world and all of it's maps feel much more alive than in previous games, but the story ends up resulting on a smaller global scale. Yes, MD's story does take place on a smaller scale, and the events at the end of the game only affect a smaller portion of the world than the events at the end of Human Revolution did. Some people find this to be extremely annoying, but I don't. Why? Because MD's story shows how UNATCO, the NSF,  Sillouette, and the Council of Five came to be, which are key groups in the original Deus Ex, and all of these groups have major global consequences in DX 1. I am not sure how a lot of people feel about this, but in Human Revolution, the story almost seemed too unrelated to the original game (even though HR was an amazing game on its own). MD helpes to glue HR to DX1 in order to provide a consistent lore throughout the whole series. MD's story is essentially easier to wrap your head around. Also, just because the story in MD is smaller in the global scale by no means makes this a shorter game than HR, which I see a lot of people complaining about. The side missions are muchhhh more complex now. It took me about 120 hours to fully beat HR and it took me about 170 hours to fully beat MD. I did walk everywhere as opposed to running in each gamming because running kept breaking my immersion. Basically, the main story is more simple, the side stories have much more story content, and the game is thus longer. I didn't think this game ended on a cliffhanger.
Gampelay Mechanics:
The gameplay mechanics of MD are the best in the series, hands down. Social battle's are a lot more realistic and fluid, shooting is much more intense, shooting and sneaking are much more versatile, hacking is more challenging, everything is just better and more solid than ever before. The added augmentations are beautiful. YOU HAVE SO MANY CHOICES ON HOW TO ACCOMPLISH ONE THING, even more than in HR. Plus, experience is now allotted in a more equal manner, which encourages doing things that you wouldnt have done in HR. For example, you can get 125 xp for finding a code in a pocket secretary and using it to open a door without hacking. sometimes, this get's you more xp than if you just hacked the terminal. Very interesting manner of alloting xp. All in all, I think remote hacking and the nanoblade aug are my favorite gameplay additions. The new method of hacking took a bit to get used to, but it ends up becoming easier than in HR if you get used to it.
Sound Design:
Sound design is one of those things that you don't notice but it can end up making or breaking your game. And boy did Eidos nail the sound design on this game. Everything from sfx to bgm feels like eidos made the best decision regarding the resources they had at hand. The main ambient Bgm is highly dynamic, changing from dark and moody to profound and uplifiting, which adds to the overall vibe of the game. Plus, the over all music selection is very versatile. When you walk outside of clubs, you hear house, acid house, tech house, electro house, and trance styles of music. Each electronic style is pretty experimental too, which adds to the musical value. Get into a firefight and the music turns into this ambient/metal hybrid in weird time signatures. Wait till the ending credits role by and you hear a Djent track with a heavy breakdown produced by Misha Mansoor from Periphery, who happened to be one of my favorite bands when I was a teenager. Not only music, but the sounds/sfx in general have been revamped. Everything from the foley such as AC humming to each aug having it's own unique sound (and there are a lot of augs in this game) is highly believable. As a sound engineer, I am seriously impressed by this game. I will say though, that I think the default loudness level for the games music is a bit too loud. It makes certain voices unintelligable, such as Eliza's voice on TV, But you can turn this volume down super easily in the games settings. I left my music at about 60 - 65 %.
Level design:
Okay these maps are huge. Like, HUGE. The main city hub is larger than Hengsha and Detroit put together. Some maps have instances where you can icarus fall through seven stories. There are also much more enemies in areas. There are even more vents to explore within each map. Overall, the level design is much more grand and realistic. Also, just to clarify an improper complaint I see being spouted, there are technically no loading screens when you travel through the main city hub. Only if you choose to take a train do you see a loading screen, just like when you fast traveled in skyrim you saw a loading screen. You have to endure a loading screen when going from Prekazka district to any other district because THERE IS A GIANT WALL SEGREGATING THE AUGS FROM THE REST OF SOCIETY AND YOU HAVE TO TAKE A TRAIN TO LEAVE. The whole map is loaded even in your district, but for story purposes, you have to take a train and therefore endure a loading screen. Again, nothing immersion breaking.
The Bad:
Nothing in this life is perfect, nor will anything ever be perfect. So, we can expect some mistakes, even in AAA games. MD is no exception to this rule, This game does have it's fair share of bugs, but nothing gamebreaking or severe enough to warrant an overall negative response. Most of this game's bugs have to do with dialogue and not the gameplay mechanics themselves, though very rarely a gampelay mechanic can bug out for a split second. The major cons are some lip syncing issues within some dialoges, and some of the dialogues have unnatural pauses between each speaker. But seriously, it's not gamebreaking or immersion breaking. There are some reported instances where saving might become unnavailable when it's supposed to be, and this can be pretty bad. Just make sure you save a lot (F5) and if you don't see it save when it's supposed to, then exit the game and reload. But this has only happened to me once in my 185 hours of playtime. I can't speak for everyone, as each rig is built differently, but these were the bugs I experienced.
In conclusion, this game deserves much more praise and much less heat. Longer game, more alive, and narratively cohesive in respect to the rest of the games within this wonderful and life-changing franchise. Choice has always been the primary focus of this series, and it is exectued much more smoothly than ever before in MD. Graphics are amazing (just dont use any MSAA), mechanics are polished, and execution is smooth. As a hard core fan of this series, having beaten literally every game in the series, I can definitely recommend this game with no remorse or frustration. The only time I became made while playing was when the game ended, because I did not want it to end. This is seriously such a good game!

Brawlhalla is a surprisingly well made game, only had a few hours, only played custom matches with friends as well as online 2v2.
Each character is fairly similar, with identical sets of standard attacks and stat differences in Attack, Attack Speed, Defense and Agility. Each also have two weapons they can possibly get from weapon drops and gives them there characters uniqueness.
The weapon archtypes are sword, axe, spear, hammer, lance, scythes, gauntlets, twin blades, guns and bow. Each again have similar light attacks but each character uses two, and has unique heavy attacks with each. There are also bombs, mines and a horn which sends a fireball across the screen at the height your standing, and when it is done gives you a weapon.
Me and a few friends have been playing it together nearly none stop, trying new characters and weapons and finding who we will be playing most. Most of this consists of timed FFA but also some of its many, MANY modes.
There is of course your timed and stock modes similar to smash brothers. Strikeout is pick 3 characters and you play them all over 3 lives. Switchcraft is similar but it randomly shuffles your characters weapons between eachother so you don't know what weapons you will pick up with each character.
As well as the less normal modes. Brawlball is a game of football as well as a battle, Snowbrawl is a snowball fight, Dodgebomb is exactly how it sounds as is beachbrawl. Basketbomb you pick up bomb drops and throw them at the target.
All modes have team options and up to 8 players
This game is incredibly fun, I might enjoy it more than smash. Each weapon has similar light attacks making picking up other characters with similar combinations easier, however their unique flare makes them completely diffirent on how you want to use each one. The animation is great, the characters have a lot of personality in there movements and unique attacks, and you never feel like one weapon archtype or character is superior. Well balanced and fun to play, sudden death can be intense too, a race to the first weapon spawn and then a epic moment of dodging and trying to attack. Me and a good friend had a 2 minute sudden death where both of us refused to be hit for ages, which was intense
My only gripe in the whole game is with basketbomb, it seems fairly underwhelming compared to the other modes. A king of the hill mode would be amazing, as would capture the flag or even a 'Juggernaut' mode.
Me and 5 other friends all got the 'All Legends' pack and we already sank hours into it. Love this game, hope it does well!

First off, a small disclaimer; like many LOTRO players, I migrated to Steam after having played for many years before, so I have many many more hours in game than my Steam activity indicates.
Lord of the Rings Online is a truly impressive diamond in the rough, when it comes to traditional "themepark" MMOs. The gameplay, while standard, is solid and does exactly what it needs to. Some classes are a bit slower and simpler than others. For instance, Guardian is a dead simple sword&board tank for the most part, while a warden is much more complicated hybrid. Different classes cater to different playstyles, and that is a good thing.  In terms of functionality, they are very well balanced; all classes are perfectly viable for their given party roles as well as solo play. It probably helps that there is very little in terms of PvP (which may be a big drawback for some), so the devs don't have be delicate with balancing.
Without a doubt, LOTRO's biggest pro is it's world. The world is MASSIVE and truly detailed. There are bonafide Tolkien scholars on staff at Standing Stones, and it really shows (to clarify, Standing Stones is the current developer, but really they are basically the same core team that have been working on the game for years. They have just finally moved out from under the heel of Turbine and have been able to move the game forward ever since). The various stories of Middle-Earth, the limited voice acting, and the score are really well done and make the world feel very vibrant.
So, the game itself is definitely worth playing, but what about the payment model? Yes, this game is F2P, and there is a LOT of content given for free. However, note that once you get to a certain point, you do have to either be a subscriber or purchase what's called a "quest pack" in order to complete various stories and side quests, however the Book quests (think, "Main Story" quests) are free for the most part. There's also a lot of instanced content that can only be completed if you have purchased unlocks from the cash store, or are a subscriber (basically if you are a subscriber, there is almost nothing that is limited). So, the payment model is a bit of a mixed bag. Putting content behind paywalls is always a bit problematic, but you still get quite a lot of content for free and can eliminate most immediate limits with a relatively small amount of cash (think a few dollars for a quest pack for an entire region, which can give you several hours of playtime if you work on completing them all).  In my opinion, the game is well worth paying for and a much better experience overall if you do. Give it a try; even as F2P the game is worth playing and trying, you really have nothing to lose. If you are a Tolkien fan, you will find a LOT to love here.
Finally, a note on the community: LOTRO has, without a doubt, one of the nicest communities of any MMO on the market, past or present. There are many active players who seek to engage their fellow players with Tolkien-lore friendly events, and every year the devs encourage a large amount of participation in the Child's Play charity.  Veteran players are by and large, very helpful and encouraging to new players, so don't let the game's size and long history deter you from getting into it.

Warlock II: The Exiled is the kind of game that I should have written a review for a while ago, but because of the size of the game, and the VERY slow pace the game takes, I am now finally able to write up a review. First off this is a fantasy turn based adventure game where you are going to play the part of a powerful warlock who saved all the realms, but in his absence from the main realm became exiled. You will now have to gather troops, heroes, knowledge, and more if you are going to be able to retake what is rightfully your's. There will be many portals you will have to transverse, but if you can make it out to the other side you might just find your chance to exact your revenge.
Graphically this game is not going to blow you away, but at the same time it looks well done. I do like the concept that every realm is a floating island, and that there is a wide variety of lands that you will have to deal with. You might be dealing with snowy lands, deserts, lava, cursed lands, and water. You never know what the next world will bring. There's also a very wide variety of enemies to face off against, you will get the chance to battle sea serpents, minotaurs, elementals, dragons, bats, and more. The one thing that I wish had a little bit more TLC to it was the city screens. I understand that there was definitely a minimal approach to it, but it doesn't feel as polished.
The music does a great job of blending into the game to the point that you don't really notice it after a while.
The controls are pretty straight forward, you are going to be using the mouse almost exclusively, with the exception of WASD when you are playing on dual monitors. If you don't you will notice that you are constantly clicking out of the game when trying to scroll across the map.
Even though there is a story to follow, most of the game is randomly generated and is customized to the experience you want to have. You can choose the size of the land masses, the number of warlocks you will have to deal with, and of course the difficulty. Now I will say this, no matter what you are going to have to deal with micro-managing of resources until you can't take it any more. This game hinges on the fact that it plods along slowly so if there were issues you wouldn't see them. There's also a large amount of randomly generated neutral enemies that will pop back up after a while to keep you on your toes in areas that you have removed all your troops from. Speaking of troops, it is damn near impossible to be able to successfully sustain more than a handful of troops. The cost of gold, food, and mana per turn for each unit, hero, building, it will drive you made. There were only a very few times in the game where I was actually gaining on all 3 and that was when I didn't do anything on those turns. The one thing that did completely drive me up the wall was the fact that you have a limited amount of towns that you are allowed to have, and out of those you can only change the ones that you personally settled to specialty towns to help with your micro-managing and decrease your town count. Here's the problem, I'm a conquerer, I never built a second town, I've capture all the cities I've found, and yet I get penalized for it.
At the end of the day the thing about this game that you are going to NEED to have is the editor. This is probably one of the best and most in-depth editors I've seen in a long time. You can build an entire game out of it utilizing Warlock II as a backbone. If you are willing to put in the time you can EASILY make something light years better than what comes out of the box. So with that I have to give a grade on the game, as is, and not what the game can potentially have with user contributions. This game gets a 6.5 out of 10.

My favorite MMORPG of all time. This game and the people who play it are a very rare breed.
A truly massive world full of beauty and secrets. A player community that is smart, mature, and friendly. There is a true dedication to the depth and gravity of the original intellectual property. I pay for subscriptions even when I'm playing different games, because any money I donate to LOTRO is a good investment
When it came out LOTRO was pretty much a WoW clone, and that disappointed me. Today it is one of the things I like about it, considering vanilla WoW was so chill. The game is built on the same solid fundamentals that took the genre to the mainstream.
The art in LOTRO is excellent. They managed to balance the realistic landscapes and characters so that even 10 years later the game looks pretty damn good, and even stunning at times. It's a lower polygon count than we're used to in 2017, and the textures won't sear your corneas, but everything feels very solid. The basic art design is excellent, and fun to look at. The landscape is beautiful, and the map is MASSIVE. From the Misty Mountains to the plains of Rohan, the places do justice to the pictures my mind rendered reading the books as a small boy.
The community is just the best in any MMO I've played, and that's just about every western MMO. I've never had anybody question my sexuality or intellectual capacity, and after like 7 years of playing I can't remember meeting a single jerk.
One of the most unique things in the game is that there are bands of players who play music at the inns, festivals, or sometimes just along the roadside. As music is central to Tolkien's world, LOTRO has the ability for players to play a broad range of instruments, playing notes either manually with the keyboard, or by loading ABC files. People get really into it with huge orchestras or just a nice little trio. I'll never forget the first time I heard the Final Fantasy 5 theme playing in an inn before I realized that this feature existed. The player-bards of LOTRO are very creative in finding new songs, and playing interesting sets. I once spent an hour listening to a group that  did all Led Zeppelin covers. Awesome. Awesome. Awesome. Once ran into a hobbit playing Leonard Cohen in the swamp at night. Was cool.
Buy this game, and support it. If you enjoy LOTR, fantasy in general, old school MMOs, or just making friends with cool people LOTRO is a masterpiece.

Masquerada has an engaging and exciting story, both heartwarming and heartbreaking moments and a cast of lovely characters. The combat is quite fun and the locations throughout the game look gorgeous.

Reviews aren't really my jam, but I like Masquerada. Disclaimer: Yeah, I backed the kickstarter.
Don't step into Masquerada expecting a Pillars of Eternity-style experience. It's very much a linear story game (if the tags don't give it away). If you're a completionist then make sure you're done with an area before moving on! Very rarely do the blue-teleporter-whatsit-circles have a return trip.
Pretty much all interaction points are coloured-whatsit-circles. General rule of thumb is yellow = key dialogue/progression or crafting, purple is optional/collectable and blue is moving to a new area. The exclamation mark on the edge of the screen points to the real quest progresser, which is good to keep in mind when there's more than one yellow point.
If you don't like Codexes then bare in mind that Masquerada really does - if you want to avoid them I'd say you can skip the lore. Towards the end of the game they start tossing extras at you that didn't fit neatly into a scene but, wahey, they wrote it, so here you go. That said, the entries are at a really nice length and I found all the Character entries particularly good reads as they're from the point-of-view of the main character, Cicero. I can't buy into lore for a world I'm not going to see but I'm always down for seeing more of a character's thoughts.
It has bugs, but none are game-breaking and no more than you'd expect. Their chapter system makes it easy to jump back if you feel you've missed something. It's an auto-save system so watch out for the notification in the bottom-left of the screen before quitting.
It's not really a micro-manager experience. I ended up sticking to one character and occassionally skipping to one of the two teammates to use certain skills, but largely I let the AI handle who to auto-attack. I've only played the game through on NORMAL (it may be very different on higher difficulties). There's a Party Behavior menu which offers some extra customisation and the Pause still came in incredibly handy. I couldn't just mindlessly send them into combat, and in the early stages of the game I felt the pain of not optimising my (then) meagre skill points.
I've only played it through once with Air where I went for teleporting around the map. This made any 1 v 1s Cicero had unintentionally hilarious. Totally winnable... if a bit slower than other playstyles. There's some depth to the combat and I didn't dig deep beyond respecs to pay better attention to Threat and Focus.
Thankfully, they introduce you to a skill-reset which you have access to in one form or another for the rest of the game. You only get enough skills points to max out a character's Passive and the 4 skills they get additional to that. There's really no point investing in more than 4 skills - you can only use 4 at the time. Experiment with what works best for you and read ahead in the skill trees to see what'll work out best. I'd reccomend making Kalden into a beefy heal tank ASAP. He's fantastic by the end of the game but my poor choices made him into floor-decor for most of the early-game.
I really enjoyed it and would buy a sequel (which they certainly set up a hook for), but I very very very much buy into story-based games. The voice-acting is stellar and really helps in that regard. It also has little snippets of non-voiced dialogue that you can find in the world, the standard "oh we're just funny little NPCs making Dragon Age references" or "we're an ongoing side story that will probably end in tragedy". I appreciate that, especially when I'd find those same NPCs later on in the game.
Don't expect any animated master pieces. When in-game visuals don't cut it for the scene they want they go for a pseudo-comic/still-frame approach instead. (You can see one in Steam's preview images.)
Give the demo a try but bear in mind that the bulk of your in-game time will be the story. Not the gameplay.

The story was decent, unfortunately the other areas got to be bad enough that I lost interest about halfway through and focused on finishing than enjoy the story.
Things I didn't like so much about the game.
-It's way too linear.  I'm a big RPG fan and in general they are linear, but this took linear to the point of dragging you around by the nose.  It's rare if there were two exits to an area.  You can pretty much only go directly to the next scene/location.
-There's no option to interact with the world. You cannot talk to a random NPC.  At all.  As much as they rarely say anything all that useful one of the things I enjoy upon going to a new town in a game is running around and hearing all the random stuff the NPCs have to say.  There is some talking in the background that helps, but it's not common.  This ties in with the previous complaint.
- Battles.  Maybe I chose a poor element, or a bad skill set up, or I'm just bad, but it felt like the best tactic for me would have been just putting the character on autopilot.  It didn't feel like I was effective at all in battle.  Also the targetting for me was a bit wonky as you both right click to target an enemy and right click to swap to an ally.  So when your ally is in melee you can accidentally swap targets instead of attacking.  I did that... a lot.  I didn't usually micromanage my allies and in general the ai was fine, but there was one boss battle where one of my allies just sat there in the middle of the map because she was too far away from my party.
- Skill points - I liked the magic in general, but the game uses on a progression based system where after certain fights/bosses you get skill points to allocate.  My issue with this is that it makes me feel like the other fights where you don't get skill points are a waste of my time that I would want to avoid, but can't.  Since I don't enjoy the battles in general this quickly made some areas feel like a slog.
- Masquerine customization.  While this seemed like a nice thing I don't think I ever once noticed the effect as they're all fairly small effects with only a chance of happening.  I'm sure it helped a lot, but it just wasn't noticeable so it kinda felt wasted.  Also the engravings could have used more variety.
- Complete lack of agency.  I've kinda already touched on this, but it just didn't feel like I got to make any real choices other than do I want to collect and read the lore/talk to my allies or not.
All in all if you enjoy a very story driven game and don't have the same issues I did with the combat you may enjoy the game, but I wouldn't recommend it to anyone without highlighting my issues with it.

This is actually my first written review, and I'm doing it as this game doesn't have many and deserves some praise.
Pros:
Visuals- everything looks beatiful and there are short comic-book like cut scenes that help add to key scenes.  Animations are simple but smooth, very pretty overall asthetic.
Characters - I don't think I've enjoyed characters so much in a game since dragon age: origins, I genuinely cared for them.  I'd say the only downside is that one of the characters seems to get a lot more character development than some of the others, he's an awsome character, but I would have liked to have seen some more of the others as well.
Combat mechanics - live action combat with tactical pause function works really well, the fights are usually pretty quick but definitely allow you to plan tactically.  There are qite a few abilities you can choose from and you can upgrade them as well.  It's done well.
Story/lore - This game has a ton of background information that you can look up in your journal as you find codex entries.  There is a lot of information that you can dig through if you want to learn more about the world but you are not forced to read it all.  The story is pretty engaging although I think I enjoyed the characters interacting with each other more than that story itself.
Cons:
Replayability: The story is predetermined, you do not actually make any choices in the game, at least choices that affect the outcome of the plot.  What you do get to choose is what type of element you want to be (earth, fire, air or water) and these do play quite differently from each other in combat with completely different skills and playstyles.  You also get to choose which companions you take with you so you can switch up your party composition.  However, the story will play through pretty much the exact same way every time you play the game.
However, my first playthrough took 12 hours, which, considering the price of the game is perfectly reasonable to me, as I thoroughly enjoyed the experienece from start to finish.  highly recommended

Firstly, this game has been sitting in my Steam library for actual years now. I kind of forgot it existed until I was doing some spring cleaning on my computer and decided I would give it a shot before just deleting it. I'm so glad I did.
The world it creates is memorable, magical and absolutely beautiful. It's sense of scale is fantastical in a way that few games can match. It tells it's story through imagery and emotion, with absolutely zero dialogue to move it along. You become attached to everything and everyone around you. You feel a sense of purpose and wonder. You want to complete this task on a personal level.
The story, even void of dialogue is one of the most thought provoking and special things I've experienced in a long time. It's rooted in fantasy but also doesn't shy away from hitting you with some incredibly gritty and dark realistic moments that life is truly all about. One minute you're experiencing something out of a Pixar film and the next is something that you could only ever beg whatever God you believe in to never experience.
From beginning to end, this game was masterful in it's execution and while the dual analog stick controls can feel frustrating at times, it also uses this to create wonderful puzzle elements and keep it simplistic enough that you only focus on your environment and the wonderful world that they've crafted.

It was an island of death; one more ship of conscripted gnomes was heading to the large outcropping of rock to re-establish Roanoake.  What was it, the fifth...sixth failed colony?  The new colonists were grim faced indeed.
Trading missions reported on the first three established outposts to find the fortress absent of life.  Known yak milk drinkers, it appeared that having comfortable beds created a shortage of fodder for the beasts, which died and caused the first brave gnomes to slowly die of thirst.  In each sucessive wave the town was  even more established, going as far as to inviting trading missions to barter for their fine lumber and trinkets.  Each time successively larger fields of grain waved in the fouled wind that carried the sweet scent of dried corpses.  The abundant grain harvests seemed to taunt the stilled gnomes as their stalks bent in the wind, chanting "race with death, pray for grain crops to feed the yaks".  How the colonists must have felt as one by one, over the course of a week, each gnome succumbed.  The last gnome died face down in the fields; the yaks long gone.  They had gambled against fate, and lost.
The fourth expedition was led by a military gnome, well trained, and well aware that securing resources were imperitive.  His attempt at a permanent settlement looked almost perfect; vast fields flush with crops, giant groves of fruit trees, industry set in an organized manner.  It looked impossible to fail...but of course it did.  The walls outside the impressive entrance were splashed with crimson gore and visible trails of blood dragged within the hold.  Following along the proud halls, the scouts came upon a first aid station and a ring of corpses, almost as if they had been engaged in a card game.  Every body was bloodless and still.  Prominently displayed by the door was a box labelled "bandages"...and it was empty except for a small paper IOU.  Sadly the gnomes didn't die from terrible injuries, but from the inability to staunch their minor wounds and they eventually succumbed.
The next expedition, forcibly sent and comprised of convicts and heretics, fared no better.  The fields and hall were strewn with corpses that appeared to have died of thirst.  A trench had been dug from the nearby mountain lake to almost the front doors of the keep, and perched on it's end was a well in all but name;  it needed but one final piece of wood to hold together and dispense life-giving water...but there was no wood for the mill, the mill couldn't make planks, and the gnomes must have been too weak to chop wood.
Naturally, the latest wave of gnomes had prayed copiously, and said goodbye to spouses and children with little expectation of seeing them again.
........
Two years later, three gnomes slowly gathered food stores and brewed beer in halls that had once been full of companions.  In the first year, the colony had been a victem of it's own success, and so many people rushed to make the town their home.  Sadly greed was on everyone's mind and most gnomes focussed on mining and making trade goods, with noone to notice that food and drink stores were nearly gone from all the extra mouths.  When the latest batch of hopeful candidates for the colony disembarked the all-too-farmiliar scene of bodies strewn about was heartrending.
Inside the colony there was one survivor, and though the body was strong, the mind had snapped.  Having discovered that with the use of a still fruit could be made into nourishing wine, the lone gnome was able to eke out a lonely existance for nearly a year alone.  Noone made any mention of the goblins and hallf dozen gnome corpses in the cold storage pantry, or that some of them had been nibbled by rats, but there were no rats to be seen.
With determination in their eyes, the newest batch of colonists took up the reins, re-started the industrial machinery, serviced the farms and started to dig a well.  But it was not to be.  Obsessed with a marble tile mosaic that the insane survivor was laying in the great hall, many gnomes stopped by and sat at the tables for hours, lost in thought as they contemplated the spiraling patterns in the stone.  Many forgot to eat, all forgot to drink.  The survivor, having finished the pattern in the floor, dropped dead in the exact center of the room.  He was ringed by a dozen corpses.
These colonists were more determined though;  they had faced goblins, hell badgers, a strange beast that assembled from ore deposits in the deep mines, famine, and thirst...always thirst.  Yet this time there were three survivors, and they were determined to hold out as long as they could, hoping for reinforcements before more goblins found out the defenses were unmanned and took the keep for themselves.
Gaunt, dark-eyed, swaying from weakness, they stirred cauldrens of mysterious meat and brewed beer to gradually restore the food stocks for the next group of foolhardy gnomes...if they ever came.  When not preparing substinance, they wandered outside like mobile scarecrows, snatching the random strawberry or apple from the ground and bringing it back inside to toss in the cauldren.
Will they hold out for help?  Only the god of gnomes could say.
