This is a thinking game.
You play the 'overseer' of a band of gnomes. You cannot control the actions of the gnomes directly, you have to assign tasks and the gnomes will complete them in order, based on the priority of their occupation and the priority of the workspace, both of which can be customized. You can trade with other nations, which show up on your Kingdom list, for things you need that you cannot produce yourself, or just choose not to produce. If your gnomes die, there is a good chance that some, if not all, will be replenished at the beginning of the next season by new immigrants from these other nations.
The first year is fairly simple, as you won't encounter too many hostile challenges unless you dig too deeply. After that, the Goblins come. Their strength is based on the value of your kingdom, so the more powerful you become, the more powerful they become. They come to slaughter your livestock, kill your gnomes, and steal whatever they can carry away... and they will love every minute they are murdering your gnomes. Building walls is no absolute security either. If they cannot find a path to your gnomes, they will employ 'diggers' after a while to get through your walls.
As if goblins were the only problem, underground you can encounter beetles which breed terrifyingly fast, zombies (which infect your gnomes!) and skeletons. Allow your food or drink stockpiles to grow too large, and the smell will attract mants, which are man-ants (gnome-sized) which will also come to steal your food, kill your livestock, and kill your gnomes if they get a chance.
To defend yourself, you can have your gnomes craft armor, weapons, traps, and even design elaborate death-traps to kill off invaders, if they work, once you have had a gnome research the tech they need. They can build practically anything out of the materials they find around, even bone can be a building or armor material.
A good game that requires almost no hand-eye coordination but a great deal of planning.

This game is fun enough, but the learning curve is super steep. There's no tutorial, so expect to dig into Youtube and/or the Steam community for how-to videos if you want to do even the most basic of tasks, like making a farm or building a wall. Once you have a handle on things, it's entertaining, but if you want something you can jump right in and play, this is not the game for you.

My first reaction when entering the game: "WTF?!"  If there was ever a game that WTF could summarize a first impression, this would be it. But not necessarily in the way one might expect.
My "WTF" moment wasn't due to anything offensive nor was it due to nonsensical or buggy content. In fact, there's nothing offensive in it, no gore, no bad language. There are  no noticeable bugs, no fps drops, no graphic glitches or crashes.  Instead, my immediate WTF reaction was due to just how bizarre and unique this game is compared to anything else I've ever played...and that's a GOOD thing.
You are one of many in an army of bunnies, attempting to cleverly outwit both other bunnies and the "master" bunny (who takes control of a giant, stationary yet deadly robot of death). The object of the match is to merely end up with more cash than your peers. You can do the master bunny's bidding and get paid for the tasks he creates to be completed or become the "master" bunny yourself and control the deathbot (which earns you cash more quickly).
Do you simply do what you are told and hope the other bunnies' greed will set them back? Do you work with a buddy to overtake the others and eventually, take control of the giant bot?  Are you willilng to backstab the others or do you insist on working as a team? Do you complete the assigned tasks to gain trust and favor from the mighty bot of doom all the while formulating and employing a master plan to overtake him and weilding the mighty power for yourself?  And if you do take control, who do you trust? Are you paying handsomely for the tasks to be completed to gain favor from your underlings even if it means they may start to catch up monetarily? Are you able to notice when a bunny starts to plot against you? Do you destroy the resistence with your mega machine gun or fry them with nepalm?  All questions that you'll be faced with in this game.
Despite it's cutesy look, it's a very deep, strategic game.
There is a lot of potential here. It's still in early access. Stability wise it seems solid. I think the tutorial could use some help as right now it's more of a text based instruction and it's difficult to remember what everything is and how to use them. There's no much in way of strategy guidance either.
The biggest criticism from me about its current state is the lack of consistent players online at any given time. The weekends seem to be more active of course, but during the week, good luck finding anyone online...at all.
I think easing new players into the game better will retain them. I think better marketing will open up the game's demographic. And if that happens, I think this little gem has the potential to be a sleeper hit.

OBEY is a very fun cooperative (or should I say uncooperative) multiplayer game. I originally had mixed feelings about this game due to a relatively poor tutorial, but once I managed to understand how OBEY is truly played, it became a blast. The two-faced style of gameplay can lead to some hilariously memorable moments. A couple words of advice before purchasing this game. The player base is still relatively small, and that is something that can only be remedied with you and your friends’ help. The purchasing format heavily discounts a 4-pack purchase. If you decide to go in on OBEY, I would recommend getting some friends in to help with a 4-pack purchase.
----11/25/2015----
There are two positions you may take part of when starting the game. You may play as a cute little bunny, scheming, plotting and looking for ways to overthrow the evil overseer controlling the robot of doom while maintaining a very obedient front in order to survive. Alternatively, you may play as the evil overseer controlling the robot of doom ensuring that those lying little devious monsters do your bidding. The main actions that the robot can take include killing the bunnies, deactivating hidden mines to help the bunnies stay alive, change pay scales in order to incentivize the bunnies to give you certain supplies (needed for ammo/security) etc. The main actions that the bunnies can perform include purchasing and feeding supplies to the robot, setting up security for the robot, warning the robot of bunnies making a break for the robot control room, or make a break for the robot control room.
Coordinating is much easier using a microphone. Although there are forms of communication without it, warning the robot of bunny locations can be difficult.
There were no noticeable bugs found in my short play through, however there are couple important suggestions I feel if implemented will help improve the gameplay.

For an early access multi-player only game, I think this game has huge potential.
There is a learning curve to understanding every concept that it throws at you. You can either play in this huge bot that can ask the bunnies running around to OBEY and trust you, so you won't shoot them. But they can also lie to you and trick you into thinking they will help you and take over the robot.
The whole goal is to get to 10,000 points, depending on how you pay out using the robot or by getting paid as a bunny on the battlefield; it can get really tricky. Using a microphone is part of getting the most out of this game, since you can talk to everyone on the server and potentionally give them tasks or they can tell you something, and bamn, they either will subvert you or go with what you ask. But only one player can win, and that is whoever achieves 10,000 points.
I recommend this game with a small con against it, it's tutorial is simple and may need more polishing and a little more handholding to give you a better understanding of the game before you start playing on a live server. It tries to break down what each mechanic does, but it's not in depth. This is a social game and you can play with bots, but the most fun is when playing with real players.
The game also has it's charm, since you can either play a bunny or a huge bot that kills the bunnies or helps them. Overall I think with some more polish on the tutorial and a bigger player-base this game has all the qualifications of a fun multi-player only game.
Also Dez (the developer) really wants to help the community either learn his game and/or get feedback to better his game and get the most out of his project. I will definitely be coming back to this game as more patches and more content gets in place. I would love to try a new tutorial when Dez has time to work on it.

OBEY is truly a great game. It has one of the best concepts in a game that I have ever seen - it just needs polishing. As with most indie multiplayer-only games (there are bots but the experience is not the same), it is often difficult to find a match when it has just joined the market recently and is early in development. But I can say the games I have played were very fun. I've only had it for 2 days and have played 10+ hours already.
The main objective of the game is to earn the most money, and whoever gets to $10000 (default) first wins the match. Each person controls a bunny, and one player controls the robot (or "robosaru"). The robot has a range of weapons and must force the bunnies to give him more ammo, more money or snitch on other players in return for cash. The robot however earns cash must more quickly and easily than the bunnies, so to prevent them form winning the bunnies must try to sneak into the robot's door and take it over without the robot noticing.
There are much more elements of this game that play large roles in deciding who wins, such as lying, deception and other psychological and game aspects.
The game has quite a steep learning curve, and the tutorial is not very clear, but the developer (who seems very nice ;) ) is often on the servers teaching people how to play and develop strategies. That's how I learnt anyway.
The game does recommend a microphone, but so far I've done quite well without using mine all the time - maybe only using it once or twice to give long commands.
One big issue I have been having is the game having a 19/20 chance of crashing when i connect to a server. This has been found to be a problem with unity and the dev says if they do not fix it soon then he will make a workaround.
Definately consider buying this game, or at least following it to see how it develops :)

I've only played a couple hours, but honestly, this game annoyed me so much, so quickly, that I doubt I'll ever play any more. I loved the original Overlord; it was charming and fun to play. But this game took the playful satire of the first game and cranked it so far up it's well beyond annoying. They took the mopey elves of the first game and turned them into the most annoying caricatures possible. Their lines and voice acting are so over the top and so exaggerated that it's not even remotely funny, just obnoxious. The formerly mostly silent minions now seem to have plenty of their own obnoxious voice overs, and they are clearly trying so freaking hard to be "quirky" that all the charm they had in the first game is obliterated.
The animations are also horrible. Every cutscene features characters snapping from odd unnatural poses to bizzare puppet-like poses constantly, completely independent of whatever they're saying or whatever else is going on. It is incredibly jarring and obnoxious to look at. Instead of a smooth flowing minion horde following you around like in the first game, your horde is now jittery and spastic, every movement being overly abrupt and poorly animated to the point that they all look like living embodiments of glitches. The AI also seems to have gotten dumber, which is sad, since the first game already had its own problems with the minions being sometimes incapable of figuring out what you're directing them to do.
If you loved Overlord, I suppose this sequel is better than nothing. But it falls short in so many areas, and seems like such a step back from the original game that I genuinely don't understand why it has such a high rating here.

Ziggurat is a major throwback to the olden days of Heretic and Hexen (two games that I absolutely love), and the game pays major homage to those golden oldie titles.  Not a bad thing.  However, the game can become very repetitive at times as you trudge your way through the same five levels over and over again.  While the level layouts and the enemies are different every time, the environments and the music stay the same through every run.  But enough of that nonsense, on to the review!
The gameplay and the controls of this game are incredibly solid.  Turning and aiming can feel very loose at first, but these settings can be changed in the options menu (and I strongly recommend turning down the default sensitivity unless you like spinning around and trying to aim until you throw up).  Other than that small starting fluke, cannot fault the gameplay at all.  Basically the player is a sorcerer-in-training that is sent to take the ultimate test!  Cue the Ziggurat!  A five floor dungeon filled with everything from giant, poison spitting mushrooms to carrots that want to tear your eyes out (along with particularly angry flamingos).
The enemies are part of what make this game great in the fact that there is a massive variety of them, especially for an indie game.  Every enemy is unique, and must be handled in a particular fashion which makes the combat very diverse and interesting.  Granted a majority of the fighting is strafing and shooting, but then the world of spells, staves, and alchemical weapons comes into play and there is no shortage of uniqueness when it comes to these either.  Whether you find the mighty Skull of Xanatos that homes in on enemies and explodes on impact, or the ever-awesome Eye of Twilight that can eradicate bosses in a single strung out volley of green power, you are unlikely to become bored while finding and trying new weapons.  Add in some big boss baddies, and you have yourself a fantastic RNG-based dungeon crawler that won't get repetitive until the 20th or 30th time you defeat the last boss (who's mother is a ♥♥♥♥♥).
Unfortunately the one minor complaint about this game is the RNG factor.  Yes, I understand it is a roguelike game so it sounds like I'm just QQ'ing, but hear me out.  The RNG factor when it comes to weapons works very well in a game like Binding of Isaac, because there is one manner of attack that can get upgraded or changed in a variety of manners.  In Ziggurat however, the player starts with a rather useless wand (on most characters) and finds different spells, staves, or alchemical weapons to dish out the real damage throughout the dungeon.  However, it is completely RNG based on what weapons will appear.  It is possible (and has happened) that in a single run, the poor wannabe sorcerer will obtain 4 alchemical weapons in a row, therefore robbing them of unique opportunities that present themselves in different rooms, and quite possibly destroying the run altogether because they were never given a spell or a staff.
The visuals in this game are top notch.  Smooth movement, no screen tearing, bright colorful environments for the most part, and incredible enemy design make this game a feast for the eyes.  Especially in a world where 2D pixel graphics have become the mainstay in a majority of roguelike indie games.  Only complaint here is that the floors are very, very similar looking when it comes to the environment.  This can get very repetitive if you decide that you love this game and want to play it a lot.  Was hoping for maybe some alternative environment designs to be thrown into the mix, but like the song goes, you can't always get what you want.
When it comes to the sound effects, this game is pretty incredible.  Everything from firing the spells, to the enemies exploding, to the lava flowing under the bridge is, for lack of a better word, awesome.  Only complaint here is the music, but I'm a big music critic when it comes to games.  The music is pretty generic and forgettable, and you'll often find yourself turning it off and listening to your own music (at least I certainly did).
Ziggurat really shines when it comes to replayability.  Tons of unlocks.  Perks, spells, staves, alchemical weapons, and a plethora of characters that are all somehow very unique.  Throw in a bunch of achievements and you'll end up dropping a lot of hours into this one.
TLDR: Game is definitely worth your time and money.  Great gameplay, unique weapons, characters, and enemies, make this game a must-buy.  Oh and did I mention the developer is very active in the forums?  Replies to just about everybody in a very friendly, helpful manner and is STILL updating the game with new stuff every few months.  Much respect for professionalism and dedication.  SUPPORT THIS DEV!

If the discussion and critique swirling around DE:MD had any upside, it's that I was able to pick up the game at a decent discount in late 2016. Getting a Deus Ex fix without breaking my budget definitely sweetened things (games are expensive here in NZ), but I found the game a pleasant surprise. I only wish there were more of it, in this game, and in the next.
DE:MD contains one of the more complicated set of story threads I can remember encountering in a game, which can make it a bit challenging to jump into from the beginning. Some reading around the game informs me that the beginning is kinda sorta not exactly the beginning of protagonist Adam Jensen's story since the end of the last game, but I found myself able to follow the major plot points developed in DE:MD without needing the additional backstory from the books and comics. Your mileage may vary, of course, but by the end I was eagerly anticipating the continuation of the story.
Set in 2029, the game centres around Prague, a city wracked by anti-augmented tensions, and where the highly augmented Adam Jensen is now located as part of Interpol Task Force 29. Both as a story hub and gameplay space, Prague provides plenty of mysteries to solve and secrets to discover between main missions. I absolutely recommend you aim to follow and complete as many of the side quests as possible, as some of them explore elements of Deus Ex's augmented future not touched by the main plot. I spent plenty of time between main missions crawling through Prague's hidden corners, and the developers have ensured these kinds of forays are rewarded. Throughout the game you will find a huge amount of background details, flavour text, and mysteries in various reading material scattered around the world. The decision to focus so much of DE:MD in one place is a departure from Human Revolution, but you may find that in this city, not everything is as it seems.
Running a stealth (well, mostly) playthrough, I found the gameplay to be compelling and engrossing. Even among the game's weaker elements, playing as Adam Jensen always convinced me of DE:MD's reality as I utilised Jensen's cybernetically enhanced capabilities to traverse the environments and infiltrate enemy installations. New, more advanced experimental augmentations add new gameplay elements here. I came to rely in particular upon the remote hacking skill, triggered on valid targets by a timed button press minigame, which becomes surprisingly challenging when trying to avoid detection or bullets. But there are always other options depending on which approach you favour, and depending on which augmentations you've prioritised. The somewhat more forgiving energy system adopted in this game also helps, and will be familiar to players of Dishonoured. Minus the activation cost, energy will recover to previous levels after using augmentations, but regen is cancelled by the use of any other energy consuming abilities.
Less convincing, at times, were the conversations I engaged with other characters. Some encounters involve negotiating or persuading other characters through dialogue choices. At least Eidos avoided the trap of vague dialogue wheels, as all of Jensen's responses are written out for clarity in tone and intent upon mouseover. However, the responses of at least one character during these moments  gave me a distinct sense of the recording booth. Depending on your dialogue choices, their reactions can swing wildly in different emotional directions if you subsequently adopt a different tone in the next wheel of choice. The sudden and jarring shift broke the social simulation that these characters were actually talking to each other. For most of the important characters at least, these aren't issues.

If you're on the fence, my advice is to give DE:MD the benefit of the doubt. I thoroughly enjoyed exploring almost every inch of the game Eidos created, only to go wiki-hopping afterwards and learn I'd still managed to miss quite a few things. I only hope this isn't the last we see of Eidos' work on Deus Ex.

The problem with Warlock 2 is not that it's a bad game; rather, it doesn't add enough to justify the 'sequel' tag and $30 price point.  Exiled mode is merely a focused string of 'pocket dimensions' (that already existed in the first game) in a campaign format -- no more innovation than the Armageddon mode for Warlock 1.  The other improvements and additions are arguably ones that should have been included in a patch or, at most, a $10 DLC.  Unrest is the only truly new mechanic and its implementation is primarily intended to cap the number of cities you can build.  This ultimately has little bearing on the game as you can win on even the hardest difficulty with a few lords and a couple of complimentary units.
The Great Mage edition for $50 is particularly laughable as it merely adds a few lords I've never even seen in 30+ hours of play, a few spells I've never bothered to cast, and a dragon mage hero that doubles as a capital -- the latter being the only one I'd recommend buying separately for a couple of bucks.  The other extras are a bunch of out-of-game materials most people won't listen to/read.
Edited: And now in the recent patch they've added an in-game store selling things like the privilege of starting on a certain plane/shard for $3.  Warlock 1's Armageddon DLC cost the same and added a new mode.  The Elf DLC added a new race for the same price.  Paradox is definitely on the decline with all these cash grabs.

If you haven't played Warlock before, it's a Civilizations-style 4X strategy game set in a fantasy world, streamlined to require less micromanagement than Civ, but with a healthy dose of wild, interesting monsters and extra worlds in each game to place emphasis on exploration and colonization over internal economic management.  In my opinion, it plays faster than Civ at the expense of some depth, but makes up for that depth with rich, large worlds and a wide range of gameplay options on the combat level.
If you have played Warlock before, then Warlock 2 is pretty much exactly what you want in a sequel.  The Exile campaign mode sets players on exterior shards in a labyrinthine web of interesting miniature worlds to fight your way to the central hub world and beat the AI-controlled boss for control - which is interesting and compelling, if surprisingly difficult.  The new worlds add a wide variety of resources, monsters, and terrain to the game, which was not lacking in the first game but is a welcome addition.  Furthermore, the number of playable races has practically doubled, offering a great deal of replay value and a ton of new options for tech trees and internal management as you expand your empire to include a wider variety of creatures and troops.
On the downside, the game discourages vast empires with a city limit - which does prevent turns from going too long - but that option can be turned off on the menu.  Resources for creature upgrades are now limited to a set number of uses per resource, but that works as an incentive to do more exploration and expansion.  On the truly minor gripe level, the achievements are a bit glitchy at time of writing, but I suspect they'll be repaired in due time.
In short, Warlock 2 is a solid improvement on the already-solid Warlock formula.  If you're a Warlock fan, you should absolutely make the investment; if you're a Civilizations fan or a strategy fan, you should definitely try it out.

Warlock 2 and Its predesesor, Warlock Master of the Arcane, are among the best games that I have played on any platform. Having logged inumerabe hours in Civilization, the granddaddy of turn based strategy games, I actualy tjhink I prefer Warlock. Perhaps it is because the units in Warlock have more personality, thus I feel more emotionally invested in them.
A couple things  that I love about Warlock...
1. The controls are silky smooth and emipire management is simple and easy to deal wiith compared to any other TBS game I think of. Each turn icons representing different types of actions cascade down the right side of your screen- at least that is what they did in Master of the Arcane. In Warlolck 2 you have to expand a single action button to see the colulmn of icons- I prefer the icons in the previous game. In any event, management of your cities and units is quick and efficient- you are prompted to make decisions so there is no reason you will forget something important, allowing  to concentrate on strategy. Battles are on the campaign hex map and not on a separate battle screen.
2. The random map generator does a great job of changing things up. As in CIV you set the parameters, and the random geography created will have a huge impact on gameplay. Thus each camapign feels unique and replayability is thru the roof.
Comparing Warlork 2 to Warlock Master of the Arcane, they are virtually the same game with a couple races added, some new rules and options. They also added a spell tech tree which is an improvement. Master of the Arcane DLC was inexpensive and greatly enhanced the Warlock experience- the Dremor DLC was mind blowingly challenging, but I was up for the challenge- so I will expect the same from Warlock 2. Yes! Warlock 2 is worth the $30 price tag. How could I think not since it is one of my favorite games ever?

***There are no spoilers; only a full review of what I took from this game. ***
I do recommend this game. The 16.4 hours is what it took to complete it. But honestly I approve this purchase only for the quality voice acting and storyline put together in a graphic audiobook format. The gameplay, on the other hand is severly lacking.
The voice actors I was already fans of.  Brought from both the Geek & Sundry (how I found out about this game) and Nerdist websites the actors give depth to the characters to build the connection throughout.  If you are looking for a decent written story set in a graphic novel theme you will come to the right place...
But if you are looking for a game similar to a Dragon Age or Mass Effect...disappointment will follow you.
The art is beautiful. Designers took time making the city this takes place in. Its definately fantasy by nature and beautiful nonetheless.
Don't expect to explore it though. This game is STRICTLY linear in a isometric POV. One path to follow (albeit one section deviates from this) from beginning to end. There is no interaction with the environment, except buckets of fruit you can kick around. Principle charcters are set to move the game forward. All the other NPCs are there for show. Some will have bubbles over their head in conversations with others talking about what's going on and you will have to stop your running (there is no walk) to read these bubbles which will distract from the play because they will go on for a bit. Safe to ignore unless your goal is to read everything......because that in itself is a chore.
PREPARE TO READ A LOT. Codexes for backstory and history, characters, settings. Almost everything has a codex, set in a way that is so distracting from what you were doing that you might forget what you were doing before you decided to read the entry (some are extensive in text).  Except for the character codexes I pretty much ignored the rest of it, but you might get upset if you don't get all of them. They sit in the path so easily seen (for the most part),  I honestly wondered how I missed a few (which also ruins an achievement). The codexes are designed to enrich the story, but it becomes very tedious and doesn't effect the current events because...
...the story is already written for you.  There are times in the dialogue where there are choices present (making you wonder in a Dragon Age sort of way if I choose this what will happen) but in this reality only one choice exists and the other...is why there are checkpoints. So there are no player choices to worry about. Whatever control scheme you choose just button mash to glory (with some battle strategy mixed in) because even though there are skill trees and inks and such all the characters and all the skills really do the same thing:  to get you moving with the story (the difficuly does spike at times making the use of ill-placed checkpoints and restarts a chore but trial-and-error will rue the day).  Speaking of spoken dialogue...they are ALL TEXT-BOXES. I found myself closing my eyes and listening or lowering the scale of the GUI because they were so distracting. Reading along to spoken texts is OK when its paced right. This isn't that. I found I sped up the dialogue in places because I read faster than they did (which I think ruins other achievements as well).  But the character animation is also these boxes (which they did a real good job with the sync), so having an option to remove these from play removes a lot of design (and so the option doesn't exist).
The music reminded me of 2 things...1. Final Fantasy where the music never stops and doesn't match the situation (most of the time) and 2. That Knight Rider made-for-TV  movie with the mall chase scene where this calming soothing music existed instead of exciting get-you-pumped music (to this day I still wonder why).  I turned off the music because I found it distracring but then turned it on because silence during scenes needing music is even more distracting.
With all this you could be asking yourself "he's recommending this?" The combat isn't satisfying. The lack of environment depth (you will feel compeled to roam and be saddened with the waste of time). The tedious reading and visual distractions that take you away from the story and gameplay...
But the story IS awesome. The dialogue and the voice acting DO bring to life this story. You will laugh. You may tear a little. You will feel connected even if the try of backstory and history is forced.  If you are anywhere familiar with the voice actors you will smile with the knowing "it was her" or "that was amazing".
There is minimal replayability. If you are a completionist and didn't get all the achievements the first time you may go back but for as rail-linear as it is and all the chapters to choose from, getting those last few codexes isn't worth the extra time IMO. Even though it crashed on me twice near the end (restarting the game fixed both) I felt satisfied and not-at-all cheated. I adjusted how I played and thought less comparing it to another game I was used to.
Is it worth the price? I paid $25. For the quality acting and artwork it is.  But with the lack of player involvement in the direction (think any game where it shows you a button to press to survive peril) of the game, it would probably sell better as a graphic audiobook.
There is no surprise why the file size is so big. There are a ton of voices and its visually appealing.
But, unless the story plot draws a hectic situation, there really isn't a sense of dread or peril to rush for anything from a player standpoint. It is a very-elaborate storytelling game.
I don't regret buying this....(The quality is there. It just could have been so much more.)...
but you might.

Saw this at GameStart 2016 and was immediately hooked by the prologue (and the fact that the creative director promised that I'll cry many times in this game). I cried, 3 times, but I won't reveal where. I'm not even much of a sentimentalist but their writer has a way with knowing when to squeeze your tear ducts, punch you in the gut, and choke your trachea.
The first half is a little sloggish as there is quite a learning curve in picking up the terminology related to the lore of Ombre. But once I had party members recruited, I was well acquainted by then. I also really enjoy the pacing at which these lores get revealed, so it doesn't feel like an information dump all at once. With that said, I'm the kind of person that can enjoy a wall of text, but not others. I get the feeling that you might miss the immersion if you decide to skip the text though.
The second half of the story picks up the pace of the story as you're hit by how much bigger the investigation has become. Many characters will die, and it sucks because through the game you'd actually grow close to them before their untimely demise.
I share the grievances of your AI doing some pretty stupid things. This is evident mostly in difficult boss fights where they go ahead and run up to get themselves killed, so micromanagement is necessary when faced with a tough foe. There was also an instance where near the end of the game the program crashes, so I had to restart the entire battle. This is frustrating because everything is only via autosave.
However, I do like the simpler skill tree system and equipping with different masks and boosts, as opposed to most RPGs with an inventory system and leveling up. It's different, and takes away some elements of the classic RPGs, but it allows for more of the story to seep through.
I'll eventually return to the game to fill up the codex entries. The missing ones are bugging me :P

To keep this short and to the point, I would wholeheartedly recommend this game.
Story- The story that Masquerada brings starts rather slow, but amps up to become a very engaging and satisfying story. The world created  in Masquearada contributes to making the story so great. To truly experience the world and story of Masquerada, I would implore any would-be players to pick up and read every codex entry they find. Than you can thank me later.
Characters- You start the main game as Cicero Gavar, an exiled inspettorre who's called back to his home city of Ombre. There he is given the task to search for a missing scholar of the city he once called home. Along the journey you pick up companions, face villains, and meet important figures of the city. I can honestly say that every character I came into contact with was memorable. The voice acting of the characters helps make them so memorable. I can say that i definitely had my favorites, but they were all good. It's been a while since last I played a game where I hated some characters not because they were badly written, but because they had done something ingame that I did not agree with or offended the main character in some way. Slight spoiler: the dual with a figure head of the city was so satisfying... I wanted to bash the guy's head in since the first time he was introduced lol.
Gameplay- The gameplay is essentially a linear rpg. You start the game by picking one of four elements to play throughout the game: fire, water, air, or earth. Each element has abilities that allow it to tank, dps, support, and cc, so I would recommend chosing whatever element is your favorite. Along your journey, you pick up companions, one for each of the elements. You chose 2 of them to go on missions with you, and sometimes 1 is a must-go due to story reasons. People complain of the combat, but I found it enjoyable and satisfying. Let me preface this and say that I played on the hardest difficulty. Fights were definitely hard, but they were not impossible. Whenever I found myself taking multiple tries to get past a battle, it was always due to my strategy rather than the game being unfair. The enemies do hit hard, but you cannot just rush in and button mash your way to victory. Placement, comboing abilities, cc'ing enemies, enemy prioritization, reading of enemy tells, and use of pause are all key to beating this game on hard. Once I got the hang of things and realized the flow of combat, I found it to be very enjoyable.

If you're reading this, you are likely apprehensive about this game's free to play status. But there really isn't any reason to be. Although there are microtransactions, this game couldn't be further from the pay to win formula.Virtually everything can be purchased via microtransaction, and paying with real world cash really only advantages you if you want cosmetic items.
Every week a set of six characters will become available to play for free, and these are the ones you'll be playing as if you're just starting and don't want to spend any money. As aforementioned, characters can be bought outright with real money, but they can also be bought with a large sum of in game currency. After every match the players are awarded a small amount of gold and bonus gold can be obtained by completing daily missions, by participating in weekly game modes, and even by logging in daily. Once you have a few thousand gold you can buy a character to own from then on. This might seem skewed against those that don't want to pay, but the way the game is designed actually discourages buying characters outright. First of all every character only has six signature moves. Every other move is shared by some, or all other fighters. This means that the differences between characters is often infinitessimal. If you're anything like me you'll probably take a liking to one or two legends, spend your gold on them within the same week, and then start buying other legends simply because its the only thing you can do with your gold. Throw in the fact that you can try any character in training mode before you buy, and you have very little reason to spend a cent.
On the other hand, this also makes the game a lot less interesting than it could be. Most other games claiming to fighters have characters with apparent differences, and every character seems deep enough that they could take years to master. In this game almost every character feels the same, and I can dominate free for alls and 1v1s with relative ease after playing a legend for an hour. For that reason I usually log in for the daily bonus, finish my missions, and logout. To be fair the game is fun in short bursts, but I think I would want much more if it wasn't free.
If you still have doubts, just play the game. It's free, it doesn't take up much disk space, you can run it on almost anything, and its fairly fun.

This game. It's...well it's different. If you like survival games then you should enjoy the bleak atmosphere and setting, but as the levels aren't massively open world, looking for supplies only requires you to take the less obvious route to your goal.
Gunplay (and later on, arrow play) requires thinking and timing, as you only have 1 bullet vs 4 enemies at many points in the game. Again this adds a survival aspect to the game. If you are a fan of bleak miserable stories, then also conisder buying this game. It is one of the few arcade games that actually has a decent story.
The thing this game is probably most well known for, and hated for, is the retry system. You pick up "retries" through the game by helping people, (by giving them your supplies) or just finding them lying about. Retries basically let you start from last saved checkpoint. Out of retries? Then you will have to start that level that you have been playing for an hour all over again. It's quite similar to Dead Space 2's Hardcore mode, where you only get a few saves (albeit not as harsh).
The last gameplay element I will look over is the most important, and may influence you buying it. The stamina bar. The stamina bar is used up for almost anything except walking. It regenerates very quickly but only when walking. If you are halfway up a building, you can't just stop and rest, you either use up precious supplies, or die. When your stamina bar is empty you enter a mode called "extreme effort" which lets you push on through whatever you are doing (climbing, walking through dust clouds etc.) but then actually drains the capacity of your bar, which means less stamina regenerates each time you rest. This therefore, means climing is more supply dependant, unless you refill your bar to full capacity. For people who tend to not think things through before doing something, this game will not be for you. Unless you don't mind starting a level over every time you die.
I played the game on the hardest difficulty from the outset and have only died 5 times between level 1 and 11, so it is easily done.
In conclusion, this game I recommend on sale, as it only lasts about 5 hours but the story and satisfaction of surviving will make sure you do not regret the price.

This is a very unique multiplayer game. You are a bunny, that is trying to gain control over a huge dictating robot on the map. Once in control you try to convince other "bunnies" (players) to follow your orders. You win by collecting the most money.  But beware for some bunnies might disobey you and will try to take control over the robot themselves, so be on your guard.
Any bunny can take control over the robot, by just entering the front door, but when you control the robot, you have a few weapons at hand to protect yourself, like a flamethrower, sentries and a minigun. The downside is that other bunnies supply you with ammunition for these weapons.
It doesn't mean that you can only win the game by entering the robot, you can even win by never setting foot in it, by cleverly picking what materials to deliver to the feed box. Not every player that controls the robot is vicious or cruel, some might rule with a benevolent spirit and choose to share the wealth with the hardworking bunnies. That's what makes every game completely different and utterly fun.

Early Access Review, 11/21/15
Unusual multiplayer game featuring diplomacy and negotiation alongside stealth and strategy.  Conversing with your opponents is practically required, so beware purchasing if your rig lacks a mic or you don't enjoy, you know... talking.  Otherwise, have fun playing as Little Bunny FooFoo hopping through the forest, jumping into the giant killer robot of doom and extorting money and guns from all your little bunny friends via bribery and threats of flamey death!
OBEY is a remarkably strange, fascinating game with a steep learning curve.  The tutorial is an absolute must, and even that doesn't cover all the tactics involved - although hopefully this will be improved before the game's final release.  The game is also multiplayer only, so if you prefer sticking to single player games, you can skip this game (and the rest of this review).
Remember those "friendly"(ha!) tabletop sessions of Risk where you tried to convince good ol' Bob spread across Asia that it was completely in his own interest to invade Canada in order to wipe out Evil Overlord Fred, all while you hunkered down in Austraila peacefully hoarding billions of troops to win you the game a few turns later?  Or that one game of Monopoly where you convinced your little sister that giving you a monopoly on Boardwalk and Parkplace in return for Reading Railroad would actually win HER the game in the end?
Well, OBEY is just that; a game of dirty diplomacy and friendly manipulation.  In OBEY, your goal as a tiny, cute little bunny rabbit is to take control of a giant deadly robot with laser-eyes and a flamethrower, then somehow convince all the other tiny, cute - and extremely treacherous - little bunny rabbits that feeding you the money you need to win and the weapons you need to kill them dead is definitely a good idea.
The gameplay smushes together stealth, observation, strategy, and game theory into a 3D world populated by you and all your bunny rabbit friends waddling slowly around and trying to make money, along with one giant killer robot with laser eyes of doom who can make money faster than anyone.  The robot can be taken over by anyone who sneaks inside, but it can also lay the smack down on any bunny who twitches their nose the wrong way -, or 'generously' pay an allowance to the bunnies who play nicely.   To win, you must pay close attention to your surroundings and what every other player is up to, negotiate with - and lie to - other players , and above all not aggravate the giant robot with laser eyes of doom before you can shuffle your cuddly little bunny butt inside to kick out the current occupant and take it over.
All in all, if you have a microphone and sometimes like thinking, strategizing, and negotiating in your games instead of the usual run-n-gun, I recommend you give this quirky game a shot.  However, this comes with a strong 'buyer beware': as with any multiplayer game, enjoyment depends on the people you play with, so you will need to bring friends or be OK relying on random strangers (who hopefully speak your language and have mics of their own).
---
Note:   Due to the social nature of the game, you may want to split a 4-pack with friends.  If that doesn't work for you, at least the developer seems to be quite active and doing his best to help people learn the game, so it seems likely that even games with strangers will be fun.   Of course, keep in mind that OBEY is in Early Access, so it is difficult to tell how popular it will be down the line, and how easy it will be to find quality random matches.  Thus, your final mileage may vary.
Note 2:  The giant killer robot of doom may not actually have laser eyes.  But it should.

I guess it may resemble arena games a little; the game requires a mix of social skills, strategy and decision making, although a bit of luck won't hurt.
In this game, you're mostly a small rodent - except when you aren't. Your purpose in the scary little world you're in is to follow orders - except when you'd rather not. Sounds a little confusing I suppose. But basically you could be an obedient little worker bee and keep big brother happy, or you could pretty much do anything you want as long as you don't get caught. Talking to the other players in this game is a big part of the experience, and the push to talk and push to mute options built into the game work very nicely. The atmosphere created by the dark environment, the flood lights, and the rodents fragility is Orwellian, I found myself thinking about old school Sci-Fi books. The Robot is a lot like big brother, something in the game also kept making me think of Asimov, though I'm not sure what. On the whole the game is very good at pulling you in, just alt tabbing from it feels like you're going to another world.
That said, it's not easy figuring out what you want to do in the game, and if you ignore the tutorial like I did (you really shouldn't), you'll just find yourself working like an obedient little sheep, and you'll miss out on all the hidden little things you can in the game. (Tip: try crashing the carrier, the little marshmallow in a campfire explosions are worth it)
Techinically the game has a goal and a win condition, but it's not enforced, and I like that.

This game, as I'm sure is well advertised, is a more approachable take on the Dwarf Fortress formula.  Think Minecraft meets the Sims, but instead of a house, you build a small settlement (or a huge sprawling, multi-level fortress that goes 40 stories below the earth).
+Begin with a small group of workers with various skills.
+Assign them tasks, giving priority or preference to those you deem more vital.
+Watch them execute the tasks and make logical adjustments, altering terrain and tasks to meet needs.
+Harvest resources, build structures, and defend your settlement until new immigrants arrive.
+Defend against enemies, both natural and fantastical, preparing your workers through acquisition of resources, trading, and training their skills.
+Workers get better at tasks the more often they do them, with each having their own hunger, thirst, and stats. Can change occupations or create your own custom classes using a system of priorities for each task (Agriculture, Smithing, Mining, etc).
It's one of those games you begin at 1800 and take a break, check the clock, and curse the fact that somehow it's now 0600 the next day and you only get 2 hours to prep for work.  Strongly recommended for weekend play only!
Developer is regularly updating this game, putting it beyond the immediate competition in that regard.  Given time, it could rival the Hallowed DF in terms of content, but for now it merely noses past by a slight margin due to graphical and interface simplicity that make it a joy instead of a chore (sorry, DF, but you are a bit on the exclusive side).
Strongly recommended to fans of simulations, creative world-builders, and hoarders.

Let's get this out of the way. Is Gnomoria a good game? yes. Should you play Gnomoria right now? not unless you're exceptionally talented with city simulation games.
In case any person reading this review somehow missed it, as of this review, Gnomoria is still an Early Access game. As such, the game is not feature complete. One of those missing feature is a comprehensive tutorial. That's right, gamers have to learn everything the game have to offer through trial and error. Which I can imagine being a barrier for anyone who lacks experience with this genre. Most of the game's core feature seems to be there already. And my only problem with the game so far is that my control over my gnomes is somewhat looser than I'd like; the game's control revolves around this priority system. Which sounds like you can tell a Gnome what's important and what's not; but the problem seems like either the Gnome doesn't always listen, or the command take quite a few hours (in game time) to take effect. Once I have several wounded combatant bleeding all over the place (which is so ridiculous that it's actually quite ammusing to watches my Gnome nonchalantly going about his business while his arterial spray hastily colored my kindom red like his life depends on it, WHICH IT IS!!!), but even though I hastily push the priority of hospital to the top of priority list for several workers, and made sure someone produced several bandages, those two workers still bleed to death anyway. Another issue I saw so far is the lack of assignment for certain post such as grove, which made it that much harder to micromanage you kingdom. But enough of my complain, let's get down to the pros and cons:
Pros:
-Visually appealing graphics.
-Birds eye view with option to rotate camera and ascend/descend height is the ideal choice for camera control.
-Can build structure of any size and shape, then define it's use.
-Multiple combination of meterial and product, i.e: can build chair from 4 different type of wood.
Cons:
-Lacking a proper tutorial.
-Background music is present but lacks variety (only classic, and orchestrated).
-AI either broken, or intentionally difficult to control.
-Player controls the task, but not the worker. Which makes it hard to rush urgent job at a moment notice.
-texture of stone is too dark, making it hard to see underground when all the blocks blended into a grey mesh.
Score: 8/10

Dead Space 2 is one of my favorite games of all time, and with good reason. Nowadays there seems to be a popular trend in horror games to make the protagonist a twinkle-toed pansy with a simple flashlight, or a photo of their missing loved one as the only weapon. Sometimes they make it scary just by making the control scheme so terrible that you feel like you're playing hog-tied and with oven mitts on. While there is no doubt at all that it creates more tension when you're forced to run and hide, or have limited ammo, that's not really what I'm interested in doing. When I play a horror game, I want to single-handedly annihilate the enemy scourge, while still feeling a steady level of tension. This game nails both aspects perfectly. The combat is amazingly fluid, which is so much more than you can say about many horror titles. When you die, it's because you screwed up, not because the controls were designed to make you fail. Also, few things are as satisfying as prying off a razor-sharp limb from one enemy, only to use it like a rail gun to impale another against a wall.
There is no real shortage of health or ammunition, weapons are upgradeable to the point of being ridiculous, and your character is sufficiently badass. Yet despite all this, you can't help but feel genuine psychological terror throughout most of the experience. Your character Isaac feels distinctly human, and is clearly haunted by the recent traumatic events in his life, losing his grip with reality more and more as you progress through the story. The environments are meticulously detailed and fit perfectly in what you may expect from a futuristic space station, such as the equivalent of a Scientology church, a daycare facility, a shopping mall, etc. Even though it is ultimately a linear experience, it is so well done that you wouldn't want it to be any other way.
The weapon upgrade system is also so well done that it easily lends itself to multiple playthroughs, and I really wish the system was more common in other games, regardless of the genre. In short, it is impossible to upgrade all your weapons to max in a single playthrough, but you are able to carry their current level straight through to the next. This means you could easily do 2-3 playthroughs before your favorite weapons are maxed, and 5-6 before all the weapons in the game, including your rig, are maxed out completely.
All in all, if you are a fan of the horror or sci-fi genres, you can't miss this. I would be hard-pressed to find too many cons, although admittedly there were some parts I liked more than others. In the end, though, you realize that you could easily start a new game immediately after finishing the last, and that's always a good sign for any video game. Dead Space 2 was so good that it led EA to eventually hyper-commercialize and ruin the franchise, but that's not saying much since they ruin everything they touch.

Mankind Divided is a clunky game should be titled Human Revolution 2. If you're looking for more Deus Ex and more of the Human Revolution story and gameplay then by all means, buy this game.
However if you're looking for something that pushes the gameplay of Deus Ex forward or advances the narrative in a meaningful way then feel free to give Mankind Divided a pass. It's a nice looking game but the gameplay is IDENTICAL to Human revolution with a few more augs added, most of which honestly add nothing new. PRO TIP: get remote hacking, it's the one truly good new thing.
I appreciate what the devs were doing trying to tell a more focused, localized story but honestly I found it boring and muddy. Lots of new questions are asked and never answered in a frustrating way. There's only one major environment in this game too, Prague. The city of Prague is extremely detailed but obnoxious to travel around and there's not a whole lot to find and do in it. You go to a few other locations for single missions but they're all WAY simpler than in previous games.
Mankind Divided was also unstable and buggy for me. I regularly had hangups on game/level loads, crashes, and the sound would disappear requiring a full restart. I also don't recommend trying DirectX 12 mode with a 900 seires nVidia card as it didn't work at all for me.
tl;dr - Mankind Divided is a poor major entry in a series where up until now ever big sequel has done something truly new. It's buggy and tells a boring story and is functionally identical to Human Revolution. Play if you want more Deus Ex, skip if you're on the fence.

It's alright....
In all seriousness though, this MMORPG is great, even through it's ups and downs. The main quest is captivating and emotional in places, the end game content tends to be difficult (not always, but we'll discuss that at a later point), and the graphics hold up nicely for being a 2007 MMO release, and now that we're starting to see the effects of the transition away from Turbine, I thought I'd give you a reveiw to read.
****DISCLAIMER****
My Steam hours are not an accurate reflection of the actual time spent in game! I have more than whatever it's showing right now! Also much of this will be subjective.
****End Disclaimer****
THE BAD
Lets start out with the bad because that's where this tale begins, but please keep reading through this section and onto the good, because this game is a flawed gem.
To begin with, the game has one major flaw that is, for the most part, the cause of all others: It's engine is absolutely ancient. The game started development way back in very early 2000s, with a set release date of 2004, and a title of Middle Earth Online, but after many delays, and several major reworks of the entire game, it was released as The Lord of the Rings Online in 2007. The game still uses many of the same assets from it's early development (which is actually incredible as they don't look that old... Ok they've aged, but they're not the worst assets we've seen from that era), and the engine is being pushed to it's absolute limits, both in terms of graphically, and in terms of scripting and coding. What this translates out to is lag. For about the first 60 levels, you won't run into too much lag however, but after that, it starts getting progressively worse. Riders of Rohan, released at the level cap of 75 and raising it to 85, did a massive number on the game. With the introduction of Warsteeds and mounted combat, the engine was pushed to it's breaking point; it wasn't designed to handle people moving at the speed of a warsteed (not sure on the exact stats, but it's faster than a normal mount) and combat at the same time. Rubber banding, lag, and a plethora of other issues popped up, and couple that with Warner Bros. making the game change direction, and not letting Turbine fix the issues that needed fixing, and you get a hot mess. An enjoyable mess (imho), but a mess none the less. The endgame was a fight against RNG, raiding was dead, the hard core playerbase started leaving the game for FFXIV. It was a mess, and then came Helm's Deeps to add more oil to the fire. The Helm's Deep expansion (released at the 85 cap, raising it to 95) contained many massive changes, some for the better some for the worse, most prominent among these were the total lack of captivating endgame content, and the Trait system overhaul. Raiding was replaced by Epic Battles; laggy, boring, and extremely repetitive with hardly any challenge. This was the new endgame. The Trait system overhaul is more complex and I will discuss that below, but it was a two edged sword with both good changes and bad changes. During this expansion came a mass migration of Raiders leaving the game for FFXIV or WoW, and the hardcore playerbase virtually dried up. The already shrinking subscriber count fell throught the floor, leaving only the loyal hardcore Tolkien fans. The Lag was getting worse, the quests were (and still are) bland.
Then came the Western Gondor update....
THE GOOD
Update 14 rolled out, and for the first time in the game, we were setting foot on Gondorian soil. New gearing mechanics, new dailies that were challenging and required a group, and a return to the more traditional zone building. This is the turning point in the game. The lag in the new zones, while present, wasn't nearly as bad, they looked amazing, the new gearing system was unique and, for the most part, fun. There was also a 5 level increase to make the cap 100, along with many smaller changes. Update 15 rolled out with several new zones, a new Epic battle (this one offensive and not defensive, which is more fun), new emotes, and several new cities. The lag was still present, but Turbine was getting back into the swing of things. We were going through iconic locations, experiencing Aragorn's story, and while fun, it was too small of a content update. Then came update 16: Ashes of Osgiliath, with a return to challenging endgame dungeons, a new weapon system that while not perfect, is better than what we had. The White City visible in the background, we marched through Osgiliath, and onto update 17 and the Siege of Minas Tirith. This update brought many new problems to the table, with a memory leak bug that causes a major crashing problem, and heavy lag in Minas Tirith (understandable however due to the size and design of Minas Tirith; it's almost impossible to optimize the place properly). Then came The battle of the Pelennor Fields, and with it, a new and challenging raid. The story reached a new height here. Then came the march of the King with update 19, with the story progressing forward, new gear, new regions, followed by update 20 and the battle of the black gate with it's climactic battle.
So now that this brief history has been stated, why did I split it up? Well simply put, ever since update 14, the game has been moving forward and getting better and better, and while the lag is still present, the new developers, Standing Stone Games, is actively working on it, to the point where they are trying to get a 64 bit version of the game working. The dev team is passionate about the game again, and it's showing. The love they have poured into the game shows with every little detail. So now that that's out of the way, do I reccomend you play it? Yes! If your a Tolkien fan, then it's a double yes!
So lets now turn our gaze onto the stuff that matters; the stuff you'll run into if you play this game.
Starting off this game is like any other MMO, with a more fleshed out world. You have your basic stats, hot bars, skills, gear, inventory. It's essentially a WoW clone in this aspect. Then you run into one of the changes I mentioned earlier; at level 5 you unlock your skill trees.
SKILL TREES AND THE TRAIT SYSTEM CHANGES
Skill Trees weren't always a thing in LotRO. In fact, up to Helm's Deep, the games traiting system was entirely unique. You did deeds (read acheivments), usually to the tune of "Use [Skill] X times." The number ranged greatly, but generally speaking it fell between 100-400 times depending on how core of a skill it was. The reward for these deeds was a Trait which modified that skill, or provided some bonus to a certain play style to which that skill was core (I.E. "Use Relentless Strike 200 Times" unlocked a trait that changed it to Remorseless Strike which hit harder). These traits further had quote unquote "set" bonuses (IE if you slotted two yellow line champion traits, Swift Strike would change to Swift Blade). This was changed in Helms Deep to be more accessible to newer players. This was a double Edged sword, as the original trait system was more customizable than the Skill trees, but they gave new players a better and more visible sense of progression. Some classes also fared much worse than others with the system change, with certain classes becoming blatantly overpowered and some being nerfed into the ground. This has been addressed, and all classes are more or less viable now. However, much of the uniqueness of the classes was destroyed. That being said, I do see the good in the changes, but I still begrudge them.
STATS
Why on earth would I need to discuss stats? Well, other than to say that there has been no need for a stat squish in 10 years and 105 levels.... *glares at Blizzard* Other than that... Stat's are normal and simple enough to understand. Math comes into play at endgame.

I love the original but the problem here is this feels like paying again for the exact same game. Put it in sandbox mode and you would be very hard pressed to tell the difference looking at it. This should have been an expansion. £44.99 for the base game and 0 day dlc..... It staggers my mind.

This is a fun game to a shortened extend. At first it seems really neat to play a civilization styled game with fantasy elements such as having hero units with great power, gearing them with artifact gear, and even casting spells as a great mage. However, as a game progresses there are a few definite faults. The most prominent of such is having an "optimum city limit". A mage can start out with a max of 5 cities (7 with perk) to be able to occupy and retain good benefits. Unfortunately as the game progresses many cities are captured and not nearly as productive. In one of my games i have about 22 cities and only 8 or so optimal max. Now a solution could be just to raze everything and then use a settler to place a stronghold on said area for defense against ever occuring moster spawns, it is at the same time somewhat redundant since in order to defend against these attacks, one needs troops. The other main annoyance is having only 6 available opponents. I always play in the biggest setting possible, so when i chose a huge game universe and could only face 6 other mages i was dissapointed. Part of what makes these games fun is forming alliances in order to conquer enemies, but I was able to obliterate my opponents before even making contact with the others. In summation i would say its worth maybe 20$ and as for the great mage pack, the contents arent nearly as neat as it may sound. Considering that 3 of the 7 perks are lords that can be hired in the beggining, but fairly soon through playing the game you cant either use the call of suzerain or just find better lords to hire. Well if you could have more then 4 lords total at once it would be better i suppose, but, you cant.

A very good story-driven RPG that is only held back by a not so tactical combat system.
The story itself is excellent, the characters are extremely likeable and all have some sort of unique story they go through as the game progresses. The main character Cicero also has a lot of backstory you can pick up by reading the in game codex entries, which are very well written and not a pain at all to collect. The OST is incredible, it always was adding to whatever scene was happening in game. The art is also amazing, it's a very distinct look that works very well for this type of game.
My only gripe with this game comes from the combat, and how it can be a little clumsy at times to wield. Combat in this game can be played in either a tactial pause mode, or a real time action mode. On the easier difficulties, you rarely need to use tactical mode unless you really want to, but on hard you do not have that luxury. Unfortunately, the AI for your partners is not the best, and they have a habit of doing things that get them killed. The devs know this however and are working on some balancing patches, as well as adding a New Game+ mode.
Aside from a slightly clumsy combat system, this game is one of the best narritive experiences I've played in years, and I hope they have more in store for us in the future.
P.S. Please go easier on Kalden next time devs :(

At first I didn't understand what was going on and how the combat was meant to be played. But a few hours in, I lost track of time completely. The gameplay became more and more addictive as I gathered new spells and party members, and the fights became more intense as I refined my tactics. Found myself clenching my buttcheeks during the major boss fights.
During the course of the game, you are forced to play with party members not in your A-team, posing new strategic questions. All the while the story pummels you with catastrophe after catastrophe. My internal monologue was filled with battle cries like “get out of my way, you sycophants!” or “oh no you didn’t!”. The soundtrack was immersive, haunting, and the animation was just sublime.
This is one of those games you must complete to see the full picture. Near the end, while some things still didn’t make sense to me, the battles became so tightly woven with the story that I didn’t care. There were gut-punches that shocked me and made me uncomfortable with how the characters were behaving, but at the end, for all his flaws, I identified with Cicero – a try-hard who just never wins.

Are you tired of grinding, chasing carrots or sniffing out every corner of an open world?
Do you want to read a book? Listen to an audiobook? Play a visual novel? Try your wits in tactical combat? Why not all at once?
Masquerada is a unique game that offers both the expected quality of an indie game, as in - great story, beautiful soundtrack and, in this case, incredible voice acting; as well as a chance to test your skills in pausable combat.
In short - this is almost like a casual, more calm and relaxing version of Dragon Age. Complete with lots of lore and engaging world.
Whatever issues this game may have - come from misinterpretation. Of course, if a person wants price\value or replayability... that's something for F2P skirmishers or grand AAA games. Let's not forget that this is an indie game, and, to be honest, I wouldn't say it falls far behind titles like South Park, it's even ahead in some departments. So - money should not be the question. Experiencing the story should be, and, as even the negative comments have said - this story is one worth experiencing.
Another issue that people have - is the combat. Well, to be honest that's why there are various difficulties. I can't speak for all of them, I'm playing on Hard, but I see that they can be changed at any time. So while I do find myself struggling and replaying some fights - I realize that this is MY choice. And if I ever find it too much - I can always drop the difficulty to continue. More often than not - I can just analyze my mistakes and do better. Of course, in some cases - the set-in-stone character development might become an obstable(as the game does not have a strict RPG role trinity), but that's.... what you can call replayability. Want to ever replay the game, maybe on a higher difficulty? Do better this time. You know what you are dealing with.
Without tank-healer-dps trinity, the combat system might seem weird, but let's understand that wierd does not mean wrong, it means unqiue. And, in fact. the ability of your tank to also be a healer, or for your protagonist to be a flexible jack of all trades - is better than just, you know, building a tank, a healbot and a glass cannon.
Get to know this sytem better. See what you can do if you've chosen something wrong. Reduce the difficulty if necessary. What's the one thing that people always blame games like Diablo 3 for? Everything is TOO LINEAR. You make a cookie-cutter build and you win.
This is one of the game where you actually have to think outside of the box, live with consequences and get over any obstacles. And, let's be realistic, this isn't Diablo 2. You are bound only by your profile\current storyline. If things go wrong, you don't lose hundreds of hours...
So, to conclude, this is the game that you play for the experience. Not another space pirate simulator. Not another skirmisher. Not another annual AAA flick. Many people can say they've enjoyed a GTA game before, but how many people can say they've experienced To the Moon?
Well, why not experience a beautiful world inspired by west-european traditions, where you play as a detective who has to lead his party on a perilous quest to unravel a mystery that can change everything?

Dead Space 2 is full of changes and overall a mess...but in a good way. It is for the most part true that the longer a horror franchise keeps running the faster it gets stale but this one is arguably the pinnacle of the franchise. I am nostalgic towards the original Dead Space, I'll have to admit, but Dead Space 2 balances action and horror almost perfectly.
The Necromorphs don't scare you anymore with their mere presence but numbers. You'll be well aware of the dangers ahead yet if you take a moment to realize the body count it is indeed shocking. The game throws so many of these things at you it's downright scary at times. To compensate Issac has a lot more mobility now but this is still a horror game and far from the mechanics of run'n'gun types like Call of Duty or DOOM.
As far as you're concerned the controls allow a lot more freedom but just the right amount. We're still talking about a third-person shooter, after all. It seems a lot more optimized and fluid than the original was regarding controls. Zero-G sections are now more fun as you can thrust to one side or the other while shooting.
The weapons themselves are a lot more varied too: besides the new types of Necromorphs added there are also at least twice the amount of weapons from the original to choose from and they all fit in the "tactical dismemberment" principle of the game. If you're like me you can also finish the whole game with the most basic of loadouts (Plasma Cutter, Plasma Rifle, Ripper, Line Gun). There is a lot to choose from and even more so if you activate that CD Key given to you by purchasing the game on Steam (maybe other platforms as well).
Clearing one concern that I had is that no, you don't need to install Origin to play this game and not even for the multiplayer. You will only need to create an EA Account to join servers but that can be done in-game. So far aside from two individuals I met everything is pretty much dead unfortunately.
Story-wise the game journeys into Issac's mind and there are a lot more setpieces scattered around. I won't spoil much for ya but they can form a bit of a mess at times. One moment you have this big gargantuan Necromorph running after you which might as well serve as a boss fight and then you have human encounters the next. Speaking of which you do not fight humans directly in this game (not that the series would ever need it).
It is overall a bit of a mess but in the long-run it's beautiful and should be experienced first hand if possible. It takes pretty much everything the original had and raises the stakes. The level design is beautiful, maybe twice as large with distinctly different areas and tremendous skyboxes.
On the downside though this experimental approach comes with a bit of a downside. The regenerating ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ doesn't appear again after a short run in this one.
Overall Dead Space 2 is a must-buy along with the original and if you're a fan of the series I ought to say no more. It experiments a lot with new ideas but in the end it all comes to a good product. Usually going on sale for 2,50$ it's totally worth it and will last you about as much as the original (if not a bit less, it fluctuates but lasts more than your average shooter to say the least).
One dead, one space, two Dead Space.

Right after I finished the first Dead Space I went right to this one. Many people say it's not as great as the first, and many others say Dead Space 2 is superior to the first.
Personally, in terms of action, this game takes it. Dead Space was all about taking your time, getting immersed in the tense, creepy atmosphere, and managing your ammo/resources. It was thrilling, but it never was not as in-your-face action packed as Dead Space 2. Also, it had a couple neat boss fights which I enjoyed. Dead Space 2, however,  lacks in the boss-fight catagory. Dead Space was a horror/survival game first, and an action game last. This game is much more fast paced and action oriented.
Dead Space 2 holds onto that creepy atmopshere from the first, and in some cases shines a little brighter in that aspect. In terms of what the game gives you to work with, like ammo and health packs - Dead Space 2 hands it out like candy compared to the first. This made me play more reckless and careless. You can make more mistakes in this game and not pay that high of a price for it. This can be seen as good or bad depending on what kind of player you are. For me, I enjoyed the added action to the Dead Space universe.
Don't get me wrong, there are still some bits that will scare you. Eventually, though, you will learn to predict when something is about to jump out at you. Overall, it's all still great fun shooting the limbs off these creatures and stomping the hell out of them until they're motionless. The story is more present here, and there's some more character development.
My only cons with the game are with the final two chapters of the game, and the thruster sequences. In the last two chapters of the game you are bombarded with enemies from all directions, and it makes the game feel cheap and it can get very frustrating very fast, no matter how ready you are. Then there are sequences where you have to steer yourself in space and dodge debris with your thrusters on your suit. I did not enjoy these sections whatsoever because you have such low mobility and you will die over and over trying to find the right path.
Overall, one hell of a game. I enjoyed it a lot, maybe a tiny bit more than the first. Dead Space 3 is next on my list.

Ziggurat is a FPS-roguelike hybrid that features procedurally generated levels and permadeath. The gameplay is kind of similar to tower of guns except with more mobile enemies that sometimes swarm you like in serious sam. Your weaponry includes a weak starter wand, various shotgun like spells, wide spread and rapid fire staves, and alchemy items that are typically explosives or arrow types. Every attack you use draws from one of four pools of mana (wand/spell/staff/alchemy) and proper management of your stocks is crucial to surviving each level.
Movement is very slick and you will probably find yourself sprinting a lot since the game lets you ice skate around at high speeds making it easy to get across levels and to avoid monster attacks. There are a few jumping puzzles in the game which is kind of a pet peeve for me in any FPS but they aren't such a big deal once you get used to the fact that you stop moving forward the moment you release the key.
Monster difficulty ranges depending on the type of monster and weapons you have available and some types, such as the fire imp, can quickly flood the room with difficult to dodge attacks when in large numbers, making it very difficult to deal with them if you don't have some sort of crowd control weapon. To add to the difficulty, all items in the game will despawn after a set period of time (including the experience gems which you need to level up!) so not only do you have to take down everything in a room but you also have to dance in between monsters and grab up all the mana gems, health, and experience before it disappears. This can be annoying at some times but it does add to the overall challenge and prevents the player from simply sniping at things until everything is dead.
Overall I would recommend this game to anyone who likes old-school style hectic single player FPS play since it gives off that kind of vibe with the cramped rooms and monster spawns.

I could not do anything to influence the outcome, I could not fail and the success scenario is frankly still pretty♥♥♥♥♥♥ so it was a pointless exercise altogether.
A game is supposed to be something you can win. Or even interact with the world at all outside of the boundaries of "do the one thing it's possible to do, or walk the one direction it's possible to walk."
