This game is, in a word, an expansion. But it is priced as an expansion, unless you plan on getting the great mage edition. It adds what amounts to a campaign mode, retools the spell research system, adds 2 new races, and includes a race that was DLC for the first game. If you never played the first warlock, but are interested in the series, get this one. If you do have the first game, then whether you get this is entirely dependant on how much you liked the original. If you did like it, well, this is more of the same, and some solid additions. For $30 I can certainly recommend it, but I can only recommend getting the great mage edition if you have money to burn, or really REALLY like the series. If you DIDN'T like Warlock: Master of the Arcane, and were hoping that the sequel would fix everything you hated, well, then this probably isn't the game for you, because all they really fixed was the research system.

Have you played Civilization and mostly enjoyed the experience?  Did you ever want something that was a less involved in juggling the requirements of building a long term successful civilization and at the same time gave you the feeling of building an expanding empire?  Oh, and did you ever ponder what Civilization 5 would be like if it didn't take itself so serious?  Well, that pretty much sums up Warlock 2.  The comparison is unavoidable between the two since much of the interface is similar.  Much of what you do in the game will be familiar to Civ 5 players, just less involved and deep in its potential.  Diplomacy - check.  City building and development - check. Resource management - check.  Build troops to decimate the enemy - check.  Now, with all that said, the one area where Warlock 2 is possibly ahead of Civ 5 is the actual combat game.  Between the variety of combat types, upgrades, and magic types vs melee and ranged troops Warlock 5 shows itself to be more designed to be a pure combat empire builder than Civ 5.  Sure there are other types of victory conditions, but in the end most will play to dominate the enemy on the field of battle since the other types of victory are not nearly as deep and satisfying.  At times there is even an RPG component to Warlock 2 that some may find appealing.  The joy in Warlock is that it presents a fun and playable game that doesn't take itself too serious and at times even manages to laugh at itself.  For those that prefer there is a campaign game that unfold a story along with a more scripted gameplay, but for myself it is best as a sandbox where you can dapple in all the absurdity of a fantasy world inhabited with giant rats, vampires, and creatures normally found in mythology.

Paradox took Warlock: Masters of the Arcane, slapped a novelty glasses-and-mustache disguise on it, and called it Warlock 2.
Warlock 2 is essentially Warlock 1, and, in my opinion, definitely not worth the launch price.  There's minor differences here and there, but unless you squint really hard, it's still the same game.  The units are the same, the spells are the same, the voice clips are the same, the soundtrack is the same, and even the ridiculous AI is the same.  The biggest feature to the new game, the world shard system, has been more annoying than anything.  It's such a chore getting your units from shard to shard, and it takes 'forever' to do so when you have a large army, because you're constantly bottle-necking at the portals.  I can only see it getting worse and worse as I'm forced to travel to more and more shards.
I really like Warlock, and Warlock 2 is fun (because it's the same thing, essentially), but I don't recommend paying the full price for it.  If you can skip it, wait for this game to go on sale.  It'll be a steep discount.

TL;DR:  warlock 2 is a great game, and IMO improves upon Warlock 1 and is worth the $30 price.
i understand the criticism that this game seems more like an expansion than a sequel.  IMO, whichever side of the fence you are on.. its a subjective opinion... and honestly, if you feel that way, i totally get it.
here's how i look at it though..
one:  you are paying the same price you would for most stand alone expansions.
for $30 you get the standard edition, and you get everything you need minus the bonus content, which is bonus content if you want it.  i dont consider anything in the Great Mage edition a must have.
thus, you are essentially getting the full game for $30.  the price seems pretty reasonable to me - even if we are saying this is just an expansion.
two - Exiled Mode:
first, its unique.  instead of one large map where you go out adventuring, collecting stuff, building your empire, conquering other civilizations,  all on a single plane..  you have a ton of smaller maps which you access by opening portals.. each with their own unique flavor to them, and you STILL have the adventuring, loot finding, conquering, etc.
and what makes things even more unique is that each of the maps have a different element effect.  one will be undead, one will be lava lands, one will be winter/frost based, etc.
ive started a few games and i can say from experience that you dont start on the same environment every time so you have to modify your strategy a little each time you play.. there are some scripted moments that dont change.. but beyond that you can have a different experience each time you play the game.
the above mode, along with all the improvements like tech/spell trees, etc is enough for me to recommend Warlock II.
a few criticisms:
the units seem kind of useless for the most part.  you have many summoning spells available to you, and what you get can be quite powerful.  especially the dragons and spirit wolves.  also, you will get 4 heroes as you progress through exiled mode which can also become quite deadly.  you use those 4 heroes, a high level summoned dragon and maybe a unit or two for good measure and you are pretty much set.  yes, you need to defend your cities as you play.. but honestly, once you reach the optimal city limit, which you can usually manage on two continents.. the cities can become expendable.
also, sometimes the random monster encounters you get can become frustrating.  they always seem to happen right around the time you are fighting a rival great mage.  some may consider this a positive.  myself, i just find it tedious.
one final minor criticism.. the diplomacy mechanic.  there really isnt one.  lets say you declare a seize fire on a rival so you can clear out some monsters.  its almost a guarantee that the AI will attack again real soon, sometimes even on the very next turn.  basically diplomacy comes down to  accepting the seize fire to get a spell, gold, and mana and thats about it.
conclusion:
IMO, the amount of content in the game is enough to consider it worth the price - whether you consider it an expansion or not.. ask yourself, in the end, is it worth $30.  me.  i say DEFINITELY.

Do not buy this game!
On paper this is pretty much Warlock 1 with a few additions which mostly amounts to 2 extra races (which feel samey), a few extra spells (along with a new research system), as well as a new playing mode where you start of in other planes of existance. In fact those are where the game shines the most as the plane to plane gameplay is actually quite interesting and some of the random events really shake up the gameplay and can make even raising your army interesting as the conditions of the universe change on you.
The issue though is that all the problems with the first game rather persist. The game has the same glitches including a crash bug that still goes unfixed from Warlock 1, the same imbalances, an unbalanced mage creation system, poor braindead AI, Overpowered heros, useless ordinary units (with exceptions).
Then there are the problems unique to this game. The planes never feel fully fleshed out with their own resources, the races barely take advantage of the planes, the quest system will constantly bar you from progress and ask you to either defeat an excessively tough enemy that can span you hundreds of turns to defeat or require you to pony up resources obscene to collect. Then there are some planes that are neigh on impossible to explore. As well while the events are quite interesting a lot of them only serve to harass you, don't be surprised if the game just decides a volcano would look rather nice next to your capital.
Finally these features don't mesh well with eachother, for example the mage creation system doesn't take into account the new research tree.
Ultimately this is a stand alone expansion of Warlock 1. Which would be fine but they just didn't care to put the time and attention that this game needed to shine. It needed to be balanced better, with more features to fill out those planes, A good AI, As well as an overhaul to the random events and quests. In spite of all the effort they clearly put into this game, it still somehow feels like a cheap cash in.

Warlock 2 does, at least in my humble opinion, exactly what a good sequel should do.  There are no sweeping changes here, there are no completely different mechanics, there's no arbitrary new mini-game that fundamentally alters how you play.  Warlock 2 takes all of what made the original fun and polishes it, adds to it, develops, evolves and improves.  City and army building has been greatly improved with more transparency of 'tech trees', unit-improvement resources are now handled better and spell research is leaps and bounds better, with direct and clear choices offered to the player at each step of the way.
While many of the art and sound assets  are direct from the first iteration, everything seems just a little more nicely rendered, a little more well built and just, well, better.  The UI is clearer, there is far more help available in-game and everything seems more to-hand than the original did.  With the new game mode and the editor, the wider selection of races and units, there's a lot of content to explore and consume before the well runs dry.
Overall, this game is a superb example of what happens when you build a sequel not by reaching for new faddish quirks, by trying to cater to the lowest common denominator or by bloating the game up with reams of pointless minutiae that require advanced statistics and spreadsheets to manage, but by playing the game and understanding that the game was already fundamentally good and simply tweaking and polishing and improving every point.
If you liked the original, you will love Warlock 2: The Exiled.  If you didn't like the original, there's a very good chance that whatever put you off has been addressed and improved in this new edition.

I Am Alive? More like I Am Alpha!
Because it's a clearly rushed product that's not very well optimized, is ugly, is short as hell and ends strangely and abruptly.
It's also one of the best B-games I've ever played.
I Am Alive drops you into a world torn asunder by a cataclysmic event. You're just a guy looking for people from his past, trying to help those in need, and trying to survive in a harsh reality where everything's out to get you. Your main ability is climbing, and the climbing system of IAA is really well-done: it controls a lot like Uncharted or Tomb Raider, but with the addition of a Stamina system: the longer you climb, the more your bar depletes. If it gets to the end, you'll still be able to climb, but your maximum stamina capacity will slowly dwindle until you get to a resting spot. You can restore your max stamina with items, but it's a neat take on providing urgency to a system that's been used before.
The combat is the second tier of the game, and it's also exceptionally well-done: the game utilizes an Intimidation system, which allows you to bluff your opponents using an empty gun while you try to control fights to your favor. Sometimes they'll call your bluff, and you'll have to either shoot them or go for a machete kill; other times, you might want to approach hostiles unarmed, wait for one to get close, and then attack with your machete, surprising everyone and giving you the upper hand. Ammo is scarce, and you don't want to waste a bullet: chances are if you miss a shot, you're about to die. The guns feel good, and the fact that unarmored foes die in one hit is an absolutely incredible way of finally adding realistic gunplay, which makes every encounter memorable. If you come across guys with guns, you either need to be unarmed and hope they come to search you or shoot them first. You will probably die a few times before you get the hang of things, and enemies flanking you might surprise you.
You later get a bow, which leads to interesting combat encounters since arrows are recoverable and the bow is silent.
The story, largely, is told by victims you save and the few friendly people you encounter on your journey and is well-written. The dynamic you have with the first friendly character you meet is the best, leading you to develop an emotional attachment to them. It's not going to win any awards, but it certainly helps to keep you motivated.
The game's not without its flaws, however; the ending is rushed, unsatisfying, and leaves you with a lot of questions, and there are times when the checkpoint system can get very annoying. I played the game on Normal and it was pretty tough, but I never had to restart a chapter. There are segments where you wander aimlessly through the streets, hoping to find something climbable to either save you from the dust storms or lead you to the next destination. The game is also (not, in my eyes, a negative) very short (I clocked in at 4h059s) which could leave some people thinking they overpaid.
I really liked my time within I Am Alive's world, and a fully-developed sequel or spin-off in the same world would be more than welcome.

M. Stands for Masterpiece.
This game is wonderful. It's surely unusual because not many people do such games these days and that's why I think it got quite a few negative reviews. People mostly criticize gameplay and system features and surely there are some flaws, but that's irrelevant. The essence of this game is a STORY, and a truly heartfelt one. It's a story about people, their character and their relationship, about a fantasy world crafted with love and soul put in it. This game has really touched the strings of my souls and is a great proof that game development is truly a form of art.
TL;DR - If you want to play classic RPG with many choices, go Pillars of Eternity. If you prefer tactical fights with deep strategy and mechanics, play XCOM. If you desire to live through a breathtaking adventure alongside unforgettable characters with vibrant personalities in a meticulously designed and truly enchanting fantasy world, Masquerada: Songs and Shadows is your choice.
Characters: Every person in the game is vivid, they don't just SEEM alive, they actually ARE alive. Usually characters in games are developed by people who don't really have much social experience (or so it seems) and don't really understand how people's relationship work, but luckily that's not the case with Masquerada. Due to the small number of characters introduced the devs showed us each and every one of them with their virtues and flaws, with their own stories, in all their uniqueness. They may behave irrationally succumbing to their emotions, but that's realistic, that makes them more alive. These are not your typical "heroes" who despite having a few bad traits are 90% good, brave and righteous (or 90% evil). The characters of Masquerada, including main ones, are humans who lie, fear, despair, but also hope, fight for what they believe and, what's most important, they EVOLVE throughout the story, and that's exactly what makes them alive.
World: The world of Masquerada if full of minute details that make it much more vivid. A lot of information about the world's features as well as background lore given to us in a form of Cicero's records (or the ones he finds) is simply amazing. In-game we can only see a small part of this world, a city of Ombre with its rich history and peculiar society structure, all though-out very carefully. But we can also get a glimpse on the other nations and territories through the notes, and it gives us more or less full picture of the world, which is quite rare for such games. Numerous minor details and descriptions is what really made a strong impression on me.
Sound: Music is quite simple, but really fitting. It helps a lot to immerse in the atmosphere. And the voices! Damn, they're so good. They help to form images of characters so much better and really plays a great part in their vividness! The voice cast  is quite starry: Felicia Day, Liam O'Brien, Matthew Mercer and many other people lend their voices to the characters of Masquerada.
Visual Design: There are many bright colors in the game that in my opinion make the game even more lively. The art style is quite simple and yet eye-catching.
Mechanics: Combat system is not complicated at all: elemental tags work pretty straightforward, most descriptions are not overloaded with numbers (much to mucnhkins' distaste). AI is doing weird things sometimes so you always need to keep an eye on your party members, but with the help of tactical pause it's not that hard (may be annoying sometimes though). On the hard difficulty the game is…well, hard. But perfectly manageable. I completed it on hard with the party of characters that I like for personalities rather than for abilities (don't get me wrong, I love all the main characters, but to take along some of them in some situations were more fitting that the others) and although it was a bit harder than if I always had a good-all-around party, it was by no means exceptionally difficult. Even if you think you had built your characters wrong, by the time it starts to matter there will be a skill reset option, so it's quite user-friendly.
Story: I dare to say that people who designed the story are true geniuses. There are quite a few twists and turns of the plot, with many tales unfolding along the main storyline, closely intertwining with it and eventually everything being woven into the grand canvas of an adventure one can never forget. It's not particularly complicated or always unpredictable (some moments are really mind-blowing), but it somehow absorbs you. And, what's important, it's perfectly logical. Not rational, but logical, and definitely realistic. Many important questions arise as you progress and later you can see what answers Cicero and his friends find, how they resolve difficult situations and how it all affects them. All the characters' personalities as well as the word's lore are instrumental in creating this unique feeling of involvement in the story, the feeling of living through it.
Verdict: It's one of the best games I've ever played. I even see it not like a game, but rather an experience I lived through myself. In my opinion this masterpiece can actually influence one's perception, maybe teach some lessons and is definitely a source of inspiration. I doubt I managed to describe the game in all its brilliance and that's why I encourage everyone seeking a vibrant story to try out this game.
To the Developers: Thank you guys for creating such a magnificent game. It was a truly unforgettable experience, Cicero and his friends now hold a special place in my heart.

I'm a Kickstarter backer. I've seen more of the game than what my gameplay time says, no worries. (We finished the game at the 20 hour mark)
Okay, so there's a very specific group of people out there who would love this game, and also a very specific group that would hate it. This is entirely due to design and what this game is, and what some people expect it to be even though it's not.
FACTS:
- There are NO branching storylines here, and NO decisions that "get you to an alternate ending". There is ONE storyline, and that's the one story line there is. Not a pro nor a con, it's what it is.
- The game is EXTREMELY linear. In the sense that you proceed forward, forward and forward. It's like Transistor in that regard: you always went forward, and there's no real point to going back. (Not one of those CRPGs where you get quests from random people and stuff, you mostly go do the main quest and that's that).
- The game is fully voiced, all dialogue between characters is voiced, it adds a lot to the gameplay value. (By the way, it's very high quality voice acting too! Names like "JENNIFER HALE" the Female Shepard from MASS EFFECT, or "CRISPIN FREEMAN", these names might ring a bell?)
- The game is text-heavy because people talk to each other. So if you just want hack and slash, there are less dialogue-heavy games out there for that, in which case go play some Bastion or something.
But if you want lore and codex entries like back in the Dragon Age Origins games, you'll be pleased. The game is heavily focused on telling its story.
- There is skill customization. Multiple skills to choose from, different upgrade "paths" to take on said skills. They differ from character to character, element to element. Fun times.
- The music is superb.
- The art is pretty.
- The battle system is okay. The companion members' AI is downright stupid, so you need to tell them to stop being stupid manually.
- Auto-saves on screen transition only. No manual saving. An odd design choice. Not really a fan.
- Recommended because of the music, story (from beginning to end!), and world design.
Final verdict:
- If you have enough money, this game is definitely worth buying, even full-price (if you believe this is something you'll enjoy)
- If you don't have enough money, wishlist it and buy it on a sale, you should definitely get this one (if you believe this is something you'll enjoy)

It is difficult to reccomend Masequerada, eventhough I adore it.
Reasons being that it barely qualifies as a game. The only area in which the player has any agency, being combat and the trappings thereof, this making up perhaps 1/4 of the "game". That being said, the combat is proportionally well developed considering how little  there is of it or perhaps it is that, it is adequate and you dont get bored in your short time with it. This fact might be a con or a pro depending on the buyer. You fight at the appointed venues and level up, allocating points via a system reminiscent of Dragon Age: Origins. It is all very linear and the fights only occur because they are narratively appropriate. You will not be hunting for bear asses nor taking on lucrative contracts, there is no buying or selling nor gear as such - not beyond the mask you choose to wear. The "game" has a very deliberate pace and mood and there are no extras, one might expect, to detract from this.
That being as it is, by now you might be wondering; what of the other 3/4? Well my friend, it is storytelling. This thing masquerading as a game is a tool for the developers to tell a story via heaps of lore codexes - which could of used some narraration -, character development and the superb voice acting. They do no require your input nor ask for your opinion, you will traverse from point A to point B with the sole task of initiating dialogues and fighting the odd battle here and there. For most of the time you will sit either bored or enraptured by the story unfolding. It is more akin to a radio play or full blown theatre play than it is to an RPG. Indeed there is no roleplay to speak of in the direct meaning of the word. You are a mute witness and at the end of it, you can applaud if yo so wish.
All I can add is that the characters are very human, they will grow, they will falter and pick themselves up again. The backdrop to their personal conflicts being a civil war where indeed the fabric of reality will be set in peril. If this nonegame intriques you, go ahead and buy it. Perhaps the developers will be enticed to make an actual game with similar levels of storytelling.
P.S: I do not reccomend playing on hard, as the mechanics are not very refined and commanding the party can be clunky. This combined with the archaic savepoint system will have you hating the experience of being set back to the start of an area each time you die. Not even the subtle inflections of Matthew Mercer will make it tolerable, you have been forwarned.

A fairly unique multiplayer game of being a Bunny and trying to take control of a giant gun and earn power and money using a combination of honesty, deception, obedience, mutiny, servitude, manipulation, lying, cheating, stealing and all the other C.V. ruining human traits. It's the first Steam release from an American developer with a brief history in game art and development, and comes with a unique mix of gameplay elements which sometimes make for really interesting player interactions and psychological situations.
After playing for just a couple of days I found myself beginning to analyse people mid-conversation in my day to day life, wondering if they were lying to me about trivial things for monetary gain, half-expecting them to hide in a piece of furniture and rush at me when I wasn't watching. It's a game which undoubtedly gets in your head when you play too much.
Full disclosure: I have no affiliation with the developer, but did recieve a key.
Consisting of a medium sized map with up to 10 Bunny players, the sole objective in OBEY is to amass as much money as possible, but the methods for accomplishing this vary based on the current player:power scenario and can shift in an instant. One central gun/watchtower called the Robosaru exists per map, a Power Plant which generates money for the player inside the Robosaru, and a Feed Box where Bunnys can deposit items to generate money for the Overlord, and usually make money for themselves in the process.
Whoever commands the Robosaru has a distinct advantage in the form of 10x passive income, and of course deadly control, but it comes at the cost of everyone trying to steal that control either through direct attacks, or by lying, manipulating and sabotaging the Overlord or any combination of their fellow Bunnys in persuit of their own paycheck. Because it becomes increasingly difficult to watch more than a Bunny or two, the Overlord must work together to keep himself safe, similarly Bunnys want to stay alive and profit more, which means that the dynamics constantly change based on how many players are in the game, how much money they have, what they're assumed attitude towards each other is, and what they actually accomplish.
At a higher level OBEY about out thinking your fellow players. In the early stages I routinely found myself asking for more money for performing actions, and being a sort of salesman for myself. When I learned that I could cheat my fellow Bunnys by lying about their actions, a new avenue of options opened up. This lack of strict limitation and the utility of psychological warfare via spoken commands and text brings the gameplay to a higher level than simply running around trying to earn money and directly sabotage the current winner, and it's where the game shines.
The visual style is also very worth pointing out. Maps tend to be very simple, and I personally love the low polygon approach to the assets. The animations and movement are also well correlated with the visuals, and having a group of Bunnys all turn their heads to stare at me in the hull of a gloomy-lit ambient Dropship ended up being far more creepy than it rightfully should've been.
Being in Early-Access, technical issues are less of an issue and though I had a few small technical problems every single one of them was mentioned on the development panel as currently being worked on. There are still technical issues worth bringing attention to though, like lag and server drops which are common. The server console is fairly flat and bland and utilizes an IRC channel which comes with pros and cons, and the server client for hosting your own games is completely unmentioned in game, and I only found it through a mention on the website.
There's also a real lack of options for play just now. There are a handful of dedicated servers with various configurations, and each round has a small pool of maps to select from, but there's currently only a couple of US server and maybe a handful in the EU, so if your ping isn't particularly good you're probably going to be limited to a server or two at best, and if you're inexperienced or looking for different gameplay types, you're going to be waiting for far too long to connect to a good server.
Which brings up the biggest problem with this title: the lack of players. It's great fun when there are enough people around, and genuinely addictive and intense gameplay takes place, especially with people you know, but currently the community is only really palpable during a very specific set of hours and if you know more than a handful of players then you're unlikely to play with people you haven't mostly already seen. This wouldn't be a problem in most games, but here if you know what to expect from a player or they remember what you did the last few games, there's probably a disadvantage for one of you and a bias towards the same gameplay unfolding.
I expect this game to grow over time, and it's a game more than any other I've found that will become better with a larger community in place, so it's a real problem when there's no effort to grow the player base other than perhaps a Steam group and the developer forums. While the current community is definitely great fun to play with, and well in tune with the spirit of the game, it's still both drastically dependent upon, and lacking in players.
You can pick up OBEY just now for £10.99/14.99€/$14.99 or your regional equivalent, and the 4-Pack option saves you a chunky 40% if you have a couple of friends. As with all multiplayer games, your value for money is subjective based on how much you're likely to play, but when compared to other popular multiplayer titles on Steam, this is priced on the higher end, though it doesn't have in-game purchases or DLC to worry about.
While finding people to play with can be an issue, if you expect the player base to grow then this is a fair buy, and good value for money if you go for the 4-Pack option. If you need a good multiplayer scene then you might want to wait til after release, for a sale, or until the player levels reach a better level.

Right after I finished the first Dead Space I went right to this one. Many people say it's not as great as the first, and many others say Dead Space 2 is superior to the first.
Personally, in terms of action, this game takes it. Dead Space was all about taking your time, getting immersed in the tense, creepy atmosphere, and managing your ammo/resources. It was thrilling, but it never was not as in-your-face action packed as Dead Space 2. Also, it had a couple neat boss fights which I enjoyed. Dead Space 2, however,  lacks in the boss-fight catagory. Dead Space was a horror/survival game first, and an action game last. This game is much more fast paced and action oriented.
Dead Space 2 holds onto that creepy atmopshere from the first, and in some cases shines a little brighter in that aspect. In terms of what the game gives you to work with, like ammo and health packs - Dead Space 2 hands it out like candy compared to the first. This made me play more reckless and careless. You can make more mistakes in this game and not pay that high of a price for it. This can be seen as good or bad depending on what kind of player you are. For me, I enjoyed the added action to the Dead Space universe.
Don't get me wrong, there are still some bits that will scare you. Eventually, though, you will learn to predict when something is about to jump out at you. Overall, it's all still great fun shooting the limbs off these creatures and stomping the hell out of them until they're motionless. The story is more present here, and there's some more character development.
My only cons with the game are with the final two chapters of the game, and the thruster sequences. In the last two chapters of the game you are bombarded with enemies from all directions, and it makes the game feel cheap and it can get very frustrating very fast, no matter how ready you are. Then there are sequences where you have to steer yourself in space and dodge debris with your thrusters on your suit. I did not enjoy these sections whatsoever because you have such low mobility and you will die over and over trying to find the right path.
Overall, one hell of a game. I enjoyed it a lot, maybe a tiny bit more than the first. Dead Space 3 is next on my list.

First, a short explanation of why I dont recommend the game (an actual review will follow).
Unfortunately, the Steam version of this game is incomplete.  The DLC that goes with this game is console exclusive which, besides being total ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, means you will never have the full experience if you purchase this game here.  Too make things more depressing, this was a PS3 release, meaning the only way to experience the full version of the game (if you cannot find a used version) is through the PS Now as either a rental or through the subscription service.
Now, all that is a shame, because I ♥♥♥♥ing love this game.  (I recommend playing Overlord: Raising Hell before Overlord II, and this review will assume that you have and will contain spoilers from the previous game)
Overlord 2 takes place after Overlord: Raising Hell and you play as the new child of the previous Overlord (by Rose) retaking the world from the "Glorious Empire" which arose since your sire's unfortunate incarceration in an Infernal Abyss (It happens).  You do this by raising a horde of minions and proceeding to ram them headfirst into the enemy until the enemy drowns in the bodies of your dead servants.  Well, I suppose you could use the guard system and the new tactical considerations (like various mounts for your Brown, Green, and Red minions) and overcome the enemy with your strategic brilliance.  But, to be honest, I often would start like that, lose my horde to an ill timed exsplosion, and then proceed to simply throw minions at my opponenet until the blood of my minions choked their airways.
Your horde will consist of the classic specialized minions from previous installments (convienetly color coded by evolution) whose special abillities will allow you to progress further and strike at your enemies in new and often amusing ways.
Browns are your front line fighters, they can both take a punch and dish them out.  But they cant really do anything else.  Reds are ranged attackers who through fireballs and can set your enemies ablaze and leave them screaming and running in panic, but are so fragile that a light breeze could kill them.  They also can absorb fire that blocks your path allowing you to progress.  Greens much like the browns, only weaker, but with the abillity to stealth on guard markers and jump on to enemies back and deal massive damage.  They also absorb poison, much like the Red's absorb fire.  Finally the Blues, which are even weaker than the Red's, dont really deal any damage, but can ressurect minions who fall in battle and swim.  As Gnarl says, "Browns, Reds, and Greens cant swim.  They are, however, remarkably good at drowning."
The story isn't particularly noteworthy, and actually feels quite short.  (hence the complaint about the missing DLC)  Still, it covers its bases and gives you reasons to use the new and improved magic system.
You still do collect spells as you go along, but upgrades for the spells take on new and excitting possibilites depending on whether or not you feel like Dominating a population, or Destroying them.  Your Evil Presnce spell allows you to dominate weak minded individuals, making them your slaves to fight with your minions in battle, or support you in towns by mining gold and making weapons for minions.  Or, you can use the spell to turn them into ash and have done with it.
Whichever way you choose affects how you can upgrade the spell.   A Domination Overlord will eventually be able to subdue entire crowds with ease, and a Destruction overlord will get better at reducing them to ash.
All of the other spells have similar choices as well.  Buff a minion to be incredibly strong, or consume its essence to restore your health.  Increase the power of your horde temporarily, or release a massive shockwave.  The choice is yours... mostly.
See, this is where the lack of the DLC really hurts, because it introduced three more obtainable spell catalysts (which you use to upgrade your spells.) lacking those, you cannot upgrade all your spells and have to pick and choose.  Which sounds like fun decesion making, but actually takes away from the feel of being an Evil Overlord of supreme power.
This is a shame, because I really really love this game.  I picked it up here because of how much I loved it when I first played it on console years ago.
But sweet as it is, it leaves a bitter taste in my mouth to know that if I want to have the full experience I have to subscribe to PS Now.

I came into this game not expecting anything.  It was a dollar on sale.
However I came away from this with my expectations vastly exceeded.
This is a short game, probably four hours of content in all, but to be honest that doesn't bother me.
What I got out of this was a fun tidy platformer with a sprinkling of humour that I enjoyed.
That seems like good entertainment value to me.
The original quest is quite short, but leaves a mark.  There is plenty to think over as you race through this colorful platformer.  What would you do for an achievement?  Are you really gun safe?
And after years of living in the world of freemium have we really been programmed to play games like this?
Is this game a silly prediction that creeps closer to coming true?
Or you can just race about jumping around like a mad person looking for secrets.  Thats mainly what I did.
And then there is the Game of The Year quest.  Its noticeably longer in length if you like your games that way, and creates a story that builds on the original game quite nicely. I remember seeing a demo for this game somewhere, can't remember. Anyway, that’s not the point. The point is this game looked really good from what I saw, a fun and fast paced FPS roguelike. Roguelikes are very common these days so seeing something a little more innovative, such as Ziggurat, is always refreshing. The platforming and 2D level design isn’t here. Ziggurat is a fully fleshed out 3D game that’s has a variety of roguelike elements. Some it does extremely well, whereas others, it doesn’t.
First of all, the FPS gameplay in Ziggurat is extremely fun and smooth. It’s extremely fast paced and it works for a game like this. In saying this, the shooter combat isn’t as deep as other FPS games, but this isn’t a downfall for the game, as it is extremely easy to adapt to, especially for the four types of weapons that your character possesses. This isn’t Call of Duty, so don’t expect it. Speaking of the weapon types, there are four for each character. The wand is your base weapon which you start with and it shoots normal damage dealing bolts. The other weapons, ranging from magical to arcane are better than the wand, must be found by the player, and ammo conserved, unlike the wand. This makes Ziggurat a lot more strategic and challenging and gives it that true roguelike feel.
Perhaps the most important element of a roguelike after combat is the levels. Random level design is what makes a roguelike a roguelike. In Ziggurat, the levels are a bit of a disappointment. They are random, but not entirely. The main levels are easily traversable, but they are not like other games such as Rogue Legacy, where the level design was extremely random and couldn’t be played the same way again. Ziggurat is not at all like this. The main levels stay almost identical during the time you spend trying to survive the Ziggurat. The level design makes the player feel like they been there before, and it makes the game feel more repetitive, which is what a good roguelike shouldn’t do. Replaying the game multiple times after death made playing the game much like a chore after a while.
The enemies in Ziggurat are varied, but not to the extent where there are random enemies each round that you play. Ziggurat has its fair share of enemies to face, and the more you play, the more experience you gain with taking these enemies down more efficiently. Some enemies are tougher than others, thus more thought is required in dealing with their attacks. This is another great aspect of the game as it gives that true roguelike feel of learning enemies and killing them, whilst taking the least amount of damage as possible. Dying is common in the game, but can be prevented, and survival prolonged, if the enemies are understood well. The bosses however are disappointing. They are an identical copy of the enemies, but just bigger and with more health. They are also ridiculously easy to take down if the right weapon is equipped and their attacks learnt. Bosses also spawn enemy minions which make the overall fight harder, but more chaotic, resulting in lower framerate. The framerate issues in the game are easily noticed, especially on low end systems. On higher end GPU’s, performance is excellent, even on the highest settings. But, even when getting 150+ frames, drops are noticeable as 30-40 frames can easily be noticed. This doesn’t detract from the overall experience, but can nag some gamers, especially ones with low end GPU’s. This shows the inconsistency with the game engine as enemies and certain areas are very intensive on frames. In saying this, Ziggurat looks truly gorgeous as a next gen game, and getting high frames whilst observing detailed lighting, shadows and textures, makes it a very immersive experience.
Although the game can get very repetitive due to the poor layout of the levels, the perks and the different characters adds incentive to play again. The perks are well designed and impact the game in a considerable way when leveling up, so choosing perks relative to the build of the character, is a vital factor for survival in Ziggurat. Secret rooms, such as trap rooms and treasure rooms, add to the games overall roguelike feel as players can get an advantage or get killed if they are not careful whilst in these rooms. Characters in Ziggurat can be unlocked by fulfilling certain objectives within the game, such as killing X amount of enemies or getting X amount of kills with a weapon. These tasks are rewarding as unlocking characters adds a more strategic feel because every character is different in the way the game is played, or will be played, depending on the player. Some might choose to have more arcane ammunition whilst sacrificing ammo for every other weapon type, whereas others might choose to be weaker at the start but level up quicker to give an advantage late game. This ensures that all types of players can gain mastery with their desired character, making the game appeal to all types of roguelike players. New or veteran.
In conclusion, Ziggurat is an extremely enjoyable and innovative roguelike game that features a host of different enemies, perks, and characters to experiment with and learn. The level design however isn’t up to par with the other elements of the game, making it ultimately feel stale and repetitive after a while. For the 14.99 asking price tag, is Ziggurat worth it? I would say yes, not absolutely or no way. It won’t suit everyone, but it can be seen that it has developed with the purpose of attracting more gamers to the roguelike genre. Just don’t expect to sink 100 hours into this.

As much as i want to, i can't recommend this game.
The matchmaking is awful.
You constantly get placed against people who are either a much higher elo/rank than you are,usually with hundreds of hours difference between you, or people who are just smurfing and enjoy destroying you even though you're playing at a very low rank/elo. ( The game is free, so it's very easy to smurf on).
A lot of the weapons are very spammy, and you sometimes get to spend entire matches just being ragdolled from Orions Lance dash spam or  the light attacks of any bow character who chain you into an 50% of your hp light attack combo.
There's a "dodge" system, which is like an invincible frame that is your only saving grace from being killed by a single staggering combo. however the dodge mechanic is every iffy, it has weird hitbox's sometimes caused by latency,
even when you do hit someone and hear the impact sound, they still somehow dodge, or when you are certain you did dodge, you get hit during the animation.
People who play enough time learn how to abuse the mechanic, and always hit you right at the end of the invisiiblty frame, and also circle around your attacks without you almost ever hitting them.
Usually in any video game that involves skill, reviews and comments like mine , are followed with "Get gut" responses.
Had it was any other game, such as Darksouls, i would agree with them,however In brawlhalla, the skill is to play enough time, until you :
Eventually memorize the combo that stagger the enemies the longest.
Learn to abuse the already mentioned broken dashing hitbox.
And if you play against newer players, you just spam the same heavy attack move over and over again.
Not to mention you'll play against people who are by default better than you most of the time, which is not a fun experience for any new player.
Ironically i'm still playing it from time to time, but that's mainly because of my tight schedule, and matches on brawlhalla don't last longer than 5 minutes. When i'm done playing i always feel annoyed and stressed, rather than relaxed, which is the feeling you're supposed to feel when playing video games.

A decent game that requires a lot of climbing. Combat is not the main focus here as melee combat is quite dangerous and ammo for guns are very very rare. Like "1 bullet from a dead villain" rare. From the same creators of Assassin's Creed, you're placed in a post apocalyptic world where you have to navigate your way through climbing, jumping and avoiding dangers.

IAA far exceeded my expectations. Its reception was lukewarm--often characterized by extreme and vocal loathing; it's a modern Ubisoft title; Stanislas Mettra said some very stupid things that got a lot of equally stupid reactions; &c.
It feels like the budget title it is, so gameplay mechanics are stiff and it often feels like a poor man's Uncharted set in a poor man's McCarthy-obsessed-with-fetchquests copycat's creation when you're climbing outcrops or buildings or trains--whatever. I liked this. I did. It felt old school, and since the game was going for an old school, very difficult fight for survival, it seemed right.
The game's difficulty, I felt, was perfect. I never died, but I was always coming close. There's a genuine sense of desperation start to finish, not only from you but from every NPC, enemy or friend--except maybe those aggressive armored ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s introduced at the 2/3rds point. Weird, annoying inclusion. You might find yourself sympathizing with many baddies.
"Stick-ups" surprisingly lack the feeling of repetition from poor AI; despite their frequency, I always found myself with that feeling of desperation again, trying as quickly as possible to spot the guns before being forced to act and save some asses.
The storyline is lacking and feels more like a prelude than anything (reminiscent of Hard Reset), but the atmosphere makes up for its inadequacies, ash and dust falling everywhere, choking the environment and its people--you--stressing that Road inspiration. (If I were to guess--and I really want to--I'd say The Event was an exaggerated eruption of one or more supervolcanoes.)
I loved the feel of this game, and I'll definitely replay it, hoping for further, bigger-budget sequels all the way through. I'd love to see how the world fairs outside of this game's geographic boundaries.

even when you do hit someone and hear the impact sound, they still somehow dodge, or when you are certain you did dodge, you get hit during the animation.
People who play enough time learn how to abuse the mechanic, and always hit you right at the end of the invisiiblty frame, and also circle around your attacks without you almost ever hitting them.
Usually in any video game that involves skill, reviews and comments like mine , are followed with "Get gut" responses.
Had it was any other game, such as Darksouls, i would agree with them,however In brawlhalla, the skill is to play enough time, until you :
Eventually memorize the combo that stagger the enemies the longest.
Learn to abuse the already mentioned broken dashing hitbox.
And if you play against newer players, you just spam the same heavy attack move over and over again.
Not to mention you'll play against people who are by default better than you most of the time, which is not a fun experience for any new player.
Ironically i'm still playing it from time to time, but that's mainly because of my tight schedule, and matches on brawlhalla don't last longer than 5 minutes. I just finished the game, and its pretty much what you'd expect from a modern Deus Ex title. I very much enjoyed it personally.
While the main story is hard to follow, and overall pretty weak, my main enjoyment from this game came from the side quests, exploration and that feeling of progression & badassery as you unlock more augmentations.
The side quests are typical DE fare, you encounter civilians/criminals/cops etc in your travels around Prague who enlist your help. These really flesh out the world, and I found myself caring more about these than the main quest story.
As for the exploration - I'm someone who could never run past a cave in Skyrim and just leave it unexplored. In DE I have to break into every locked room, explore every vent, climb every building. I hate to feel like I've missed anything. Prague is a pretty open hub. The only things stopping you from going places are either your abilities to break/hack through locked doors or how capapble you are of stealthing past guards. There are a ton of ways to navigate through the remote quest areas as usual to suit your chosen playstyle.
The main story as I mentioned is pretty convoluted I feel. The illuminati are involved, as well as several different nefarious insitutions and businesses who all want.....something. It didn't feel cohesive to me. There's very little context given about why we're in Prague, and the events between Human Revolution and Mankind Divided are, IMHO, left lazily unclear.
Finally, Prague as a hub gets a bit repetitive and stale. I'd love to see multiple hubs in the next title.
TLDR - If you liked Human Revolution, you'll like this. It's not quite as good, but I absolutely think it's worth the asking price.

This is a highly underrated game, and it's sad to see people get so up in arms against the developers over decisions forced on them by the publisher. It's painfully clear that the developers did their best to hide the microtransactions and roll back the preorder bonuses. Behind all that is a game that I feel surpasses human revolution and consistently reminded me of the original. Yes, it's not a globe spanning adventure with massive conspiracies to uncover, but the story becomes a much tighter crime drama that hints at really exciting stories to come.  I was thrilled at how this story began to introduce characters and plot points from the original. It's a slow burn, but well worth the effort if you've played the original deus ex. This game really shines in it's level design though. The changing context of revisited areas and watching them slowly expand as the story progresses and the players augmentations allow for increased exploration is only rivaled by the originals. This game takes Warren Spectors idea of making a couple city blocks with as much depth as can be possibly squeezed out of them to its extreme. To see one city hub used so effectivelly and now learn that the game was severly cut down in order to allow for the rest to be made into sequels is an absolute tragedy. And to rub salt in the wound, Square Enix's crippling of this game caused a bad reception, which now has led them to put the series on hold. I was never a fan of the story of Human Revolution, and Mankind Divided is the prequel I've always wanted. Seeing such a passionate dev team get so close to wrapping up the whole franchise and perfecting and modernizing deus ex/immersive sim game design, to then be completely halted by a publisher for a bad reception caused by publisher intervention is infuriating.  Please buy this game and support the devs. This game shows they were taking this franchise in an incredible direction that lives up to the original. Too many games focus on art and story, and have lackluster gameplay, but this game shows how story and art can be expressed through gameplay. This game has so many surprises up its sleeve, and its clear the devs were just getting started.

As for all most recent AAA games, the beginning was difficult for Mankind Divided. Day 1 negative reviews popped up and almost everybody mentioned the microtransactions as well as the game's bad optimisation. I, for one, cannot refer to these since 1) microtransactions I couldn't care less about 2) the game is now properly optimised. My current rig - coupled with a GTX 1060 - could put a smile on Jensen's face even in the heat of battle.
Marvellous! Just marvellous! It was the very thing I was missing from Human Revolution. Most notably, the facial animations (if you remember the artefact issues all pertained to the facial animations). Everything else, of course, looks tremendously good. Especially when you stroll down on the streets of Prague late at night when a curfew is in effect. Well, strolling is an exaggeration - cops shoot on sight so your best bet is to move while cloaked. Still, the sirens lighting the surrounding area in the heavy rain look great. For this to happen you need to wait a while when it comes to story progression - but to marvel at the sights in the distance during the early Dubai mission you do not!
It was a bit of a letdown. Human Evolution was just so perfect with its great ending and boss battles. For a sequel it is always difficult to live up to its predecessor. And of course to the expectations of players. This is now a different environment: Jensen works for Interpol and is based in Prague. Unfortunately, we only have this one hub in the game (as opposed to HR's Detroit and Hengsha). Still, the area is big and offers a dozen side missions at least and of course many collectibles. We have a new nerd (Koller is great but his hipsteresque style can never match the rude remarks made by Pritchard), a new pilot, a partner-in-crime lady and a new boss (with a lot less appealing office compared to that of Sarif). Here and there we get glimpses of what happened to our "old" friends, still, the new guys simply are not that great. And while the story is good the "global threat" is nowhere as imminent as it was in HR.
This has been brought to perfection. You can perform takedowns anytime an enemy gets close regardless of how Jensen is positioned compared to the NPC. HR went far by allowing us to take out those sitting (and showing a cool animation) but MD takes a step further: even when he crouches behind a box Jensen can quickly get up and do fistycuffs. After that he pulls the unconscious body back. The best is when you are in an office: you just start throwing some boxes about and wait for the patrolling guards at the door one by one.
We have a couple of new augs that are devastating. Most emphasize combat gameplay so much so that very soon you completely forget what Typhoon is. Plus, our Remote Hacking allows us to disable turrets, cameras and drones for a short period of time and even to turn off the lasergrid for good. This coupled with the above-mentioned improved stealth mechanics results in a much easier game - provided you have the necessary patience and can ditch the Rambo approach. The experimental augs can do some harm to Jensen so you are required to turn off another, already purchased aug. However, a side mission later on completed eliminates this issue and when you start New Game+ and a couple of hours in you max out Jensen you realise just how amazing it is to play this game with the stealthy approach!
Well, beside the nuke software (that wins us a node immediately but with 100% detection rate) we now have furtivity, overclocking and reveal. The game mechanics are the same but some added software give it variety. Nothing we actually needed but then again some people expect new in all walks of Jensen's life otherwise that's a wrongly spent 60 bucks! It should also be noted that weapons can be upgraded (their magazine size or damage output) since there are many crafting parts scattered across the levels. You also have EMP rounds for the pistol, shotgun and even rifle. Its nice to ease the combat style approach, however, I was never really keen on doing a walkthrough this way.
Beside the fact that there are a lot of collectibles the game has another gameplay mode called Breach. You practically do the same stealth or combat approach but in a virtual reality this time. You have dozens of missions and before each you can pick a loadout. You have to approach databanks and once the necessary amount of data is downloaded from them you have to quickly leave by going to the spawning point before the timer runs out. There are challenges, leaderboards and achievements here. Breach items found during Jensen's story can be unlocked here.
Yes it was. This is a great game still and while it is a bit rough around the edges when it comes to its story I liked solving another case with Jensen and even better is the fact that this game brings us closer to getting to know the real people behind the game's events. While many were disappointed in the ending it should be noted that it prepares us for the oncoming 3rd episode. Too bad the developers announced they'll be focusing more on the Marvel universe. Instead of a lengthy expansion we'll get short DLC stories - an expansion is better but this is simply not the direction the market is currently going in.
After approximately 80 hours by barely checking what Breach is I can safely say this is a great sequel. It could have used a little more polish (especially story-wise), still, this is a great purchase for those who liked Human Revolution.

Masquerada has been a overwhelming joy to play. Marry a brilliant story, star-studded voice acting and solid mechanics, the game does live up to the promises made by the development team - and more.
Challenging and intriguing, it's a must for rpg lovers who are looking for the twists and turns of a plot that unravels only to bind you.
I would say more, but doing so would only give away what we, the player, must experience for ourselves.

I backed Masquerada on Kickstarter and I'm so glad this game has finally been released!
The art and voices are definitely the highlights of this game. I enjoyed looking at all the little details in the maps and the rich colour palette. The voice acting is top notch, lending an incredible amount of immersion to the world. I can feel that a lot of love went into making this.
Although the story is linear (you don't get to make any dialogue choices to pursue story branches), it unfolds at an engaging pace so I hardly minded.
Highly recommended if you like: rich world-building, isometric games, art history (seriously - check out some of the handdrawn details on the maps and buildings), and tactical pause-and-play (great for people like me who get easily flustered by real-time combat).
EDIT: I have finished the game, after sneaking in a few hours here and there over the past few nights.
I have to say - I was blown away by the ending. The game was trotting along merrily as an investigative mystery (see the earlier part of my review), and then shifted tone in the third and fourth Acts. I won't spoil it, but suffice to say, I was tearing hard at the credits. I give it a solid A+ for handling such deft storytelling.
After moving onto the harder battles, I feel the key is to pause often (and pause at the start of the fight) and plan your movements. You need to pause and reposition every few seconds to line up a combo, but when you do, the fights are much smoother than fighting in real time which often leads to companion AIs going kamikaze. I think the latest patch also improved the companions AI a lot more, especially the ranged fighters.
Unfortunately, due to the nature of the story, there is no replay value for more plot (only 1 main storyline).

I was a backer for Masquerada’s Kickstarter campaign at the basic game tier, and it’s yet another quality Kickstarter game that I would have thrown some more money at if I knew it was going to be this good.
Masquerada is a Real Time with Pause RPG that feels more like a JRPG to me in structure. The game is very linear, there are no sidequests, dialogue choices, and world maps and stuff like that. But that is not really a negative, because Masquerada makes sure that the journey is a real engaging one. When it comes to the combat the game still needs some work, mainly in that unlike in most RTwP RPGs you can’t select your whole party. This becomes an issue because the Party AI is rather weak and won’t get out of the way of stuff like AoE attacks. On Normal this isn’t much of a problem, but I’d advise against playing on Hard for the time being. Also a few bosses and enemies seem rather unbalanced, able to do obscene amounts of damage that just feels kind of broken. (Like one mid-game boss does more damage than even the final boss does.) The core of the combat is quite fun though, it’s fast paced and feels good, especially the late game when you have real good abilities. So any problems the combat has can probably be fixed, the devs have said they’ll be on it. The game also has no manual saves, which is a rather dumb decision nowadays. (Though it never became problem for me) But yet again that’s a problem that can be patched. (Hell Shadowrun had that same problem too at first, and I love Shadowrun.) I’ve also ran into some bugs, one game-breaking in the tutorial, but as I said the devs will be on it, they seem real receptive.
Visually the game looks really pretty. I’ve ran into some graphical glitches, but overall the game does a bang up job for an indie game on a budget. The soundtrack is also real good stuff too. Overall the game has a nice atmosphere, filled with color and beauty.
Now when it comes to narrative, Masquerada is real damn good, standing toe to toe with some of the recent RPG greats. The game creates an interesting world with fleshed out and likable characters. The game is also filled to the brim with codex entries that you find strewn throughout the game.  I read everyone that I could find and you know a game’s narrative is good when you want to read all the text it gives you. Many of the codices are also used to flesh out the protagonist, Cicero, and his past.  The main cast all have depth and are likable. The characters are also really brought to life by the excellent voice acting brought by some of the industry’s VA veterans such as Jennifer Hale, Liam O’ Brien, Dave Fennoy, Matthew Mercer, Crispin Freeman, and more. Masquerada’s narrative kept me engaged the whole way through. The ending is the right kind where they are some loose ends that can be taken up with a sequel, but pretty much the main narrative of the game has been resolved so it’s not an unfulfilling sequel hook.
So in conclusion while there are some flaws that can be fixed, Masquerada is a damn fine game that deserves to stand shoulder to shoulder with recent indie RPGs like Shadowrun, Aurion, and LISA and Undertale. I definitely recommend any RPG fan to buy it, it's well worth it.

It's immediately apparent that Masquerada was lovingly crafted, and the game is charming with its stylized art direction, rich backstory, and ample voice acting. The RPG elements are rather lightweight, limited to ability trees and switching between masks. Experience points/levels and equipment (other than your mask) are absent--perhaps most frustratingly with that last RPG convention.
I find the writing in this game to be a bit of a double-edged sword. Again, I can tell a lot of thought and care have gone into crafting the dialogue and descriptions in the game. At the same time, the wording often comes off as overly flowery, stumbling in its own attempts at eloquence. This is a minor quarrel, probably one that few players will have, but after reading and listening to a few hours of the game's writing as of this review, I feel it is worth mentioning.
I hope the game's AI will be refined in an upcoming patch. Characters currently need near continuous micromanagement, since they tend to wander off and switch targets almost immediately after initiating your command. Getting your party to concentrate on a single enemy in a group is a chore. Telling every member to hold their position helps, but isn't foolproof, and still requires more party-sitting than I think should be necessary.
That all being said, I'm impressed by Witching Hour Studios' polish on its focused feature set. Masquerada does what it does well, even if "what it does" may feel a bit limited from a gameplay perspective. If you view this as a visual novel with RPG enhancements, you won't be disappointed.
EDIT (Oct 3): Removed the complaint about lack of respec. Apparently, I'm not far enough in yet. :)

As a kickstarter, I was REALLY looking forward to this game. And in some cases, it delievered. In others...not so much.
First off, setting, story, voice-acting: all was superb. Everything I wanted. I found myself wanting to explore and learn everything I could about the Citte and all of its inhabitants and hidden histories. I was drawn in by the superb performances of the voice actors, and the story was gripping that one doesn't mind linearity, if that is a hang-up for you.
I was also a huge fan of the magic system; sure, it followed the Last Airbender formula, but the incorporation of not only masks, but the design, decoration, and stances made it feel far more vibrant and its own thing rather than a carbon copy: each mask/weapon can be coated in a concoction of special inks and herbs to give it more properties, and different masks have different "Specials" that can be activated.
So why did I say 'no' on recommending? Well, others have touched upon it. Combat is heavily, and I mean HEAVILY micro-manging. Unless you are hitting the SPACE BAR and bringing up the tactical screen, your companions will go off do whatever they want. They obey only the first command you give them, then the AI decides whether to follow suit or do its own thing. Nor can you scroll through the battlefield while the tactical screen is up; it's frozen in place.
EDIT: Apparently you CAN move the tactical screen by moving the mouse to the edges of the screen. Being one of the things I tried (and didn't work) I can only assume a buggy glitch on my end and not a knock on the game itself.
And yet despite having to so closely manage everything, combat is very simple: Right click a target, click a special ability if you want to use it, MAYBE engage in flanking manuevers if you aren't so ridcioulously outnumbered, and that's about it. If direct combat is going to be so simple, than more tactical options would be nice.
The "searching" in the game when not in combat is also disappointing. Just find where the colored circle is, step in it, click "E". Congratulations, you found the pokeball. I'm not exactly expecting a full on investigative system, but something a bit more involved than, 'point and click' WOULD be nice. You feel less like a bad♥♥♥♥♥Inspetorre and more like Inspector Gadget, following bread-crumbs so obvious it becomes monotonous. Every once in a while you learn about the lore through observation or listening to people's conversations, and then it feels organic. Otherwise, it's to the PC's Encyclopedia Britannica!
As those are the only two real GAME mechanics, I find those to be harsh criticisms of a game. While the power selection IS nice, some paths are clearly better than others (don't go the magician/distance fighting route; it just isn't worth it. Leave that to your designated distance NPC instead...or do what I did and never use him, because he sucks).
I mentioned the story just now, and that is true of the main one. However, I have two further (spoiler-free) critiques of thath, which adds to the "No" column. One, the main villain's motivation is clear, and makes a certain amount of sense, but HOW the villain came to this view point is never explored. Perhaps I missed something, but there seems to be a gap between how the villain got from point A to point B.
Second, your companions. Okay, in these games, it's almost a given that every companion will have a side-quest that you must help them overcome some personal demon to get closer to them. Except...you only get one side-quest. One that deals with a sensitive issue with such heavy-handed hamminess I needed several slices of bacon afterwards. People who play the game know of what I speak. Now, it isn't totally useless creator-preaching; we get to see an important aspect of the secular relgion/cultural beliefs of the Citte, and how it can affect, influence, and motivate lives.
However, it is VERY jarring that it is the only such side-quest we get. You read that right; we get no such similar sidetracks for our other characters. Two of them are handled almost off-handedly during the main quest-line, and the other...DOES your fourth companion get anything? After hinting at some hidden relation to the main character and talks of avenging someone's death...it never goes anywhere.
Oh, and sequel-baiting. I can't abide by the damn sequel-baiting.
So yeah, this game has problems. Glaring ones, actually. And yet...and yet, I want to love it, want to see it do well, and see more about this very inventive world we have been given a glimpse of. The relations of a powerful and vibrant port city who's gift of magic helps make them a center of their world...yet only so far as their borders stretch. A nation that fled religious oppresion for freedom, only to engage in social (and worse) oppresion within its own walls. Factions and politics and people in between, just trying to make a living; the city felt ALIVE. That's a feat to be celebrated in any game. Plus, it's not like this is some $60 AAA title; the game is 25 bucks, hardly a rip-off by any stretch of the imagination.
So I guess I have to say, No, I don't recommend it...but at the same time I don't tell you to turn away and run in horror. Look at the premise. Read through the reviews, and make your own choice. I can vouch for the story (mostly), the world, the music, and the voice-acting. Characters are interesting (if at times 2-D) and the game looks pretty (it should; that's where the kickstarter money was supposed to go). A host of skills for each of your four magic paths, plus three "styles" on how to use all of them, give you (on the surface, at least) a lot of options in combat. However, the gameplay is not the greatest in the world; micromanaging companions, the at-times stupid AI, borderline hands-off controls, and an almost useless tactical screen can make combat a chore at times. When not in combat, searching is really look around room, find purple/blue/gold circle, click E, watch cutscene. If those don't bother you, then ignore my 'No' and give the game a go.

I backed this game on Kickstarter.
Pros:
+They kept their promises on what this game would deliver.
+The sound track is very good and goes well with the story the game is trying to portray.
+The story is well thought out and is enjoyable to play through.
+The artwork is well done and the characters are rememberable.
+Combat system is unique and challenging.
+You can build how you want your characters to be. There are many different upgrades you can choose from as the game progresses (how your weapons work, what kind of buffs you will receive, and the regular upgrades on skills).
+The lore is very well done.
+There are hidden conversations and lore you can find by fully exploring levels.
Con (or possible con):
+Combat has a high learning curve. If you're looking for a game that is more casual and easy to pick up skip this game.
+Levels are linear and not open world. Also, some of the hidden content appears the 4th time you go to a place but not the first 3 times so its easy to miss.
+If you want to power through the game, you miss most of the story.
+If you want to change your element because you don't like the playstyle, you have to make a completely new character.
Overall I'm pleased with how the game came out. I'd rate it 8/10.

First off before anything, you have to understand what kind of game this is. This is not a dungeon crawler like Diablo, this isn't a super action game like other games of this genere. This is a very story driven game, with a solid plot and a lot of backstory. This game is very linear, you pretty much are driven through the story and can probably beat the game without diviating off course. There are tidbits of information that you can find if you search for a bit, also some masks that you can find if you search a bit, but for the most part it is very linear.
Think of it as a new style Visual Novel Game.
So yes there is tons of text. Just walls and walls of text. I personally like it a lot. I love reading about the worlds history and about each character. I love reading about tidbits and finding new tidbits to read about. It makes the game that much more enjoyable for me. I can understand how people don't like that and don't want to do that. That is why before you think about this game, know that you're going to do a lot of reading. If you're okay with that, carry on. If you're not, stop now.
Pro's
- Beautiful Voice Acting
- Beautiful Art
- Amazing story
- Gameplay is challenging yet fun
Con's
- AI is kinda dumb
- LOTS of information/tons of reading (I don't see that as a con but I know others do)
- Linear Story
First off I'll start with the cons because I know thats what everyone reads first rather than pro's.
The game's AI definitly does need some tuning up. You can change the battle formation and styles in game, but I feel that they need a bit tweaking.
Like I said before, there is lots to read. I have enjoyed reading all of it to be honest. It is a journal entry written by the main character so you get a lot of first person opinions on a lot of things. It gives you more of a view of what kind of charachter Cicero is and you get to understand his psyche a lot more. But all in all, there is a ton to read. Even if you don't read the other stuff, the stuff you need to read to understand the plot and what's going on is a lot.
The story is very linear. Extremely linear. This game isn't meant for a hardcore gamer. This game is meant for someone who wants to enjoy an amazing story, a person who doesn't skip over cutscenes and listens to the characters talk it out. Very beautiful to me, however extremely linear.
Now the pro's are pretty self explanitory.
The voice acting is superb. Top knotch. Every single one of them, every single character, truly brings their character to life. I watch every single cutscene and don't skip over them because I want to hear the characters talk to each other. It truly is amazing.

This game is beautiful. I'm not sure if there is any other word I can use.
I wasn't expecting much when I picked this up. I wasn't one of the Kickstarter backers and I hadn't heard of it at all before. But I gave it a try, and I don't regret it at all.
Gameplay-wise, Masquerada is a very linear adventure featuring party-based, tactical combat. It's not the best rendition of this by any stretch, but the combat does its job well enough. Characters gain skills and weapon upgrades as they progress through the story. The combat system encourages flanking of enemies and tactical play, though at lower difficulties it can be played more directly with little trouble. Outside of combat, the game is mostly about moving from one story point to the next, while searching for additional lore notes and upgrades scattered across the maps.
The game follows Cicero in his investigation of a missing person. That sounds simple enough, but things get a lot more complicated, and tragic, as the game goes on. The story is what really elevates this game over others. Cicero and his friends are all generally good, but deeply flawed, people. The story that follows is as much about them overcoming their personal demons as it is about Cicero's investigation, and this is a good thing as the entire cast are so lovable. This is one of the few RPGs I've played where I can genuinely say I love all of the characters, and watching them overcome the tragic circumstances that befall them was the true drive for me to finish this game.
The voice-acting in this game is excellent, which helps keep the story moving.
If anyone really wants a good story in an RPG, I'd highly recommend this game. I found myself enthralled and playing it from beginning to end without pause, and that almost never happens to me.
