TL;DR: in the end, Overlord II is a rather ordinary >>ADVENTURE<< game with a satisfying amount of dark humour, nice visuals and some variety to keep it fresh. As a somewhat original take on the adventure genre, it is a game you would play more for the eye-candy, originality, story and laugh than for the gameplay itself. These goblinish minions are as funny as their yellow counterparts (from the movie Despicable Me, if you really managed to miss them by now), but they can't completely redeem this game.
Personal Rate: 6.5/10
---------------------------------
I strive to provide somewhat brief reviews for games, so I try to focus on the essentials instead of covering everything it could be said about Overlord II. If you feel you need more details or a second opinion (which I recommend you do get), read other reviews and check YouTube videos. Also, English is not my native language, so be forgiving if you find any error, and kind enough to let me know about it.
Having that said, I must get this straight out of the door: every single written review I've found about this game, both official or player-made, fails to mention that THIS IS NOT a strategy game / RPG blend, as you'd be forgiven for thinking given the game description, the pictures and the Steam Tags.
It is actually an adventure game with some very light strategy / RPG gimmicks. Do not expect to command troops in open battles, to decide where to strike or defend next given your enemies' movements, neither to truly customize your Overlord avatar: this is nothing like Sacrifice or other RTS / RPG / Open World games out there, and the Store description is very misleading.
In very few words, your goal is to complete levels in a quasi-linear sequence, using the iconic minions to solve puzzles and complete several tasks while searching for hidden items. Enemies generally do not respawn, grow in numbers, move around the map nor follow any general strategy, so you can consider them part of the puzzle: you must beat them with minimal loss of minions when you get to their area of the map, and to do this you usually need to get the right number of the appropriate minion types, and use them accordingly. Each finished level unlocks more tools to complete the next ones while progressing the story a little.
There are a lot of different, marginal things to do in this game, and this sets Overlord II apart from other adventure games. For instance, you get to do some sidequests. You may improve / slightly customize your Tower of Evil and forge different items to use (but with a very poor set of items to choose from). You may visit the same level several times (although enemies generally do not respawn, as said before) to unlock previously blocked areas, you will conquer towns (as part of the storyline) and may reap the benefits from them (weapons and, ultimately, minions) from time to time. You get to choose a mistress.
However, these are all gimmicks with little usefulness: ultimately, the game is level-based and linear, your choices have little to no consequence both on the story and on the gameplay, and all those gimmicks are there more for aesthetics, amusement and sense of novelty than for real gameplay value.
Also, as many others have said, the PC controls are somewhat clunky and there are some bugs, but nothing major or unbearable IMHO.
In the end, Overlord II is a rather ordinary >>ADVENTURE<< game with a satisfying amount of dark humour, nice visuals and some variety to keep it fresh. As a somewhat original take on the adventure genre, it a game you would play more for the eye-candy, originality, story and laugh than for the gameplay itself. These goblinish minions are as funny as their yellow counterparts (from the movie Despicable Me, if you really managed to miss them by now), but they can't completely redeem this game.
Do I recommend it? If on sale, yes. Otherwise, I think you can find better games out there with a similar price tag.

Gnomoria is an isometric civilization builder. It is clear that Gnomoria is heavily influenced by (because saying 'steals from' is frowned upon) the incredibly popular but also incredibly difficult and intimidating game Dwarf Fortress (which I also love) but makes it more user-friendly and forgiving.
The game can be both brutally punishing and immensely rewarding. Playing your first game will end in inevitable death, probably during the first enemy invasion or your first winter. It is to be expected. As you gradually push further and further with each new civilization you found, you become more attuned to the importance of certain resources and the nuance of city design. Finding ways to optimize building and planning are not taught to you by the game, but learned through bloody trial-and-error. Six or seven games, you'll find your stockpiles bursting before the start of your first winter and the initial goblin invasion cute at best.
Gnomoria is a game where you need to be willing to fail (and fail hard), but also be ready—perhaps even eager—to try again. You'll reach a point where all of your gnomes have tasted delicious goblin sausage and are waiting, steel armor and swords gleaming in the summer sun, sweating with anticipation at the next attack, ready for their next meal to charge into battle with them like the little monsters they are.
I should point out that your gnomes are the monsters in the scenario, not the goblins, and you will be proud of them for it.

Gnomoria is a town building game that involves moderately sophisticated combat. By "town building game", I mean the game features a economic model where industries of tools and products to sustain your workers, keeping them healthy and happy, and equip them for work and battle. In this sense it's similar to games such as Caesar.
It also features digging, which is similar to Dungeon keeper exepct that 1) goblins invade instead of human heroes 2) instead of many flat dungeons on many different maps, you focus on building one dungeon that can span ~200 levels.
The combat is moderately sophisticated because you control the production of equipments and roles of your soldiers but not directly moving them to battle. You are allowed to say "charge" or "fly", but that's about it. Your gnomes level, but without a skill tree you do not micro-manage them.
In it's current status (0.9.13, July/15/2014), the game is sufficiently sophisticated, although no way as sophisticated as Dwarf Fortress. It's a nice "tutorial mode" if you plan to eventually move onto Dwarf Fortress.
The game definitely worth it at below $10, a steal if below $5.

Edit 3:
When I originally posted this review, I was a bit upset after having beaten the game. I stand by what I said originally, but didn't really articulate why I disliked this game so much very well. However, in a comment following this review, I ended up getting what I wanted to say a bit better. As such, I am appending those thoughts after the original review, as I feel the initial emotion is as important as the more calculated response.
Original Review:
Waste of time. Finished the game in, what, 15-20 minutes? It trys to be profound or enigmatic, but ultimately misses the mark. Minimalistic approach fails to either engross nor inspire curiosity. Of course, the first 15 minutes of the game is going to be the most important to make an impact. But this game manages to complete its entire experience in that time, without even a hint at a greater world, even when you don't know what you are doing.
Honestly, it just feels like another pretentious art piece that doesn't even manage (or attempt) to communicate anything at all. The "story" doesn't even connect to the game in any way, and is instead just thrown in there without thought, seperate from the game entirely. Its attempt to be cryptic will leave you almost wishing that there was more to it. But then the ending tells you all the mystery that might exist. Not even worth the time for free.
Thoughts from Comments:
I mainly play games for what they can do uniquely. I appreciate a fantastic art style, but I see no reason that the art needs the game to complete it. Like I said, I think this games art could be better enjoyed as a poster or part of a gallery. I genuinely feel that adding interactivity took away from the experience. I enjoy the pixel art as a separate work far more than the actual game. The artist is clearly very good, and I would love to work alongside them.
But the world isn't fleshed out very well, and I feel that takes away from [the game] a lot. Ultimately, Steam is a platform for games. If an art piece can't utilize the interactive medium in an effective manner, then the creators should ask if they really need to utilize that medium. I'm not saying "add combat" or more "gamey" elements, but rather find an interesting way to utilize the interactivity at the artists disposal than a bog standard platformer with a shell of a story.
I'm just so disappointed with my short time with this game. There is so much that could be there, but just isn't. If you disagree (as many evidently do), I can't take away your enjoyment. Have a blast! But I can't justify recommending it for anything but the poster DLC.

Just make sure to be smart about which character combinations you choose.  Hint:  the dice are the important part,  if you don't have two dice with bolts you are doing a very bad job of choosing characters.  You'll have dozens of opportunities to add new team members.  You amass tons of food in the game (I usually have 40-50 food stockpiled at the end),  so you'll have plenty of opportunities to reroll if you get unlucky.  Just make sure to give yourself the dice you will need to make the roles.
Decisions do matter in this game.  Think about your route,  and which buildings your characters can handle (you can check out building before entering them),  think about your party contruction,  strategize about which goals to prioritize.  Play smart and its easy to win (as long as you make it past the first 10 turns).

After an hour of the RNG throwing horrible things at me constantly, I had to quit because my stress levels had simply gotten way too high.
I don't know if I was just unlucky, or I didn't know what I was doing (possibly both?), but the game -really- feels incredibly stacked against the player, to the point that it feels absolutely impossible to make any positive headway.
It's a losing battle from the beginning, and just keeps getting worse.
The concept is interesting, but I found the actual experience of it so utterly painful that I doubt I'll play this game again unless I feel particularly masochistic.
I barely paid a dollar for it (on sale), and I'm almost tempted to get a refund. I won't, since it's only a dollar, and I'm lazy, and on the off chance that I ever decide to give it a shot.
I really want to like the game... there's certainly some interesting elements here, and I like the whole board game/cards/rebuild the city thing, but man... it's just too relentless.
You go around the map, searching through locations for useful things (items, characters to join you, food) and doing quests, all the while dealing with the infected rat threat. You deal with these things by rolling dice, each character having a dice pool.
Dice aren't numbered, but have icons representing certain skills/abilities like awareness, endurance, etc.
To "clear" an event (whether you're searching, or fighting rats, or whatever), it "costs" a certain amount of skills/abilities (which you must roll with your dice). For example, defeating some rats might require you to roll one die of agility and one of endurance; if you succeed, you defeat the rat, if you fail (don't roll what you need), the rat hurts you.
When you get hurt, you receive a wound of some kind, which usually makes you lose dice rolls of a certain type.
There are also random events (I had nuclear fog, a thunderstorm, and a heatwave) which can all negatively impact your dice rolls as well (basically "stealing/eating up" certain rolls).
The problem is that there are so many bad things constantly happening that it's basically impossible to get anywhere, as things beyond your control will constantly "eat up" your rolls, making it hard to impossible to progress.
If you enjoy board games and are a glutton for punishment, maybe give this game a try.
Otherwise, stay away.

This is a peculiar title, in that I enjoy it quite a bit, but would have a hard time recommending it to someone who played the original Warlock.  The game has traditional 4x gameplay in a fantasy setting, with hex-based territory management and some interesting spins on the world map and city management.  There are even some very nice quality-of-life features, like the building progression map or the spell book.  These features are all very competantently implemented; the problem is that the previous game did these exact same things as well.  In terms of game rules and over graphics, the game is essentially the same, aside from a new game mode entitled Exiled mode, which puts a new spin on the classic Campaign paradigm used in such games.  However, aside from all that, I dont think there is enough here to justify someone who owned the original to upgrade to the sequel.  I enjoy this game a great deal, and if this is your first foray into the Warlock series, do buy it, as its a fantastic title, I just dont know if returning Warlock players would be justified in spending $30 price tag for a game that is essentially a DLC updated version of the original.

I've been enjoying this game immensely, but I can't recommend it until some issues in game receive some much-needed attention. In exiled mode, there are a few critical quests that can break via various common conditions in game, causing them to never be able to be completed. Though it won't halt your progress, it may create cripplingly challenging conditions (Think of all the land you own slowly falling into the ocean turn by turn.) that can be impossible to recover from. The AI behaves much like a stuntman running through glass windows, and it can create an unintentional mess (Or is it intentional?) when an AI settler barges into a dangerous dimension and invites an army of shadow dragons into your shard to do battle with  your tier 1 archers. Also sometimes you read a description just to discover that is basically what they just told you by voice. At least mark those stuff as read already.
Voice acting and track is great so far, what I'm really not sure about is the combat system.
Don't get me wrong, I'm enjoying fighting. I even set "Hard" difficulty and was enjoying it. However the checkpoints makes VERY PAINFUL dying in this game: for example I changed the AI right before a big fight (takes a while to change the AI), learned some new skills and went in. Died and all my changes were not saved. I'm fine with check points, but KEEP my changes to the character and AI. This is very important for an RPG. In addition, is not clear at all when the game it's saved, you must be really careful to the "autosave" text to appear, sometimes you want to go to bed and you just have to keep playing to notice that Autosave message...
Anyway, the combat lacks so far because it's chaotic and the skills are not that inspired. I picked fire (who was so crazy to tell you to pick between 4 elements without giving you any direction or information about skills!?). You can't properly tell "all characters attack this guy" (yes you have to go over them one by one and tell to attack), in addition there is an entire combo system around "elemental tags", but only 2 skills per character have them and only if you pick a specific upgrade in a skill.
I'm still early in the game. The combat system is "enjoyable", but not great. While I value the story, honestly I consider the combat system more important in ANY videogame, because it's the thing that you "repeat" during the whole game, so being lacking in that is equivalent in saying the gameplay is not good enough.
Hopefully I'll be able to change this review in a few boss fights, but I wouldn't recommend this game for this price tag, the gameplay is too lacking.
That being said, graphics are amazing, plot is great and soundtrack is good, together with nice setting.

Kickstarter backer here. This review was edited after I finished the game.
Let me start with that I really like about the game:
1. the voice acting. It is superb
2. I really like the graphics
3. edited: I love the story...absolutely love it, from the first to the last moment.
I don't mind the game being as linar as it is as it is leading me through an immersive and captivating story.
To understand all the points you have to know that I have problems with my hands and cannot do action stuff or anything like that where the hands have to be in movement and active all the time. Also, I am playing the game on OS X so some problems may not apply to you.
With that said, here the points I really dislike:
combat
1. micro management: it is impossible to set things up and expect your chars to keep to the setup. "Hold" keeps until the very first action and after that it is turned off again. So you are constantly tabbing through your chars, setting them up once again just to see it's all gone again
2. targetting: just like holding...it is temporary and changes whenever the chars feel like it. Again, yet another point where you have to micro manage over and over. Also, it sometimes seems to me the chars love to run into the enemy aoe fields to suicide.
general
1. the checkpoint system: It is setup in a way that you have to repeat the same combat over and over if you fail the 2nd fight in a row.
2. the checkpoint system: due to the constant micro management in combat, I often end up with hurting hands after only 1 combat and I'd like to quit the game for a bit to recover them from the strain of the micromanagement. But, unless there happens to be a checkpoint after a fight I'd just have to repeat that fight if I did that.
3. added: this is the only game in my library where I looked forward to loading screens because that meant the game would be saved :)
progression
1. At some point, I realised that the element I had chosen wasn't what I wanted and decided to restart and choose another element. Well, that won't work...all these decisions are saved and cannot be changed even on a restart...I had chosen water and water it was going to be...even the 2nd time around. I often restart in RPGs when I see I made a mistake or realise I'd prefer another choice in eg. skills, etc. that I didn't take the first time around. Well, no luck here.
Your element will survive a restart and can't be changed
Your skill points and how you distributed them will survive a restart and can't be changed
and as a consequence, you won't gain any skill points in any of the fights you do the 2nd time around until you are back at the point where you chose to restart.
Added: in response to comments
For me, going back in time, call it restart/rewind or something else means undoing all I've done and that includes decisions, choices, etc.. On the other and, I freely confess I normally keep far away from games with checkpoint systems so my understanding of the system may be wrong.
Yes, I could have created a new profile at that point in time to "properly" restart, especially after seeing that restarting a chapter isn't a proper restart but, tbh, going through all of it a 3rd time was a bit much at the time.
Summary (now, after finishing the game)
I am much more torn now...on one hand, I truly loved the story (I can't remember when a story in a game caught my attention like this the last time), otoh, the problems didn't get less but more over time...so I stand by my original vote:
A beautiful game marred by too many problems...what a pity

I will recommend it, but this game has lots of the problems.
This is a detective story, set up in really interesting world. You can not compare it to BG, or any other CRPGs cause it's not. It is feels like narrative story, where the combat is just a complex QTE.
PROS
- The story of the world is fascinating. Rich with lore, factions, conflict.
- The characters are rich, but the game really struggles to explain it. However I loved the fact that everyone is somewhat "grey". No pure good & evil.
- The fabula is unique (at least for me). Brings the Vampire: The Masquerade fascination to the table.
- The story might be just engaging enough for you to continue.
- Estetics, music, atmosphere are really nice.
CONS
- The mechanics. It might be the prefference, but it does not force you to conserve your spells (they are a based on cooldowns). It's really hard to pull combos, which should be the shining jewel of the system. The combat is just too noisy for that.
- The story is very linear. No searching, no secrets, no reward for curiosity.
- The surroundings are bit rushed. Many of the areas are just boxes with texture, no context, couple of extra items.
- The controls do not feel responsive. The actions are not instantaneus, thus its really hard to tell whether you botched sequence or it's still pending. It might be related to the enemy hit boxes.
- The checkpoint system is abnoxious. No decent saves.
- Zero replay value.
- The prologue served really bad for the game.

is a game with a very interesting concept which I will describe in the next paragraph. It is entirely multiplayer as interaction with other players is crucial. It's unlike any other games I've played before and its concept is very well made.
If this review is too long for you, I suggest you to only read the first paragraph about the game's content and the final verdict at the end.
In OBEY, one player is a leader and controls all the other players from a giant robot. This robot has the ability to shoot bullets and rockets that kill the disobeying players, if the leader sees them and shoots them.
Other players, bunnies, have to listen to the leader. They have to wear tracking collars and carry weapons into the robot's feedbox. The leader pays them for that, but the point of the game is for the bunnies to sneak into the robot and take the leader's position. In other works, you have to obey until you have the chance to hide and sneak to the robot.
More players would be much appreciated, but the game is never really discounted a lot. Bringing more players would bring some energy to the community and the developer would have a much easier time getting new ideas and improving the overall impression of the game.
The idea for this game is amazing and, in my opinion, it is worth supporting the developer, although the price is a bit high for the current amount of content. Interaction with other players adds a whole new level to player experience. This game is really great at making you think how to free yourself while not raising any suspicion and, when you manage to get in charge of the robot, you actually feel rewarded and accomplished.
The game is well made, still missing some options and players, but is overall in great shape. I certainly recommend it.

"Corpsing" is perhaps the most major mechanic, if you are killed by a laserwall or flames then you will leave a corpse, if you drop this corpse into the feederbox the robosaru will lose a fairly significant amount of money, so it gives incentive for the robosaru to be very careful, oh and it's also possible to destroy corpses by shooting them as the Robosaru, so you don't have to worry about a whole ton of rabbits running corpses constantly, though they probably will try to do so anyway if you give them reason to.
Collars increase your money gain per in-game tick from 2 to 6, and provided you have a kind but controlling overlord, also lets him/her keep easy track of where you are and, if particularly kind, the robosaru might even give you extra money for ratting out runners and such.

Not a great game by any stretch of the mind, and far from the best Deus Ex game.
Having said that, here is a list of interesting things that Deus Ex: Mankind Divided is doing that deserve to be acknowleged:
- Densely packed small open world feels more detailed and alive than should be possible.
- Obsessive attention to detail.
- Art direction is beautiful.
- The juxtoposition of old prague archetecture and newer technologies is fitting thematically.
- Non-augmented humans wear transparent clothing to show they have human limbs. Nice touch.
- The world is a maze/network of security exploits, and it's puzzles are downright enthralling.
- Hacking minigame doesn't suck. I didn't think that was possible!
- Grid based inventory is easy to understand and manage.
- Cyberpunk with crazy global conspiracies galore!
- DLC is friggin great.
- Jensen is sexy as ♥♥♥♥.
Here are a few things I don't so much like about this game:
- Writing isn't half as smart or deep as it thinks it is.
- Game is MUCH less ambition than Deus Ex: Human Revolution, and suffers for it.
- Jensen Stories feel tacked on. Weird way to access DLC and side content.
- A Deus Ex game that doesn't visit China or America feels... weak...
- Some augmentations feel samey, and aren't worth investing in parralell.
- Game is content to tell rather than show how Jensen ended up where he is. Missed opportunity.
- Jensen is angsty as ♥♥♥♥.

First off, DO NOT LISTEN TO PEOPLE TELLING YOU THIS GAME IS BAD OR SHORT!
Now that we got that out of the way, Mankind Divided is a solid successor to Human Revolution and the Deus Ex franchise in general. The game has improved gameplay from HR, especially when it comes to stealth, beautiful graphics (if you have powerful enough machine) and excellent level design with multiple paths how to accomplish pretty much everything.
The lenght of the game very much depends on your playstyle. If you like to explore everything, do every little side mission, hack every computer, talk to everyone and play stealthily, you're easily looking at 40 to 50 hours of amazing gameplay. If you like to play guns blazing, shoot everything and not care about exploration, then you can see the end credits in less then 10 hours. But you haven't really finished the game. Deus Ex was always about exploration. If you want simple FPS, this game isn't for you. If you want an immersive world with complicated story that makes you think, buy this now.
However, the game does end on a HUGE cliffhanger, and if the rumours that the sequel was put on hold by SE are true, we may never see the ending of Adam Jensen's story, which would be a shame. So BUY THIS NOW!

Pros:
-Great gameplay (gunplay, conversations)
-New augs are great
-Prague is a great hub
-Story is well constructed
-Sidequests are really good in the way that they are implemented
-Microtransactions are there but they're not shoved in your face
-The final boss can be approached in any way
Cons:

-There are microtransactions if you're annoyed by that kind of thing
-Only one city hub
Final Verdict: 8.5/10

There are so many phenomenal aspects to this game.
Gameplay Mechanics: This game requires the use of a controller to play because you move each brother with one half of the controller. This concept is so revolutionary and fits so well into the game that I will always be impressed by it. Sure it can be hard to get used to and you may mix up which brother you are attempting to control, but it's 100% worth it. It really adds to the gameplay experience and emphasizes the brothers' cooperation as they go on their journey.
Visuals: In this game there are several points where there is a bench where you can have the brothers sit and admire the view. This is not an overestimation of the game's beauty by the creators. This game is absolutely stunning. I found myself sitting there for a couple minutes simply taking in the surroundings.
The Brothers: Each brother has their own distinctive personality and it truly shines throughout the game. I found myself interacting with everything twice (once with each brother) just because I wanted to see their reaction.
The Feeling: This game is a very emotional game. It deals with some heavy themes and it really made me stop to think about how these characters truly feel. It became more than a game to me. Couple this with the outstanding musical score and you might want to have a box of tissues handy.
I could probably talk about how much this game means to me for hours, but I think I will cut it here.
I hope you try this game and experience it for yourself.

Brothers, A Tale of Two Sons is a game about two brothers who set on a adventure in search of a cure for their sick father.
This is an adventure game that's mostly without dialogue, and dialogue that does occur between characters does so in a fictional language without any translation for the player. You're left to your imagination to interpret what they could be saying, which isn't that difficult due to the gestures characters make.
It's short, visually stunning game with beautiful locations and simple but often interesting puzzles. For the most part the game is not so much about the story, but about the adventure and interactions of the two brothers with the world. It's fantastically well designed and I thoroughly enjoyed the experience.
When it comes to gameplay you can control both brothers simultaneously, each with one thumb stick and each has their own action button (you can use keyboard as well, but controller is heavily recommended). There are things one brother can and the other can't do, so they will have to work together in many situations to overcome puzzles and other problems on their way.
Overall I would highly recommend the game, even though it's relatively short it's an experience you won't forget.

A beautiful and emotional roller-coaster, Brothers feels more of a journey, than a game.
Set in a nordic-type fictional world, you simultaneously take control of two brothers, that have to embark on a dangerous journey to find a cure for their father's illness. What striked me first was the fact that the characters speak a non existent language and, without even being provided with subtitles, you have to understand what's going on in the whole story just by the characters actions and context! I found this to be a very innovative and different approach to convey each of the game's parts.
Subsequently, while the graphics were good enough, the scenery more than made up for it. Each stage was like a fairy tale brought to life (with giants, ogres and other creatures), but make no mistake, this is not a children's story, as evidenced by some of its final parts.
The ending was a real tear-jerker and hits you hard, especially since I couldn't believe that was it for the game. I thought there would be some kind of twist and it would complete on a more cheerful note... but no! Bravo to the developers for taking such a bold step.
The music is more or less constant throughout the game, with a specific tune that fits the game's environment, especially in the end.
Its length is also very short, about 3-4 hours long and the achievements are mostly easy, though not story related. Also, there are no collectibles at all, something I appreciated, considering how many modern games adopt this method to pointlessly prolong the game's duration.
Lastly, the game's controls were, probably, its weakest point. On one hand, they were kind of unique, making you control both brothers at the same time, with each analog stick, while on the other hand, that very fact made them confusing at times, as to which brother you were controlling. Thankfully there weren't any complex actions in it and the length was too short to make you worry about it.
All in all, I would even go as far as to call it more of an interactive movie, than a game and that's exactly why it's worth it.

Spend a lot more time in GTA IV without playing through the story and without add ons and without online content. Thats a giant step backwards.
The mechanic regarding the saving of cars is bad - like sitting at your desk screamingly bad. Every protagonist has a car that will respawn at their home every time. You also can upgrade cars as well (better looks, performance, stuff) and you can spend quite the fortune on your car. You can also save any car that you find in a garage at your home. This however does NOT replace the constantly respawning verhicle of your hero. So if you do not like your car you can get another one and you can save it. However if you lost your car (during a mission for example - and this will happen in like 90% of the missions) you might - you might! - be able to get it back by going to the police station and paying a small fee but sometimes your precious baby will be gone forever. Even going to the police station is a pain after a while. So only upgrade your base vehicles and dont bother with anything else. I always wanted a gamemechanic to save cars - but this sucks and could've been easily fixed.
Money. Money is actually worth something in this game which is good. However getting money is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥since there are not enough ways to actually earn money. Most missions have zero payout. F###ing ZERO. There seem to be no generic missions that allow you to repeatably earn money (car racing or stuff like that). I earned my cash through taxi driving. There is only one way to earn money effectively and thats buying shares at the right time. Some missions will affect shares drastically and you need to save money until that point and invest everything, do the mission and sell everything. ♥♥♥♥ this up and you'll be low on cash for the whole game.
The only missions with noteable payout are the robberies. Those are great! Awesome missions. You gather stuff and information and make a plan, hire crewmen and rob a bank or something. Bad (and cheap) crewmen might screw up parts of your robbery increasing difficulty and/or loosing cash in the process. Crewmen also have some stats and they will improve if you take them on more robberies. BUT there is only 4 of them. Four! One beeing the final mission. And you cant repeat them later! This feels like a lot of content has been cut out.
Also the 3 distinct character that you can play, while the immersion is great, their indivdual story gets lost rather quickly since most story missions include all three of them as soon as you unlock the third guy. And you'll notice really fast the following: You play one character, do everything, every sidequest and so on and then you have to switch to another dude (since theres nothing else to do), have some story progress with that one to unlock another mission for the first dude. This gets really annoying, especially because it disrupts some great storylines.
GTA V does right what all GTA titles do right so I think I dont really need to go into that. And still: It's too short. Theres no generic missions, the story is over really fast and feels cut in many ways. It's not the GTA that it is advertised to be. Maybe GTA VI will do the job.

Nyheim takes the setup of Rebuild and tweaks it more resemble a dice driven solitaire boardgame. Instead of zombies, it's killer mutated diseased rats. Move around searching, getting new characters and items, averting random event crises, and trying to fulfill quests. You can win by upgrading your HQ to max level, completing the string of primary quests, or simply surviving for one full year.
A lot of negtive reviews say the RNG is too hard. You can dismiss that as people who don't know what they're talking about, BUT I've played plenty of of "player(s) vs. the system" board games (Pandemic, Arkham Horror, Eldritch Horror, Elder Signs, Ghost Stories, Mansions of Madness, Yggdrasil, and others), so I'd like to think I can comment on the mechanics. I was looking forward to Nyheim because it looked like they were trying to emulate this experience.
Nyheim screws it up. Badly.
The dice system is like Elder Signs. Each die is 8 sided and there are 4 different symbols: hearts, eyes, lightning bolts, and lightbulbs. Thing is, not all dice are equal. Each party member gets to roll a die each turn and each character will have different symbol distributions on their die. Some might have an even spread. Some might have 4 bolts and a heart but nothing else. Every time you try to search, fight off rats, or solve challenges, they will each have certain symbols that need to be rolled to beat them.
The problem is you WILL get screwed when a challenge comes up requiring symbols you just don't have. Need 2 hearts? Too bad, there's only one die with hearts on it. 2 bolts? There are only 2 dice with one bolt each so it's a 1/64 chance each turn, and if you miss it then you get an injury which will eat a bolt roll every turn and the only way to get rid of it is to spend a turn resting but you to roll a bolt during resting and that's after it eats a bolt so again that's only a 1/64 chance of getting the double bolts you need to heal it and you have to do that 3 times to get rid of the injury. Then it's back to hoping for that 1/64 chance again and another injury every time you mess up. It's supposed to be a "strategy" to get characters or items with the right symbols, but you have no control over the options you'll get and will often be locked out of symbols no matter what.
These kind of games need a resource to fudge rolls. Usually it's to buy rerolls or guarantee a certain result. Nyheim does use the food resource for rerolls but that doesn't make any difference if you don't have the symbols in the first place. Some items can convert certain rolls to others, but it probably won't be the ones you need, you can't control which items you get, and each character can only carry one item. Other games solve this by making all dice the same so you always have a chance of rolling what you need, or wildcard symbols. Elder Sign lets you burn resources for rerolls, guaranteeing facing, or adding dice with better symbols on them. Nyheim tries to be these games but doesn't understand the balancing mechanic.
What these games also do is make defeat a matter of accumulated bad luck or bad decisions. Nyheim screws you with a single random result far too early and often. You have to establish a headquarters early on, and many important quests and crises happen at the HQ. Each search has a chance of spawning killer rats that will attack you every turn you're there. Spawn killer rats at the HQ the 2nd turn? "You're ♥♥♥♥ed; might as well start over" should be the game's slogan.
But you can't just start over. You have to play each defeat out to the very end if you want experience points, which are used to buy modifiers in future games. You can buy a perk with strengths and drawbacks for 50xp (more survivors spawn, but more rats show up, etc.) or 250xp for the perk without the drawback. You get maybe 50-150xp each run and the perks only last one game. Grind 5 runs to save up for a bunch of perks you buy for one game for your serious attempt at winning? Well the random number generator just ♥♥♥♥ed you that game so you die and all your perks are wasted. Have fun grinding more for another shot.
Nuts to that. This game BADLY needs to impliment some kind of system that allows wildcard rolls. Powerful rat swarms should not spawn early game (especially on your HQ) (and seriously, it gets to the point where searching isn't ever worth it unless it's for a quest). Injuries shouldn't be so severe (at least make the symbols they discard different from the ones required to heal them). Changes need to happen before this stops being anything but a futile RNG grindfest. I regularly play solitaire boardgames where 70% loss rates are the norm, and even I'm calling the RNG difficulty here B.S. And I really hope they do improve it, because the premise, basic setup, and polish are all good. If it was actually balanced to not be total B.S. anymore then this would be a great fun little game.

TLDR: Gameplay is bad due to bad controls, bugs are present in a non-early access game, art and story and music are fine but failed at simple step of gameplay. Price is a bit too much, episodic nature makes no sense. Want HM on PC? Just get Stardew Valley.
I really want to like this game. I backed it on Kickstarter and had high hopes for it, being completely unaware of Stardew Valley's production. Again, I utterly HATE to compare this game to another, as I like to look at games on their own, but no matter how biased I am, I can't bring myself to enjoy Wild Season.
Buggy, and awkwardly controlled are two major descriptions I'd give the gameplay. It just doesn't feel smooth, natural, or enjoyable, and for a farming simulator that is a HUGE mistake. Fluidity of controls is a MUST have when you're sitting at a computer for hours pressing buttons. You must enjoy your farm work, but if it's uncomfortable or frustrating, then you fail no matter how good the music, graphics, or story is. It's a game first, an experience second, this rule applies to all games. Wild Season fails at this first step.
Art is fine and pretty. I greatly enjoyed it, though I had a friend say that the portraits and the sprites give them an uncanny feeling. It is our opinions, and I do not fault this game for it's art style whatsoever. It looks cute and pretty, it's fine.
I don't know about the story, as I couldn't freakin' play the game! 1.6 hours is all I could manage, with additional time spent as I got an early demo being a kickstarter backer (gave a lot of freakin' money to have the access to that demo...).
Price is utterly stupid and ridiculous. I don't care what your reasoning is, the episodic nature of this game is doomed to fail, and I don't understand how the developers thought it was a necessary idea. Even if they were strapped for cash, common sense would tell them that this incredible price and separation of gameplay would only lead to people having complaints. It's not a freakin' telltale game with a story that can justify it, remember, gameplay should come FIRST in a farming sim, and I really feel the devs forgot this simple rule.
That, or they got utterly demoralized by it.
Too expensive, no consistency or communication with the fans in regards to updates, and completely unstable. When I first heard of this game, I was prepared to buy a five or four pack to give this game to many of my friends. I was so excited and hopeful for this.... I was a fool.
Lastly, and this is just utterly unfortunate for this game and the poor developers, why in all holy heck would I ever recommend this game when Stardew Valley exists? Stardew is solid in gameplay and story, it's a full and complete game, it's reasonably priced. There is NO reason to consider this game unless you just... like to buy badly made games???
I wish I can love this game. I'm EXTREMELY biased for this games favor, I really am, I loved many things about this game and waited for years for it, watched many streams of developers talking and streaming other HM games using them as inspiration and guidance. But even someone as biased as me would say this is a horrific choice. Just. No.
This game would've failed regardless of Stardew Valley. But then Stardew Valley DID come out, and that just make it even worse for this game. I hate jumping on the bandwagon of Stardew love but the fact is, that game is solid and decently designed, while this one is not.

Brawlhalla is a brawler that tries to do things a bit differently from the Smash Bros franchise. The game is centered around weapons you pick up during the fight, as they determine your entire moveset. Every Legend has two weapon types associated with them that has the same light attacks, but unique strong (signature) attacks. The game has a few unique features such as gravity cancelling, allowing you to execute any ground attack in mid-air. This allows for a lot of unpredictability and combo options.
The game has great netcode that uses servers, and a ranking system so you'll be fighitng people close to your skill level.
Having played a lot of Smash Bros in the past, I found it tricky to adjust to the lack of shielding and a cooldown on dodging. However the close-range nature of the fights feel personal and intense. You should definitely give it a chance if you're a fan of brawlers!

I Am Alive is such a peculiar game. It's one of those games that I play, and don't really enjoy, but want to keep playing. I mean, The game is very ambitious, and I'm having some amount of fun with it, but there's just some things about it that you can't help but think how this game may have benefited from some different design choices.
I enjoy the challenge that the limited continues provide.  It makes you want to play the game more carefully. I feel like the game rewards you for exploring, as you find additional items, and sometimes survivors to help, which will give you an additional retry, but it also punishes you by making your stamina go down, making you almost not want to explore.
It's little things like that where the game is sending you mixed messages where it starts to feel like a chore to play. Yet, then I end up raiding an area with a whole bunch of enemies, and I have to carefully pick & choose my next move, trying to make people surrender, or pushing them far enough back to kick them off a ledge, or getting close enough to stab them with my machette. all the while, I'm making sure I do them all in the right order and quick enough in order to avoid getting hit, and conserving my ammo, which is very precious.  Some might find this tedious and complicated, but I find it tense & exhilirating.
After you get through an area, just fighting group after group of guys, the game just makes you feel like this awesome Mad Max kind of character, and it's those moments, and the story (which is somewhat basic but kind of intriguing) that keeps me coming back to it.
The game is definitely not for everyone, and it has it's flaws... but for people who enjoys survival horror games, or just games with interesting systems and mechanics, I'd say to definitely check it out.

An excellent, relatively short game (5-9 hours) characterized by realistic-looking post-apocalyptic settings that are quite stunning to behold. The level of attention to detail is downright impressive and really helps to immerse you within its story that is rather simple at its core but is enhanced by endearing moments & characters that feel and act like living, breathing human beings. I found that I cared about the main character's plight and mission and was invested in trying to make this hellish future into a better place by saving an adorable little girl, helping to reunite her with her absent mother, encountering other survivors and aiding them when I could and murdering opportunistic SOBs that preyed on the weak and innocent, JUSTICE IS SERVED beeyatches! xD
The gameplay itself is well-balanced with platforming elements that emphasize managing your limited stamina during its many awe-inspiring climbing portions that have you scaling the side of unmaintained skycrappers, clambering across elevated scaffolding and more while using pistons to pause and recuperate at opportune moments. It made these sections feel tense, as close to reality that a game can get and a lot of fun.
Finally, the combat is also quite well-done as you can make charging gang members halt in their tracks by whipping out a gun, frightening them into holding their hands up as you either use this opportunity to back them into hazardous elements of the environments which is always a riot to watch unfold or blast them apart with well-placed shots. This is especially fun as you can do this while out of ammo but take too long and your opponents will wise up and charge you.
9/10

This game may look a lot like the original Warlock: Master of the Arcane, but it's got a lot more under the hood, besides new content.
Be prepared to experience something new, as a lot of the game mechanics have evolved and the old metagame is dead. As is always the case with innovation, things aren't necessarily right the first time but it's fair to say the devs and the producers have made substantial communication efforts with the community and have managed to instantiate a healthy feedback cycle.
Modding has also received official blessing and an editor has been developed to help create and edit maps and game content. There also appear a mysterious "campaign mode" but nothing is clear yet as to what this will be.
Anyway I could keep writing about the merits of the game but I'm drawn back that "one more turn" addictive feeling and I'll leave it at that. I hope to see you in the game lobby soon!

In general, I think it is a good game with great over-arching strategic decisions and gameplay.  The AI could certainly do with some improvements, but they're somewhat tough at high difficulty.  However, as a player of the original Warlock, I can't help but notice that this is almost the same game with a new campaign, a couple of new races, and some stragegy tweaks.  Would be better suited to be called a standalone expansion rather than a sequel.  So it is up to you if you think the price is worth it,
The good:
- Plenty of room for strategic mastery.  An example is: which cities to have included in the main cities (the one with the gold and iron resources, or the one with 2 pigs and a donkey? Or do I just keep both and just deal with the riots that arise?)
- Somewhat interesting storyline with some good challenges that hit you throughout the campaign
- "Just one more turn..." addictiveness that I haven't seen since Civ 3.  You always seem to be on the brink of achieving something.
The bad:
- Looooong drawn out campaign.  By the time I had reached Ardania, I was already sick and tired of the grinding.  And that was only on Medium size.  It needs a bit more depth to keep things interesting.
- Predictable AI.  Oh, you're amassing your troops near my city?  You must be declaring war in 3 turns.
The other:
- "Campaign" option in the menu (currently empty, but being pre-sale I can't complain, but I'm hopeful this will give some good replayability to the game)
- Spawns, spawns, and more spawns.  Just when you think you're done with those giants, the game decides to spawn 2 red dragon nests on the other side of the map so you basically lose the city before your troops can cross.  Good income, but very tedious after a while.  Also - why do so damn many of the spawns fly?  My patrolling army was made up entirely of archers/wizards since the soldiers were just completely useless.

I have completed the 1st two acts of the game so far on Twitch and am about 7 hours into the game. I dont know how many acts there are so unsure how much more there is. But I believe I have got far enough to have learned what the game has to offer.
To start the art style and animation really stands out, the voice acting is top notch and the voice cast has a large collection of recognisable names. When you realise how much dialog there is in the game you will learn to appreciate that the voice acting works very well. I wouldnt be surprised if over half of the time I have spent in game so far was listening to the characters talking. The lore is very deep and I am enjoying the story, I paused the game at the end of Act 2 where there was an interesting story plot point. It really took me a while to come to terms with the fact that this is an RPG without loot to collect.
My only real gripe is the party AI, you have limited control over automating them and they have no knowledge of the one rule of any RPG (Dont Stand in Stuff). I was constantly finding myself pausing the game to direct each member of the party to run out of the AOE.
That and I REALLY miss the ability to drink a health potion or switch to a character that has a heal to keep my party members alive. Some of the characters have indirect healing abilities but there is no real "healer" type character which makes some of the encounters require a lot of micromanagement to try to keep people together for a chance of the small healing available.
Overall I am really enjoying the game, a primary reason I play games is for the story and that is definitely here. I am not someone that is an expert of the genre which could partly explain the issues I was having managing my party. I am very much looking forward to finishing up the story on Sunday and seeing where the story leads.

Really hard to choose between yes and no, but, I guess, for an average gamer that is a no. I did enjoy the game somewhat, but the combat mechanics made me say 'screw it' and put the game aside from now.
TLDR: Pros:
* Stylish, beautiful, eye candy from the get-go
* Original game world, reminding of many things at once (Cadwallon, anyone?)
* Solid voice acting
* Pretty decent plot, dramatic moments sound pretty real
Cons:
* Walls of text (might be a pro if you're into it)
* Learning curve that goes from 'I did nothing and won' to 'I did everything and lost' almost instantly
* 'AI' that isn't really intelligent at all and just operates based on (very limited) options that you control (not without a lot of trial and error).
More about the cons in detail.
TEXT: the investigative nature of the storyline is enforced by 'case notes' and overall thoughts and memos by our character about everything he sees. You don't exactly NEED to read them asap to understand what's going on, but it really helps - without it you lose some immersion and quickly enough go into 'click through the blablah, get to action' mode. Otherwise you get hit with a lot of info all at once.
LEARNING CURVE: The game teaches you controls and _one_ basic interaction in combat. Then you get a second character. And a third. And they have abilities. And you don't get enough easy fights to check how they should work or when you should use them. Abilities and upgrades also come with ZERO hints.
COMBAT: If you go microcontrolling the combat, the game is pretty much Aarklash Legacy wannabe without the tactical depth, and probably a little too frantic for my liking. I immensely enjoyed AL, and here I more often than not yell in frustration at things the characters do (or refuse to do).

Note: I was a Kickstarter backer for this game.
So far, it reads like a BioWare or Bethesda game in terms of lore (and I'm not kidding about the "reads" part -- walls and walls of text in the codices) and essentially plays like a better managed Diablo. The characters are so far pretty interesting and I really like the set-up of the world and how the class conflict is playing out (though the sociologist in me cries at some of the text in the codex about why the underclass/poor stay in the Citte where they're "unwanted"). I can tell the devs put a lot of work into the world-building and the lore behind the game and, for the most part, have built a realistic feeling society given the context of the world. I'm still pretty early in the game, so I assume this changes more later, but I have been slightly disappointed with character development so far, as most of it has taken place through the walls of text in the codex rather than through the story or interactions with other characters. The interactions I have seen, however, such as between Tristan and Cicero, while short have been deep enough that it's fairly easy to get a picture of that person's character pretty quickly. The world interaction is a little frustrating as everything but movement -- conversations, condexes, switches between phases -- are instigated by stepping into a bright colored circle and clicking E to activate. It takes away a lot of the immersion because it's rendered the backgrounds and environments into pretty pictures in the background that happen to be very very linear. I also have to definitely shout out to the voice actors, all of whom are great (though I don't think I'll ever be able to picture the Glorious Gilmore as anything but Cicero now, since Matt Mercer often uses the same voice). The sound editing could maybe use a little tinkering, though, as I had to turn up my sound, turn down the music and make sure the voices were up to 100% so I could actually hear the dialogue. The music is great but not so great I want it to drown out the voices, which is what happened in the tutorial when I played it.
The combat is.... Well, let's just say I liked classic Diablo so it's no surprise I like this, even with its issues (such as companion clustering in AOE). But it's definitely nothing groundbreaking in either the combat or the skills (again, unless something changes later in the game).
My only major complaint would be the lack of a manual save system, which is more of a quality of life issue than anything game-breaking. I'm just the kind of person that would prefer to have a save right before the boss or, in a story-driven game, a save before an awesome cutscene and I can do neither. The game is on an autosave/checkpoint system instead.
Still, the game seems WELL worth the money I added to the Kickstarter and I think it's been given a fairly reasonable Steam price for what you're getting.

Intro:
The Dead Space games are survival horrors!! The series takes place in outer space in the 26th century. Mankind has expanded into space and colonized other planets, but Earth herself is in ecological crisis, having been drained of resources. EarthGov currently resorts to "planet-cracking" - the processing of mining entire planets for the recovery of raw materials, with a fleet of specially constructed space-faring vessels. However, EarthGov is investigating a second possibility. During the 23rd century, the Chicxulub crater was found to contain a "Marker" - an artifact of extraterrestrial origin which acts as a relay for a persistent electromagnetic field signal, with no apparent source.
Dead Space 2 (released in January 2011) is the follow up to the Dead Space game released in 2008. It follows the further adventures of Isaac Clarke in his encounters with the mysterious Marker.
The game is set three (3) years after the events of the first Dead Space, the game follows protagonist Isaac Clarke's fight against a new Necromorph outbreak on the Sprawl, a space station surrounding a shard of Saturn's largest moon, Titan. In an asylum on the Sprawl, Isaac Clarke awakens with no memory of the past 3 years since Aegis VII, having just been awoken by Franco Delille (protagonist of Dead Space Ignition), an engineer on the Sprawl who was sent by Daina to rescue Isaac. With the already-ongoing Necromorph outbreak, an Infector kills and mutates Franco into a Slasher in front of Isaac, leaving Isaac to escape on his own... Play the game to see what happens next!!!
A central theme in the games is the fictional antagonistic cult religion "Unitology". To me, there are many similarities between the fictional Unitology and the real-world Scientology, which I found interesting. (I am not a Scientologist, BTW).

If you liked the past Deus Ex games this one is pretty much the same but with a few more powers and more story, not a bad thing of course.

In Deus Ex Mankind Divided, man has fused with adolescent cybernetic technology and the results are…erratic.
Media propaganda is spoon-fed to the public by corporate controlled intelligence, while revolutionary journalists coordinate their counter insurgency beneath the streets of Prague.  Cultural uncertainty in regards to a marginalized augmented population devolves into virulent paranoia, as law enforcement deploys brutal tactics to handle the “opposition”.  Political leaders seek to destroy autonomy via the guise of benevolent technological innovation for all.  In the shadows, a clandestine group seeks to establish governance without opposition by obliterating civilized institutions with carefully calculated maneuvering.  This is the world of Deus Ex Mankind Divided, a future gone astray…a future not far off from our own.

After 60 hours of exploring every nook and cranny of an exhaustively detailed Prague 2029, I am fixated on a discomfortingly plausible future, in which the technological singularity is knocking on the door of artificial general intelligence.
In Mankind Divided, the primary narrative handles these themes overtly and tends to take a backseat to the well-crafted subtlety of its side missions.  While the main story ends abruptly, the side missions are well fleshed out and provide consequential and meaningful resolutions for each action and decision you make.  Side missions offer compelling twists and turns while exploring the more existential themes the game has to offer.
Mankind Divided retains the same stealth/action and RPG elements of its predecessors, while vastly improving the fluidity of its mechanics by allowing the player to efficiently implement a strategic chain of augmented maneuvering at a faster pace than prior iterations.  The developers have incorporated more limiting energy usage mechanics this time around, which require calculated movements throughout the environment if the player wants to remain the hunter and not the hunted.  A plethora of interesting augmentation options open up several creative avenues for the player to navigate the environment and snuff out the enemy.  The new “experimental augmentations” enhance the protagonist with prototype technology, such as remote hacking, and my personal favorite, the Tesla, which functions as an offensive stealth option, projectile stun with multi-targeting functionality.  These new augmentations are not only a blast to use, they’re viable and just as accessible as their more “standard” counterparts.
Stealth in Mankind Divided is relatively the same as it was in its predecessor, Human Revolution. Unlike Human Revolution, a more aggressive style of play is enhanced by complimentary augmentations such as Titan armor (temporary invulnerability) and a more expansive set of weapon handling augments.  I decided to go with a non-lethal ghost playthrough my first time around, after briefly experimenting with a lethal approach which felt a bit clunky in terms of target acquisition.  Environmental exploitation, coupled with hastily adaptive stealth, made for some truly memorable moments that left me feeling like a cybernetic predator.
Exquisite, gothic architecture overshadows the cobbled streets of Prague.  Claustrophobic and dizzying corridors harbor the occult and criminal alike below.  Graffiti and ivy contest one another over surface domain, while alleyways shelter capitulated prey within the shadows.  Ebony towers loom ominously over denizens with a scornful facade.  Streets are illuminated by the glow of screens perpetuating 24 hour propaganda, while flyers rallying the resistance occupy every corner.  Colossal, prisonlike structures harbor the demonized and afraid within a maze of wire and metal.
The environment is alluring and immersive, as it pulls the player through a nebulous glimpse of a future slowly overriding antiquity.  The experience is enhanced by the games wonderful lighting and nuanced textures, which meld the noire and dystopian themes into a plausible glimpse of the future.  The graphical fidelity of this game does come with a hefty cost for graphic enthusiasts looking to run ultra-settings on PC.  My GTX 1070 goes from 65 fps avg. with MXAA off, to 40 fps avg. with MXAA 2x enabled.  Fortunately, the graphics options are expansive and allow the user to manipulate multiple, lighting, shadow and anti-aliasing settings.  The Dawn Engine is quite capable of rendering large, intricate maps without additional loading; however, I feel there was room for further optimization.
Sweeping orchestral piano, layered overtop trip hop and ambient electronic elements provide an ethereal, resonant backdrop for the environment.  The soundtrack, composed by the brilliant Michael McCann, ebbs and flows with the pulse of the games action.  Activated augmentations provide a satisfyingly unique sound cue just before the bone crushing impact of a takedown.  Shots from a tranquilized sniper rifle utter a muzzled wisp just before they strike their target.  Mechanized enemies vibrate the floor with a threatening stride of hydraulic impact.  The atmosphere is a richly innovative blend of visual and sonic ambition.
Deus Ex Mankind Divided offers the player a chance to explore its expansive universe with freedom and creativity.  Each encounter provides the opportunity to navigate challenges in uniquely satisfying ways.  Viable stealth, action, lethal, or non-lethal playstyle hybrids provide enough replay value, coupled with a multi-layered narrative that rewards environmental exploration with context.  Fully realized, gorgeous environments within the alluring, dystopian world of Deus Ex challenge the player to embrace the future of humanity and all of its consequences.

We've reached the fourth entry in the 17 year old series, and we've seen two games followed by two prequel games. The series famously started with the approach "all conspiracy theories are real", but the most recent entries, Human Revolution and Mankind Divided, have skewed away from the most outlandish conspiracies and closer to cyberpunk influences. Still conspiracy is at the center of the theme, and they're beginning to run out of steam with Mankind Divided.
You are once again Adam Jensen, mechanically augmented ex-cop, ex head of security for an augmentation manufacturer, now Interpol agent. You're based in Prague after The Incident, in which most augmented people lost control of themselves and attacked others until their controlling entity was stopped by Jensen. The world is now deeply divided into pro-augmentation and anti-augmentation, with a UN vote removing rights for augmented people coming soon. From this stage, Jensen must investigate the bombing of a subway station that is blamed on pro-aug extremists.
Mankind Divided takes the "any approach to a problem works" philosophy all the way through. If you're sneaky, there's cover to hide behind and venting ducts to crawl through everywhere. Are you shooty? Get your guns out, there's plenty to shoot. Want to hack computers and talk your way out of problems? That works! Lethal, nonlethal, silent, noisy, it all works. An amazing amount of work went into this game to give you the ability to play it as you like.
This is also reflected in Prague itself. By the end, you'll feel like you know the city because every neighborhood and location is well detailed and obviously lived-in. The amount of detail in the levels and thought that went into the gameplay really reflects the love the developers have for the game.
One of the hallmarks of Deus Ex is a globe-hopping plot. That doesn't exist here, but it's not necessarily a detriment. You'll spend almost all of your time in Prague. Again, Prague is so well fleshed-out that it's not Dragon Age 2 situation, but I did absolutely get worn out seeing the same subway train loading screen.
With so much attention given to the gameplay and the city, the conspiracy and the plot as a whole are fairly weak. It tells a very simple story with a lot of the more compelling elements taking place as side missions. It's got one beat (augs vs. non-augs) that it hits over and over. It's not a new beat, as this conflict has been at least touched on by all previous Deus Ex games, and that's a big disappointment. It also suffers from feeling under developed. It's not a short game by any means, but it feels like it ends just as it's picking up. The ending also obviously leads into the next game. This is a real bummer because it seems that the studio is moving on to Marvel games in the near future.
On a not-unrelated note, I would be remiss if I did not mention the presence of expendable microtransactions in this single player game. You can pay real cash for in-game cash or praxis points, the ability development currency. It is utterly unnecessary as I found no need for any more praxis points or cash to support my personal playstyle, but you could make the game a lot easier on yourself with straight cash. And, like currency in the game, once you use it, it's gone. It's not like you're buying yourself a permanently larger chest of cash for every playthrough. You spend your cash and your praxis points and they're gone. It doesn't detract from the game because the game is clearly balanced and designed to be played without external influence, but that just highlights how utterly unnecessary the microtransactions are.
With the future of the series in doubt, this isn't exactly the note that I wanted to see it go out on. Mankind Divided is fun and open-ended in ways that many games can't get close to, but it's hampered by a thin story in a series that used to get high marks for complex storytelling. I don't think Deus Ex is dead by any means, but Mankind Divided makes the case for spending more time on the Marvel games that are sure to bring in piles of money with less effort necessary to impress. Deus Ex: Mankind Divided is a good game that should have been great.

I think it's funny that while I had a lot to praise about the first Overlord, it's harder for me to do for the sequel. It doesn't do a lot different and there's the idea that, well, it doesn't really need to do anything different. You control your minion types, wreak mayhem and destruction, and retake your domain from the Glorious Empire aka Romans.
I guess I'll start with the positives. Minion pathing is a little better, and if you get seperated from your horde, they'll just teleport back to the spawning pits, meaning you won't lose minions to glitches this time around. On top of that, Blues have gotten magic blink powers so you can move them through objects to pick up unfortunate dead minions, rather than having them attack yet another obstacle in their way. Battles typically are structured with you taking your minions and strategically throwing them against an equally large horde set up a la Legionaire style, which kinda feels cool. And finally the scale has been upped, locations are vibrant and alive while feeling suitably epic when it matters. It ends up blurring that line between dark epic fantasy and comedic romp at times, but unfortunately never enough to strongly stand for one over the other or blending the two seamlessly, it just feels a little muddled in the wrong places.
As for the negatives... Minions are sadly pretty damn stupid still, blues will try to do resurrections nearby where a minion died rather than fall back to a safe horde like they did in the first game. But that doesn't matter too much as you don't get Blues this time around until over half the game has passed. Yeah, for some reason you don't quickly build your army back up compared to the original where you got all four types within the first couple of hours. Enemy types are varied in some places, but you're dealing with the Glorious Empire Legionaires for nearly half of it, so most of your memories are focused more on the chaotic pile of bodies clashing with one another with no real strategy to it. The game itself is also structured very linearly, while the original was also rather linear, it hid that illusion well through branching paths that eventually came together at the end. This time around you go from location to location - typically by teleporation - with the occasional very short almost pointless sidequest.
Finally, I have this nagging sensation that Overlord 2 - despite its grander scale - is actually a step down from the original Overlord. The original has you fighting corrupted heroes in a normally generic high fantasy world, it works because of how different it is to be playing the villain against the sometimes more villainous heroes. Overlord 2 has the same fantasy world with some different scenery, but against Romans with the feeling of progression being in conquered towns rather than growing hero body count. It handles its setting at face value rather than spitful sarcasm and dark humor with underlying tones of "sometimes heroics isn't far from villainy."
Overlord 2 plays well and is an exciting romp through a high fantasy landscape - with all its flaws included - but it may wear a bit by the end despite how the larger scale. Because like the Glorious Empire you're facing, there's a lot of style in place but not quite enough substance. At least the game sells for ridiculously cheap these days. Recommended, but more to fans of the original who want a little more. Newcomers may enjoy it but that's a big if.

Minion management and mayhem continue in the sequel to the evil domination themed game, Overlord II. The story begins with a lone demonic child sought out by the forces of the previous overlord whose kingdom had come to ruin as the result of a magical cataclysm. You must reclaim your magical minions, fight bosses, and solve puzzles all the while dominating or destroying everyone in your path.
Most mechanics such as minion movement and combat remain the same as the previous game, although the spell system has been simplified. Now instead of having to have a specific spell selected, you have different types of magic depending on whether you have no target, an enemy target, or a minion target. Spell effects are also changed by how dominant or destructive you are; a result of either enslaving or purging the cities and leaders you come across respectively.
Your brown, red, and green minions also receive specific mounts which allow for new strategies to be employed such as wall ambushes with spiders, formation breaking charges with wolves, and drive-by fire balls with salamanders. Enemies are tougher this time around, with the empire forces in phalanx formations that are difficult to break without killing their commander. Your evil self is tougher too, and you can now charge into battle alongside your minions, doing considerable damage with the right equipment.
One thing that might bother fans of the previous game is the new forge system. In the first game, all you had to do was grind gold and souls to eventually unlock every armor or weapon you could ever want. In Overlord II there are a finite number of dark crystals and spell catalysts which means you’ll need to pick your upgrades carefully as you can’t get all of them (I found health-stealing weaponry  and fire minion upgrades to be particularly useful). It’s not that big of a drawback though and even a casual explorer will have more than enough materials to get the job done.
Overlord II is a straight upgrade made in an era where sequels were generally about keeping most of the good ideas unchanged while adding new gameplay to keep things interesting. As such it’s a bit of a rarity and definitely worth picking up along with its prequel for the full experience.

OBEY,
What an awesome game. I'll get this said early and go into more detail after.
If you like online multiplayer games and want to try one with a twist like no other.
Then OBEY is a game worth picking up immediately.
I've been playing OBEY for 6-7 months now before it arrived here on Early Access on steam.
I have 100+ hours pre-steam at least. Its been one of the most enjoyable Indie, Alpha experiences I've had.
OBEY has a one man development power house. Who is passionate about his game. He works on fixes and has been updating the game often with fixes and balances pre-steam and that trend continues here on early access. I have seen this game grow into something incredible and its great to finally see it in a place where more will have access to it.
Lets get onto the game and its mechanics.
OBEY IS an asymetrical multiplayer game. Its not skill based in the way that most multiplayer games are. Twitch reflexes wont help you here. Its more about working out your enemies strategies, their game plans while also working to control your opponents to make them obey you to help you win the game.
I'll break it down more simply.
It works best 4-8 players in my opinion.
Its in a sense free for all. (altho an alliance system is planned for the future)
So you all start out as cute little bunnies. The goal of the game is to reach $10000
As a bunny it is difficult to earn money. Thats ok because there is a appartment block sized robot in the map armed with a minigun the size of a school bus.
Now as the robot, which you can enter by walking in a door at its base you will earn money more quickly.
You can call a drop ship. Which will allow you to buy supplies to help you earn more money and defend yourself with ammunition and other items to help you keep control of the robot. The robot is only able to drop these supplies on the map. He has to get the other players to feed him these items. Which will take good leadership and control. A happy bunny is a less likely to subvert you. Now as a bunny. You can choose to either OBEY you're leader or Subvert him.
I have done some videos which will give you a better idea oh how this works.
But yes if you wanna label an number score on it, It'd be 10/10 / 100% / 2 Thumbs Up.
Indie Game of The Year Contender.
This is even better with friends. 4 Packs are available and recommended in my opinion.
It works really well with strangers also. Its interesting working different people's strategies out.
There is a detailed wiki and an active ever growing community.
Join us.
I OBEY you to.
