You won't get ganked by a bored high level player and I've yet to see any unpleasentness in the world chat. Also it's free. Pay a little for a mount is probably a must but it's still a good time!

In Batman: Arkham Asylum, you truly ARE Batman.  I've played a few Batman games through the years, but none really gave me the feeling of entering his world like Arkham Asylum did.  The fighting system is intuitive, and there's enough variety of minor enemies that it rarely gets dull.  By far my favorite moves are the takedowns, especially using a gargoyle to swoop down from above and string a thug up by his ankles.  The puzzles are also challenging while not being unfair.   You earn a significant number of upgrades, both to your armor and to your gadgets.  The only minor complaints I have are the relentless backtracking through the same terrain throughout the game, and the generic, one-size-fits-all boss battles, which require little more effort than stunning with the Batarang, dodging their charge, and beating them up.  Still, the overall game is so good that it's easy to overlook minor annoyances.  Now I can't wait for Arkham City this fall.  If you like Batman, BUY THIS GAME!

Warlock: Master of the Arcane is a very good game. Warlock II: The Exiled surpasses it every way! First let's talk about changes! Spells now have a meaningful tech tree and this tree is expecially useful as spells are grouped such that researching stage one spells for instance will unlock access to stage two spells - more powerful - and so on. Also, depending upin what you research, you gain favor with certain gods and disfavor among others. If you play Magic: The Gathering, think of the color pie on the back of a card. If you curry favor with a god, you also gain some favor with the godto the left and right ofit while simultaneously losing favor with opposition gods. I really like this mechanic as it really makes you think about your spell research more carefully, that is to say, youare not just thinking of your immediate offense and defense but also the longer term metagame.
Gone are the downward planes. Instead, similar to Eador: Masters of the Broken World, you play on "shards" and portals must be found that connect to other worlds. Space game vets who remember Conquest: Frontier Wars will remember this type of mechanic. And unlike Eador, in this game, you are creating a power base that carries over seamlessly to each new plane you visit. But, the futher you move away, the shards become (naturally) more dangerous. I like Eador, but, THIS is the superior game - the game Eador SHOULD have been.
Quests are numerous and interesting and the game retains a nice bit of humor, but happily, it feels a little more serious than the first Warlock. Even if you are a Warlock I veteran, I would advise you to play the tutorial to get comfortable with the changes.

I'll preface this review by saying I've played every Deus Ex game to date. I played the original Deus Ex to death when it first came out, and I've replayed it almost yearly for almost 2 decades now. I still consider it one of the best games ever made.
And I'll say this about Deus Ex: Mankind Divided - it is quite worthy to be called a Deus Ex game. Anyone who says otherwise knows nothing about the Deus Ex game series and what it represents.
The game is not short. It took me about 50 hours to fully clear the main game - that's without any DLC's or the Breach. Sure, I took the classic "non-lethal, ghost" approach which is known to take the longest, but again - that's what Deus Ex is all about. Exploring every corner of every area, making sure you know every option available to you, finding every secret piece of loot and lore and then finally executing your mission with full clarity.
If you rush in guns blazing with a pathing of point A to point B as your mission requires, you can certainly clear the game faster, but you're also ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ on the biggest strengths of Deus Ex - which is incredible level design and attention to detail.
MD has some of the best level design of any DE games to date. There are so many ways to approach every mission that you never feel lost or deprived of options.
At the same time there's so much to explore. Countless pieces of lore scattered on computers, notepads and more. All of it draws you into the world of Deus Ex.
And that takes me to people crying about there only being one "hub" area. Well, technically that's wrong, since you also get to visit another smaller hub - and I call it a hub because it had a ton of NPC's, stores, and some side-quests of its own.
Also, things change in the main hub after enough story missions. Not wanting to spoil things, I'll just say that the main hub goes through a couple of iterations which not only gives a different visual look to it all, but also creates new quests and more context for a lot of the areas you visited earlier.
---
Deus Ex: MD takes a slight turn from previous games by going mostly with the idea that: side quests are nothing but main quests without someone important looking over your shoulder as much.
This is the true strength of the game. There's so much to discover and complete when it comes to the side-quests of Deus Ex: Mandkind Divided. Off the top of my head - you get to solve a complicated murder, you get to dig into your own past, you get to smuggle out augs, bust a forgery ring, help an underground resistance, rob a bank and more.
Everything you do in the game feels like part of the Main Story. You're thrown into the world where everything is connected. No quest feels like "oh, this is nonsense, who cares". No. Every quest feels like it matters, like it's relevant to what Adam is doing in some way. Even exploring every nook and cranny feels relevant as you're trying to expose a mystery where anyone can be involved - and often is (you find quite a few ties to the illuminati and such even in the computer files of completely random apartments and characters).
That said, DE:MD was meant to be a "middle chapter" of a bigger overarching story that began with Human Revolution. And this is probably why a lot of people are acting up. But asking for the main story in MD to end more conclusively would only mean the likely end of the DE prequels. The developers only have so much story depth and story-years to work with due to the limitations set by the original game.
The story of MD is definitely a lot more localized compared to HR or the original (even though technically you do visit multiple areas across the world), but that in no way makes it bad. You can defifnitely see the massive implications of it for the entire world.
---
I for one recommend Deus Ex: Mankind Divided for all Deus Ex fans who are smart enough to realize that not every game in the series can have a massive global showdown fiesta ending.

When I first saw this game, I thought it would be a Smash Brothers clone. In a few ways I was right; it's a platforming fighting game boasting a set of characters similar to that of League of Legends.
However, upon playing the game, I found it to have different aspects that really enticed me to play more.
Every character has two weapons, with weapons fitting into certain catagories (Spears, guns, swords, ect.). All weapons in a catagory function basically the same way, but with slight variations to the characters who wield them.
I figured out that the main reason for the large set of characters is so that any combination of weapons is avalable. For example, if you wanted to use a bow and an axe you would pick the undead lich Azoth. If he was on the rotation, that is.
This brings me to my main problem with the game. There is a weekly rotation of six characters, blocking off use of the others. If you want, you can buy the characters through in game money or via microtransaction. However, gold in game is extremely tedious to get. You have to play countless online matches to be able to earn the gold. This puts you in a corner. Should you grind battle after battle just to get that one character you want really badly, or do you cave in and spend your hard earned money and go the easy way.
Another problem with the game is the AI. They have 3 settings: easy, medium, and hard. All the settings play like button mashing 4 year olds. The game is made for multiplayer, with several choices for competitive play and for couch parties.
Summary:
Brawlhalla is a fun Smash Bros style fighting game with a unique weapon mechanic. It is plenty of fun to play with friends or online, but you have limited options for single player. While the characters seem very different from each other in designs, they play mostly the same and can lead to repitition. The game also pressures you into microtransactions in several different ways.
I recommend it if you have a few friends who will play it with you, but if you don't and won't go online, this game isn't very fun.

Diablo advantages:
Seasonal play with ladders (Reaper of Souls)

better mechanics as far as toon control (movement flows easier)
more classes (Reaper of Souls)
Torchlight II advantages:
Mod support

Torchlight II is a must have for any fan of action RPGs and fans of Diablo

Mandagon is a beautiful, sort of puzzle-platformer adventure game.
It is difficult to write about it without spoiling the game, because part of the fun is figuring out what is this all about, what do you need to do, and what does it all mean. In a way, in terms of narrative, it resembles Dark Souls - you are given bits and pieces that come together to form a meaning behind the game.
The visuals are beautiful and I guess that I missed a lot by not knowing more about Tibetan beliefs and symbols that the game utilises as it's thematic background. Throughout that the game tells its unique story.
Mandagon is not difficult, not very challenging, it is not even long. The whole game is pretty much a single level that can be beaten within 40 minutes including the time for figuring out your goal and mechanics.
It is free, but now after completing it, not only I want to play it again, but I want to give my money to the people who created such a wonderful thing. (There's a paid DLC with music and artwork, so there's a way).
If, like me, you don't really have time and patience for lengthy games (30+ hours) - this might just be for you.

This gets a thumbs up SIMPLY because it's an Early Access game that is FREE and not hidden behind some $30 paywall just to play an unfinished game. That alone is worth praise, and I really wish more developers would go back to the "free playable demo" age of gaming instead of what has become the norm of selling unfinished products. However, this game is going for the "free-to-play upon release" route I'm assuming because it's littered with microtransactions that change the appearence of basically everything on your character. Real-money purchases are purely cosmetic though, and, unless I missed something, you can only unlock new characters through the in-game currency (earned by playing the game) which really keeps players on an even scale, avoiding a pay-to-win fiasco.
That aside, it's a super fun game. A controller is obviously mandatory being a fighting game, at least in my opinion,  so without one you may have a bit of trouble. I was impressed by how fast you can start the game up and get into a match, making it a GREAT game to play inbetween other tasks. Rounds are short and require virtually no time investment. I've only seen maybe a third of the character roster but everyone seems to be different enough without being too overpowered, barring a few exceptions. The artsyle is ok, every character is obviously made from the same base model, which is fine, but every single character seems to have the Dreamworks Face (google it if you don't know) which I'm not crazy about, but that's just a personal opinion.
Overall it's a fantastic game for where it's at, obviously could use more content but that's a given being EA. Definitely a great party game for you and a few friends, and being free of cost and very low computer resource demanding, there's no reason not to check it out.

The game is one of the best looking platformers around and can be fun with friends but other than that I think the game suffers with a few core problems and in my opinion highly overrated.
Pros:
-Visually stunning.
-nice reward/progression system.
-good gameplay mechanics.
-Very easy to get a hang of it.
-Fun if you have 2 other friends since this game is a 3 player co-op.
Cons:
-May need freinds to have fun or if solo may be a bit more difficult.
-Level design is long and tedious and usually very easy with annoying obstacles in the way but overall the game is short and can complete within a few hours if you do not try to get every collectible in the game.
-Story is not engaging and you don't really care for the characters or their quest.
-Experiance points may glitch when you kill an enemey and he does not drop it or if you kill them by dropping them off a cliff if you are the type of person who wants to unlock everything which can be very annoying.
-The Thief character is pretty much useless until you get the low gravity ability which combined with the wizard you could overcome any obstacle with ease but you do not need her for anything to progress through the story.
-Lack of replyability since there are long levels that are just boring to play through with the same traps, puzzles, obstacles etc.
-Puzzles are useless if a puzzle requires you to get somewhere high as you could just use the wizards 4 boxes skill, even easier if you have the option enabled for same characters to be on at the same time with other players, you could have 12 boxes in total.
-Lack of mods, the modding support has been out for a very long time with only about 12 custom maps/mods made, also I heard the editor is a pain to work with.
I would recommend this game ONLY if it is on sale and if you have friends to play with as this game is very boring solo, not worth the full price which atm is 16,99 euro. I was fortunate to get a 3 pack on sale for only 5 euro which is 3 times cheaper than the full price for 1 copy which was a very good deal, I like this game but only for the price I bought it at, but for the full price I have to thumbs this down. ):

Dead Space 2 is everything a sequel should be; not only does it cling onto the concepts that allowed the original to flourish, but it improved upon them. Mechanics are polished to such an extent that it feels ageless and nowhere near outdated, even in 2017!
Dead Space, had me struggling to really connect with its main protagonist, Isaac Clarke; but with the addition of 'cutscenes' and voice acting, Isaac became someone believable. I found myself caring for his survival, desperately shooting the limbs off those pesky necromorphs, so that they couldn't split Clarke into two pieces.
Dead Space 2, whilst more "action-packed" is the pinnacle of the franchise. Its rich narrative and gameplay mechanics make it a timeless classic. However, keep in mind, the Steam version of the game does not include achievements and unlocks all armour/weapons at the start of the game. If you want the "proper version" of Dead Space 2, I would purchase it through Origin (ew) or on console!

Released as it was back in the heady days of rail shooters there is so much about dead space 2 that makes me think .. what the hell this is awful. There's the sticky controls, the god awful minigames from before the revolutionary discovery that minigames had to be fun topped off with the crunchy mechanics of wolfenstein 2D or CoD single player updated to make sideways more useful. And then there are the tunnel crawling .. why the hell am I doing this stupid bits. They are really stupid.
But I've just replayed this for the second time and screw all that cos holy **** is it good. The slicing mechanics are actually quite fun, the story is hugely engrossing and the immensity of it's impact buried within the mechanics actually matches the immensity of the story, the set pieces work better than almost any set pieces I've ever seen (lifts are the safest way to travel .. aren't they?) and most of the non-minigame mechanics are immensely effective from audio and text logs to just looking around rooms and working out what had happened before an inanimate object falls on you. The pace .. oh my god that's perfect and relentless and it makes it all so obvious why interaction is better than passive in the horror genre. The overall balance between difficulty, scares, claustrophobia and the desire to push forward could probably be shown to substitute for meth without any of the drawbacks except the lack of toilet breaks.

I wish, I WISH I could give this a positive review but I just can't. Sure, it's fun for a few days but then it slowly starts to sink in: All of the characters are essentially just reskins of each other, with a slight difference, (Character A has the two weapons: Guns and Hammer. The character rotation is one of the dumbest ideas I've ever seen, and it's a wonder that it became so popular aside from the obvious cash-grab. Sure, you can pay using in-game currency, but how do you get said in-game currency? Online battling. And if the current character rotation is full of legends you are absolute trash with, you're outta luck, mate. And even if the character rotation is good, the very next day it'll be snatched away from you, leaving you in the hands of RNGesus. Overall, this game tries way too hard to be Smash Bros, but when it comes to what makes Smash Bros what it is, it proverbally falls flat on it's proverbal face. The items are VERY, VERY, VERY lackluster, aside from the weapons, which might as well be required to have for a win unless your some kind of Spiderman predecessor with your keyboard/controller. "Oh, it's Early Access!" Don't care. Doesn't make the items any less useless, for example:
Spike Ball: You throw it at the enemy and if it hits them does a small bit of damage, despite the fact that you LITERALLY THREW AN IRON BALL COVERED IN SPIKES AT THEIR FACE.
Assist Horn (don't know what it's called): Your character sounds the horn and your little assist guy you get to buy at the in-game store sets himself on fire and rushes across the stage. Sounds good right? **insert family forture buzzer sound** Wrong. Because much like the Spike Ball, it does a very minimal amount of damage, not to mention it is almost impossible to land unless you're stun locking your opponent(s) in place.
Mine: Oh come on now, ARE YOU KIDDING ME. HOW IN THE EVER LOVING EXISTANCE OF GABE NEWELL DO YOU MESS UP THIS BADLY. Basically, this works as you would expect a mine to work like, you toss it, imbeds itself inside the ground and explodes when someone walks over it. However. If it makes direct contact with a person before armed, it will do very small minimal damage (Seems to be a running theme with this game's items) and plop on the ground. Problem, it does not arm. Meaning your opponent is able to pick up your own mine and use it against you, but that's not the only issue I have with this item. You see, while making it get into the ground is rather easy once your opponent is off screen/recovering to safety, (which you practically need another item for, namely the weapons) the issue is getting them to stand on it in the first place, as you overall have very little control over your opponent except for tossing them off the sides of the screen/stomping them Mario style from above in order to force them down a bottomless pit. Most of the time I find myself purposefully landing on it myself in order to just get it off the screen, in fear a weapon will land on it and overall be wasted/tossing it off the screen the first time I see it just to save myself the hassle.

I really, really wanted to like this game. I love Harvest Moon, and the idea of Harvest Moon with some lurking, dread secret sounded wonderful to me.
But part of the charm of games like Harvest Moon is the environment. Simply walking around and enjoying the small town. It needs to be a character, too. And there are some enjoyable visuals in certain areas. But much of the town is blank space, making it hard to navigate. You shouldn't feel lost in a tiny, homey town.
Also, while I like the idea of the townspeople not wanting to have you there, in practice, it doesn't lead to them being likeable or interesting characters. This sort of thing could be used to build intrigue, with glimpses of who they really are peeking out between the cracks. But I never got the mystery-solving itch. I just wanted to leave. It's also easy to either sleep through cut scenes, or cause weird bugs when the game insists on showing them anyway.
Currently, this game is episodic, which boggles my mind. A farming simulator is a time-eater. This genre is not one meant to be broken up into little bits. And after a kickstarter and early access, this game should be complete. Worse still, the game is buggy, and core elements of gameplay are still being built.
I'll praise Quickfire for not giving up on the game, as they still do regular updates. It's the sort of thing where I'm tempted to leave a "don't buy it yet" sort of review. Because I want to view this game as a work in progress. But Wild Season isn't in early access anymore, and the game is still being debugged. And I can't recommend a game based on hope. I dropped $30 on the game before it went episodic, and feel incredibly foolish having done so. It doesn't deliver on the simple pleasure of growing lots of different crops. It doesn't feel like I've been invited or challenged to solve an interesting mystery. I don't care about the characters. The ads and information released by Quickfire make it look like there's so much to this game, but in my playthrough, it just didn't deliver on any of it. I appreciate them working hard to try to deliver their own spin on Harvest Moon, but your money would be better spent on a copy of virtually any other Harvest Moon game.

Torchlight II is a quite enjoyable ARPG dungeon-crawler with a huge amount of loot, fun, and exploration to be had! I've enjoyed this game since 2013, and I still play it with friends.
Torchlight II has some very enjoyable gameplay, and its visuals are pretty cool and its soundtrack is good too, and they both compliment the game and give it its cool style. The environments in the game are pretty cool, and sometimes quite varied, and there's many places to explore and quite a few side quests to participate in, too. Its combat is also incredibly satisfying.
Throughout the game, there is a huge variation of armor, weapons, and enchantments that you will find, and you can also transmute items and enchant things at an enchanter. You can also find "ember" to socket items with that will give you a boost in elemental strength, from defense to attacking with that element.
There are four classes in the game: The Embermage, the Berserker, the Engineer, and the Outlander. Each class has different skills and weapon specializations, although you can use any kind of weapon that you want, no matter what class you play as. You can also customize the characters a bit and choose a pet, although the default options aren't very extensive.
Torchlight II is also a mod-friendly game, and it has plenty of cool mods that can change the gameplay, add areas, give more customization options, and add convenience features.
Overall, I have no complaints about Torchlight II. The story isn't very fleshed-out, but I find that it's still sufficient for the game nonetheless, and its gameplay is very satisfying and quite fun! I would definitely recommend Torchlight II to anybody who enjoys ARPGS, Co-op games, and loot games. ^.^

DLC Quest is simply put, one of the best satire games that I've ever played. It mocks bad game design, cliches, memes, storytelling Micro-transactions in video games, and pretty much everything else. This gives the game a charm that not many others have. It's funny and it's entertaining. It intentionally makes bad game design choices to mock the game with them. This is the game's biggest edge over its competition, it really justifies the purchase and is the only reason you need to play this game. And that's great, cause it's just about the only thing the game has over other games.
Yes, aside from the satire there is no reason to play this game. No great story, no amazing game-play, there's nothing here. But that's all the game needs, because it's the best satire I've seen. The big thing here is how you need DLC to do EVERYTHING, even to jump and move to the left, or merely pause the game. This is one of my favorite parts of the game, because it's so darn funny. There's even DLC that does nothing except wast your coins. The way that it mocks DLC practices is just... Hilarious, and one of the main draws here. I don't want to ruin any more of the game since that would be a disservice for anyone who hasn't played the game, but it's great.
The game is actually split into two different campaigns, the first one is just called DLC Quest, it's shorter and gets the joke across quickly. The second is Live Freemium or Die, it's longer and, in my opinion, funnier. Both of these campaigns call out the issues plaguing the industry today, but present them differently. Live Freemium also drags on significantly longer, but can still be beat rather quickly.
Unfortunately this isn't a perfect little gem. It has flaws. First and foremost, it's extremely short. This is the biggest fault the game has, you can beat it in an hour or two. For a 2.99 game though, you really can't complain. Additionally the game has a LOT of backtracking Even though it makes fun of backtracking you still have to do it, and it gets painfully repetitive. One more fault I saw it that the game's lack of game-play does make a great point about free-to-play and DLC heavy games, but nonetheless can be very... Shallow and boring.
All things considered, this is a good game. The satire is really what makes it so, because it's extremely funny. While it's so short and rather shallow, it's worth the money. Really, it's only $2.99! What do you have to lose?

Dead Space 2 is everything a sequel should be; not only does it cling onto the concepts that allowed the original to flourish, but it improved upon them. Mechanics are polished to such an extent that it feels ageless and nowhere near outdated, even in 2017!
Dead Space, had me struggling to really connect with its main protagonist, Isaac Clarke; but with the addition of 'cutscenes' and voice acting, Isaac became someone believable. I found myself caring for his survival, desperately shooting the limbs off those pesky necromorphs, so that they couldn't split Clarke into two pieces.
Dead Space 2, whilst more "action-packed" is the pinnacle of the franchise. Its rich narrative and gameplay mechanics make it a timeless classic. However, keep in mind, the Steam version of the game does not include achievements and unlocks all armour/weapons at the start of the game. If you want the "proper version" of Dead Space 2, I would purchase it through Origin (ew) or on console!

Released as it was back in the heady days of rail shooters there is so much about dead space 2 that makes me think .. what the hell this is awful. There's the sticky controls, the god awful minigames from before the revolutionary discovery that minigames had to be fun topped off with the crunchy mechanics of wolfenstein 2D or CoD single player updated to make sideways more useful. And then there are the tunnel crawling .. why the hell am I doing this stupid bits. They are really stupid.
But I've just replayed this for the second time and screw all that cos holy **** is it good. The slicing mechanics are actually quite fun, the story is hugely engrossing and the immensity of it's impact buried within the mechanics actually matches the immensity of the story, the set pieces work better than almost any set pieces I've ever seen (lifts are the safest way to travel .. aren't they?) and most of the non-minigame mechanics are immensely effective from audio and text logs to just looking around rooms and working out what had happened before an inanimate object falls on you. The pace .. oh my god that's perfect and relentless and it makes it all so obvious why interaction is better than passive in the horror genre. The overall balance between difficulty, scares, claustrophobia and the desire to push forward could probably be shown to substitute for meth without any of the drawbacks except the lack of toilet breaks.

Trine 2 will be a game that I always remember fondly.  I bonded with my children as we escaped into this 3-player adventure.  The varying difficulty levels were appropriate given our varying skill levels.  Trine 2 is more beautiful, plays more fluidly, has more variety in level design and enemy types, and is simply a better experience than Trine 1.  Trine 2 is a less frustrating and a much longer experience than Trine 3, which we eventually abandoned after an ill-advised preorder.
If your kids are young enough, they will enjoy the fantasy story line and might really get into 'being' the character they identify with most, even though the game luckily allows for each player to switch on the fly between the wizard, archer, and knight throughout the game.  In our household, 'being' the characters transitioned into a recurring bedtime story full of wizards, archers, knights, kingdoms, princesses, and all sorts of goblins, gouls, and orcs.
If you are looking for a great side scrolling adventure game to play with your children, this should hit your sweet spot.  Highly recommended.

> Using the Rogue's grappling hook to get on to a platform from underneath is much easier
> The ability for my character to make it onto a platform with a jump is much more lenient
> Easier to summon and destroy things with the Wizard (quick squiggle = box, botched line = plank (yay) instead of box (boo), which was frustrating from the first game)
- I can read the narration and skip faster to get into the level as a result
Cons:
- The only thing they haven't improved from the first game is that the Rogue needs a grappling hook aim when using a controller as she often latches onto the wrong platform or the wrong part of a platform. The grappling hook should also be able to retract further making it as easy as it should be to get on to platforms (despite that they somewhat improved this from the first game).
- Things that are CLEARLY made of wood can't be grappled on to
- Spiders sometimes spawn camp and this can become a little annoying
- The camera is appalling in so many instances (normally too zoomed in) and it would be far better with a player controlled zoom function!

However, I was soon hooked into the storyline and gameplay of Trine.

We have now moved on to Trine 3.
Now this is the one I was actually looking forward to more, having owned this first because it was recommended to me as being like Gauntlet Legends.. But now having played both Trine 1 and 2 I'm really looking forward to Trine 3.
From what we've played so far, Trine 3 is also looking to be very promising and multiplayer appears to also work seamlessly.

There's something special about the Trine games. They combine the best parts of artistic design and exploration for the sake of beauty with a thinking mans puzzle mechanics which can be combined and utilised in interesting and unexpected ways. Along with fantastic extras like co-op, challenges and the likes (all of which are actually worth trying out and fun in their own rights) this is one of the games I've loved from the moment I first picked up.
As for the rest of the series, Trine 1 holds a special place in my heart because I picked it up first and because it set the bar so high, but Trine 2 raises the bar and takes nothing away- it's prettier, it has more content, it's more responsive and technically improved and it's just an all round improvement, and then Trine 3, while I appreciate it a lot more than most despite its failings is still the lesser of the three.
Picking up the whole series is absolutely my recommendation, but if you only have time for one, Trine 2 is my suggestion.

True successor to the original Trine with added online co-op.

The music is charming and the puzzles are satisfying to solve.

Upon entering Rhovanion we were set upon by a new type of enemy. This enemy would forever change my perception of this game, as I stood there, awestruck by the brilliant mechanic before me I could not help but to contemplate the big questions. How was this not caught in testing? Worse yet, if it was caught in testing, who thought it was a good idea to let it through?
As my initial shock vanished, I came to the conclusion that something of unfathomable importance had just happened on this Tuesday morning in the Norcrofts. I must admit I had my doubts as to what was happening after having first acquired my Glider in the Wold, but this.. no this was something different entirely.
In all of this I could not help but think to myself that "This may have looked dumb, but in all honesty these graphics somehow still holds up fairly well." This thought was destined to continue for some time but as I spotted some gathering nodes I swiftly went into a state of blinded greed where I threw all safety and precaution to the wind as I dashed over to mine it. Sadly, I was still in combat.
At this moment I realised that the mighty fine enemy who previously had left me awestruck still remained in existance. Unfortunately it was nowhere to be seen. I decided to cut my losses and move forward with my quests. Close to ten minutes passed as I was flailing away at seemingly unendless quests including the slaughter of what I now presume to be a close to extinct race of Goblins (Seriously, if you don't like beating up Goblins, this game is not for you, theres millions of them and you WILL have to kill every. Single. One. Twice.), I was monitoring my minimap as usual. An old habbit from my days of playing Delta Force 2. Granted, there was no radar in Delta force 2, but still the point stands. I should say that there was a minimap in Delta Force 2, but this one only displayed the topography of the landscape and did  in no way alert you to the potential hazards of an enemy that had attacked you over ten minutes ago charging back at you from nowhere. This minimap however, does precisely that. I watched a red little marker on the minimap come charging at me at inhumane speed. Inhumane for two reasons. Primarily because it was not human. But the fact that this tiny goblin was also mounted seemed to also contribute to this partcular notion. The lil' guy attacked me. Once. Before charging off into the distance once more.
At this point I could but embrace one simple fact: I will never get out of combat, that superbly speedy and obnoxiously sneaky Goblin will keep me in combat until one of us perish. Being stubborn, rather than lazy, I opted to simply track down the bugger. This, I might add, is where my true adventure began. For the next thirty minutes, I would walk back and forth in the middle of Norcroft (For those of you who have never seen Norcrofts, its just a huge plains.), Every once in a while my good friend the mounted Goblin, whom I after the third time attacking me had been baptized George, would attack me to keep me in combat. All while dashing off into a different direction than which I was traveling towards before in an feeble attempt to catch him. Fed up with this little concept of a mounted enemy who apparently does not know how to stop, I opted for running to the edge of the map and await Georges return next to one of the many mountains that encircle the plains.
As George had a tendency of walking by roughly every ten minutes I decided to go grab myself a drink. Not that it is relevant for the review, but I should probably inform you that it was a cup of Tea, Lemon green tea. Highly recommended.
Upon returning I was, to my dismay, at about 3% hp with a Norcroft Field-bear happily chipping away at my health. However this was not all! Looking at my minimap I fondly observed how George was, indeed, nearby. The poor little fellow had got himself lodged into the mountainrange on the side of the map and tried incredibly hard to get himself dislodged. This process, apparently, took around ten minutes, then he would charge off and slap someone, most recently: me, in the face before dashing off and getting himself stuck on the other side of the map.
It was with resounding joy I found myself dying to that Field-bear and watching Dear old George finally reset and return to his appropriate location in the fields where he belongs and will graze away peacefully until he runs into another player who will undoubtedly rejoice in the idea of never having to leave combat ever again.
Unfortunately however, the gliding characteristics of the mounts in Rhovannion prohibits me from ever moving past the area due to sheer amusement, but other than that..
10/10!

I've really had a lot of fun on this seemingly simple, but highly addictive game! The gameplay allows the player to be both creative and to manage production efficiently as they chose. Although there are no explicitly defined objectives, the player will need to set their own objective in order for their kingdom to thrive
PROS
The game is fun to play and you have good control of the game settings.
Allows you to be creative and make your kingdom look how you want with a wide range of cosmetic features, or alternatively make a crude factory that pours out weapons to destroy your enemies with.
There is a huge amount of objects in  the game your gnomes can make, although many have seemingly little use as of yet.
It's the sort of game you can keep playing, there's always something you can do in your kingdom. You may occaisionally find yourself watching your gnomes advance, but that's a great opportunity to tidy up your great hall or something!
There is always motivation to increase your score in the game (called kingdom wealth) as the higher it is the more gnomes join your kingdom.
Game is still under development so new features are released periodically.
It has a slight personal feel as your gnomes each have their own name and attributes, and you can chose where they live and their job. I like watching them gradually get better at their job.
CONS
Some may find the game quite slow paced. You only start with 9 gnomes and it can take quite a while to get things done.
You can only have one savegame per kingdom. this makes the game more challenging, but it's very fustrating if you save the game, then are defeated soon after, as you don't have enough time to change that outcome and your kindom is lost forever.
There are a lot of objects that don't actually do anything but increase your score. It makes sense to have a few objects for this purpose but there are more than necessary.
There's a whole section on cooking food to make better food, but from a stragetic point of view there is no reason to actually do this as the 'better' food is worth the same as the raw food and altough fills your gnomes up more, is no justification for the amount of labour it takes up.
The graphics are very primitive - I tihnk it suits the game quite well but this may be a con for some.
There is no way to 'win' the game, although there will become a point where all the ores have been mined (days and days of gameplay) and continuing on may seem dull. I feel like perhaps the developers could add in a story mode as there are assesable objectives.
These are all minor setbacks, the worst problem is the lag. This is a pixley 2D sprite game, so why in god's name does it lag a reasonably alright i7 laptop? You have to be playing the game for quite a while for the lag to occur and there are things you can do to reduce it, but it's still a pain.
So overall, would definitely recommend this game to anyone who likes the continuous stragety and is intersted in creativity and/or designing production systems. Really hope they fix the lag, but I will continue to enjoy the game nethertheless and look forward to any new features.

I've thought about this for significantly longer than this game deserves and have come up with a couple of conclusions on what I think of it.
You're just not going to get Upton Sinclair's The Jungle in the 21st century, certainly not some type of work that makes people reevaluate what they're doing, what they're giving, and what they're getting in return. So a satirical game like this with seemingly good intentions, created to poke fun at a poor industry practice is likely the only way to make a strong political statement, at least one that gets any attention. The fact that DLC Quest came from Greenlight makes it all the better.
However, I'm not recommending this game for several reasons.  The primary reason is that it's just not very good. Gameplay is very Super Mario Bros: Sidescroller, very rudimentary exploration, spend most of your time collecting coins, there's something about a princess. Part of the impact of the satire is more or less aimed at this similarity. There's an unspoken message that says, essentially, "imagine this is the late 80s, early 90s and you can't even have sound because Mario was made by Ubisoft". That's an amusing concept on paper and an arguably effective way to make your statement, but it's not all that enjoyable to experience.
Quests in this game have to live within that Mario framework, balance simplicity, but also try to tell a basic story that further supports the dev's point. The result is endless hide and seek coin collecting and busywork tasks that prolong the time you have to play the game and delay the hour you'll put it down. Yeah, that's basically what all quests in all games do, but they're typically more interesting an involved than "travel to the other side of the map and press E. Travel to the other side of the map again and press E." When the top two rarest achievements in the game are "do the entire thing again - but faster!", you get an idea of what you're getting into. Ultimately, there are two ends you can reach with this playstyle. The first is that the dev doesn't know what quests are or how to make enjoyable "meat and potatoes" content for a game (which is likely), or the dev is making a larger statement that 90% of real life is collecting coins and busy work (which is naïve - look, I have time to both play this game
criticize it! :P).
One other reason that I'm not much of a fan of it is that this is marketed as a full-fledged video game. In 1985, if it wasn't a satire game and had different theming altogether, it would still be decidedly short on content. You can finish this in two to three hours. Today, it's easy to make a game of this quality and spam them out on the internet. This is how Miniclip and other flash game websites are alive.
Now, with that in mind, I'm going to list some of the top-rated reviews for this game:
"You can buy more DLC than Borderlands 2 has. 10/10" - Hammercorps
"Download the Review DLC to access this review." -GmCity
"Had to spend extra to pause the game. 10/10" - Fatal'z Nutz
That's it. Those aren’t snippets, those are the full reviews. Indicated by the fact that these, among others,
top reviews, the basic atmosphere of DLC Quest feedback is basically "I agree with this game's premise" and "Gosh, I don't know, I just like it". This is actually not far removed from how DLC, itself, is marketable. Notwithstanding publishers that pride themselves on actual expansions to a game, which introduces 30-50% of the initial content they originally didn't intent on developing, let's take more rampant publishers as an example.
Let's take a game like Crusader Kings II, published by Paradox Interactive, which is a lovely game by the way, although it suffers from rampant DLC release. As of February 2015, there are 52 DLC items which includes four major additions, two ebooks (of all things) seven music additions, and 39 glorified reskins of ruler clothes or soldier uniforms. Why do people purchase these things? Basically, for the same reason behind the reviews for DLC Quest. They agree with the premise of the original game...plus a healthy mix of "I just feel empty inside without it".
So really, by marketing a flash game as a full fledged video game, at a DLC price, with a satirical premise, Going Loud has actually (rather impressively) created a game that functions as DLC normally would. As a result, they've published very little content, but to an extraordinary amount of profit.

Ziggurat is a first-person magic based rogue-like. The game is based around three different pools of magic that power different categories of weapons. Blue mana powers spellbooks like basic fire and ice spells, Green mana powers different staves which shoot smaller, more spread out projectiles, and Orange mana powers heavier weapons like magic grenades. The story is basically you are a magic wielder who must complete the five floors of the "Ziggurat" to test your magic abilities. There are a lot of characters, weapons and perks to unlock throughout the game so becomes more fun the more you play. I felt it getting a bit stale after a while, but then I unlocked new stuff to try out and it was fun again. Only other complaint is that the game doesn't tell you much about it, so a lot of it is trial and error. I feel like the game would be better with more updates, but as it is now it is still really solid. Ziggurat is really fun if you like quick, pick-up-and-play rogue-likes. Basically a less-polished, first-person Binding of Isaac.
A great dungeon-crawling arena-based magic shooter. Fast paced, well balanced.
You are a mage.  But you are a mage who has to aim!  Can get pretty hectic at times, and difficult.  It's fun!

Harry Potter meets The Hunger Games in this First-Person Shooter. The game is reminiscent of the classic Heretic and Hexen games, which themselves were fantasy spinoffs of the Doom games. That being said, don't go into this expecting a traditional FPS experience, Ziggurat is a roguelike action shooter that requires quick reflexes instead of puzzle solving.
You are essentially an apprentice wizard going room to room (and level to level) facing challenges with the ultimate goal of escaping the "Ziggurat". I was initially concerned that the fighting might be a monotonous grind, but each battle is fast and furious with a multitude of room and monster variations. The fighting is broken up with trap rooms, secret rooms, and treasure rooms. There quite a few characters, perks, spells, and weapons to unlock as you play through the game.
I hate any form of grinding, but even after 13 hours of game time I haven't found it repetitive and I am still enjoying Ziggurat. It is definitely worth playing and ultimately conquering.
A very good game and addicting roguelike. A plus for replayability. Wizard blasting at its finest.

Very difficult and very fun, I've seen a few mage FPS like this, but nothing near this complete and polished. If you want to play an aggressive, fast paced, spell flinging wizard who dies all the time, this game is for you.

While visually polished and presenting straightforward mechanics, Ziggurat's gameplay feels quite bland. The level design is boring and predictable; levels are broken down in rooms with specific features and purposes (combat, shrines, etc.) rather than generating a random dungeon with its own twists and turns. Every room is a box devoid of interesting elements. Combat is lackluster as well; all the player does is run around in circles spamming attack.
If you're expecting either a shooter or a rogue-like, it will dissapoint you in both areas.

Feels like an interactive movie, not only in terms of ambience but also in terms of moral decisions.
The game is based on 3 major concepts:
A)  Carefully manage your human constitution and dexterity. I Am Alive does its best to constantly remind you that you  are human and fragile. A realistic moving/climbing system alongside a revolutionary psycological combat system play their part in this as well.
B) Explore. But do so with consequences. You might find something of use or you might use all your supplies for nothing.
C) Help others in need, however make sure that helping them doesn't jeopardise your own survival. Moral decisions are often in I Am Alive and the game does not really reward you for the right choice. There is no right choice and the only reward comes from your own morality and mentality of living.
If you are a fan of I Am Legend, but you are too old for mindless zombie killing then this is the title for you.

It's not a bad game but ultimately it's simply not worth your time.
The minion mechanic is very interesting and I applaud the devs for trying it, but the game itself is probably a solid example as to why other devs have ignored the idea.  On top of that,  the implementation is unnecessarily  clumsy, cumbersome and imprecise - significant problems given this is the core mechanic in the game and the tool you employ against just about everything.
Similar things can be said of every design decision in this game - it's not awful, but simply playing it is a chore. A basic awkwardness premeates the entire game as your minions are annoying to control, your avatar is plods around the map, mini-games are chores to complete and the game is seriously padded out in places.
Finally the fortress that serves as your hub between missions is aesthetically suitable but in all over ways awful. I understand why they didn't simply use a menu to organise your empire but plodding back and forth down hallways and through multiple loadscreens to do two buttons worth of work is nightmarish. And much of what the Fortress offers (customisation and minion management) is grossly unrewarding.
The setting and dialogue is novel enough, I didn't find it particularly funny though it tried hard to be, but it didn't annoy me either, which is notable enough as most 'funny' games tend to be outright annoying.
Visually it's actually pretty decent for its age.
Overall, there's some cute ideas here but the implementation isn't good enough. It's not even really 'if you can stand X you'll like Y". Just play something else.

Dead Space 2 was a pleasant surprise for me. Which is odd considering it is a game all about dismembering nightmarish alien monstrosities in the sci-fi equivalent of a haunted house; pleasant is hardly the adjective I might expect to use. But after the disappointing experience I had with the first game of this franchise, it was a welcome change.
The biggest improvement was to what I consider the major failing of the first game: Dead Space 2 is actually a creepy experience. Scary? Well, I might be too jaded for that (and let's face it, the monsters in this series are just too comic book to inspire real terror) but I'll admit some of its scripted sequences did make me jump in my seat (just a little bit, of course). The levels are meticulously designed, with excellent lighting and some good texturing, all of which work together to set the proper mood. And while the story and characters are also still sophomoric it was head and shoulders above the simple fetch-quests by characterless officers of the first game.
The gameplay was improved too, leaning more towards pure action run-n-gun and discarding most of the chaff of the survival-horror genre (with the exception of save-points -whose presence I accept since I felt they heightened the tension of the game- and the limited inventory space, which I despised since it was a pointless and tedious bit of micro-management that distracted from the game's otherwise impressive pacing). The AI was a satisfactory mix of predictable and chaotic, interspersed with a handful of the mostly scripted sequences.
Oh, there were a few rough edges; some levels overstayed their welcome, for instance and there were a handful of minor bugs but on the whole I can't look too unfavorably at this latest iteration of the Dead Space franchise. Its a good-looking, well-playing game with lots too see, even more to kill and lots of memorable (and often creepy) moments.

Just finished this, for the TL;DR -- a game with no words can still tell one hell of a story, and this game is a shining example of storytelling in my book. Backed up by mechanics both solid and maddening in equal measure and a soundtrack that fits just right, Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons is worth the buy.
Brothers follows two siblings on a quest to find a cure for their ailing father shortly after the tragic passing of their mother. The game is told without written text, but it doesn't need words to convey the personalities of the steadfast older brother and the mlschievous younger one, or to give the world and the people in it character and charm. I really enjoyed the experience this title put forth and the emotions it continued to evoke from me as I experienced one thing after another -- this game continued to subvert my expectations, and I respect it for that.
The controls will either not bother you at all, or drive you absolutely out of your senses. In Brothers, you control each of the titular characters at the same time, one with each analog stick. Once you get the hang of it it's surprisingly fluid, but until you get the hang of it, it's... fairly miserable. But that's part of the challenge of the game, really, and it's not bothersome enough to skip the title altogether -- far from it. Some of the later climbing areas felt incredibly satisfying to traverse thanks to these mechanics, and overall it's not that much of a hindrance. Plus you can ride goats at one point.
The game runs fluidly as can be and it looks great for its era, at least on my sytem. I never had a framerate shudder or an instance of slowdown -- which is good, because this game doesn't really have any graphical settings -- fair warning for those to whom this is important.
But overall, the real draw of Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons, is the namesake Tale itself. The storyline, in all of its unspoken glory, is phenomenal, and will get under your skin. It's cute and charming at times to watch the brothers interact, and other times it's harrowing to try and escape something dangerous with both of them at once -- you come to care for them, or at least I certainly did. The world is full of colorful creatures and characters both good and bad, and some of the areas I explored will stick with me for a while -- this game has surreal, haunting imagery at times; sometimes, it's even a little disturbing. It fits the piece -- and it's all really complemented by one of the best cameras I have encountered in years. This game reminded me what good camera work looks like. I never had a quibble with what it was doing, it literally never caused an issue, and it's probably been years since I could make that claim.
Brothers was crafted with a lot of love, and all that work shows in the world and the narrative which frames it. It's fun to play, and jut the right amount of challenging as you figure it all out, and it's really, really wonderful overall. I'm so thankful to the friend who introduced me to this game -- and I hope that reading this might encourage someone else to take a look at it as well.
Thank you for reading.

This game is a very good and unique variation of the knockback-based fighters out there. The weapons play extremly clean and smoothly. The animations for attacks and such are hands down one of the best things about this game, all of them look great and fit the overall art style of the game well. Almost none of the combos in this game are true, which can be annoying at times but fits the rest of the gameplay and pace of the matches.
Even on the old laptop that I play the game on it still runs at a pretty much locked 60 fps and the connection to other players ingame offers no input delay at max connection - which is not the case for any other fighter i've played online. The game runs on a modified Adobe Air platform with essentially homemade framework for the rest of the engine, which is why it takes minimal processing power to run at 60 fps and why the onine connection has zero delay.
Overall this game is very fun to play and I don't see myself stopping anytime soon. 9/10

TL;DR VERSION:
Pros:
-Good stealth
-Versatile map design with many stealth routes to take
-Rather interesting story
-A lot of customization for different styles of gameplay
Cons:
-Eats up a lot of RAM (with 8GB you will still sometimes experience lag spikes even on medium settings)
-The ending isn't satisfying, probably setting up for a sequel
-Numerous bugs, some annoying, some even worse
Verdict: The game is good for stealth fans and when it works is engaging and fun but after half a year of being out it has too many bugs to be worth 50€. Buy only at a significant discount.
LONGER VERSION:
Despite reading mixed reviews about the game, I decided to buy it since it was 70% off. And the game has been a bitter-sweet experience so far.
Seeing as this is the first Deus Ex I've played, I can't compare it content or story wise to any of the previous games. That being said, I'll just say that the story is rather interesting albeit short and unfinished in my opinion.
Now onto the gameplay.
Going in fresh it really did feel like a good game at the beginning: the stealth worked reasonably well and the AI wasn't too dumb, there were always multiple ways to stealth through a mission depending on how you spec’ed your augments and of course if you ever got tired of sneaking around, you could try to slaughter your way through. Of course the enemies are rather tough and you are squishy, especially at the beginning so the game probably won’t appeal to those looking for an FPS.
So far so good, right? Well it would be if everything worked as intended.
The first bug I encountered was my screen filling up with random projections of particles, which blocked my view and was generally annoying. Thankfully it stopped after I left the area I had been in at the time.
After that followed some minor bugs with me not being able to draw weapons or the game treating walking as sneaking (aka slowing me down and not producing noise) until I restarted from a checkpoint. These further lessened the immersion and were frustrating to deal with when in the middle of a mission.
Then when I got the active camouflage augment, every time I deactivated it the game decided to teleport me to a security checkpoint where an NPC would repeatedly ask for some papers, this stopped only when I killed her.
And last but not least towards the very end of the game it straight up crashed on me twice in a row, which prompted me to write this review.
So the best way to sum up the game is that it is indeed bitter-sweet. The gameplay and the story are good but both are dampened by bugs and an unsatisfying ending. In my opinion, the game is definitely not worth 50€ but for at least half that price it would be a fair deal.

A frustrating mix of great concept and terrible execution. I can't tell if I had more fun than controller-hurling rage.
Every challenge is a wall of invulnerable guards that you get past by positioning a horde of reds at just the right spot to take out the captain. Sometimes you get to use a catapult or ballista. Strategy is fairly irrelevant.
Every game has bugs, but it's the design choices that will drive you batty. What should have been a simple set of menus accessed from a keypress is instead a vast dungeon with rooms spread to the far corners, where your slow-walking avatar must trudge too, then wade through pointless "elevator" animations, and then even more animations before you can interact with the ungangly UI to manage a single resource. We're supposed to feel like we're entering a whimsical world, but mostly you just cry when you realize you have to trudge back across the entire dungeon to perform an upgrade.
The magic system could have been completely removed without any loss to game play. You get four spells. You'll see a tutorial once. Then the spells seem to work by context, but despite a lot of experimentation, I couldn't figure out what the parameters were. I suspect it requires very precise targetting and timing that is more likely to happen by chance than by intent. But when you do get a spell to work, the effect is so underwhelming that it never seems worth the bother, and you certainly don't need them to complete the game, nor do they make it any easier.
Then you get awarded women as trophy mistresses. It's just as shallow and pointless as it sounds.

Despite reading mixed reviews of this game I was surprised it was actually this good. The world has been struck by earthquakes and it's up to you, a survivor, to try and find your family.
The graphics are dark and moody; you can only see a few metres ahead which makes it difficult to differentiate friend from foe. It really adds to the tension. That, and the lack of bullets. You have to pick targets carefully, and even decide if you want to kill them. It's not always needed, you see, and you really need to preserve your ammo.
There are also other survivors to be found and they might need your help. It's up to you. Helping them will grant you a retry. So in the event that you are killed you'll be able to try it again.
Besides killing and helping people you'll be climbing around like the PoP and AC games, which feels natural by now, and is cool.
Too bad the game is a bit short; it will take most people around 4-6 hours to complete.
Yet another game that has to be experienced, people.

Gameplay is fun until you get to the last boss. Then it just gets stupid. Several of his attacks are effectively unavoidable, so unless you managed to get lucky with your build and items you're screwed. They advertise this as being a game of skill and it largely is, but the final boss kind of goes against this. Don't be deceived by the gameplay of your first few hours, they really messed up the design of the final boss. What's worse is that you can't really improve quickly against the final boss because you then have to play through all the stages again, even though you probably don't feel like they're worthy of your time because you've already gotten to the boss. This is one of the design issues with roguelikes and they haven't solved it here. How are you supposed to get better at fighting a boss if you only get to make one attempt every hour? This is fine in a turn based roguelike because you have all the time in the world to think, but in an FPS you don't have time to process everything so it really hinders learning a bosses patterns. Too bad, the rest of the game is quite fun. It's all just preparation for major disappointment as you get to the final boss.

I want to start off by saying to anyone avoiding this game because of the notice that says a controller is required, it's actually not required. It's much easier to play with a controller because of the single player co-op mechanic, but it is not actually required.
Keep in mind, there is no voice acting or subtitles for this game either. If you're someone who likes story handed to you via direct dialog, this may not be what you're looking for. Though, I personally feel this game doesn't need dialog to function properly, the story is made very clear just through actions.
I went into this game expecting a fun little short story but came out with so much more. This game is packed with emotion, and for a game that has no English voiceovers or subtitles, I feel like that's a feat in itself. The graphics and storyline make this game feel very Jack and the Beanstalk with a touch of Brothers Grimm. It's an adventure packed with emotion and sadness like no game I've played in a long time. Along the way you can interact with most of your surroundings, including the people and animals, which is a small but effective touch to make the game feel all the more real. The game centers around the theme of death, with small breaks of joy in between.  If you want a game that'll make you cry in both joy and sadness, this is one for you.
Aside from the story, are the puzzles scattered throughout your journey. Realistically if you really wanted to play this game with someone you could, as each brother takes up half a controller, but the puzzles are simple enough it can easily be played alone. At no point did I feel like I needed a walkthrough because I was stuck on a puzzle, and even most of the achievements are right next to where you need to go, but not so obvious that you shouldn't look for them. Most achievements are located on a side-path from the main storyline.
I highly recommend giving this game a shot, especially if you like short adventure games packed with storytelling and emotion.

The story mode of gta v has it's points, but some of the writing is a bit pathetic.  They could have provided a better experience for players.  Most of the gameplay does work and can be fun.  It has some weird side quests and some unusual events to experience.  Though you end up having to use a guide or a walkthrough to experience more than half of the things because too many of these events are so obscure that people couldn't find them even while trying to find the ufo.
Another aspect of gta v is the online multiplayer mode.  They really did provide some good things to do online.  You can get involved with other players and play a decent version of gta with friends.  The key problem with their online though is a constant shoveling of newer better stuff to get you to spend the in game money because they don't really want you playing, the want you buying shark cards which get you in game money.  It is heavily marketed that way and can be annoying at times but is not the worst issue.  It really is just a small issue that they nearly harass you with in game coments from npcs and constant beeps from the "phone" about things you should be buying.  It would not really be a problem if the game was normally playable.
Lately the game isn't particularly playable.  The methods they used to provide the online content leaves it vulnerable to some versions of cheating.  Because of the vulnerabilities mod creators tend to provde lots of cheats for some people to abuse the game with.  Those people start to make sure that no one else can play the game.  Rockstar does attempt to ban wave at times as they detect the cheats, and they do have a ban system in place that can permanently remove an account from playing online.  But they don't do any more than that.  Cheater takes away all your progress, well if they got detected, then they get a temporary ban first, then a permanent ban on second offense.  You on the other hand after a week of contacting support usually get some of your stuff restored, but glitches end up leaving some things inaccesible for weeks or months.
Cheaters abuse everyone constantly for multiple days at a time, and Rockstar merely just lets it happen.  It may not be easy for any developer to prevent cheating, but lately I would say that Rockstar makes an effort to endorse cheating because they are not doing anything about these issues anymore.  If you want to play gta online, then play only in private sessions where you can't access the good content or meet other people that you have not already made friends with.  In other words, until you see proof that Rockstar has done something about the cheating, don't play gta online.

Batman: Arkham Asylum was the best action game of 2009.  I originally played this game on Xbox 360, but revisited the PC version and enjoyed it again even more with crisper graphics.  While the game does have some beat 'em up elements to it, it won't tire you out on them.  Though, if you do enjoy them, like I did, the game offers a challenge mode that lets you enjoy the wonderful contextual combo system.
Much of the appeal is the puzzle-like approach to clearing a room, or getting to your next objective by sticking to the shadows and using the fear tactics that Batman is known for.  The story is compelling, and the gameplay offers just enough variety to keep it from feeling bland.  There is a pleasant mixture of brawling, stealth action, story sequences, and detective work to keep your attention.
If you haven't yet played Batman: Arkham Asylum, I would highly recommend the PC version using either mouse/keyboard or a 360 game controller, especially before the sequel arrives!

Since my gametime (off Steam hitting around 10k) is ridiculously high i figured i'd give an in-depth review of the game both on a leveling and end game basis for both new players and potential returning players as well.
This review will be done on a positive/indifferent/negative basis.
Positives:
+ Class variation and static roles: . You play as a Minstrel, you'll be healing. You play as a Guardian, you'll be tanking etc. Some classes such as Beornings and RKs can do multiple jobs, but the game follows the old school MMO system (as expected given its age). Over 9 classes to choose from all with unique roles both end game and unique abilities and playstyles while leveing and questing.
+ Graphics:     The game graphically has aged like fine wine and is still appealing to the eye, especially in the more recently released zones. The revamped zones in low level areas and the new regions in Gondor are more up to date and places such as North Ithilien are breahtaking. The artstyle that LOTRO offers fits the game perfectly.
+ The Main Story:   The overarching plot is fantastic at least in Volume 1 + 4, with Volume 2 being good and Volume 3 being 'okay'.  There are currently 4 volumes (the latter still underway).
+ Music/OST:     This has always been top notch and they've done a great job, especially in places such as Moria, Angmar, Rohan & Gondor to truly capture Tolkiens works in the flesh through the music that is played while venturing around.
+ The Lore:    This is without doubt the closest to the literature source you can find in game or video form. Fantastic job in sticking and expanding upon Tolkiens works.
+ F2P:   I could go on about this for hours but looking at it from the perspective of a new player, and the ability to buy the content with in-game currency and not pay a single penny (Unless you want to PvP) is pretty astounding. Naturally it's grindy as hell but it's free, so you can't really complain.
+ Raiding:  At the time of this review there is plenty of end game content to keep you busy, some more difficult than others that require a kinship (Guild), voice communication as well as understanding the instance and your class respectively.
+ Landscapes/Open World: This speaks for itself. LOTRO is huge, and the atmosphere and immersion in some locations is phenomonal. Places such as Moria, Lothlorien, Minas Tirith, Mirkwood etc really stand out as the pinnacle of world building in this game.
Indifferent Points:
=Optimization: Game crashes are a thing as is lag, especially in highly populated zones. Can be game/immersion breaking.
= PvMP:   PvMP (Player vs Monster Player) has so many positives but also a few negatives (as well as lack of any development pretty much since its release from the Developers in 10 years except for attempted balances between classes). The skill level for PvP is insane and that makes it both fun and enjoyable. If you enjoy a challenge PvP is definetly the hardest part of the game to play well. There are plenty of great and friendly players in PvP on both sides, but also a very negative and childish community that ruins it which can potentially  make you lose interest if you don't learn to ignore the chat. That's PvP for you. There are, as in many MMOs 'flavour of the month classes' that are OP with updates, the only issue is that given how small Standing Stones team are and the lack of monthly updates (Updates are released less frequently than in bigger MMOs such as ESO, FFXIV, WoW etc) it's an on going dilemma.
= Developer Interaction:   This isn't really a positive or negative but in comparison to how the game used to be (under Codemasters in Europe) when developers and GameMasters used to interact with the community very frequently, the lack of actual interaction between players and the Dev Team (outside of the Community Manager through Twitch & Forums) leaves room for improvement and more engagement. Despite this in recent months this has improved slightly, so hopefully we'll see more involvement from the team with in-game events in the future.
= Roleplaying:     I'm not someone who roleplays in LOTRO so i can't offer much feedback on this. The community is, for the most part really friendly and welcoming and there are servers specifically for Roleplaying, so it must be good!.
=Crafting:     Crafting is something, in most MMOs (with the exception of ESO) that i've never really enjoyed. I don't mind crafting in LOTRO when i need too but i don't take any particular pleasure in doing it.. If you enjoy crafting in other MMOs you'l likely enjoy it in this game as it has many viable purposes (from leveling gear, to consumables to end game relics). It's also part of questing as many of the crafing items you need can be found while playing and leveling through the game in each area. I'd stick this as a positive except it honestly isn't anything overly special that stands out. It's just 'there'.
Negatives:
- End Game Grind:     While people seem to enjoy leveling alts (and while you can skip it with Valar upgrades to boost your character, bearing in mind you'll have to go back and do your deeds and learn your class anyway so it's pointless) you will pretty much have to go through the exact same content again from 1-105. While you can level in certain different areas for some levels you will have to venture through Moria, Rohan, Gondor on multiple toons. The issue isn't so much leveling (which is fun) but the grind you need to achieve a playable character for end game content. I could write an entire paragraph detailing how bad grinding to be 'raid ready' is (in an effort by Devs to keep people in game between major updates i assume) if people want an overview, but in a nutshell you have to; Obtain 83 Class Points, Get around 10+ Virtue Traits to level 20 Each. You'll have to level, upgrade, reequip and grind items for your legendary weapons. You'll have to grind essences and then craft them by obtaining crafting items from many different sources through grinding them to get the required essences you want, and even then you aren't guaranteed the best essences.
^ If Standing Stones made this less grindy (especially the essence and legendary item grind) for ALT characters, it would make the end game grind more approachable for people to do it more than once without making it feel like a chore.
- Class Development:   In a nutshell; Beornings were released and are a broken mess and have been with only one patch since they were released. An introduction to a new race/class and little changes shows a lack of care, at least in my eyes for the finished product or player feedback. I haven't seen a new skill (or ability) on my main class in years. What happened?! Further more there are now MANY useless skills on multiple classes that haven't been made viable or addressed in years. This also goes for legendary legacies on legendary weapons. An example on Loremaster (My Main) is; Gust of Wind on Loremaster. Completely pointless. Ents go to War is no longer as viable as it used to be and Natures Fury is pretty much pointless as well in class rotations except for its pretty animations.
- Side Quests/Missions:     This is more nitpicking but the sidequests in LOTRO (There are exceptions) are.....typical MMO fetch or kill quests. While some of the side quests have interesting stories and background with the lore, nothing has ever really stood out when questing in LOTRO outside of the Main Quest and stories. The actual stories that go along with the quests have improved considerablly since release, so perhaps i'm being abit harsh here. Despite this if you've played through Minas Tirth and done the questchain there, you'll know where i'm coming from when i say it's far from enjoyable at times. It has its ups and downs..
- Mounted Combat:   Speaks for itself. It wasn't asked for and hasn't been used since Rohan effectively or at all outside of a couple of scenarios.
End:
Recommended :)! Thanks for reading

It's basicly "Guess Who" with Edmunds art style and humor, where each round you are given four clues to eleminate as many innocent as you can figure out to figure out who the guilty person is. As you get further and further it adds more twists to how the clues work, but the order of the people you have as clue givers each time is always the same, so its not like one time you will have the third person telling things always in negitive tense, then the next time the third person always saying things oposite of the truth, and then the next time the third person never repeating their clues... the mods for round 3 are always the same the mods for round 10 are always the same, etc, just the clues and line up are different.

-----------------------
Motion Sickness Tips
-----------------------
When i first started up the game, the first thing that i noticed was the unnatural movement.
You have motion blur, zooming while sprinting and above all, your camara wobbels to the left and right when walking.
I turned off motion blur right away since this is a bad thing in any FPS game since you want clear view when shooting enemies, and to get good situational awareness.
However for the first time i can recall i actualy got sick while playing a game, after a mere 40~ minutes, i started feeling dizzy.
Since not everyone knows what names gamedesigners give to camara changes (with an exepetion of motion blur maybe) i decided to write this to help anyone that finds the previous mentioned anoying or feels sick from it.
You can turn all of it off both in the Menu but also while playing.
Go to  >Settings<  and then  >Game<
Here you can turn off the wobbeling of the screen and sprint zooming.
Turn off  >Vieuw BoB<  to stop the screen from wobbeling left and right when moving.
Turn off  >Spring FOV Change<  to stop the screen from zooming in while sprinting.
The last option is under  >Settings<  and then  >Graphics<
Here you will find the  >Motion Blur<  that you can turn off to stop the screen from fading when moving.
