Try to remember the most cheesy action flicks of the 80s you can think of. You know, the usual suspects - films with Chuck Norris, Dolph Lundgren, Steven Seagal, etc. And of these, pick those with the most hilariously absurd sci-fi settings. You know, the kind where every major plot item either has "Cyber-", "Hyper-", or "Lazer-" as a prefix.
Now mash all those titles into one, turn them into a video game, and raise the comical absurdity by 210%. Bang, Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon. You play as Sergeant Rex Power Colt, a cyborg commando sent out to investigate the actions of the rogue Colonel Sloan, who plans to bombard the world with the blood of the eponymous Blood Dragons (essentially dinosaur-like lizards that can shoot laser beams from their eyes) because Washington wants to make piece with the Red Menace.
If you now think "Hey, that sounds disturbingly like every plot for a trash action movie ever", you're just about right. The entire game more or less exists solely to satirize the glorious age of VHS (although it also pokes fun at modern video games i.e. by lampooning the overly long and often annoying tutorials of today's FPS games). The combat system is solid but not spectacular, but you'll nonetheless be grinning or laughing for the better part of your playtime because of the gloriously bad one-liners of Colt and the dialogue in general (my favorite:"Rex, there is death behind this gate" - "What kind of death?" - "The dangerous one"). The only disappointing part of the game is its rather short length (~10 hours if you bother to get all collectables), but considering its price and the fact that this originally was planned as a Far Cry 3 DLC (it's a stand-alone game now), this is acceptable.
Long story short - if you've ever watched a single bad action flick from the 80's, Far Cry 3 - Blood Dragon will  have you laugh your♥♥♥♥♥♥off.

Truth be told, before I started writing reviews, I told myself that I would always finish the game before reviewing, but at this point, I'm not sure if the developers sooner finish developing the game and adding new content, so I can finaly end it, or I die. Now I would risk it and wait, but lately I've been watching a lot of hentai videos, so I'm not sure if my heart keeps beating or gives up from the excitement.
The main implication of the previous paragraph and the reason why I wrote it (other than attracting your attention), is that the game takes god damn forever to finish, even with the amount of content that is currently out, it takes months, possibly years to complete 100%. It's thanks to the mechanic of "restarting" progress - every time you feel like the pace is too slow, you can reset the game, which will make your next playthrough faster, so instead of waiting weeks to "finish" the girl (haha), you "only" have to wait days. Which is neat, at first. As you progress and unlock more girls and girlzlies (yes, it's a bear pun), the game gets insanely fast... and insanely tedious. Clicking through 10 different girls and achieving whatever their hearts desire take forever. At some point I started to feel like I'd rather just wait out those weeks, to get more boost (the further you progress with the girls, the higher the boost will be), just so I don't have to go through the process of clicking again.
Obviously resetting often and thus farming boosts efficiently would be a much faster way to progress... but honestly, ain't nobody got time and energy for that. So that's the main downside to the game. If I were to recommend the game 20 hours in, I'd rate it as positive for sure, but after all this time I spent "playing", or rather - mashing my left mouse button (just kidding, I use AutoHotKey), I really can't give it a thumbs up. It's way too painful, I just wanna finish this stupid game. Please, let me finish it.

Crush Crush is the perfect backup game...  But you intend on playing Crush Crush, make sure that you have a primary game to play while you're "playing" this game.
I've been a sucker for date sim games for over ten years now, and if you're a long time player of the genre, you should also enjoy this game, too.  The girls are good looking, the dialogue is fun, and the types of dates you can take are plentiful.  The large number of jobs that are available adds to the variety, and the large number of gifts you can get for the girls also adds to the variety the game has to offer.
Unfortunately the way Steam reviews work, they're an all or nothing proposition, so while I can recomend this game in good faith, the review system makes reviews an "all or nothing" proposition, and alas, this game is anything but perfect!
I don't know if the frequent typos and sometimes odd syntax is the result of a lack of proofreading or if Sad Panda Studios is intentionally making the game in Engrish (sic) as a means of paying homage to Japanese date sim games that predate Crush Crush, but if you cannot take typos and occasional odd syntax in good humor like I can, you'll probably be agitated by this game.
By all means, Crush Crush should be a backup game to any other video game you're playing.  I made the mistake of downloading Crush Crush when I fell into the mindset where all the other video games I enjoy have gone stale, and that turned out to be a huge mistake.  I just wanted to play a video game, and while you can make remarkable progress early on (especially on Cassie, the first girl you encounter), the amount of money you will need for going on dates and purchasing gifts goes up (there are girls who require over $15 billion in gifts to satisfy a signle requirement) while the rate at which you gain skills and job promotions goes down.  (You're going to find yourself playing professional sports to satisfy one girl's requirement, which is a drag, because it pays far less than being a hunter or a lawyer, and the amount of free time you have to have on your hands to indulge in the sports career is very high.) (Edit:  The number of time blocks required to engage in the professional sports career decreases dramatically with promotions.  This is true of many of the occupations in this game.)
This game is going slow for me despite having purchased $10 of actual (RL) money for diamonds to speed up the game.  And if you don't plan on spending any money on this game, then you should make absolutely certain that you have at least one more game to enjoy while you're waiting to fulfill the requirements needed to win over the girls, because you are going to be waiting an incredibly long time!  Fortunately, the game plays itself while you're not actually in game, so you don't need the game (or even your computer) to be running just to make progress in this game.  (Although you are more than free to sit back and do nothing while you watch the game play itself for you.)
This game has an unusual educational quality to it:  I never learned in school (not even in college) what comes after a trillion, and I had to look up the names for quadrillion and quintillion so I could tell friends of mine about the sort of money one can expect to earn in Crush Crush, and how much they're going to have to pay to buy certain gifts for girlfriends.

I absolutely love this game. Maybe not quite as much as the first one but I still love it. I admit, it really grew on me after some time. Just like in the original, you assume the role of an evil Sauron-lookalike and rain absolute hell on the world as you embark on a series of quests to ultimately subdue it. There is always the option of being a nice(r) guy but the primary goal is to be the nastiest SOB the land's ever seen. Story progression is quick, but it will, in turn, slow down considerably which can bore some. You're crossing stuff off a to-do list the whole time. Regardless of these shortcomings, I still consider myself part of the cult following the series has.
Some nitpicking as referenced by the cons index:
(1) Your minions are stupid, demented, unhinged, and unfathomably cute, but this is no excuse for their shortcomings. Targeting an object/enemy on a ledge is not worth attempting since your minion will probably run to the ledge, stare a bit, and run back even if there is an obvious path leading up to the target. You must either sweep by stick/mouse or confirm they can run straight forward to what you are aiming at. Even the gimped Wii side game developed by Climax has pre-mapped courses; one instance is if there is water blocking a path, your minions will fall back and, in record time, follow a detour and make it to where they're going. None of that here, or the first title. The same bug with spawning minions from a pit and having them clip walls is a nuisance even though they warp back to the Netherworld after about a half a minute of realizing they're stuck.
(2) Overlord originally encouraged you to be a wicked harbinger of destruction with its story-altering irreversible controversial decisions. This time around, you step down to lesser power often throughout the game (some might argue said instances only demonstrate the incredible strength at your disposal) but most of the time, you're just a threat to an always-present higher power and only fundamentally equally-as-powerful as those who occupy your Netherworld "home".
So, with that mouthful out of the way, I very much recommend this game even with its problems. It has all that made the first game good but it also brought along the same exact problems that plagued the first one, and then some. You should enjoy the game but you cannot reject the presence of the flaky stuff.
If all this looks good to you, buy this.
If you are new to Overlord and seek a spin of the unusually original gameplay the main series has to offer, demo or play the superior first game.
If you play primarily for the humor and minions, you will be more than pleased. Buy this.
If you play for the story and gameplay, watch some videos and play the demo before making the plunge and tread lightly. (Let's be honest, controls and gameplay were never a strong suit of the series, your minions clobber everything for you as-is.)
If you enjoyed the original as much as I did (VERY thoroughly), buy this.
If you thought the first game was alright and you expect real improvements this time around, steer clear and perhaps take a look at Dark Legend for the Wii for a more traditional experience.

I did truly enjoy this game, the story was amazing and thrilling on so many levels, the metaphors and presentation of the metaphors was brilliant. The aspect of personal programming was spot on.
The writings and the depth of the story were and are obviously presented on several levels, and the real-time rendition was and are great. The syncs were at times amusingly flawless.
Everything from the visual art, to music and voice-acting proves the amount of work that went into this. I also enjoyed the multilinguistic aspect of the gameplay, it added a lot to the illusive space. The amount of fluff were amusing, and some of the patterns and references were absolutely enjoyable. This game nails why I 999 time out of 1000 dislike 'cat people', especially the crazy ones.
Other from that, the only thing that really got to me at a few times was the physics engine, both irritatingly and amusingly. I found it fun that the copy-machine was to heavy to lift without augmentation, but if you got a trashcan and pushed it towards it, it took off faster than Apollo 4. (Wooow, that metaphor right there)
Then I had some minor problems with the graphics where I got stuck, and Mr Jensen got severe seizures all over the screen, which kind of demoralised the will to explore a little, poor Jensen (and they all occured after Koller did his♥♥♥♥♥♥.
- But hey, that is to be expected I guess, especially with such graphics this game offered.
Although some of the shooting were really annoying, when one missed a target at almost point blank. One should not really have to use a long range weapon with a scope if the target is about five meters away just to be on the safe side.
But then again, it is not like I could make a better game myself, but to be nuanced in my review; as those parts got the best of my patience at some occasions.
Nothing that would prevent me from recommending this game anyhow. Because one should play it if one is interested in really anything that is on 'that' side of the Internet these days, to be fair and honest. And if not that, then to stay in touch with some parts of the most cutting edge science of this momentum.
Because in terms of information and knowledge embedded, well, what more can really be said other than it is spot on, on several levels simultaneously.. there are obviously (as always) room for expansion in the story and illusive space, even though I have not played all the games, and scientifically and progressively, there are interesting lines which could be taken in eventual upcoming sequels. For me, Grand Theft Auto V’s extraordinary scope is summed up in two favourite moments. One is from a mid-game mission in which I flew a plane into another plane, fought the crew, hijacked the thing, and then parachuted out and watched it crash into the sea to escape death at the hands of incoming military fighter jets. Another time, whilst driving around in an off-road buggy, I got distracted by something that looked like a path up one of the San Andreas mountains. Turns out it was a path, and I spent 15 minutes following to the summit, where I nearly ran over a group of hikers. “Typical!” one of them yelled at me, as if he nearly gets run over by a rogue ATV on top of a mountain every time he goes on a hike.
I could go on like this for ages. GTA V has an abundance of such moments, big and small, that make San Andreas – the city of Los Santos and its surrounding areas – feel like a living world where anything can happen. It both gives you tremendous freedom to explore an astonishingly well-realised world and tells a story that’s gripping, thrilling, and darkly comic. It is a leap forward in narrative sophistication for the series, and there’s no mechanical element of the gameplay that hasn’t been improved over Grand Theft Auto IV. It’s immediately noticeable that the cover system is more reliable and the auto-aim less touchy. The cars handle less like their tires are made of butter and stick better to the road, though their exaggerated handling still leaves plenty of room for spectacular wipeouts. And at long last, Rockstar has finally slain one of its most persistent demons, mission checkpointing, ensuring that you never have to do a long, tedious drive six times when you repeatedly fail a mission ever again.
Grand Theft Auto V is also an intelligent, wickedly comic, and bitingly relevant commentary on contemporary, post-economic crisis America. Everything about it drips satire: it rips into the Millennial generation, celebrities, the far right, the far left, the middle class, the media... Nothing is safe from Rockstar’s sharp tongue, including modern video games. One prominent supporting character spends most of his time in his room shouting sexual threats at people on a headset whilst playing a first-person shooter called Righteous Slaughter (“Rated PG – pretty much the same as the last game.”) It’s not exactly subtle – he literally has the word “Entitled” tattooed on his neck, and the in-game radio and TV’s outright♥♥♥♥♥♥takes don’t leave much to the imagination – but it is often extremely funny, and sometimes provocative with it. Grand Theft Auto’s San Andreas is a fantasy, but the things it satirises – greed, corruption, hypocrisy, the abuse of power – are all very real. If GTA IV was a targeted assassination of the American dream, GTA V takes aim at the modern American reality. The attention to detail that goes into making its world feel alive and believable is also what makes its satire so biting.
Grand Theft Auto V’s plot happily operates at the boundaries of plausibility, sending you out to ride dirt bikes along the top of trains, hijack military aircraft, and engage in absurd shootouts with scores of policemen, but its three main characters are what keep it relatable even at its most extreme. The well-written and acted interplay between them provides the biggest laughs and most affecting moments, and the way that their relationships with one another developed and my opinion of them changed throughout the story gave the narrative its power. They feel like people – albeit extraordinarily f***ed-up people.
Michael is a retired con man in his 40s, filling out around the middle as he drinks beside the pool in his Vinewood mansion with a layabout son, air-headed daughter, serially unfaithful wife, and very expensive therapist – all of whom hate him. Franklin is a young man from downtown Los Santos who laments the gang-banger stereotype even as he’s reluctantly seduced by the prospect of a bigger score. And then there’s Trevor, a volatile career criminal who lives in the desert selling drugs and murdering rednecks; a psychopath whose bloodthirsty lunacy is fuelled by a combination of methamphetamine and a seriously messed-up childhood.
The missions flit between their individual stories and an overarching plotline that involves all three, and it’s a credit to GTA V’s versatility and universal quality that each character has his share of standout missions. As their arcs developed I felt very differently about each of them at different times – they’re not entirely the archetypes that they seem to be.
This three-character structure makes for excellent pacing and great variety in the storyline, but it also allows Rockstar to compartmentalise different aspects of Grand Theft Auto’s personality. In doing so, it sidesteps some of the troubling disconnect that arose when Niko Bellic abruptly alternated between anti-violent philosophising and sociopathic killing sprees in GTA IV. Here, many of Michael’s missions revolve around his family and his past, Franklin is usually on call for vehicular mayhem, and extreme murderous rampages are left to Trevor. Each has a special ability suited to his skills – Franklin can to slow time while driving, for example – which gives them a unique touch. Narratively, it’s effective – even off-mission I found myself playing in character, acting like a mid-life-crisis guy with anger issues as Michael, a thrill-seeker as Franklin, and a maniac as Trevor. The first thing I did when Franklin finally made some good money was buy him an awesome car, because I felt like that’s what he’d want.
Trevor feels a like a bit of a get-out-of-jail-free card for Rockstar, providing an outlet for all the preposterous antics and murderous behaviour that otherwise might not fit in with GTA V’s narrative ambitions. I found his violent insanity a little overblown and tiresome at first. As get-out clauses go, though, it’s pretty effective, and Trevor’s over-the-top missions are some of GTA V’s action-packed highlights. It’s a successful way of solving a problem that’s prevalent in open-world games: the tension between the story that the writers are trying to tell, and the story you create yourself within its systems and its world. Grand Theft Auto V accommodates both, masterfully, allowing neither to undermine the other.
The actual act of switching between them also provides a window into their individual lives and habits, fleshing out their personalities in a way that feels natural and novel. Pick a character and the camera zooms out over the San Andreas map, closing back in on wherever they happen to be. Michael might be at home watching TV when you drop in on him, or speeding along the motorway blasting ‘80s hits, or having a cigarette at the golf club; Franklin might be walking out of a strip club, munching a bag of snacks at home, or arguing with his ex-girlfriend; there’s a good chance that Trevor could be passed out half naked on a beach surrounded by dead bodies or, on one memorable occasion, drunk in a stolen police helicopter.
It could be nearly anything, because there is a bewildering multiplicity of things to do in the new San Andreas – tennis, yoga, hiking, racing on sea and on land, flying planes, golfing, cycling, diving, hunting, and more. The missions are an able guide to both San Andreas’ locations and its activities, touring you around the map and whetting your appetite for independent exploration of it all. The way that we’re introduced to San Andreas never feels artificial – the map is completely open from the start, for example – which contributes to the impression that it’s a real place, somewhere you can get to know. If GTA IV’s Liberty City feels like a living city, San Andreas feels like a living world. Even so, I would STILL recommend this game. I reported the bug and the developer responded within the day. Either way, it's a wonderful game and I'm in love. Thoroughly.

Simple and sweet, a town-management game where you can't directly control your subjects.  Lead a small band of adventurous gnomes into the founding of a new colony, and defend them not only against starvation, but also hostile goblin raiders and hungry beasts!
Simple and fun once you get the hang of it, with a basic 'dig and build' approach to the world controls.  Randomized terrain and gnome stats make this a slight blend into roguelike, which has both ups and downs.  The in-game orchestra sound track is quite nice, and the game sounds are decent quality for a beta.
The combat is not difficult to understand; you can give instructions to your gnomes on how to conduct themselves in battle (I favor a kamikaze rush), and the enemies present a bit of variety in tactics as well; animals will run if hurt, and goblins will happily test your defenses.
Poor graphics* and terrible default sound track.  There's not very much to do (still early access at time of writing), and so the game can be very slow after a while.  Strong learning curve with no starting instructions, and at time of writing resources can be difficult to get together for items needed for the game.  Few explanations and warnings for events makes some facets of the game a bit challenging.  The pathing AI can be a bit funny.
* 8-bit, might be your thing.

I bought the game last week, game wasn't properly published (thus unplayable) until I had a chat with Steam Support. That said, here's the review after the game became playable.
The Return Home is a game about a rabbit thrown out of its home by lizards for an inexplicable reason and now the rabbit's after revenge.
From the time I've spent playing the game, I'd say you can beat this game in about 20 minutes or less. The first half of the game is you just running around on a fetch quest, the second half is a sketchy FPS against the shoddy AI lizards you spent the first half running away from, after which the game just ends out of the blue.
The graphics are okay and it's always neat to see some cel-shading. However, several problems arise with broken lighting and other visual effects, causing significant performance lag, especially on the second half of the game.
The in-game music is mostly just a semi-repetitive beat akin to certain tracks from the Serious Sam games. The cutscene music is excessively loud in comparison. You can't skip the cutscenes and the options only become available after entering the game itself.
In short, despite its low price tag, the game is not currently in a state you'd get much bang for your buck. It'd probably last you longer than a candy bar, but the aftertaste isn't as pleasant. Don't get it.
Also, what's up with that completely empty "About" button in the main menu?

Trine 2 is a side-scrolling adventure game of puzzles and platforming where you play as one of three heroes who make their way through dangers in a wondrous fairytale world.
It is playable as single- and multiplayer. In single player mode there is only one hero at a time playable but you can switch between the others as often as you want, to use their individual powers.
Each hero has its own special abilities which helps you to complete certain tasks to progress through the levels and strike down enemies. Often there are different ways to solve puzzles which require to use your environment surroundings.
You can level up by picking up experience orbs. Some are easy to find but there are much trickier ones to get and even secrets to discover. There are small talent trees for each hero to improve and gain new abilities.
What makes Trine 2 so unique is the mesmerizing and enchanting world you're facing.
The great artworks and many lovely details stood out for me the most.
The beautiful fitting music combined with the dazzling illustrations are creating a stunning atmosphere.
Worth mentioning is also the brilliant narrated story and poems within the game.

To conclude, this game is amazing and I can definitely recommend it.
The amount of gaming hours you'll spend playing it alone or with your friends will be a great experience and is totally worth the purchase.

is a tower defense game with real time strategy resource management elements. It’s this resource management which is both a highlight of the game and -in my opinion- its downfall. A core mechanic is sending worker bees to collect pollen, nectar and water to build and maintain towers, which does keep players on their toes having to keep an eye on resources as they fight enemy waves. However, the game is short and relies on grinding a certain resource to unlock good upgrades, adding on a lackluster story it ends up being a missed opportunity and something most will skip over in favor of other tower defense games that can offer more.
There is a story element of the game but it’s pretty uninspired. You’re in control of a bee colony who is trying to find a new home but along the way are being chased by enemies who are after your honey supply. The main enemy is Queen Hornetta, as wasp who needs honey to wax her legs. It was finding this out which really cinched things for me that the story is pointless and while has a few humorous moments doesn’t add much of anything. While a game like this doesn’t need an deep story, they tried to add one and I wish it were better.
This game is played with a mouse, most actions require you to click and drag your worker bees where you need them as well as creating battle towers along the path. As with most tower defense games, the main objective is to keep enemy forces away from your main base, they come in waves and the difficulty increases as a level progresses. There are six tower types and each one has two different upgrades which alters how they work somewhat and can change your gameplay options. However, the only way to upgrade them is Honey Dew, the biggest problem with the game. You get this resource by collecting it in certain levels as well hitting certain goals at the end of a level, however you need thousands of units of the stuff to upgrade towers which means a lot of grinding. You can also use Honey Dew to advance your technology giving nice boosts like faster moving bees among many others but again, it becomes very costly. The game is short with only twenty levels but the grinding makes it a slog and feels much longer..

Crush Crush is the perfect backup game...  But you intend on playing Crush Crush, make sure that you have a primary game to play while you're "playing" this game.
I've been a sucker for date sim games for over ten years now, and if you're a long time player of the genre, you should also enjoy this game, too.  The girls are good looking, the dialogue is fun, and the types of dates you can take are plentiful.  The large number of jobs that are available adds to the variety, and the large number of gifts you can get for the girls also adds to the variety the game has to offer.
Unfortunately the way Steam reviews work, they're an all or nothing proposition, so while I can recomend this game in good faith, the review system makes reviews an "all or nothing" proposition, and alas, this game is anything but perfect!
I don't know if the frequent typos and sometimes odd syntax is the result of a lack of proofreading or if Sad Panda Studios is intentionally making the game in Engrish (sic) as a means of paying homage to Japanese date sim games that predate Crush Crush, but if you cannot take typos and occasional odd syntax in good humor like I can, you'll probably be agitated by this game.
By all means, Crush Crush should be a backup game to any other video game you're playing.  I made the mistake of downloading Crush Crush when I fell into the mindset where all the other video games I enjoy have gone stale, and that turned out to be a huge mistake.  I just wanted to play a video game, and while you can make remarkable progress early on (especially on Cassie, the first girl you encounter), the amount of money you will need for going on dates and purchasing gifts goes up (there are girls who require over $15 billion in gifts to satisfy a signle requirement) while the rate at which you gain skills and job promotions goes down.  (You're going to find yourself playing professional sports to satisfy one girl's requirement, which is a drag, because it pays far less than being a hunter or a lawyer, and the amount of free time you have to have on your hands to indulge in the sports career is very high.) (Edit:  The number of time blocks required to engage in the professional sports career decreases dramatically with promotions.  This is true of many of the occupations in this game.)
This game is going slow for me despite having purchased $10 of actual (RL) money for diamonds to speed up the game.  And if you don't plan on spending any money on this game, then you should make absolutely certain that you have at least one more game to enjoy while you're waiting to fulfill the requirements needed to win over the girls, because you are going to be waiting an incredibly long time!  Fortunately, the game plays itself while you're not actually in game, so you don't need the game (or even your computer) to be running just to make progress in this game.  (Although you are more than free to sit back and do nothing while you watch the game play itself for you.)

Tower defense, with some RTS.
So far I am only 7 episodes in.  Each episode (map) has been fairly short (less than 10 rounds).
The RTS adds some interesting elements.  However, I prefer my TD to be a leisurely contemplation of strategy while I do other things such as watch TV.  In this game, the RTS element requires more active attention, such as making sure that while the bees are flying back and forth harvesting, they don't run into the MOBs (which results in the bees becoming imprisoned).

You can watch some gameplay which includes my level 17 honey dew farming method here
or read the written review below.
Beefense is a really fun tower defense game. With an added RTS twist.
Its a pretty standard tower defense setup but it adds a resource gathering requirement.
You start with a few bees on a level. You have to command bees to harvest different resources and pilot towers.
You harvest pollen as a resource to buy and upgrade towers, and also to buy more bees.
You harvest nectar which will keep your towers operating at a sustained damage output.
You harvest honey dew which is used to upgrade and improve towers and bees globally between levels.
You harvest water which if enough collected will allow you to activate a water boost power up.
This makes all of the towers on the map much more effective with increased damage and range.
Towers must also have a bee inside them to actually function. If no bees are in a tower it will not fire.
This leads to lots of micromanagement that keep games feeling engaging throughout.
So most levels start out with 1 bee, You make another bee and get those gathering pollen.
Usually the first 3-4 bees I have gathering pollen. Then I'll buy my first few towers using the pollen gathered.
The next 2 bees I will have harvesting nectar to keep my towers firing at full capacity.
Set the next couple on bees to pilot the towers. I usually start with a gatling and a long range rocket tower.
Then build more towers and bees over the coming waves. When all the pollen is harvested I'll switch them to harvest water for the water boost power up.
There are 20 levels to play, each with 3 in mission objectives. Which made coming back and trying to beat the mission in a different way enjoyable. The towers and bee upgrades are purchased with honey dew which is acquired during levels. These upgrades includes 2 unlocks per tower eg. on the gatling tower you can unlock a snail variant which slows down enemies and an incendiary ammo variant which will do damage over time. There are also bee unlocks which increase harvest speed and speed up bee flight speed etc. Most of these are easy to get. There was one upgrade which boosts all your placed towers to a upgraded level. Which is very powerful. Unlocking the last stage of this required 50000 honey dew which took awhile to acquire. The fastest farming method I found was level 17, which netted me 1500-1700 honey dew for each 4minute run.
If you are a tower defense fan this is a no brainer. You should pick this up immediately. Its very reasonably priced even when not on sale. The main mission will take you 4-6 hours to complete. This probably stretches to 10 hours if you want to farm honey dew for every single unlock. I've played 20+ hours. I enjoy going back to levels and attempting them in different ways. Definitely worth your time.
A review code was provided for free by the developer.

Cute tower defense game with an 'unbeelievable' amount of bee puns. Takes the same tower defense mechanics that you know and love and crosses it with a kind of RTS resource management side where you need to decide what tasks to assign your bees to at any given time. Do you need them manning the towers? Or collecting the various resources scattered throughout each level? 
 
If you like your tower defense games this one is worth picking up for its current price of under a fiver. 
 
 
Beefense has a cute story for the campaign, it's not going to win any Oscars but is a nice detail that is often overlooked in the tower defense genre. Thought has gone into the level design. The game eases you in gently but you will have to use some strategy to beat the later levels. 
 
Managing your bees adds an interesting twist but it can be easy to lose track of how many bees you have assigned to each task. It would be good to have a panel showing how many bees were assigned to each task. 
 
There is a persistent upgrade system which gets you thinking which upgrade to buy for maximum effect. But Beefense's free to play origins can make earning these upgrades a bit grindy. It would also be good to get some Steam achievements added. 
 
Mrs Biscuit loves her tower defense games and gives Beefense 9/10. Better than Go Home Dinosaurs but it's no Desktop Tower Defense. Worth a look.

For me, Grand Theft Auto V’s extraordinary scope is summed up in two favourite moments. One is from a mid-game mission in which I flew a plane into another plane, fought the crew, hijacked the thing, and then parachuted out and watched it crash into the sea to escape death at the hands of incoming military fighter jets. Another time, whilst driving around in an off-road buggy, I got distracted by something that looked like a path up one of the San Andreas mountains. Turns out it was a path, and I spent 15 minutes following to the summit, where I nearly ran over a group of hikers. “Typical!” one of them yelled at me, as if he nearly gets run over by a rogue ATV on top of a mountain every time he goes on a hike.
I could go on like this for ages. GTA V has an abundance of such moments, big and small, that make San Andreas – the city of Los Santos and its surrounding areas – feel like a living world where anything can happen. It both gives you tremendous freedom to explore an astonishingly well-realised world and tells a story that’s gripping, thrilling, and darkly comic. It is a leap forward in narrative sophistication for the series, and there’s no mechanical element of the gameplay that hasn’t been improved over Grand Theft Auto IV. It’s immediately noticeable that the cover system is more reliable and the auto-aim less touchy. The cars handle less like their tires are made of butter and stick better to the road, though their exaggerated handling still leaves plenty of room for spectacular wipeouts. And at long last, Rockstar has finally slain one of its most persistent demons, mission checkpointing, ensuring that you never have to do a long, tedious drive six times when you repeatedly fail a mission ever again.
Grand Theft Auto V is also an intelligent, wickedly comic, and bitingly relevant commentary on contemporary, post-economic crisis America. Everything about it drips satire: it rips into the Millennial generation, celebrities, the far right, the far left, the middle class, the media... Nothing is safe from Rockstar’s sharp tongue, including modern video games. One prominent supporting character spends most of his time in his room shouting sexual threats at people on a headset whilst playing a first-person shooter called Righteous Slaughter (“Rated PG – pretty much the same as the last game.”) It’s not exactly subtle – he literally has the word “Entitled” tattooed on his neck, and the in-game radio and TV’s outright♥♥♥♥♥♥takes don’t leave much to the imagination – but it is often extremely funny, and sometimes provocative with it. Grand Theft Auto’s San Andreas is a fantasy, but the things it satirises – greed, corruption, hypocrisy, the abuse of power – are all very real. If GTA IV was a targeted assassination of the American dream, GTA V takes aim at the modern American reality. The attention to detail that goes into making its world feel alive and believable is also what makes its satire so biting.
Grand Theft Auto V’s plot happily operates at the boundaries of plausibility, sending you out to ride dirt bikes along the top of trains, hijack military aircraft, and engage in absurd shootouts with scores of policemen, but its three main characters are what keep it relatable even at its most extreme. The well-written and acted interplay between them provides the biggest laughs and most affecting moments, and the way that their relationships with one another developed and my opinion of them changed throughout the story gave the narrative its power. They feel like people – albeit extraordinarily f***ed-up people.
Michael is a retired con man in his 40s, filling out around the middle as he drinks beside the pool in his Vinewood mansion with a layabout son, air-headed daughter, serially unfaithful wife, and very expensive therapist – all of whom hate him. Franklin is a young man from downtown Los Santos who laments the gang-banger stereotype even as he’s reluctantly seduced by the prospect of a bigger score. And then there’s Trevor, a volatile career criminal who lives in the desert selling drugs and murdering rednecks; a psychopath whose bloodthirsty lunacy is fuelled by a combination of methamphetamine and a seriously messed-up childhood.
The missions flit between their individual stories and an overarching plotline that involves all three, and it’s a credit to GTA V’s versatility and universal quality that each character has his share of standout missions. As their arcs developed I felt very differently about each of them at different times – they’re not entirely the archetypes that they seem to be.
This three-character structure makes for excellent pacing and great variety in the storyline, but it also allows Rockstar to compartmentalise different aspects of Grand Theft Auto’s personality. In doing so, it sidesteps some of the troubling disconnect that arose when Niko Bellic abruptly alternated between anti-violent philosophising and sociopathic killing sprees in GTA IV. Here, many of Michael’s missions revolve around his family and his past, Franklin is usually on call for vehicular mayhem, and extreme murderous rampages are left to Trevor. Each has a special ability suited to his skills – Franklin can to slow time while driving, for example – which gives them a unique touch. Narratively, it’s effective – even off-mission I found myself playing in character, acting like a mid-life-crisis guy with anger issues as Michael, a thrill-seeker as Franklin, and a maniac as Trevor. The first thing I did when Franklin finally made some good money was buy him an awesome car, because I felt like that’s what he’d want.
Trevor feels a like a bit of a get-out-of-jail-free card for Rockstar, providing an outlet for all the preposterous antics and murderous behaviour that otherwise might not fit in with GTA V’s narrative ambitions. I found his violent insanity a little overblown and tiresome at first. As get-out clauses go, though, it’s pretty effective, and Trevor’s over-the-top missions are some of GTA V’s action-packed highlights. It’s a successful way of solving a problem that’s prevalent in open-world games: the tension between the story that the writers are trying to tell, and the story you create yourself within its systems and its world. Grand Theft Auto V accommodates both, masterfully, allowing neither to undermine the other.
The actual act of switching between them also provides a window into their individual lives and habits, fleshing out their personalities in a way that feels natural and novel. Pick a character and the camera zooms out over the San Andreas map, closing back in on wherever they happen to be. Michael might be at home watching TV when you drop in on him, or speeding along the motorway blasting ‘80s hits, or having a cigarette at the golf club; Franklin might be walking out of a strip club, munching a bag of snacks at home, or arguing with his ex-girlfriend; there’s a good chance that Trevor could be passed out half naked on a beach surrounded by dead bodies or, on one memorable occasion, drunk in a stolen police helicopter.
It could be nearly anything, because there is a bewildering multiplicity of things to do in the new San Andreas – tennis, yoga, hiking, racing on sea and on land, flying planes, golfing, cycling, diving, hunting, and more. The missions are an able guide to both San Andreas’ locations and its activities, touring you around the map and whetting your appetite for independent exploration of it all. The way that we’re introduced to San Andreas never feels artificial – the map is completely open from the start, for example – which contributes to the impression that it’s a real place, somewhere you can get to know. If GTA IV’s Liberty City feels like a living city, San Andreas feels like a living world. It's difficult for me to recommend this game because my review of it would be something akin to a 6/10, but that's being kind. I got the game on sale because of the reviews I heard about it, and most of the reviews had to do with the game's performance during launch. I normally find this a great inconvenience but not ultimately damaging to a game or game franchise unless the issue is not eventually settled. I can say that I ran into no such issues with this game; it ran smoothly on my system, but that may be due to the fact that I bought this game months after launch and therefore probably fixed for the most part.
Having said that, the reason I am giving this just a little over a half-descent game is because of the gameplay. I thought the gameplay was not terrrible to get the hang of. There were some hang ups here and there, but overall, I thought the gameplay was cool. The cover system has some cool expansions, but again, there are some hang ups here, too. I like the ability to switch cover and to have the waypoint path that Jensen will follow visible when he changes cover, but it seems like Jensen only goes so far in a waypoint path before he just stops moving. If my next point of cover is just four-five feet away, no problem. Any farther, Jensen goes about four-five feet and just stops. The additional augmentations were real cool, and the story behind their addition to the game cool as well.
My biggest beef is with the story. Conspiracy is obviously the primary theme of the Deus Ex story. The first Deus Ex had an incredible storyline to it, and one that kept you constantly wondering who was who, what was next, where the next twist or revelation was, and who could be trusted and so forth. In other words, it maintained a good element of mystery necessary to conspiracy. You're an agent sent on a mission, come to discovery a massive global conspiracy against the world by a secret society. Human Revolution I thought delivered on this as well. I loved the mysterious nature of the Illuminati in Human Revolution, and the attempt to discover how and why they would attack an augmentation company. Why would a mere augmentation company become a threat to the Illuminati? There was a big mystery to it all you uncover as the story unfolds, and you uncover everyone's role in the whole conspiracy too.
In Mankind Divided, the storyline was so utterly predictable and bland. It is nothing more than your typical scapegoat story where the real badguys disguise themselves as someone else, commit terrorist attacks and then begin a propaganda campaign on destroying that very group. It is so obvious in all the news stories present throughout the game that this is the case. The only mystery you have to unravel at this point is who, if anyone, on your side is with the conspirators. I don't know if it was the plan for the developers to make it clear that augs were not the real problem but a planted group among them you need to find, but if it was, it just ruined the story and any interest in uncovering the plot. Literally the only reason I finished the story was to get the +New Game and play the whole story as one bad♥♥♥♥♥ fully augmented Jensen. I had absolutely no interest in the story whatsoever. Personally, I would think a more compelling story would be augmentations becoming more and more cool and inviting. People exchanging their humanity for machine under the propaganda of 'human evolution', when in reality, the Illuminati is using augmentation technology and its appeal to push people further into its own control. If advancement in technology is the goal of the future, why on earth would humanity detest augmentations? This would in fact be the next rennaisance. This would be a field trip for propaganda for the Illuminati, provided they are in control of the technological revolution. Society today has become so reliant on technology that kids today can barely even solve simple math problems without a calculator, or even spell without spell-check present. It's so pervasive that it makes us more and more dependent upon the technology. The government watches us through our cell phones that we can't live without. It would be more realistic for globalists to further propogate growing closer to these things and the advancement of technology, not away from it. But I digress. Nevertheless, terrible story development with a bland and predictable outcome. Storywise, this game gets a solid 2/10. For gameplay, because of the added features, but still with gameplay hick-ups, I give it a 5/10, and an all-in-all 6/10.
If you love the Deus Ex franchise as it once was, you won't like this one at all. Bad story, descent gameplay, but that's really it. It was definitely not worth $59.99; glad I got it for 75% off.

I am appalled by the amount of negative reviews this game has gotten, which is VERY undeserved in my opinion.
It's like Human Revolution, but better. I wasn't expecting much from the new augments, but remote hacking, integrated P.E.P.S. and Icarus dash are mad useful.
Energy usage is far less of an issue in this title than it was in Human Revolution, which speeds up the gameplay significantly.
Level design is top notch and the amount of detail in the game is insane. Human Revolution could be quite restricting in it's own way, but in Human Revolution verticality is embraced and encouraged, along with the usual many nooks and crannies. Don't get me wrong; it's still a path from A to B, like Human Revolution, but you'll have plenty of ground to cover.
There's a good amount of side-missions with varied objectives and there are always multiple manners to complete your tasks.
Pocket secretaries, emails and ebooks are back in large numbers and it's very much worth reading all of them.
The game is absolutely gorgeous. It runs at a very solid 60fps on very high, 1440p, though with the sidenote that this is on a GTX 1070 + SSD combo. Keep in mind that Ultra was created for those magic future computers, alike Crysis back in 2007.
Levels are packed to the brim with props and civilians. You'll find some model clipping here and there, especially in Golem City, but I figure that as a necessary evil considering the amount of stuff they crammed into it.
Unfortunately, dialogue animation is a right mess. I don't know whether it's due to a bad character animation lead, management or Square Enix rushing the developers (read: most likely the latter), but they really are ridiculous. At least the humans actually look human now.
Cutscenes are horribly compressed and the actual game looks far better. In-engine cutscenes next time, kthnx. If there is a next time.
I'll keep it short.
Hnnnnnng.
I must admit I can't comment much on this yet considering I haven't finished the game yet, but it's not as good as Human Revolution's. That doesn't mean there isn't plenty of stuff going on here. This is a dialogue-heavy game and the voice acting is very good. I really appreciate the scripts, 'cause they divulge meaningful backstory, explore the emotional state of characters and their environments and to me it feels quite genuine. Some may take offense to the stereotypical harsh, offensive slavs you run into from time to time, but this was charming to me. It's not like there aren't plenty of other character archetypes in the game.
The most important bit; atmosphere a plenty.
Choices you make throughout the game will be reflected upon throughout the game, not just at the ending.
And to the people that go "hurr durr bad ending"; Human Revolution had a disgusting excuse of an "ending" and that game got glowing reviews. And I enjoyed that game greatly too, despite it's very weak ending and very weak boss fights. I don't care how soured anyone may be by the (lack of) ending in Mankind Divided; I know how important proper closure is, but to give a game that's superior to Human Revolution gameplay-wise a negative review purely for it's ending and the microtransactions, is criminal to me.
It's a seperate option in the menu. I have not encountered it in-game.
You get PLENTY of credits and praxis kits in-game.
So, it's there for casuals or people that don't have time to explore every nook 'n cranny 'cause of work/life/family, and I never run into it and am actually better off not purchasing it due to balancing reasons.
The pre-order scheme was absolutely terrible and Square Enix has definitely been punished for it, but that's no longer an issue.
So, why exactly does a feature that can so easily be overlooked influence the review scores of so many?
A flawed game due to Square Enix rushing the developers, but an absolutely brilliant game nonetheless. It looks amazing, it sounds amazing, it plays amazing. Whilst the storyline doesn't surpass Human Revolution, the story in it's place is fulfilling and the amount of well voice acted dialogue makes for a very atmospheric game.
Whilst there are less levels and hubs than Human Revolution or other past Deus Ex titles, they are immensely detailed and well designed.
To be honest, I enjoy this game far more than Human Revolution.
It'd be a fool's choice to disregard this game 'cause of people leaving negative reviews for the microtransactions, which are not encountered or needed at all in-game.

The original Deus Ex, from the year 2000, is still in my opinion, the greatest game of all time. And with that in mind Mankind Divided is simply disappointing.
It is far too short and DLC should not be a thing in a single player game. It does the franchinse a disservice.
The world feels very small in MD... you bounce around to a handful of places.. but spend most of your time in a hub city... while the original had you going all over the world with each location having various side locations to explore.
Set well before the original game, all the nods to the original just felt like easter eggs more than anything. The story ended before any of those nods could be seen as anything more. The original Deus Ex was a massive self contained story. There was so much to love about it.. but ultimately you felt like you got a great story and thus a great game out of it. MD just feels like its the second act in a trilogy, with Human Revolution being the intro to the characters and setting.
As much as I love the franchise, I think I will hold off on the next sequel at least until any launch issues are sorted and to see the reviews. I don't want to buy it if it's not a complete game. It needs to live up to the franchise... which does feel impossible.. but it needs to be a better attempt than this.
Now, visually the game was amazing. I rarely experienced issues during my playthough.. The odd crash held me up initially, but those issues have since been sorted. On that note, the dev support for the game has been really great. I think most issues stem more from the publishes trying to milk it rather than developer decision.
Overall though, I cannot recommend this game. I would rather urge you to get the original, it can generally be found for less than $5... and it is simply amazing.

Ok. Deus Ex: Mankind Divided!

The visuals are pretty average, but the level and art design is really nice. They have kept the same theme from Human Revolution, but improved on it.
One thing I noticed is that most of this game takes place in the daytime. I think it diminishes the 'cyberpunk' feel, and when the game changes to the rainy night (sadly towards the end of the game), it shows what I reckon was missing. A proper day/night cycle along with dynamic weather could have done wonders!
Also of note here, is that when I first played this at it's initial release, the performance was abysmal. It has improved greatly but it is still rather demanding, considering the visuals and effects themselves are not that great. Mess with a couple of different graphical options though, and it is no drama's. I maxed everything out minus a couple of things.
The voice acting is great, but the lip synching is not. I like all the different accents used in the game, gave it a really 'international' feel. The music is your usual lovely Deus Ex style, and changing from mellow to chaotic when you go from stealth to gun's blazing.
Everything does it's job, but I did notice it doesn't use audio channels as well as it could.
I also noticed that when it's raining, standing in a doorway can be dead quiet, but as soon as you take literally one step forward you can hear it raining heavily. Almost like the ambient rain sound is missing or something. Channel problems due to bad coding?
The story is where every Deus Ex shines, and this is no exception. The side missions were also great to get into, and a welcome addition that added a lot more to the game. Obviously not much can be said without spoiling things, but if you are going to buy this then make sure you do them and follow them through one at a time! They are worth it.

Dead Space 2 in the broadest sense is a direct upgrade of the first game, however it also carries some of the same problems that the first game has.

The atmosphere, lighting, and just gameplay in general are amazing. Playing through the campaign you won't be disappointed.
My biggest problem with the game is the lack of horror elements as described earlier. The game is perfect when it comes to building up to the scare, however when it does deliver the payoff it's usually as over the top as possible. An example of this is during the first cutscene in the game, where it builds up to the scare, however, it immedietly goes too far and just becomes confusing to say the least.
The multiplayer in this game is practically dead, however you might find a match with 2-4 people in it.
Overall this game for me is a 9/10.

Dead Space 2 is a great game 8.5/10!
The story is pretty good 8/10. Several twists and turns. It sure helps to have played Dead Space first.
The difficulty settings give is some extra play through value. Along with the option to start a new game with all the items you gathered in a previous game. 10/10
The game is really linear 5/10. If you like linear games it's great, but I'd rather explore and have to figure out may way. If Dea Space 2 was an open wolrd (for the most part), being able to go all over an entire space station, where enemies could pop up at any moment, this game would get max score. Because it's linear the enemies have predefined appearances and so the second go around you know where the enemies pop up. Very much tied to a set story.
If the story was more tree like, with other endings or outcomes this would really bring this game over the top, but it doesn't do that.
The graphics are great, nuff said.
The movement is a bit restrictive, but they do this to add to the horrer effect. It's great that the enemies move much faster than you, other wise you would be shocked when something pops out.
Enemy variety is lacking 6/10. Later in the game you see the same monsters but with slightly different color that have more hitting power and health, but their tactics are the same. They should come up with better kill strategies that are more complex than just shooting, like adding some environmental things into a strategy to kill bosses.
They need to have a bit more movement in the charater, like jumping, which is none existent. But the zero-gravity sections are great, where you get to fly around. I wish there were a lot more of this kind of stuff though. 7/10
The game mechanics are good. 7/10 They have leveling of items and a growth tier system, so you have a sense of progression, unlike Gears of War. It's nice to have a progression system but it is minimum, they should have a bit more with regard to progression systems.
Sounds are great 9/10
Overall, dead space is a safe game to add to your collection. Most of these recommendations are for the devs who should build out the game a bit more to make it a stellar game.

Excerpt from my blog review on Wild Season:
First off, Harv---I mean, Wild Season has a lot of potential. Since it IS in its early stage, Wild Season is plagued by hilariously wonky bugs and glitches in which I actually I had to stop playing it after 3 or 4 days. However, it shares the same addictive qualities as the beloved Harvest Moon games with, of course, its own spin on it.
What separates Wild Season's storyline from HM is its dark, suspenseful storyline. When you first start, you'll quickly notice that everyone in this town hates you. While the filler of the game is farming, taking care of animals, etc the storyline keeps you hooked to find out the answers and improve your relationships. Wild Season has done a good job on character development giving each NPC unique, intriguing personalities.
One of the unique features of Wild Season is its quest board where NPC's enlist your help by putting up timed errands. Problem is there are just too many bugs and glitches it's almost unplayeable. The funniest glitch that made me laugh was seemingly switching bodies with an NPC in front of me during a quest. Keyboard shortcuts don't register right away so I had to spam a key like 10 times to talk to NPC's.
The game needs a bit more polishing before it's truly ready. Moreover, the way the game is right now doesn't justify its absurdly high price of $30. I would ONLY recommend this game if it's on sale.

As a Harvest Moon fan I really recommend this game. This is the "Harvest Moon" game that I would believe those whove played Friends of Mineral Town and Back to Nature would enjoy. As did Friends of Mineral Town, Wild Season is bringing in all what makes the RPG Farming Simulation genre good and addicting. In its current state it is still heavily buggy and lacking in many areas but judging what I can see in game, I believe it is headed in the right direction. With a bit more polishing and a whole lot more content I would really think this will be one of the best RPG Farming Sim games available.
+Great Farming Action
Its not like Farmville or anything like those online clicker games. Its old school RPG Farming. How it should be. Youve got a variation of crops and trees. Using different (hopefully upgradeable) tools you tend to them, from plowing to watering to sowing and eventually selling them for profit. Not only that, you also have a variety farm animals to tend to such as cows and chickens.
+Active-Time Farming
Time moves on as you do things in the game and in this certain characters will have their own schedules and  will be found in different differnt places in differet times of the day. As more work is to be done in your farm youll have less time to do other errands like buying seeds, getting your groceries, wooing women and celebrating birthdays.
And when I said birthdays, yes, there are birthdays. Other than an active clock to keep you on your toes, there is also a calander that shows you the season, holidays and events. Most crops only grow on certain seasons so you need to work hard and quick to get the most profit since they wither as the season ends.
Time really adds to the game and makes it more immersive.
+Alot of characters
Your Farm is not only the place youll be in for the entirety of the game. Youll get to visit the town and meet the colorful (and friendly?) townspeople. The Townspeople provide you with what you need such as seeds and farm animals, if you have the coin. There are characters that are viable for marriage too.
+/-Nice Artstyle
The game has an interesting artstyle similar to that of the old handheld Harvest Moon Games (sort of like RPG makers-esque). That is a cute and colorful and kinda tiny. It does look nice but its honestly nothing we havent seen before. Im sort of hopeful of changes to be had in some areas, like it just feels sort of flat (I know its a 2d game) and lifeless.
+/- Decent Soundtrack
Wild Season got it right to get the sound of an anime RPG farming sim but its sort of lacking. Like footstep noises and such. It may sound like a nitpick but things like these and to the immersion and it just sounds sort of really quiet without those. Sometimes the soundtrack repeats cut and the repeat doesnt sound seemless.
-Buggy as all hell
As do most Early Access games, Wild Season is really buggy. From messy button inputs to characters that seem to be out of place this is what truly breaks the game. The controls are sometimes unresponsive and characters just bug in and out (sometimes they get stuck in a loop within conversations/cutscenes and you cant progress.
-Really expensive
As of the state of the game it does not really justify its hefty price tag.
Overall the game is fun but it heavily needs more work. I am excited to see it finished.
8/10

First of all, as of now the game is still in early beta stage, version 0.7.0.12 in 8 November 2015. It indeed has quite a few bugs and requires polishing, as the devs themselves state in the store page.
That being said, this is shaping up to be great fun. Everyone who's familiar with the original Harvest Moon on the Super NES will know it as the inspiration behind Wild Season, tho this game aims to go above and beyond. Adding extra skills in the form of cooking, mining and fishing, there are a lot of extra activities to fill up your time after you're done taking care of the crops.
Particularly noteworthy is that it allows your character to be female or male, and the townsfolk include several different eligible bachelors and bachelorettes. Add to it a plot regarding a secret of the town, and it's clear that this has had a lot of effort and care poured into it.
But I feel I must repeat: currently this is still decidedly unfinished, and players are acting as playtesters. If you don't mind bugs and rough edges, you can find a lot of fun, but if you want your game experience unspoiled, I advise waiting.
I am really enjoying the game. Controls are a bit clunky, but after re-assigning are much better. Some hiccups, but are expected in an early access. Looking forward to more developments.

Amazing ARPG game. Would definitely recommend playing the game one play through and then downloading synergies mod. TLII is a big improvement over TLI.

A very good Diablo II-esque hack'n'slash.
are nice, if fairly basic by today's standards. The art style is hit or miss, it's very colourful and almost cartoonish across the board, giving the game a distinctive vibe. I like it.
is mostly fine, some voice acting is borderline garbage, the soundtrack is really nice though.
is as basic and unengaging as it gets, and the fact that you only get walls of text with no voice acting for sidequests doesn't help either, but you know what? I don't care. I play games like this for the beatdowns, not storytelling.
is exactly what you'd expect from an ARPG - kill things, get loot and experience, optimise your loadout and build, rinse and repeat. And it does all of this pretty well.
- What I like about this game as opposed to Torchlight 1 is that it incorporates large open areas so you're not just dungeon crawling all the time (in fact you're likely to spend MOST of the time in overworld areas if you want to explore them completely). The environments are largely varied and nice to look at.
- Four character classes focusing on melee, heavy weapons, ranged weapons and magic. You can use most weapons with any class (and some crossover builds may be viable) but it's obviously most efficient to use the ones you have bonuses for.
- Lots and lots of loot to go through, with numerous things to take into consideration, like "is 20 more armour worth giving up my +10% crit damage bonus?", you'll probably need to do some serious math if you want to get the absolute most out of your gear.
- A wide range of active and passive skills that are only limited by level - no skill requires you to unlock a different one first (although there are cases where getting one skill is pointless without having another). A considerable downside is that there's no full respec option in the vanilla game so if you pick a subpar skill and don't realise until later on, you're stuck with a broken build.
- Like in TL1, you have a pet who helps you in combat and you can send it to town to sell items and (unlike in TL1) even buy some consumables (e.g. potions or identify scrolls), saving you a lot of warping back to town.
- Four difficulty levels (plus hardcore mode where dying means game over) allow casual players and masochists alike to have some fun.
- New Game Plus (being able to play through the game again at higher level with the same character) and The Mapworks (where you pay to enter randomly generated dungeons with modifiers that may noticably alter gameplay) make sure there's always something you can do with your character.
I picked this game up when I was feeling nostalgic for the old Diablo games and it more than delivered on what I expected from it. An absolute must-play if you're into ARPGs and worth checking out even if you're not.

Multiplayer: You're either going to love it or hate it. Don't feel ashamed if you can't get into the Online portion of this game.
Final note: If you wanna play for just the Single Player, I'd say wait for a sale unless you don't mind paying full price (god bless you). As for Online Mode, play at your own risk.

Great game!   Simple though hard.  With a great theme.  A horror themed game just in time for Halloween.
It's a pretty small and simple Tower-Defense type game.   The objective is to keep this enormous orange a** (I guess a TYRANTasauras Rump, or a T-Rump)  from getting to the White House.  And let me tell you, you do NOT want this a** getting anywhere near the White House.  The last thing you want is for T-Rump to get its hands on nuclear weapons or the world is doomed.  Dooooommed!   In other words...  Game over man.
You have Big Beautiful Walls which are preventing the giant a**  from getting to the White House.   To complicate things the a** keeps flatuating out its devoted minions called Trumplings who will attack the walls.    They are pretty efficient at getting through the walls.  Let me tell you the walls aren't all that Yuuuge, believe me, but I don't think it would matter if they were 10 feet higher and someone else was paying for them,  the Trumplings aren't human so they chew right through them.   Trumplings are mean nasty vicious little creatures, deplorable even,  though generally pretty mindless.
You can place big American Guns in various locations to take out the Trumplings.  The guns will fire automatically at the Trumplings, though at a slow rate.  You can manually take control of any gun to fire much faster.  Though it seems Trumplings are most vulnerable when attacked from the front.    Unfortunately the T-Rump is invulnerable to the guns.   So it will only be stopped by the walls, which will cause it to turn around and go the other direction.
To help you out, the Trumplings when killed by your ample supply of guns on every street corner, will sometimes drop kernals of truth.   You can pick these up and when you've gotten 5 of them you can launch the Fist of Truth.  This will temporarily stun the T-Rump, buying you some time,  and also  help to deflate the T-Rump's massive ego (its health bar).   If you can get its ego down to zero you can save the day!  Sometimes you can get the T-Rump to go in the opposite direction when hitting it with the Fist of Truth, though I've not figured out if there is a way to reliably do that.    If there is a trick to getting the T-Rump to do that, it would help out a lot.
All-in-all it's a simple fun little game, with a pretty basic story line.   Granted it's not very realistic. A giant orange a** trying to get to the White House to destroy the world!    Seriously, where do people come up with these crazy ideas?   Still it is a game and a halloween themed horror game at that, so I guess being the halloween season explains the crazy concept  of this game.
Good thing something like this could never happen in the real world.

The CEO of Take 2, GTA's publisher talking about how he will force microtransactions into every single one of their games, they want more the $60+ that we all pay for the game but hundreds over the course of your play time regardless of the game.
Educate yourself, read how bad these people are know your enemy as a gamer, as a consumer, is:
Single player, still good, as with most if not all GTA titles thus far, playing 3 different characters is both at times tiring and fun.  One of the 3 is the least interesting, that being Franklin, his character was the least fleshed out yet was made out to be the glue to the group.  The gameplay is mostly better and for it's time it looked great though not visually not as impressive, there are however still instances where the world lives and you just sit back and watch.
By now you already know what the story is about, you do heists, which compared to PD2, are quite well done and make you feel like you're actually getting something out of it after you've planned for several set-up missions.  Your characters level up their traits so the now bog standard RPG elements are built into the game, for better or for worse which means at times a lot of grinding in order to get better which again is forced and boring in any game.  All in all the story is worth it so long as you find the game on sale, NEVER pay full price for this title as it is simply not worth $60 for a 4 year old game, period.
Now the online aspect of GTA5, where to start.... well it WAS a fair sandbox where you could enjoy getting killed by random a-holes in the server but now you can get that same feeling while you're flying, riding in a tank, anywhere you go you will be harried by other players in Freeroam.  It was a horrible design choice and I will never understand what they ultimately thought would happen.  That's just the crappy overworld, joining matches is a chore if you can even find anything then have fun with the infinite number of game modes that Rockstar keeps shoving out of the door to keep people playing because you'll never find a game mode beyond it's initial introduction.  By the way that’s if you aren’t killed by the countless modders that have been a problem since day 1 of the PC release but does Rockstar do anything?  No they go after the victims rather then the offenders.
On the subject of stability or how good of a port GTA5 is over all, it is pretty good but it also isn't, the load times are insane, even having the game on an SSD it can take at times an unlimited amount of time to load/connect to an offline lobby.  While the game runs fairly well Rockstar clearly did not make sure that stability and reliability was mirrored during loading and connecting to a lobby.  Sorry but a 4 year old game if it's well optimized should not take 5+ minutes to load on an SSD or any hard drive for that matter, period.
How they treat their paying customers and loyal player base is also shameful, their support staff, if you can call them that, do nothing but read from prefabricated responses and treats you like you caused the issue to happen.  They constantly suggest over the top things to fix completely separate issues, like uninstall our 50+ gigabyte game and reinstall it in order to fix a connection problem.  Not to mention the countless false positives for account bans and account wipes, which means that even a straight as an arrow player can and will get banned or have all of their cash wiped entirely from their character just because their “state of the art trusted anti-cheat” system flagged your account.  They constantly blame the victim rather then the cause and their support staff are instructed not to speak to anyone regarding bans or said money wipes.  They have constantly denied any and all wrong doing on every account even when given mountains of evidence they are staunch in their “belief” that you are the problem and not their system.
Making money, which is the only way to really get anywhere in the game, because it's not like I want to play the game that I bought, no I want to literally work for hours at a time grinding missions, heists, game modes, etc.  Just to get anywhere in the game.  If you don't grind for cash or pay for in game money you will suffer, the poor are indeed the lesser class in GTA Online with no real way to gain serious money if they can't find the means or the tools.  You can't get the tools if you don’t have the money and if you don’t have the tools you can't make the money.  It's a horrible circle and it does not make a fun game to just enjoy, because you can't because it's work, you're quite literally working within the game universe.  If you own a business,  you're doing work, if you're trying to make money via heists (which is no longer the best way to make money these days, anymore anyway) you work and grind for DAYS on end.  With the amount of time that I spent working in GTA Online, comparing their own pricing for Shark Cards I would have spent thousands of dollars to give you some perspective and I still don't own everything, not even close.  Everything in Online is now priced so that it all but forces you to buy Shark Cards which Rockstar's fee to pay microtransactions.  The best part about them now is that they are totally worthless, with each update that Rockstar releases the items get more and more expensive to the point where even the $100 Shark Card for $8 million, won't even buy you a car or two, where as before when the game was first out you'd be hard pressed to spend all $8 million.  It is done on purpose and now that Take 2's CEO has consistently come out to the public and investor meetings and stated that he treats customers by how they spend on his games.  That should tell you what kind of horrible person and horrible company Take 2 and Rockstar have turned into.
Their CEO is on record comparing paying human customers to minnows, dolphins and whales, these dehumanizing categories put gamers into their spending habits, if you spend very little and simply grind for days on end for your cash well you’re a minnow, if you buy money constantly then you’re a whale.  These are the people running Take 2 and Rockstar, these are the people saying making games is too expensive, the “people” who compare human beings to aquatic creatures based on their spending habits.
Do yourself and your fellow gamers some respect and avoid this title, educate yourself on how badly Take 2 and Rockstar have been treating their own paying customers for the past 4 years and realize that it will NEVER go back to the way it was.  Take 2 and Rockstar will never be the same again, and when this microtransaction bubble bursts, because it will, Take 2 and Rockstar will be gone because they've now made sure that if their ideas fail their companies fail.  It's better to please your investors then your actual customers, the ones who make  your fame possible.  Spend your money on another more deserving company, please.

As you go through the process of playing this game, it is clear that this game is a labor of love. The attention to detail in the enviroment, sound design, and overall design of the necromorphs makes this game some of the best sci-fi horror ever made. Every necromorph has something especially disturbing that you notice about them after the first time you see them, wether that be the way that the pukers crawl after you with a vengance after you take out their legs, or the way those walrus lookin♥♥♥♥♥necromorph's jaws are horribly distended. I highly reccomend this game for its atmosphere and chilling enemy design.
Things to consider:
-The game is frame locked at 30 FPS if you enable some settings in the game. I wont explain it here, but just do some quick research if it bothers you, it is very easily fixed so you can play at 60 FPS with AA.
-My personal reccomendation is on your first playthrough start on the easier difficulties: That way, you can focus less on being frustrated because you are constantly dying and more on the how fast things are going to hell
-If you want to win, upgrade the crap out of your plasma cutter and keep the semiconductors the game gives to ensure you always have ammo for it (sell the semiconductors and buy ammo at the shop)

A lot of people on steam are whiny entitled babies. Here's a few things I'd like to debunk from playing this game for 500 hours.
1. Hackers are common. ♥♥♥♥♥♥ ones are rare, it happens. If you don't enjoy it just switch sessions. (Or play jobs I literally never see any hackers when I am out doing races, deathmatches, survivals, etc. They all frolic in free mode.)
2. Anyone down here crying that they were banned for literally no reason saying "I ground so hard for all that money!" is probably lying trying to get un banned for their stupid♥♥♥♥♥cheating. I've played this game for years, and really the only way to get banned is dropping money for yourself/others. Or getting so many reports that rockstar actually does something about it. I have been friends with countless modders and hackers and they are pretty power drunk people most of the time if I'm honest. But sometimes they can make the session better if you're not a baby. If you start telling modders to ♥♥♥♥ off and that you're reporting them they ARE going to ruin your fun. If you don't like it that much find a new session, easy as Pause < Online < Find New Session.
