3. You CAN legitimately afford the stuff rockstar markets. You want a Luxor Delux? Buy a hangar, buy regular Luxor, paint it gold. Badda Bing Badda Boom. Back in my days on PS3 I could probably make 200 grand a night grinding missions. All you need to get started is to buy a Bunker, I say the bunker because you don't need to also buy a warehouse like the CEO Offices. Normally people don't mess with gunrinning shipments. 90% of the time they destroy your stuff it's just for the sake of destroying your stuff to♥♥♥♥♥♥you off. Because people are like that. Whenever you want to sell mass amounts of goods, you're gonna need a few friends and there's plenty of guides on how to get a solo public session you can just invite your friends back to, then sell your stuff before anyone joins.
4. There's a lot to do in this game, I find myself patrolling free mode basically allll the time and I have personally gotten bored doing it. Many people do this and then get mad that they can't go inside perticular buildings, and do this and that, and give it a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ review. Me and my friend were bored in free roam one time and I asked him if he wanted to play from versus missions and races and stuff. So we went and tried it out and we actually had a lot of fun. Wild Season is a very difficult game to give a yes or no reccommendation to at the current state the game is in. The game has to be one of the most fun RPG maker games I've ever played and is truly impressive considering it was made using that platform. On the other hand there are so many bugs and issues with the game that it is hard to reccommend it at the moment. Some of these issues can be forgived as the game is in early access, but it seems as though the developer should have fixed some of these problems before putting it up on Steam.
Pros
- Amazing visual style and graphic design. Honestly, the visuals are probably the best part about this game.
- Very familiar "Harvest Moon" style gameplay.
- Fairly interesting story.
- Developer appears to be working to fix issues and bugs.
Cons
- Insane amount of bugs (Often I'd find myself walking through walls and other people, cutscenes glitching out, etc.)
- Wonky Controls (For example, the only way to save is by pressing "J" while facing foward in a bed. Planting crops is also difficult alot of the time as a result of these controls.)
- Very Dialouge Heavy at beginning of game. Takes about an hour or so to get into any real gameplay.
- High Cost (Even while it is on sale at the moment for $16.49. For the regular cost of $29.99, it is even more ridiculous. I mean honestly, go buy Cities: Skylines or something.)
- Very Repetitive Music (What little music is in the game is actually pretty good, but it loops wayyyyy to often.)
Overall Wild Season is a game that shows a lot of potential, but for the state that the game is in at the moment and the fairly high pricetag I don't believe it is worth your purchase. In the game's current state, I would only reccommend if you have an obession with Harvest Moon, or if it is on extremely high discount.

Disclaimer: Received a key for review purposes
One thing you have to realize about Wild Season is that it's very much an Early-Access game. At its current state, the game is pretty buggy and needs a lot of fine-tuning. Currently the gameplay and controls are a bit frustrating. This game is a farming life sim, yet I found it difficult to work on my farm for extended periods of time because of how slow it took for my character to perform actions. Sometimes it took more than a couple of seconds for my character to pick up weeds or crops and then put them away in my bag. Even working on a 3x3 plot is time-staking. This is a shame because I was looking more forward to the farming-sim aspect of the game than the RPG/ Visual Novel aspect of the game.
The controls also need to be better mapped AND/OR better noted ingame. WASD for movement was fairly easy to figure out but J K L for actions was not as obvious. This should have been told from the beginning, not an hour into the game.
There are also a lot of immoveable cutscenes from the very start. I understand this is also a visual novel and an RPG so there are bound to be many cutscenes to move along the story, However I wish the game wouldn't heavily depend on cutscenes to progress. Even just letting me open the door myself when someone knocks on my house door, or entering a store and walking towards the NPCs myself would be better than waiting constantly for the cutscenes to end and for me to finally do something and move around. All the cutscenes made me feel very constrained and I would have liked the option to meet the characters at my own pace.
One thing I really like about the game is the story and characters. I'd certainly like to know why the townpeoples are acting so xenophobic and what my farm has to do with anything. Some of the characters are very charming and interesting. Your task is not just maintaining your farm; it also includes building platonic or romantic relationships with your neighbors. But once again while I'd love to explore more into the story's lore and story, the poor controls make it difficult for me to play for a long period of time.
I like the concept of this game, and personally I think this game would be a lot more enjoyable if the developers fixed the controls. However this game needs a lot of work. At the current stage of development, I cannot find myself recommending this game.

Every once in a while, I love to smash everything and everyone in sight - then I turn to a something like Torchlight II. Hack & Slay is the name of the game, and it feels just as satisfying as the rich booty from those battles. The enemies and surroundings are diverse enough, and some bosses look relatively awesome. I say "relatively" because overall, the graphics have not aged well. On the other hand, the music is still excellent. Dialogues are short and do not involve any important decisions or moral dilemmas, which is an advantage because the voice acting is mostly sub-par.
Grim Dawn is superior in this regard and managed to create a lot more depth of atmosphere (e.g. the Steampunk setting with fireweapons side by side with swords and maces is more plausible in a post-apocalyptic scenario - Torchlight does not bother with giving you that kind of background). Also, it is four years younger and has better graphics. If in doubt which one you should play, I would prefer Grim Dawn.
Nevertheless, Torchlight II is well done, it offers consistently engaging gameplay and character progression as well as several options for you to keep on playing after finishing the main story. The feature that you can use your pet as a connection to town markets is not realistic, but innovative and conveniently saves your hero some annoyingly repetitive errands, which is why I make this honorary mention here.
I recommend this game to fans of the genre and give it a 7/10 in this comparison group.

This is one of those "Best way to kill 5-10 minutes" games.
After some trial and error, the first 9 levels will be "2ez4u", but after that you either have to take guesses or double-check if that guy you're suspecting to be the perpetrator really IS the guy the witness describes.
It becomes extra hard when 2 of the 4 clues are basically the same (e.g. "He's not small" and "He's kinda big") and the other 2 describe more than two suspects (e.g. "He looks messy" and "He's a hippie").
It not only depends on your judgement when it comes to looks, you actually have to look through the witness' eyes.
An example being Bigot Barny: He's racist. At least that's what his description says.
When he says "He looks like someone I'd hate", then it's definitely NOT a white guy.
It gets extra tricky when there's a timelimit or when the witness influences the scene (e.g. a magician turning the faces of some suspects into his own).
All in all, it's a nice, little, and especially challenging game. It shouldn't be played for several hours, though.

This game is very fun, unfortunately, it has a slight issue of not closing properly.  After telling it to exit and all, it will still 'exist' as a process in memory, steam will refuse to open it and say that you're currently playing 'Fingered.'  If this were a rare occurance, I wouldn't mind, but it has happened every time I have played this game.  Killing the process with Task Manager just gives you an "Access Denied" message, the reason for this is because Task Manager cannot kill an exiting process.  3rd Party software is unable to kill the process either.  I wouldn't say this is the first game I've run into an error like this, but this is definitely one of the most annoying.  So far, the only way I know of to get rid of it is to Reboot your PC.
(BTW, Running Windows 8)

Look beyond all the pre-order shenanigans and the silly (and completely unneccessary, as in you won't ever feel a compulsion to buy them, at least outside of Breach mode) microtransactions and you are left with the best stealth/action RPG since Deus Ex: Human Revolution. It maybe doesn't quite hit the level of the 2011 game, but then the bar was set very high.
It feels like Eidos Montreal have tried to directly address the issues that effected the original game, maybe to the point of it being slightly detrimental to the overall product. The "boss" fights aren't separate to the rest of the game anymore, and there's few if any situations where you have to go into direct combat with enemies.
Well thought out maps (albeit with the usual tropes of man-sized ventilation systems, everyone leaving passcodes on pocket sectretaries, etc - but these are tropes of the genre and whilst they may be cliched, it's hard to think of alternative mechanics to subert it), engaging side quests full of interesting characters.
I will say it feels like the game tries too hard at times perhaps to make you think a certain way or make certain parallels with real situations (apartheid, police states, etc).
However, I have not seen a city hub in any game that offers anything close to what Prague has if you're willing to spend the time looking around, you can genuinely spend a good 10 hours across the three Prague visits just exploring the city, finding notes, items, environmental story telling all over the place. People compared Mankind Divided to Human Revolution by saying the halved the number of locations (Detroit and Hengsha to just Prague) but that doesn't do justice to the level of detail and design (and sheer size) of Prague. I wonder if they'd split what they've designed across two or three cities and had you fly between them might have mitigated some of the critism? But content-wise there is plenty there.
If you avoid this game because of the controvesies around Square's business practices, you really are missing out on one of the greatest games of it's genre. Not quite as good as Human Revolution in some respects, but superior in others.

SUMMARY: Excellent game. If you like story driven games that reward exploration and deal with deep philosophical issues, this is a must buy. If you liked Human Revolution, you will like this one too.
Take Human Revolution, improve every single aspect of it and you get Mankind Divided. An excellent addition to the franchise.
Unfortunately, there was this wave of negativity against the game at the beginning because of Square Enix meddling with their pre-order fiasco, microtransactions and Breach. I can assure you that none of those things affect the game and they are there for people who want them. If you are not one of them just ignore it. Eidos Montreal really delivered this time.
Now, I see people complaining about many things so let me address them below:
Lie #1 -  Game is too short
Couldn't be further from the truth. I have around 100 hrs on the clock and it could've easily been more as I haven't explored and done everything. I tried to explore as much as I can before going to Golem City but once arriving there I did only the main storyline until the end as I wanted to see how the story ends. Try doing everything the game offers you and you will se that this game is much longer than Human Revolution ever was. Human Revolution had a lot of revisiting of the same areas. In Mankind Divided you don't have that. Also the sidequests in Mankind Divided are much more refined.
Lie #2 - Game lacks content
Seriously? Just because you were too lazy to explore, it doesn't mean the game lacks content. Try exploring and you will see how much the game rewards you. Deus Ex has always been about exploring.
Lie #3 - Game is unfinished/divided in two parts
While it is true that Mankind Divided opened a lot of questions at the beginning without resolving all of them by the end of the game, I don't think that it means the game is unfinished. The developers made it very clear that the Jensen arc is going to be a trilogy (together with Human Revolution). Human Revolution appears to be a self-contained game because no sequels were planned. Mankind Divided instead was made with a sequel in mind which will resolve all the pending plots (and all pending plots are not main story related, but related to the wider Deus Ex universe). In any case the main storyline was opened and ended in Mankind Divided.
Lie #4 - Game has only one hub
The game has two major hubs, Prague and Golem City. The fact that both are in Europe makes no difference as they are still two different hubs. If they put Golem City in Asia, I am sure nobody would complain about the number of hubs. And these two hubs offer more things to do than the whole Human Revolution. The hubs are incredibly dense and this is the only game where I've seen that. The vertical design of the levels is amazing as it really rewards exploration.
Lie#5 - Microtransactions ruin the game
Yes, there are microtransactions and as we've heard it was because Square Enix wanted them in the game. However Eidos Montreal did the smart thing and designed the game in such  a way that you don't need to use microtransactions. If you wish, use them, if you don't, don't use them. It doesn't affect the game at all. Everything that can be bought with microtransactions, can be found for free in game

Wild Season is a story-centric farming simulator with a lot of potential. You just invested all your money into the purchase of a farm which turns out to be not quite what you expected, in a town full of people who clearly do not want you around. You now have to try and restore the farm while figuring out why the community is so hostile towards you.
The art style is well-done and reminiscent of classic jRPG titles. The sprites and characters are beautifully drawn. The music is nice and suits the game very well. Sound effects are also decent and get the job done.
There is a good number of NPCs and locations to visit, friends to be made as well as people trying to convince you to leave town.
The pace of the game is quite slow and while it's okay when working on your farm, people who aren't fans of visual novels will probably be put off by the lengthy dialogues sequences. Between the intro and the tutorial, it will take you over 30 minutes before you can actually start to play on a new game. While it does a good job of setting the back story, this should definitely be reworked to get the player into the game sooner. (You can bypass most of it with the Quick Start menu option, but then you don't get to choose your character's name and characteristics.)
At the time of writing this review, the game is still in early access and a lot of bugs are currently present in the game as well as large chunks of contents missing. Interactions with other NPCs are limited and they don't remember your past conversations between sessions. There's a lot of features mentioned at some point in the game that don't seem to be implemented yet. Also, saving the game doesn't always seem to work so you need to double check if you don't want to have to revert to the last auto-save. The developers appear to be active and are adding depth to the game and fixing bugs, so it look like it's headed in the right way.
Controls currently feel very disconnected. Using the keyboard and mouse doesn't quite feel right, yet when playing with a controller it doesn't feel very responsive. Plus, not everything is currently mapped to the controller so I end up going back and forth between the keyboard and mouse  and the controller. Some actions, like closing an inventory window are mapped to the same button as using the tools, so you often end up spending energy needlessly by swinging your tools around when you simply want to close a dialog.
Overall the game is nice and, with the right tweaking, can really evolve into something worth playing. Right now, I can only recommend this game if you want to support the developer and don't mind playing it in it's unfinished state. The price tag for this game seems quite steep for what you're currently getting and even for the final product, I would expect the sweet spot for a game like this to be around the $20 mark.

First of all, I can't clearly say that I'm a huge admirer of farming/grinding games, so my impressions might not convey what I actually felt while playing this. Still, I was quite surprised to see how many possibilities are there, and can certainly say that one won't get bored soon enough and will find some in-game activity to enjoy with.
Wild Season is still in Early Access phase, so of course, you can expect some "issues" which can slightly distort gaming experience. Although, so far I haven't met anything critical which would affect the session. Nevertheless, it is worth mentioning that once I was a witness to the bug whether characters were continuously going through the door, sort of being stuck there, but dialogues went just fine, so it wasn't a real problem.
It cannot be denied that I actually loved artwork and character portraits which, being a cliche to mention, still feel really nicely done and look rather lively. However, I think that some of used assets could be sharper, while some can say they seem a bit blurry. Same goes for the fonts, and perhaps dialogue windows as well.
You won't find a lot of witty dialogues, but they can't be referred as "fillers like" or blank, just to be, too. Town and its outskirts are big enough, so there is a lot of place for you to hang around. Although, there is only one jiggle melody playing for each location, and I must say, you may not feel satisfied while listening for it over and over again.
The only noticeable flaw I've met is the quite distracting beginning of the game. Not by a matter of the story, but mostly for its unhelpful introductory part. You are following numerous cutscenes and dialogues, but don't get explained what it is for and whether you should do "this" or "that". Tasks-to-do keep appearing in the right corner of the screen, but there doesn't seem to be any quest log, so you could check whatever activity you should be doing. Also, short controls guide would come very handy, as you may change buttons for actions, but nothing tells you what each action does. You may not even learn that you can save the progress unless you go next to a bed in your house and randomly press "J" on it. Also, some commands like toggling of "running mode" aren't listed at all, so you might take a time to figure that it goes by "R".
Meantime, I would really love to be able to use my mouse instead of a keyboard for some activities. since you have to handle both left and right of letters keyboard while still controlling the mouse for dragging items and some other things. In addition, sometimes it's required to press action button twice in order to perform something, and skipping dialogues with a button doesn't work very well.
Long story short, while not covering all aspects of Wild Season and not advancing too far in the story, I've tried to shed some light on it. If you are a fan of Harvest Moon and acknowledged with words such as farming/gathering not only in real life but in-game as well, you might want to try out this project and maybe find it addictive enough to play on a regular basis. Otherwise, you may prefer waiting for a sale, and for a game to meet further development. Still, despite some minor [for me] issues, WS has a lot of potential and with necessary effort and polishing it can certainly become one of a few gems you rarely meet this time, not a big one, but one which is absolutely worth meeting with.

Wild Season is a refreshing take on the farming RPG (think Harvest Moon), with an intriguing story and loveable characters. Normally I only play games with a strong narrative aspect, so the original Harvest Moon games, while fun to me when I was younger, were somewhat difficult for me to stick with because they couldn't hold my interest for long periods of time. I was pleasantly surprised to discover that Wild Season does have an overarching mystery story--I bought the farm and moved into the town like normal, BUT, from the beginning it was pretty clear that a lot of people were UNHAPPY about the fact that I moved in. Some of them even asked me outright to leave, which only makes me more interested to find out what it is they're all hiding! Even so, a lot of the characters are really fun to interact with, and have their own unique personalities and ways of speaking. The dialogue definitely doesn't suffer from the usual cliches, so I enjoyed talking to everyone I encountered.
The art and the animation is great; everything looks super clear, and is the HD quality we deserve from a 2D game in this decade. I wasn't able to test all of the features yet, but my farming ventures seemed to go fine, and so did the couple of times I tried fishing.
Although I did encounter both major and minor bugs from time to time, from what I've seen, the devs are constantly releasing updates to fix them, and they also respond quickly to questions! The game is in Early Access and still unfinished, but even so, I'm happy with what I've experienced so far, and I'll be waiting on tenterhooks for the full release. Kudos to the developers; keep it up!

One of the major fantasies I've had since childhood, is that of being a strong warrior. The concept of destroying hundreds of enemies with ease, facing legendary monsters, and having reality-breaking abilities, have been inspired through countless forms of media. Whether you're a superhero fanboy, or you're grounded in reality, the
concept is always fascinating to explore. Torchlight 2 takes the simple hero concept, gives you a story, and some excellent gameplay to boot. With an overall rating of Overwhelmingly Positive, is it really worth the acclaim? In this review, we'll find out.
Torchlight 2 at its core is an action RPG, in which you slay monsters, collect piles of loot, and clear countless dungeons. Taking inspiration from games such as Diablo, Mythos, Fate, and of course its very own predecessor Torchlight, this game expands upon a fairly well known formula, and creates something rather unique. You see, this game has the makings of an online MMORPG, but can be played completely offline. The loot-focused, grind-oriented nature of the game is something that is frequently delivered in a variety of games, but is not often done well. To my relief, this particular game really shines in this aspect.
You generally take quests from NPCs, which you will find primarily in the base camps. There are many other quests to be found in the world as you explore, so there's never a moment where you should be lacking in direction. I particularly liked the feeling of having so many quests to complete as I journeyed. It reminded me of some of my favourite MMORPGs, and I finally realized what it was that I liked about them; direction. Don't worry about being overburdened, Torchlight 2 strikes a very fair balance between quantity, and quality. To my recollection, I never had more than about 3 active quests at a time.
Torchlight 2 is a story-driven game. It's about as predictable as one could expect, though this does not make it a
story by any shot. A good story gives the player a real motivation; a reason to exist. No longer was I just your everyday hero. Instead, I was a pivotal character in this world. I was important, and I felt a sense of purpose as I cleared hallways and caverns of monsters, getting closer and closer to my end-goal.
The story is divided into 3 major sections, exposing you to different environments with each, and bringing you closer to the final showdown.
You start out by choosing between four distinct classes: Engineer, Berserker, Outlander & Embermage. Each one specializes in the use of unique weapons and armor, and each one can have a widely flexible play-style. To allow this, each class has 3 skill trees that they can allocate points to. Depending on your preferred gameplay style, you can take a melee or ranged approach. From bows, to dual swords, to staves, and even cannons, you'll find a rather large arsenal available to you, depending on your class. The number of potential builds are quite limitless, so it really inspires creativity and flexibility.
In addition, you are given a permanent companion; a pet. This pet will usually serve as secondary storage, as well as additional damage if you so desire. I really love the pet selections, the ability to change its nature, and the ability to send it to do my shopping whilst deep inside a dungeon.
The combat in this game is one of its greatest strengths. Each character has a wide selection of abilities. You can assign each one to a numbered hotkey, as well as your Mouse 2 button for easy casting. You can also have two separate weapon loadouts! This allows you to swap between two different weapons in the middle of combat, to further suit your play-style.
During large battles, you'll find yourself running around trying to avoid dangerous monster abilities, while dealing damage at the right time. This is even more crucial for boss fights, as they often have unique mechanics which you need to play around with. There are a wide variety of monster abilities and strategies to be used, so you'll have a bit to learn.
While being primarily story-driven, Torchlight 2 extends the re-playability with New Game Plus, Mapworks (special dungeons for your grinding needs), and LAN or Online Co-Op. It's an absolute pleasure to have a game that caters to multiple gaming needs in this way. Whether you're home alone, or you want a great LAN party game, Torchlight 2 has you covered.
You may be able to finish the story at level 50, but chances are, you'll probably not stop until you reach closer to level 100 thanks to the addictive nature of the game.
In addition, Torchlight 2 supports MODS! Hell yeah! Thanks to the ease of modding, and the large community behind the game, there is an absolute ton of mods you can use to enhance your gameplay experience, and change almost everything about the game. If something about vanilla didn't appeal to you, chances are, there's a mod for that.
While being slightly dated as of 2017, the graphics aren't the worst I've seen. In fact, they hold up quite well. While not being the primary area of concern, Torchlight 2 delivers a pleasant visual experience, filled with colours, particles and effects galore. Prefer something less fancy? Turning the settings all the way down is perfectly fine, and can help framerates on weaker PCs. Overall, while not being the primary focus of the game, I never found the graphics distracting or hideous to complain about. Many of the effects were quite beautiful, and perfectly suited their environments.
From wide platforms, to tight corridors, the world of Torchlight really felt immersive and really gave me a desire to explore every inch of it. To my knowledge, many (not all) of the maps are procedurally generated, which added to the
feel of each new environment.
From the soundtrack of the game, to the varied sounds and effects of combat, I had a great experience with this game's sound design. Each shot from my Engineer's cannon felt powerful. You could really hear the kick of the blast, followed quickly by the sound of monsters dying and loot being dropped.
There was a substantial amount of narration, mainly for the story, but it was well done. I had initially been uninterested in the story, but listening to it being read really gave it life and energy.
Torchlight 2 is possibly one of
games to play if you're interested in great combat, unique classes, and abundant mods. It's one of those
types of games that you really shouldn't be skipping unless this type of game doesn't appeal to you in the slightest.
At $20 you could easily spend hundreds of hours playing this game and it would be worth it. However, this game frequently goes on sale for a quarter of that price or less, so you really have no excuse not to get it.
I rarely ever replay games, but I found myself coming back to this one, again and again.
For excellence in the action RPG genre, I give Torchlight 2 a:
10/10 - Addicting gameplay, Wide appeal, High re-playability & great fun!

+ Very solid plot that faithfully continues the series
+ Looks and art style have aged well
+ Magnificent visual storytelling
Cons
--------------------------------
- The villains could use more character development
- Value of multiplayer in a horror game is iffy

Wild season is basically a farm game with some sim aspects thrown in there. There's a rather mysterious story to keep things moving together, which works alright.
While this is not particularly my kind of game, it does it's best to keep you hooked and you can see right away that the developer has put a lot of effort into it.
It's still absolutely filled with bugs, but as long as the game stays in early access, I don't think that's something to be upset about.
I kinda liked the art style they are going for. It's somewhat reminiscent of those older flash games you used to play when you were young, with a bit of JRPG anime and portable console nostalgia thrown into the mix.
Music sets the mood just fine and the sound effects are on point.
Animation quality is somewhat above your standard indie JRPG quality, but nothing to be exited about (bugs really bother here right now).
Right now I've seen quite a few things that definitely need to addressed on the way, and as this kind of games only work with constant playtime and player progression, I can't recommend to throw in your game time hours just yet.
Still, as a whole, I think fans of the genre will be pleased to have this on PC once it's finished and achieves the console-like quality it's clear it's aiming for. It will definitely have it's place at the steam store if it ultimately gets there, so thumbs up for the dev and the hard work that awaits!
Final veredict: Wait for early access to end if you expect the full experience right from the start. Buy now if you wish to support the idea and help the developer get it just right. Not sure about the price though, I would wait for good a sale.

Wild Season is quite a neat little game, and has a lot of potential once the small errors are fixed, of which there are many. For example, the controls are different from a lot of other games, and are not explained at any point, so it's quite tough figuring them out. Also, often certain keys become unresponsive for a period of time.
Other bugs include me getting the Welcome to Bedford Valley achievement whenever I enter a room, and people having a conversation with "William" in the general store but him not actually appearing in game (I'm not sure if that's a bug or if he was just speaking from another room, but when he did appear he was walking through walls)
I am aware that the developers are working on fixing these bugs and it's good to see they are actively working on the game.
Now onto the gameplay - from what I have played so far, the game has quite a good storyline. However, conversations with people at the beginning (when you are meeting everybody) take quite a while and leave you sitting pressing the RMB constantly for quite a while. The game has quite a nice concept - you've /accidentally/ bought a derelict farm and have to fix it up and start a buisness (at least that's what i can figure out)
The music is interesting, but the loop is quite short and gets repetitive after a while. The art style is neat, and I've found the game similar to Animal Crossing in many ways, although in animal crossing you aren't required to become a farmer.
Overall, it's an enjoyable game. I wouldn't really recommend it at it's current price, but I haven't seen the whole game yet, it may have much more to offer. If it's on sale for less than £10, I'd recommend you pick it up.

A game with great potential. Yes, this game is still in early access and it shows. There were a few things that I came across which I believe need to be fixed before I can fully enjoy this game.  To name a few issues , the frame rate, the characters skip around the screen with movements like a bad horror movie. There also seems to be quest updates and completions of the same thing repeatedly. One of the major issues I had was the lack of instruction or misdirection (the mayor tells you to go south east when you're meant to go south west). I didn’t know how to save my progress after putting in over an hour into the game and when it came around to planting my seeds I couldn’t get around to doing just that. I couldn’t find help in game and online has yet to post any useful information. But put a side the pixilated opening animation and misdirection of the characters and you have what will eventually be a great game. I can see this being one of those games people call a hidden gem. The story actually kept me in the game to see what was going on with the farm and why people wanted my character to leave. The music and art was good for this particular game. Of course I have to add that the game being made with Unity was a good choice. Simply because I have played plenty of games and every game made with Unity worked perfectly. As far as not crashing, freezing or not running the game at all. But to put in my two cents , Wild Seasons  is definitely worth buying , just wait until after early access. Unless you want the experience of being a game tester. Then pick it up and have fun.

I find the artwork inspired and quite polished. Loading times are sometimes extremely long and without an obvious cause. Pay also attention to the hardware requirements to enjoy the graphics at their best.
Gameplay has been improved since DEHR and the effort of the team to bring the consolidated Deus Ex game mechanics even further is obvious. AI however has to be improved to behave correctly in specific situations (e.g.: a soldier will react to the opening of a door in front of him only in rare cases). BREACH isn't in the style but quite enjoyable.
I recommend the purchase since now the prices are quite low and it is worth a try.

Graphically, Gnomoria is somewhat inferior to the much-maligned and unsuccessful Towns - that being said, in every other way it is superior to that now-defunct game. Gnomoria is better designed, with an interface that gives you many more options for terraforming and production and allows you to keep better control of all aspects of your settlement (if you so desire). The citizen and soldier AI is much better, resulting in more production efficiency and fewer random casualties. Unlike Towns, Gnomoria provides a slew of pre-game customization options to fine-tune your game, and there are no 'unused' or 'useless' objects - everything you mine or forage can be crafted or re-purposed into something else. Gnomoria's audio - both in sound effects and music - also enjoys much better quality and diversity, providing alot of good atmosphere. Think of this game as a graphically-superior, 3D version of Dwarf Fortress, with the capacity to be made less utterly brutal. While it lacks the hero/dungeon crawling aspect of Towns, its sheer superiority in nearly every other category, combined with the clear dedication of this developer to keep working on it (unlike its now-completely unsupported genre step-sibling) makes Gnomoria the clear choice for anyone wanting a deep and engaging fantasy kingdom-building sim.

Essentially Dwarf Fortress-lite, and I mean that as a compliment rather than "hurr durr lacking depth like acorn falling engine". It's very enjoyable, even in this state. Updates are slow as one man alone is working on this, but progress has been moving along at a regular pace, if not a blistering one, which I find more refreshing than having major updates at unnanounced intervals that could be a long time apart. If you wanted to check out DF but like me was very intimdated with the, well, everything, check this out, it's well worth it, even at thi stage and especially for this price.

Overlord's a pretty unique game. You play as an evil Overlord who commands a small army of goblin-like minions to do his dirty work for him. At the outset, you'll be able to keep 15 under your control at a time, and that number will rise as you move forward in the story. There's something viscerally satisfying watching your minions wreak havoc on an enemy town - the little guys gleefully destroying everything in sight while the occupants run around in terror, many of them with a minion or two clinging to their backs and clubbing them to death. Mayhem and chaos ensues and it's entertaining to watch, and you can wade into the fray and knock things around with a huge axe if you don't feel like sitting on the sidelines.
If it sounds too dark, don't worry - the game has a great morbid sense of humor and doesn't try to play it straight, so it's never depressing or disturbing. The game pokes fun at fantasy conventions too - early on you make enemies of the elves, who are literal tree-hugging hippies who are pretty upset that you've been clubbing baby seals to death to harvest life force for your growing army. The primary villians are a Roman-style Empire, who are rounding up and killing magic beings (like you and your minions), and the story takes jabs at ancient Rome sterotypes. Your senior minion advisor also narrates things for you, and the detest he expresses for the more beautiful side of fantasy settings is pretty hilarious.
The game plays well, but there are problems with the controls. Later on, combat demands precise control over your minions, and the game doesn't really do that well enough. It leads to some frustrating moments where you're fumbling around trying to give the right orders to your minions, while your enemies are picking them off - giving you a taste of the confusion you normally cause. Some of the genre's typical sins come here too - there's a couple of clunky vehicle sequences, and at least one forced stealth section. To the game's credit, these segments aren't nearly as infuriating as you'd expect, but they still felt unnecessary and weren't very fun.
Overall it's a fun game, and I recommend it despite its shortcomings - especially to players who enjoy "summoner" type characters in other action RPGs (such as Diablo), or those who are looking for something different in the genre.

Add to all that it has fantastic mood setting music you've got a class A product. Many players simply can't stop at a single character and over the years I have kept on coming back to this game. Without a doubt my favourite MMO ever. It's also great to see the dedication of Standing Stone in keeping their work alive and keeping lotro safe for the future years with a decent, not overly greedy free to play system. Much of the content can be enjoyed for free and extras can be bought as required. The only time you may consider spending money is to open up quest packs in different regions and expansion packs. But considering the size and amount of time you could foreseeably spend in this masterpiece, it is well worth it!

Imagine a game with everything you hate about 21st Century shooters; limited weapon loadout, mixed gameplay, collectibles, XP and leveling. Add a dash of what you love; open(ish)-world, great visual direction, satisfying 'splosions, solid shoot-bangs. Throw a late '70s-early '80s Tron glow and VHS filter on it, then coat the whole damn package in a laquer of bad clichés and mixed metaphors. That's Blood Dragon.
Blood Dragon is a laughably simple story containing all the classic elements of a Karate Kid-meets-Rambo II, playing as the cyber-Predator. The best part of the game is how serious it takes itself. As in, not ever. At all. It's in on the joke. Spectacular voice acting during the (affordably animated) cutscenes and every line of in-game dialogue is delivered perfectly straight, as though the actor did not know they were reading cheesed lines from 30 years ago.
The game starts strong and ends strong. The bits in the middle are OK, but enjoyable overall. I don't recommend clearing all the garrisons before the final encounter like I did as gameplay afterward suffers if you do.
I recommend this, even at $15 for the experience. Although I strongly recommend it at >$10, so snap it up if you see it on sale.

Crush Crush is a unique game in that it can make a man feel chill and relaxed and also very aroused at the same time.
The idea of the game is simple; you combine the mechanics of an idle/clicker game with that of a dating sim. So just like in a dating sim you need to work jobs for money and perform hobbies to raise stats. But because it is an idle game, you need to wait around for the money and stats to build up. It sounds simple, and kind of boring doesn't it? But the game has a really interesting charm that keeps it from that.
First off you get a little story sequence with each girl, explaining how you end up meeting said girl and it's almost always under unfortunate circumstances where you cause an issue, such as crashing into one girl and putting her in the hospital, all the way up to accidentally landing on the girls ancient prison and awaking her from a 1,000 year slumber.  No, the game doesn't take itself very seriously at all. Also, all of the girls are unique and have different personalities; a nerdy gamer, a busy narcoleptic, a rainbow haired tomboy, and yes, a female bear as shown in the trailer. Suffice to say you can always be entertained by the girls. Each one of them is cute in their own special way, as conveyed through the lovely artwork and through the dialogue present in the game. You do start to feel an attachment to them as you go along, with the first girl Cassie being a personal favorite of mine.
The way it all works is that each girl has levels of their relationship with you, as you progress from an annoyance to an awkward best friend all the way up to lover. Each girl has their own requirements per level, which means taking them on a crazy number of dates, and buying a large number of absurdly priced gifts, starting with $400 sea-shells through $13,000 cocktails and new cars that cost somewhere in the millions or higher. But the fact you can end up working a dozen different jobs at one point means money isn't exactly scarce. Each relationship level will require a certain number of gifts and dates, and even a level in a particular stat or a specific rank in a job, and none of them are exactly the same.
The other part of levelling up with each girl is the number of hearts you have with them; this is primarily where the clicking part of the game comes in, as you will click a button saying "Apologize" or "Flirt" or "Seduce" depending on the relationship level and each time you do so you get hearts. The gifts and dates do this as well, but you need a certain heart requirement to get to the next level, no matter what way you do it. As well, if you have points in a certain stat then the girls get hearts automatically, allowing you to leave the game idle and not only get better stats and more money, but to make the girls grow more fond of you.
At some point, you won't be able to make meaningful progress without resetting. This sets all of your progress back to nothing, but depending on how far along you've gotten with each girl, you receieve a multiplier to make the next time squicker. This is a necessity to get far in the game so you will have to do it eventually.
Now yes, this is a freemium game. You can spend *real* money to buy diamonds to use in game, which in turn are used for skipping ahead a day or seven, buying more 'time blocks' so you can work more jobs or do more hobbies (not recommended because you get many free blocks as you go), buying bonuses to your multiplier or even allowing you to skip resetting but still get the multiplier in the process. The diamonds can also be used to buy gifts and go on dates if you have no cash but this hardly ever is the case. And lastly, you can buy special outfits with the diamonds at the highest level, including rings for wedding dresses with are quite nice to look at. Yes folks, polygamy is a thing in this game and you can have several wives!
In all seriousness it is a fun little time waster. You probably will need to spend a little to avoid the game dragging on and on, and I personally have spent between $30 and $40. I do this gladly because the devs are active on the forums, provide constant updates to the game, and their dedication to it shows through. This game crushed all expecations I had of it, and with its charm these ladies took a bit of my heart as well. It's fun, enjoyable, engaging, and worth at least checking out.

I bought Deus Ex MD at the discounted price of around $18, and for that price Deus Ex offered quite a spectacular experience. I enjoyed Human Revolution quite a bit when it came out, and on seeing the negative backlash this game was getting soon after release I was worried about the product that we were receiving. After reading a few reviews, it seems like most of the problems have to do with Square Enix pimping out the game here and back with micro transactions, and some poor optimization.
As far as the optimization goes: by the time I picked up the game in late Feb of 2017 I had very few issues with the game and it ran at a consistant 60fps on my GTX 970 for the duration of the game.
As far as the microtransactions go, while I do detest their inclusion in this product, it is very clear that the game was not designed or balanced around buying additional credits or praxis. By the time I was done my first playthrough I was swimming in more credits than I knew what to do with, and had enough praxis to fully upgrade the vast majority of my hacking, stealth, and mobility trees. Enough that I felt like I could perfectly specialize in whatever way i chose to play the game, without having so many available that i felt over powered. I don't like that they're available, but the game functions as though they don't exist, so it's about as good of an outcome as we can hope for without removing them.
For people who are upset at the length, it certainly isn't as long as human revolution, and for every interesting thing the main story tries to do, it usually doesn't end up accomplishing what it sets out to do. That said, I did manage to get almost 30 hours out of the game, and while I played it pretty lesiurely, going for a mostly stealth run, I certainly didn't waste any time. There's a lot to explore and do if you look for it.
For the weaknesses that the game's story has, I found the fluidity of the combat and stealth mechanics to be a lot better, and the augments from the first game have been majorly simplified to create room for the new experimental augs. A lot of the upgrades in HR were very unsatisfying to purchase, like buying an additional 2.5 seconds of sprint time, or spending additional praxis to upgrade stealth movement from running, to sprinting, to falling. Investing a total of 5 praxis into your legs just for stealth falls. Ultimately what the game lacks in story it makes up for over its predecessor with a more satisfying and diverse gameplay experience.
One of the other things MD does VERY right is boss encounters, and how it really doesn't have any until the very end of the game. Human Revolution had this problem where it allowed you to play the game full stealth and non lethal, until you got to one of 3 different boss fights in the game and you were forced to confront the boss in open conflict and kill them. Escaping the fight, or taking them out non lethally were not options. When I tried to beat the game without killing anyone i had three weapons in my inventory. The stun gun, tranq rifle, and a gattling gun that i held exclusively for use in boss fights. It was dumb.
CONCLUSION: At the end of the day, Mankind Divided is NOT a perfect game. However, the gameplay and combat alone are incredibly polished and satisfying. Stealthing your way through levels, or even taking enemies out head on are both incredibly enjoyable, and you have a large number of lethal and non lethal weapons at your disposal to replay the game in a number of unique ways. The main story is serviceable, with side missions managing to help pull the player along in finding more enjoyable story lines to explore. This game is definitely worth the price of admission now that it's floating around $20-30 duing a sale, and I encourage anyone who wants a very strong and satisfying gameplay experience to come and enjoy what Deus Ex: Mankind Divided has to offer.

With the final piece of DLC released, I feel like I am finally ready to write this review.
I was incredibly hyped for the launch of Mankind Divided. And when it did, I was not disappointed by the gameplay or technical aspects of the game. Playing through the Director's Cut version of Human Revolution and listening to every piece of Creator's Commentary, I understood just how much the creators of Human Revolution wanted to do, yet couldn't because of an incredibly limited game engine and relatively low budget (DX:HR was a suprise hit, and was not given an incredible budget to work with).
The success of Human Revolution meant that Mankind Divided had a much higher budget, and the developers created a new engine with that money. Both of these really showed. The game is beautiful both technically and artistically in a subtle way (hence many who have gotten used to the overabundance of lens flare and bokeh etc in the modern AAA market call this an ugly game). The environments are carefully crafted and overflowing with detail (even more than HR). And the gameplay is the logical step up from Human Revolution: exploration stealth with multiple ways to get to where you want no matter your character build or playstyle (so many modern AAA games promise this but fail to deliver, MD is the real deal.)
But it isn't enough to have top notch gameplay, environments, and graphics to be a good Deus Ex game. Deus Ex is known for its story: a huge world-wide adventure to uncover a global conspiracy while juggling alliances and allegiances. Following HR I wanted to see where and what Jensen will go through, how he will handle his relationships with characters like Megan Reed, Sarif, Pritchard, Malik etc...
Yet we have none of that. Or rather, we have a part of that: Mankind Divided is Act I of a Deus Ex story. An incident in the beginning of the game drops Jensen down a rabbit hole of conspiracy theories, but ends a quarter of the way down the hole. We started the game with 5 questions that needed answering, yet by the end the game has only answered 2 of them while giving us 10 more questions. The final boss is clearly just a pawn of a greater force, the mid-credits "twist" can be seen from 10 miles away if you are paying any attention as the game literally chucks hints in your face halfway through the game. It just feels... hollow. There aren't even good characters this time. MD abandones pretty much the entire cast of the previous game for a new one, yet does little to make the new cast as likable as the previous.
And all of this can be explained by Square Enix's corporate greed. Coming from reputable sources within SE, Mankind Divided was originally meant to be the full Deus Ex story, but Square Enix decided to cut that story in half and make two games out of it.
The Deus Ex franchise is in a terrible spot right now. Mankind Divided has failed to meet SE sales expectations, and information from inside sources has confirmed that the game that is being developed from the second half of the cut story has been canceled or at least put on hold. We may never get to see the end of Jensen's story, and that truly saddens me.
But as for Mankind Divided, all I can say is that it is a great game, but only half of a great Deus Ex game.

Surspisingly polished indie game, with lots of attention to detail and high replayability, as long as you don't dislike rogue-lite FPSs. For me it was the first game of the genre, and I am positively impressed.
It has beautiful environments with constant framerate (no drops at all!), fluid and fast quake-like movement and a huge variety of enemies who provide a REAL challenge. You will die a lot, and come back for more! Random combat modifiers, procedurally generated dungeon layouts and a simple-yet-interesting skill system, which occasionally presents meaningful strategic choices, complete the picture and provide a new spin at every run.
Most importantly, each character class requires a totally different appoach to the game (some can "tank" damage, others are powerful but fragile and have to constantly evade, others have starting perks...) Even the "basic" unlimited-mana weapon (which you might use a lot, or not at all, depending on your build choices) differs significantly among the available characters. How... I'll let you find out :)

I've been playing DX since the original; I've played all the previous games at least twice and sometimes three times.  I've never been so frustrated with a game, mainly because of the constant crashing. At times it will go for an hour without crashing, other times no more than a minute.  For example, I spent a half hour trying to get past Otar somebody; I kept making the wrong conversation choices and getting into fights I couldn't win -- then after innumerable reloads I finally I got through the conversation and that was when the game froze with Otar mid-sentence.  Had to reload and replay the entire thing all over again AGAIN.  In researching this, apparently my experience is not unusual and I could never find any kind of definitive fix for it.  Apparently some people aren't affected, so if you're one of the lucky ones, or if you can just get past the frustration of the constant crashing, the gameplay is good, the world is interesting and the story eventually becomes quite absorbing.  I'm torn between recommending and not recommending this game -- I just can't excuse the crashes because even my Fallout 4 is more STABLE. In recent reviews, people have complaints about long installation times, trouble with registering, and not being able to play the game. For me, this was not the case. I don't have a powerful rig (and also not the best wifi), and I downloaded this game in under an hour. With quick account registration and patches installed, I was soon on my way to explore Middle Earth.
As for the game itself, for being almost 10 years old, it's incredible. As a fan of Tolkien, it's astonishing to run into iconic landscapes and characters. The game is beautiful for being 10 years old, and you don't need a high performancing PC to run it. There's a main quest line that follows the books and plenty of interesting side quests. Combat is fun and engaging for a tab target MMORPG. The music, oh the music. If you're a fan of the Lord of the Rings film scores, then you'll love the music in game. There's nothing more enjoyable than the ear-gasm of riding into Rohan and hearing the sweet sound of violins accompaning your journey.
On the contrary, the game can become a bit grindy. Lower level quests can become quite repeditive with the feeling of "kill 10 spiders and collect 5 bear hides.," can be a bit overwhelming. I know. I've almost stopped playing again because of it. But, if you pick an advanced and interesting class, it can be less mind numbing. At the time of writting this review, I have a level 52 Minstrel, and the quests definitely become more engaging the further one progresses. Skirmishes, epic battles, and instances are a great break from these grindy experiences, and epic battles are available at low levels.
As for the F2P model, it's one of the best ones available. It's incredibly fair and there really isn't any P2W instances. Some higher level quests and expansions require LOTRO points, but these points can be acquired in game (if you're up for some serious grinding). Most of the equipment found in the LOTRO store are cosmetics, mounts, and chracter boosts. I started out as a F2P player, but fell in love with the game; and became a VIP member, spending some money on additional LOTRO Points.
So download the game. If you don't like it, then all you have done is wasted a bit of your time. It's free to play people. This 10 year old game just came out with a new expansion that includes a new race, the High Elf. The future of LOTRO looks brighter than ever. Download it now and enjoy an authentic Middle Earth experience.
EDIT: Because of the outdated graphics and combat style, this game won't appeal to everyone. If you're looking for an enjoyable MMORPG, then this game might not be for you. If you're looking for an MMORPG set in the Tolkien universe, then this game is for you. If you're not interested in LotR lore, then this game might not hold your attention for long.

If you're looking for a coop game to play with your friends, Trine 2 definitely delivers. At it's core it's a three-player cooperative physics-platformer, set in a fairytale environment with gorgeous, colorful graphics.
You assume the role of one of three heroes: a wizard, a thief and a knight. Each character has unique abilities and progressing through the level requires each hero to utilize them accordingly: the knight will swiftly tackle foes, the thief can use a grapling hook to reach far away places and the wizard can conjure up boxes and planks that can either simplify platforming or block certain traps and enemies. If you happen to play by yourself, you can switch between the three characters at any given time (which, incidentally, is cannon) .
The levels are pretty short and usually end with some sort of crescendo: either a boss fight or a particularly tricky platforming segment. Throughout the levels are several checkpoints, so dying isn't too stressful and playing on normal difficulty one can breeze through the game quite quickly. So how did I manage to clock in 35 hours during a single playthrough? The answer lies in the difficulty setting - one of the overlooked but definetely more important aspects of Trine 2. As mentioned, the game can be beat casually pretty quickly; however, if you decide to play the game on hard difficulty WITH checkpoints disabled, the game suddenly becomes incredibly challenging and cooperation between all three characters becomes essential for survival. It's what makes the game appealing to a more hardcore, veteran audience. It is imporant to note though, that this means replaying the same levels over and over and that - understandably - isn't everyone's definion of fun or a challenge.
Summary/TL, DR: Trine 2 is a very beautiful cooperative platformer designed for everyone, regardless of age, gender or skill level. With the extra levels and ridiculously low price, it would be a real shame for people to overlook it!

+ Refined controls and more interesting plot twists entwined around a more solid core.
+ A huge graphical boost
+ Runs very well on older machines and is still able to run smoothly and without fault
+ Much like the first, the initial atmosphere is well maintained due to the crippling sense of dread and helplessness during the first portion of the game.
+ Replay value is still present with plenty of upgrading and a lot of Titan station to explore with New Game Plus.
- Horror isn't subtle, for horror hardcores this wouldn't appeal as jumpscares and cheap tactics takes the horror core of the first game and adds an action twist making it easier and overall less scary if played on the easier difficulites.
Overall, very cheap and runs well. Controls are excellent and hasn't aged a day since its 2011 releaase. The horror is toned down and a good introduction to the horror genre.

Torchlight 2
This game is good for 8-10 hours of play, especially on LAN with some friends. However, this game becomes a chore to play through and finish, as it turns out to be a very lightweight RPG. You will end up ploughing through endless waves of enemies with tactics rarely playing any part, only some bosses are tough enough to even bother trying to play better. You will end up spam clicking to such an extent that after a few hours my primary mouse finger was literally sore and aching, so i ended up rescheming the controls to the keyboard so i could spam hit some rarely used keys and distribute the load over to multiple fingers, not just my index mouse finger.
Storyline? There is one but its very poorly fleshed out. I felt virtually no connection to the events and the worldbuilding was poor. Its hard to people people could exist in this monster-spammed world. The towns are nothing more than bases to gear up and refresh. I never felt like there was any people in this world or that my actions could impact them in any way.
Balance. The game gives you 4 classes with a large amount of skill trees to customzie them with but the problem is each class has some stand out choices that are so good it makes everything else obsolete. One classes basic ability is so overpowered you can simply focus on it entirely and obliterate everything simply spamming it. Item gear is another problem, you can enchant items with attribute bonuses and these bonuses stack up to such huge levels they provide more stat points than your characters base stats. Its like going from level 20 to 60 all of a sudden and makes an easy game a cakewalk. Although the tens of thousands of enemies are so dreary to face i wouldnt want them tough, either.
Looting. You are spammed with a literal flood of items, 90%+ of which will be either worse than what you have or useless to your character. You will end up sending your pet off at regular intervals to sell your entire inventory of items for cash. This was fun at first as getting loot in RPGs is quite enjoyable but they overdid it big time.
Fishing. Like most games with a fishing minigame, this game doesnt have a detailed zelda-style mode but instead opts for the ''click when ready'' model, so it really provides no good gameplay here. Most fishing minigames suck and this fits in with the crowd to a T.
BTW, who or what is the boss of this game? Some alchemist? Ive never seen such a no-presence villain in any game before, ever.
